Author: Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgiśa Commentator: Aghoraśiva Editor: Caṭṭopādhyāya
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark Dyczkowski. Revision 0: 27/09/2007. Publisher: Dhundhirāja Gaṇeśa.

The Essence of the Great Tantra,
Chapter One:
Now, the auspicious invocation and the indication of the contents of the work.
Having bowed to the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, which are worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, and to his guru, the bestower of knowledge, the wise Kṛṣṇānanda [composed this work]. || 1 ||

Having understood the meaning from various passages found in those respective texts, and for the sake of ease, the *Tantrasāra* is here set forth in brief. First, the definition of the teacher and the disciple is stated. (2)
Now, the characteristics of the Guru:
He is peaceful, self-controlled, of noble birth, humble, and possessed of pure attire;
he is of pure conduct, well-established, pure, skillful, and highly intelligent; he is a member of a spiritual order (āśramī). || 3 ||
One who is established in meditation, proficient in tantra and mantra, and capable of both restraint and grace is designated as a guru.
In the Āgamasamhitā: "The best of Brahmins, who is capable of both uplifting and destroying, who is ascetic and truthful in speech, and who is a householder—he is called a Guru. (5)

Now, on the greatness of the Guru: In the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said that one who perceives the Guru as a mere human being, the mantra as a mere collection of syllables, and the image as a mere stone, shall go to hell.
Indeed, one's parents, who are the cause of birth, should be worshipped with great effort;

the preceptor, moreover, is especially worthy of worship, as he is the one who reveals what is dharma and what is adharma. The preceptor is the father, the preceptor is the mother, the preceptor is the deity, and the preceptor is the refuge. When Śiva is angry, the preceptor is the protector; but when the preceptor is angry, there is no one at all [to save you].
8 || One should perform what is beneficial for the guru through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
O Goddess! From practicing what is harmful, one is born as a worm in excrement. 9 || O Goddess! The father is the giver of the body, and the guru is indeed the giver of knowledge.

There is no one more venerable than the Guru in this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra. From whose mouth issues forth the body consisting of the perfect Brahman; he certainly delivers one from the ocean of hell—of this there is no doubt. By abandoning the mantra, [misfortune] would arise...
From abandoning one’s guru comes death; from abandoning the guru’s mantra, one goes to the Raurava hell. He who, while the guru is present, worships other deities, goes to a terrible hell;
that worship becomes fruitless. (12–13)
In the *Śrīkrama*: "Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda (*brahmadātṛ*), the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;

one should always regard the Guru as superior even to that father. One should behave toward the sons of the Guru as toward the Guru himself, and toward his daughters and so forth as toward the Guru; worship should be performed in the same manner."
One should please [the teacher] and carry out his commands; one should always worship the lineage of the teacher as if they were the teacher himself.
In the *Nigamakalpadruma*: Whether ignorant or possessed of knowledge, the guru alone is the deity;

whether standing on the wrong path or the right path, the guru alone is the eternal refuge. One should go before him as he approaches, follow him when he does not move, and [attend] him even on his seat or his bed.
One should stand before the guru; having obtained permission, one should remain [there], for in this way one will not incur a curse.

Likewise, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The Guru is the mother, the father, the master, kinsmen, and Śiva himself; having thus fixed this in one's mind constantly, one should worship the Guru with one's whole being."

Now, the characteristics of those who are censurable and unfit to be gurus, as stated in the *Kriyāsārasamuccaya*: "One afflicted with vitiligo, one with oozing leprosy, one with eye disease, a dwarf, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one conquered by women, and one with an extra limb. (21)

One who is deficient in limbs, deceitful, diseased, a glutton, or a talkative chatterer—freed from these defects (or, according to another reading, "devoid of them") is a teacher approved by his disciples. || 22 ||
In the *Yāmala*: "One who is cursed, one without a son, a miser, a gambler, likewise one devoid of ritual action, a rogue, a dwarf, and one who reviles his guru. (23)
A wise person should always avoid those who are afflicted by diseases of the blood and bile,
and one should always avoid, according to the tantra, a teacher who is possessed of envy.

The Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā states: "One who is childless, one whose sons have died, one who is impotent, and likewise one who is a dwarf"—this and other such cases should also be understood [as qualifying for initiation]. || 25 ||
Now, the characteristics of a disciple:
one who is peaceful, disciplined, pure in soul, endowed with faith,
capable of retention, competent, of noble birth, wise, and of virtuous conduct— such is the ascetic (yati), and so forth.

A disciple becomes endowed with virtues, and not otherwise. Furthermore: one who is meritorious, righteous, pure, devoted to the guru, and has conquered the senses—he indeed becomes a fit disciple, being intent upon charity and meditation.

Now, the characteristics of a prohibited disciple: To a sinner, one of cruel conduct, a rogue, a miser, one who is wretched, devoid of right conduct, and one intent on mechanical ritualism and malice; || 28 ||
It should not be given to one who is a reviler, to a fool, to one intent on hating sacred sites, to one devoid of devotion to the guru, nor to one who is impure. (29)
In the *Āgamasāra*: "Laziness, impurity, being drenched [in sin], hypocrisy, and likewise miserliness; poverty, sickness, anger, passion, and longing for sensual enjoyments. (30)
Those who are seized by envy and avarice, who always speak ill of others, who have acquired wealth through unjust means, and who are devoted to the wives of others; (31)
Those who consider themselves learned should avoid the enemies of the wise, as well as those who have fallen from right conduct, those of miserable livelihoods, backbiters, and the wicked. (32)

Those who eat excessively, those of cruel conduct, the wicked-minded, and those who are censured— these and others such as these, who are base men and devoid of virtue, should be rejected even if they have been accepted as disciples. || 33 ||

Now follows the procedure for the status of teacher and disciple, as well as the determination of what should and should not be done in the presence of the teacher: "The status of teacher or disciple [is established] by their dwelling together for one year. (34)

And so it is said in the *Sārāraṅgraha*: "A true guru should examine (or wait for) the disciple who has taken refuge in him for one year. (35) However, there is no restriction regarding time in dreams;
for according to the words of Nārada: "In dreams, indeed, there is no fixed rule. (36)
In that very same [text]: "The fault arising from the lack of self-control in a king falls upon his subjects; likewise, the sin of a wife falls upon her husband;
and similarly, the sin acquired by a disciple is certainly incurred by the teacher. (37)

In one year, a Brāhmaṇa endowed with good qualities becomes fit; a Kṣatriya in two years, and a Vaiśya in three years; a Śūdra becomes fit in four years—thus has the fitness of a disciple been described. (38)
In the *Tārāpradīpa*: "In the Kali age, the wise person should worship the deities according to the procedures taught in the Āgamas;
for the deities do not become propitious in the Kali age through other methods. (39)

Likewise: In the Kṛta age, the path declared by the Śruti prevails; in the Tretā, that arising from the Smṛti; in the Dvāpara, that spoken in the Purāṇas; and in the Kali, that approved by the Āgamas. Brāhmaṇas born in the Kali age are impure and perform the duties of Śūdras.
Their accomplishment is achieved through the path of tradition (āgama), not by the Vedic way.
The syllables of the mantra are to be known as deities, and the deity is in the form of the guru;
one who desires his own welfare should not make a distinction between them. (42)

In the *Devī-āgama*, the word of Śiva is as follows: "One must never step over the teacher’s bed, seat, vehicle, sandals, shoes, or stool; likewise, one should not step over his bath-water or his shadow. One should avoid performing a separate worship in the presence of the teacher, as well as arrogance. (43)
One should renounce the explanation of initiation and one's authority before the Guru. || 44 ||
In the Rudrayāmala: Having become a disciple, one should never at any time engage in lending money, taking loans, or the buying and selling of goods with the guru. (45)

Now, regarding the meaning of the word *guru*, it is said in the *Tantrārṇava*: "The letter *ga* is declared to be the bestower of accomplishment; the letter *ra* is the burner of sin; the letter *u* is said to be Śambhu. The supreme *guru* is the essence of these three."
From the letter *ga* comes the perfection of knowledge; the letter *ra* is the burner of sin;
from the letter *u* one receives identity with Śiva—thus is the Guru traditionally remembered.
The syllable *gu* signifies darkness, while the syllable *ru* signifies its obstruction;
because it obstructs darkness, it is called *guru*. (48)

Now, the determination of the Guru according to the distinctions of the stages of life (āśrama) and so forth, as well as what is to be done toward the Guru based on the distinction of distance or proximity, is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "One who is a householder [should serve] those who are householders; one living in the forest, those who dwell in the forest; and one who is detached, those who are detached."

A renunciant is declared to be the teacher for renunciants, and a householder for householders. Furthermore, in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, a Vaiṣṇava should be accepted; likewise, in the Śaiva tradition, a Śaiva. In the Śākta tradition, one should know that all three are [acceptable];
he is the master of initiation, without a doubt. Even the guru must indeed be a householder.
In the Kulārṇava, it is stated that a householder who understands the meaning of all the scriptures is called a guru. || 51 ||

And so it is said in the Kalpa: "A Brahmin who has a wife and sons, who is compassionate and esteemed by all, should act as a guide for householders in matters concerning the gods, the ancestors, enemies, and friends. (52)
In the *Kulacuḍāmaṇi*: "One should serve as a guru that person by whom one has been instructed in this tantra—be it father, mother, brother, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle.
And from the *Hayaśīrṣa*: "Neither a child, nor an old man, nor a lame person, nor likewise one who is emaciated."

And so it is said in the Nityānanda: "One should not perceive the Guru as a mortal; if one should so perceive him, then for that person there will never be accomplishment through mantras or the worship of deities. (55)
Likewise: A disciple, remaining with one-pointed mind, should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
staying within the distance of a krośa, he should bow to the guru every day. (56)
A disciple should prostrate at the five parvans from a distance of half a yojana;

starting from one yojana up to twelve yojanas. A disciple situated in a distant land, having approached the presence of the Guru with devotion, should prostrate to the Guru there according to the number of yojanas mentioned for each month.

57–58. O lady of beautiful limbs! Even if the city of one's own guru should be far away, one must perform the salutation of the guru’s feet every year. 59. And this should be performed once during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) and once during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
Now, the prohibition regarding initiation from one's father and others:

In the *Yoginītantra*, it is said: "One should not receive a mantra from one's father, nor from one's maternal grandfather, nor from a younger brother, nor from one who has taken the side of an enemy. (60)

In the *Gaṇeśa-vimarṣiṇī*: "The initiation of an ascetic, the initiation of a father, and the initiation of a forest-dweller—the initiation of one belonging to a secluded stage of life does not bestow auspiciousness. (61)
In the Rudrayāmala: A husband shall not initiate his wife; a father shall not initiate his daughter;
likewise, a son shall not [initiate his father], nor shall a brother initiate his brother. (62)

"If the husband is one who has already mastered the mantra (*siddhamantra*), then he should initiate his wife as his *śakti*, O Varārohe! She shall not be [regarded] as a daughter. From such prohibitive statements, the meaning is that one should not receive the mantra from them; however, this refers to those other than those who have mastered the mantra. Not [from] one who has mastered the mantra...
Because of the statement, "it becomes corrupted. || 63 ||

The initiation of an ascetic (yati) is also described in the Śaktiyāmala: "A mantra-practitioner endowed with the conduct of a holy place, possessed of knowledge, well-composed, constantly devoted to his duties—such a person is known as an ascetic and may serve as a Guru even in the worldly realm. (64)

And so it is stated in the Siddhayāmala: "O Dear One, if by the power of fortune alone one should obtain the *siddhividya*, then at that very moment one should initiate them, setting aside any deliberation regarding a guru. (65)
Likewise: "Due to negligence or due to ignorance, one may perform the initiation of a father;

having then performed an expiation, one should perform the initiation of a sage (i.e., a second initiation). The term "father" is illustrative and includes the maternal grandfather and others as well.
The expiation, however, is the recitation of the Sāvitrī ten thousand times, because it is seen [prescribed] in all cases. || 66 ||
Śaṅkhā: By reciting [this] ten thousand times, it destroys all impurities. || 67 ||

Likewise, in the Matsyasūkta, the statement "the mantra of the father is devoid of potency, yet it is not defective in the Śaiva or Śākta [systems]" refers specifically to the initiation into Kaulika mantras.

The reason for this is stated in the *Yoginītantra*: because initiation is prohibited with reference to the *vidyās* beginning with the *Śākta* (such as the *Tārā-vidyā*). (And thus the meaning is that a *Viṣṇu-mantra*, however, should be received from one's father and so forth. Alternatively, [it is stated] in the *Matsyasūkta* regarding the *Śākta* *Tārā-vidyā* and others.
Because it is taught in that manner with reference to her; and likewise [it says], "One should give to one's eldest son, the ornament of his own family," and so forth. || 68 ||
Also in the Śrīkrama: "The mantra, having been reflected upon, should be given to a wise eldest son;
when there is a solar or lunar eclipse at a great sacred site (tīrtha), there is no fault anywhere. (69)
And likewise, concerning the Viṣṇu-mantra: "O Brahmin, you have asked well;
I shall tell it all to you. It was previously told by Brahmā to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha himself gave it to my father, his own son. (70)

"My father, whose heart was serene, pure, and a treasure-house of compassion, bestowed upon me this great sacred site at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse. These and other words were spoken by Vyāsa to Śaunaka in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā.

In the Yoginītantra: "A mantra of a father that lacks potency, as well as one from a maternal grandfather, or one obtained in a dream or given by a woman, is purified only by means of consecration. (73)

As for that which was said: "A woman who is virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, with senses subdued, who knows the true meaning and essence of all mantras, well-behaved, and delights in worship—she indeed shall be fit for the guru;
for initiation by a woman is declared auspicious, provided she is not a widow."
And it is taught that [the qualities of] a mother are eightfold. This [verse], however, concerns one who has mastered the mantra through service to the guru. 74.

Likewise, in the Bhairavatantra: "In the case of receiving instruction in one's own mantra, one should not entertain thoughts of [another] guru. (75) The meaning is that if [the mantra] is worshipped as being that of one's mother, it yields eightfold [results]; if not so worshipped, it bestows auspicious fruits. Some say this refers to the subject of a perfected (siddha) mantra; however, in reality—
In the Yoginītantra, the word "woman" (strī) refers to a widow, by virtue of the force of syntactic consistency.

A widow acts by the instruction of her son, and a maiden by the command of her father; since a woman has no independent authority—whether as a married woman acting by her husband's command or otherwise—the term "lack of authority" refers to the absence of independent entitlement. This applies to women in general and those who are pregnant.
There is no fault whatsoever in the initiation; one should not perform it in the tenth month, for having done so, one becomes a denizen of hell.

If one obtains a mantra in a dream and subsequently meets a true guru, then one should receive that very mantra from him; if not, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) over a jar filled with water, [one should take] the mantra written with saffron on a *vaṭa* leaf.
The meaning is that, having cast it into the jar and lifted it up, one should take hold of the mantra. || 79 ||
For it is said: One should infuse the breaths of the Guru into a jar obtained in a dream;
having written [the mantra] on a banyan leaf with saffron during the auspicious planetary conjunction (*grahaṇa*), one then attains success;
otherwise, it shall be fruitless. This [is to be done] in the absence of a true Guru.

Therefore, one should receive the mantra from that very person; for there is no restriction regarding dreams, according to the statement of Nārada: "In that case, there is no restriction concerning [the guru's] being a Siddha or otherwise. (80)
Likewise, there is the statement of Jāvāla, preserved by the Vidyādhara Ācārya:
"Those born in Madhyadeśa, Kurukṣetra, Naṭaka, and Koṅkaṇa;
those from Antarvedi, Pratiṣṭhāna, and Āvanti—these are the most excellent gurus. [Madhyadeśa...]
Āryāvarta. || 81 || The Gauḍas, Śālvas, Suras, Māgadhas, Keralas, Kośalas, and Daśārṇas—these seven are the central Guru countries.
Likewise, those born in Karṇāṭa, Narmadā-rāṣṭra, Kacch, Tīra, and Kālinda [are also included].
The Kalambas and the Kāmbojas are considered the lowest. || 82 ||
Now follows the determination of initiation (dīkṣā), the deliberation on it, and so forth.
Since recitation (japa) is defective without initiation, that initiation is first described:
because it bestows divine knowledge and effects the destruction of sin.
Therefore, she is called "Dīkṣā" by the sages who are knowers of the Tantras. || 83 ||
Now, the necessity of initiation (*dīkṣā*) in all stages of life (*āśrama*): "All recitation (*japa*) has initiation as its root; supreme austerity (*tapas*) has initiation as its root.
One should dwell taking refuge in initiation, regardless of which stage of life one inhabits. (84) Those who are uninitiated...

They perform rituals such as recitation and worship; yet, O Dear One, for them there is no fruit, like a seed sown upon a stone. O Goddess, for one devoid of initiation, there is neither spiritual perfection nor a blessed state.
Therefore, with every effort, one should be initiated by a Guru.

Even one who is uninitiated shall go to the Raurava hell at the time of death; for the uninitiated, the state of being a Piśāca does not leave them upon death. Therefore, one should always diligently receive initiation from a Tantrika. 87.

And so it is stated in the *Navaratneśvara*: "The fruit of all initiations (*dīkṣā*) is the unbroken state of liberation (*mukti*). Enjoyments (*bhukti*), however, occur as incidental results because they do not contradict [the goal]. O Goddess of the Gods, [initiation] burns away hundreds of thousands of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and tens of millions of major sins (*mahāpātaka*) in an instant."

For initiation must indeed be performed according to the prescribed rule. But that lowest of men who, having merely seen a mantra in a ritual manual (kalpa), takes it up for himself—no atonement arises for him even in thousands of Manvantaras.
For one who has not been initiated, [liberation] cannot be achieved through austerities, restrictive observances, or vows; nor by visiting sacred fords, nor by bodily mortifications. (91)
In the Matsya-sūkta: "O fair-faced one, hear the fault of those who die without initiation! Their food is considered equal to excrement, and their water equal to urine."
Any śrāddha performed for him, or by him, all indeed goes downward. || 93 ||
Then: "The initiation bestowed by a true guru shall purify all karmas.
Now, regarding the mantras forbidden to a Śūdra, another Tantra states: "A mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) must not be given to a Śūdra."
In every respect, one should [conceal] the mantra of oneself, the mantra of the guru, and the mantra known as ajapa.
If a twice-born man gives a mantra joined with *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra,
the Śūdra falls into hell and the Brāhmaṇa goes to a downward state.
The Śruti also says: "If a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, the Yajus, or Lakṣmī, he goes downward after death. (96)
The *Vārāhī* states the distinction: "The mantra of Gopāla and Maheśa should be given at the feet;
likewise the mantra of his wife, of Sūrya, and of Gaṇeśa.
One would be entitled to this initiation [only by these]; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of sin. (97)
Now follows the consideration of the success (siddhi) and other qualities of mantras.
In that regard, one should initiate [the disciple] into a mantra that is favorable. Because it protects through contemplation (manana), it is therefore proclaimed as a "mantra. || 98 ||
And thus: one should employ those mantras that are favorable to one's own natal star and zodiacal sign.

In the *Siddhasārasvata*: "One need not purify the Siddha and other [qualities] of the mantras consisting of the Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha [mantras], nor of the Prāsāda and Praṇava, nor of mantras whose syllables are already perfected. (100)

In the Vārāhītantra: "The Tārā-cakra, the Rāśi-cakra, and likewise the Nāma-cakra—if the mantra possesses these qualities, one need not contemplate any other cakra. This, however, should be understood as being stated by way of primary importance.

And so it is said: "One should not accept a mantra from a wealthy person, nor likewise from one of low birth," and because such [rules] are seen in other passages, the investigation of the respective *cakras* (lineages) is necessary; therefore, that is first described. [This applies to] a mantra obtained in a dream, one given by a woman, or a three-syllabled mantra.
In the case of Kālī, Tārā, Maṇi, as well as Chinnamastā, and in all Vedic mantras, one should not examine the Siddhas and other such factors.

Regarding the *mālāmantra* of Vārāhī: "Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are proclaimed as *mālāmantras*. One should not purify a neuter mantra by means of the *siddha* and other [categories]; the same applies to the eight-syllable *haṃsa* mantra."
And for the five-syllabled mantra, as well as for mantras with one, two, three, or more seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should not examine their status as *siddha* and so forth;
likewise, O Pārvatī, for a single-syllable mantra, a garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*), and a Vedic mantra, one should not examine their status as *siddha* and so forth. [This applies to] male mantras...

Those ending in *huṃ phaṭ* are considered male; those ending in *svāhā* are considered female; and those ending in *namaḥ* are neuter. Thus, mantras are said to be of three kinds. This [mantra] is a great vidyā devoid of [these genders], and it is conveyed by the word "great" (*mahā*). || 5 ||

In the *Mālinīvijaya*: Now I shall declare all those Great Sciences (*mahāvidyās*) that exist upon the surface of the earth, which are untouched by webs of defects, together with their fruits: Kālī, Nīlā, Mahādurgā, Tvaritā, Chinnamastakā, and Vāgvādinī.
Furthermore, Annapūrṇā, Pratyaṅgirā, Kāmākhyāvāsinī,
Bālā, Mātaṅgī, Śailavāsinī, and all such goddesses bestow full fruit in the Kali age; because their mantras are already perfected, there is no [need for further effort] in this regard.
The labor of practicing these [mantras] throughout the ages is such that these great vidyās are not obstructed by the defects of the Kali age. || 7 ||
And so it is said in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra: Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī,
Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī, Vagalā, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalātmikā— these are the ten.

The great vidyās are proclaimed as perfected vidyās; herein there is no dependence on perfection [attained through other means] and so forth, nor any consideration of lunar mansions and the like. There is no purification of time and so forth, nor any defect regarding enemies, friends, and so on. Because they are perfected vidyās, there is here no laborious service to the yugas.

"O Great Goddess! there is nothing whatsoever that can ever be accomplished through hardship"—from such statements as these, no deliberation is required in these matters. In reality, however, this is merely intended as praise;
for the necessity of deliberation exists everywhere, though it may be obscured by the influence of adverse fortune (*duradṛṣṭa*).
The traditionalists maintain that this is because the fault of such [mantras] has been observed through the acquisition of hostile mantras in dreams and other such states. || 8 ||
Now, the *Kulākula-cakra* (see Figure 1):

I shall here explain the divisions of the *Kulākula* for the practitioners (*mantrins*). Thus, it is stated in the *Nibandha*: "The letters of the fifty [syllables] are, in order, wind, fire, earth, water, and space."

The five short vowels and the five long vowels ending in the bindu (anusvāra), produced through euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), are proclaimed; likewise, the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ya*, *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha* are declared in groups of five. And thus: *a, ā, e, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, ṣa* are the winds (*māruta*). *i, ī, ai, kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, ra, kṣa*... [and so forth].

The letters *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *ga*, *ja*, *ḍa*, *da*, *ba*, *la*, and *lā* belong to Agni (Fire). The letters *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *aṃ*, *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*, *śa*, and *hā* belong to the Ether (Nabhas). The letter of the practitioner comes first, and that same letter belongs to the mantra as well. *Ṭa*, *ṭha*, *tha*, *dha*, *pha*, *ra*, *ya*, *va*, *sa*, and *kṣa* belong to Varuṇa (Water). One should know that for one's own family to be beneficial, it must have the same elemental deity (bhūtadaivata);
the earth element is the friend of the water element, and the wind element is the friend of the fire element.
The wind element is the enemy of the earth elements, and the fire element is the enemy of the water elements. (9)
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of the earthly elements" (*pārthivānām*), it is implied that the fiery element is the enemy of the earthly elements.

The ethereal element (*nābhasa*) is a friend to all; one should never practice what is contrary [to this]. Thus, it is said in the Rudrayāmala: "In relation to the earthly, the watery is a friend, while the fiery is declared to be an enemy."

"The enemy of Aindra and Vāruṇa is proclaimed to be Māruta; the enemy of Taijasa is said to be Mitra. From this statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, it follows that there is enmity between water (jala) and wind (māruta), while success is attained with Mitra.
It is declared that there is nothing at all for one who is indifferent; death and disease occur for an enemy, while supreme success is attained within one's own family. 9ka.

Now, the zodiacal circle (*rāśicakra*): (see Figure 2). As stated in the *Āgamakalpadruma*: "One should draw two lines from east to west; from their center, [draw two more] toward the south and the direction of Kuvera (north); and one each toward the northeast (*īśāna*) and the moon (north)."
Then one should write the syllables in the southeast (Agni) and northwest (Vāyavya) squares.

One should write all the letters starting from Aries (Meṣa), numbering four, three, two, three, two, seven, two, five, five, five, four, and five; then one should write those letters situated in Virgo (Kanyā).

[The letters] beginning with *pa* [are assigned to the signs]. In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "The letters *va*, *la*, *ga*, *ra*, *kha*, *ra*, *śo*, *na*, *śa*, *mī*, *śo*, *bhe* are distributed among the signs (*rāśi*) in sequence; in the sign of Virgo (*kanyā*), the letters beginning with *śa* are traditionally taught. Therefore: *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī* are Aries (*meṣa*); *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ* are Taurus (*vṛṣa*); *ḷ*, *ḹ*...

Mithuna (Gemini); *e* and *ai* are Karkaṭa (Cancer); *o* and *au* are Siṃha (Leo); *aṃ*, *aḥ*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* are Kanyā (Virgo); *ka* and *va* are Tulā (Libra); the *ca*-group is Vṛścika (Scorpio); the *ṭa*-group is Dhanus (Sagittarius); the *ta*-group is Makara (Capricorn); the *pa*-group is Kumbha (Aquarius); and the *ya*-group is Mīna (Pisces).

One should employ mantras that are favorable to one's own zodiac sign (*rāśi*). Likewise, according to the words of Nārada, "one should employ those mantras that are favorable to one's own *tāra*, *rāśi*, and *koṣṭha*. One should know the purity of the signs and should abandon [those signs associated with] the *śakra*, *mṛti*, and *vyaya* [positions].
The wise should calculate from the sign of one's own name up to the sign of the mantra. However,
when there is no knowledge of the sign of one's own name, one should take the sign associated with the first syllable of the sādhana and perform the calculation from that.

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "When the zodiac sign (*rāśi*) and lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) are unknown, one should count from the first letter of the name up to the final letter of the practitioner's (*sādhaka*) syllable-group," as this is also maintained in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*. || 11 ||

In the *Tantrarāja*: "If one counts by means of the first letter of the mantra and the first syllable of the name, and finds the sixth, eighth, or twelfth [letter], then the first letter of the mantra will be an enemy; by that, harm shall come to him. (12)
In the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*: "The first, fifth, and ninth [houses] are remembered as kinsmen;
the second and those in the sixth and tenth are servants; the third, eleventh, and seventh are nourishers;
and the fourth and eighth are destroyers—indeed, the fourth and eighth are destroyers."
This concerns the domain of Viṣṇu, as it is contained within the *Rāmārcanācandrikā*.

(13) In the Śākta and other traditions, the sixth [day] should be avoided, according to the statement: "The sixth, eighth, and twelfth days should be diligently avoided," and because this is also contained within the *Tantrarāja*. (14)

In another tantra: These are the designations for the twelve zodiacal signs (*rāśi*), and their results correspond to their names: the ascendant (*lagna*), wealth (*dhana*), siblings (*bhrātṛbandhu*), children (*putra*), enemies (*śatru*), wife (*kalatra*), death (*maraṇa*), virtue (*dharma*), action (*karma*), income (*āya*), and expenditure (*vyaya*).

There are twelve zodiac signs (*rāśis*). One obtains their auspicious or inauspicious results according to their names. In the *Vaiṣṇava* [system], however, there is the reading: "In the house of friends, an enemy; in the house of enemies, a friend.
(15) There is constant success in the ascendant (*lagna*), and likewise, an abundance of wealth in the second house (*dhana*).

If it falls upon a brother, there will be prosperity for the brother; if upon a kinsman, he will be dear to his kin. If upon a son, there will be an increase of sons; if upon an enemy, there will be an increase of enemies. If upon the wife, it is said to be middling; if upon death, death itself shall occur. If upon dharma, there will be an increase of dharma.
It bestows success and is established through ritual action; in the first house there is abundance of wealth, and in the twelfth house there is expenditure of what has been accumulated. || 16 ||
Now, the wheel of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatracakra*): (see Figure 3). *a*, *ā*—Aśvinī, divine; *i*—Bharaṇī, human; *ī*, *u*, *ū*—Kṛttikā, demonic;
*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*—Rohiṇī, human; *e*—Mṛgaśiras, divine; *ai*—Ārdrā, human; *o*...
Au: Punarvasu, the deity; ka: Puṣyā, the deity; kha ga: Āśleṣā, the Rākṣasa;
gha ṅa: Maghā, the Rākṣasa; ca: Pūrvaphalgunī, the human; cha ja:
Uttaraphalgunī, the human; jha ña: Hastā, the deity; ṭa ṭha: Citrā.
Rākṣasa: Ḍa Svātī; Deva: Ḍha Ṇa Viśākhā; Rākṣasa: Ta Tha Da Anurādhā; Deva: Dha Jyeṣṭhā; Rākṣasa: Na Pa Pha Mūlā; Mānuṣa: Ba Pūrvāṣāḍhā; [Deva]: Bha Uttarāṣāḍhā.
Mānuṣa: Ma; Śravaṇā: Deva; Ya; Gha; Niṣṭhā: Rākṣasa; La; Śatabhiṣā: Rākṣasa; Va; Śa; Pūrvabhādrapadā: Mānuṣa; Ṣa; Sa; Ha;
Uttarabhādrapadā: Mānuṣa; Aṃ; Aḥ; La; Kṣa; Revatī: Deva.

In the *Vṛhacchrīkrama*: "O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should draw four lines from north to south, and ten lines from west to east; then one should again write the lunar mansions (*tārakā*) in the order beginning with Aśvinī, starting from the letter 'A' [and so forth]. (17) Akārādi—

O Dear One, [the letters] from *kṣa* onwards consist of two moons, fire, and Vedas; earth, moon, and eyes; moon and eyes; up to the end of Aśleṣā, there are sky and birds; twice earth, eyes, and pairs of eyes;
and moon, eyes, fire, and moon.

From Maghā to Jyeṣṭhā, there is a second group of nine stars. Their letters, divided by four, are assigned in order to the portions of Revatī: three, one, one, one, one, two, one, two, and three. (18)
And so it is stated in the Nibandha: "The three [asterisms] preceding and following [Punarvasu], as well as Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī—these the wise call the human asterisms. (19)
Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Mūlā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā, Citrā, Maghā, and Viśākhā are the stars whose presiding deities are Rākṣasas. Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣyā, Svātī,
Hastā, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Śravaṇā [are the stars whose presiding deities are gods].
The stars are the deities. || 21 ||
Likewise: "The highest affection is toward one's own kind, moderate toward those of different kinds;
there is destruction between Rākṣasas and humans, and enmity between Dānavas and gods. Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, the enemy, the seeker, death, and the friend—"
And one should avoid being born under the third, fifth, or seventh asterisms; these are to be shunned for births and other such occasions. || 23-24 ||

And so says Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "The eighth, ninth, and auspicious [asterisms], as well as those situated in pairs and pairs, are auspicious; the others are not auspicious and should be avoided by the wise," and so forth. In that regard, the asterism should be counted starting from one's own natal asterism.
If one's own birth star is unknown, the star should be calculated starting from the very star associated with the first syllable of one's name.

In the *Piṅgalātantra*, it is stated: "For one whose birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*) is manifest, [the calculation] should proceed from that birth asterism; for one whose birth asterism is lost, it should proceed from the name asterism (*nāmarkṣa*). Accordingly, one should count in a clockwise direction starting from the first letter of the practitioner's name.

"Thus says the *Sudhī*. According to another method in the *Nibandha*: 'From the letter *pra* up to the attainment of *lā*, [the letters] *pa*, *ṭu*, *pra*, *hya*, *ru*, *dra*, *syā*, *dri*, *ru*, *ru*, *ka*, *ra*, *ma*, *lo*, *ka*, *lo*, *pa*, *ṭu*, *prā*, *yaḥ*, *kha*, *lo*, *gha*, *bhe*, *ṣu*.'"
They have been split apart. || 25 ||
The syllables [of the mantra] are derived from the hands [in this order]:
one, three, four, one, two, one, two, two, two, one, moon (one), fortnights (two), fire (three), and moon (one);
three, moon (one), earth (one), one, fortnight (two), moon (one), eyes (two), fire (three), and Vedas (four). From the hands [the syllables arise].

Both [the first and last] signs of the zodiac have their final degrees situated in Revatī; therefore, one should count from the nakṣatra of the reciter according to the sequence of birth and prosperity, because of the statement: "O wise one. (26)
Then Akathaha Vaktra said: (see Figure 4) "One should write the letters in a square consisting of four compartments;
that is to say, in sixteen compartments, formed by four sets of four compartments. (27)
In the *Viśvasāra*: "The wise one should draw a square grid consisting of four compartments;
there, he should again draw a set of four in sequence. Then, within the sixteen compartments, he should write the letters beginning with 'A' in a clockwise direction."

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: the wise man should write the letters born of the alphabet in order within the squares corresponding to the moon (1), fire (3), Rudra (11), nine (9), eyes (2), the Yugas (4), the sun (12), and the directions (10); in the seasons (6), eight (8), sixteen (16), fourteen (14), and the elements (5); and in the netherworlds (7), fifteen (15), fire (3), and the moon (1).

Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, place one letter in each of four squares; thus there are four squares. Then, within the squares of the grid, starting from the left, [place the letters] corresponding to the name: *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*.

This should be understood in sequence by the wise: from left to right and from right to left. According to the *Kalpadruma*, having drawn five lines extending from east to west, one should likewise draw five lines in the order from south to north, so that there are sixteen squares.
One should write them in such a way that they are properly accomplished. || 29 ||

In the *Viśvasāra*: "The wise one should write the letters from 'a' to 'ha' starting from the root-square (mūlakoṣṭha) in a clockwise direction within the squares; it is taught that the counting should be performed by the very same method used for writing. [The letters are classified as] *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth.

The "well-accomplished" (susiddha) enemy is to be known by the wise as such through the sequence [of syllables]. The "accomplished" (siddha) [enemy] becomes effective in time; the "to-be-achieved" (sādhya), however, [is subdued] by means of recitation and fire-offerings. The "well-accomplished" [enemy] cuts the very root [of the practitioner] from the moment of its seizure.
In another tantra it is said: "The accomplished letters are declared to be friends, while the to-be-achieved..."

The *sevaka* (servant) is remembered [as the first type]; the *poṣaka* (nourisher) is to be known as the *susiddha* (well-accomplished); the *ghātaka* (destroyer) is remembered as the enemy. Through recitation (*japa*), the *bandhu* (friend) becomes accomplished; through excessive service, the *sevaka* [becomes accomplished].
The *poṣaka* nourishes what is desired, while the *ghātaka* certainly destroys it.

A *siddha* [mantra] becomes a *siddha-sādhya* when recited twice as much as prescribed; a *siddha-susiddha* is achieved by half that recitation, while a *siddha-ari* destroys one's kinsmen. A *sādhya-siddha* requires double the recitation, a *sādhya-sādhya* is useless, and a *sādhya-susiddha* is attained by double the recitation.

A *sādhyāri* (enemy of the *sādhya*) destroys those born of one's own lineage. A *susiddhasiddha* [destroys] by half the recitation; a *sādhyasiddha*, by more than double; a *siddhasiddha*, by the mere planets; and a *susiddhāri* destroys one's own clan.

An enemy that is "accomplished" (siddha) will kill one's sons; an enemy that is "to be accomplished" (sādhya) will kill one's daughters. An enemy that is "well-accomplished" (susiddha) will kill one's wife, while an enemy that is itself an "enemy" (ari) will kill the practitioner (sādhaka).
Now, the Tantra states the measure for the abandonment of hostile mantras:

"One should recite eight hundred mantras over a *droṇa* measure of cow's milk; having drunk that milk, one should likewise utter [the mantra] into water and then abandon it. By this very procedure..."
One is liberated from the mantra of an enemy. Having recognized it as an enemy mantra, one should not recite it again;
having abandoned that, one should resort to another mantra of that deity. || 38-39 ||
Regarding the measurement of a *droṇa*, as stated in another treatise (*tantrāntara*): "Two *pala*s make one *prasṛti*; four of those make a *kuḍava*. Four *kuḍava*s make a *prastha*;
four *prastha*s make an *āḍhaka*. Four *āḍhaka*s are said to constitute a *droṇa*."
By those who know the Mānava [Kalpa-sūtra]. || 40 ||

He states another method in the *Rudrayāmala*: "Having written the enemy's mantra on a banyan leaf (*vaṭapatra*), one should cast it into a stream; in this way, there shall be liberation from the mantra," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva. (41)
Now, the *akaḍama*-cakra (see Figure 5):

One should draw two lines from east to west, and from their midpoint, [two lines] toward the south and toward Kubera (the north), respectively; likewise, [two lines] across toward Maheśa (the northeast) and the Lord of the Rakṣasas (the southwest).

[This is] by means of wind and fire. Then one should write the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, excluding the neuter ones. The two vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ*, as well as *ḷ* and *ḹ*, are indeed declared to be neuter.

One should write them out one by one in sequence, from Aries to Taurus; O auspicious lady, the wise practitioner should count them in order, beginning with the first letter of the name. From Aries to Pisces as well, the wise one should count them in sequence for the mantra-reciter according to his own name.
Up to the first syllable of the mantra and so forth.

In the *Ratnāvalī*, [it is said]: "In the twelve-spoked wheel of the zodiac, one should write the letters starting from the first (A) and ending with the last (Ha), excluding the *kūṭa* syllables, from the east up to the northeast. Then, [one should mark] the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* [categories]."
Furthermore, regarding the Siddhas and others: the *Siddha* is in the ninth, first, and fifth;
the *Sādhya* is in the sixth, tenth, and even (second); the *Susiddha* is in the third, seventh, and eleventh (*rudra*); and the *Ripu* (enemy) is in the fourth (*veda*), eighth, and twelfth.
This, O Goddess, which begins with *akaḍa*, has been told to you as the supreme. But this—
This refers specifically to Gopāla, because of the statement: "In Gopāla, 'aka' is remembered as 'kaḍama'. || 45 ||

Regarding the subject of Śiva as well: "The Vaiṣṇava [system] is known to be pure in its astrological configuration (rāśi), while the Śaiva is remembered as being free from impurity (akaḍama)," according to the *Yāmala*. (46)
And so it is stated in the Vārāha-tantra: "The purification by the *tārā* [syllable] is for the Vaiṣṇavas;
the purification by the *koṣṭha* is for Śiva; the purification by the *rāśi* is for the Traipuras; and in Gopāla, the *akaḍama* is prescribed. (47)
Now, the wheel of debtor and creditor (see Figure 6): It is as follows—eleven squares filled with the Vedas;
the knower of reality should write the letters from *a* to *ha* within those squares. First...

In the five squares, the practitioner should write two letters each, following the sequence of short and long vowels; in the remaining [squares], the wise one should write the consonants one by one in order. Likewise, there are two vowels each in the five squares, and the rest [are the consonants].

One should write the six vowels, one in each of the six [cells]. Then, one should write the remaining consonants beginning with *ka* (the *ha*-group excluded) in the eleven cells, one by one. These are indeed: six, six, zero, three, four, four, zero, zero, three, and two.

The letters of the name to be proven (the *sādhya*) are as follows: 2, 5, 0, 1, 6, 1, 0, 4, 1. The letters of the practitioner's name (*sādhaka*) are indeed: 1, 8, 4, 1, 0, 4, 1. Having determined the remainder of the vowels and consonants from the name, and the remainder of the letters starting with *a*, *ka*, *ṭha*, *va*, and *da* after subtracting the "elephant-eaten" (i.e., the consonants), one should know that the greater remainder of the two constitutes the debt (*ṛṇa*).
There would be wealth. || 50 ||

The meaning of this is as follows: having separated the letters of the name of the person for whom the rite is performed (sādhya) according to vowels and consonants, and having multiplied them by the numerical values beginning with six (ṣaṭkāla),
one likewise separates the letters of the practitioner's name (sādhaka) into the form of vowels and consonants.

Having multiplied [the numbers] by the pairs and so forth, and divided them by eight, that which is greater between the two—the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka)—is a debt (ṛṇa), and that which is less is wealth (dhana). Having understood this, one should give the mantra. If the mantra is in debt, then:
The mantra becomes bestower of auspiciousness, provided it is not [otherwise] wealthy. || 51 ||

And so it is said in another Tantra: "If the mantra has an excess of digits, then the wise man should recite the mantra; he should also recite the mantra when the digits are equal, but he should not recite it when there is a deficit.
One should know that in the case of zero (śūnya) there is death; therefore, one should avoid zero. [In the case] of a deficit..."
In wealth. || 52 ||
Likewise: the Sādhya planets are multiplied by 14, 27, 2, 12, 6, 5, 3, 4, 3, 8, and 9;
and then [the others] are multiplied by 10, 1, 7, 4, 8, 7, 7, 3, 4, 6, and 3.

[The phrase] "the letters of the practitioner" [is used]. Some maintain that the passage beginning with "at six times" (*ṣaṭkāla*) and so forth refers specifically to Viṣṇu, because it is cited in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*. However, in reality, this is merely an elaboration of what preceded it. || 53 ||
And likewise, having stated "Indra, the bear, the eye," and so forth,
one should then multiply the numbers from the grid of the letters of the names in sequence, starting from one and ending with eleven (the number of Rudras). || 54 ||

It is clearly stated in the Rudrayāmala: "One should fill the squares of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the practitioner (sādhaka) according to the number of the planets. When multiplied and divided by eight, whatever remainder clearly arises—that figure I shall describe here as it resides in the eleventh house."
Having said this, it is stated that he is the Time of the six times (ṣaṭkāla-kāla). || 55 ||
In the Tantrārṇava: "A mantra that is a debtor may yield auspicious results, while one that is wealthy is inauspicious;
when they are equal, it is declared by the lords of sages to have balanced results. (56)
Elsewhere: In an empty house one meets death; with wealth it becomes fruitless;
but in the case of debt, by its mere acquisition, all prosperity arises. (57)
Another method: Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, divide [the sequence] into three parts and differentiate them by the vowels;
the other is the reverse of that. The meaning of this is: starting from the first letter of the practitioner’s [name]...

By counting up to the first syllable of the mantra and multiplying that number by three, dividing by seven, the remainder will be either a surplus (debt) or a deficit (wealth). "The other" refers to the sequence starting from the first syllable of the mantra up to the first syllable of the practitioner's name.
Having multiplied that number by seven, one should divide it by three.

Furthermore, in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), doubled and joined with that of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), should be divided by eight; the remainder is [the result], while the other is the reverse.
The meaning of this is: the name of the one to be accomplished is doubled according to the distinction between vowels and consonants.

Having combined [the letters] according to the distinction between vowels and consonants by means of the syllables of the practitioner's name, one should divide by eight; thus the debt and wealth are to be known. "The other" refers to the syllables of the practitioner's name, which are doubled according to the distinction between vowels and consonants.

Having combined [the name] with the letters of the *sādhya* according to the distinction between vowels and consonants, and having divided by eight, the remainder—whether it be an excess or a deficit—is to be known as wealth (*dhana*). || 59 ||

Sanatkumāra describes the method for taking the names: "Having abandoned the names given by the father and mother, including [the suffixes] -śarman and so forth, as well as those ending in -deva, and having then removed the syllable 'Śrī', one should apply [the remaining parts] to the wheels (cakras) in sequence. (60)

Regarding the manner of taking the name, Piṅgalā says: "The name that is well-known, or his birth-name, or that which may have been given by the Guru through the falling of flowers for ascetics (yatīs). (61)
In another tantra: "Or it is well-known in the world, or performed by the mother or the father."
In the Rudrayāmala: "That by which one who is asleep wakes up, or one who is far away converses, or one who speaks even while his mind is elsewhere—that name indeed must be grasped. (63)
The necessity of investigating the *cakra* according to the distinction of deities is stated in the *Vārāhītantra*, the *Yāmala*, and other texts:
"For the Vaiṣṇavas, there is the purification of the *tāra*; for Śiva, the purification of the *koṣṭha*."

The purification of the zodiacal signs (*rāśiśuddhi*) is for the Traipura [deity], and the *akaḍama* is prescribed for Gopāla. The *akaḍama* is for Rāmacandra; for Gaṇeśa, the *haracakraka*; for Varāha, the *koṣṭhacakra*; for Mahālakṣmī, the *kulākula*; and for all [others], the *nāmādicakra*.
Likewise, the Bhūtacakra; at the Tāraka-cakra, the wise man should recite the pure mantra of Traipura.
Likewise: that which is purified by the [Vaiṣṇava] zodiacal signs is known as Vaiṣṇava, while the Śaiva is remembered as Ākaḍama; and for Kālikā and Tārā, the Tārā-cakra brings auspiciousness.

In the Tāraka-kṣetra of Caṇḍikā, Akadama is prescribed for Gopāla; in the Cakra of Hara, it is for all mantras. One should not resort to this when there is an excess of wealth. One should know it to be auspicious when there is an excess of debt, but it is not the rule when there is an excess of wealth. Having purified the defects—

One should accept [the mantra] originating from the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa). A mantra that is a debtor yields auspicious results, while a mantra that is a creditor bestows inauspicious results; when they are equal, it yields auspicious results—so it has been declared by the best of sages.
Elsewhere, even in an empty place, one meets death; wealth becomes fruitless;
and in the case of debt, upon its mere acquisition, all success is lost. (71)
Now begins the section on initiation (dīkṣā):
On the day preceding the guru’s initiation, he should consecrate his disciple with mantras;
having prepared a bed of darbha grass, he should cause the disciple to lie upon it. (72)
The knower of mantras should bind the child’s topknot with the sleep-mantra;

at the time of sleep, the child should recite that mantra three times. Having meditated upon the sandals of the venerable Guru, fasting and with senses subdued, [he should recite] *Tāra* (Oṃ) followed by *Hili* twice.

The syllable *dviṭha* is declared for Śūlapāṇi. Having recited this three times, fasting and with senses subdued, one should meditate upon the sandals of the venerable Guru and sleep upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.
This is another mantra; this mantra was taught by Śambhu for one who is sleeping.

Thus it is proclaimed: "Homage to the victorious, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul; homage to Rāma, the universal form, the Lord of Dreams! Tell me the truth in my dream regarding all matters without exception;
I shall bring about the accomplishment of the task."

"O Maheśvara, by your grace!"—having thus prayed to the God with this mantra, the good disciple may either sleep or remain awake. In the morning, the Guru should ask the disciple what was seen in the dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious: [did he see] a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a temple, a lotus, or a river?

Having seen an elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, a serpent, a tree, a mountain, a horse, pure meat, raw meat, liquor, and spirits— all such things as these— one shall attain success; this is for the purpose of indicating the attainment of mantra-siddhi.
The consecration of the disciple. || 76 ||
Now, the determination of the time for initiation (*dīkṣā*):
In the *Gautamīya*: "The commencement of the mantra should take place in Caitra, as it bestows all human goals (*puruṣārtha*).
In Vaiśākha there shall be the acquisition of jewels; but in Jyaiṣṭha, death would occur. In Āṣāḍha..."

In Śrāvaṇa, there will be the loss of kinsmen and a full lifespan; in Bhādrapada, there will be the loss of life (or loss of progeny); and in Āśvina, there will be an accumulation of jewels. In Kārttika, there will be the accomplishment of mantras, and it shall be the same in Mārgaśīrṣa; but in Pauṣa, there will be affliction from enemies.
In Māgha, there shall be an increase in intelligence. In Phālguna, all desires shall be fulfilled;

one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa). In Caitra, however, the domain of Gopāla [is prescribed], because it has been stated in the Gautamīya: "Initiation in the month of Madhu leads to suffering and even death. Thus.
It is not found elsewhere than in the Yoginītantra. || 81 ||
Likewise: "In Jyeṣṭha, the Vidyā bestows death; in Āṣāḍha, it brings happiness and prosperity.

Thus, according to the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, there is no fault regarding Śrīvidyā in the month of Āṣāḍha. In that context, the month is indeed solar (*saura*); for it is said: "Initiation is auspicious in a solar month, not in a lunar (*cāndra*) nor in a sidereal (*tāraka*) one."
According to the Gautamīya and the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā: "The commencement of a mantra on a Monday (meṣa) results in the loss of grain; on a Tuesday (vṛṣa), one meets with death."
In Cancer, there is the loss of offspring; in Leo, there may be the failure of mantra-siddhi; Virgo constantly bestows prosperity;
in Libra, all accomplishments are attained; in Scorpio, there will be the gain of gold; and Sagittarius causes the destruction of men.
Capricorn is said to bestow merit; Aquarius grants the abundance of wealth; Pisces always brings suffering—such is the sequence of the monthly rules. 82.

Now, the determination of the days for initiation (dīkṣā): on Sunday there will be wealth; on Monday, it is said, there will be peace; Mars destroys longevity, so one should avoid initiation on that day. On Wednesday, one attains beauty and knowledge.
If it occurs on a Thursday, one attains prosperity; on a Friday, one gains good fortune; and on a Saturday, there is a loss of fame.

Now, the determination of the lunar day for initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the *Āgamakalpadruma*: "Initiation performed on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is considered to cause the destruction of knowledge;
on the second day, knowledge arises; on the third day, one becomes pure. (85)
On the fourth day there shall be loss of wealth; on the fifth, an increase in intelligence;
on the sixth, a decline in knowledge; and on the seventh day, one obtains happiness.
On the eighth day there shall be destruction of the intellect, and on the ninth day there is the decay of the body.
On the tenth day there is royal prosperity; on the eleventh day, one should become pure.
On the twelfth day there shall be complete purity; on the thirteenth day, poverty. (89)

On the fourteenth day there is birth as an animal; at the end of the month, there is decline; at the end of the fortnight, there shall be an increase in dharma; one should avoid Vedic study [on these days]. 90.
He states what constitutes the suspension of Vedic study:
"The thundering of clouds at the twilight hours, a roar [of thunder], an earthquake, and the falling of meteors. (91)

One should avoid these and other days mentioned in the Śruti; specifically, the second, the fifth, and the sixth. It may also be performed on the twelfth or even on the thirteenth day. Thus it is said.

The injunction regarding the sixth and thirteenth lunar days pertains to Viṣṇu, because it is contained within the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*. The fifth, seventh, sixth, second, full moon, as well as the thirteenth and tenth lunar days are likewise praised. (95–96)
"Granting all desires"—from this statement of Sanatkumāra, the prescription for the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also established.

Regarding the domain of Śiva, he states the prohibition for the tenth and seventh days: "The tenth and especially the seventh day of the bright fortnight are always censurable; the sixth day (*ṣaṣṭhī*) likewise should always be avoided."
In another Śaiva Āgama: || 97 ||
Now, the determination of the lunar mansions for initiation:
In Aśvinī one attains happiness; in Bharaṇī death is certain;
in Kṛttikā one becomes miserable; in Rohiṇī one becomes a master of speech. (98)
In Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness; in Ārdrā, the loss of kinsmen;
in Punarvasu, one becomes wealthy; in Puṣya, the destruction of enemies; in Aśleṣā, death may occur;
in Maghā, liberation from suffering; [and] beauty...
And one attains [the fruit] under Pūrvaphalgunī; of this there is no doubt. || 100 ||

One born under Uttaraphalgunī becomes wise, and under Hastā, one becomes wealthy. Under Citrā, there shall be attainment of knowledge; under Svātī, the destruction of enemies. Under Viśākhā, there is happiness; under Anurādhā, the increase of kinsmen. Under Jyeṣṭhā...
There would be a loss of the thread in the case of the root [vowel], whereas there is an increase in fame. || 2 ||
Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā bestow fame; one becomes miserable under Śravaṇā, and there is poverty under Dhaniṣṭhā. Under Śatabhiṣā there is intelligence, and one becomes happy under Pūrvabhādrapadā.
There is happiness under Uttarabhādrapadā, and an increase in fame under Revatī. || 4 ||
The prohibition regarding Ārdrā and Kṛttikā applies only to [the initiation of] mantras other than those of Śiva and Agni;
for it is said: "The commencement of a mantra is praised under Ārdrā and Kṛttikā, provided it is the commencement of a mantra for Īśa or for Kṛśānu (Agni) respectively. (5)
In another tantra: "In the asterisms of Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Hasta, as well as in Jyeṣṭhā and the three Uttarās—thus [is it]. 2.135.
One should perform the consecration with mantras. Thus, whatever procedure is prescribed for Jyeṣṭhā and Ārdrā applies here as well, because it has been stated in the Agastyasaṃhitā.
Now, the determination of the yogas:
Śubha, Siddha, and likewise Āyuṣmān; after that, Dhruva-yoga;
then Prīti-saubhāgya-yoga; then Buddhi-yoga; and Harṣaṇa.
Likewise, in every tantra, such yogas bring about auspiciousness. || 7 ||
In the *Ratnāvalī*: The yogas are Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Sukarman, Sādhya, Śukra, Harṣaṇa, Varīyān, Śiva, Siddha, Brahma, and Aindra—these are the sixteen. (8)
Now, the determination of the *karaṇas*:
Vava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, and Vaṇija—these are the *karaṇas* that are exclusively auspicious; so it is declared in all the Tantras. (9)

Now, the determination of the ascendant: One should undertake the commencement of initiation when the ascendant is Taurus, Leo, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces, and when the moon and the stars are favorable.
Likewise: a fixed ascendant is auspicious for a Viṣṇu-mantra, while a movable ascendant is auspicious for a Śiva-mantra;
a dual-natured ascendant is praised for a Śakti-mantra. (11)

In the Agastyasaṃhitā: "Malefic planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and benefics situated in the angles (kendras) and trines, are auspicious for initiation; however, all [planets] situated in retrograde motion cause total destruction. (12)
Now, the determination of the lunar fortnight: Initiation is auspicious in the bright fortnight, and also in the dark fortnight until the fifth day.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā: "Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, initiation is auspicious in all cases. (14)

In the Kālottara, however, it is stated: "Those desiring prosperity [should worship] always during the bright fortnight; those desiring liberation, during the dark fortnight"—this is the implied meaning. Regarding the months prohibited for practice, specific details have been declared by the sages.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: the sixth [day] in the month of Bhādrapada; the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Āśvina (Īṣa);
the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika; the third day of the bright fortnight in Mārgaśīrṣa;
the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Pauṣa; the fourth day of the bright fortnight in Māgha; and the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Phālguna; [and so on] in Caitra...

The fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika [is known as] Kāmacaturdaśī; some say it is the thirteenth. In Vaiśākha, there is Akṣayā, and in Jyeṣṭha, the Daśaharā lunar day. In Āṣāḍha, the fifth day of the bright fortnight, and in Śrāvaṇa, the fifth day of the dark fortnight—these are the festivals of the gods; one obtains the fruit of ten million holy fords (tīrthas) by observing them.

In this matter, initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed; one need not wait for a specific month, nor examine the day of the week, nor the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), nor defects such as the lunar date (tithi), nor even the astrological conjunctions (yoga) and lunar phases (karana); so it was declared by Śaṅkara. || 17–18 ||

And another opinion is as follows: the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in Caitra, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Vaiśākha, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Jyeṣṭha, and the fifth day of the [bright] fortnight in Āṣāḍha, known as Nāgapañcamī. (19)
The eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Śrāvaṇa, O auspicious lady, and the eighth day conjoined with Rohiṇī;

the highly meritorious Mahā-aṣṭamī in Āśvina, which also grants desired boons; the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, and likewise the sixth and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight in Mārgaśīrṣa; and the sixth and fourteenth days in Pauṣa.
The eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Māgha, and the sixth day of the bright fortnight in Phālguna—this is the determination of the proper time. || 21 ||
In the Yoginītantra: "O Sovereign of the Gods, during the solstices and equinoxes, during the eclipses of the moon and sun,
on the day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), on the first days of the Yugas, on all the Manvantara transitions,
and on the days of great worship (mahāpūjā)— as well as on the fourth and fifth lunar days."

The fourteenth and the eighth lunar days are likewise declared to be auspicious for the rite of receiving initiation (*dīkṣā*). Based on such statements as "on the [fourteenth] and so forth," the mention of the fourteenth and eighth days refers to the domain of Śakti. (23) The mention of the fourth day refers to the domain of Gaṇeśa, because it is so stated in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*). (24)
Even during months that are otherwise censured, initiation is declared to be auspicious;
there is nothing on earth equal to the time of a solar eclipse, especially for the rite of receiving initiation, O Great Goddess. Whatever is performed there yields infinite fruit.

It should be so: at the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) and likewise during a solar eclipse, there is no obstacle whatsoever regarding the ascendant (lagna) or other factors in any way. At the sun’s transit, nothing else need be sought; there is no requirement for purification based on the day of the week, lunar date, month, or the like.
This applies to the solar eclipse; likewise, it also applies to the lunar eclipse. || 25 ||

And so it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "One should not perform a Śākta initiation during an eclipse of the sun, nor indeed should one perform a Vaiṣṇava initiation if there is an eclipse of the moon. This, however, refers to cases other than Gopālavidyā and Śrīvidyā. [This applies] to other auspicious conjunctions (parva-yoga).

"During an eclipse of the moon or the sun"—thus from the *Gautamīya*. "The entire initiation is auspicious on its own respective day; however, at the time of a solar eclipse, nothing else need be sought. Thus also from the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.

Now, regarding the specific details for the [initiation] of Tārā and others, as follows: "I shall proclaim the time for initiation according to the Nīlatantra: on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, under an auspicious lagna and at a favorable moment, when the moon is in conjunction with Pūrvabhādrapadā or the Maitra (Anurādhā) nakṣatra."
Or it is also highly commended under Anurādhā or Revatī.
One should know the auspicious time for the reception of the mantra, especially during the month of Īṣa (Mārgaśīrṣa) and particularly in Kārttika. || 31 ||

Regarding the specific [efficacy] during a solar eclipse, the *Yāmala* cited in the *Ratnāvalī* states: "The seed-syllables of Śrī, Parā, and Kālī, as well as the mantra of Lopāmudrā and that of Aghora—when obtained during a solar eclipse, these bestow the fruit of liberation upon men. [This applies on] the new moon day, on Monday, or on Tuesday.
The fourteenth day, the seventh day, and a Sunday—these are equal to a hundred solar parvans. || 33 ||

In the Kulārṇava: "The seventh lunar day on a Sunday, likewise the new moon (darśa) on a Monday, the fourth on a Tuesday, and the eighth on a Thursday—these should be known as equal to the festival days of the gods;
on these one should perform initiation. (34)
In the *Yāmala*: "At Puṣyatīrtha, Kurukṣetra, the four Devī-pīṭhas, Prayāga, Śrīgiri, and Kāśī, one need not purify the time. (35)

In the *Viṣṇuyāmala*: "Beginning from the awakening of the Goddess (Devī-bodha) until the ninth lunar day (*navamī*), initiation (*dīkṣā*) performed by the wise during those days bestows all desired fruits. (36)

Especially during the bright fortnight, and even then on the eighth lunar day; and even there, when the goddess Śāradī Durgā is present in every house— that is the time when initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed, without scrutinizing the month, the asterism, or other such factors.
Likewise, in the case of awakening Durgā, one should not examine whether the time is auspicious or inauspicious;
whether it be on the eighth day known as Aśoka or the ninth day known as Rāmā,
whether under a favorable or unfavorable astrological rising (lagna), or on any lunar day whatsoever, [it should be done] in accordance with the command of the Guru.
The initiation (dīkṣā) should especially be performed on the fourth lunar day, on a Tuesday, and on a day that touches three [different] zodiac signs;
on such an occasion, one should not consider the ascendant or other astrological factors in any way whatsoever.

In the *Samayātantra*: "On the birthdays of those who mark the beginning of the ages (*yugādi*), as well as on the day of marriage, and during the two solstices (*viṣuva*) and equinoxes (*ayana*), one should not deliberate upon anything at all. (40)

Likewise: if the Guru, out of compassion, bestows [the initiation] upon his disciples, then he need never consider the astrological moment (lagna) or other such factors. On that day, all weekdays, all planets, all lunar mansions (nakṣatras), and all zodiac signs (rāśis)—all these belong to the Guru who knows the mantra.
They bring about auspiciousness. || 42 ||
In the Yoginītantra: "And during an eclipse or at a great sacred site (tīrtha), there is no determination of time."
Now I shall describe, according to the Tantras, the locations for initiation (dīkṣā):

in a cow-pen, in a cow-shed, in a temple, or in a forest; likewise in a sacred field (puṇyakṣetra), in a garden, on a riverbank, near a dhātrī tree or a bilva tree, or on a mountain peak—these are the places for the knower of mantras.
And in caves, or even on the banks of the Gaṅgā, it shall be multiplied by ten million times ten million.

He states the prohibited places: "O Pārvatī, one should not receive initiation at these holy sites: at Gayā, in the field of Bhāskara (the Sun), at Virajā, on Mount Candraparvata, at Caṭula, at Mataṅga, and likewise in the hermitages of Kanyā. (45)

In the Vārāhī Tantra: "If Venus is in its setting or its retrograde state (vṛddhi), or if Jupiter and the Sun [are unfavorable], there is no fault at all when [the practice occurs] during Aries, Scorpio, or Leo;
for in all the Mahāvidyās, there is no consideration of time and such. Thus it is said.
In the *Muṇḍamālātantra*: "There is no purification of time and so forth, nor any defect regarding [the presence of] enemies and the like.
Now, the determination of the rosary (*mālānirṇaya*):
In the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*: "The index finger, the middle finger, and the ring finger..."

And the little finger—these [fingers] are, in order, three-fingered with three joints each, while the middle finger has only one joint. One should designate two joints of the middle finger as the *meru* (the central peak).
Regarding the sequence therein, the *Satkumārasaṃhitā* states: "The ring finger—"
Starting from the middle finger and beginning with the little finger, one should perform the recitation across the ten joints up to the base of the index finger.

Likewise: "Starting from the root of the ring finger and from the little finger itself, one should perform the recitation (*saṃjapet*) across the eight joints ending with the middle finger of the index finger. This statement, however, refers to the context of one hundred and eight repetitions and pertains to Viṣṇu. (49)

Furthermore, regarding the [proper] application of power (*śakti*): "The three joints of the ring finger, the three joints of the little finger, the three [joints] of the middle finger, and the base joint of the index finger—[if one recites] on the tip or the middle of the index finger, he is a doer of evil. Thus says the *Śrīkrama*.
Thus it is said in the *Haṃsapārameśvara*:
"By the successive turning of the three joints of the ring finger, one should take one joint of the middle finger and one joint of the index finger;
and two joints of the index finger—know that, O Pārvatī, this is the Meru, the Garland of Power (*śaktimālā*)."
Thus has been fully explained the Illuminator of All Tantras. || 51 ||
Likewise: beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction up to the base of the middle finger, one should recite [the mantra] over the eight joints.
This also applies to the context of one hundred and eight recitations and so forth. || 52 ||
Furthermore, regarding the Śrīvidyā: O Goddess of the Suras, the root and tip of both the ring finger and the middle finger, as well as the three joints of the little finger and the index finger,
and the two "merus" (knuckles) of the ring finger and the middle finger [are to be joined].

"Auspicious! O Goddess, one should recite [the mantra of] Tripurasundarī in a clockwise order," according to the statement in the *Yāmala*. (53) Beginning from the base of the little finger and proceeding in a clockwise manner up to the base of the index finger, one should perform the recitation across the eight joints.
This [topic] also concerns one hundred and eight subjects.

In the *Muṇḍamālā-tantra*: "The finger-garland (*karamālā*) is proclaimed as beginning from the two joints of the ring fingers in sequence, starting with the little finger, and ending at the base of the index fingers."
The fingers should not be separated even slightly when the palm is slightly contracted;
for if the fingers are separated, the recitation flows away through the gaps.

Elsewhere it is also said: Whatever is recited upon the tips of the fingers, whatever is recited while crossing over the *meru*, and whatever is recited at the joints of the fingers—all that becomes fruitless. (57)
Since Rākṣasas seize that recitation which one performs by transgressing the rules of counting, a wise person should count [the beads] in every respect. (58)
In the Viśvasāra: "The number of recitations must be performed; a wise person should not recite without counting. For one who acts without counting, everything becomes fruitless. (59)
In the Tantra: having placed the hand upon the heart and turned it toward the left, covering both hands with a cloth, one should always recite [the mantra] with the right hand. 60.
Now, regarding the holding of the count of recitations (*japa-saṃkhyā*), there are prohibited and permitted items:

one should not perform the counting of recitations with unhusked grains, nor with the joints of the fingers, nor with seeds, nor with flowers, nor with sandalwood, nor with clay. [Likewise,] not with lac, usury...

Having mixed vermilion, cow dung, and dried cow dung (karīṣa), one should form them into pills and perform the prescribed number of recitations (*japa*). Kuṣīda, red sandalwood, karīṣa, and the ash of dried cow dung—this is to be understood as pertaining to the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the purpose of recitation. Regarding the recitation:
And the garland is exactly as it is in its enumeration. || 61 ||

Now, the Garland of Phonemes (*varṇamālā*) according to the *Sanatkumāra-tantra*: The garland consists of the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*), including the letter *kṣa* and the vowels (*eruka*), arranged in direct and reverse order, accompanied by the nasal bindu and the eight groups of consonants, for the purpose of internal worship. [The sequence begins with] *ā*, *di*, *ku*, *cu*.
The eight syllables ṭu, tu, pu, yu, śa, vo, ṣṭa, and u are proclaimed [as the seed-syllables]. || 62 ||

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: having added the bindu (anusvāra) to each letter beginning with 'a' and having recited them one hundred times in both direct and reverse order, one should first utter the final letter of the vowels beginning with 'a' and the consonants beginning with the 'ka'-group, making it possess the anusvāra.

Thereafter, the recitation of the mantra (mantrajapa) should be performed; in this manner, the recitation reaches the count of one hundred and eight. "Internal worship" (antaryajana) is used here as an illustrative term. || 63 ||

And thus: "Having pronounced the letter together with the *bindu*, the wise man should subsequently recite the mantra; having meditated upon [the letters] from *a* to *kṣa* joined with the *bindu*, this is declared to be the garland of letters (*varṇamālā*) in both direct and reverse order"—so says the statement of Nārada. (64)
Another method for purification is taught by Viśuddheśvara:
"By means of the division of the eight groups [of consonants] in both direct and reverse order, one should interpose the letters with the mantra and the mantras with the letters;
thus one should construct a garland composed of syllables that illuminates all tantras."
One should never attempt to leap over the final letter, which has the form of Mount Meru.

Likewise, in the *Mālinīvijaya*, there is a rule regarding the Sūtras: "The serpent-like [energy] shines within as the form of the letter *Rūm*; it blazes like one who has just awakened from sleep, consisting of a hundred ascents and descents, and the eight groups plus eight. (66)
Now, from the *Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā*:
"Previously, in the form of Rudra, [the seed] was extracted from the fire of dissolution;
therefore, at the end, one should employ that seed of the earth which was rescued from the dissolution. This is the seed rescued from the dissolution.

Furthermore, from the letter *la* and fire (*ra*), one should again apply two *la*s at the end in this rule for the production of the double *la*. By this, it should be understood that there are two *la*s. || 67 ||
Now, regarding the determination of the gems for a rosary: listen to those [rosaries] made from lotus seeds and so forth for external application— [those] made of rudrākṣa,
conch, lotus seeds, japa beads, and pearls.
The rosary of a householder may be made of crystal, precious gems, gold, coral, silver, or kusha grass roots. (68)
Now, regarding the fruit of the rosary:
counting with the fingers yields one; with knots, it becomes eightfold;
with *putrajīva* seeds, tenfold; and with conch shells, a hundredfold; [with rudrākṣas], it is a thousandfold.

A rosary made of coral and precious gems is said to be worth ten thousand; that same rosary made of crystal is declared to be worth one hundred thousand, while one made of pearls is said to be worth one million. One made of lotus seeds would be worth ten million, and one made of gold is said to be worth a hundred million. With a rosary of *kuśa*-grass knots, the merit is a billion, and with *rudrākṣa* beads, it is ten billion.
It may be infinite. A garland fashioned from all [of these] bestows the fruit of liberation upon men.
(69) In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "If one performs recitation with rudrākṣas, indrākṣas, or likewise with crystal beads, one must not insert anything else in between, such as putrajīva seeds and the like."
If one should employ any other [beads] in the rosary during the act of recitation, that "Beloved" [rosary] will grant neither his desires nor liberation.
In the *Muṇḍamālā*: "A garland made of *dhustūra* flowers from a cremation ground is to be known for the ritual of Dhūmāvatī. A garland fashioned from human fingers and bones grants all desires.
It should be strung with sinews and likewise wrapped in a red cloth; it must always be kept secret."
With effort, O beloved, [he was treated] by his mother like a paramour. || 71 ||
Regarding the difference in specific desires: A rosary fashioned from lotus seeds is considered destructive of enemies; a rosary made of knots of *kuśa* grass destroys all sins;
one constructed with *putrajīva* fruits brings about the attainment of sons. [Constructed...]
A rosary made of silver and gems, when used for recitation, grants one's desires; a rosary fashioned from coral bestows abundant wealth.

Regarding the ignorance of Bhairava, it is stated in the Vārāhī-tantra: "One should make a rosary of gold, coral, crystal, or fashioned from conch shell, or indeed of corals alone; one should avoid the *putrajīva* fruit, but especially the lotus seed (*padmākṣa*), the *rudrākṣa*, and the *bhadrākṣa*."
