73. However, for the recitation (*japa*) of the *Tripurā* mantra and similar practices, a rosary made of red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), seeds (*bīja*), and so forth, is highly recommended.
Thus it is said in the Tantra: "A rosary of red sandalwood bestows both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*);
likewise, for a Vaiṣṇava, a rosary of *tulasī*; for Gaṇeśvara, one made of elephant tusks; and for Tripurā..."
For recitation, the rudrākṣa is recommended along with red sandalwood. || 75 ||
In the *Muṇḍamālā*: "A garland made of great conch shells [is prescribed] in the rite of Nīlasārasvata. (76)
Regarding the *mahāśaṅkha* in the Tantra:
"O Dear One, a rosary fashioned from a fragment of the bone of the forehead is a *mālā* made of *mahāśaṅkha*, used for the recitation of the *Tārā-vidyā*.
The bone situated between the ear and the eye is proclaimed to be the *mahāśaṅkha*. (77)

Regarding the rules for the gems, the *Munḍamālā* states: "They should be uniform in shape with one another, neither too thick nor too thin, free from defects such as insect holes, and indeed neither worn out nor brand new."
Now, according to the Gautamiya: "A rosary of fifty beads is prescribed for all rites.

The rosary of beads is proclaimed to begin with the letter *a* and end with the letter *kṣa*. O best of sages, one should designate the syllable *kṣa* as the summit (*meru*) there. By means of this [rosary], [one performs] all mantras..."

Recitation (*japa*) bestows all prosperity. In the *Cāmuṇḍātantra*: "One should always perform recitation with the hand, but not for the sake of specific desires, due to a lack of understanding. O beautiful one, one may indeed perform recitation with the hand in the absence of a rosary."
Regarding the distinction of desires, it is stated in the Gautamīya: "In this context, the specific prescription for the rosary (akṣasūtra) is observed: with twenty-five beads, there is liberation;
with thirty, for the attainment of wealth; and all goals are achieved with twenty-seven."
Fifteen repetitions are for malevolent rites; with fifty, there is the accomplishment of desired objects;
likewise, with one hundred and four, the accomplishment of all things has been declared by the wise. (79)

Now, regarding the varieties of seats, the *Haṃsamāheśvara* states: "A seat made of kaba, mla, komala, or kuśa grass, or one made of wood, serves as the instrument for ritual action; it may be white or black, though the former is specifically preferred."
"Regarding 'the red blanket': O Goddess of the Gods, their pure seat is a skin-seat (carma-āsana). If one sits upon hair, then everything is destroyed;
by the mere touch of hair, the loss of accomplishment (siddhi) arises. [This is] for the sake of desired goals..."

A woolen blanket is excellent, as is a red woolen blanket. On a black antelope skin, there is the attainment of knowledge; on a tiger skin, liberation and prosperity. On a seat of *kuśa* grass, there is the attainment of mantras; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. On the bare ground...

The arising of suffering and misfortune result from a seat made of wood (83). One becomes poor on a bamboo seat; on a stone seat, there is affliction by disease. On a seat of grass, there is loss of fame; on a seat of leaf-sprouts, there is mental confusion. Indeed, [a seat] made of cloth causes the destruction of recitation, meditation, and austerity.

For this very reason, a seat consisting of cloth alone is prohibited, because [the scripture] states that a "cloth-seat" removes disease and so forth, thereby indicating that it produces a specific result;
and also because of the Lord’s statement: "With cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass as the uppermost layers. || 85 ||
And likewise in the Gautamiya: "In the same way, the mantra-practitioner [should sit] on a soft seat covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and kuśa grass. (86)
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "One initiated into the channels (nāḍī) may enter [the cremation ground] clad in the skin of a black antelope;
likewise, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a celibate student, and a mendicant may enter. (87)
In the *Āgamanakalpadruma*: the skins of the ram, tiger, elephant, camel, bear, and serpent are prescribed as seats for each of the six ritual acts (*ṣaṭkarma*). (88)
Now, regarding the consecration of the rosary (*mālā-saṃskāra*), it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"If a person recites a mantra with rosaries that have not been consecrated, one should know that all of it is fruitless, and the deity becomes angry. (89)

Sanatkumāra said: A thread produced from cotton bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa; and that which is beautifully fashioned by the daughters of the foremost Brahmins is likewise auspicious. It may be white, red, or black, or even made of silk thread (paṭṭasūtra).

Or: for pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), and malevolent rites (abhicāra), as well as for liberation (mokṣa), sovereignty (aiśvarya), and victory (jaya), the colors are white, red, yellow, and black respectively. For all castes (varṇas), however, the red [thread] bestows all desired objects. Having tripled it three times, one should tie the knots.

According to the treatises on craftsmanship, the wise one should prepare the thread for the measurement of the gems and jewels. The intelligent practitioner should recite each letter of the alphabet together with the *tāra* (OM). Taking the rosary, he should string it upon the thread at regular intervals, forming the *brahmagranthi* (Brahma-knot) [at each junction].

Having thus fashioned Meru along with the knots, and having tied the rosary in front, one should then begin the consecration (saṃskāra). According to the opinion of some, one should tie it with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā);
and likewise in the Ekavīrākalpa: "One should tie the knot according to the letters of the Mātṛkā and with the mantra."
Or else, the supreme practitioner should have it made; or he should string it together with qualities such as gold.

Then he should apply the *brahmagranthi* or even the *nāgapāśa*; then, intent on meditation, he should bind the garland with the *kavaca* mantra. Finally, he should [place] the *meru* at the end of all.

Endowed with two threads, the supreme practitioner should weave them together by means of the *tāra*-yoga and bind them. O Goddess of the Gods, having thus completed this, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
In the Gautamīya [Tantra]: "Having joined mouth to mouth, one should join tail to tail;
the garland should be like a cow’s tail, or auspiciously shaped like a serpent. (96)

Regarding the rule for the mouth and tail according to the *Chandaḥsāra*: for the *rudrākṣa*, the elevated part is said to be the mouth and the depressed part the tail; for the *kamalākṣa*, the subtle portion with two dots is the mouth; [likewise] for the *savinduka*.

The thick portion is known as the tail (puccha) and the smooth portion as the face (mukha). Having thus understood the face and tail of the Rudrākṣa and the lotus-seed (ambhoruhākṣa), you should place a single bead of the same species at the front as the Meru. Taking each individual gem, [one should apply] the Brahma-granthi.
One should arrange them; however, one should recite each individual letter of the Mātṛkā at the beginning of the stringing. || 98 ||
The rule for the knot is stated in that very same place: "It is prescribed by means of three repetitions of the knot, or likewise by half [that amount];
one should make the knot as firm as possible by means of two and a half revolutions. Thus, there is an option according to one's preference. 99.

From the Kālikā Purāṇa: "One should fashion each seed bead with a *brahmagranthi* (Brahma-knot) as it naturally occurs, or otherwise without knots but provided with a firm cord. Having thus prepared the rosary, O best of sages, one should indeed purify it. (100)

One should fashion a lotus shape using nine fresh leaves of the *aśvattha* tree; in its center, one should place the rosary while reciting the root mantra of the Mātṛkā. One should then wash it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and pure water, reciting the *Sadyojāta* mantra.

The mantra for Sadyojāta is: *oṃ sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi sadyojātāya vai namaḥ | bhave bhave nātibhave bhajasva māṃ bhavedbhavāya vai namaḥ*. One should rub [the substance] with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra.
The Vāmadeva mantra: Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva, salutation to Jyeṣṭha,
salutation to Rudra, salutation to Kāla, salutation to Kalavikaraṇa, salutation to Balavikaraṇa,
salutation to Balapramathana, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana.
For the purpose of churning the mind, one should fumigate her with the Aghora mantra.
The Aghora mantra is: *Oṃ aghorebhyo 'tha ghorebhyo ghora-ghoratarebhyaḥ | sarvataḥ sarva-sarvebhyo namas te 'stu*.

To those in the form of Rudras; one should smear [the image] with the Tatpuruṣa mantra. The Tatpuruṣa mantra is: *oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt*. One should thus consecrate it with the fifth [mantra].

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times for each [deity], and likewise one hundred times with the root mantra for Meru. In the *Muṇḍamālā*, it says: "With the fifth mantra itself, one hundred times for each."

One hundred times; one should consecrate Mount Meru with the fifth mantra in that same manner. Or rather, it may be done once for each. In that very [text] it says: "The practitioner of mantra should consecrate each one individually with the fifth [mantra], once for each."

And likewise, with reference to the *samudāyamālā* in the *Gautamīya*, it is stated: "One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times using the fifth hymn alone, even if it is slightly less than a hundred"; thus, in the case of a *mālā*, the recitation of a hundred [times] should be performed.
The fifth mantra is: *oṃ īśānaḥ sarvavidyānāmīśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmādhipatirbrahmaṇo'dhipatiḥ brahmā śivo me'stu sadāśivom*. This may be recited once for each [mantra] or [all together].
And likewise in that very [text]: "The mantra-practitioner should consecrate each [bead] with the mantra, and once with the fifth [syllable].

Therein, one should worship the deity externally with extensive offerings according to one's means. (3) After the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the life-force) of the rosary, one should worship the deity.

And so it is stated in the Sanatkumāra-tantra: "Having thus consecrated the rosary, the wise one should join the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of that [deity] into it; then, O best of the twice-born, he should worship that rosary with the root mantra. (4)

In the Vārāhī Tantra: "O Mālā, O Mālā, O Great Mālā, whose nature is that of all reality, you in whom the four aims of life are established; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me. Having performed [the ritual] beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should worship with red flowers. This concerns the Śakti [deity]. (5)
Regarding Viṣṇu, however, it is stated in the Yāmala:

"One should worship with this mantra—the Vāgbhava [syllable], likewise Lakṣmī, and the rosary beginning with the letter 'akṣa', ending in the dative case and the letters of the heart; one should consecrate [the deity] with the root mantra."
In the same manner, the knower of mantras should consecrate the thread with the letters of the Mātṛkā, according to the sequence of ascending and descending order.
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Thereafter, one should perform the rite of fire-oblation (*homakarma*) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*) [into the vessel]. (7)

If one is unable to perform the fire sacrifice (homakarma), one should perform double the recitation (japa). The practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should not recite another mantra; he should neither shake nor tremble [the body]. From shaking, there is a loss of accomplishment (siddhi);
from trembling, it bestows much suffering. When a sound arises, disease occurs.
If it falls from the hand, it causes destruction; if the thread is snapped, death will occur;
therefore, one should be diligent in this matter.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should place the rosary either at the level of the ear or in a high place, having spoken thus:
"Oṃ, O Rosary, you are considered the bestower of all accomplishments for all the gods; by that truth, grant me success, O Mother! Salutations to you. Then, having worshipped it with offerings...
The householder should guard it with great effort.
Regarding the specific requirements for different desires, the *Gautamīya* states:
"In the rite of subduing enemies, [one should use] the union of the index finger and the thumb;
from the union of the thumb and the middle finger, the attainment of all perfections is certain. (12)
The union of the thumb and the ring finger is intended for eradication and suppression; the union of the index finger and the little finger is considered the destruction of enemies. (13)

In the *Saṃhitā* by Vaiśampāyana: "One should move [the beads] from the very middle with the thumb and the middle finger; one should not touch them with the index finger—this method of counting bestows liberation. When the string is worn out, having tied on a new string, [one should recite it] a hundred times."
One should recite [the mantra]. If it falls from the hand through negligence, one should recite one hundred and eight times.
Having washed away any forbidden contact, one should recite as prescribed.
Even when [the thread] is broken, one hundred and eight recitations must be performed.

As it is stated in the *Kubjikātantra*: "When the thread is broken, having woven the thread again, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times. This is because falling from the hand and being broken yield the same result. || 16 ||

Another method is found in the *Āgamakalpadruma*: "Having completed the worship beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the knower of mantras should invoke Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, and Durgā there and perform their worship. Then, having cast [the offerings] into the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)," (17).
The knower of mantras, having lifted that garland with a mere glance, should place it in a golden vessel; then,
having treated it in sequence with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, interspersed with water and incense.
The wise one, having established the procedure for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) right here in due order,
should bathe [the image] with cool waters. Then, having anointed it with sandalwood paste, musk, saffron, and so forth, he should mutter the *Hṛdaya-mantra* one hundred and eight times.
In that [consecration], one should worship the nine planets and the guardians of the directions;
then, having worshipped the Guru, one should receive the auspicious garland. || 21 ||

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Having received the command of the Guru, a person whose inner organ is purified should then perform the preliminary rite with the desire for the accomplishment of the mantra. (22)

He states its necessity: "Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any action, so too is a mantra proclaimed to be ineffective when deprived of the *puraścaraṇa*. Therefore, at the outset, the wise person should perform it himself or have a guru perform it; in the absence of a guru, [he should have] a Brahmin [perform it]. (23)

Or one should employ a friend who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings, affectionate, learned in the scriptures, and endowed with various virtues; or a woman possessed of good qualities, who has excellent sons. || 24 ||

Now, regarding the determination of the location for the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite), the *Yoginīhṛdaya* states: "First, the determination of the location is declared in order to perform the *puraskriyā*:
a sacred field (*puṇyakṣetra*), the bank of a river, a cave, or a mountain peak."
Sacred sites, the confluence of rivers, and purifying forests. || 26 ||
Secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, a mountain slope, a grove of tulasī, a cow-pen, a temple of Śiva devoid of bulls, the root of an aśvattha or āmalakī tree,
a cow-shed, the midst of water, a deity’s shrine, and the shore of the ocean.
These are the places recommended for practitioners as their own dwellings during the performance of spiritual rites. || 28 ||
Japa is recommended when performed in the presence of the sun, fire, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, brahmins, and cows; or else, one should dwell wherever the mind finds serenity. (29–30)
Likewise: one should know that [the merit] is a hundredfold in the home, it becomes a hundred-thousandfold in a cow-pen, ten millionfold in a temple, and infinite in the presence of Śiva. (31)

In the Brahmayāmala: Recitation performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; in a cow-pen, it is ten-fold; in the interior of a forest, a hundred-fold; and by a pond, a thousand-fold. On a riverbank, it is a hundred-thousand-fold; on a mountain peak, it is equal to ten million-fold; in a temple of Śiva, it is a hundred times ten million-fold, and [in the presence of the Guru] it is infinite.
In the presence of the guru. || 33 ||

Likewise: "In a house, a cow-pen, a forest, a grove, by a river, on a mountain, in a temple of Śiva, or in the presence of the Guru—wherever [these conditions are met], that recitation is considered supreme (34). [It should be] in a secluded and pure place, free from barbarians, wicked people, wild animals, and thorns, and devoid of censure."
O beloved of penance, one should dwell in a place endowed with devotion, in a righteous land that is well-supplied with food and free from calamities,
in a beautiful region inhabited by devotees, in the presence of gurus,
and likewise in a place where the mind is one-pointed.
Resorting to any one of these places, one should perform the recitation (japa). Wherever the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) performs the recitation, there he should contemplate the tortoise (kūrma).

In the *Gautamīya*: "If one performs the *puraścaraṇa* on a mountain, on the bank of a river, in a sacred forest, or on the shore of a stream, one need not contemplate the tortoise (*kūrma*). But if it is in a village, a settlement, or a house, one must contemplate that [tortoise]. (39–40)

Now, regarding the rules for food and so forth during the *puraścaraṇa* rite, the *Gautamīya-tantra* states: "The practitioner of mantras performing the *puraścaraṇa* should distinguish between what is fit to be eaten and what is not. Otherwise, from the fault of improper eating, the loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises. (41)
One should eat approved food with the desire for the accomplishment of mantras; therefore, a person should always be diligent in eating approved food. (42)
In the Agastyasaṃhitā: Cow’s curd, milk, and ghee; sugarcane products excluding jaggery; sesame seeds, white mung beans, and tubers excluding the kemuka variety. (43)

The coconut fruit, the plantain, the lavalī, the mango, the āmalaka, the jackfruit, and the harītakī are considered by the wise to be excellent *haviṣya* (sacrificial food) during the interval of a vow; or rather, the reading is "at the commencement of a vow" (*vratārambhe*). Winter rice, white sugar, and steamed [grains]... [44]

Grains such as mung beans, sesame, barley, peas, kaṅku, and nīvāra; potherbs such as vāstuka, hilamocikā, ṣaṣṭika rice, kāla-śāka, radish, and all types of greens except for *kemuka*; salts such as *saindhava* and sea salt; cow products such as curd and clarified butter; and milk from which the cream has not been removed.

The jackfruit, mango, myrobalan, long pepper, cumin, orange, tamarind, plantain, lavalī, and emblic myrobalan— these fruits, along with non-sugared molasses and products of sugarcane, when not cooked in oil,
are declared to be *haviṣyānna* (sacrificial food) for a sage. Or, one who eats such *haviṣyānna*...

Vegetables, or even barley-gruel; milk, roots, or fruits—whatever is available at any place [is permitted]. The fruit of the plantain, the tamarind, the lotus, and the orange: these fruits are to be eaten; others than these [are not].
One should avoid [it]. || 47 ||

As for that which is stated in the Yoginītantra: "In the vow, one should avoid the tamarind, the nālikā vegetable, the pea, the breadfruit, the kadamba, the coconut, and the pumpkin"— that should be understood as referring to a different type of vow.
Now, the things to be avoided during the *puraścaraṇa* [preliminary rite]:
One should avoid honey, alkaline substances, salt, and oil;
as well as betel-leaf, vessels of bell-metal, and even divine food (*divyabhojana*). Likewise: alkaline substances...
Salt, meat, garlic, eating from a bronze vessel,
black gram, adzukis, lentils, kodrava, and chickpeas as well— food that is stale, devoid of oil, or defiled by insects. (50)

In the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*: One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it. Except during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), the practitioner of mantra should not touch his own wife. [One should also avoid] salt, whatever is alkaline, and likewise honey.
A change of flavor; crookedness; oil for the head; oil for anointing the body; and eating food that has not been announced. || 52 ||

One should avoid actions performed without prior intention, such as massaging the body and so forth. One should bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with pure myrobalan (amalaka). Having recited the mantra, one should perform bathing, sipping water for purification, and eating, according to the prescribed rules.

One should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day (trisandhyā). One should recite the mantra at the three junctions, or at one junction, but never without [the ritual context]. According to one's capacity, one should bathe three times a day; if unable, twice; or at least once. There is no fruit for one who does not bathe, nor for one who does not offer libations to the ancestors (pitṛs).

If one recites while having unwashed hands, or while naked, or even while standing upon the head [of another], or while talking, it is said to be as fruitless as that for which long was intended. (56)
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "The practitioner should indeed take food that is soft, lukewarm, well-cooked, and light;
he should eat in such a way that there is no increase in the senses."

In the Kulārṇava: "If one whose body is nourished by another's food and drink performs an accumulation of merit, half of the fruit belongs to the giver of the food and half to the doer; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, with every effort, the wise person should avoid the food of others. (58)

O Śaṅkarī, during the time of *puraścaraṇa* for all rites, the tongue is scorched by the food of others, the hands are scorched by accepting gifts, and the mind is scorched by the wives of others; how then, O fair-faced one, can there be success? [Note: "The food of others" refers to food obtained other than through alms; regarding alms—] In alms...
Because it produces its own [result]. || 60 ||
And likewise: "For the twice-born who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, virtuous, born of noble lineage and station, and subsisting on alms—" (61)

In the Vāmakeśvaratantra: "Except for fire, no object whatsoever should be accepted from others when it is possible; but if it is impossible, one may accept it from a person purified outside a sacred site (tīrtha), provided it is on a day other than a festival. From such [a person], one should perform recitation (japa).

In that case, one who is incapable [of the full practice] should daily seek pure food and so forth, taking only as much as is required for a single day's meal. If, out of attachment, he takes more than this, no success will arise for him even in hundreds of kalpas.

When a sound is uttered once, one should recite the *praṇava*; when a sound is proclaimed by another, one should perform *prāṇāyāma* once. If one speaks much in chatter, one should sip water (*ācamana*), perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs, and then recite the mantra. The same applies when one sneezes, as well as when touching places that should not be touched.
And even regarding touching [impure things], one who performs the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should observe such rules as these.
O Dear One, whatever recitation, worship, or other rites one performs while possessed by the urge to void urine or feces and so forth, all of it becomes impure.

The deity, abiding in the state of secrecy, quickly consumes that person who performs recitation while possessed of dirty clothes, hair, and so forth, or afflicted by foul odors from the mouth; as well as one who suffers from laziness,
yawning, sleep, sneezing, spitting, fear, touching the lower parts of the body, or anger.

One should avoid [these] at the time of recitation. (67) Thus, according to the prescribed method, without delay or haste, one should perform the recitation for the stated number of times for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*. (68)

Contemplating with his intellect the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the mantra, he should recite it with a one-pointed mind from the morning until midday. Whatever number of recitations was commenced, that many must be performed day and night; if he should perform fewer or more, he falls from his vow.
such a man shall become. || 70 ||
In the Gautamīya: One should not look upon an outcast, a Vratya, a slanderer, or one who reviles the gods;
likewise a Brahmin who does not belong to an āśrama, as well as one who reviles the universe. (71)

In the *Muṇḍamālā*: "One should recite daily the same number with which the practice was begun; one should never make it less or more until its completion, and should always perform the recitation. In the Kali age, the recitation should be four times the stated number. (72)
Elsewhere also it is said: "The recitation prescribed for the Kṛta age is doubled in the Tretā;
it is declared to be tripled in the Dvāpara, and quadrupled in the Kali age. (73)
Also in the Kulārṇava: "Deficient or excessive rites never bear fruit;
indeed, those rites alone bear fruit which are performed according to the rules. Sleeping on the ground, celibacy, silence, service to the teacher, and the daily three-fold ablution..."
Bathing, avoidance of trivial activities, daily worship, constant charity,

chanting the praises of the deity, occasional rites of adoration, faith in the guru and the deity, and devotion to the recitation of mantras— these twelve dharmas bestow the accomplishment of mantra. (75)
One should avoid speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts (patitas), those who have fallen from their caste through neglect of sacraments (vrātyas), atheists, and those who are impure;

likewise, one should avoid speaking untruths and yawning. Even when speaking the truth, one should not do so during the performance of recitation (japa), fire-oblations (homa), worship (arcana), and other such rites; otherwise, everything performed becomes indeed ineffective.

It is useless. || 76 || But if a death-impurity (mṛtasūtaka) should occur during the time of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), even then one who has made the formal resolve must not abandon the vow at all. || 77 ||
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Always wearing clean garments, one should daily wash the bed that has been spread with *kuśa* grass; alone and fearless, one should sleep upon it. (78)

One should avoid speaking untruths and abandon all forms of deceitful speech; one should also refrain from listening to singing and instrumental music, and from watching dances. One should likewise avoid oil massages, the application of perfumes and ointments, and the wearing of flowers.

One should abandon bathing with hot water and the worship of other deities. In that very place, one should recite the mantra neither dressed in only a single garment nor while overwhelmed by many garments.

In the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā: "A person performing the *puraścaraṇa* should never, even out of delusion, cause a reversal [of the order]; whether the cloth is above, below, or outside, there shall be no lack of rule whatsoever regarding the application (*viniyoga*) of the procedure. (82)
Upon seeing, speaking to, or hearing the mention of those who have fallen from their caste or the lowest castes,
or upon sneezing, passing wind, or yawning, one should cease the recitation. Having likewise sipped water (ācamana) when these occur,
and having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with its six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga), one should properly resume the remainder of the recitation.
Or rather, [the term "etcetera"] refers to the sight of the sun and so forth, as well as the beginning of the day and a Brāhmaṇa. || 84 ||

In that regard: withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra, freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of *japa*.
One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one with disheveled hair, or one surrounded by a crowd [is disqualified].

One whose hands are not purified, who is impure, or who is talking, should never perform japa. Nor should one do so while not seated, or while lying down, walking, or eating; nor with uncovered hands, or even if covered, with the head wrapped;
nor while the mind is distracted by anxiety, agitated, or bewildered.

One who is afflicted by hunger should not recite [mantras] on a street, in an inauspicious place, or in a place shrouded in darkness. Nor should one recite while one's feet are covered by shoes, or while seated on a vehicle or a bed. One should not recite with the feet stretched out, nor while sitting in the utkaṭāsana posture. One should not recite while standing on sacrificial wood, on a stone, or on the bare ground.

While seated on his seat, having seen a cat, a cock, a crane, a dog, a Śūdra, a monkey, or a donkey, he should sip water (ācamana) and recite the remainder [of the mantra]; having touched them, bathing is prescribed.
This rule applies everywhere regarding the recitation of mantras; however, for mental recitation, there is no such restriction at all.

And so it is said: "Whether impure or pure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping, the wise person who has the mantra as his sole refuge should always practice with the mind alone. There is no fault in mental recitation (*jāpya*) at any place and at any time. This applies to the recitation of the *Śyāmā* and other such vidyās.
The specific details regarding that matter are to be observed in the relevant section. || 88 ||
Now, the fruit of recitation (*japa*):
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "The best of the twice-born who is devoted to recitation obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
he becomes one who yields great fruit for all sacrifices indeed, through recitation. (89) By recitation...

The deity, being constantly praised, becomes pleased; being pleased, she bestows abundant desires and eternal liberation. Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, grahas, and terrifying serpents, overcome with fear, do not approach one who recites [this].
On all sides. || 91 ||

From the *Padma* and *Nārada* [Purāṇas]: "Whatever ritual sacrifices there may be, as well as the rites of consecration and ascetic penances—all these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*). This greatness of the vocal sacrifice of recitation has thus been proclaimed."
Therefore, the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundred times more effective than that, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is said to be a thousand times more effective.

Mental recitation is prescribed for those whose desires have been fulfilled, while the whispered recitation is for those desiring nourishment; vocal recitation is declared to be the most excellent for the purpose of subduing.
According to the Gautamīya: "One should bathe three times a day according to one's ability; if unable, twice or even once.
One should recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day, and the worship shall be equal [in frequency].
Because it is an ancillary part of the worship at the three junctions, the meaning is that the recitation should be one hundred and eight times. (95)

Either worship may take place once, and one should perform the recitation (japa) even without that worship; or worship may take place at the end of the recitation, or one should recite the mantra at the end of the worship. Beginning at the time of dawn, one should recite until midday. (The phrase "until midday" is not intended as a restrictive rule.)

However, this refers to the delimitation of an extended period of time; otherwise, if there were a rule for recitation at that specific moment, then due to the tongue's occasional dullness or alertness, there would be a violation of the rule if the fixed number of recitations were either incomplete or exceeded. (97) [The mind]...
Having withdrawn the senses and having focused the mind on the meaning of the mantra, one should recite it neither too quickly nor too slowly,
like a string of pearls.
Now, the definition of *japa*:

*Japa* is the repetition of syllables, performed mentally, in a whisper, or aloud. That which one utters by means of the intellect, aiming at the meaning, as a sequence of syllables consisting of phonemes, accents, and words, is *japa*.

That is known as mental recitation (mānasa-japa). One who has fixed his mind on the deity should move the tongue and lips slightly; that which is somewhat audible to the ear is known as whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa). || 99-100 ||

In the Viśuddheśvara Tantra: "That recitation which is beyond the range of one's own ears is known as mental (mānasa); that which is within the range of one's own ears is proclaimed as whispered (upāṃśu). (1)
One should recite the mantra with speech; that is known as vocal recitation (*vācika-japa*).
Whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is ten times more distinguished than loud recitation (*uccair-japa*).
The whispered recitation with the tongue is said to be a hundredfold [more effective], while the mental recitation is a thousandfold. || 3 ||

In another Tantra: "O Goddess, whispered recitation (uccair-japa) is declared the lowest; the low-voiced (upāṃśu) is remembered as the middling; and the mental (mānasa) is the highest—thus recitation is said to be threefold. Recitation with the tongue (jihvā-japa) is to be understood by the wise as that performed solely with the tongue. One that is too short is a cause of disease, and one that is too long..."
This is the destruction of wealth. One should recite [the mantra] joined with the syllables and the imperishable [seed-syllable], like a string of pearls. || 5 ||
Whatever hymn one may recollect with the mind, or whatever mantra one may recollect with speech—
both become fruitless, like water poured into a broken vessel.

In the *Gautamīya*: "The mantras, existing in the state of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*), are said to be merely phonemes; when uttered as the resonance of the *suṣumṇā*, they attain sovereignty. (7)
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being woven into the power of consciousness (cit-śakti),
which resides within that very supreme void (paramavyoman) expanded by supreme bliss (paramānanda); [thus] it reveals the true nature of the Self even without worship, fire-offerings, and the like.

In the *Daśākṣarapaṭala* of the *Gautamīya*: "Having meditated again and again upon the root mantra at the base of the *suṣumnā* with the awareness of the vital breath, one should contemplate its meaning, its consciousness, and its life-force. (9)

Also in the Kulārṇava: "If the mind is in one place, Śiva in another, and Śakti in another, while the vital breath (māruta) is elsewhere, O beautiful lady, one does not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (10)

Birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs at the beginning, and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) at the end. A mantra that is joined by these two types of impurity does not attain success. Having removed those [impurities] from the mantra, one should recite it with the intellect as much as possible; freed from the two types of impurity, that mantra bestows all perfections (*siddhi*).

In that very same [text]: "Therefore, O Goddess! having encircled the mantra with the *dhruva* [syllable] with effort, one should recite it one hundred and eight times, or even seven times, from the beginning of the recitation. At the end of the recitation, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*), one should place the seed-syllable of Brahman at both the beginning and the end of the mantra."
O Supreme Goddess, one should recite the mantra seven times for the sake of liberation from the two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka).

He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*, will find no accomplishment even by reciting it a hundred million times. O Dear One, those mantras whose seed-syllables (*bīja*) have been lost will not yield fruit; however, mantras endowed with consciousness bring about all accomplishments.
[These] are remembered [as such]. || 15 || Mantras devoid of the Caitanya (consciousness) are said to be mere phonemes;
they do not yield fruit at all, even through hundreds, tens of millions, or hundreds of millions of recitations.

|| 16 || Whatever the original nature of a mantra may be when its utterance is performed, that same nature remains whether it is recited a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times, or ten million times.
That is not its fruit. || 17 || There shall be the breaking of the knot in the heart and the expansion of all the limbs;

tears of bliss, horripilation, and possession of the body arise, O Kuleśvarī, as well as stammering speech suddenly—of this there is no doubt. Even when the mantra is uttered but once, such [results] occur. || 18 ||
Where conditions (pratyayas) are observed joined with the Caitanya [consciousness], that is called mutual interaction (pārasparya).
One should recite the mantra for exactly one month, combined with the Bhūtalipi and so forth; by reciting it a thousand times in both direct and reverse order, that mantra becomes perfected (siddha).

Therein, the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) consists of the five short vowels, the conjunct letters (*sandhivarṇa*), and the letters of space, air, fire, and water; these follow the sequence of the last, the first, the second, the fourth, and the middle [of each group], being the syllables of the five classes (*pañcavarga*). (21)

With the addition of the *tasa* (the three *ta*s), *dhā*, *sta*, and the white moon (*śvetendu*), this *bhūtalipi* consists of forty-two syllables. Having first performed the recitation (*japa*) in this manner, [one perceives] the form of radiant energy (*tejorūpa*).
One should offer [it] into the right hand of the deity with kusha grass, flowers, and arghya water. || 22 ||
Having thus contemplated that as fruitful, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform three [prostrations] at the beginning of the recitation and three at the end. Regarding the capacity [of the practitioner], this is done with the left hand of the Goddess.
And thus: having first performed the recitation in this manner, [one should worship] with perfumes, unbroken rice, and water mixed with *kṛśara*.
The wise practitioner should offer the recitation (japa) into the left hand of the Goddess.

At the end of the daily recitation, O Goddess, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of a tenth part of that number. O Sage, one should likewise perform libations (tarpaṇa) and ritual ablutions (abhiṣeka), each being a tenth part of the respective [homa], and one should feed Brahmins every day.
To pacify any deficiency or excess; or else, when everything is complete, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites. || 26 ||

In the *Muṇḍamālā*: "Whatever number of recitations (japa) has been prescribed for whom, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) daily at the end of that recitation, consisting of one-tenth of that amount, using the respective substances. Alternatively, when the count reaches one hundred thousand, one should perform the homa. (27)

Likewise, regarding the inability to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites, the *Sanatkumāra-tantra* states: "Whatever limb [of the ritual] should fail, the recitation (*japa*) must be performed twice that number. In the absence of the fire-oblation, the recitation should be four times the number of oblations. (28) [This applies] to Brahmins and Kṣatriyas...

It is recorded that the quality is measured by the number of tastes; for Vaiśyas, it is the number of the Vasus (eight), and this is the rule for their women. Whatever caste a Śūdra has taken as his refuge, he should follow the rule for that [caste]; for a Śūdra who has no such refuge, the number of directions (ten) is prescribed.
For a Śūdra who is devoted to a Brāhmaṇa, his recitation (japa) is equal to that of the Brāhmaṇa's wife. || 31 ||

In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "For Brahmins who are unable to perform the rite of fire-offering (*homakarman*), the recitation (*japa*) is double. For all other castes, however, triple and so forth is prescribed. 'Triple' means that for a Kṣatriya, the recitation must be performed at three times the number of fire-offerings."
By a Vaiśya it is fourfold; by a Śūdra it is fivefold. || 32 ||

As it is stated in the *Kulaprakāśa*: "If any limb [of the ritual] should be deficient, the twice-born should perform a recitation (*japa*) double that number; [specifically], three, four, or five times, according to their respective order. By this [same rule], [the requirement applies] to women and Śūdras."

The section on the entitlement to perform *homa* (33). Likewise, in the section on sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa-prakaraṇa*) in the *Śāradā-tantra*, it is stated that for Śūdras a triangular pit is prescribed, and there is also the entitlement of women to perform *homa*.
In that very same [text]: "A maiden performs *homa* with parched grains (*lāja*) mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhura*). By this...

By following the prescribed rite, a maiden obtains her desired husband; for this very reason, women have the right to perform the fire-oblation (homa), and that [rite] is to be performed through the agency of a Brāhmaṇa.
And likewise in another Tantra:

"From the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*, from performing fire-sacrifices (*homa*), from worshipping the Śālagrāma stone, and from sexual union with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla. Thus it is said.
Because there is an explicit prohibition.
Likewise: because it is established everywhere that women are equal to Śūdras in all Vedic rites;
for there is a saying of the Blessed One: "The touch of the hand of a woman or a Śūdra is like a thunderbolt falling upon me. (35)

In the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya* as well, it is stated: "They do not desire the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, the Yajus, or Lakṣmī for women and Śūdras; he who desires them goes downward after death. This passage, ending with the words "they do not desire," is also cited by Govindabhaṭṭa in his commentary on Parāśara.

If a twice-born man gives a mantra joined with *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra, the Śūdra attains hell and the Brāhmaṇa goes to a downward state. (From the Yajurveda. *Lakṣmī* means the seed-syllable of *Śrī*. || 36 ||

Likewise, in the *Nārāyaṇakalpa* it is said: "The great mantra of eight syllables [is for all], while the seven-syllabled one is for Śūdras and women. Furthermore, any mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) is not recommended for women or Śūdras. Thus, everywhere the treatment of women is the same as that of Śūdras; and this applies to the Śūdra as well.
Some say that the homa is performed by oneself as the agent. || 37 ||

And so it is stated in the Vārāhītantra: "If one here is desirous [of worldly results], even a Śūdra, during the core ritual of the fire-oblation (homa), should abandon the wife of Fire (the *svāhā* suffix) and perform the oblation with the ending of the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (38)
For all [of these], there is a twofold recitation.

And so it is stated in the Vasiṣṭha-smṛti: "If any limb [of the rite] is omitted, a double recitation (japa) must be performed out of devotion by one who is unable [to complete it], for the sake of perfecting that limb. If no limb is omitted, one shall obtain the specific result [of that limb] merely by feeding a Brāhmaṇa."
Whatever the twice-born eats, whether it be defective or complete, that very thing is certainly eaten by Hari himself in person. (40)

Likewise, in the Agastyasaṃhitā: "O Noble One, if one is unable even to perform the fire-oblation (homa), or the worship (pūjā), or the libation (tarpaṇa), then the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) shall be accomplished by means of these two limbs alone— namely, by recitation (japa) performed that same number of times and by the propitiation of Brahmins."
Indeed. || 41 ||
In the *Vīrātantra*: "The observance (*niyama*) is to be understood as applying to the male practitioner, and never in any way to women.
For women here, there is no ritual placement (*nyāsa*), nor meditation (*dhyāna*), nor worship (*pūjana*).
By mere recitation (*japa*) alone, the mantras are accomplished for women—this is the opinion of the Teacher (*ācārya*)."
There is also a secondary rule regarding the feeding of Brahmins.

And so it is said in the Muṇḍamālā: "O beautiful one, if one is unable to perform worship and the like due to a lack of material resources, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is prescribed by means of recitation alone. In this case, the feeding of Brahmins is indeed mandatory.
In this manner, one should feed the twice-born for the sake of accomplishing one's resolve;
by the mere propitiation of the Brahmins, that which is deficient shall certainly become complete. (43)

In the Kulārṇava: "O Supreme Goddess, he who feeds uninitiated paśus in his own home goes to twenty-one hells. O Beloved Goddess, he who performs the purificatory rite (puraścaraṇa) in this manner shall be liberated from all sins and attain union with the Goddess."
Likewise: one should then feed Brahmins who follow the Kaula tradition with a tenth part of that [number], preceded by great honor and with foods such as milk and sugar-candy. 46.
And then: One should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Guru with food, clothing, and so forth.

By the mere satisfaction of the Guru, the accomplishment of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) will certainly occur. In the absence of the Guru, one should offer it to his son or to his wife. In the absence of those two, O Goddess of Gods—

One should offer [the remains] to the Brahmins. O Kuleśvarī, for one who has correctly mastered a single mantra through the worship of its five limbs, all mantras become perfected by his grace. Those who know the Tantras say that everything has the Guru as its root.

Remaining always in a single village, he should go and pay homage to his guru; for the guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, therefore he should worship him first. At the conclusion of that, the best of practitioners should perform a great worship with ornaments for the married woman and the maiden.
One should adorn [the deity]; sweet food should be prepared in abundance, and one should eat together with one's kinsmen.
Thus, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected shall accomplish all desired objects. (49)
In another school of thought, the procedure for *puraścaraṇa* is stated in the *Tantra*: "Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
during an eclipse of the sun or the moon, being pure and having fasted on the preceding day, [one should perform it] at a river..."
Standing in water reaching up to the navel at a river flowing to the ocean, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind from the time of touch until liberation is attained. (50)

If the river is defiled by crocodiles and the like, then that which must be done is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "Even after bathing in pure water, being composed in a clean place, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind from the beginning of the meal until its conclusion. Having done this, [one is purified].
One who has doubt shall become a partaker of the fruit of recitation. || 51 ||

In the absence of a river: "Alternatively, having bathed in sacred water, being pure and having previously fasted, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind from the moment of the eclipse until its release. (52)

But for one unable to observe the fast, it is said in that very same text: "Alternatively, there is another method according to the Pauraścaraṇika rite: having bathed during an eclipse of the moon or sun with a restrained mind, one should recite the mantra from the moment of contact until the end of the release."

Being composed in meditation, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) at one-tenth the number of recitations (*japa*); likewise, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed at one-tenth the number of oblations.
One should perform the ritual ablution (*abhiṣeka*) at one-tenth the number of libations;
and with one-tenth the number of ablutions, one should provide a meal for Brahmins. Having done this, indeed—
The supreme accomplishment of the mantra arises. || 53 ||
In the case of the Gopāla mantra, however, the number of libations (tarpaṇa) is equal to the number of fire-oblations (homa).

For example: "In this [practice], the libations for the Gopāla mantras are according to the number of oblations," and so forth. Having bathed and made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should perform the recitation (japa) until its conclusion with liberation (vimokṣa).
A pure man should perform sacrifices and other rites until the end of the eclipse;

by reciting [the mantra] in this manner, the perfection of the mantra will surely come to pass—of this there is no doubt. [This concerns] the necessity of recitation during an eclipse. If, due to the requirements of a *śrāddha* or other such rites, one [cannot recite],...
"A man should abandon [the rite]; he becomes an offender against the deity and leads seven generations of ancestors to the nether regions.

This is because of the statement of Sanatkumāra. In reality, however, this refers to the subject of a *puraścaraṇa* that has already been commenced. For it is said: "If an eclipse should occur while the *puraścaraṇa* has been commenced, then..."
"One should never abandon the recitation of mantras (*japa*) on account of a *śrāddha* or similar obligations," because of this [scriptural] consistency:
"A *śrāddha* must indeed be performed even at the cost of one's entire property during a lunar eclipse (*rāhudarśana*); for one who does not perform that *śrāddha* sinks like a cow in the mud."
"And because it is contradicted by contrary statements"—this is an additional reading found in the *Āgama-tattva-vilāsa*.
In this same manner, it should be understood that even during the night, specific rules for *puraścaraṇa* apply. Thus, everything is entirely consistent. || 56 ||
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the *Kalpa*, one should perform the mantra-rituals such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth;
or else, one should perform the oblations and other rites with a tenth part of that [number]. (57)
Likewise: immediately thereafter, one should perform the rites beginning with *dhī* (the *dhī-homa*) in sequence, using a tenth part [of the total].

At the conclusion of that, one should perform a great worship and the gratification of Brahmins. Then, for the sake of the mantra’s accomplishment (*siddhi*), one should fully honor and satisfy the Guru. In this way, the accomplishment of the mantra occurs.
And the deity may become pleased. || 58 ||
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "O Supreme Goddess, he who feeds uninitiated souls (*paśus*) in his own home goes to twenty-one hells. (59)
Although the term *puraścaraṇa* refers to the five-limbed [rite], as it is said:

"Recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), ritual bathing (*abhiṣeka*), and feeding Brahmins—this five-limbed worship is called *puraścaraṇa* in the world"; nevertheless, the term *puraścaraṇa* [is used] at times such as an eclipse.

The term "secondary" (gauṇa) refers solely to the act of recitation (japa). This is because it is observed in such passages as: "O Maheśānī, that which is recited beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise is desired as the *puraścaraṇa*. [Objection: Since there is an absence of fire-oblations (*homa*) and other rites therein, how then [can it be so]?

If it is argued that the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) for an eclipse consists of *homa* (fire-oblation) and so forth, this arises from the scriptural injunction itself. Nor should it be said that because the *puraścaraṇa* has five constituent parts (*pañcāṅga*), those very same rites must apply in every case;
for if that were so, the specific prescription for the eclipse would be rendered purposeless. Rather, in the case of an eclipse—

Due to the restrictive rules regarding the *homa* and other rites, there is no *homa* and so forth elsewhere. However, the prescription of *homa* and other rites for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) performed at home is intended to indicate its equivalence to the standard five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*) *puraścaraṇa*. For this very reason:

It has been established by the authors of the Prakaṣas that when the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consisting of the five-fold nature is performed during the time of the eclipse, one possesses the qualification for the primary ritual application; however, it is universally agreed that if this is not performed, and only the preliminary rite consisting of mere recitation (japa) is done, there is no such qualification. || 61 ||

Regarding the time for *puraścaraṇa*, the Vārāhī Tantra states: "One should commence the *puraścaryā* when the moon and stars are favorable, during the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day; however, one should not perform it while Hari is asleep. (62)
Regarding the counter-exception, however, it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:

"Initiation and *puraścaryā* are recommended in the months of Kārttika, Āśvina, Vaiśākha, Māgha, Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, and Śrāvaṇa; and during an eclipse or at a great sacred site (*mahātīrtha*), one need not observe the [specific] time. (63)

Regarding the prohibition of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) when [the sun] is eclipsed or has just risen, another Tantra states: "O Dear One, one should certainly not perform initiation or recitation (*japa*) when [the sun] is eclipsed or has just risen; if it is done, there will be a swift destruction of longevity, fortune, progeny, and prosperity. (64) In that regard:

Having first taken possession of the ground, and on the third day prior to the preliminary rites, having performed the shaving of the head and other such acts, one should designate a square area of one or two *krośas* in each of the four directions around the altar as a field for food and other necessities for the sake of the retreat (*vihāra*), and therein—
Having constructed a pavilion in accordance with the *kūrmacakra*, one should observe the practice of eating only once a day (*ekabhakta*).
Then, on the following day, having performed the ritual bath and other duties and being purified,
[one should place] branches of either the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, or *plakṣa* tree in the four directions of the altar.

Having consecrated ten stakes, each measuring one *vitasti* in length, one hundred and eight times with the mantra "Oṃ, to the Sudarśana weapon, Phaṭ," he should plant them in the ten directions of the altar [with the words]: "Oṃ, those who are here causing obstacles on earth,
in heaven, or in the intermediate space, and whoever else has become an obstacle..."

"May they all depart far away, abandoning this field of mine which is secured by my mantra; may there be success for me without obstacle. Having buried [the stakes] with this [mantra], one should worship the weapon-mantra upon them with "Oṃ, to the Sudarśana weapon, Phaṭ! and then [proceed] upon them.
One should worship the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, in the order starting from the east.

For example: having invoked [Indra] with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O world-protector Indra, come here!", one should worship him with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). In this same manner, one should worship the others as well. || 65 ||

And likewise, in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "Having gone to a sacred field or similar place, one should perform the consecration of the ground; for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of such-and-such a mantra, I take possession of this ground for this mantra."
"May it be accomplished!
And likewise: "In a village, a place measuring one *krośa* is considered suitable according to one's own desire;
in a city or similar location, [one should choose] a *krośa*, two *krośas*, or even a *kṣetra*."

One should prepare as much space as desired for the monastery; one should occupy as much ground as is required for the purpose of the monastery, including food and other necessities. One should drive stakes made from milky trees, consecrated with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), into the ten directions, and [recite] the weapon-mantra over them.
One should worship them; furthermore, the wise man should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) among them with perfumes and other offerings.
66. Then, having worshipped the Kṣetrapāla and the Vāstveśa in the central space, one should worship Gaṇapati for the sake of destroying all obstacles.
As follows: Oṃ, today, etc., [I], belonging to the [amuka] gotra and named [amuka] Devaśarmā...

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the purpose of destroying all obstacles in the rite of the preliminary service (puraścaraṇa) of such-and-such a mantra for such-and-such a deity to be performed by me, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇeśa," one should worship Gaṇeśa in the center of the altar with the five articles of offering (pañcopacāra). || 67 ||
As it has been said: "Then one should worship the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) and others there according to the rules;

one should duly honor the Lord of the Field (kṣetreśa), known by the name Vāstu, and Vighnarāja. One should offer an oblation (bali) to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), and then enter the field. Thereafter, [one should subsist] on food restricted to a month and so forth."
One should offer the *bali* to the deities who have been worshipped.
Then: *Oṃ*, those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce abodes;
the Mothers of terrible form, and those who are lords of the hosts (*gaṇādhipatayaḥ*), and those who are obstructors (*vighnabhūtāḥ*).
"And others who dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions— may they all, with joyful minds,
accept this offering. With these words, one should offer the *bali* to the beings in the ten directions,
and then recite the *Gāyatrī*.
And likewise, the teacher Vidyādhara states: "Having bathed in the morning, one who is self-restrained should recite the Gāyatrī a thousand times;
this is first for the sake of destroying both known and unknown sin."
One should satisfy the Brahmins with wealth, food,
clothing, and seats; having honored one's own guru with many garments and ornaments, one should thereafter commence the recitation (japa) preceded by his permission.
Furthermore, regarding the *gāyatrī* of each respective deity, as stated in the *Govindavṛndāvana*:
"Before chanting [the mantra], one should chant the *Kṛṣṇa-gāyatrī*, which destroys all sins,
ten thousand times (*ayuta*) for the purpose of diminishing transgressions."

Because it is established by the *Kṛṣṇāgāyatrī-svara*, the same applies elsewhere as well; for this very reason, Mādhavācārya states that it is common to both women and *śūdras*. As for the statement, "Having bathed in the morning, one who is self-restrained should recite the Sāvitrī ten thousand times," that refers instead to cases where there is a suspicion of extremely grave sin. [The formula begins: *Oṃ adya...* and so forth.

"I, [Name], of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious [Name] Devaśarman, desiring the destruction of known and unknown sins, shall perform the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra one thousand and eight times. Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), he should recite it, or alternatively, perform ten thousand recitations (*ayuta*). Then, he should observe a fast or eat light food. On the following day at dawn:
Having performed the ritual bathing and other preliminary rites, one should make the formal declaration (saṅkalpa) preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions (svastivācana). || 68 ||

Oṃ. From today [and so forth], I, of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious Amukadevaśarman, desiring the accomplishment of the mantra of such-and-such deity preceded by the destruction of all evil obstacles that hinder the attainment of that mantra’s siddhi, shall practice from this day until the time when it is accomplished.
For that duration, [perform] so many recitations of such-and-such a mantra, a tenth-part homa of that, a tenth-part tarpaṇa of that,
a tenth-part abhiṣeka of that, and a tenth-part feeding of Brahmins.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) thus: "I shall perform the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for the form," and having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth, one should bind the respective mudrās and worship the deity according to the sequence prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*paddhati*), [offering] into the lamp.

Having placed the deity of blazing form within one's heart, one should perform the recitation (japa) starting from the morning until midday; thereafter comes the fire-oblation (homa), and then the libation (tarpaṇa). || 69 ||
In the Kulārṇava:

"Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with water from sacred fords mixed with camphor; having invoked the Deity into the water, one should worship Him according to the rules with devotion, using water-based offerings such as the foot-water (pādya) and others."

Accompanied by his retinue, one should satisfy each member of the retinue with a single handful of water. Then, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity with a tenth part of the number used for the *homa*. When the count is complete, once again offer a single handful of water to each. As for the formula for the libation (*tarpaṇa*):
This is to be stated in the section on bathing. || 70 ||
Now, the words for the consecration:
having recited the root mantra ending with "namaḥ," one should consecrate oneself on the crown of the head with the vase-mudrā, saying, "I consecrate myself as the deity [Name]."
And likewise in the Gautamiya: "Having uttered the root mantra ending with 'namaḥ', followed at its end by the name of the deity in the accusative case, one should then say, 'I consecrate [you]';
and with this, one should sprinkle one's own head with water using the mudrā known as the 'water-pot' (kumbha). (71)
Regarding the ritual for a *śakti*, the *Nīlatantra* states: "At the end of the root mantra, having uttered the name, one says 'I sprinkle,' followed by 'namaḥ' and 'pādam.
Then, having fed the Brahmins, one should offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), beginning with: 'Oṃ, today... etc.
For the sake of completing the ancillary rites of the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the mantra of such-and-such a deity,
I offer this gold, whose presiding deity is Agni, as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you, the preceptor of such-and-such a lineage. I bestow it upon you.
Then, one should perform the determination of being free from defects.
Now, the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) during an eclipse:

it is as follows: *Oṃ*, on this day, etc., while the sun or the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu, I, [Name] of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), the illustrious [Name] Devaśarman, [for the sake of] such-and-such deity...

"Desiring the accomplishment of such-and-such a mantra, I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa* consisting of the recitation of the mantra of such-and-such a deity for such-and-such a number of times, beginning from the first morsel of food until its cessation. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should perform the recitation. Then, having performed the ritual bath on that day or the following day, [one should recite] *oṃ*.

"Today," and so forth: [this refers to] the taking up of such-and-such [substance] for such-and-such mantra; at this time, the recitation (*japa*) of such-and-such a deity’s such-and-such mantra for a certain number of times, followed by its one-tenth part (*daśāṃśa*) as a fire-oblation (*homa*), its one-tenth part as a libation (*tarpaṇa*), its one-tenth part as a consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and its one-tenth part—

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall perform the rites for feeding the Brāhmaṇas," and having performed the rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth, one should offer the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and other items as before;
this is the procedure for the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa). || 73 ||
Now, the Tortoise Diagram (*kūrmacakra*) (see Figure 7):
"An action performed by relying upon the location of the lamp (*dīpasthāna*) yields its fruit.
That place where a person shines is called the 'location of the lamp'. [74] [One should divide] the ground into a square...

Having divided [the space] into nine squares, one should write the seven groups [of consonants] in sequence, beginning from the eastern square. In the central square, which is presided over by Lakṣmī, one should write the vowels in pairs; then, starting from the east, one should place the vowels in the directions where the first letter of the [relevant] field is situated.

One should know that its mouth is where the arrangement of the syllables of the field (kṣetra) and so forth is situated, with those two [parts] standing on either side. One should know that its mouth is where those two stand on either side. Both feet are said to be in the two cavities (koṣṭha) and the belly (kukṣi), and what remains is declared to be the tail.

By this sequence, one should divide even that which is situated in the middle into parts: that which is situated in the mouth attains success; that which is in the hand has a short life; that which is in the belly is indifferent; and that which is at the feet shall experience suffering. That which is situated in the tail causes the practitioner of the mantra to be afflicted.
Through [the rites of] binding, eradication, and so forth, this Kūrma-cakra is proclaimed as that which bestows success upon practitioners of mantra. (77)
In the Piṅgalāyāma: "He who performs the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) without knowing the Kūrma-cakra obtains no fruit from that sacrifice; it leads only to all manner of misfortune.
Now, the ten purifications of mantras:

In the *Gautamīya*: "Birth, life, subsequent beating, awakening, then consecration (*abhiṣeka*), purification (*vimalīkaraṇa*), nourishment (*āpyāyana*), satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*), illumination (*dīpana*), and concealment (*gupti*); these ten are the purificatory rites (*saṃskriyā*) of mantra. Having inscribed [these] in a vessel made of gold or other materials.
The Mātṛkā-yantra is supreme. O virtuous lady, it may be drawn with saffron, sandalwood paste, or even with ashes.
Saffron is prescribed for the purification of Śakti, sandalwood for Vaiṣṇava rites, and ashes are declared for Śaiva rites when drawing the Mātṛkā-yantra.

Now, the Mātṛkā Yantra (see Figures 8 and 9): its pericarp consists of the syllables of space, moon, and earth; its filaments flash with pairs of vowels; it shines with the [consonant] groups as its eight petals; and it is encircled by the abode of the earth.
In the three directions beginning with the East, it is surrounded by a flood of earth (Kṣauṇipūra) joined with the letters ending in *la* and *laṅgali*;

this is declared to be the supreme Yantra of the Formed Body (*Varṇatanu*), which bestows good fortune and prosperity. One should write *vaṃ* in the cardinal directions of the Yantra and *ṭhaṃ* in the intermediate directions. || 81 ||

And likewise in the *Gautamiya*: "One should place the groups of consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* in the directions starting from the east; those beginning with *ya* and ending with *va*, and those beginning with *śa* and ending with *ha*, one should duly place upon the *lakṣmī* [seat] in the northeast. [One should draw] a square with four doors, with the syllable *vaṃ* in the cardinal directions and *ṭhaṃ* in the intermediate directions. Thus it is said.
The Mātṛkā Yantra. || 82 ||
Now, the ten purifications of mantras:
the extraction of mantras from the *mātṛkā* diagram is known as "birth" (*janana*);
this has been determined by the sages according to the rules of the sequential arrangement of lines.

The wise one should recite the syllables of the mantra, interspersed with the *prāṇa* (the breath), one hundred times for each; that is declared to be "life" (*jīvana*). Alternatively, the recitation may consist of ten counts. || 83 ||

In the *Viśvasāra*: "The wise one should mutter the letters of the mantra either separately a hundred times or ten times. Having written down the letters of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water; the striking is performed for each [letter] individually with the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Yam), as before.
It is held that there shall be a flogging of a hundred strokes. || 84 ||
And so it is said in another Tantra:
"One should strike all the phonemes with sandalwood water; then one should awaken the mantra either a hundred times or ten times. (85)
In the *Viśvasāra*: "O Goddess of the gods, listen to the tenfold method proclaimed for striking (*tāḍana*).

Having written the letters of the mantra with oleander (*karavīra*) flowers, one should strike them with as many [flowers] as there are letters in that mantra; awakening is performed with the letter *ra*. (86)

In another tantra: Having drawn [the maṇḍala] with flowers equal in number to the syllables of the mantra— specifically red *hayāri* (lotuses)— and having consecrated each syllable of the mantra once with fire,
the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is proclaimed according to the procedure stated for that particular mantra, using *aśvattha* sprouts.

The practitioner of mantra should sprinkle [water] a number of times equal to the syllables of the mantra. Having mentally contemplated the mantra at the root and center of the *suṣumṇā*, the ascetic should duly burn away the three impurities with the light-mantra (*jyotirmantra*), beginning with the *tāra*.

The *jyotirmanu* is considered to consist of the sky, fire, mind, and the staff. *Tāra* is the *praṇava*. The sky is the letter *ha*; fire is *ra*; mind is *u*; and the staff is the *anusvāra*. Thus, [the mantra is] *oṃ hrauṃ*.
With that mantra, [one should perform the rite] using gold, *kuśa*-water, or water with flowers.
The ritual procedure for satiation according to the rules is thus remembered. Satiation with water accompanied by a mantra is considered to be "mantra-satiation. || 90-91 ||

For the Śakti-mantra, libation with honey is prescribed; for the Vaiṣṇava, with water mixed with moon-juice (soma); for the Śaiva, with ghee and milk—this is declared as the proper method of satiation (tarpaṇa). The same applies to the consecration (abhiṣeka) as well.
The conjunction of *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* is called the "illumination" (*dīpana*) of the mantra.

The concealment (*gopana*) of the recited mantra, however, is its non-disclosure. These ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) have been proclaimed in all the Tantras; having performed them according to the tradition, [one attains success].
The minister shall obtain his desire. "The three impurities" refers to the impurity of individuality (āṇavīya), the impurity of illusion (māyika), and the impurity of karma (kārmaṇa).

In the *Prapañcasāra*: "The impurity called *māyika*, namely that which belongs to woman (*yoṣit*), the *pauruṣa* [impurity], and the *kārmaṇa* impurity—these two are declared to be *āṇavika*. These three impurities are forbidden. Thus it is said regarding the conjunction of *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā*.
The meaning is that one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, encased by the seed-syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā*.

And so it is stated in the Viśvasāra: "Encased by the seed-syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā*, the best of practitioners should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and thus kindle [the fire]. (96)
Now, the procedure for the initiation of Kalāvatī:
the disciple, having previously fasted and performed his daily obligatory rites, shall make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) preceded by the recitation of benedictions.

For example: *Oṃ*, beginning with "Today," etc., [he] makes the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I, of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious [Name]-devaśarmā, desiring the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, shall perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into the mantra of such-and-so-many syllables for such-and-such deity; having thus resolved, [he approaches] the Guru."
He should choose [the teacher]. The response is: "Oṃ, may you be seated; Oṃ, I am seated.
"Oṃ, we shall honor you"; the response is: "Oṃ, honor [me].
Then, having honored the guru with perfumes, flowers, garments, ornaments, and so forth, [he should touch] his right knee.
Having held [the vessel], one should recite: "Oṃ, today, etc., the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such lineage,

in the rite of initiation into the mantra of such-and-such deity performed by me, having worshipped the venerable Amukadevaśarman of such-and-such lineage with these [offerings] beginning with fragrance, as my preceptor..."

"I choose you as my guru," [he says]; "Om, I am chosen," is the reply. "Om, perform the duties of a guru as prescribed," [the guru says]; "I shall do so according to my knowledge," is the response. Then the guru, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), should prepare the general offering (sāmānyārghya) at the doorway.
Namely: having drawn a triangular circle upon the earth-element [mandala] on one's own left, and having worshipped it with "Oṃ,
obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," and having washed the arghya vessel with the mantra "Phaṭ," and having placed the conch together with its base therein, [one worships it] with the mantra "Namaḥ."

Having filled [the vessel] with water, one should invoke the sacred waters (tīrtha) from the solar orb by means of the *aṅkuśa* mudrā and the mantra beginning with "oṃ gaṅge ca," etc.; then, having offered perfumes and other substances with the *praṇava* (oṃ), and having displayed the *dhenu* mudrā, one should recite "oṃ" eight or ten times. || 97 ||
And so it is said: "Then one should fashion a mandala consisting of a triangle, a square, a circle, and a lotus.

Having worshipped the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti), one should place the vessel upon it. Having purified the vessel with the Weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should fill it with the Heart-mantra (hṛnmantra). One should then pour in holy water (tīrtha) after invoking it."
"One should offer the fragrance and other items with the *praṇava* and indeed show the *dhenumudrā*;

this is remembered as the general *arghya*. According to this statement from the *Gautamīya*, there is an eightfold recitation of the *praṇava*. Since it is not seen to be so in the case of the special *arghya*, [this applies] to Śyāmā and others.

Because it is seen to be worthy of that [offering] in ten ways, one should then fill the vessel with water and mutter the *praṇava* ten times; thus it is stated in the Bhairavīya. Then, having sprinkled the door while muttering "phaṭ," one should perform the worship of the door.
Namely: at the upper aperture (ūrdhvoḍusvara), *oṃ vighnāya namaḥ*, *oṃ ahālakṣmyai namaḥ*, *oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*. On the right branch, *oṃ vighnāya namaḥ*.
On the left branch, *oṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*. Beside those two, *oṃ*...
Salutation to Gaṅgā. Oṃ, salutation to Yamunā. At the threshold, Oṃ, salutation to Astra. Thus one should worship with flowers and water.
According to the Nibandha: having sprinkled the door with water empowered by the Astra-mantra, one performs the worship of the door.
One should perform the worship: [one should worship] Vighna, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī on the upper part of the door-arch (ūrdhvoḍumbaraka).
Then, on the right branch, Vighna; Kṣetreśa on the other [left branch]; and on both sides of those two, Gaṅgā and Yamunā with flowers and water. On the threshold (dehalī), one should worship Astra.
"Prati dvāram" (at each door) is the sequence. If one is unable, then merely "namaḥ dvāradevatābhyaḥ" (salutation to the deities of the doors) [is sufficient]. || 99 ||

In the *Svatantra-tantra*, regarding the worship of Tripura and other deities, there is this specific instruction: "The yogi should likewise [worship] Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Yoginī, and Vaṭuka; then he should recite the names of Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī. Thus is the distinction. 100.

In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however: Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Bala, Prabala, Bhadranāman, and Subhadra are the Vaiṣṇava Vighnas. One should worship them with their names as mantras, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*. Then...

Preceded by the placement of the right foot, touching the left side [of the entrance] while contracting the right limb, one should enter the interior of the pavilion and worship in the southwest with: "Oṃ, homage to Vāstupuruṣa; Oṃ, homage to Brahmā. Then...
Having dispelled divine obstacles by looking with divine vision while reciting the *deya* mantra,
having dispelled atmospheric obstacles with water while reciting the mantra *astrāya phaṭ*,
and having dispelled terrestrial obstacles by striking the ground three times with the left heel.

Taking the ritual substances over which the mantra *phaṭ* has been recited seven times, he should scatter them [while reciting]: "Oṃ! May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth; may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. Thus he should scatter them. || 2 ||
Roasted grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice grains are designated as *vikira* offerings;
they are the destroyers of all multitudes of obstacles. || 3 ||

Likewise: Immediately thereafter, the lord of teachers should dispel the divine obstacles with glances from the Vidyā-vision, those moving in the intermediate space with water empowered by the Astra-mantra, and those on the ground with three kicks of his heel; thus he should ward off the obstacles. || 4 ||

Then, taking unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the right hand in the *nārāca-mudrā*, one should cast them with the *astra-mantra* for the pacification of obstacles within the house, respectfully reciting the mantra "apasarpantu te" (May they depart). Thus it is stated in the *Śāradīya*. 5.
