In the *Sammohana-tantra*: "One should scatter there arrows that have been consecrated seven times with the *śara* mantra.

Then, having worshipped and assumed the seat with the mantra: *hrīṃ ādhāraśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*, one should recite [the following]: for this seat-mantra, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*) and Sutala is the meter (*chandaḥ*).
The Tortoise is the deity; this is the application for taking possession of the seat. Having recited: "Oṃ! O Earth, by you the worlds are supported;
O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. Do you likewise support me always and make this seat pure," one should sit upon a swastika or similar seat with the *sana* mantra. Having sat down...
One should dispel the obstacles. || 6 ||

In another tantra: "First, having dispelled the obstacles, one should thereafter arrange the seat; or else, the wise practitioner, remaining on the seat, should dispel the obstacles. Then, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the root mantra...
One should purify the pavilion.
Regarding its dimensions, the *Gautamīya* states: "One should purify that house and the pavilion with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (8)

Regarding the proportions for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), it is stated in that same source: "One *pala* of milk is the portion, and cow urine is desired to be of the same measure; clarified butter should be one *pala*, and cow dung two *tolakas*; curd should be the measure of a *prasṛti*. This is remembered as the *pañcagavya*."
Alternatively: equal portions of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed;

having consecrated them with the root mantra, one should purify [the area] with that very [mixture]. By that, there shall be universal purification and the eradication of all sins. Then, on the southern side, the materials for worship [should be placed].

On the left side, one should place a jar filled with pure water for washing the hands, and another vessel behind; having placed ghee lamps in all directions and joining the palms in reverence, one should say "Oṃ, obeisance to the Gurus" on the left. Oṃ.
Salutations to the Supreme Gurus. Oṃ, salutations to the Higher-Lower Gurus. To the south, Oṃ, salutations to Gaṇeśa. In the center, Oṃ, salutations to [Name] Devatā.
And likewise: having joined the palms in reverence, one should worship the three Gurus on the left.

One should meditate upon the Guru, the Paramādi, and likewise the Parāpara-guru, as well as Gaṇeśa on the right and the Lord upon the head. Then, having purified both hands with sandalwood paste and flowers while reciting the mantra "Phaṭ," [one should proceed].
Having raised the hands three *tāla*-lengths above the head, one should perform the binding of the ten directions with finger-snaps (*choṭikā*).

Then, with the syllable *raṃ*, one should visualize a rampart of fire by means of a stream of water. Then follows the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), then the placement of the *mātṛkās* (*mātṛkānyāsa*), then breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and then—
The placement of the syllables (pīṭhanyāsa); then the placement of the seers and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa); then the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa);
then the display of mudrās; then meditation (dhyāna); then mental worship (mānasapūjā); then the setting out of the arghya vessel. || 13 ||
Namely: there should be three vessels for the *arghya* and likewise three for the *pādya*;

similarly, there should be separate vessels for the *ācamanīya* and so forth. However, due to weakness in physical capacity, it is recommended that there be only one; thus, there are six *ācamana* vessels.
In another scripture, it is the sixth. || 14 ||
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*: "Alternatively, one may arrange the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the other offerings in a single vessel. This refers to an extreme case of necessity;
however, there is an absolute requirement for both the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) and the special offering (*viśeṣārghya*). || 15 ||

And so it is stated in the *Navaratneśvara*: "One should not share a single vessel [even] if it be Maheśvara himself; the mantras will turn away, and there will be calamities at every step. In this world one shall be poor, and after death one shall fall into the state of a beast. (16)
Likewise, there is a statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "In all cases, the *aja* is praised, except for the worship of Śiva and Sūrya; *aja* means a conch shell. (17)

Regarding the measurement of the *arghya* vessel, the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* states: "A vessel of thirty-six *aṅgulas* is proclaimed as the best; the middling is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve *aṅgulas*. Having drawn a triangular mandala to one's left, upon it—
Having placed the tripod and, with the syllable *phaṭ*, having washed the conch and set it upon that [tripod],

one should cast perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, and so forth into it with the mantra *namaḥ*. Then, one should worship it with pure water using the reverse-order alphabet (*vilomamātṛkā*) and the root mantra (*mūla*).
For example: kṣaṃ, laṃ, haṃ, saṃ, ṣaṃ, śaṃ, vaṃ, laṃ, raṃ, yaṃ, maṃ, bhaṃ, baṃ, phaṃ, paṃ, naṃ, dhaṃ, daṃ, thaṃ, taṃ, ṇaṃ,
ḍhaṃ, ḍaṃ, ṭhaṃ, ṭaṃ, ñaṃ, jhaṃ, jaṃ, chaṃ, caṃ, ṅaṃ, ghaṃ, gaṃ, khaṃ.

With the mantra: *kaṃ aḥ aṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ aṃ*, [one should worship]. On the tripod, [one should say]: *maṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the fire-maṇḍala, whose self consists of ten parts);
and *aṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane namaḥ* (Salutation to the sun-maṇḍala, whose self consists of twelve digits).

Thus, having worshipped in the conch with "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar maṇḍala, the essence of sixteen digits," and in the water with "Oṃ, Gaṅgā and Yamunā, Godāvarī and Sarasvatī, Marude, Sindhu, and Kāverī—
be present in this water," [one should do so] by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.

Having invoked the sacred sites (*tīrthas*) from the solar disc with the mantra "O [Name], come here, stay here," and having invoked the deity there from one's own heart, one should veil it with both index fingers while reciting *huṃ*,
display the *gālinī* mudrā while reciting *vaṣaṭ*, and gaze at that water while reciting *vauṣaṭ*.

Furthermore, having performed the ritual of complete identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), one should worship the deity there with the words "Obeisance to [the deity] with perfumes and flowers. Then, having covered it above with the fish-seal (*matsyamudrā*), one should recite the root-mantra eight times. || 19 ka ||

And likewise in the *Gautamīya*: "Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should join [the vessel] there with that which is called Kṛṣṇa; one should mutter the mantra eight times and place the *gālinī* mudrā with the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Here, the word 'Kṛṣṇa' refers to the respective deity. Then, [one recites] *vaṃ*.

Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* with the mantra and protected [the water] with the *astra-mantra*, one should pour a little of that water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel; then, having sprinkled oneself and the articles of worship three times with that water using the root mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body according to the sequence for the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
One should worship Dharma and the others. || 21 ||
Namely: on the right shoulder, *oṃ dharmāya namaḥ*;
on the left, *oṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; on the left thigh, *oṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ*;
on the right thigh, *oṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; on the face, *oṃ adharmāya*; on the left side, *oṃ*.
For ignorance, at the navel: *oṃ* to Avairāgya; on the right side: *oṃ* to Anaiśvarya.
In all cases, one should worship with [the mantra] ending in *prāṇāya namaḥ*. || 22 ||

And so it is said in the Śāradā-tilaka: "The wise preceptor, proceeding clockwise, [should place] Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in order upon the two shoulders and the two thighs; [then] on the face and the sides—"
One should visualize Adharma and the others in the navel and the sides. In the heart: *Oṃ* to Ananta;

*Oṃ* to Padma; *Oṃ* to the solar disc (*arkamaṇḍala*) consisting of twelve digits (*kalā*); *Oṃ* to the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*) consisting of sixteen digits; *Maṃ* salutation to the fire-disc (*vahnimaṇḍala*) consisting of ten digits.

In this manner, one should worship with the syllables *saṃ* for *sattva*, *raṃ* for *rajas*, *taṃ* for *tamas*, *āṃ* for the *ātman*, *aṃ* for the *antarātman*, *paṃ* for the *paramātman*, and *hrīṃ* for the *jñānātman*, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. || 24 ||
In the Śaradā: "Then, by means of the sequence of nyāsa, one should worship Dharma and the other [qualities] within the bodies;

with flowers and other offerings, up to the end of the *pīṭhamantra*, and upon that, the Supreme Deity. Then, having worshipped the *pīṭha-śakti* in the filaments of the heart-lotus starting from the east, [one worships] in the center."
One should worship according to the *pīṭha*. There, in the heart, one should worship the root deity with perfumes and other offerings, excluding the food offering (*naivedya*). || 26 ||

And likewise, in the Nibandha: "One should worship with offerings such as perfumes and the like, even without the food offering (naivedya). Then, one should offer five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali) with the root mantra upon the head, heart, mūlādhāra, feet, and all the limbs."

Having given according to one's ability and having recited the mantra, one should offer the recitation with the verse beginning: "Oṃ, you who are the protector of the most secret of secrets," and so forth. || 27 ||
And so it is stated in the Nibandha: "Then, with one-pointed mind, one should perform five handfuls of flowers;
one should place [the mantras] upon the head, the heart, the navel, the feet, and all the limbs."

One should perform all of this with the water contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel. Then, having discarded the water from the *prokṣaṇī* and refilled it as before, one should begin the external worship. Therein, one should prepare either the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala or another, as described in the *Śārada* [Tantra].

One should worship there with the Vidyā. Having worshipped the maṇḍala with "Oṃ, obeisance to the maṇḍala," one should worship there with śāli rice. Having worshipped the maṇḍala with "Oṃ, obeisance to the maṇḍala" and having filled the pericarp (karṇikā) with śāli rice, upon that—

Having scattered rice grains and spread *darbha* grass over them, one should place a seat (*viṣṭara*) together with unbroken rice (*akṣata*) upon it; then, one should worship these [deities] within the mandala as follows:
in the center of the seat, "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," and "Oṃ, obeisance to Kūrma."
One should perform the worship of the *pīṭhas* as described in their respective chapters, beginning with "Namas" and ending with the *pīṭha-mantras*.

Then, one should worship these [deities] in the maṇḍala, proceeding clockwise; having assigned the ten kalās of Fire to be described hereafter, beginning with "Oṃ Ya Dhūmrārciṣe Namaḥ," one should worship them. Then...
Having washed the pitcher made of gold or other materials with the mantra *phaṭ*,
having fumigated it with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and having wrapped it with a triple-stranded thread, one should worship it with scents and flowers while reciting *oṃ kumbhāya namaḥ*.
Having scattered a seat, unbroken grains, and new jewels,
and while uttering the *praṇava*, having meditated upon the oneness of the jar and the pedestal, one should place it upon the pedestal.

Regarding the procedure for the pot according to the Gautamiya: "One may [make it] of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to one's own capacity. One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth;
if [this is done], one obtains a fruitless result. (30) Thirty-six finger-breadths [in size].

One should have the *kumbha* (pitcher) characterized by a width and height equal to that [of the base]; it should be sixteen or twelve [aṅgulas], but one should not make it less than that. Then, having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the twelve digits (*kalā*) starting from the east upon the *kumbha* in a clockwise direction—beginning with "Oṃ Kaṃ Bhaṃ, obeisance to Tapinī"—one should worship them. Then...

One should worship the jar with the thought that it is the deity itself, reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order and the *deya-mantra* while identifying oneself with [the deity], using a decoction of milky trees, or one derived from the bark of the *palāśa*, or with water from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), or with water well-scented with perfumes and flowers.

Then, having placed the sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon, beginning with *Amṛtā*, in the water in a clockwise direction, and having worshipped them with "Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Amṛtā," and so forth, one should fill the interior of the conch with substances such as the decoction of milky trees and the like, and stir in the eight fragrances (*gandhāṣṭaka*).
Having invoked all the arts (kalās) into that water, one should worship them. || 32 ||

In the Śaradā: "The eightfold fragrance is indeed threefold, consisting of Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, cora, saffron, gorocana, jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi—these they know as the eightfold fragrance of Śakti. (33)
Sandalwood, agallochum, hrīvera, kuṣṭha, saffron, sevyaka, jaṭāmāṃsī, and surabhi—
these are known as the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, tamāla, water, saffron, kuśīda, and combined with kuṣṭha— this is known as the eightfold Śaiva fragrance.
The meaning of this is as follows: sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, black *śaṭhī*, saffron, *rocanā*, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and *gāṭhiyālā* constitute the eight-fold fragrance (*gandhāṣṭaka*) of Śakti.
Sandalwood, agallochum, *bālā*, *kuḍa*, saffron, the root of white *vīraṇa*, and *jaṭāmāṃsī* [constitute another formulation].

*Devadāru* is for Viṣṇu. *Candana*, *agaru*, *karpūra*, *tamāla*, *bālā*, *kuṅkuma*, *raktacandana*, and *kuḍa* are for Śiva. (36) Therein, first one should worship the ten kalās of Agni as follows: "O ten kalās of Agni, beginning with Dhūmārcis, come here!"
One should invoke [the deities] with the words: "Come here! Stay here! Stay! Be present here!
Then, reciting the root mantra in reverse order while mentally meditating on the deity of the mantra, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (installation of the vital breaths) for them.
Namely: *Āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ haṃ saḥ*.

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of the ten digits (*kalā*) of fire, beginning with *dhūmārcis*, are here; thus, *ām* and so forth. The individual soul (*jīva*) of the ten digits of fire, beginning with *dhūmārcis*, is situated here; thus...

ĀM, and so forth: may the ten kalās of fire, beginning with Dhūmārcis, as well as all the sense organs—speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath—of these ten kalās of fire, having come here, remain happily for a long time; svāhā!

Having thus established the vital breaths (prāṇas), one should worship with perfumes and other offerings. One should worship with the five types of service (pañcopacāra) using [mantras] such as: "Oṃ, this perfume is offered to Dhūmārcis and the others; obeisance. Thereafter, one should worship each [deity] individually. || 37 ||
Namely: Yaṃ, homage to Dhūmārcis; Raṃ, homage to Uṣmā; Laṃ, homage to Jvalinī; Vaṃ, homage to Jvālinī; Śaṃ, homage to Visphuliṅginī;
Yaṃ, homage to Suśrī; Saṃ, homage to Surūpā; Haṃ, homage to Kapilā.
*Namaḥ*. *Laṃ*, obeisance to Havyavāhanā; *Kṣaṃ*, obeisance to Kavyavāhanā.

If one is capable, having invoked each individually, one should worship them with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings. Then, as before, one should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), and so forth, for the twelve digits (*kalā*) beginning with Tapinī, which reside in the mouth of the Sun.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and having worshipped, one should worship each [deity] individually.
The twelve *kalās* are as follows: Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvalinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. These are the *kalās*.
[The deities] of the Sun are situated within the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*).
They are as follows: *kaṃ bhaṃ*—homage to Tapinī; *khaṃ baṃ*—homage to Tāpinī; *gaṃ phaṃ*—homage to Dhūmrā; *ghaṃ paṃ*—homage to Marīci.

Ṅaṃ naṃ, salutation to Jvalinī; caṃ dhaṃ, salutation to Ruci; chaṃ daṃ, salutation to Suṣumnā; jaṃ khaṃ, salutation to Bhogadā; jhaṃ taṃ, salutation to Viśvā; ñaṃ ṇaṃ, salutation to Bodhinī; ṭaṃ ḍhaṃ.
"Salutation to Dhāriṇī. Ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ, salutation to Kṣamā. Thus one should worship.
If capable, one should invoke each individually and worship each with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings.
Likewise, it is stated in the Nibandha: "The solar [deities] beginning with Ka and Bha and ending with Ṭha and Ḍa are the givers of wealth."

The twelve have been described [in verse 37a]. Then, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) and so forth for the sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon, such as Amṛtā and the rest, one should worship them as before.
It is as follows: *aṃ* homage to Amṛtā; *āṃ* homage to Mānadā; *iṃ*...

Salutation to Pūṣā. Īṃ, salutation to Tuṣṭi. Uṃ, salutation to Puṣṭi. Ūṃ, salutation to Rati. Ṛṃ, salutation to Dhṛti. Ṝṃ, salutation to Śaśinī. Ḷṃ, salutation to Candrikā. Ḹṃ, salutation to Kānti. Eṃ, salutation to Jyotsnā.
Aiṃ, salutation to Śrī. Oṃ, salutation to Prīti. Auṃ, salutation to Aṅgadā. Aṃ, salutation to Pūrṇā. Aḥ, one should worship the fifty kalās beginning with Sṛṣṭi, as follows:
the ten kalās of the groups beginning with Sṛṣṭi, namely the *ka*-group and the *ca*-group.
Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) and other rites as before, one should worship each [deity] individually.
As for the individual worship: *kaṃ sṛṣṭyai namaḥ*, *khaṃ ṛddhyai namaḥ*, *gaṃ smṛtyai namaḥ*, *ghaṃ medhāyai namaḥ*, *ṅaṃ kāntyai namaḥ*.
Caṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī; chaṃ, obeisance to Dhṛti; jaṃ, obeisance to Sthirā; jhaṃ, obeisance to Sthiti; ñaṃ, obeisance to Siddhi.
If one is capable, one should invoke each [deity] individually and worship them with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. Therein: Oṃ haṃsaḥ.

Having recited "He who dwells in purity, he who dwells in wealth, he who dwells in the intermediate space, the Hotṛ priest, he who dwells on the altar, he who dwells in the sacred ford, he who dwells in the house, he who dwells among men, he who dwells in the best, he who dwells in truth, he who dwells in the sky, born of the cow, born of truth, born of the mountain—
he is the Great Truth," one should invoke [the deity] and worship him in the conch. Then...
Having performed the installation of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and so forth as before for the ten digits (kalās) beginning with *jā* and ending with *ṭa*, one should worship them. || 38 ||

For example: Ṭaṃ, obeisance to Javā; Ṭhaṃ, obeisance to Pālinī; Ḍaṃ, obeisance to Śānti; Ḍhaṃ, obeisance to Aiśvaryā; Ṇaṃ, obeisance to Rati; Tai, obeisance to Kāmikā; Thaṃ, obeisance to Varadā; Daṃ, obeisance to Hlādinī.

*Dhaṃ*—salutation to Prīti; *Naṃ*—salutation to Dīrghā. If one is capable, one should invoke and worship each [deity] individually. Then: *Oṃ pratadviṣṇustavate vīryeṇa mṛgo na bhīmaḥ kucaro giriṣṭhā yasyoruṣu triṣu...* [etc.]

Having recited "vikramaṇeṣvadhikṣiyantī bhuvanāni viśvā" and having invoked [the deity], one should worship. Then, having performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and so forth for the ten digits (*kalā*) of the groups beginning with *Tīkṣṇā* as before, one should worship them. As follows: *paṃ*...
Tīkṣṇāyai namaḥ, Phaṃ Raudrāyai namaḥ, Baṃ Bhayāyai namaḥ, Bhaṃ Nidrāyai namaḥ, Maṃ Trantryai namaḥ, Yaṃ Kṣudhāyai namaḥ,
Raṃ Krodhinye namaḥ, Laṃ Kriyāyai namaḥ, Vaṃ Utkāriṇyai namaḥ.

"Śaṃ mṛtyave namaḥ. If one is capable, one should invoke [the deities] individually everywhere and worship them with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. Then: "Oṃ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ puṣṭivarddhanam | urvārukamiva bandhanānmṛtyormukṣīya māmṛtāt ||" (We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may he deliver us from death, as a cucumber from its stem, while we are not separated from immortality.)
Having thus recited the mantra, one should invoke [the deity] and worship with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings.

Then, having performed the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and so forth as before for the five kalās of the yellow and other groups of six vowels, one should invoke them and worship with water for the feet and other offerings. For example: *Yaṃ pītāyai namaḥ*.
Saṃ, obeisance to Śvetā; Haṃ, obeisance to Aruṇā; Laṃ, obeisance to Asitā;
Kṣaṃ, obeisance to Anantā. If one is capable, one should invoke and worship each individually. Then:
Oṃ, the wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, as if [the sun] in the sky...
Having recited "The eye is extended," one should meditate upon Viṣṇu. Then, having performed the opening [of the eyes] and so forth, as well as the sixteen-fold [rite],
the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and so on, as before, one should invoke [the deity] and worship with water for the feet and other offerings.
For example: Aṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti; Āṃ, to Pratiṣṭhā; Īṃ, to Vidyā; Īṃ, to Śānti; Uṃ, to Gandhikā; Ūṃ, to Dīpikā; Ṛṃ, to Recikā;
Ṝṃ, to Mocikā; Ḷṃ, to Parā; Ḹṃ, to Sūkṣmā; Eṃ, to Sūkṣmāmṛtā.
Aiṃ, salutation to Jñānāmṛtā; Oṃ, salutation to Āpyāyinī; Auṃ, salutation to Vyāpinī;

Aṃ, salutation to Vyomarūpā; Aḥ, salutation to Anantā. If one is capable, having invoked each [deity] individually, one should worship them with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. Oṃ, those wise ones, seeking wealth, remain ever vigilant.
They kindle that which is Viṣṇu’s supreme abode; may Viṣṇu prepare the womb, and may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. May Prajāpati sprinkle [the seed], and may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
Oṃ, bestow an embryo, O Sinīvālī; bestow an embryo, O Sarasvatī; may an embryo be yours.
Having recited, "May the two Aśvin deities, adorned with lotus garlands, bestow [blessings]," one should invoke and worship them;

then, one should pour that decoction, which consists of the constituent parts (kalās) and resides within the conch, into the pitcher. Then, [one should cover it] with the sprouts of the Aśvattha, Panasa, and Cūta trees entwined with Indravallī.

Having covered the mouth of the jar with the thought that it is a *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree), one should place upon that jar-mouth a cup containing fruit and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), with the thought that it is the fruit of the *kalpavṛkṣa*. Then,
having wrapped the jar with a pair of stainless linen cloths, [one should worship] the jar with the root mantra.
Having conceptualized the form and meditated upon the deity in the manner described, one should perform the invocation therein and worship. || 39 ||
Then, reciting the root mantra: "O [Name], come here, come here;
stay here, stay here; be present here, be present here; remain firmly established here."

Having thus performed the invocation and other rites, having veiled [the deity] with "Hūṃ," having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the limbs of the deity, and having rendered [it] nectar-like with the "Vaṃ" syllable by means of the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*),
one should consecrate it as supreme by means of the supreme-consecration mudrā (*paramīkaraṇamudrā*). Then, [one should perform] the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
Having performed [this], one should worship with the sixteen types of offerings. || 39 ka ||
For example: having recited the root mantra, one says, "This seat [is offered] to such-and-such deity;

obeisance," and then says, "Welcome, such-and-such deity. Then, having recited the root mantra, one should offer water for the feet at the lotus-feet, saying, "This water for the feet [is offered] to such-and-such deity; obeisance."

This *arghya*, consisting of fragrant paste, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and *dūrvā* grass, is offered with the formula: "Svāhā to the deity [Name]! It is prepared with *śyāmā*, *dūrvā*, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*.
One should place it on the head. Regarding the Vaiṣṇava rite, however, they say it should be offered following the sequence beginning with the *arghya*.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one should place the *ācamanīya*—consisting of jasmine, cloves, and kakkola—into the mouth, saying: "This *ācamanīya*, svadhā, for [the name of] the deity."

Regarding the statement, "One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) into the mouth with the *svadhā* mantra," those who read the word *sudhā* instead [of *svadhā*] argue that since the word *sudhā* denotes nectar (*amṛta*), and since this water for sipping is nectar-like, they say, "This water for sipping is *vam*. || 40 ||

And thus it is said: "Then the preceptor should offer the *madhuparka* with the water-mantra. Nor is this [rule] restricted solely to the *madhuparka*; for it is stated: "Then one should offer the *madhuparka* into the lotus-face with the *svadhā* mantra; by that very mantra..."
"One should provide the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) with water," according to this statement;
likewise, because of the contradiction with such statements as, "One should offer the water for sipping with the Vāruṇa mantra. Some maintain that this statement refers specifically to the Śūdra.

In reality, however, it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on desire. The people of Mithilā, for their part, read the word as *svadhā* rather than *sudhā*, because the substitution of the letter *va* does not convey the sense of renunciation (*tyāga*). Furthermore, since the offering of the *arghya* water is prescribed with the word *svāhā*, which signifies renunciation, [the reading *svadhā* would be inconsistent].

They say that when the *ācamanīya* (water for sipping) is offered in conjunction with that [libation], the *svadhā* mantra is appropriate because it conveys the sense of relinquishment (*tyāga*), but the *sudhā* mantra is not. || 41 ||
Likewise: "With 'svadhā', [he offers] water for sipping three times into the lotus of the mouth;
with 'svadhā', the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and again water for sipping"—according to this statement cited by Somaśambhu. Some teachers, however, [prescribe this] with the water-mantra.

Regarding the phrase "with the *vāruṇa* seed-syllable," those who maintain that the third case ending here expresses accompaniment (*sahārthe*) consider that one should say: "This water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is for such-and-such deity; *vaṃ* *svadhā*.
Then, one should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) with the formula: "The honey-mixture, *svadhā*. [Then] the clarified butter (*ājya*).

The wise know *madhuparka* to be curd mixed with honey; likewise, the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is offered with the formula *svadhā*. Then one should present the materials for bathing (*snānīya*), followed by the garments and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Then, "Adoration (*namaḥ*)" for the ornaments; this is the fragrance (*gandha*).
Salutation; and that fragrance is prepared from sandalwood, camphor, and black agallochum.

Then, having worshipped the respective locations for the nyāsa with the letters of the Mātṛkā encased in mantra, [one offers] "these flowers, vauṣaṭ. In every offering, there is the utterance of the root mantra.
Then follows the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā). || 45 ||
Then, one should offer incense consisting of guggulu, aguru, uśīra, sugar, honey, sandalwood, and clarified butter.
And in the *Śāradā-tilaka*:
"The preceptor should incense the deity from below with guggulu, aguru, uśīra, sugar, honey, and sandalwood, mixed with clarified butter. (46)

The specific detail regarding that is as follows: Guggulu, agallochum, and sandalwood, mixed with sugar, clarified butter, and honey—this six-component incense is always dear to all the gods. [Furthermore,] the *roga*, *rogahara*, *rogadaka*, *īśa*, *surataru*, *jatu*, *laghu*, *patra*, and *viśeṣa* [are the specific types].
O beautiful one, here the auspicious incense wick is the mudrā of the lotus, free from curvature.
The meaning of this is: *kuḍa*, *harītakī*, molasses (*guḍa*), *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *devadāru*, lac (*jatu*), *aguru*, *tejapatra*, *sarala*, *nakhī*, and *muthā*. || 47 ||
Likewise: guggulu, sarala wood, pine resin, leaves produced from the Malaya mountains, hrīvera, aguru, kuṣṭha, jaggery, resin (sajjarasa), ghanasāra, harītakī,
nakha, lac, jaṭāmāṃsī, and realgar— this is the sixteen-ingredient [incense].

They know that incense is used in rites for the gods and the ancestors: honey, musta, ghee, fragrance, guggulu, agallochum, śailaja, sarala, śihla, and siddhārtha—this is called the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga-dhūpa). || 48 ||
Then, one should offer a lamp using a wick containing camphor.
And thus it is said in the Śāradā-tantra: "Having prepared wicks filled with camphor and using either ghee or sesame oil, one should raise and display lamps that are intensely fragrant."

The specific detail, however, is as follows: one should offer water at each interval between the ritual services (*upacāra*). One should also offer the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) during the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and when offering the garment. Thereafter, one should present the food offerings (*naivedya*).
Regarding the specific details for the offering of fragrance and so forth, it is stated in another Tantra:
O Pārvatī, the practitioner should offer pure fragrance with the tips of the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, while reciting the root mantra. (51)
One should offer a flower upon the wheel with the thumb and forefinger; O Goddess, the wise practitioner should offer incense in the same manner as the perfume.
O Goddess of the gods, the preceptor, holding the incense with the tip of the thumb upon the middle joint of the middle and ring fingers, should offer it;
having raised it three times with the Gāyatrī and the root-mantra, O Goddess, by means of the mudrā known as Tattva.

One should present the food offering (naivedya). With the root mantra, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) and betel-leaf with the Tattva-mudrā. Having sprinkled the incense vessel with the incense-vessel mantra and worshipped it with this heart-mantra, one should ring the bell—which has been worshipped with the Astra-mantra—while offering guggulu incense.
One should burn [incense], and then offer incense amidst the sounds of bells, musical instruments, and cries of "Victory! (jaya). || 56 ||
Likewise: "Victory! and "O Mother of Mantras, Svāhā!"—uttering these, one should ring the bell after having performed worship, and then one should fumigate with excellent incense. || 57 ||
In the Tantra: "One should not offer incense upon the ground, nor on a seat, nor likewise into a water-pot. (58)

And likewise in the Gautamiya: "Having drawn back the bell, which is positioned to the left at the limit of one's vision, one should ring it with the left hand while offering [the oblation] with the right hand."
Likewise, when offering a lamp, one should ring a bell. || 59 ||
In the *Yāmala*: One should offer perfume, flowers, and ornaments in front;
one should give the lamp on the right, or in front, but not on the left.
Likewise, the incense should be on the left, or in front, but not on the right. The food offering (*naivedya*) should be on the right or the left.

Neither in front nor behind [the deity]. The left and right sides belong to the deity alone, and not to the practitioner; for it is seen [in scripture] that one should offer incense, lamps, and excellent food before the deity.

That mixed with ghee is on the right, and that mixed with oil is on the left. Likewise, if the wick is white it is on the right, and if it is red it is on the left; however, there is no fixed rule for that which is placed directly in front.
Furthermore, cooked food is on the left of the deity, and raw food is on the right. (64)

And so it is stated in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*: "If one sets aside the right side and places [the food] on the left, that food shall become unfit for consumption, and the water shall be like liquor. Thus say the traditionalists. (65)

And likewise, in the *Yāmala*: "The lamp filled with ghee is on the right, and that filled with oil is on the left; on the right is a white wick, and on the left a red wick. Regarding food offerings (*naivedya*), the rule is according to whether they are cooked or uncooked; there is no such restriction for those placed in front."

In some cases, [this is done] with the lamp and the food offering (naivedya). Then follows the salutation (vandana). Then, having performed the recitation (japa) one thousand and eight times or one hundred times, one should offer the recitation with the mantra beginning with "guhyātiguhyam" and so forth.
Then, the Guru, having performed the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the mantra according to the previously mentioned method—
Having led the disciple forward and covered the disciple's eyes with a cloth while reciting the mantra *vauṣaṭ*,

the Guru himself, uttering the mantra, should cast a handful of flowers into the water-pot (*kalaśa*) for the pleasure of the deity, after having filled the disciple’s joined palms (*añjali*) with flowers. Then, [he removes] the eye-bandage.

Having moved [the disciple] away from the darbha-grass mat and seated him, and having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth according to the sequence of his own ritual worship, he should perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) prescribed for the respective mantras upon the body of the disciple. Then, having again worshipped the deity residing in the water-pot with the five types of offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [he should proceed].

One should cause the adorned disciple to sit upon another [seat]. Then, having raised the water-pot preceded by auspicious rites, and having placed the sprouts in the form of celestial trees situated at its mouth upon the head of the disciple,

While mentally reciting the *mātṛkā*, he should consecrate him with water prepared by means of the root mantra and the consecration mantras taught in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*. Then the disciple, having sipped the remaining water and put on two garments, [should approach] the Guru.

He should sit in close proximity. Then, the Guru, contemplating the oneness of those two—the disciple’s own deity having been transferred to him—should worship that very deity with perfumes and other offerings. Then, with the mantra "Oṃ sahasrāre huṃ phaṭ," [he should touch] the disciple's crest-lock.
Having bound [the disciple] and protected him, one should perform the ritual placement of the *kalās* (*kalānyāsa*) upon the body of the disciple.
It is as follows: with three blades of *kuśa* grass, from the soles of the feet up to the knees, one says: *oṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ*. From the knees up to the navel, one says: *oṃ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*.

From the navel to the throat: *oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*. From the throat to the forehead: *oṃ śāntyai namaḥ*. From the forehead to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*): *oṃ śāntyatītāyai namaḥ*. Again, from the aperture of Brahmā to the forehead: *oṃ śāntyatītāyai namaḥ*.
From the forehead to the throat: *oṃ śāntyai namaḥ*. From the throat to the end of the navel: *oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*. From the navel to the knees: *oṃ pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*.
From the knees to the feet: *oṃ nivṛttyai namaḥ*. Then, [of] the disciple...
Placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, having recited the mantra to be given one hundred and eight times,
he should place water in the disciple's hand, saying, "I give this such-and-such mantra to you";
then the disciple should say, "Give it."

And so it is stated in the Vāsiṣṭha: "Then, having placed his own hand upon that person's head, he should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, he should bestow the mantra preceded by water, pronouncing: 'May it yield equal fruit for both of us. Then...
Having caused the mantra, joined with the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs], to be heard three times in the right ear by the guru, he should cause it to be heard once in the left ear.
And so it is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "The guru, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the water upon her body..."
With effort and a full mind, one should recite the mantra three times into the right ear;
the phrase "into the right ear" refers specifically to the twice-born (dvijāti). || 71 ||
And likewise in that Tantra: "One should recite the mantra three times into the right ear with a single utterance;
this is the rule for the twice-born, while for women and Śūdras it is from the left. (72)

In the Rudrayāmala: The Guru, facing east, [should place the mantra] three times in the right ear and once in the left ear of the disciple who is standing facing west; the reverse of this should be known for women and Śūdras, [placing it] from the left. Then...

He should remain prostrate at the feet of the Guru and say: "O Lord, by Your grace, I am fulfilled in every respect; I am liberated from the great noose of illusion and death, and I am Śiva. Thus he should speak. (74)
Then the Guru should say: "Rise, child! You are liberated; be possessed of perfect conduct.
May fame, prosperity, splendor, sons, long life, strength, and health always be yours. Thus he should cause him to rise. || 75 ||
In the Viśvasāra: "One should recite the mantra, complete with its seer (ṛṣi) and other attributes, into the right ear;
likewise, O Goddess, at that very moment, one should mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times. (76)

In the *Śāradā*: "The wise one should mutter eight times the supreme Vidyā received from the Guru, while contemplating with his intellect the identity of the Guru, the Mantra, and the Deity. This statement refers to the subject of recitation accompanied by that specific contemplation; however, in the absence of such contemplation, [the number of repetitions is different].
One thousand [times]. || 77 || For the sake of protecting his own power (*śakti*), the Guru should recite [the mantra] one thousand or one hundred times.
In another Tantra: "He should recite it one hundred times in her presence and dwell near her for three days;
otherwise, there is no doubt that the mobile power (*sañcāriṇī-śakti*) will not come to the Guru. || 78 ||
In the Viśvasāra: "Then, for the sake of protecting his own power, the Guru should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times, or even one hundred times, according to the prescribed rule. (79)
In the *Yāmala*: "O Goddess, having given the mantra, one should then recite it one hundred and eight times.

Then the disciple, taking kusha grass, sesame seeds, and water, [says]: "Om, today, for the sake of the reception and consecration of the such-and-such mantra of the such-and-such deity, this gold is [offered as] the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."

"I offer this gold, whose deity is Agni, to you, the Guru, of the [so-and-so] lineage, named Devaśarman, who has been liberated. (81) One should dedicate one's body, wealth, and life—all of it—to him. From that time forward, one should act as the Guru's [servant].
With a mind focused on nothing else, he should offer into his mouth whatever is most beloved in the world. 82.

Regarding the rule for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the *Svatantra-tantra*: "One should give a sacrificial fee to the Guru, who is the manifest Śiva himself; either one's entire wealth, or half of that, or half of that again, according to his command. Otherwise, how could his power be mobile?"
It will come to pass. || 83 ||
In the *Kulāmṛta*: "Abandoning stinginess regarding wealth, one should accomplish all rites;
for stinginess quickly destroys sons, longevity, fame, and wealth. (84)
Having honored the Guru as a deity, whoever should amass wealth, that wealth is enjoyed by him alone;
it is not seized by kings or thieves. One should offer a seat to the Guru, as well as a red woolen blanket, and one should give necklaces and other ornaments, and a cow.
One should give a milch cow;
one should give land that provides a livelihood, which follows after one's sons and grandsons.
Likewise: One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru consisting of gold accompanied by clothing;

by the mere satisfaction of the guru, even a corrupt mantra becomes effective. Otherwise, it will not be successful at all and will instead lead to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). [The materials for] the reception of initiation...

Then one should inform the preceptor; furthermore, one should diligently satisfy other Brahmins there as well. Then, having satisfied the Brahmins with sweet food, drink, and so forth, one should eat oneself. || 89 ||
And likewise, in the *Nibandha*: "Afterwards, the initiated man should feed the Brahmins according to the rules;
he should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins and eat himself while remaining silent.
Regarding the fast of the teacher and the disciple on the day of initiation, the *Yoginītantra* states:

If a preceptor, having imparted a mantra, observes a fast, he becomes a worm in a hell of great darkness; it is not otherwise. If a practitioner of mantra, having performed initiation, observes a fast, the deity is always enraged and, having uttered a curse—
One should go to the city. || 92 || If the fire-oblation (homa) is performed here, we shall then explain its procedure. Thus ends the ritual application for the initiation of Kalāvatī. || 93 ||
Now, the initiation of the five deities (*pañcāyatanī dīkṣā*) [is described] in the *Yāmala*: "When one worships Bhavānī in the center, one should worship Acyuta in the northeast,
Pārvatīnātha in the southeast, Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest, and [Śiva] in the northwest."
The procedure for heating and worship has thus been declared. || 94 ||
But when one worships Govinda in the center, Śaṅkara in the northeast, Gaṇanātha in the southeast, and likewise Tapanam in the southwest; || 95 ||
One should worship Ambikā, who is the sole ground for worldly enjoyment and liberation, in the northwest; Śaṅkara in the center; Acyuta in the northeast;
Tapana in the southeast; Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest; and Pārvatī in the northwest.
[She is] the bestower of heaven and liberation. || 97 || When Āditya is in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast and Gaṇanātha in the southeast;
and when Āditya is in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast and Gaṇanātha in the southeast.
Likewise, one should worship Keśava in the southwest;

the goddess Ambikā, who is the ground for attaining heaven, in the northwest; Gaṇanātha in the center; and when [Gaṇanātha] is in the center, one should worship Keśava in the northeast, Īśvara in the southeast, and [the Lord] in the southwest.
Likewise, one should worship Tapanī and Pārvatī, who brings about liberation, in the northwest. Deities who are removed from their proper places bestow suffering, grief, and fear. 100.

And likewise, in the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*: "When Śambhu is in the center, Hari, Naha, Hara, Bhū, and Devī are established; when Harī is in the center, Śaṅkara, Bhāsī, Anagāsuta, Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, and Ajaṃbikā are established; and when Devī is in the center, Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Ravi, and Ya."
O Lambodara, O Unconquerable Lord, may those [obstacles] which are very friendly toward women from the side of Śaṅkara result in loss for you. || 1 ||

In the *Rāmārcanacandrikā* and the *Gautamīya*: "When, however, one has worshipped Govinda in the center, Gaṇanāyaka in the southeast (Āgneyī), Haṃsa in the southwest (Nairṛtī), Śivā in the northwest (Vāyavī), and Śaṅkara in the northeast (Aiśānī)... (2).

"For the attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. Regarding this, some maintain that the worship of Gaṇeśa and others in the southeast (Āgneya) and other directions during the worship of the limb-deities is intended specifically for Rāma and Gopāla. However, the traditionalists hold that it is optional. || 3 ||

Regarding their worship, according to the *Gautamīya*: "Having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, as well as performing the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) worship, one should recite the mantra twenty times and conclude by offering obeisance. Now, as for the time for the worship of the deities of the limbs:
Immediately after the worship of the deities of the sacrificial ground (pīṭhadevatā).

And so it is stated in the Sanatkumāra-tantra: "The worship of the pedestal, the sacrifice to the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās), the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), then the invocation, the fashioning of one's own mudrā, meditation on the Lord, and the offering of worship. (5)

As for the statement that one should worship the deities of the limbs after offering a handful of flowers to the principal deity, that refers specifically to consecrated images, yantras, and the like.
Regarding worship on a support other than a yantra, the Kulāvalī states:
"He who performs separate worship on a single pedestal without a yantra incurs the curse of the deity by abandoning the relationship of limb and possessor of limbs. (7)
And thus: "Having invoked one deity, if one worships another deity, the practitioner of mantra receives curses from both and becomes evil-minded.
This [statement], however, refers to cases other than the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*). Regarding all the ancillary mantras, there is an investigation into their attainment (*siddhi*) and so forth.
It does not exist.
And thus: "The purification of the Siddhas and so forth is not for these [mantras], since they are subordinate members, like a king. (8)
However, in the case of Śyāmā and others, there is an absence of the five deities (pañcāyatana).

And so it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "In the case of Śyāmā, Māyā, Bhairavī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, and Bhairavī, as well as Mañjughoṣa in the Raudra [tattva], the five limbs (pañcāṅga) are prescribed by the wise. This applies to all secondary sciences (upavidyās) and to the six ritual acts (ṣatkarma) and so forth."
In this practice, there is no requirement for initiation and the like, nor is there the worship of the limbs and the principal deity.

In the *Tattvasāra*: "In all the secondary sciences (*upavidyā*) as well as in the performance of ritual applications (*prayogasādhana*), instruction must always indeed be given even without initiation (*dīkṣā*). (11)
Now, the abbreviated initiation (saṃkṣepadīkṣā):
At an auspicious moment, having placed nine jars filled with water, honored with perfumes and flowers, and wrapped in cloth upon a Sarvatobhadra diagram;

Combined with all medicinal herbs, nine jewels, and five sprouts, one should then perform the worship of the deity and offer one hundred and eight oblations. Regarding the "five sprouts," these are the *panasa*, mango, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *vakula*.
And so it is stated in the Vāsiṣṭha: "The panasa, āmra, aśvattha, vaṭa, and vakula—these are declared as the 'five leaves' by the sages who know the tantras. (13)
The nine gems are, in their respective order: pearl, ruby, lapis lazuli, hessonite, diamond, coral, ruby, emerald, and sapphire. (14)

In the Nibandha: One should cause the well-adorned disciple to sit upon the altar near the fire, having been consecrated with the waters of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel as well as the water from the *śāntikumbha*. (15)
One should perform the consecration with the root mantra recited one hundred and eight times;
"one hundred and eight" means one hundred plus eight. || 16 ||
Then, while placing his hand upon the head, he should accomplish the mantra;

saying "Salutation be [to you]," he should offer unbroken grains (akṣatāḥ), and thereafter the disciple should worship the guru. Or else, at another initiation, having worshipped the conch along with unbroken grains—
Having sprinkled that water eight times on the head while reciting the root mantra and placing the hand there, one should mutter it eight times into the ear; likewise,
if someone is unable even to do that, they should worship a lotus flower along with rice grains.

Having sprinkled that [water] eight times with the root mantra alone, one should place it [in the disciple's hand] and recite it eight times into his ear; this is the procedure for the oral instruction. Thus ends the abbreviated initiation. || 18 ||

Another instruction is stated in the Viśvasāra: "The mere recitation of the mantra at a lunar or solar eclipse, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a site of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva—that is called 'instruction' (upadeśa)."
In the Viśvasāra: "The Great Initiation (mahādīkṣā), as well as the [ordinary] initiation (dīkṣā), and thereafter the instruction (upadeśa);
in every age this must be performed, and in the Kali age, the instruction [is paramount]. (20)

Now, the *Sarvatobhadra* mandala (see Figure 10). In the *Śāradā*: "In a square divided into four compartments, provided with diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*), one should likewise draw four diagonal lines within each of the four compartments, in their respective centers."
The practitioner of mantra should cast two fish-marks extending from east to west and two extending from south to north; then, upon those fish-marks, he should cast four equal lines.
As before, he should cast the diagonal lines (karṇasūtra) in the corner squares. From that, [the grid] arises.

One should lay down four lines among the fish; then, within the resulting squares, there shall be fish, and upon them one should drop lines. The practitioner of mantra should drop the lines there according to that very same procedure, until there are two hundred and fifty-six squares.
21. With thirty-six squares in the center, one should draw a lotus possessing all its characteristics;
with the outer row there should be the pedestal (pīṭha), and with a pair of rows the pathway (vīthikā);
one should arrange the doors, the arches (bhobha), and the side-ornaments (upaśobhā) using the remaining [squares].

Then, following the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, the wise mantra-practitioner should draw a lotus. Having set aside one-twelfth part of the lotus-area on the outside, he should divide its center into three circles with equal proportions. The first...

The first [measurement] should be for the location of the pericarp (karṇikā); the second for the filaments (kesara); the third for the lotus petals; and the tips of the petals by a quarter-part. Having established these according to the measurement and rule of the space between the outer and inner circles, the wise one [should place them] at the tips of the filaments.
Having drawn [the petals] on all sides with half-moons at their joints, one should drop lines there; and having drawn a circle with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals,
the wise person [should proceed] within that space, on both sides of the central line.

One should draw the tips of the petals all around with the outer hand; at the bases of the petals, one should arrange the filaments in pairs. This lotus is declared by those who know the tantras to be the common [form]. One should erase three squares for the meaning of the word "pad" (square) and one square for the pedestal (*pīṭha*) in the corners.

With the remaining squares, the wise man should fashion the seats and the limbs; he should sweep out the squares situated along the pathways according to their rows. Then, he should construct the doors in the cardinal directions using four squares each, and the *śobhās* (ornamental projections) using three and one square respectively.

There should be side-decorations on both sides of the doors. Immediately thereafter, there should be secondary decorations made with one and then three squares. With the remaining six squares, there should be a set of four corners. One should color that captivating maṇḍala with five colors.

21kha || Yellow is from turmeric powder; white is derived from rice; red is from safflower powder; black is produced from burnt chaff; and dark green is said to be from the leaves of the *bilva* and other such trees—thus is the pentad of colors described. 22.
The white lunar lines, auspicious and one finger-breadth in height and width, should be colored;

the pericarp with yellow pigment, the filaments with reddish-pink, the petals with white, and their junctions with dark-blue. Alternatively, the practitioner may color them with red powder, or the pericarp alone may be yellow.

The filaments (keśarāḥ) should be colored yellow, the petals (dalāni) reddish, and the joints (sandhayaḥ) black; or alternatively, one may color them with yellow or black. The interior of the pedestal (pīṭhagarbhāṇi) should be colored, while the feet (pādāḥ) should have a reddish luster, and its limbs (gātrāṇi) as well as the walkways (vīthīṣu) should be white.
On the four [sides], one should draw wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*) provided with leaves and flowers;
they are variegated with various colors and enchanting to the sight of all. The doors are white in color, the *śobhās* are said to be red, and the *upaśobhās* are yellow in color.
And the corners should be black. Three lines are to be drawn on the outside, white, red, and black in sequence.
This mandala, known as Sarvatobhadra, is considered common to all.

Now, the *Svalpasarvatobhadramaṇḍala* (see Figure 11): Having divided the square ground into twelve parts from each direction, the wise practitioner should drop threads therein; thus, one hundred squares are seen.

One should fashion the pedestal (pīṭha) with forty-four squares, followed by thirty-six lotuses; there is no pathway here arranged in rows. The door-ornaments (dvāraśobhe) are as before, but the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) are not seen; [this is done] with the remaining squares.
The knower of the tantra should form the corners with six [lines]; he should perform the remainder as before—thus is the maṇḍala remembered. (24ka)
Now, the nine-navel mandala (see Figure 12):
The wise practitioner should arrange sixty-four squares within a square [area]. With four squares, there shall be a lotus in the center; furthermore, one should create four walkways surrounding it.
These conclude the mandala. One should draw lotuses (*paṅkajāni*) in the four squares located at the cardinal directions.

Having divided the four squares situated at the intermediate directions into sixteen parts, the wise one should erase them into the form of svastikas using white, yellow, red, and black lines (*rājas*).

One should fill those svastikas starting from Śiva according to the very path previously described; one should complete the rest in the same manner. This mandala, called the Nine-Navel, is said to bestow all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). || 25 ||
Now, the mandala of five lotuses (see Figure 13):
This mandala of five lotuses is said to be devoid of the svastika. There are four types of mandalas for the purpose of worshipping the deity during initiation, according to all the tantras.
It is declared to bestow all prosperity. || 26 ||
Now, the Trilauhīmudrā: Next, for the benefit of practitioners, the Trilauhīmudrā is described.
The three metals correspond to the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; silver is the Moon.
Gold is remembered as the sun, and copper as fire. (27) The portions of metal are specified by the number of vowels and consonants;
with those metals, one should have a seal made that is unalloyed and well-proportioned. Among these, the vowels are traditionally taught. (28)

The vowels are gentle and belong to Saturn; they bring about auspicious results. The consonants are all pervasive and have the Moon, the Sun, and Fire as their deities. The sixteen vowels are well-known, while the consonants are twenty-five in number. Those ten pervasive letters bestow desire, wealth, and dharma.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times,
the practitioner should then touch it and offer oblations into that [fire] with clarified butter according to the previously mentioned number.
Having cast that mudrā into the pitcher by way of the procedure prescribed for consecration (abhiṣeka), he should invoke [the deity].

One should worship the Goddess with ritual services according to the prescribed injunctions. Having performed the consecration, the Guru should give the seal-ring to the humble disciple. This seal-ring destroys minor ailments, poisons, and fevers; it provides protection against wild beasts, thieves, predatory animals, and the like.
One should especially perform [this]; by wearing it, a lord of men attains victory in battle. It brings about the perfection of mantras for men and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
a person who wears it constantly shall become equal to a god on earth. Having thus consecrated [it]...

Having established the water-pot according to the sequence prescribed in the previously mentioned initiation manual (dīkṣāpaddhati), and having invoked the deity specified in the respective ritual manual (kalpa), one should worship with the prescribed offerings according to the sequence stated in the initiation manual.

The meaning is that, having worshipped the sādhya and consecrated him, one should give [the object] to him; then, having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, one should hold a great festival. || 36 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya Śrī Kṛṣṇānandāgamavāgīśa. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter:
Now, the Procedure for General Worship.
Therein, having risen during the *brāhmya* muhūrta, having abandoned sleep and discarded the night-garment, [one should place it] upon the head.

Having meditated upon the Guru, white in color, seated upon the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus, with two arms making the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, adorned with white garlands and unguents, his form being self-luminous, accompanied by his own left-side seated Śakti, who is deep red and likewise self-luminous in form.
Having propitiated [the deity] with mental offerings, one should pay homage as follows:
"To that which has the form of an unbroken circle, by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded..."
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state has been revealed;
salutations to that venerable Guru by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance with the ointment-stick of knowledge.
Then, one should contemplate the root-vidyā from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
that is, the root-vidyā as Kuṇḍalinī.
And so it is said in the Yoginīhṛdaya:
"The Vidyā, in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, pierces the three maṇḍalas. (1)
Elsewhere also:
"One should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who dwells in the Mūlādhāra, subtle,
having the form of the deity Tāmisṭā, and endowed with three and a half coils."

Having risen with a firm posture, the practitioner, using the *prāṇamantra*, should gaze at that Great Goddess— who is encircled by self-manifested lingas and possesses the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes— as long as he can hold his breath, while she shines like the rising sun.
With a concentrated mind, for the sake of pacifying all misfortunes without exception,
one should contemplate the body as auspicious and pervaded by a mass of its radiance.
Regarding its permanence, it is stated in the *Gautamīya*: "Now, in this context, I shall tell you what was done previously;
by performing which, one attains eligibility for the worship of mantras, yantras, and so forth."
Without which [the goal] would not be accomplished, and one would fall into hell. || 3 ||
And in the *Yāmala*:
"If one worships the Goddess with devotion without first performing the morning duties, his worship shall be fruitless, just like a ritual action devoid of purification. (4)
Also in the *Lakṣmīkulārṇava*:
"He who is devoid of the twilight worship (sandhyā) shall not obtain the fruit of initiation.
Thus, by this statement, its necessity is established. || 5 ||
After the Vedic *sandhyā*, the Tantric *sandhyā* should be performed.
As it is said:
"The Vedic and Tantric *sandhyās* [should be performed] according to their sequential order. (6)
Now, the procedure for the twilight worship (sandhyā-prayoga):
therein, according to one's capacity: *oṃ ātmatattvāya svāhā*, *oṃ vidyātattvāya svāhā*, *oṃ śivatattvāya*.
One should sip water with the utterance "svāhā";
otherwise, there is merely the act of sipping water.
And so it is said in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"The foremost of practitioners should sip water with the principles (*tattva*) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva;
then, O Dear One, having uttered the wife of Fire (*svāhā*), he should [rinse] with pure water."
In the *Mālinītantra*:

"One should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) with the principles of the Self (*ātmatattva*) and so forth, preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with the *dviṭha* [syllable]. Then, having invoked the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) in the water with the mantra beginning "O Gaṅgā," and so forth, one should [perform the sipping] three times with *kuśa* grass while reciting the root mantra (*mūla*).
One should pour water on the ground.
With that water, one should sprinkle one's head seven times.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), [one should place] water in the palm of the left hand.

Having placed [the vessel] with the right hand and covered it with water, one should consecrate it three times with "haṃ yaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ. Then, while reciting the root mantra, one should sprinkle the head seven times with the dripping drops of water using the *tattvamudrā*. The remaining water is held in the right hand.

Having taken hold [of the breath], meditated upon it as a form of fire, drawn it in through the *iḍā*, washed away the sins within the body, visualized that water— which is black in color— as the very form of sin, and expelled it through the *piṅgalā* with the mantra "phaṭ" onto the previously imagined adamantine stone (*vajraśilā*) before one;
One should cast that water, which has the form of the "sinful man" (pāpapuruṣa), [into the water]; this is the Aghamarṣaṇa rite.
One should also recite the mantra beginning with "Gaṅge ca" at a sacred ford (tīrtha), for according to the Smṛti, the fruit at a sacred ford is double.
And likewise in the Gautamiya:
"Having sipped water according to the rule, the practitioner should lie down in a clean place;
having united the sacred sites (tīrthas) with water three times by means of the root mantra."
One should cast [the water] upon the ground with the tip of a *kuśa* blade and sprinkle it seven times upon the head.
In another tantra:
Having sipped water again and performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), the knower of Dharma takes water in his left hand and, with the falling drops of water, [performs the sprinkling].
Having performed the sprinkling seven times while reciting the mantra over his head,
the wise one should take the remaining water in his right hand,
draw it into the interior of his body through the *iḍā* [left nostril], and thereby wash away the accumulated mass of sins.

The practitioner of mantra, having visualized that black-colored water as the form of sin, should expel it through the right channel; then, while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*), he should cast it onto a diamond-stone (*vajrapāṣāṇa*) in front of him with his right hand.
Elsewhere it is also said:
Having performed the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), the wise one should then take water in the left hand and form a hollow cavity with the right hand.
Having consecrated it again three times with the seed-syllables of Śiva, Vāyu, Jala, Pṛthivī, and Agni, and seven times with the root-mantra using the *tattva-mudrā*,
one should sprinkle that water upon the head and place the remainder on the right side.

The foremost of practitioners should wash away the sin residing within his body. Then, having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should offer an oblation (arghya) to the Sun with the mantra: "hrīṃ haṃ saḥ oṃ ghṛṇi sūrya āditya."
Likewise, in the Sammohana Tantra:
"O Goddess, one should write the seed-syllable of Śiva situated in fire (ra), adorned with the left eye (ī), consisting of the bindu and nāda; then one should write the word 'haṃsa'."
By means of this mantra, which is dear to Bhāskara, one should offer the *arghya*—this is the remainder [of the sense].
The specific details, however, shall be stated in the section on bathing (*snānaprakaraṇa*). || 9 ||

Then, having poured water three times with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to [Name] Devatā residing in the solar disc," or with her specific Gāyatrī, one should recite the Gāyatrī of that respective deity. || 10 ||
And likewise, immediately after the *arghya* offering, it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Then the wise one should mutter the Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable.
As for the Gāyatrī, she shall be discussed in the section on ritual bathing (*snāna-prakaraṇa*). || 11 ||
In the Nandikeśvara Saṃhitā:
"As long as the arghya offering is not given to the high-souled Bhāskara, so long one should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or Maheśvarī. (12)
In the Gautamīya:
Thus have the junctions of the mantra been described to you for the attainment of the fruit of the mantra.
If one does not perform them out of delusion, one shall not obtain the fruit of initiation. [This concerns] the three junctions.
A Brāhmaṇa should perform it according to the prescribed rules;
a Śūdra, however, should perform the Sandhyā according to the rules declared in the Tantras.
Or, if he is unable, the practitioner (Mantrī) may indeed perform the abbreviated Sandhyā.
Having meditated upon the Lord at evening, morning, and midday, one should mutter the mantra;
however, if the twilight prayer has been omitted, one should mutter the Gāyatrī ten times.
Now, the procedure for bathing:
having offered [libations] in a river or similar body of water and performed the Vedic bath, one should perform the Tantric bath. || 15 ||

And so it is said in the *Gautamīyatantra*: "Now, one should perform the bath according to the prescriptions of the scriptures; one should carry out the bath that washes away impurities as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch."
Then one should perform the mantra-bath by means of ritual action for the sake of attaining success.
It is as follows:
"Oṃ, today [and so forth], for the sake of pleasing the deity named so-and-so, I shall perform the ritual bath"—thus one should make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa). || 17 ||
And so it is said in the *Kulacuḍāmaṇi*:
"Taking a copper vessel together with *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and water, one should perform the ritual bath for the pleasure of such-and-such a deity. (18)
Then, having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and the two breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*), [one recites]: *Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva Godāvari Sarasvati Narmade...*
"O Sindhu and Kāverī, be present in this water!

Having thus invoked the holy water from the solar orb with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, having rendered it nectarine with the syllable *vaṃ* and the *dhenu-mudrā*, having veiled it with the *kavaca-mantra*, and having protected it with the *astra-mantra*.
Having consecrated [the water] eleven times with the root mantra, having poured twelve streams of water while facing the sun,
and having immersed oneself three times in that water which has issued from the lotus feet of one's chosen deity, [one should worship] the deity...

Meditating on the root mantra and reciting it according to one's capacity, one should sprinkle oneself three times with water while reciting the mantra three times using the *kalaśa-mudrā*; having performed the Vedic *saṃdhyā* rites,
offered the *arghya* to the Sun, and completed the Tantric rites beginning with the *aghamarṣaṇa* and ending with the stream of water (*vāridhārā*).
One should perform the ritual action. || 19 ||
And so it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"Having meditated thus, one should offer handfuls of water and satisfy one's chosen deity. (20)
Regarding that, he states the sequence:

"Oṃ, I satiate the gods; Oṃ, I satiate the sages; Oṃ, I satiate the ancestors. Having thus performed the libation, [one should likewise satiate] the guru, the paramaguru, the parāparaguru, and the parameṣṭhiguru.
One should satisfy [them].
And so it is said:

Having first gratified the lineage of gurus, one should then satisfy the gods, the sages, and the ancestors according to the procedure prescribed for the Kalpa, and finally satisfy one's chosen deity. (21)
But there is a distinction regarding the libations:
one should thrice satisfy Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśaṭha, Uddhava, Āruka,
Viṣvaksena, Śaineya, and the Guru.
The formula, however, is as follows: "Oṃ, I satiate Nārada," and so forth, according to this sequence. || 22 ||
Then, having recited the root mantra, one says, "I satiate such-and-such deity; *namaḥ*"; this is the procedure regarding Viṣṇu.
And likewise in the *Gautamīya*: "First, having fully recited the mantra, [one says] 'Śrī' followed by 'Kṛṣṇa'."
Having uttered the word "tarpayāmi," one should then perform the libation ending with "namaḥ."
Elsewhere, having uttered the root [mantra], one should say: "I satiate the deity Amukā.
And likewise in another tantra:
"The word 'I satiate' (tarpayāmi) should be joined at the end of these names [of the deities] within the mantras."
And with the words "and [the name] ending in the dative case," such is the mantra for the libation (tarpaṇa) as it is remembered. || 24 ||
Furthermore, regarding the scope of one's capacity: "Having first performed the root-utterance, I satiate such-and-such goddess, svāhā.
This is because the words "svāhā" are prescribed for each respective mantra in the contexts of both fire-oblation (homa) and libation (tarpaṇa). || 25 ||
And so it is said in the Nīlatantra:
"Having pronounced the name at the end of the mantra, one says 'tarpayāmi' (I satiate) thereafter;
ending with 'svāhā', one thus satiates," and so forth. || 26 ||
In the Viśuddheśvara [tantra]: Having first uttered the vidyā, at its end one should pronounce the name of the deity;
having said "I satiate" (tarpayāmi), it is held that the libation (tarpaṇa) ends with "svāhā."
"Or twenty-five times, or tenfold, or even threefold;
having recited the root mantra, the wise one should satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa"— according to this statement from the *Gautamīya*, one should perform the libation twenty-five times, ten times, or three times.
In this context, "Śrī Kṛṣṇa" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).
Regarding the Śakti, there is a threefold libation.
When the rite of bathing has arrived, the practitioner of mantra should offer a handful of water upon her head.
Then, having performed the rite three times with the Vidyā, one should drink the purified water three times.
Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Kulāmṛta*, "The libation (*tarpaṇa*) is threefold, and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is likewise threefold by means of that [water]. (28)
Then, one should satisfy each of those deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇa-devatās) once.
And so it is said in the Kulārṇava:
"One should satisfy the retinue with water, offering one handful (añjali) for each."
If one is unable to do that, one should recite the root mantra and satisfy the chosen deity alone. || 29 ||
And likewise:
"In case of inability, having uttered the root mantra, one should satisfy the Goddess alone. (30)
Then, having risen from the water, put on two washed garments, and sipped water (ācamana), [one offers] "Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ, this arghya, svāhā!
But when preceded by the Tāra (Oṃ), it is "Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ, to Mārttaṇḍabhairava."
"To the one endowed with the power of light, this arghya, svāhā!
In another tantra:
"Having recited the mantra of the Sun, [one offers it] to Mārtaṇḍabhairava."
Then one should recite: "To the one endowed with the power of illumination, this is the *arghya*.
Having uttered the mantra ending in *svāhā* and offered the *arghya*, one should mutter the mantra. (31)
Regarding the Śrīvidyā, however: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ, to Mārttaṇḍabhairava, together with Prakāśaśakti.
Having offered this *arghya* with the words, "To the one accompanied by the retinue of planets, zodiac signs, lunar mansions, lunar days, yogas, and karaṇas, svāhā!
This *arghya*," one should recite the *gāyatrī* of each respective deity a hundred times. || 32 ||
And so it is said in another tantra:
"The wise person should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
even one burdened with great sins should recite it ten times."
"Truly, O Great Goddess, one becomes liberated at that very moment"—
thus [it is said] in ten ways, according to the distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable.
Or, after the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one may perform the prostration (sarpaṇa).
And so it is said:
"Thereafter, [one should offer salutation] to the Deity residing within the solar orb."
Taking the *arghya* water in his joined palms (*añjali*), he should offer it three times with the *gāyatrī* mantra.
Thereafter, he should recite the Goddess Gāyatrī as much as he is able.
Then, for the purpose of the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the practitioner should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
"Having meditated and cast a handful of water, one should satisfy the chosen deity," according to the statement in the *Yāmala*. (34)
The Gāyatrī mantra is as follows: "We know the one who deludes the three worlds; we meditate upon the god of love; may that Viṣṇu inspire us."
Thus is the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī:
"We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu inspire us.
Thus is the Nārāyaṇa-gāyatrī.
We know the one with adamantine claws; we meditate upon the one with sharp fangs; may that Narasiṃha inspire us. Thus is the Nṛsiṃha-gāyatrī.
"Vāgīśvarāya vidmahe, Hayagrīvāya dhīmahi, tanno haṃsaḥ pracodayāt. This is the Hayagrīva-gāyatrī. Now, the Gopāla-gāyatrī:
"Kṛṣṇāya vidmahe, dāmodarāya dhīmahi, tanno Viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt"— this is the Gāyatrī of Kṛṣṇa. "Daśarathāya vidmahe, Sītāvallabhāya dhīmahi, tanno Rāmaḥ pracodayāt"— this is the Rāma-Gāyatrī.
"Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us. This is the Śiva-gāyatrī.
"Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa; may Dantī impel us."
Thus is the Gaṇeśa-gāyatrī:
"We know Dakṣiṇāmūrti; we meditate upon Him who is established in meditation; may He, the Lord of Wisdom, inspire us."
Thus is the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Gāyatrī:
"We know Āditya; we meditate upon Mārtaṇḍa; may that Sūrya inspire us.
Thus is the Sūrya Gāyatrī.
"May we know Kāmadeva; may we meditate upon him who possesses the flower-arrows; may that Anaṅga inspire us.
Thus is the Gāyatrī of Kāmadeva.
"Let us know her who deludes all; let us meditate upon her, the mother of the universe; may that Śakti inspire us.
This is the Śakti-Gāyatrī.
"Let us know Tvaritā; let us meditate upon Mahānityā; may that Goddess inspire us.
Thus is the Gāyatrī of Tvaritā. "Aiṃ, let us know Vāgīśvarī; klīṃ, let us meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; sauḥ, [may she] inspire us."
By the impelling of power:
the Gāyatrī of Kālabhairavī is:
*Aiṃ* we know the Goddess Tripurā; *Klīṃ* we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; *Sauḥ* O you who are moist with longing! *Klinne*.
"May she impel us.
This is the Gāyatrī of Tripurāsundarī.
"We know Tripurā; we meditate upon Bhairavī; may that Goddess impel us."
Thus is the Bhairavī-gāyatrī:
"We know the Great Goddess; we meditate upon Durgā; may that Goddess inspire us.
Thus is the Durgā-gāyatrī.
"Let us know Nārāyaṇī; let us meditate upon Durgā; may Gaurī inspire us.
This is the Jayadurgā-gāyatrī.
"Let us know Mahālakṣmī; let us meditate upon Mahāśrī; may Śrī inspire us."
Thus is the Lakṣmī-gāyatrī:
"We know the Goddess of Speech; we meditate upon the King of Desire; may that Goddess inspire us.
Thus is the Sarasvatī-gāyatrī.
We know Nārāyaṇī; we meditate upon Bhuvaneśvarī; may that Goddess inspire us.
This is the Bhuvaneśvarī-Gāyatrī.
We know the Blessed One; we meditate upon Māheśvarī; may that Annapūrṇā inspire us.
Thus is the Gāyatrī of Annapūrṇā:
"We know Mahiṣamardinī; we meditate upon Durgā; may She, the Terrible One, inspire us.
Thus is the Gāyatrī of Mahiṣamardinī.
"Vairocanīye vidmahe, Chinnamastāyai dhīmahi, tanno devī pracodayāt. This is the Gāyatrī of Chinnamastā. "Kalikāyai vidmahe, Śmaśānavāsinyai dhīmahi, tanno devī pracodayāt."
Thus is the Kālikā-gāyatrī:
"We know Tārā; we meditate upon the most formidable one; may that Goddess impel us.
Thus is the Tārā-gāyatrī.
"Let us know Garuḍa; let us meditate upon Suparṇa; may that Garuḍa inspire us.
Thus is the Gāyatrī of Garuḍa. || 35 ||
As for meditation: at dawn, one should meditate upon Brāhmī, who resembles the rising sun, holds a book and a rosary in her hands,
wears a black antelope skin, and dwells in the starry sky.
At midday:
one should meditate upon the Goddess of dark complexion, four-armed, with hands resplendent with the conch and discus, holding a mace and a lotus, seated upon the solar throne. || 36 ||
In the evening, the ascetic should meditate upon the boon-granting goddess Gāyatrī—
white-complexioned, clad in white garments, seated upon the bull, three-eyed,
and holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a trident, and a human skull.
Meditating on the Goddess as residing in the center of a solar gem, one should practice her worship.
The specific visualization for Tripura and others is as follows:
At dawn, upon the fire-mantra (raṃ) in the ādhāra lotus,
one should contemplate the Goddess in the form of the Vāgbīja, radiant like a mass of lightning.
Her hands were beautiful, holding a flower-arrow, a sugarcane bow, a noose, and a goad;
she had assumed a body by her own will and was composed of the syllables of the Great Vidyā.
At midday, upon the solar disc in the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
one should meditate on the Goddess, whose essence is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), who is as red as liquid lac, and who holds a flower-arrow,
a bow of sugar-cane, a noose, and a goad.
[He is surrounded] on all sides by the thirty-six powers of the principles (tattva-śakti), with his own self as the foremost. || 39 ||
In the evening, when the moon resides in the lotus of the Command (Ājñā), one should meditate upon her who possesses a luster equal to the moon,
who is composed of the seed-syllable of Śakti, who holds a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad,
whose form consists of four syllables, and who is adorned with crystal ornaments.
Having meditated upon the Blessed Lady, who is eternally surrounded by her retinue.
In the case of Tārā and others, however,
having offered the arghya for the Sun with "hrīṃ haṃsaḥ," one should place sandalwood, arka flowers, and aparājitā flowers into a vessel made of copper or similar material.

Having offered the arghya with the mantra: "Svāhā to the glorious Ekajaṭā, who dwells within the rising orb of the sun, and who is ever-arisen as pure consciousness," one should recite the Gāyatrī; this is the specific instruction.
As it is stated in the Nīlatantra:

One should extract [the mantra] ending with "to her who resides in the orb of the rising sun" and "svāhā to her arisen as eternal consciousness"; this is remembered as the mantra. Elsewhere, in the Kālikā-mantra, the word *kālikā* is to be employed in place of the word *ekajaṭā*. || 41 ||
