*Māyā* is Bhuvaneśī; armor (*varma*) is *huṃ*; prosperity (*ṛddhi*) is the letter *kha*; and Īśvara is the letter *e*.
*Kūrma* is the letter *ca*; its final is the letter *cha*. *Bhaga* is the vowel *e*, joined with which [the letter] *kṣa* is formed.

*Strī* is the essential form [of the seed-syllable]. *Dīrghatanucchada* is *huṃ*. *Saṃvarta* is the letter *kṣa*; *bhaga* is the vowel *e*, joined with which [the letter] *kṣa* is formed. Again, *Bhuvaneśvarī* is *phaṭ*. || 73 ||
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Arjuna, the meter (chandas) is Virāṭ, the deity (devatā) is Tvaritā,
and its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of accomplishing the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha).
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
The sage is declared to be Arjuna, the meter is said to be Virāj, and the deity is proclaimed to be Tvaritā, who bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence. || 74 ||
The procedure for its worship (*tvaritāyantra*, Figure 17):
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus upon a purified base, with the *dakṣiṇāmūrti* [mantra] [at the center], and draw a circle of earth-elements (*bhūvindu*) on the outside.
One should write the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) eight times in each of the eight corners;
in the center, one should encircle Bhuvaneśānī with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
This is declared to be the yantra named "The Maker of All Protection" (*sarvarakṣākara*).
Having invoked Maheśānī there, one should worship her with ritual offerings.

Then, having performed the morning rites and completed the ritual actions up to the *nyāsa* on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and so forth, one should install the pedestal-energies (*pīṭhaśakti*) beginning with Jayā as prescribed in the *Bhuvaneśvarī-mantra* upon the filaments; then, in the center, [one installs] "KṢAṂ HŪṂ HAṂ VAJRADEHA GHURU GHURU HIṄGULU HIṄGULU GARJA GARJA HAṂ HŪṂ."
One should place the mantra "KṢĀṂ PAÑCĀNANĀYA NAMAḤ. And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
The *saṃvartaka* (the letter *ha*) joined with the *bindu*, the armor (*ka*), the entire *viyat* (the letter *ha*),

*vajradeha* (the letter *ra*), the pair of *ghuru* (the letters *gha-ra*), and indeed the two *hiṅgulu*s (the letters *ga-gha*). Then "roar, roar" (*garja garja*), *viyat* (the letter *ha*), the moon (*i*), the armor (*ka*), and the final [letter] possessed of a long *bindu* (the letter *au*).
The heart-mantra of Pañcānanā is proclaimed to be the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra). || 76 ||
Then follows the Nyāsa of the Seer and others:
*namaḥ* to the Seer Arjuna on the head; *namaḥ* to the Virāṭ metre on the mouth; *namaḥ* to the deity Tvaritā on the heart.
Then follows the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*):
*oṃ namaḥ* on the head; *huṃ namaḥ* on the forehead; *khe namaḥ* on the throat;
*ca namaḥ* on the heart; *che namaḥ* on the navel; *kṣa namaḥ* on the secret place; *strī namaḥ* on the thighs; and *hūṃ* on the knees.
*Namaḥ* to the two calves; *kṣe namaḥ* to the pair of feet; *phaṭ namaḥ*.
One should perform the pervasive application (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra. || 77 ||
And likewise in the Nibandha:
"One should place the letters, excluding the *māyā* [syllable], on the crown, the forehead, the throat,
the heart, the navel, the secret place, the pair of thighs, and on the knees, shanks, and feet."
Having performed the placement, the practitioner should effect the pervasive [consecration] with the entire [mantra]. || 78 ||
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*ca che aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *che kṣa tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*, *kṣa strī madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ*, *strī huṃ anāmikābhyāṃ huṃ*, *hūṃ kṣe*.
With the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*; with the [two] thumbs, *phaṭ*; and with the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
In this manner, one performs the placement on the heart and other limbs, beginning with "to the heart, *namaḥ*," and so forth.
And thus it is stated in the *Nibandhana*:
The best of practitioners should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using seven syllables beginning with *kūrma*, omitting each preceding one in sequence, by taking them in pairs. (79)
Then comes the meditation:
[one should visualize her] as dark-complexioned, adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, wearing a garment of woven leaves,
her breasts radiant with a necklace of *guñjā* berries, and bearing eight serpents.
I worship the three-eyed Goddess, who has been endowed with the tinkling of bracelets, armlets, girdles, and anklets, and whose hands are raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.

Then, having performed the general worship of the pedestal as prescribed, one should worship Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā upon the filaments of the lotus, in order starting from the east, using mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
In the center: *kṣaṃ hūṃ haṃ vajradeha ghuru ghuru hiṅgulu hiṅgulu garja garja haṃ hūṃ kṣāṃ pañcānanāya namaḥ*.
Then, having meditated as before, perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the other rites.
Having performed the rites up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjalidāna*), one should begin the worship of the protective enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
In the corners beginning with the southeast: *cache gāyatryai hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *chekṣa gāyatryai śirase svāhā*; *kṣastrī gāyatryai śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; *strīhūṃ gāyatryai* [kavacāya huṃ].
"Huṃ for the armor; Hūṃ-kṣe, vauṣaṭ for the three eyes of Gāyatrī;
Kṣe phaṭ in the directions, phaṭ for the weapon of Gāyatrī.
Having thus worshipped, one should worship Praṇītā and Gāyatrī in the north and northeast respectively.
And likewise in the Nibandha:
"One should worship the limb [Aṅga], the Praṇītā, and the Gāyatrī in sequence upon the filaments;
one should worship these [goddesses] on the petals, preceded by the Śrī-bīja and well-adorned."
[He saw] Huṃkārī, Khecarī, Caṇḍā, Chedinī, Kṣepiṇī, and Strī;
Huṃkārī and Kṣemakārī, adorned with weapons in this world;
and Phaṭkārī at the front on the exterior, bearing a bow and arrows.
The mantra is as follows: *Śrīṃ huṃkāryai namaḥ*; on the exterior, in front, *Oṃ phaṭkāriṇyai namaḥ*, and so forth;
on both sides of the door, *Oṃ jayāyai namaḥ* and *Oṃ vijayāyai namaḥ*.
Outside of that, one should worship Kiṅkara with the mantra: "O Kiṅkara, protect, protect! Be firm at the swift command! Huṃ Phaṭ!
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:

On both sides of the door, one should worship Jayā and Vijayā, who hold golden canes and lotuses in their hands; then the words "kiṅkarāya," followed by "rakṣa rakṣa," and at the end of those words, "tvaritājñāsthiro bhava."
Outside that, one should worship the servant (Kiṅkara) with the mantra ending in the armor-weapon (varmāstra) syllables;
he is dark-complexioned, holding a club, and has black, curly hair.
[One should worship him] with wild, reddish flowers that are exceedingly beautiful and fragrant.
"One should worship with incense, lamps, and so forth, with dances, songs, and great festivals.
Herein, there is no worship of Indra and the other deities, because it has not been mentioned. (80 ka)
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings.
For this [mantra], the preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand repetitions.
One should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with fuel-sticks of *vilva* wood, anointed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), numbering one-tenth of that amount.
And so it is said:

Having mastered one hundred thousand [recitations] of this mantra, the knower of mantras who has conquered his senses should perform a fire-oblation with ten parts of the best *vilva* fuel-sticks smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). (82)
Now, the mantra of Nityā:
Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, "Nityaklinne," then "madau" and "drave," followed by Vahni-vadhū (the consort of Fire). This twelve-syllable mantra has thus been declared. (83)
The procedure for her worship is as follows:

having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa), one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the filaments in the order starting from the east with the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of all powers" (hrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ), ending with Jayā and the others.
One should perform the Nyāsa of the Seer and the rest as follows:
*Namaḥ* to the Seer Sammohana on the head; *namaḥ* to the Nivṛt-chandas on the mouth; [and] on the heart...
Salutation to the eternal deity.
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"The seer is Sammohana, the meter is Nivṛt, and the deity is Nityā. || 84 ||
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*aiṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *aiṃ tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*, *aiṃ madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ*, *aiṃ anāmikābhyāṃ huṃ*, *aiṃ*.
With the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*; with the palms and backs of the hands, *aiṃ phaṭ*.
In this manner, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the six limbs, beginning with the heart, using the formula *aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"Having performed the six ancillaries with speech, one should meditate on the Nityā according to the rule. (85)
Then the meditation:
[She who has] the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, who is ruddy in hue, who is saluted by the immortals,
and who holds in her hands a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a full skull-cup.
One should meditate upon the consort of Śiva, whose limbs are overwhelmed with intoxication, possessing three eyes and adorned with red unguents, garments, and ornaments.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) and worshipped the pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśaktis), such as Jayā and others, in the filaments (keśaras), one should worship in the center with the mantra ending in "hrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ. Having meditated again, [one should perform] the rites from invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali).
Having performed the visualization, one should begin the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*):
(The Nityā Yantra, Figure 18).
It is as follows:

In the four corners beginning with the southeast, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions: *aiṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *aiṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *aiṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *aiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; in the center, *aiṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; and in the four cardinal directions, *aiṃ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*.

On the eight petals, one should worship with the mantra beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*: *Oṃ nityāyai namaḥ*, *nirañjanāyai*, *klinnāyai*, *kledinyai*, *madanāturāyai*, *madadravāyai*, *drāviṇyai*, *draviṇyai*.
One should perform the worship everywhere using this formula.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"Nityā, Nirañjanā, Klinnā, Kledinī, Madanāturā,
Madadravā, Drāviṇī, and Draviṇī— these are the eight powers."
"Her hands are enriched with a blue lotus and a skull-cup, and she possesses the luster of a clinging lotus.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the incense offering up to the dismissal. || 87 ||
The preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of four hundred thousand repetitions.
And so it is said:
"Having performed four hundred thousand recitations, [one should offer oblations] with *madhūka* flowers smeared with honey."
Having offered ten thousand oblations with flowers, he should satisfy his own guru.
Now, the mantras of Vajraprastāriṇī:
immediately after the *vāṅmāyā* [syllables], the mantra "nityaklinne madadrave svāhā" consists of twelve syllables and bestows subjugation (*vaśya*). (89)
The yantra for her worship consists of a hexagon, a twelve-petaled lotus, four gates, and a square. || 90 ||

(Plate 19) Then, having performed the worship beginning with the morning rites and ending with the placement on the pedestal (*pīṭhanyāsa*), [one should place the deities] in the filaments (*keśara*).
Having performed the placement [of mantras] from Jayā up to the Pīṭha-mantra, one should perform the placement of the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth:
"Salutation to Aṅgiras, the seer, on the head; salutation to Triṣṭubh, the meter, on the mouth; salutation to Vajraprastāriṇī, the deity, on the heart."
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"The sage is said by the sages to be Aṅgiras; the metre is Dṛṣi-triṣṭubh;
and the deity is declared to be Vajraprastāriṇī, the bestower of desired boons. (91)

Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs: "Aiṃ, salutation to the two thumbs," and so forth; and with "Aiṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth, [the assignment] is made upon the heart and other parts.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"The best among those who know mantras should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (92)
Then the meditation:
seated within a red lotus with eight petals upon a red boat in a red ocean,
she has red eyes, a crescent moon shimmering upon her red crown, a smiling face, and three eyes.
We take refuge in Ambika, whose body is bent by the weight of her breasts, who holds in her hands a citron, a noose, a goad, the bow of Madana, and excellent skull-cups, and who is stooping low. 93.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the installation of the conch as before, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), and having meditated again,
one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañca-puṣpāñjali*).
One should begin the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
Having worshipped in the intermediate corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions with "Aiṃ, obeisance to the Heart" and so forth,
one should worship on the twelve petals in order starting from the east with "Oṃ, obeisance to Hṛllekhā."

In this manner, one should worship Kledinī, Klinnā, Kṣobhiṇī, Madanāturā, Nirañjanā, Rāgavatī, Madanāvatī, Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, Vegavatī, and Smarā, everywhere using the formula beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"Hṛllekhā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Kṣobhiṇī, Madanāturā,
Nirañjanā, Rāgavatī, and the seventh, Madanāvatī."
Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, Paścātvegavatī, and Aparasmara— these Śaktis, holding skull-bowls and lotuses, have red bodies. Outside of that, one should worship the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements.
Accordingly, it is stated in the Nibandha:
"The Mothers are to be worshipped in the cardinal and intermediate directions; furthermore, the lords of the directions are to be worshipped."
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 93ka ||
The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa).
And so it is said:
"The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, he should then perform a fire-oblation."
Ten thousand oblations should be offered with the best fuel-sticks from the rājavṛkṣa tree, sprinkled with ghee;
the rājavṛkṣa is the śoṇālu.
Now, regarding the difficult mantras:
next, I shall describe the Durgā-mantra which bestows both seen and unseen fruits.

[The seed-syllable] preceded by *māyā* (the letter *i*), joined with the mountain (*ga*), the ear (*ra*), and the bindu (*m*), and further endowed with the creative emission (*visarga*), becomes [the mantra].
The mantra ending in the five [vowels] (pañcāntaka), possessing the *pratiṣṭhā* [vowel], having *māruta* as its seat and the *bhautika* [vowel] as its base,
beginning with *tāra* and ending with *hṛdaya*, consists of eight syllables.
Here, *adri* is the letter *da*, *karṇa* is the letter *u*, *pañcāntaka* is the letter *ga*, and *pratiṣṭhā*...
The letter *ya* is Māruto; the letter *ai* is Bhūtika.
(Another measure): Tāra, Māyā, and its own seed-syllable, followed by "to Durgā" and the heart-mantra.
Thus says Bhaṭṭa. || 95 ||
The procedure for her worship is as follows:

having performed the rites from the morning duties up to the placement of the throne (pīṭhanyāsa), one should place the powers of the throne (pīṭhaśaktis) upon the filaments and the center of the heart-lotus.
Namely: Āṃ to Prabhā; Īṃ to Māyā; Ūṃ to Jayā; Eṃ to Sūkṣmā; Aiṃ to Viśuddhā; Oṃ to Nandinī; Auṃ to Suprabhā; Aṃ to Vijayā; Aḥ.
To the giver of all accomplishments, *namaḥ* everywhere.
Above that, one should place: *oṃ vajranakhadaṃṣṭrāyudhāya mahāsiṃhāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha: "Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, and again Nandinī,
Suprabhā, Vijayā, and Sarvasiddhidā— these are the nine Śaktis."

One should worship these [deities] with the vowels, excluding the three short ones and the neuter [e and o]. Following the *praṇava* (oṃ), the mantra for the Lion is considered to be: "To the one whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs, to the Great Lion," ending with the armor-syllable (*vaṃ*) and followed by the salutation (*namaḥ*).
One should offer a seat with this [mantra], and one should fashion the form with the root mantra. || 96 ||
Then follows the Nyāsa of the Seer and so forth, as follows:
*namaḥ* to Nārada, the Seer, on the head; *namaḥ* to Gāyatrī, the Metre, on the mouth; [and] *namaḥ* to the Heart on the heart.
Salutation to the goddess Durgā.
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"The seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra is Nārada, the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, and the deity (devatā) is Manu."
Durgā is proclaimed by the virtuous as the one who wards off the removal of misfortune. || 97 ||
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*hrāṃ oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*, *hrūṃ oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai*.
To the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *hraim oṃ hrīṃ duṃ* to Durgā, to the two ring fingers, *huṃ*; *hrauṃ duṃ* to Durgā, to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*;
*hraḥ oṃ hrīṃ duṃ* to Durgā, to the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
In the same way, for the heart and other limbs, one should recite *hrāṃ oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai namaḥ*, and so forth.
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"The practitioner [should worship] with the root mantra, even when devoid of the word of salutation (*namaskāra*)."
One should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) according to the prescribed rule, together with *hrām* and the other [syllables]. || 98 ||
Then comes the meditation: she is seated upon a lion, crowned with the moon, resembling emerald in hue, adorned with three eyes, and holding a conch, a discus, a bow, and an arrow in her four arms.

May Durgā—the remover of misfortune—be for your protection; she whose bracelets, necklaces, and bangles are fastened, whose girdle tinkles and whose anklets jingle, and who shines with jeweled earrings.
Having meditated thus and worshipped her mentally, one should perform the installation of the conch. (99)

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*), [one worships] in the filaments and in the center: *Āṃ* to Prabhā, *Īṃ* to Māyā, *Uṃ* to Jayā, *Eṃ* to Sūkṣmā, *Aiṃ* to Viśuddhā, *Oṃ* to Nandinī, *Auṃ* to Suprabhā, *Aṃ* to Vijayā, and *Aḥ* to Sarvasiddhidā; above that—
One should worship with the mantra: "Homage to the Great Lion, whose weapons are diamond claws and fangs, hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
And likewise:
One should worship these [deities] with seed-syllables (ajp) excluding the three short vowels and the neuter ones.

Following the *praṇava* (oṃ), the mantra for the Lion is considered to be: "To the one whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs, to the Great Lion," ending with the armor syllable (*vaṃ*) and followed by the salutation (*namaḥ*). This is the Lion-mantra.
One should offer a seat with this [mantra] and fashion the form with the root mantra.
Then, having meditated again and performed the rites beginning with invocation up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers, one should commence the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
Namely:
one should worship with "hrāṃ oṃ hrīṃ duṃ, obeisance to the heart of Durgā," and so forth, in the southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast, the center, and the cardinal directions. || 100 ||
Then, on the petals: *jaṃ* for Jayā, *viṃ* for Vijayā, *kīṃ* for Kīrti, *prīṃ* for Prīti, *praṃ* for Prabhā, *śraṃ* for Śraddhā, *śruṃ* for Śruti, and *maṃ* for Medhā.
On the petals: *oṃ* for the conch, the discus, the mace, the sword, the noose, and the goad.
To the bow and the arrow;
outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense up to the final dismissal.
The preliminary rite for this [mantra] consists of reciting it eight hundred thousand times.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times with sesame seeds soaked in honey."
Or, one who has conquered the senses may offer a thousand oblations of milk-rice;
by that, the eight-thousand oblation prescribed by the sacred texts is accomplished.
Now, the mantras of Mahiṣamardinī as given in the Śāradā-tantra:
the radiant sky [H] with eyes [Ī], followed by "white" [Ś], "O crusher! [MARDINI], and two *ṭha*s [ṬHA ṬHA].
The eight-syllabled mantra of Mahiṣamardinī is proclaimed as follows in the Nārāyaṇī Tantra:
*viṣa hi majjā kālo'gniradriristho ni ṭha dvayam*.

The syllable *ma* is poison (*viṣa*); the syllable *ya* is the marrow (*majjā*), which is its own nature; the syllable *ma* is time (*kāla*); the letter *ra* is fire (*agni*); the letter *da* is the mountain (*adri*); and because it is said to be "joined with *i*" (*istha*), the letter *da* is joined with the vowel *i*.
This nine-syllable mantra begins with Tārā, or Māyā, or Kāmā, or Vāgbhava, or the Seed of the Bride (Vadhūvīja), or Kavaca. || 3 ||
And so it is stated in the Viśvasāra:
"The wise man should recite the vidyā beginning with the Praṇava, or he should recite it beginning with Māyā;
or likewise, he should recite it beginning with the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū-bīja), or beginning with the Kavaca."
At all times and in all places, the wise one should recite me, beginning with the syllable *Ā*.
One should recite that Goddess beginning with the *Vāgbhava* syllable for the purification of speech.
Without the seed-syllables (*bījas*), the Great Vidyā is proclaimed to be devoid of power.
Enclosed by a pair of seed-syllables at the beginning and at the end of the pair of locations,
there is no ten-syllable Vidyā equal to this Mistress of the Three Worlds.
Furthermore, with the Praṇava and Māyā added, the Vidyā becomes ten syllables again.
The Kāma is said to be the Praṇava, while the Vidyā consists of ten syllables. || 4 ||
The worship of these [deities] consists of the following:
one should perform the placement [of mantras] upon the seat (pīṭha) starting with the morning rites;
then, having performed the previously mentioned placement of the sages (ṛṣi) and so forth, one should perform the placements on the hands and the limbs (karāṅganyāsa). || 5 ||
Namely:
*mahiṣahiṃsike hūṃ phaṭ*—homage to the two thumbs;
*mahiṣaśatrośārvi hūṃ phaṭ*—svāhā to the two index fingers; *mahiṣaṃ heṣaya*.
HŪṂ PHAṬ with the two middle fingers, VAṢAṬ; "Slay, slay the buffalo, O Goddess!
HŪṂ PHAṬ" with the two ring fingers, HŪṂ; "O Slayer of the Buffalo! HŪṂ PHAṬ" with the two little fingers, PHAṬ.
In this manner, for the heart-mantra and others, such as *mahiṣahiṃsike hūṃ phaṭ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth;
likewise, wherever there are five limbs of a mantra, one should exclude the eyes (*netra*).
One should perform the five-limbed rite devoid of the eyes.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"HŪṂ PHAṬ for the slayer of buffaloes is proclaimed as the heart;
MAHIṢATROŚĀRVI HŪṂ is declared to be the head."
"Mahiṣaṃ heṣaya"—this pair ending in *hūṃ phaṭ* is for the tuft (*śikhā*).
"Mahiṣaṃ hana" followed by a pair [of syllables] at the end, O Goddess, *hūṃ phaṭ*, is the armor (*tanucchada*).
At the end of "Mahiṣa," [followed by] "sūdani *hūṃ phaṭ*" is declared to be the weapon (*astra*). (5 ka)
Then comes the meditation:
I bow to her who resembles a garuḍa-stone, adorned with a jeweled crown and earrings,
possessing an eye in her forehead, and seated upon the severed head of Mahiṣa.
She who bears upon her own arms a conch, a discus, a sword, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a trident, and a threatening gesture, and who has the moon as her crest-ornament.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the placement of the *arghya* water and the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), one should worship the previously mentioned pedestal-mantra both in the center and upon the *kaśara* grasses.
Regarding the *arghya* vessel, the *Viśvasāra* states:
"One should worship the Goddess as one worships Kālī; one shall obtain the fruit as one does when worshipping Kālī.
One should never worship the Goddess with Vaiṣṇavas, nor ever with *tulasī*."
"A vessel for the *arghya* offering should not be made of conch-shell; this was declared by the Lotus-born [Brahmā]. One may worship Śiva with a vessel of Viśvāmitra or even one made of clay.
From this statement, the prohibition of the conch-shell follows. (7)
Having meditated again and performed the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali),
one should commence the worship of the protective enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
One should worship the limbs (aṅga) in the directions starting from the southeast (agni), as before.
Then, on the petals starting from the east and so forth: *Āṃ* salutation to Durgā; *Īṃ* to Varavarṇinī; *Ūṃ* to Āryā; *Ṛṃ* to Kanakapratibhā; *Ḷṃ* to Kṛttikā; *Aiṃ* to Abhayapradā;
*Auṃ* to Kanyā; *Aḥ* to Surūpā.
Likewise, in another tantra: "First Durgā, then Varavarṇinī, the one called Mādhyaṃkā,
Kanakapratibhā, Kṛttikā, and Abhayapradā."
And one should worship a maiden of beautiful form, starting from the east in due order;
for these [deities], there is the substitution of the long vowel for the initial [consonant]. || 8 ||

"One should worship the goddesses beginning with *Duḥ* and preceded by long vowels on the eight petals," because it is stated thus in the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*, and also because of the statement in the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "In sequence, with the long vowels. (9)

On the tips of the petals: *yaṃ* for the discus (*cakra*), *raṃ* for the conch (*śaṅkha*), *laṃ* for the sword (*khaḍga*), *vaṃ* for the shield (*kheṭaka*), *śaṃ* for the arrow (*bāṇa*), *ṣaṃ* for the bow (*dhanus*), *saṃ* for the trident (*śūla*), and *haṃ* for the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
The word *namaḥ* is to be applied everywhere.
And likewise in the Nibandha:
"One should worship the weapons— the discus, conch, sword,
and shield— along with the arrow, bow, trident, and the threatening gesture— at the tips [of the fingers], in sequence, using the letters beginning with *ya*."
One should worship Brāhmī and the others at the tips of the petals.
Then, outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements, in the cardinal directions.
Thereafter, one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the offering of incense and ending with the dismissal of the deities.
And so it is said in the Kulacuḍāmaṇi:
"Thereafter, one should perform the practice consisting of the Siddhas, including Brāhmī and the others, then the world-protectors outside of that, and then the armor. (10)
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times and performing a fire oblation (*homa*) of eight thousand sesame seeds.
As it is said:
"One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times and perform [an oblation] with auspicious sesame seeds one thousand times."
Because of such statements as these. || 11 ||
Prior to the offering of the *japa*, one should draw a triangular mandala in the northern direction and present the oblation (*bali*), reciting:
"Come, come! Grasp, grasp! [the two words] twice."
And for my own offering, O Goddess, [the mantra is] "lulāpakapadadvayam" (the two words beginning with *lulāpa*).
One should utter "sādhaya" twice, then "khādaya" twice; thereafter, one should say "sarvaṃ siddhipadaṃ dehi" and then the word "svāhā."
This mantra for the offering of the sacrifice (bali) is proclaimed as that of Mardinī. || 12 ||

Now, the mantras of Jayadurgā: *Tāra* (Oṃ), *Durga*, the pair [of consonants] *Ra* and *Kta*, followed by *Locana* (Na), ending with *Sva* (Sa), and concluding with *Dviṭha* (Svāhā)—this ten-syllabled vidyā of Jayadurgā is to be known. (13)

The worship of this [deity] is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth, including the ritual actions prescribed in the Durgā-mantra up to the placement of the ṛṣi and others (ṛṣyādinyāsa), one should perform the placements on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa).

Oṃ Durge, salutation to the two thumbs; Durge, svāhā to the two index fingers; Vaṣaṭ to Durgā with the two middle fingers; Huṃ to Bhūtarakṣaṇī with the two ring fingers; Oṃ Durge Durge Akṣaṇi, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers; Oṃ Durge Durge.
With the palms and backs of the hands, [one performs] protection at the heart and other locations; *phaṭ*. || 14ka ||
Then comes the meditation:
[one should visualize her] with the luster of a dark cloud, inspiring fear in enemies with her side-long glances, with a crescent moon bound upon her crest,
holding in her hands a conch, a discus, a sword, and a trident, and possessing three eyes.

One should meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, who is seated upon the shoulders of a lion, filling the entire three worlds with her splendor, surrounded by the thirty gods, and served by those desiring spiritual perfection.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should prepare the place for the *arghya* water.
Then, having performed the previously mentioned worship of the *pīṭha*, one should perform the worship as before.

The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of five hundred thousand recitations (*japa*). The fire-offering (*homa*) should consist of one-tenth that number, performed with clarified butter.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:

"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with the aim of [hitting] a banana tree, and thereafter offer oblations of clarified butter in the consecrated fire for one-tenth that amount; one should also feed Brahmins."
On the pedestal described as having eight syllables, the wise one should perform worship as before.
Now, the mantras of Śūlinī:
at the end of the words *jvala jvala*, the word *śūlanita* follows;
then, ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) *duṣṭagraha-hūm*, the mantra concludes with the fire-seed-syllable (*vahni-bīja*).
It is said that [this mantra], consisting of the elements, the senses, and the imperishable, brings about the destruction of seizing spirits and minor ailments. || 17 ||
For her worship, having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the *pīṭhanyāsa* as prescribed for the Durgā-mantra, one should perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*.
As follows:
Salutation to the sage Dīrghatapas on the head; salutation to the Kakup meter on the face; salutation to the deity Śūlinī on the heart.
(From the Nibandha:)
The sage is declared to be Dīrghatapas; Kakubha is cited as the metre;
Śūlinī, who is worshipped by all the gods, is declared to be the deity. || 18 ||
Then one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs as follows:
"O Śūlinī Durgā, huṃ phaṭ, salutation to both thumbs; O Śūlinī Varadā, huṃ phaṭ, svāhā to both index fingers; O Śūlinī Vindhyavāsinī, huṃ phaṭ..."

*Vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers; *O Śūlinī, O enemy of the Asuras, O lover of battle, terrify, terrify! Huṃ phaṭ!* with the two ring fingers; *Huṃ! O Śūlinī, well-worshipped by gods and Siddhas, O Nandinī, protect, protect, O Mahāyogeśvarī! Huṃ phaṭ!* with the two little fingers; *phaṭ*.
The same applies to the heart and the other limbs.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha: "O Durgā, [the mantra] 'hṛdvarade' is for the heart; 'śīrṣe vindhyavāsini' is for the head; and 'tat' is for the crest-mantra (śikhā)."
O beloved, [the mantra] should be preceded by battle; then "mardini" at the end of the *asura* [syllables],
followed again by "trāsaya" twice, then the armor (*varma*), and finally "devasiddhasupūjite," "nandini" joined with "rakṣa," and "mahāyogeśvari" in sequence.
The five mantras beginning with Śūlinī and ending with Huṃ Phaṭ are indeed [to be recited] in sequence. || 19 ||

Then the meditation: [One should meditate upon her] mounted upon a lion, dark as a water-laden cloud, carrying in her lotus-like hands a trident, an arrow, a sword, a discus, a lotus, a mace, a bow, and a noose.

I meditate upon the wielder of the trident, who has the moon as her crest-jewel, possesses three eyes, and is served by four maidens bearing swords and shields, and who strikes terror into her adversaries.
Having thus meditated and worshipped with mental offerings, one should prepare the vessel for the *arghya* water. Then:

Having performed the previously mentioned worship of the seat (pīṭha-pūjā), having meditated again, and having carried out the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañca-puṣpāñjali-dāna),
one should begin the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-pūjā).
Namely:

one should worship the five limbs as previously described, beginning with "O Śūlinī, O Durgā, huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the heart," in the directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Īśāna, and the intermediate points.
Then, on the leaves starting from the east and so forth: *oṃ durgāyai namaḥ*, and likewise for *varadāyai*, *vindhyavāsinyai*, *asurabhardinyai*, *yuddhapriyāyai*, *devasiddhasupūjitāyai*,
*nandinyai*, and *mahāyogeśvaryai*.
Then, one should worship those weapons upon the tips of the petals. || 21 ||
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"Having performed the worship of the limbs, the Śaktis to be worshipped on the petals are Durgā and the others—
Varadā, Vindhyavāsinī, Asuramardinī," and so forth.
The fifth [petal] should be Yuddhapriyā, well-worshipped by gods and siddhas;
the seventh is called Nandinī, the supreme Mahāyogeśvarī.
On the tips of the petals are her weapons: the conch, the discus, and again the sword.
[He assigned] the mace, arrow, bow, and trident, as well as the noose, to the presiding deities of the western direction.
Then one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense (dhūpa) up to the dismissal (visarjana).
The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of fifteen lakhs of recitations.
And so it is said:
The wise mantra-practitioner should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times;
the fire-oblation (homa) should consist of ghee or food, and it should be performed to the extent of one-tenth of that number.
Now, the mantras of Vāgīśvarī.
Next, I shall describe her whose body consists of the phonemes (varṇa), she who awakens universal consciousness;
for when she is not perceived, this entire world is insentient.
"Vada vada vāgvādini vahnivallabhā"—this is the ten-syllable mantra. || 23 ||
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"The mountain (a) is conjoined with Varuṇa (va), then 'da', 'vāgvādini' (vā), and two 'ṭha's;
this ten-syllable mantra of Sarasvatī bestows the sovereignty of speech."
This [mantra], encapsulated by Bhuvaneśī, bestows the great Sarasvatī. || 24 ||
The worship diagram for this [goddess] is as follows:
it has the sky (the letter *ha*) and the moon (*a*) as its pericarp; its filaments shimmer with pairs of vowels;
within its petals are the five groups of consonants (*ka* to *ma*), the *ya-śalā* group, and the *ja-bh-iva* group, respectively.
The Yantra, surrounded by the earth (Kṣauṇī) and joined with the letters *la* and *laṅgali* in the three directions of Āśā,
is said to be superior to the body of the syllables (*varṇatanu*) and bestows all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*). (Figure 20) Its worship is as follows:
Having performed the rites beginning with *prātaḥkṛtya* up to the end of the *pīṭhanyāsa*, one should place [the mantras] on the filaments (*keśara*), in the center, and in the cardinal directions:
*oṃ medhāyai namaḥ*; likewise for *prajñā*, *prabhā*, *vidyā*, *śrī*, *dhṛti*, *smṛti*, *buddhi*, and *vidyeśvarī*. In the center, [one places] *varṇapadmāsanāya*.
Homage everywhere! 26.
Then, the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth:
on the head, "Salutation to Kaṇva the seer"; if it is enclosed by the syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ), "Salutation to Bṛhaspati the seer.
On the mouth, "Salutation to Virāj the meter."
In the heart, salutation to the deity Vāgīśvarī. || 27 ||
Now, the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa):
*vaṃ* on the head, *namaḥ*;
on the two ears, *daṃ namaḥ* and *vaṃ namaḥ*.
To the two eyes, *daṃ* homage to you;
*namaḥ*. To the two nostrils, *gvāṃ* homage; *diṃ* homage. To the mouth, *niṃ* homage.
At the linga: svāṃ, obeisance.
At the secret place: hāṃ, obeisance.
Then, having performed the placement of the Mātṛkās on the hands and limbs, one should meditate. || 28 ||
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"Having assigned these syllables to the head, ears, eyes, nose, mouth, navel, and anus, one should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga) as taught in the Mātṛkā. (29)
Then comes the meditation:
She possesses the pure luster of the full moon in its youth; her body is bent by the weight of her breasts, and she sits upon a white lotus.
May the Goddess of Speech protect us, she whose splendor is a book held in her own lotus-hand as a writing brush, for the attainment of all prosperity and success.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual installation of the conch.

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), one should worship Medhā and the others, starting from the filaments (keśara) and the center and extending to the directions, up to the end of the mantra; then, having meditated again and performed the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), one should perform the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
In the southeast: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ*, salutation to the Heart (*hṛdayāyai namaḥ*). In the southwest: *iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ*, *svāhā* to the Head (*śirase svāhā*).
In the northwest: *uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ*, *vaṣaṭ* to the Crest-lock (*śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*).
In the northeast: *Eṃ Taṃ Thaṃ Daṃ Dhaṃ Naṃ Aiṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *Hūṃ*.
In the center: *Oṃ Paṃ Phaṃ Baṃ Bhaṃ Maṃ Auṃ* for the three eyes (*netratraya*), *Vauṣaṭ*.
In the directions: *Aṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃ Laṃ Kṣaṃ Aḥ*.
*Astrāya phaṭ.* On the petals, starting from the east: *Oṃ yogāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ satyāyai namaḥ*, and likewise to Vimalā, Jñānā, Buddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, and Prajñā.
On the tips of the petals, the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped.
As it says in the Nibandha:
"The Mothers beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped [with mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*."
And thus:
having first worshipped the limbs, one should afterwards worship these powers:
Yoga, Satya, Vimalā, Jñānā, Buddhi, and again Smṛti.
Having worshipped Medhā and Prajñā according to the ritual, holding a seal and a book on the petals, and having worshipped Brāhmī and the others on the tips of the petals,
the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be honored outside, and their weapons outside of them.
Thus, from the *Prapañcasāra*:
"Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and the other [emblems]. (31)
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings.
The preliminary requirement (*puraścaraṇa*) for this is ten hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).
And so it is said:

One should recite the mantra one million times; thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number, using white lotuses smeared with milk, or sesame seeds soaked in honey.
Now, for another mantra:
at the end of the heart [seed-syllable], one should extract the pair of words "bhagavati vada," followed by "vāgdevi" ending with the wife of fire (svāhā),
preceded by the vāgbhava [syllable].
Manu consists of sixteen syllables and bestows the fruit of mastery over speech. || 33 ||
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:

having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa), one should place the previously mentioned powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis) and the mantra of the seat in the filaments and in the center. || 34 ||
Then, having performed the previously mentioned nyāsa of the ṛṣis and so forth, one should perform the nyāsa of the hands and limbs as follows: *aiṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*.
Homage to the two index fingers, svāhā!
O Blessed One, to the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ!
Speak, speak, to the two ring fingers, hūṃ!
To Vāgdevī with the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*;
to Svāhā with the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
In this same manner for the heart and the other [limbs].
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"With six words of the mantra, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) conjoined with the [six] classes. (35)

Then the meditation: [She is] white, with clear ointments, garlands, and garments, radiant with a piece of yellow silk, holding in her lotus-hands the gesture of exposition, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and the Vidyā.

I salute the goddess of speech, who rests upon a lotus-seat, whose breasts are like tender creepers, who is smiling, who possesses three eyes, who bestows the power of eloquence, and who grants the wealth of good fortune.
Having thus meditated and worshipped her mentally, one should perform the consecration of the conch. (36)
Then one should perform worship according to the previously mentioned sequence;
however, there is a specific distinction regarding the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra).
For this [mantra], the preliminary practice consists of reciting it eight hundred thousand times.
And likewise:
"Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times with undistracted mind;
at the end, one should offer oblations ten times that number with sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter. (37)
The other mantra consists of Tāra, Māyādhara, Vinduśakti, Tāra, Sarava, and Tī followed by the feminine suffix -ṅe;
this eleven-syllable mantra is thus proclaimed. (38)

Its worship is as follows: having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement of the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) as previously described, one should perform the previously mentioned nyāsa of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth. || 39 ||
Then follows the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa): Oṃ namaḥ to the aperture of Brahmā;
Hrīṃ namaḥ between the eyebrows.
At the eyes: Aiṃ namaḥ, Hrīṃ namaḥ. At the ears: Oṃ namaḥ, Saṃ namaḥ. At the nostrils: Raṃ namaḥ, Svaṃ namaḥ. At the mouth: Tyaiṃ namaḥ.
Namaḥ to Naṃ at the penis;
namaḥ to Maṃ at the secret place. || 40 ||
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *Aiṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*Aiṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
Aiṃ, vaṣaṭ phaṭ to the two middle fingers;
likewise, huṃ to the two ring fingers;
aiṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers.
Aiṃ, phaṭ with both palms and backs of the hands.
Likewise for the heart and other limbs: Aiṃ, obeisance to the heart (hṛdayāya namaḥ), and so forth.
And thus it is stated in the Nibandha:

The practitioner of the mantra should sequentially place the syllables of the mantra at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), between the eyebrows, and in the nine apertures; the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) is performed with the Vāgbhava syllable.
Then comes meditation:
[one should meditate on] Vāṇī, whose face is radiant like the full moon, possessing the luster of camphor and the kunda flower,
her head marked by the crescent moon, and who respectfully holds [various objects] with her own hands.
I worship her who holds a lute, a rosary, and a jar brimming with nectar; who possesses lofty breasts, whose body is adorned with divine ornaments, and who is mounted upon a swan.
Having meditated thus and worshipped her mentally, one should perform the installation of the conch.

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), one should worship the previously mentioned pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśaktis) in the filaments and in the center, as well as the mantra of the pedestal (piṭhamantra).
Then, having meditated once more, [one should perform the rites] up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā), one should begin.
To the right of the Goddess: Oṃ, salutation to Saṃskṛtā Vāṅmayī.
To the left: Oṃ, salutation to Prākṛtā Vāṅmayī.

Then, upon the filaments: in the southeast, *aiṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; in the southwest, *aiṃ śirase svāhā*; in the northwest, *aiṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; in the northeast, *aiṃ kavacāya huṃ*; in the center, *aiṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*; and in the cardinal directions, *aiṃ astrāya phaṭ*.
Then, on the petals starting from the east, one should worship Prajñā, Medhā, Śruti, Śakti, Smṛti,
Vāgīśvarī, Mati, and Svasti, everywhere with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, on the tips of the petals, the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"To the right of the Goddess, the auspicious Saṃskṛta Vāṅmayī is to be worshipped;
to the left, the auspicious Prākṛta Vāṅmayī is always to be worshipped."
As before, one should worship the limbs; then again, one should worship Prajñā and the others:
Prajñā, Medhā, Śruti, Śakti, Smṛti, Vāgīśvarī, Mati, and Svasti—these are declared to be Brāhmī and the others that follow.
Then, outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Thereafter, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense and so forth until the final dismissal. || 43 ||
The *puraścaraṇa* for this consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations;
and thus it is said:
"One should recite twelve hundred thousand [times], and likewise offer a thousand white lotuses."
Or the supreme practitioner should offer oblations with nāga and campaka flowers. || 44 ||
Another mantra is found in the *Śāradā*:
"O Vācaspati, O Immortal, may there be further floating, further floating"—this should be proclaimed.
This other mantra, beginning with *vāk*, is said to consist of eleven syllables (the number of Rudras). (45)
His worship and other rites are as before.
However, for the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), [the mantras are]: *aiṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*vācaspate* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
*Vaṣaṭ* to *Amṛta* with the two middle fingers;
*Huṃ* to *Pluvaḥ* with the two ring fingers; *Phaṭ* to *Pluḥ* with the two little fingers.
In the same way, [the procedure applies] to the heart and the other [limbs]. || 46 ||
And likewise in the Nibandha: "One should perform the limbs according to the rule with the five words beginning with 'vāk'. (46ka)
As for the meditation:
she sits upon a lotus, holding a rosary, two lotuses, and a book in her hands;
her crown is adorned with the crescent moon, and her radiance is like that of pearls, moonlight, and jasmine.
May the Goddess of Speech—who has eyes half-closed at her forehead, who is weary from the weight of her breasts, and who is constantly attended by hosts of sages—be for your protection. (47)
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of eleven lakhs of recitations.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one lakh times for Rudra, and offer oblations of clarified butter ten times that amount. (48)
And so it is stated in the Śāradā-tilaka:
"The bed of Viṣṇu situated in water consists of the four-faced one (Brahmā) together with Kevala;
[then] Vahni joined with Arghīśa and Indu; and Bhṛgu possessing Bindu, Satya, and Ambu."
The wise have declared three seed-syllables for the prayer to Sarasvatī:
the syllable *va* is water; the syllable *ā* is the bed of Viṣṇu; and with that, together with the letter *ka* alone, devoid of a vowel, one obtains speech (*vāk*).
The ultimate meaning is "Vāgbhava.
Some, however, explain it thus out of fear of the fault of *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication based on a further indication):
the letter *va* joined with the vowel *ā*, and the letter *ka* which curls at its head as a solitary *anusvāra*; by that [which is] so endowed...
Because it exists together with the letter *ka*, it is [called] *kvā*; since this is equivalent in power to a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), "vāk-vāgbhava" is a synonym.
However, in reality:

Having extracted the twelfth vowel, adorned with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, one should extract the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*. One should extract the second seed-syllable joined with the sixth vowel.
"Having extracted the seed-syllable of the Moon (ca), one should then join it with the [seed] of Varuṇa (va);
mounted upon the thirteenth vowel and adorned with the Bindu and Nāda"—according to this statement from the Viśvasāra, this is indeed the Vāgbhava-bīja. (49)
The worship of this [deity] is as before.
However, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) should be performed with the three seed-syllables uttered twice:
*aiṃ* to the two thumbs (*aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*), *rūṃ* to the two index fingers (*tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*), and *svauṃ*...
"Vaṣaṭ with the two middle fingers," and so forth.
And likewise in the Nibandha:
"The practitioner of mantra should fashion the limbs [of the deity] using [the mantras] repeated twice and joined with their respective classes. (50)
One should meditate on her as being as white as a string of pearls, adorned with a crescent moon upon her head,
and holding in her own arms a book, a rosary of variegated colors, a jar filled with jewels, and a fly-whisk.
"I praise the Sovereign of Speech, who sits upon a lotus, whose waist shines with the weight of her full and lofty breasts, and who has for a long time been bowed down by the three worlds.
Having meditated thus, one should worship as before. || 51 ||
The preliminary practice for this consists of reciting it three hundred thousand times.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and perform oblations with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter in the consecrated fire, using one-tenth of that number. (52)
Now, the mantra of Pārijātasarasvatī,
as given in the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*: it consists of the syllables *ha*, *sa*, *au*, and the *bindu*, enclosed within the *praṇava* (oṃ) and *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ).
The word *sarasvatī* ending in *ṅi* (locative singular) and the word *nati* [are also included]. || 53 ||
The worship of this [mantra] is as follows:
having performed the morning rites and so forth up to the placement of the *pīṭha-mantra*, one should perform the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the rest:
"Salutation to Kaṇva, the seer, on the head; salutation to Triṣṭubh, the meter, on the mouth; [salutation to] Pārijāta on the heart."
Salutation to Sarasvatī. || 54 ||
Then one should perform the placement of the hands and limbs as taught by the Mother (Mātṛkā).
The placement of the ten syllables is performed on the head, the space between the eyebrows, the eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the private parts, and the feet.
(Then one should perform the placement on the hands and limbs with "Hsāṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ" and so forth; everything else is as before. || 55 ||
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā, however, it is said:
"O Goddess, the knower of mantras should write the seed-syllable Vāgbhava of Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity,
having encapsulated it with the Tāra [Om] and the Parā [Hrīm]."
This mantra for Sarasvatī, ending with the heart [seed-syllable] and consisting of eleven Rudra-syllables, is thus declared.
In the *Prapañcasāra*:
"Sarasvatī becomes speech when she is situated in the middle of the Śakti, with the Praṇava at the beginning and the end."
The mantra beginning with "ṅentā" and ending with "anuraya," consisting of eleven syllables, is proclaimed as the Bhajamāna-parijāta;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is declared its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is stated to be its meter (chanda).
The goddess Vāṇī is proclaimed as the mistress of the Pārijāta tree; O Supreme Goddess, the third [syllable] is the seed-mantra (bīja), the power (śakti) is the Savior (Tāraka),
and the pin (kīlaka) bestows the great Sarasvatī.
The ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the seed-syllables differentiated by the six long vowels.
Then the meditation:
[Vāṇī] is mounted upon a swan, white as jasmine and the moon that is the smile of Hara; her face is graced with a gentle smile, and a crescent moon is bound upon her crest.
With hands radiant with the lute of knowledge, the vessel of nectar, and the rosary, seated upon a white lotus—may Bhāratī grant you the attainment of your desired goals. (57)
Her worship and other rites are like those previously described for the eleven-syllable mantra.
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations.
One should offer oblations (*homa*) twelve thousand times with *arka* flowers or *nāgacampaka* flowers.
Thus end the mantras of Sarasvatī. || 58 ||
Now, the mantra of Gaṇeśa:
Now I shall declare the mantras of Gaṇapati, which bestow the accomplishment of all aims;
knowing which, men constantly fulfill their heart's desires. (59)
They know the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati to be "pañcāntaka" followed by "śaśidhara";
"pañcāntaka" is the letter *ga*. (60)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement of mantras on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa), one should offer salutations in the filaments and the center with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Tībrā; obeisance to Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, and Kāmarūpiṇī."
To Ugrā, Tejovatī, Satyā, and Vighnanāśinī; above them, salutation to the one seated upon the lotus of all powers (sarvaśakti-kamalāsana).
One should worship everywhere with mantras beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "namaḥ."
And so it is stated in the Nibandha: "The one called Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmarūpiṇī,
Ugrā, Tejovatī, Satyā, and the ninth, Vighnanāśinī."
This is the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra), beginning with "to the lotus-seated one who possesses all powers" and ending with "the heart"; by means of this, one should offer a seat to the Lord.
Then follows the Nyāsa of the Seer and others:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇaka, the Seer," on the head; "Oṃ, obeisance to Nivṛt, the Metre," in the mouth; "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa, the Deity," in the heart. || 62 ||
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*gāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *gīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *gūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *taiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *huṃ*; *gauṃ* [to the two little fingers].

With the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*; with *gaḥ* on the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*. In this manner, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs, beginning with "gāṃ to the heart, *namaḥ*," and so forth.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"One should perform the six limbs in sequence by means of the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels. (63)
Then the meditation: [He is] red as vermilion, with three eyes and a broad belly, holding a staff, a noose, and a goad in his lotus-hands, and beautiful with a citron fruit shining in his great hand.

Worship Gaṇapati, whose crown shines with the light of the crescent moon, who has the face of a lordly elephant with temples moistened by streams of ichor, who is adorned with the king of serpents, and who is clad in red garments and smeared with red unguents.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual installation of the arghya water.
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), one should worship [the deities] in the filaments and in the center,
ending with the mantras of the Tīvra and other pedestals. Then,
having conceived the form (*mūrti*) by means of the root mantra and having meditated upon it again, [one performs] the invocation and so forth—
Having performed the ritual actions up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers,
one should begin the worship of the obstructions (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
As follows:
In the pericarp, in the directions starting from the east, [one should worship] with "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇādhipati," and likewise to Gaṇeśa,
Gaṇanāyaka, and Gaṇakrīḍa. Then, in the filaments— at the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions— one should worship Gāṃ.

One should worship in the sequence beginning with "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" (Salutation to the Heart) and so forth. In the middle of the petals, starting from the east, [one should worship] Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadanta, Mahodara, and Gajānana.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the formidable Vighnarāja known as Lambodara,
who is smoke-colored, at the tips of the petals; then, one should worship Brāhmī and the others with this mantra:
One should worship in the sequence beginning with "Oṃ, obeisance to Vakratuṇḍa.
On the tips of the petals, the Mothers, Brāhmī and the others, are to be worshipped in the order starting from the east.
Outside of that, one should fully worship Indra and the other guardians, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 65 ||
The preliminary rite for this consists of four hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and thereafter perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part [of that number],
using sweetmeats, flattened rice, parched grain, groats, and stalks of sugarcane."
Coconuts, pure sesame seeds, well-ripened plantains, and [the remaining four]—these eight substances for Vighna have been declared by the wise. (66)
Now, regarding the mantra of Mahāgaṇeśa, it is stated in the Nibandha: "One should first write down the seed-syllables of Śrī, Śakti, Smara, Bhūmi, and Vighna."
Having first uttered "Gaṇapatim" and afterwards the word "Varadam," and having said "Sarvajanaṃ me vaśam ānaya," followed by two *ṭha*s;
this twenty-eight-syllable mantra, beginning with *Tārā*, is thus proclaimed. (67)
He states the seed-syllable of Earth (bhū-bīja):
"The letter *smṛti* joined with *māṃsa* and the nasal bindu is declared to be the Earth-seed.
*Smṛti* is the letter *ga*; *māṃsa* is the letter *la*.
Therefore: Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, bestower of boons, bring all people under my control, svāhā! || 68 ||
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the ritual actions beginning with the morning duties and ending with the *pīṭhanyāsa*, and having assigned the powers of the seat (*pīṭhaśakti*) according to the previously mentioned mantras of the seats starting with *tīvra*, one should perform the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
Salutation to the sage Gaṇaka on the head; salutation to the Nivṛt-gāyatrī metre on the mouth; salutation to the deity Mahāgaṇapati on the heart. || 69 ||
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gāṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*;
likewise, *oṃ 5 gīṃ tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*, *oṃ 5 gūṃ madhyamābhyāṃ*.
*Vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ* 5 *gaiṃ* to the two ring fingers *huṃ*; *oṃ* 5 *gauṃ* to the two little fingers *vaṣaṭ*; *oṃ* 5 *gaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands *phaṭ*.
In the same manner for the heart and other [limbs].

Some, however, say "oṃ gāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth; that is not correct, because of the statement in the *Prapañcasāra*: "One should employ the seed-syllable of the [deity] itself, conjoined with its own long vowel," which indicates that only the specific [seed-syllable] is to be taken. (69a)
Then comes meditation:
one should visualize an island made of the nine precious gems in the ocean of sugarcane juice,
its shores illuminated by its waves and fanned by gentle breezes.
It was crowded with *kalpa* trees and creepers such as the *mandāra* and *pārijāta*;
its ground was reddened by the radiance of emerging jewels;
and the horizons were illuminated by the rising sun and moon. In the center of it stood the *pārijāta* tree.
One should meditate upon [the throne] as consisting of the nine gems,
constantly fanned by the six seasons that increase delight;
beneath that, upon a great pedestal fashioned into a lotus of the Mātṛkās.
One should meditate upon Mahāgaṇapati, situated within a triangle inside a hexagon;
he has the face of a lordly elephant, is crowned with the moon, possesses a ruddy luster, and has three eyes.
He is embraced with passion by his beloved, who holds a lotus in her hand and rests upon his lap, and with whom he is united.
I worship Him who holds in His hands a citron, a mace, a conch, a trident, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, His own tusk, and a jewel-filled jar;
and whose mind is intensely longing for the *pāyasa* (milk-rice) flowing from the hollow of His cheeks.
Repeatedly warding off bees with his ears and palms,
he delighted the practitioners with showers of jewels issuing from the mouths of jeweled jars held at the tips of his hands, appearing overwhelmed by intoxication.
Adorned with a crown of rubies and embellished with jewel ornaments.
Having meditated thus and performed worship with mental offerings, one should begin the external worship.
The worship diagram for this is as follows:
a triangle with a hexagon outside it; everything else should be understood to be like the *mātṛkā* diagram. (Figure 21)
Then, having performed the installation of the conch and conducted the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*),

one should worship the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*) and the mantra of the pedestal (*pīṭhamantra*) as before; then, having meditated again and performed the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*).
One should begin the offering of obstructions (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
Outside the triangle, in the four directions starting from the east: in the east, beneath a *vilva* tree, [one should worship] Śrī and Śrīpati;
in the south, beneath a *vaṭa* tree, Gaurī and Gaurīpati; in the west...
One should worship Rati and the Lord of Rati beneath a Pippala tree; to the north, Mahī and Varāha beneath a Priyaṅgu tree;
Lakṣmī and Gaṇanāyaka before the deity; and in the six corners, Āmoda accompanied by Siddhi in the front corner, and Pramoda accompanied by Samṛddhi in the southeast corner.

One should worship Sumukha accompanied by Kānti in the northeast corner; Durmukha accompanied by Madanāvatī in the west; Vighna accompanied by Madadravā in the southwest; and Vighnakartṛ accompanied by Drāviṇī in the northwest.
On both sides of the hexagon: *Oṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi together with Vasudhā; Oṃ, obeisance to Padmanidhi together with Vasumatī*.
As it is stated in the Nibandha:
Outside the triangle, the practitioner should worship, starting from the east and proceeding through the directions, two each of the trees— the bilva, the ṭapa, the pippala, and the priyaṅgu—
beneath which he worships Śrī and Śrīpati, as well as Gaurī and Gaurīpati.
One should first worship Rati and Rati-pati, as well as Mahī and Varāha; and in front, one should worship Gaṇanāyaka together with Lakṣmī;
likewise, in the front corner, one should worship Āmoda together with Siddhi.
In the southeast (Agni-kona) is Pramodaka together with Samṛddhi;
in the northeast (Īśāna) is Sumukha together with Kānti;
likewise in the west is Durmukha together with Madanāvatī; and likewise in the southwest (Nairṛta).
Accompanied by Madadravā, he is the supreme leader of the Gaṇas;
accompanied by Drāviṇī, he is likewise the creator of obstacles in the northwest;
and on the two sides of the hexagon are Śaṅkhanidhi joined with Vasudhā.
One should also quickly worship Padmanidhi together with Vasumatī.
Then, having worshipped the six seed-syllables in the filaments— at the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions—
one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and other weapons, in the outer earthen enclosure (bhūgṛha).
Then one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the offering of incense and ending with the dismissal. || 72 ||
The preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of four hundred and forty-four thousand repetitions.
Thus it is said:
"The practitioner of mantra, being composed, should meditate upon the mantra and recite it four hundred thousand times."
One should offer oblations with eight substances, such as sweetmeats and others, totaling forty-four thousand, which is ten times four thousand.
Another mantra:
One should utter one's own seed-syllable conjoined with Śakti, followed by Mahāgaṇapati in the feminine (with the suffix ṅe).
This twelve-syllabled mantra is declared to be "Agnivadhu. (74)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having established the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) along with the seat-powers (pīṭhaśaktis) beginning with Tīvra and ending with the seat-mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and the other components.
In the Nibandha:
"The seer is Gaṇaka; the metre is Gāyatrī, beginning with Nivṛt;
the deity declared in the mantra is Śaktigaṇādhipa by name. (75)
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *hrīṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*gaṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
Hrīṃ, to the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ;
to Mahāgaṇapati, to the two ring fingers, huṃ;
svāhā, to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ.
Having recited the collective [mantra], [one strikes] with the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
Likewise for the heart and other [limbs].
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
One should assign the limbs [of the mantra] using the words of the mantra both individually and collectively.
Thus:
"Salutation to Gaṇaka, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head; salutation to the Nivṛt-gāyatrī metre, on the mouth; [salutation] on the heart..."
Salutation to the deity Śaktigaṇādhipati. || 76 ||
Then one should meditate [upon him] as white as a pearl, with the face of an elephant in rut, moon-crested, and three-eyed,
holding in his own hands a lotus, a goad, and a jewel-pitcher.
We worship him who wears a jeweled crown, his hand resting upon the lap of the goddess— who possesses the luster of a lotus and whose hand clings to his banner— as he places his hand within her womb.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual installation of the conch.
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), one should worship [the deities] beginning with Tīvra and ending with the mantra of the pedestal.

Having meditated again and performed the rites from invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), one should perform the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā). || 78 ||

The four previously mentioned couples, beginning with Śrī and Śrīpati, are placed in the six corners; Āmoda and the others are in the filaments (keśaras) at the corners starting from the southeast; and in the center and the cardinal directions, one should place: *hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *gaṃ śirase svāhā*, *hrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, and *mahāgaṇapataye*.
"Hūṃ, svāhā" for the armor; "Vauṣaṭ" for the three eyes; having recited the root mantra of the entire collection, "Phaṭ" for the weapon.
Then, having worshipped the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī upon the petals, and outside of that, Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other [emblems].
One should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings;
the yantra, however, is like that of Mahāgaṇapati. (78ka)
The preliminary rite for this [mantra] is one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with cakes (*apūpa*) consisting of one-tenth of that number."
One should offer oblations into the consecrated fire; then the Lord of Day (the Sun) shall worship the Deity.
Another mantra: one's own seed-syllable constricted by Śakti, followed by "vaśamānaya" and the two Ṭha-s (ṬhaṬha).
This other mantra, preceded by Tāra (Oṃ), is said to consist of eleven syllables.
And its worship diagram is as before. || 80 ||
The limb-mantra (aṅgamantra) should be assigned by means of one, three, two, or all [of the fingers]:
*oṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
Oṃ hrīṃ gaṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers; vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers for subjugation;
ānaya, huṃ to the two ring fingers.
Svāhā to the two little fingers; vauṣaṭ [to the heart].
Having uttered the entire [mantra], phaṭ with the palms and backs of the hands.
Thus for the heart and the other [limbs].
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"First with one [syllable], then with three, two, three, and two;
finally with the whole [mantra]—this is considered the prescribed arrangement of the limbs (aṅga-kalpanā) for the weapon-mantra."
One should place these [mantras] on the thumbs and other fingers, as well as on the heart and other [parts of the body]. || 81 ||
Then comes the meditation:
[he] holds in his hands a sugarcane staff, two tusks, a noose, and a goad;
he is embraced by his excellent consort who rests upon the back of a lotus, her head touching the tip of his banner.

I constantly meditate upon the Lord who has a dark-complexioned consort holding a lotus, who possesses three eyes, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon, who is as red as the hibiscus flower, who has an elephant’s face, and who is intensely fond of worldly enjoyments;
all else is as before.
The preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra consists of three hundred thousand repetitions.
Thus it is stated in the *Nibandha*:
"One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, and [perform] the fire-oblation (*homa*) with ten thousand stalks of sugarcane."
Or one should offer oblations with cakes mixed with clarified butter for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra. || 83 ||
Now, the mantra of Heramba consists of the letter *ga* joined with the vowel *u*, accompanied by the bindu, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), and ending with *namaḥ*; thus it is four syllables long.
As it is stated in the Nibandha:

The letter Pa, the end of the pentad (Pa), joined with the Bindu (M) and adorned with the left ear (U)—beginning with Tārā (Om) and ending with the Heart (Namaḥ)—this is proclaimed as the mantra of Heramba.
Consisting of four syllables, it bestows upon men the fruits of the four aims of life. || 84 ||
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the *pīṭhanyāsa*, one should install the powers of the seat (*pīṭhaśakti*) and the mantra of the seat as prescribed for Gaṇeśa, and then perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*.

For this [mantra], the seer is Gaṇaka, the metre is Gāyatrī, the deity is Heramba, the seed-syllable is the letter *ga*, the power is the bindu, and the application is for the sake of attaining the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*).
"Salutation to the seer Gaṇaka on the head," and so forth. || 85 ||
Then, one should perform the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) with these [syllables]: *gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaiṃ gauṃ gaḥ*, thereby effecting the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
And thus:
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of a seed-syllable (bīja) possessing six long vowels. || 86 ||
Then comes the meditation:

[one should meditate upon] Heramba, who possesses the luster of pearls, gold, blue jasmine, and saffron; who is endowed with three eyes; who has the face of an elephant; whose vehicle is a lion; who bears the moon; and who shines with the brilliance of the sun.
I worship Him who holds with His arms a proud gift-bestowing [hand], a shield that grants fearlessness and joy, a sword, a garland consisting of heads and eyes, a mallet, a goad, and a trident.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the arghya water.

Then, having worshipped [the deities] up to the power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) as prescribed by Gaṇeśa, one should worship the seat with: "Oṃ huṃ huṃ, obeisance to the Great Lion, the seat of Heramba, Gāṃ.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
The Praṇava, the two armor-mantras (kavaca), "mahāsiṃhāya," then "gām," followed by the word "heramba" and ending with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) for the seat—
this shall be the seat-mantra; one should offer the seat with this.

This same mantra is also used for the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa). Thus it is stated in the Nibandha: "The mantra that is prescribed for the seat is indeed the very same one to be used for its ritual placement."
Then, one should fashion the form with the mantra *oṃ gamiti*.
Likewise, it is stated in the Nibandha:
"One should fashion its form with the seed-syllable of the obstacle [Gaṇeśa], preceded by the Tāra [oṃ]."
Then, having meditated once more and performed the rites from the invocation up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers,
one should begin the worship of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
For example:
one should worship [the syllable] *gāṃ* in the southeast corner, in the center, and in the cardinal directions with "Oṃ *gāṃ* hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth. || 88 ||
On the leaves,
one should worship Vighna, Vināyaka, Śūra, Vīra, the one known as Varada,
the elephant-faced, the single-tusked, and Lambodara.
On the tips of the petals, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), and outside of that, Indra, his throne, the thunderbolt, and so forth.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense (dhūpa) until the final dismissal (visarjana). || 88ka ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, and thereafter perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-tenth that number."
It should be offered as before. || 89 ||
Another mantra:
Gaṃ, homage to the one who quickly inspires faith.
And likewise in the Nibandha:
Saṃvartaka has two eyes and his side rests upon a seat of fire;
for the purpose of propitiation, there is the ten-syllable heart-mantra beginning with his own seed-syllable.
The worship of this [mantra] is as follows:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the *pīṭhanyāsa*, one should perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*:
"Salutation to Gaṇaka, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to Virāṭ, the meter (*chandas*), on the mouth; [salutation to the deity] on the heart."
Homage to the deity for swift propitiation.
As it has been said:
"The sage is declared to be Gaṇaka; the Virāṭ metre is proclaimed."
The deity proclaimed for this [mantra] is Vighna, who inspires swift faith.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the seed-syllable joined with the long vowel [Ā].
Having performed the placement on the hands and limbs as in the case of the single-syllable mantra, one should meditate. || 91 ||

May the elephant-faced one protect you—he who holds a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper, and a tusk; who carries a *bījapūra* fruit placed upon his own trunk; who is red, three-eyed, crowned with the young moon, and radiant with necklaces.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) and meditated again,
and having performed the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali),
one should begin the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā). [One should worship] Gāṃ for the heart in the southeast corner, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.
One should worship the six limbs with the mantra beginning with "namaḥ" and so forth. Thus it is stated in the Nibandha:
"Having first worshipped the limbs, one should thereafter sacrifice to the eight obstacles."
Immediately thereafter, one should worship these [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī upon the petals;
on the petals:
Vighna, Vināyaka, Śūra, Vīra, and the one known as Varada.
One should worship the elephant-faced one, who has a single tusk and a protruding belly; on the tips of the petals,
one should worship Brāhmī and the others, and outside of that, Indra and the other gods, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 93 ||
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"One should perform one hundred thousand recitations, and at the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds."
Or else, with the three sweets, or with the eight substances that have been mentioned.
Now, the mantras of Haridrā-Gaṇeśa:
the great one-syllable mantra ending in the letter *pa* (pañca), resting on the earth (*dha*), with its head adorned by a bindu (*m*), bestows the fruit of all desires.
Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Haridrā-Gaṇapati is the deity (devatā), the syllable *ga* is the seed-syllable (bīja), and the syllable *la* is the power (śakti).
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is performed with the seed-syllable alone. || 95 ||
As for Dhyāna:
one should meditate upon the Lord as having the luster of turmeric, four arms, and clad in yellow garments;
the God holding a noose and a goad, and likewise a sweetmeat and a tusk.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch and the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā), beginning with the intense (tīvra) seat and ending with its presiding mantra; then, having meditated again, one should worship Gaṇapati. || 96 ||
(Plate 22: Gaṇeśa’s dhāraṇāyantra) The application for the worship of the enclosures is the same as for the single-syllable Gaṇapati mantra. || 97 ||
The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of four hundred thousand recitations (japa).
Thereafter, ten thousand oblations (homa) are to be performed with rice grains mixed with turmeric powder and combined with the three sweets (trimadhura). || 98 ||
I shall now speak of another mantra, the extraction of the mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one! Having extracted the seed-syllable of Indra, one should extract one's own seed-syllable.
