*rāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *rīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *rūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *raiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *huṃ*; *rauṃ*...
With the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*; with the palms and backs of the hands, *raḥ phaṭ*.
Likewise, for the heart and other limbs: *rāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth. (3)
Then follows the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa):
RĀM NAMAH at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), RĀM NAMAH between the eyebrows, MĀM NAMAH at the heart, YAṂ NAMAH at the navel, NAṂ NAMAH at the generative organ, and MAṂ NAMAH at the feet.

Then, having performed the previously mentioned rites such as the placement of the limbs (*mūrti-pañjara-nyāsa*) and so forth, one should meditate [upon Him] thus: "He whose splendor is like that of a dark rain-cloud, who sits perpetually in the *vīrāsana* posture, and who holds with one lotus-hand the mudrā consisting of gnosis while the other rests upon his knee."
I worship Rāghava, who gazes at Sītā standing by his side— her hand like a lotus, radiant as lightning— while his own limbs shine with various ornaments such as a crown and armlets.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual installation of the conch.

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*), having fully worshipped the powers of the pedestal (*pīṭhaśakti*) and the mantra of the pedestal as taught by the Vaiṣṇavas, and having meditated once more, one should perform the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*), and then begin the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
On the left side of the deity: *Śrīṃ sītāyai namaḥ*.
In front: *Oṃ śārṅgāya namaḥ*; on the left and right sides: *Oṃ parebhyo namaḥ*, *Oṃ cāpāya namaḥ*.

Outside of that, on the filaments—in the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions—one should worship the six limbs with the mantra "rāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth. || 6 ||
Then, on the petals in the directions starting from the east: *oṃ hanūmate namaḥ*; likewise for Sugrīva, Bharata, Vibhīṣaṇa, Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Śatrughna, and Jāmbavān.
On the petals: *oṃ sṛṣṭaye namaḥ*, and likewise to Jayanta, Vijaya, Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana, Akopa, Dharmapāla, and Svamantra.
Then one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other weapons.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings.
The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of six hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the appropriate season, and perform ten thousand oblations with auspicious lotuses."
One should offer oblations into the consecrated fire and thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas.
This mantra is sixfold.
And so it is said:
"The five-syllabled [mantra] begins with one's own Kāma-śakti, Vāk, Lakṣmī, and Tārā."
The six-syllabled mantra is of six kinds and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
Brahmā, Sammohana, Śakti, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Imperishable (Avyaya), Agastya, and Śrīśiva—these are declared to be the sages here in this sequence. (10)
Alternatively, for the seed-syllable of Kāma and so forth, the sage is Viśvāmitra, the metre is known as Gāyatrī, and the deity is Śrī Rāma;
one should perform all rites such as meditation and worship as previously described. (11)
Another mantra:
"Jānakīvallabha" ending in the dative case (Ṅe), followed by the wife of fire (Svāhā) and "Hum," etc.
This ten-syllabled mantra has Vasiṣṭha as its seer (ṛṣi) and Virāṭ as its meter (chandas). 12.
Chagda is the deity; Rāma is the grasping of Sītā’s hand;
the first seed-syllable is the Dviṭha (the letter Ṭha); Śakti is considered the limb-formation by means of Kāma (the letter Ra). || 13 ||
One should place the ten syllables of the mantra on the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, palate, throat, heart, navel, thighs, knees, and feet.
Then the meditation:
In the beautiful city of Ayodhyā, within a pavilion of jewel-like splendor,
provided with canopies and archways fashioned from mandāra flowers.
Rāghava was seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot atop a lion-throne, being praised by Rākṣasas, monkeys, and auspicious gods traveling in celestial vehicles,
and graced by all-knowing sages.
His left side was adorned by Sītā, and he was attended upon by Lakṣmaṇa.
Meditating thus upon [the deity] who is dark-complexioned, with a serene countenance, and adorned with all ornaments,
one should recite the mantra ten lakhs of times with undistracted mind.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with bilva flowers mixed with honey, numbering one-tenth of the recitation.
Everything else is as before. || 15 ||
Another mantra: Vahni joined with Nārāyaṇa, and likewise Jaṭhara alone;
this two-syllabled king of mantras bestows all desired fruits. (16)
The mantra consisting of the four syllables, preceded and followed by each of the glorious seed-syllables *māyā* (hrīṃ) and *manmatha* (klīṃ), or likewise that of six syllables, bestows all desires.
A mantra may end in *svāhā*, or in *huṃ phaṭ*, or in *namaḥ*;
it becomes sixfold by means of the seed-syllables of Tārā, Māyā, Ramā, Anaṅga, Vāk, and one's own [seed-syllable].
The three-syllabled king of mantras shall be the bestower of all desired fruits. || 17 ||
This two-syllable mantra ends with "Candrabhadra," while this four-syllable mantra is declared to be the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu) for Rāma; the supreme mantra consists of five syllables.
The mantra is preceded by each of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā;
it may begin with Lakṣmī, Vāk, Manmatha, and so forth, or with the Tāra (Om), and thus exists in many ways.
By that [mantra], "tena aṃ rāmāya namaḥ" and so forth, is the six-syllable [mantra].
It is the bed of Viṣṇu situated in fire, adorned with a half-moon.
The single-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the king of mantras, the celestial tree;
Brahmā is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī its meter (chandas), and Rāma its deity.
For a single-syllable mantra, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations; for it is stated thus: "One should recite the mantra one million times."
The distinction is that for others, there is a recitation of six hundred thousand times.
The meditation, worship, and other rites for these [deities] are as previously described for the six-syllable mantra. (19)

Now, the mantras of Śrī Kṛṣṇa: At the end of the word *gopījana*, [the phrase] *vallabhāya* ending with two *ṭha*s (svāhā) constitutes this ten-syllabled mantra, which bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
This mantra begins with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).
Furthermore, in the analysis of the zodiac signs and lunar mansions, the analysis is performed without the seed-syllable. || 1 ||
"O Sage, the recitation preceded by the seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be its secret;
because its nature as a seed-syllable has been omitted, it is here called the 'Ten-Syllabled' (daśākṣara). Thus from the *Gautamīya*. (2)
And so it is stated in the *Bṛhadgautamīya*:

"O Great Sage, the ten-syllable mantra, which is the sole abode of enjoyment and liberation and whose seed has been effaced, should extract the seed of desire (Kāma-bīja) separately; through its union with that, the mantra becomes the bestower of fruits."
Otherwise, it would not lead to success. || 3 ||
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the Vaiṣṇava sipping of water (ācamana) as prescribed in the Viṣṇu-mantra, and having carried out the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), one should perform breath control (praṇāyāma).
And likewise in the Gautamiya:
"Having thus disposed the principles (tattvas), one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas).
By reciting the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) once, one should exhale the air through the right nostril."
Again, by reciting [the mantra] seven times, one should fill the air through the left nostril.

Then, holding both nostrils, one should retain the air (kumbhaka) by reciting twenty times. Again, one should exhale through the left nostril, fill [with air] through the right, and retain it through both.
Again, having exhaled through the right [nostril] and filled [the left] with air, one should retain it [in the breath] with both.
And thus:
"One should exhale through each [nostril] separately, using the very seed-syllable of desire (KĀM)."

One should fill [the breath] with that [mantra] recited seven times and retain it for twenty [recitations]. In all Kṛṣṇa-mantras, one should perform the recitation either with this seed-syllable (bīja) or with the root-mantra itself; in every case, this is the method for breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus it is said in the *Kramadīpikā*: "One who desires to recite this mantra here should first practice the restraint of the vital breath (*pavana-saṃyamana*).
If he recites the ten-syllable [mantra], then [he should do so] with that ten-syllable [mantra]."

One should exhale twenty-eight times; likewise, one should inhale from the left and retain [the breath] for that same duration. One complete *prāṇāyāma* consists of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*).
If one performs twelve [repetitions] with an eighteen-syllable mantra, it should be done in this manner; for it is stated that with other mantras, it should be according to the number of syllables.
One should perform the three [breath-controls], beginning with exhalation (recaka), according to the number of syllables in each respective mantra. || 5 ||
"One should exhale through the *dakṣā* [nostril] and fill [the lungs] through the *vāmā*;
then one should retain [the breath] through both the middle [channels], and so forth.
This, however, pertains to the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and not elsewhere. 5ka.

Then, having performed the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), and having placed the seat-mantras beginning with Vimalā and ending with the mantra of the seat in the filaments and in the center, one should perform the placement of the sages and other [limbs] (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
Namely:

on the head, salutation to the sage Nārada; on the mouth, salutation to the Virāṭ meter; on the heart, salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa; on the private parts, salutation to the seed-syllable *klīṃ*; on the feet—
" Svāhā! Salutation to Śakti!
Salutation to Durgā, the presiding deity of the mantra!"—thus one should pay homage to Durgā. || 6 ||

Then, having placed the root mantra encapsulated by the *praṇava* three times on the palms, the backs, and the sides [of the hands], one should place the letters of the root mantra, each accompanied by the nasal bindu and encapsulated by the *praṇava*, upon the joints of the fingers with the word "namas" at the end.
Namely: on the three joints of the right thumb, *oṃ goṃ oṃ namaḥ*;
on the right index finger, *oṃ pīṃ oṃ namaḥ*.
On the right middle finger: Oṃ jaṃ oṃ namaḥ.
On the right ring finger: Oṃ naṃ oṃ namaḥ. On the right little finger: Oṃ vaṃ oṃ namaḥ.
On the left little finger: Oṃ llaṃ oṃ namaḥ. On the left ring finger: Oṃ bhāṃ oṃ namaḥ. On the left middle finger: Oṃ yaṃ oṃ namaḥ.
On the left index finger: *oṃ svāṃ oṃ namaḥ*.
On the left thumb: *oṃ hāṃ oṃ namaḥ*.
This is the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (the rite of emanation).
Thus, the *sthiti* (maintenance) gesture begins with the right thumb and ends with the left little finger;
the *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) begins with the left thumb and ends with the right thumb. One should perform these fivefold, including *sṛṣṭi* (creation) and *sthiti*.
And likewise in the Gautamiya:
"The withdrawal [of the breath] is proclaimed as that which removes the collection of defects;
and the emission [of the breath] bestows knowledge upon those of pure mind who abide in their respective stages of life."
The end of the stay should be for householders; these three [stages] are according to one's inclination toward desire.
Some desire the end of the state for the forest-dweller in the stage of innate knowledge;
and for the sage who is entirely dispassionate, [they desire] the end of the withdrawal.
If one is unable, one should perform it with a single measure.
And so it is said:
"One should always perform the three-fold placement; however, if unable, indeed only one."

Thus, according to the *Gautamīya* [Tantra]. Then, one should place the ten syllables upon the fingers in the order of their positions, as follows: in every instance, they are enclosed by the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
Gāṃ, salutation to the right thumb; Pīṃ, salutation to the index finger; Jaṃ, salutation to the middle finger.
Naṃ, salutation to the ring finger;
vaṃ, salutation to the little finger;
llaṃ, salutation to the left thumb.
Bhāṃ, homage to the left index finger; Yaṃ, homage to the left middle finger;
Svāṃ, homage to the left ring finger.
Hāṃ, salutation on the left little finger. Then follows the five-limbed assignment (pañcāṅganyāsa) upon the fingers of the hands:
"To the wheel of the face, svāhā; salutation to both thumbs."
Svāhā to Vicakra; svāhā to the two index fingers.
Svāhā to Sucakra; vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers.
Svāhā to Trailokyarakṣaṇacakra; huṃ to the two ring fingers.
To the wheel that destroys the asuras, svāhā; to the two little fingers, phaṭ. || 9 ||
Then, one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā, conjoined with the root-mantra and accompanied by the nasal bindu, in their respective locations within the Mātṛkā-body.
Then, one should [place] the root-mantra conjoined with the Praṇava from the hair to the feet.
Having performed the placement three times in sequence from the feet to the hair, one should place the ten *tattvas* according to the divisions of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
And so it is said in the *Kramadīpikā*:
The best of men, having followed the path of withdrawal, shall return to the path of creation;
indeed, their extraction is as previously described, and I shall now explain the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Namely:
at the two feet, *goṃ*—salutation to the supreme self of the earth element;
at the *liṅga*, *pīṃ*—salutation to the supreme self of the water element.

In the heart: *jaṃ*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the essence of the element of fire (*tejas-tattva*). In the mouth: *naṃ*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the essence of the element of air (*vāyu-tattva*). In the head: *vaṃ*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the essence of the element of space (*ākāśa-tattva*).
"LLAṂ, obeisance to the supreme self whose essence is the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra-tattva); BHĀṂ, obeisance to the supreme self whose essence is the principle of the great one (mahat-tattva).
These two are to be deposited upon the heart."
Yaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the principle of primordial nature; namaḥ svāṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the principle of the individual soul;
hāṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the supreme principle.
These three [syllables] are placed on all the limbs.
Thus is the *saṃhāranyāsa* (the ritual placement of dissolution).
Now follows the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (the ritual placement of creation):

Hāṃ, obeisance; obeisance to the supreme self, the essence of the Supreme Reality (paratattva). Svāṃ, obeisance; obeisance to the supreme self, the essence of the Puruṣa principle (puruṣatattva). Yaṃ, obeisance; obeisance to the supreme self, the essence of the Prakṛti principle (prakṛtitattva).
This triad [is placed] on all limbs.

In the heart: *bhāṃ* namaḥ, obeisance to the supreme self whose essence is the principle of Mahat (*mahattattva*). *llam* namaḥ, obeisance to the supreme self whose essence is the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāratattva*).

On the head: *vaṃ*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the self of the ether-principle (*ākāśatattva*). In the mouth: *naṃ*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the self of the air-principle (*vāyutattva*). In the heart: *jaṃ*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the self of the fire-principle (*tejastattva*).

Pīṃ, salutation to the supreme [deity] in the *liṅga*; salutation to the self whose essence is the water-element (*jalatattva*). Goṃ, salutation to the supreme [deity] in the feet; salutation to the self whose essence is the earth-element (*pṛthivītattva*).
Thus is the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*. 10.
Regarding the rule for the fingers in the *sṛṣṭyādi-nyāsa*, the *Nibandha* states:
"The middle finger is prescribed for the head; that same [middle finger], joined with the index finger, is for the eyes;
for the ears, it is [the middle finger] without the thumb, joined with the ring finger."
All [the fingers] are placed on the face; the index finger with its string is on the heart;
the middle finger joined with the first [index finger] is at the navel; they are placed on the ear and the linga;
those same fingers, together with the thumb, are on the two knees; and [those] with the thumb are on the two feet.
There may be an exchange between the position and the syllable of the fingers;
for example: *goṃ namaḥ* on the head with the middle finger.
To the two eyes, *pīṃ* namaḥ, with the index and middle fingers;
to the two ears, *jaṃ* namaḥ, with the fingers excluding the thumb;
to the nose, *naṃ* namaḥ, with the thumb and ring finger.
At the mouth, *vaṃ* *namaḥ* with all the fingers;
at the heart, *llaṃ* *namaḥ* with the thumb and index finger;
at the navel, *bhāṃ* *namaḥ* with the thumb and middle finger.
On the *liṅga*: *yaṃ* *namaḥ* with the fingers excluding the thumb;
on the two knees: *svāṃ* *namaḥ* with the fingers excluding the thumb;
on the feet: *hāṃ* *namaḥ* with all the fingers.
Thus is the sequence of emanation. Now, the sequence of maintenance:
*goṃ namaḥ* to the heart with the thumb and forefinger.
At the navel, "Pīṃ Namaḥ" with the thumb and middle finger;
at the genitals, "Jaṃ Namaḥ" with the fingers excluding the thumb;
at the knees, "Naṃ Namaḥ" with the fingers excluding the thumb.
*Vaṃ* namaḥ to the two feet with all the fingers; *lla* namaḥ to the head with the middle finger;
*bhāṃ* namaḥ to the two eyes with the middle and index fingers.
At the ears: *yaṃ* namaḥ with the fingers excluding the thumb;
at the nose: *svāṃ* namaḥ with the thumb and ring finger;
at the mouth: *hāṃ* namaḥ with all the fingers.
Now, the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*):
*goṃ namaḥ* at the two feet with all the fingers;
*pīṃ namaḥ* at the two knees with the fingers excluding the thumbs.
At the *liṅga*, *naṃ* namaḥ with the fingers excluding the thumb;
at the navel, *naṃ* namaḥ with the thumb and middle finger;
at the heart, *vaṃ* namaḥ with the thumb and forefinger.
At the mouth, *llaṃ* with *namaḥ* using all the fingers;
at the nose, *bhāṃ* with *namaḥ* using the thumb and ring finger;
at the two ears, *yaṃ* with *namaḥ* using the fingers excluding the thumb.
*Namo* for the two eyes with the middle and index fingers;
*Hāṃ namo* on the head with the middle finger.
This is the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
Furthermore, one should perform the placement of emanation and maintenance;
and likewise:
"The seeker of knowledge and the celibate student should again perform the emanation."
Furthermore, the householder should specifically perform creation and maintenance;
then the ascetic, endowed with dispassion, should deposit [the mantra] up to the end of dissolution.
By this, [the application is] fourfold for students and celibates, and fivefold for householders.
And for ascetics, those who are dispassionate, and others, the renunciation is threefold. || 10ka ||
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"This Nyāsa is prescribed for Maskarins and Vaikhānasas as ending with Saṃhāra;
for householders (Gṛhamedhis) it ends with Sthiti; and for those in the [other] stages of life (Varṇins), they say it ends with Sṛṣṭi."
Some teachers say that for a householder endowed with dispassion, [the cycle] ends at withdrawal (saṃhāra);
likewise, for one who dwells in the forest through innate knowledge, there is stability, and for those seeking knowledge, there is emanation (sṛṣṭi).
However, some maintain that there is a reversal in the three types of placement; therefore, the placement must be performed in all three ways by everyone. || 11 ||
Now follows the placement of the cage of manifestations (*vibhūtipañjaranyāsa*).
In the *Nibandha*:
"I shall describe another excellent placement called 'Manifestation' (*vibhūti*), which bestows prosperity."
It consists of ten repetitions of the mantra, most secret, and [preserved] by the best of counselors.
Namely: *goṃ* namaḥ on the base; *pīṃ* namaḥ on the linga; *jaṃ* namaḥ at the navel; *naṃ* namaḥ at the heart;
*vaṃ* namaḥ at the throat; *llaṃ* namaḥ at the mouth; *bhāṃ* namaḥ on the two shoulders.
Yaṃ namaḥ to the two feet; svāṃ namaḥ to the two thighs; hāṃ namaḥ to the neck; goṃ namaḥ to the throat;
pīṃ namaḥ to the navel; jaṃ namaḥ to the belly; naṃ namaḥ to the heart; vaṃ namaḥ to the two breasts; llaṃ namaḥ to the two sides; bhāṃ namaḥ to the two flanks; yaṃ [to the head].
*Namaḥ*, *svāṃ namaḥ* on the two hips, *hāṃ namaḥ*. *Goṃ* on the head, *pīṃ* on the mouth, *jaṃ naṃ* on the two eyes, *vaṃ llaṃ* on the two ears,
*bhāṃ yaṃ* on the two nostrils, *svāṃ hāṃ* on the two cheeks.
Thus, there are five [deities] on the root joints and the tips of the right hand, five on its fingers; five on the root joints and the tips of the left hand, and five on its fingers.
Likewise, there are five on the root joints and the tips of the right foot, and five on its toes.
At the joints and tips of the toes of the left foot, there are five [syllables], and at its fingers, five.
At the head is *goṃ*; to its east is *pīṃ*, to its south is *jaṃ*, to its west is *naṃ*, and to its north is *vaṃ*.
At the crown of the head is *llaṃ*; at the two arms are *bhāṃ* and *yaṃ*; and at the two thighs are *svāṃ* and *hāṃ*.

*Goṃ* on the head; *pīṃ* on the two eyes; *jaṃ* on the mouth; *naṃ* on the throat; *vaṃ* on the heart; *llaṃ* on the abdomen; *bhāṃ* on the *mūlādhāra*; *yaṃ* on the genitals; *svāṃ* on the two knees; *hāṃ* on the two feet; *goṃ* on the two ears; *pīṃ* on the two cheeks; *jaṃ* on the two shoulders; *naṃ* on the two breasts.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of these syllables ending with "namaḥ": *vaṃ* on the two sides, *llaṃ* on the genitals, *bhāṃ* on the two thighs, *yaṃ* on the two knees, *svāṃ* on the two shanks, and *hāṃ* on the two feet. || 12 ||
Regarding this, the sequence in the *Gautamīya* is as follows: "Emission begins from the base of the hand; maintenance is said to be from the wrist;
and withdrawal is from the tips of the fingers. One should perform the placement of these three up to the end of maintenance."
Then, as before, follows the placement (nyāsa) of the cage of forms (mūrtipañjara).
Then, as before, follow the emanation and maintenance of that very cage of forms.
Then follow the placements of the ten limbs and the five limbs.
Namely: *hrīṃ* at the heart, *pīṃ* at the head, *jaṃ* at the crest-lock, *naṃ* on all limbs, *vaṃ* in the directions,
*llaṃ* on the right side, *bhāṃ* on the left side, *yaṃ* at the waist region, and *svāṃ* on the back.
Hāṃ at the crown of the head.
Then the placement on the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) is as follows: *Ācakrāya svāhā* to the heart, *namaḥ*.
Svāhā to the wheel of movement; svāhā to the head.
Svāhā to the excellent wheel; vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Svāhā to the wheel that protects the three worlds.

*Kavacāya hūṃ asurāntakacakrāya svāhā astrāya phaṭ*. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the mantra beginning with *kirīṭa-keyūra* as stated in the Nārāyaṇa-mantra, and having displayed the mudrās of the flute, the bilva fruit, and so forth, [one recites]: *oṃ sudarśanāya astrāya*.
One should perform the binding of the directions with the mantra "phaṭ. Furthermore, the assignment (nyāsa) of the crown and other ornaments applies everywhere in the case of Viṣṇu mantras.
Then one should meditate upon Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, who incessantly infatuates thousands of cowherd maidens in the beautiful and smiling Vṛndāvana.
With the bees of their eyes directed toward the lotus-face of her lover,
tormented by the arrows of love and long yearning for an embrace,
they were bent low by the weight of their full, high breasts shimmering with pearl necklaces.
With their lower garments slipping down and their speech faltering with intoxication,
their throbbing lips curved upward and illuminated by the luster of their rows of teeth,
they enticed [him] with various amorous gestures full of passionate affectation.

To Govinda, whose beauty is like a full-blown blue lotus, whose face is like the moon, who is fond of peacock-feather ornaments, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and wears the noble Kaustubha gem and yellow garments,
whose body is worshipped by the lotus-eyes of the cowherd women, and who is surrounded by hosts of cows and cowherds; to him, the beautiful one.
I worship him who is intent on playing the flute of the kalavesha and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) ending with the mantra of the pedestal as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava rites,
and having meditated again, one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (pañca-puṣpāñjali).
One should worship the body of the deity through the sequence of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight limbs and the five limbs pertaining to the stages of creation and maintenance.
Then, at the mouth: *oṃ veṇave namaḥ*; at the heart: *oṃ vanamālāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ kaustubhāya namaḥ*, *oṃ śrīvatsāya namaḥ*.
Thereafter, one should offer five handfuls of flowers.
One should place white *tulasī* smeared with white sandalwood paste and red *tulasī* smeared with red sandalwood paste on the right and left sides respectively, using the root mantra.
Likewise, one should place two *tulasī* leaves, two *karavīra* flowers, and two *padma* lotuses on the head;
all other flowers should be placed upon the entire body.
And so it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
To the right is the pure and imperishable consciousness known as Vāsudeva;
and to the left is the red Rukmiṇī, eternal and endowed with the quality of rajas.
On both sides is a pair of Tulasī plants, accompanied by two fragrances.
One should place a pair of horses on the two sides, right and left;
five flowers on the region of the head with the root mantra, right and left;
and with six [mantras], one should offer them over the entire body, and again all over the head.
Then one should worship the enclosure:
in the east, *oṃ dāmāya namaḥ*; in the south, *oṃ sudāmāya namaḥ*;
in the west, *oṃ vāsudevāya namaḥ*; in the north, *oṃ kiṅkiṇyai namaḥ*; and in the filaments, in the corners starting from the southeast (*agnyādikoṇe*).

Oṃ ācakrāya svāhā, homage to the heart; in the south-west, oṃ vicakrāya svāhā, svāhā to the head; in the north-west, oṃ sucakrāya svāhā, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock; in the north-east, oṃ trailokyarakṣaṇacakrāya svāhā, huṃ to the armor; in the four directions, oṃ.
*Asurāntakacakrāya svāhā*, *astrāya phaṭ*. Then, on the petals starting from the east: *Oṃ rukmiṇyai namaḥ*; likewise, to Satyabhāmā, Nāgnajitī, Sunandā, Mitravindā, Sulakṣaṇā, and Jāmbavatī.

To Suśīlā. On the tips of the petals, starting from the east and so on: *oṃ* obeisance to Vasudeva; likewise to Devakī, Nanda, Yaśodā, Balabhadra, Subhadrā, the cowherds (*gopa*s), and the cowherdesses (*gopī*s).
Outside that and in the center, in the order starting from the east, one should offer salutations: *Oṃ mandārāya namaḥ*, and likewise to Santānaka, Pārijāta, Kalpavṛkṣa, and Haricandana.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other weapons.
Then one should worship the Eightfold Kṛṣṇa:
*Oṃ śrīkṛṣṇāya namaḥ*; likewise, [to] Vāsudeva, Devakīnandana, Nārāyaṇa, Yaduśreṣṭha, Vārṣṇeya, Dharmasaṃsthāpana.
One should worship [the deity] who bears away the burden of those oppressed by the Asuras,
everywhere using the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
If one is unable [to perform the full ritual], one should worship the limbs and the vajra and other [emblems].
And so it is stated in the Gautamiya:
"Alternatively, one should worship the limbs with the lords of the directions and their weapons as well.
Worshipping Kṛṣṇa in this manner, he becomes a vessel for both desire and liberation."
One who is unable to perform this sacrifice should worship with the Ceta-Kṛṣṇāṣṭaka;
thereafter, one should complete the ritual from the incense offering up to the final dismissal. || 15 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of ten lakh recitations.
And so it is said:
"Having recited the mantra ten lakh times, which bestows imperishable fruit..."
One of pure intellect should offer ten thousand oblations into the sacrificial fire for ten days using fresh red lotuses soaked in white sugar, clarified butter, and honey.

Then, if the mantra consists of a pair of vowels, one should recite it five hundred thousand times and perform the fire sacrifice with half that number (two hundred fifty thousand) as prescribed; however,
if one lacks such purity of mind, one may offer milk-rice or lotus flowers.
One should commence the rite of fire-oblation with offerings well-sprinkled with sugar and ghee. || 17 ||

Regarding the thirteen-syllable mantras of Śrī Kṛṣṇa: when preceded by the ten syllables [of the mantra], there are three types of thirteen-syllable mantras— those beginning with Śrī-Māyā (Śrī- Hrīṃ), those beginning with Māyā-Śrī (Hrīṃ-Śrīṃ), and those beginning with Kāma-Māyā-Śrī (Klīṃ-Hrīṃ-Śrīṃ).
And thus: the three ten-syllable mantras are Śrī-Śaktimāra-pūrva, Śakti-Śrīmāra-pūrvaka, and Kāma-Śaktiramā-pūrva.
Thus, from the words of Sanatkumāra. || 18 ||
The procedure for their worship is as follows:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the *pīṭhanyāsa* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice,
one should perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*.
Namely:
salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to Virāṭ Gāyatrī, the seer of the metre, on the face; salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa on the heart.
Then follow the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
"To the Discus (*ācakra*), svāhā; salutation to both thumbs," "To the Discus, svāhā; salutation to the heart," and so forth; one should perform the placement as with the ten-syllable mantra.
Then, if one desires the fruit [of the rite], one should install the cage consisting of the ten principles (*tattva*) and the forms (*mūrti*).

Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the *kirīṭa* mantra and having displayed the mudrā according to one's capacity, one performs the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with: *oṃ namaḥ sudarśanāya astrāya phaṭ*.
Having performed [the ritual], one should meditate. || 19 ||
In the first mantra, the visualization is like that of the ten-syllable [mantra]; in the second, it is like the jewel-consecration;
but in the third, the visualization is as follows: [the deity] is ruddy in color and holds a conch, a discus, a bow, an arrow, a noose, and a goad.
Kṛṣṇa should be meditated upon at midday as blowing a flute with both his arms.
In the system of Gautamīya, however, the meditation here is also like that of the ten-syllable mantra.
And so it is stated with reference to the two mantras beginning with *Ramā* and *Kāmā*: "The practitioner, regarding these two mantras..."

The wise one should perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅgaka) with [the mantras] beginning with *āca* and so forth; he should perform everything, including meditation and worship, just as in the ten-syllable mantra.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, he should perform the installation of the conch (*śaṅkhasthāpana*). || 21 ||
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) as prescribed in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, and having meditated once more,

one should perform the previously mentioned worship of the flute and other items, up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), and then commence the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa-pūjā).
Its protective enclosures are Aṅga, Indravajra, and so forth.
Then, having worshipped the group of eight black deities, one should complete the ritual from the incense offering up to the dismissal. || 22 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for these consists of five hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"One should perform five hundred thousand recitations, and likewise ten thousand [recitations] with milk-rice (*pāyasa*)."
The practitioner of mantra should perform oblations in a consecrated fire for the sake of accomplishing all aims. || 23 ||
After uttering another mantra, beginning with the word *kṛṣṇāya*, followed by *govindāya*,
then the word *gopījana*, and at the end [the word] *vallabhāya*, ending with the *dviṭha* (svāhā).
The eighteen-syllable mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma, has been declared. || 24 ||

The procedure for its worship is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the placement of the *pīṭha-mantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other components.
For example: "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head;
salutation to the Gāyatrī metre on the mouth."
Salutation to the deity Kṛṣṇa in the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable *klīṃ* in the private parts;
salutation to the power *svāhā* in the feet.
Then, having pervaded the two hands with the mantra enclosed by the *praṇava* (oṃ) three times, one should perform the ritual assignments (*nyāsa*) of the hands and the limbs:
*klīṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
To Govinda, with the two index fingers, Svāhā! To Gopījana, with the two middle fingers, Vaṣaṭ!
To Vallabha, with the two ring fingers, Hum!
*svāhā* to the two little fingers, *phaṭ*.
In this same manner, [one performs the assignment] at the heart and other [limbs].
Then, having pervaded [the body] three times from the head down to the feet with the root mantra (*mūla*), [one should proceed].
Having pervaded [the body] once from the feet up to the crown of the head with the syllable *praṇava*, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*).
[One places them] on the crown, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the mouth.

One should place the syllables of each mantra, ending with "namaḥ," in these locations— the throat, heart, navel, hips, penis, knees, and shanks— and one should also place the Praṇava upon the head. || 25 ||
Then, one should place the five words of the mantra, ending with "namaḥ," upon the eyes, face, heart, secret parts, and feet.
These five words consist of four, four, four, and two [syllables] respectively.
Then one should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*klīṃ kṛṣṇāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*;
*govindāya śirase svāhā*.
Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock of the Gopī-jana;
Huṃ to the armor of the Beloved;
Svāhā Phaṭ to the weapon.
And so it is said:
"The knower of mantras should fashion the five limbs of the mantra in sequence with syllables numbering four, eight, four, four, and two,
conjoined with their respective seed-syllables."
The classes [of mantras] end with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*.

Then, having performed the *daśatattvamūrtipañjara-nyāsa*, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the *kirīṭa-mantra* according to one's capacity, and bind the mudrā, reciting: *oṃ namaḥ sudarśanāya astrāya phaṭ*.
Having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), having meditated upon [the deity] as described in the *Daśākṣara* [mantra], having worshipped with mental offerings,

and having performed the installation of the conch (*śaṅkhasthāpana*), one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) ending with the *pīṭhamantra* as prescribed for the Vaiṣṇavas; then, having meditated again, [one should perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth.

Having performed the rites up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers, and having worshipped with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) in the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) on the respective limbs using the syllables beginning with *klīm*— such as *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth— and then once again...
One should offer five handfuls of flowers.

Then, having performed the worship of the flute and so forth, and having performed the worship of the enclosures as prescribed for the ten-syllable mantra, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal, beginning with the incense offering.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this is as stated in the chapter on the ten-syllable mantra. || 26 ||
Another mantra, preceded by Śakti and Śrī, consists of eighteen or twenty syllables. || 27 ||
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the ritual of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa), beginning with the morning duties and ending with the mantra of the seat as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava rites, one should perform the nyāsa of the seer (ṛṣi) and the other [limbs].

Salutation to Brahmā, the seer, on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre, on the mouth; salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the deity, on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, on the private parts; salutation to the power *svāhā*, on the feet.
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*kṛṣṇāya* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
To Govinda, with the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; to Gopījana, with the two ring fingers, *huṃ*;
to Vallabha, with the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*; and with the palms and backs of the hands, *svāhā*.
Phaṭ!
In this manner, [the mantra is applied] to the heart and other parts. || 28 ||

Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, one should place the letters of the *mātṛkā* encased by the mantra upon their respective locations (the forehead and so forth). Then, having performed the placement of the ten principles (*tattva*), one should again perform the pervasive placement with the root mantra. || 29 ||
Then follows the placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*):
*hrīṃ* namaḥ on the head; *śrīṃ* namaḥ on the forehead; *klīṃ* namaḥ between the eyebrows;
*kṛṃ* namaḥ on the eyes; *ṣṇāṃ* namaḥ on the ears; *yaṃ* namaḥ on the nostrils.

*Goṃ* namaḥ to the face; *viṃ* namaḥ to the chin; *ndāṃ* namaḥ to the throat; *yaṃ* namaḥ to the base of the arms; *go* namaḥ to the heart; *pīṃ* namaḥ to the abdomen; *jaṃ* namaḥ to the navel; *naṃ* namaḥ to the generative organ;
*vaṃ* namaḥ to the *ādhāra*; *llaṃ* namaḥ to the hips; [and] to the two knees.
Bhāṃ namaḥ to the two thighs; yaṃ namaḥ to the two shanks; svāṃ namaḥ to the two ankles; hāṃ namaḥ to the two feet.
This is the emanation (sṛṣṭi).
*Hrīṃ* in the heart; *Śrīṃ* in the stomach; *Klīṃ* at the navel; *Kṛṃ* at the genitals; *Ṣṇāṃ* at the base (ādhāra); *Yaṃ* on the hips; *Goṃ* on the knees; *Viṃ* on the shanks; *Ndrāṃ* on the ankles;
*Yaṃ* on the feet; *Goṃ* on the head; *Pīṃ* on the skull; *Jaṃ* between the eyebrows; [and] *Jaṃ* on the eyes.
No; [the seed-syllables are] Vaṃ on the two ears, Llaṃ on the two nostrils, Bhāṃ on the face, Yaṃ on the chin, Svāṃ on the throat, and Hāṃ on the base of the arms.
This is the arrangement.
Hrīṃ at the two feet; Śrīṃ at the two ankles; Klīṃ at the two shanks; Kṛṃ at the two knees; Ṣṇāṃ at the waist;

Yaṃ at the base (ādhāra); Goṃ at the penis; Viṃ at the navel; Ndāṃ at the abdomen; Yaṃ at the heart; Goṃ at the base of the arms; Pīṃ at the throat; Jaṃ at the chin; Naṃ at the mouth; [Oṃ] at the two nostrils.
One should place *vaṃ* on the two ears, *llaṃ* on the two eyes, *bhāṃ* between the eyebrows, *yaṃ* on the forehead, *svāṃ* on the brow,
and *hāṃ* on the crown of the head; in all cases, these should be placed ending with *namaḥ*.
Thus ends the placement of reabsorption (*saṃhāranyāsa*).

Again, having performed the emanation and maintenance (*sṛṣṭisthiti*), and having placed the cage of forms (*mūrtipañjara*)— that is, having performed the emanation and maintenance of the cage of forms— one should place the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ, obeisance to the heart; Kṛṣṇāya, svāhā to the head;
Govindāya, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Huṃ for the armor of the cowherd women;
vauṣaṭ for the eyes of the Beloved;
svāhā phaṭ for the weapon.
And likewise:

having performed the creation and maintenance [of the mantra], one should practice the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the syllables of the mantra corresponding to the qualities, fires, Vedas, organs of action, organs of sense, and eyes. (37)

Then, having performed the display of the mudrās and so forth as before, as well as the binding of the directions (digbandhana), and having performed the pervasive projection (vyāpaka) with the Kirīṭa mantra, one should meditate while forming the mudrā according to one's ability. || 31 ||
(Śrī Kṛṣṇa Yantra, Figures 23-1, 2, 3) It is as follows:
In Dvārāvatī, with supreme palaces resplendent like a thousand suns...
In a jeweled pavilion surrounded by many wish-fulfilling trees,
with pillars, doors, archways, and walls made of blazing gems,
and with variegated canopies hanging from which fresh garlands and pearls were suspended;
In the midst of ruby plains and rivers of radiant gems,
beneath a self-sustaining tree from which streams of jewels flow incessantly,
and with the horizons illuminated by rows of jewel-lamps;
Acyuta should be meditated upon as seated upon a lotus lion-throne of jewels, which resembles the rising sun;
he is like molten gold and possesses a splendor equal to ten million simultaneously risen moons, suns, and lightning flashes.
Beautiful in every limb, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments,
he wears yellow garments; his arms shine with the discus, conch, mace, and lotus,
as he touches a water-pot from which a continuous stream of jewels flows.
With the tip of his left lotus-foot, he steals the luster of a fresh sprout;
while Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā stand at his right and left, sprinkling his two heads with streams of jewels rising from the water-pots held in their own hands.
Agnajiti and Sunandā stood at their sides holding water-pots;
and from those two, Mitravindā and Sulakṣaṇā, who were ten cubits tall,
lifted up two jars filled with jewels, which were like rivers of gems, for them.
Jāmbavatī and Suśīlā, bestowing [blessings] from the right and left [hands],
are surrounded by sixteen thousand beloved consorts;
they should be meditated upon as radiant with jars overflowing with streams of gold, jewels, and heaps of water.
Outside of that are the eight treasures (nidhis), filling the earth with wealth;
outside of that are all the Vṛṣṇis, as before, along with the Asuras and others.
Having meditated thus and worshipped them mentally, one should perform the ritual installation of the conch (śaṅkha-sthāpana).

The yantra for its worship is as follows: having drawn an eight-petaled lotus in the center of a hexagon, one should write the Kāma-bīja together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the middle of the hexagon, and with the remaining [syllables]...
One should enclose it with seventeen syllables.
Then, in the eastern, southern, and northwestern corners of the hexagon, one should write the Śrī-bīja; in the remaining corners, one should write Bhuvaneśvarī.

Then, one should write the six syllables "klīṃ kṛṣṇāya namaḥ" at the six joints. Then, in the filaments [of the lotus], one should write: "We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon the one with flower-arrows;
may Anaṅga impel us."
Thus, one should write three syllables each of the Gāyatrī mantra in order starting from the east.
Then, on the petals in order starting from the east, one should write: *namaḥ kāmadevāya sarvajanapriyāya sarvajanasaṃmohanāya jvala jvala prajvala sarvajanasya hṛdayaṃ mama*.
One should write the six syllables of the *mālā-mantra*, "vaśaṃ kuru kuru svāhā," upon the petals.
Regarding the *mālā-mantra*, the *Śāradā-tantra* states:
At the end of "namas," one should say "kāmadevāya," followed by "sarvajanasya," then "priyāya," then "sarvavarṇānām," and "janasammohanāya.
One should then say "jvalat" twice, ending with "prajvala," followed again by "sarvajanasya."
The heart-mantra is at the end of the word "mama," followed by "vaśam kuru" twice;
this is the garland-mantra consisting of forty-eight syllables.
One should encircle that with the Mātṛkā alphabet.
Then, on the mandala of the earth, one should write the Śrī-bīja in the cardinal directions and the Māyā-bīja in the intermediate directions. Outside of that, one should draw eight vajras.
And so it is said:
Having smeared [the ground] with fragrant paste, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus;
in the pericarp, however, one should draw a hexagon containing the Sādhya and there [place] Manmatha.
One should encircle that Smara with the remaining seventeen syllables.
In the directions starting from the east, the southeast, and the northwest, there is prosperity; in the remaining directions, there is wisdom.
The six-syllable mantra [is placed] thirty times each upon the filaments at the six joints.
One should inscribe the Gāyatrī of Smara and the Mālā-mantra upon the eight petals.
Having written six [syllables] six times, one should encircle them on the outside with the letters of the Mātṛkā;
and one should draw the figure of the earth (bhūvimba) on the outside, as well as the syllable Śrī-māyā in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The earth-chamber (bhūgṛha) should be square and adorned with eight vajras;
this is the yantra for those [mantras] consisting of eighteen syllables, twenty-two syllables, twelve syllables, ten syllables, fourteen syllables, and eleven syllables. || 33 ||
As for that which was said: "A lotus with eight petals, square, possessing auspicious characteristics,
endowed with four gates, and having a pericarp containing the objects of desire."
The general yantra has been indicated; now hear [the one] for the eighteen-syllable mantra. || 34 ||
One should then draw a square with four gates, containing an eight-petalled lotus;
its center is called the "Kāma" [triangle] within a hexagon, encircled by the seventeen syllables.
Thereafter, one should inscribe the excellent six-syllable mantra within the hexagon.
Thus, whatever specific distinction regarding the eighteen-syllable and ten-syllable [mantras] has been stated in the Gautamīya is intended for those who are incapable;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Tāpinī and other scriptures. || 35 ||
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) ending with the previously mentioned mantra of the pedestal, and having meditated again,

having performed the rites from invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), and having worshipped the emanation (sṛṣṭi), the maintenance (sthiti), and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), [one should offer] "Oṃ, salutation to the Diadem" (kirīṭa), and so forth.

One should worship the two earrings, the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the forest garland, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem everywhere with mantras beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with "Namaḥ.
Then, having offered five handfuls of flowers, one should begin the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇapūjā).
For example: in the six corners, beginning from the southeast, one should worship the six limbs with "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ, obeisance to the Heart;
Kṛṣṇāya, Svāhā to the Head," and so forth. Then, at the base of the petals in the cardinal directions, one should worship with "Oṃ Vāsudevāya Namaḥ" and likewise "Saṅkarṣaṇāya."
One should worship Pradyumna and Aniruddha with the mantra beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Likewise, at the bases of the intermediate petals:
*Oṃ śāntyai namaḥ*, and similarly for Śrī, Sarasvatī, and Rati.
On the petals, starting from the east as before, one should worship Rukmiṇī and the others.
Here, one should offer salutations to the sixteen thousand Mahiṣīs; outside of that, starting from the east, [one should worship] Indranidhi.
One should worship Nīlanidhi, Mukundanidhi, Makaranidhi, Ānandanidhi,
Kacchapanidhi, Padmanidhi, and Śaṅkhanidhi. Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the Vajra and the other weapons.
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 36 ||
The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of reciting it four hundred thousand times.
And so it is said:
"Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, one should recite the twenty-syllable mantra."
One should offer four hundred thousand oblations with clarified butter, and forty thousand [with other substances].
Another mantra: Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, "to Kṛṣṇa," Bhuvaneśvarī;
"to Govinda," Ramā, "to the beloved of the cowherd women," and Īśiraḥ.
Above that is Bhṛgu, endowed with the fourteenth vowel and followed by the letter *s*.
This twenty-two-syllable mantra bestows the state of Lord of Speech. || 38 ||

The procedure for its worship is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having executed the seat-consecration (pīṭhanyāsa) ending with the seat-mantra as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava rites,

one should perform the assignment of the seer and others (ṛṣyādinyāsa), as well as the hand and limb assignments (karāṅganyāsa), according to the eighteen-syllable mantra, followed by the ritual gestures (mudrā) and so forth.
And having performed the binding of the directions, one should meditate as follows:
holding in his upper left hand the book containing the entire essence of knowledge.
And in the upper right hand, he holds a crystal rosary consisting of the Mātṛkās.
He plays the flute composed of the Brahman of sound, which is held in his two lower hands.
He was singing, dressed in yellow garments, dark-complexioned, and possessing a delicate luster.
One should always worship Hari, who has peacock feathers as His crest-ornament, who is omniscient, who is served by all-knowing ones, and who is attended by hosts of sages.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with twenty syllables.
The distinction, however, is this:
there is no creation, maintenance, or worship of that [deity], because of the absence of its [corresponding] caste. || 39 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of four hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"The practitioner of mantra, being well-restrained, should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times."
With well-spoken words and *palāśa* flowers, [he performed] forty thousand [recitations].
One should perform oblations with this rite; then the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur. || 40 ||
Another mantra:
Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, followed by Māyā and Lakṣmī;
this excellent ten-syllable mantra becomes a sixteen-syllable mantra.
In the Brahmasaṃhitā:
"The seed-syllable of speech (vāgbhava), Bhuvaneśānī, the Śrī-bīja, and the Kāma-bījaka; this excellent mantra consists of ten syllables, and another consists of eleven syllables. (41)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:
having performed the morning rites and the placement of the pedestal (pīṭhanyāsa) as prescribed by the Vaiṣṇavas, one should perform the placement of the seers and other elements (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
Salutation to the sage Brahmā on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the heart. || 42 ||
All other rites, such as the ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, recitation (japa), and fire-oblation (homa), should be performed just as they are for the ten-syllable mantra. || 43 ||
But regarding meditation, there is this distinction:
one should meditate upon [the Lord] in the delightful Vṛndāvana, situated in the midst of golden ground,
strewn with various flowering creepers and adorned with groves of trees.
On the ground of the forest of the Kalpa tree, within a magnificent pavilion of rubies,
he was surrounded by Nārada and other foremost sages who were offering him praise.
One should meditate upon him seated upon a lotus atop a jeweled lion-throne,
dark as a water-laden cloud, with eyes as broad as red lotuses.
Adorned with hands and feet shimmering like red lotuses,
and further embellished with ornaments fashioned from various jewels.

His chest was graced with splendor, its garment illuminated by the shining Kaustubha gem; he was beautiful with the excellence of his bright pearl necklace, and his breast was marked with the Śrīvatsa sign.
With his locks of hair at the edges of his forehead-mark of yellow pigment acting like bees,
he was resplendent with a row of side-locks resembling the bow of Kandarpa.

One should always worship Hari, who is endowed with many jewels, whose shark-shaped earrings are shimmering, who has a crest made of peacock feathers, who is the omniscient one worshipped by all-knowing ones, and who is attended by hosts of sages.
Thus [ends the verse]. 44.
Another mantra (the single-syllabled one) consists of the syllable of desire (KĀM), situated on the earth (DHA), and adorned with the dot of peace (the nasal bindu).
Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds, has been declared to you with effort. (45)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) up to the seat-powers (pīṭha-śakti) as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, one should place the seat-mantra (pīṭha-manu) upon it, reciting: "To the King of Birds, svāhā."
Then follows the Nyāsa of the Seer and so forth.
It is as follows:
*namaḥ* to the Seer Sammohana on the head; *namaḥ* to the Gāyatrī metre on the mouth; [and] on the heart...
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds.
As it has been said:
"The seer is Sammohana, and the meter is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī."
Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds, is declared to be the deity. || 46 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs:
*klāṃ* to both thumbs, *namaḥ*, and so forth;
*klāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth.
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"One should fashion [the seal] by joining the long [vowel] with the sixth [consonant] and the seed-syllable of desire. || 47 ||
Then follows the placement of the arrows (*bāṇanyāsa*): on the thumbs, *drāṃ*, obeisance to the arrow of withering;
on the index fingers, *drīṃ*, obeisance to the arrow of enchantment.
On the two middle fingers: *klīṃ* to the Sandīpana-bāṇa, obeisance. On the two ring fingers: *blūṃ* to the Tāpana-bāṇa, obeisance. On the two little fingers: *saḥ* to the Mādana-bāṇa, obeisance.
Likewise:
one should place [the mantras] on the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
First, one should place the drying [syllable] beginning with *drām*, then the deluding [syllable] beginning with *drīm*;
then the one called inflaming beginning with *klīm*, and again the heating [syllable] beginning with *blūm*;
finally, one should install the fifth, the intoxicating [syllable], together with the *bhṛgu* at the end of creation.
Then one should meditate:
[upon Him] whose body resembles broken coral, consisting entirely of splendor,
wearing a crown and earrings, and endowed with armlets and bracelets.
Resplendent with the ends of its balance-beams adorned with pearls and excellent gems,
beautiful with various ornaments, and draped in a pair of yellow garments.
Seated upon Garuḍa, she stands in the midst of a bound red lotus;
Lakṣmī, who resembles molten gold, is seated upon his left thigh.
Adorned with all ornaments and draped in a pair of white garments.
[She saw] the God, who was playfully deluding her again and again, even though she was filled with desire.
[One should meditate upon] the Lord of the World, who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, a lotus, a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows,
and whose eyes are as red as a crimson lotus.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the installation of the conch,

and having performed the worship of the pedestal according to the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) as in the ten-syllable mantra, one should again perform the rites beginning with meditation and invocation up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers.

Having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) by means of the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should worship the five arrows within the body of the deity; then, [worship] upon the hands with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the crown (kirīṭa)," and likewise to the earrings (kuṇḍala), the conch (śaṅkha), the discus (cakra), the mace (gadā), the lotus (padma), the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the bow (dhanus), and the arrow (śara).
One should worship:
with "Obeisance to Śrīvatsa" on the upper chest; to Kaustubha; to Vanamālā on the throat; to Pītavastra (the yellow garment) on the hips; and to Śrī Lakṣmī on the left side.
One should worship everywhere with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.

Then, one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the filaments— at the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions— with "klīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ," "klīṃ śirase svāhā," and so forth.
Then, having worshipped four arrows in the cardinal directions beginning with the east, one should worship the fifth arrow in the corners.
On the petals, [one should worship] "Oṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī."
In this manner, one should worship Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi; outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas).
In this context, there is no worship of the Vajra and other [emblems], because they have not been mentioned.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 48 ||
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one million times and perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that."

The knower of the treasure-chest should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) sprinkled with the three nectars, or otherwise perform the fire-oblation for as long as it takes to equal the duration of a day and night of the Sun, and likewise satisfy [the deities]. || 49 ||
Another mantra is the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM); "to Hṛṣīkeśa" is the heart-mantra consisting of eight syllables.
And thus it is said:
The word *hṛṣīkeśa* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), preceded by *namaḥ* and followed by *kāma*, is used;
its placement (*nyāsa*), worship (*pūjā*), and all other rites are as previously described. (50)

*Lakṣmī*, *māyā*, the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*), the word *Kṛṣṇa* in the dative case (*ṅe'nta*), and likewise *svāhā*—this is the king of mantras, a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it. (51)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, including the placement [of mantras] up to the *pīṭhamantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and the other [components].
For example: "Homage to the sage Nārada on the head;
homage to the Anuṣṭubh metre on the mouth."
In the heart, salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 52 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs:
*klāṃ* to both thumbs, *namaḥ*, and so forth; likewise, *klāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth. || 53 ||
Then comes the meditation: Hari, dark as a *kalāya* flower, situated in Vṛndāvana,
surrounded by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cows, and clothed in a pair of yellow garments.
Adorned with various ornaments, his chest radiant with the Kaustubha gem,
praised with supreme joy by the foremost sages such as Sanaka and others,
his arms graced by the conch and discus, he played the flute with his two hands.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.
Then, having worshipped the pedestal (pīṭha) ending with the mantra of the pedestal as prescribed by the Vaiṣṇavas, and having meditated again,
one should perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali),
and then commence the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
For example: one should worship with "klāṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth, in the filaments, in the corners beginning with the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.

Outside of that, having worshipped Indra and the other deities as well as the vajra and the other implements, one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the offering of incense and ending with the dismissal. || 55 ||
For its preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa), the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times;
he should then perform oblations with flowers born from the Brahmavṛkṣa tree, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
Another mantra is "Śrī-Śaktismara-Kṛṣṇāya Govindāya," which is the head-mantra (śiro-manu). || 57 ||
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the previously mentioned seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra), one should perform the seat-assignment (pīṭhanyāsa) and then the assignment of the ṛṣi and other elements, as in the case of the jewel-consecration (ratnābhiṣeka). || 58 ||
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) is as follows: *śrīṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*hrīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
Klīm to the two middle fingers, Vaṣaṭ; Kṛṣṇāya to the two ring fingers, Huṃ;
Govindāya to the two little fingers, Vauṣaṭ.
*Svāhā* to the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
Likewise, for the heart and other limbs: *śrīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth. (59)

Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the body-cage (mūrtipañjara) and having executed the binding of the directions with mudrās and so forth, one should meditate upon [the deity] as described in the twenty-syllable [mantra] and worship according to that procedure.
However, there is a specific distinction: one should not perform the worship according to the sequence of emanation and maintenance (sṛṣṭisthitikrama).
Because of the absence of those respective castes, his preliminary rite consists of recitation and fire-offerings in that same manner.
Another mantra is: *Tāraṃ hṛd bhagavate rukmiṇīvallabhāya svāhā*. And likewise:

The Tāra (Oṃ), the heart (Namaḥ), the Lord (Bhagavate), ending with the dative case (Ṅe), and likewise Rukmiṇīvallabha, ending with the word for head (Śirasi)—this sixteen-syllable mantra is called the Rukmiṇīvallabha. || 61 ||
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:
having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having executed the *pīṭhanyāsa* ending with the *pīṭhamantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, one should perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*.
Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head;
salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre in the mouth;
salutation to the deity Rukmiṇīvallabha in the heart. || 62 ||
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *oṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*;
*namas tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*.
To the Blessed One, *vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers;
to the Beloved of Rukmiṇī, *huṃ* with the ring fingers;
*svāhā* with the little fingers, *phaṭ*.
In the same way, [this applies] to the heart and the other [limbs]. || 63 ||
Then comes the meditation:

[one should visualize] the beloved goddess, whose complexion is like the *tāpiñja* flower, who possesses a golden luster, whose left hand emerges from a lotus, and who embraces with her own left arm him (the deity) who smiles at her heart.

May Hari protect you for a long time— He who, wearing yellow garments made of hemp flowers and adorned with various ornaments, personally embraces her while holding a golden staff that gleams in his other hand.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch and the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) ending with the mantra of the pedestal as prescribed for Vaiṣṇavas; then, having meditated again,
[one performs the rites] from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā), one should begin as follows:
in the filaments— at the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions— [one should worship] with "Oṃ, to the Heart."
Namaḥ!
Svāhā to the head, Namaḥ!
Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock of the Blessed One.
*Oṃ rukmiṇīvallabhāya kavacāya huṃ svāhā! Oṃ astrāya phaṭ!* Then, on the eight petals starting from the east: *Oṃ nāradāya namaḥ*, and likewise for Parvata and Viṣṇu.
One should honor Niśaṭha, Uddhava, Dāruka, Viṣvaksena, and the son of Śuna (Śauneya).

Having worshipped Indra and the other deities along with their respective weapons, such as the thunderbolt, one should complete the ritual procedure beginning with the incense offering and ending with the dismissal of the deities.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"Having thus meditated upon the Beloved of Rukmiṇī, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times."
One should offer ten thousand oblations with red lotuses soaked in honey.
Other mantras are as follows: preceded by Śrī, Śakti, and Kāma, followed by Aṅga, Janma, Śakti, and Ramā;
this very ten-syllable mantra becomes endowed with Śakti and Ramā.
The mantra and the transformation are these two: the non-differentiation and the marking with the discus and other signs.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the five limbs, beginning with the ṛṣi, for these two mantras as in the case of the ten-syllabled mantra, one should perform the worship described for the twenty syllables. || 67 ||
But in the meditative state (dhyāna):

he embraces his beloved who is seated on his lap with his two hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she, with lotus and lily in her hands, embraces him who is radiant with the [other] hands holding the discus and mace. || 68 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for these two consists of ten lakhs of recitations (japa),
followed by a fire sacrifice (homa) of one thousand oblations of clarified butter (ājya) for each.
And so it is said:
One should recite the mantra one million times and offer oblations of clarified butter one thousand times.
The Praṇava joined with "namaḥ," followed by "Kṛṣṇa" and "Govinda" preceded by "Śrī" and ending in the dative case (ṅe), is proclaimed as: "huṃ phaṭ svāhā. (70)
The seer of this [mantra] is the ṛṣi Nārada; the metre is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is Hari, the Supreme Self.
The assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) is performed with the syllables beginning with *ā-cakra*.
Its worship, recitation, fire-oblation, and other rites are to be conducted like those of the ten-syllable [mantra].
And the seed-powers are equal to those. || 71 ||
Alternatively, the mantras for children and cowherds:
*kṛḥ*, which is the syllable *cakrī* (the letter *ca*) joined with the eighth vowel (*u*) and followed by the visarga (*ḥ*).
"Kṛṣṇa" consists of two syllables; it is the blackness of desire. To Kṛṣṇa, the blackness of desire; salutation to Kṛṣṇa.
Kāma, Kṛṣṇāya, Namaḥ, Antakaḥ;
Kāmakṛṣṇāya, Kāmaḥ; Gopālāya, [the two Ṭha syllables].
Kāmaḥ kṛṣṇāya svāhā.
Kṛṣṇa and Govinda ending in the dative case:
Kāmaḥ kṛṣṇāya govindāya.
*Kāmaḥ*, *kṛṣṇa-govindau* (in the dative case), and *kāmaḥ*; two *ṭha*s for the consumption of curd and honey;
*suprasannātmane* for the heart.
*Kāmaḥ glauṃ kāmaḥ*; *śyāmalāṅgāya* [is] the heart; *bālavapuṣe kṛṣṇāya* [is] followed by the fire-born consort (*vahnijāyā*);
*ramā māyā kāmaḥ kṛṣṇāya kāmaḥ*.
*Bālavapuṣe klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā*.
And likewise, in the *Nibandha*:
"The mantra is considered to consist of eight syllables joined with the vowels, ending with the letter 'sa' (visarga) and the letter 'e'."
The two-syllable [mantra] is "Kṛṣṇa"; that same one, preceded by "Kāma," is three syllables;
that same one becomes four syllables when ending in the dative case (Kṛṣṇāya); another four-syllable [mantra] will be stated as "Kṛṣṇāya namaḥ," which consists of five syllables.
That same mantra, if preceded by *kāma* (the seed-syllable of desire), is considered the six-syllabled mantra.
Another five-syllabled mantra is formed by placing *smara* (the seed-syllable of love) between [the two parts];
the six-syllabled mantra is considered to be *gopālāya* ending with the wife of Agni (*svāhā*).
Another [mantra] beginning with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma) for Kṛṣṇa and ending with the wife of fire (Svāhā) is as follows:

"Kṛṣṇa Govindaka" in the dative case (ṅe-anta) is the excellent seven-syllabled mantra beginning with desire (Kāma). Furthermore, "Kṛṣṇa Govindaka" in the dative case (ṅe-anta), preceded by desire (Kāma), is the eight-syllabled [mantra].
If the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) is placed at the beginning and the end, it is declared to be nine syllables long.
For the purpose of consuming curd, the eight-syllabled mantra ending with the beloved of Fire (*vahnivallabhā*) is prescribed;
likewise, another eight-syllabled mantra ending with "salutation to the well-pleased Self" (*suprasannātmane namaḥ*) is proclaimed.
One should again extract the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), followed by the seed-syllable of the earth (LŪM), and then desire (KĀM) once more.

This ten-syllabled mantra consists of the word "Śyāmalāṅga" ending in the dative case (ṄE) and ending with "Namaḥ. Another mantra is considered to be for the "Black One with the Body of a Child," ending with "Śiraḥ" (Svāhā).
The seven-syllable mantra for Śrī-Śakti-Kāma-Kṛṣṇa is "Māraḥ";
the one ending with the head-mantra (Hūṃ) for Bāla-Vapuḥ-Kṛṣṇa is remembered by the wise as "Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya. (1)
The yantra for their worship is as follows:
an eight-petalled lotus within a circle, situated inside a square enclosure with four gates, with the Kāma-bīja located in the center of the circle (Figure 24).
And so it is stated in the Gautamīya: "A lotus with eight petals, square, well-proportioned,
endowed with four gates, and having a pericarp containing the objects of desire."
The method for their worship is as follows:
having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having executed the *pīṭhanyāsa* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, one should perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*.
For example: "Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head;
salutation to the Gāyatrī metre on the mouth."
In the heart, obeisance to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 2 ||
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*klāṃ* to both thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*klīṃ* to both index fingers, *svāhā*.
Klūṃ to the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ; klaiṃ to the two ring fingers, huṃ;
klauṃ to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ.
*Klaḥ* with both palms and the backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
Likewise for the heart and other limbs: *klāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth.
Then, having displayed the mudrās and so on as before, one should meditate. (3)
Meditation:

May Mukunda protect you— he who possesses the luster of an unblemished blue lotus, whose eyes are like red lotuses, who stands upon a lotus, and who is a youth with tinkling bells fastened to his calves and the region of his hips.

May He who is worshipped by the universe, holding in His two arms the purest *haiyaṅgavīna* and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and whose neck is adorned with the shining nails of the cows, gopīs, and cowherds, protect you for a long time.
Having meditated thus and performed worship with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) according to the rites prescribed by the Vaiṣṇavas, up to the mantra of the pedestal, and having meditated again upon the deity born from the pedestal, one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali),
and then commence the worship of the deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā).
For example:

having worshipped the six limbs with "klāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth in the filaments, in the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions; then [worship] Nārada and others on the petals, and Indra and others outside of that.
One should worship the vajra and the other implements; then, one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the incense offering and ending with the dismissal. || 5 ||
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for these consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"Having meditated upon any one of these in this manner, one should then recite the mantra one hundred thousand times."
One should offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee and white sugar.
Likewise:
one should satisfy these Manus with libations equal in number to the oblations offered. || 6 ||
The other mantra consists of the letter *ū* joined with the upper tooth (*ṛ*), followed by *śārṅgī*, *cakrī*, and the right ear (*e*);
ending with "to the Lord" (*nāthāya*) and the word "salutation" (*namaḥ*), this eight-syllabled root mantra is as follows: *ūr-śārṅgī-cakrī-e-nāthāya-namaḥ*.
The seer is Brahmā, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Kṛṣṇa;
the five limbs are said to be formed by the pairs of syllables taken together.
Having meditated thus, one should mutter the mantra eight hundred thousand times, or at least one thousand;
then one should perform oblations with sacrificial fuel-sticks from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree or with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One should worship Kṛṣṇa, who has been installed in the temple, daily;
one should perform the rites from the worship of the door up to the final installation (pīṭha) according to the previously mentioned method.
One should worship Hari in the center, and the limbs (aṅgas) in the cardinal and intermediate directions in due order:
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
as well as Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Lakṣmaṇā, and Jāmbavatī.
One should worship these deities, beginning with Indra and Vajra, in the cardinal and intermediate directions on the exterior.
He who daily recites this mantra while worshipping Hari according to the prescribed rite shall be filled with all prosperity and shall eternally go to the pure abode.
Another mantra,
with the word "Kṛṣṇa" placed between the two words for "desire," is a mantra that bestows immediate results.
And so it is said:
I shall now declare another four-syllabled mantra that bestows immediate results;
it is proclaimed as ending with the pair of letters 'Mā' and 'Ra', followed by the word 'Kṛṣṇa'. (12)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, including the placement on the seat (*pīṭhanyāsa*) ending with the *pīṭhamantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, and having performed the placement of the directions (*dṛṣyādinyāsa*) and the placement of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), one should meditate. 13.

Vāsudeva, who is seated upon the shimmering pericarp of a lotus sprouting from the root of the glorious wish-fulfilling tree; who is consecrated by innumerable jewels streaming from the interior of the lotuses hanging from its branches; and who, golden-hued, illuminates the entire triple world with his own radiance.
May he who eats milk-rice, whose nectar-like lips are constantly moistened by fresh [nectar], protect you.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the ritual installation of the conch,

and having fully worshipped the pedestal (pīṭha) up to the mantra of the pedestal as prescribed for Vaiṣṇavas, one should meditate again and perform the rites beginning with invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*), one should begin the rite.

Having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with "Oṃ *klāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*" and so forth in the southeast, northeast, center, and the cardinal directions, one should worship the eight treasures (*aṣṭanidhi*) on the petals starting from the east, and outside of those, Indra and the other guardians of the quarters.
Having worshipped Vajra and the others, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense (*dhūpa*) until the final dismissal (*visarjana*).
14. The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of four hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).
And thus it is said:
Having thus recited the mantra four hundred thousand times, one should then perform oblations forty thousand times with bilva fruits smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu).
If there is a *repha* at the end of the two *la*s, which are the seed-syllables of desire (*kāma-bīja*) in this mantra, then it is the *Mantra-cūḍāmaṇi*.
And so it is stated in the *Nibandha*:
If there is another mantra consisting of the syllable *māṃsa* (ma) below *māra* (ma),
and the syllable *rakta* (ra) is beneath the letter *la* at the bottom of the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), then this is the meaning of "this mantra. || 16 ||
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:
having performed the placement of the [five] objects of sight and so forth as before, one should perform the placements on the hands and the limbs.
As follows:
*Klīṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*, and so forth;
*klīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth.
All [procedures] for its worship and the like are as before.
But there is a distinction regarding the meditation:

[one should visualize Him] seated upon a golden swing shimmering beneath a wish-fulfilling tree in a slightly rosy garden, appearing with the luster of a blooming fresh bandhūka flower or vermilion, while being gazed upon by two cowherd girls.

I bow to Mukunda, who is like a child with dangling locks of hair, adorned with a multitude of small bells shimmering at his waist, and radiant with the playful leap of the elephant-headed Gaṇeśa, who is as fierce as a tiger and holds a goad of desire. 18.

Having meditated thus and having worshipped Him as before, and having recited the mantra while offering oblations of fresh red lotuses mixed with the three sweets, one should worship Hari as previously described.
Now, the mantra of Vāsudeva is proclaimed as follows: *praṇava* (om), *hṛt* (namaḥ), and *bhagavate vāsudevāya*.
In the Vaiṣṇava tantra, this mantra is indeed the primary one, like a celestial wish-fulfilling tree.

Its worship is as follows: having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement of the *pīṭha-mantra* as previously described, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other components.
For example: "Homage to Prajāpati, the seer, on the head; homage to the Gāyatrī meter, on the mouth; homage to the deity Vāsudeva, on the heart. (2)
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs: *oṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *namas* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*;
to the Blessed One (*bhagavate*), to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*.
