To Vāsudeva with the two ring fingers: *huṃ*. *Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya* with the two little fingers: *phaṭ*.
Thus [the mantras are assigned] to the heart and the other limbs.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"The heart is declared with *tāra* (om), the head is said to be with *namaḥ*;
the crest (*śikhā*) is declared with four syllables, and the armor (*kavaca*) is considered to consist of five syllables."
The assignment of the limbs is said to be performed with the entire [mantra] as the weapon. || 3 ||
Then follows the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa):
on the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the mouth, the throat, the two arms, the heart-lotus,
the belly, the navel, the penis, the two knees, and likewise the two feet.
One should arrange the twelve syllables.
Then, having arranged the cage of the forms (mūrtipañjara) and performed the pervasion with the kirīṭa-mantra, one should meditate. || 4 ||
Viṣṇu, who resembles ten million autumnal moons, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus; whose abode is white and who deludes the world with his splendor;
wearing armlets, necklaces, earrings, and a great crown, with shimmering bracelets—
I bow to Him who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem, and who is praised by the lords of sages.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) as prescribed by the Vaiṣṇava tradition, and having meditated once more,
one should perform the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali),
and then begin the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
One should worship the five limbs with "Oṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth, in the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions.
Then, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others, together with the Śaktis such as Śānti, on the petals starting from the east.

Having worshipped Keśava and the others, as well as the deities beginning with Nidrā and those beginning with Vajra, one should complete the ritual actions from the offering of incense up to the final dismissal. || 6 ||
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"One who has been initiated and has conquered his senses should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable."
One should offer that thousand-fold oblation with sesame seeds drenched in clarified butter.
Now, the mantras of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa: two *māyā*s (hrīṃ hrīṃ), two *ramā*s (śrīṃ śrīṃ), followed by "namo lakṣmīvāsudevāya.
This mantra begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ).
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"The pair of *hṛllekhā* seed-syllables, followed again by the pair of *ramā* seed-syllables;
at the end of *lakṣmī*, [the name] *vāsudevāya*; ending with *hṛt* (namas), preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ)."
This fourteen-syllable mantra is declared to be the celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
Its worship and other rites are like those for the Vāsudeva mantra.
However, regarding the ritual assignment of the seers and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa), Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva is the deity.
The mantras for the assignment of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) are as follows:
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the two thumbs. Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers. Oṃ lakṣmī, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers.
Oṃ vāsudevāya, to the two ring fingers, huṃ; oṃ namaḥ, to the two little fingers, phaṭ.
Thus [the mantras are assigned] to the heart and the other limbs.
And so it is said:
"The heart is declared by means of the two seed-syllables of Śakti; the head is proclaimed by the two syllables of Ramā;
the topknot (śikhā) is spoken of by Lakṣmī; and the armor (varma) is celebrated as 'to Vāsudeva'."
Having offered salutations, one should install the entire scripture beginning with Tārā.
Then follows the meditation:
[One should meditate on her] whose body resembles lightning and the moon, who has attained the unity of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
May He, who holds a jewel-encrusted vessel adorned with ornaments dripping with the essence of nectar,
a lotus that serves as a mirror for the lotuses of knowledge, a gem-studded water-pot,
a lotus, a mace, a conch, and a discus— may He, possessing these infinite forms, eternally grant you prosperity. 8ka.
All his worship and so forth are as previously described.
His preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of fourteen hundred thousand recitations.
And thus it is said:
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables;
then one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with a thousand blossomed lotuses mixed with the three sweets (madhuratraya).
"One hundred thousand according to the syllables" means a number of lakhs equal to the number of syllables in the mantra.
Now, the mantra of Dadhivāmana: *oṃ namo viṣṇave surapataye mahābalāya ṭha ṭha*.
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
The syllable *tāra* (oṃ) is for the heart; thereafter, *viṣṇave* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), followed by *surapatiḥ*;
then *mahābalāya* and the two *ṭha*s (svāhā). This is the eighteen-syllable mantra. || 10 ||

The worship of this [deity] is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having performed the placement (nyāsa) ending with "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen digits," one should perform the placement of the seer (ṛṣi) and the other [limbs].
Salutation to the Ṛṣi Indu on the head; salutation to the Virāṭ metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Dadhivāmana in the heart. And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
One should worship [the deity] on a pedestal fashioned at the end of the moon, according to the previously mentioned method. || 11 ||
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *Oṃ*, salutation to the two thumbs;
*namas*, *svāhā* to the two index fingers.
To Viṣṇu with the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; to the Lord of the Gods with the two ring fingers, *huṃ*;
to Mahābala with the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*.
*Svāhā* to the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
Likewise for the heart and other [limbs].
And so it is said:
The heart is with one [syllable], the crest with two, and the head is declared to be with three;
the armor is said to consist of five, and the eye of that same number of syllables;
the weapon is said to be with two—this is the method for the limbs as taught by the wise.
Then follows the ritual placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*):
on the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the lips, the palate, the throat, the two arms,
the abdomen, the navel, the private parts, the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, and the two feet.
One should place the syllables of the mantra ending in *namaḥ*,
two syllables at a time, beginning with the two shanks. Then, having performed the ritual of the "cage of forms" (*mūrtipañjara*) and so forth, one should meditate.
Fair as a pearl, adorned with fine ornaments of fresh gems, seated upon the moon,
her lotus-face graced by tresses of hair shaped like bees;
with her two lotus-hands she holds a golden pitcher filled with pure water.
We worship Him who holds a golden cup filled with curd-rice;
having meditated thus and performed mental worship, one should perform the installation of the conch. || 14 ||
Then, having worshipped the seat (pīṭha) as far as the lunar disc and meditated again,
one should perform the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā), beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of five handfuls of flowers.
And so it is said:
"One should worship him in a secluded place on an imagined seat ending with the Moon (Candrānta).
As follows:"
One should worship with "Oṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth, in the southeast corner, the center, and the cardinal directions.

Then, having worshipped Vāsudeva and the others together with their Śaktis on the petals of the directions, as well as the banners and other symbols at their front, and Keśava and the others; and [finally] Indra, his thunderbolt, and the other weapons, along with Airāvata and the other elephants of the directions.
One should worship.
One should worship in the sequence beginning with "Oṃ, obeisance to Airāvata, the elephant of the direction," and so forth.
In this same manner, one should worship Puṇḍarīka and the others.
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 15 ||
The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of three hundred thousand recitations.
And thus it is said:
"One should recite the mantra three million times, and then perform ten percent of that [number] with oblations soaked in ghee."
One should offer oblations of milk-rice or curd-rice according to the prescribed rule.
Now, the mantras of Hayagrīva:
Oṃ! Utter the Praṇava and the Udgītha! O Lord of all masters of speech!
O you who consist of all the Vedas, O inconceivable one! Awaken, awaken all!
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"Having uttered the word 'udgītha' by means of the words 'praṇava' and 'udgītha',
one should then say 'sarvavāgīśvarā' at the end, followed by 'īśvarā'."
At the end of all inconceivable sounds consisting of the Vedas, one should utter "sarvam";
this mantra, ending with "bodhaya" and "dvitaya," is proclaimed as beginning with "tārā. (17)
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the *pīṭhamantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [limbs].
For example:
"Homage to the seer Brahmā on the head;
homage to the meter Anuṣṭubh in the mouth."
In the heart, obeisance to the deity Śrī Hayagrīva. || 18 ||
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *Oṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
*Udgīta-praṇava-udgītha tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*.
O Lord of all masters of speech, *vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers;
O you who are conceivable as consisting of all the Vedas, *huṃ* with the two ring fingers;
awaken, awaken everything, *phaṭ* with the two little fingers.
In the same way, [the procedure applies] to the heart and the other [limbs]. || 19 ||
Then comes the meditation:
[one should visualize] the horse-faced one, possessing the luster of an autumnal moon, blazing with ornaments made of pearls.
We worship Him whose pair of arms is adorned with the discus and the conch, and who has placed His two hands upon His two knees.

Having meditated thus and performed worship with mental offerings, having established the conch and performed the worship of the pedestal as prescribed for Vaiṣṇavas, one should meditate again while reciting "Ha-Sūm."
One should thus mentally conceive the form.
And thus:
having conceived the form by means of the seed-syllable, one should extract the seed-syllable, as follows:
the seed-syllable is said to consist of the letter *viyat* (the sky), situated upon *bhṛgu* (the planet Venus), with the lord of *argha* (the letter *ra*) and the bindu (*m*). Thus: *hrīm*.
Then, having meditated again and performed the rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the offering of five handfuls of flowers,
one should commence the worship of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).

For example: one should worship the four Vedas— the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharvan— in the four cardinal directions among the filaments, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅga), the Smṛtis, Nyāya, and all other scriptures in the intermediate directions.
One should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatāḥ) within the petals according to the prescribed rule;
outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the directions, as well as the vajra and the other ritual implements.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the offering of incense and ending with the dismissal of the deities. || 20 ||
The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of thirty-three hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times per syllable with kunda flowers soaked in honey."
The best among those who know mantras should offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire ten times the amount [of the total].
Now, the single-syllable mantra of Hayagrīva consists of the letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, the sixth vowel (*ū*), and the nasal bindu.
And so it is stated in the Kalpa:

The seed-syllable (bīja) is said to consist of the sky (viyat), the descendant of Bhṛgu (bhṛgu), the lord of the guest-water (arghīśa), and the bindu; this is declared to be the single-syllable mantra that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.

Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra]; Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas); Viṣṇu in the form of Hayagrīva is the deity (devatā); the syllable *ha* is the seed-syllable (bīja); the syllable *ū* is the pin (kīlaka); and the syllable *sa* is the power (śakti).
The assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgakalpanā) is performed with: *hsāṃ hsīṃ hsūṃ hsaiṃ hsauṃ hsaḥ*. || 23 ||
Dhyāna: [She is] seated upon a white lotus, white as milk, holding in her lotus-hands a rosary, a lotus, a book, and the gesture of granting desired boons.
I bow to that supreme Viṣṇu of knowledge, who is victorious over the horse-faced one (Hayagrīva) and who is beautiful with a multitude of stainless garments and ornaments.
Furthermore:
I bow to the horse-faced one, who possesses the luster of the autumnal moon, who is adorned with ornaments made of pearls,
whose upper hands hold a discus and a conch, and whose [other] hands are enriched by the mudrās of teaching and exposition.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the installation of the conch and the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), and having meditated again,
[one performs the rites] up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*), one should begin.
Therein, the first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*):
Prajñāhayā, Medhāhayā, Smṛti-hayā, Vidyāhayā, and Lakṣmīhayā.
The second [set] consists of the eight horses of Vāgīśī, Hayavidyāvilāsā, and Nādavimardanā;
the third consists of Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi.
The fourth [offering] is with elephants such as Kumuda;
the fifth is with Indra and the others. Then one should complete the ritual, beginning with the incense and ending with the dismissal. || 24 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of four hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).
And thus it is said:
"One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and thereafter perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth that number."
An oblation with clarified butter (ājya) ten times [the number of the previous offerings] is performed. || 25 ||

Another mantra is the word *hayaśiras*, beginning with the single syllable of Hayagrīva, ending in the dative case (*caturthī*), and concluding with *namaḥ*. Thus it is stated in the Kalpa: "One should extract the word *hayaśiras* ending in the dative case."
This mantra, beginning with its own seed-syllable, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. || 26 ||
Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], the Anuṣṭubh the metre (chandas), Viṣṇu in the form of Hayagrīva the deity (devatā);
all else is the same as for the single-syllable [mantra]. || 27 ||
Another mantra:
O supreme one, having sung forth the Udgītha, O Lord of all masters of speech!
O inconceivable one, consisting of all the Vedas, awaken me, awaken me to everything!
The mantra is said to end with "svāhā," its seed-syllable being encapsulated by the Praṇava. || 28 ||
Another mantra:
Salutations to you, O Hayagrīva, the King of Vidyās, the Viṣṇu whose essential nature transcends the universe, and who consists of pure consciousness, māyā, and bliss.
The mantra is declared to end with "svāhā," encapsulated by the syllable "haṃsa. || 29 ||
Regarding these two mantras, everything is to be understood as being the same as for the previously mentioned Hayagrīva mantra. || 30 ||
Now, regarding the Nṛsiṃha-mantra,
it is stated in the Nibandha:
"One should first utter 'Ugram' and 'Vīram', and immediately thereafter 'Mahāviṣṇum'."
Having addressed the blazing state (*pada*) that faces in all directions, one should utter "Nṛsiṃha," "Bhīṣaṇa," "Bhadra," and then "Mṛtyumṛtyu.
Then, saying "I bow" (*namāmyaham*), this King of Mantras, which is like a celestial tree, has been proclaimed. This mantra...
When it is encapsulated by *māyā*, it then bestows the fruits of all desires.
And so it is said in the *Kalpa*:
"If it is encapsulated by *hṛllekhā*, it shall bestow the fruits of all desires. (31)
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:

having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the mantra of the pedestal (pīṭhamantra) as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava worship, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and the other [limbs].
Salutation to the sage Brahmā on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre on the mouth; salutation to the deity Nṛsiṃha on the heart. || 32 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs:
the heart is assigned with four syllables, the head with that same number of letters;
the crest-lock (śikhā) is prescribed with eight, and the armor (kavaca) is said to consist of six.
The mantra for the eye-rite (nayana) should consist of that many syllables of the Karaṇa-mantra.
Then follows the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa):
on the head, forehead, and eyes; on the mouth, the joints of the arms and feet;
at the tips [of the fingers and toes], the belly, the heart, the throat, and again on both sides.
And on the rear limb and the hump, one should assign the phonemes in their proper sequence.
Then comes the meditation:
[one should visualize the Lord] whose radiance is like a mountain of rubies, who terrifies the hosts of Rākṣasas with his own luster,
whose lotus-like hands rest upon his knees, who has three eyes, and whose ornaments shine with jewels.
I bow to the omnipresent Lord Nṛsiṃha, who eternally holds the conch and discus in his two arms, whose fierce mouth with tusks has a tongue blazing with flames, and whose mass of hair stands erect.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the ritual installation of the conch (śaṅkhasthāpana),
and having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) as prescribed for Vaiṣṇavas, one should meditate again,
[performing the rites] from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā), one should begin [the main ritual].
That is to say:
one should worship the limbs (aṅga) in the filaments—at the corners beginning with the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.
For example:
"Oṃ, homage to Ugra for the heart!
Svāhā to Mahāviṣṇu for the head!"
To the blazing one facing all directions, for the tuft (śikhā), vaṣaṭ!
To the terrifying Man-lion (nṛsiṃha), for the armor (kavaca), hūṃ!
To the devourer of Death himself, for the three eyes (netratraya), vauṣaṭ!
I bow down with "Astrāya Phaṭ.
Then, one should worship Garuḍa, Śaṅkara, Śeṣa, and Brahmā on the petals starting from the east; and on the intermediate petals, one should worship Śrī, Hrī, Dhṛti, and Puṣṭi.
One should worship with [the mantra] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namas*. || 35 ||
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements.
Then, one should complete the ritual activities from the offering of incense up to the final dismissal. || 35 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of thirty-two hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables, and then [perform] a thousand [recitations] with oblations soaked in ghee."
One should offer milk-rice oblations according to the rules into the fire that has been duly consecrated.
Another mantra,
according to the *Nibandha*: "Pāśa, Śakti, Nṛhari, Aṅkuśa, Varma, Phaṭ" is the mantra.
The six-syllabled mantra of Narahari is said to grant all desires. || 37 ||

The worship of this [deity] is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the installation of the *pīṭha-mantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava practice, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [constituent parts].
Salutation to the sage Brahmā on the head; salutation to the Paṅkti metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Nṛsiṃha in the heart. || 38 ||
Then, the ritual assignments (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs:
*Āṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*hrīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
KṢRAUṂ to the two middle fingers, VAṢAṬ; KRAUṂ to the two ring fingers, HUṂ;
HUṂ to the two little fingers, VAUṢAṬ.
*Phaṭ* with both palms and backs of the hands; *phaṭ*.
Likewise [at] the heart and other [limbs]. (39)
Then the meditation:
[one should visualize the Lord] whose tongue quivers with wrath, whose own mouth is wide open, and who has the moon, sun, and fire as his eyes;
whose radiance is red from the navel down to the feet and white above, and who has torn apart the body of the lord of the Daityas.
I praise Nṛsiṃha, who bears the conch, the discus, the noose, the goad, the thunderbolt, and the mace— terrible with sharp and fierce fangs, and adorned with various ornaments made of jewels;
having thus meditated upon Him and worshipped Him mentally, one should perform the installation of the conch.
Having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) as prescribed by the Vaiṣṇavas, and having meditated again,
one should perform the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), and then begin the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇapūjā).
For example:
one should worship the six limbs with "Āṃ, homage to the heart," and so forth, in the filaments— at the southeast corner and others, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.

Then, on the petals starting from the east, one should worship the conch, the discus, the noose, the goad, the thunderbolt, the mace, the sword, and the shield, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Thus it is stated in the Nibandha:
Outside the armor-enclosure (aṅgāvṛti), one should worship the discus, conch, noose, goad, thunderbolt, the Kaumodakī mace, sword, and shield upon the petals. Then,
one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 40 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of six hundred thousand recitations.
Accordingly:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times per season, and thereafter perform oblations with clarified butter."
One should gratify the preceptor with a thousand of those [cows] and with wealth in a well-kindled fire.
Another mantra is the letter *kṣa*, mounted upon fire (the letter *ra*) and endowed with the nasal bindu;
this is declared to be the single-syllable mantra that bestows the fruits of all desires. (42)
All its worship and so forth are like those of the King of Mantras.

The distinction here is that Atri is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Nṛsiṃha is the deity (*devatā*), the syllable *kṣa* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the vowel *au* is the power (*śakti*).
The ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*) is performed with the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels.

The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times. And so it is said: "One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times," and according to such statements. (44)
And likewise, another mantra is stated in the Kalpa: "Having uttered the two *jaya*s, one should also utter 'Śrī-pūrva-nṛsiṃha'."
This eight-syllable mantra is proclaimed as a wish-fulfilling gem for those who worship it. || 45 ||

Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda), Nṛsiṃha is the deity (devatā), and the assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) is performed with the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels.
Meditation, worship, and so forth are to be conducted as in the case of the King of Mantras (mantrarāja). || 46 ||

The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times, according to such statements as: "One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times. || 47 ||
Now, the mantra of Hari-Hara is given in the *Mantradevaprakāśinī*:
Tāra, Māyā, Prāsāda, "Obeisance to Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa," and Prāsāda.
Māyā is Tāra. || 48 ||
The procedure for its worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and the installation of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa) as prescribed by either the Vaiṣṇavas or the Śaivas, one should perform the installation of the seers and other elements (ṛṣyādinyāsa).

Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre on the mouth; salutation to the deity Hari-Hara on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Hauṃ on the private parts; salutation to the power Hrīṃ on the feet. || 49 ||
Then follow the ritual placements (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs: "hrāṃ to the two thumbs, salutation," and so forth, using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels.
In the same manner, [the nyāsa is performed] on the heart and other parts. 50.
Then the meditation:
I worship Hari-Hara, who holds a trident, a discus, the Pāñcajanya conch, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands; whose half-body is the graceful sport of his own respective ornaments.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) as prescribed by either the Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva traditions, and having meditated once more, one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali),
and then commence the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇapūjā).
One should worship with "hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth, in the filaments at the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.
Then, on the petals, one should worship with "oṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī," and likewise to Sarasvatī, Nārāyaṇī, and Dharā.
One should worship Bhūdharā, Ambikā, Tryambakā, Gaṅgā, and Gaṅgādhara; outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other [guardians].
In this case, there is no worship of the thunderbolt (vajra) and so forth, because it has not been mentioned.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 52 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (japa),
and ten thousand oblations (homa) with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
And so it is said:

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then, a fire-oblation (havana) should be performed with milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in ghee, in the consecrated sacrificial fire, using a tenth part of that number.
Now, the mantras of Varāha:
*taro namo bhagavate varāharūpāya bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥpataye bhūpatitvaṃ me dehi dadāpaya ṭhaṭha*.
This mantra consists of thirty-three syllables.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"One should utter the Tāra (Oṃ), followed by 'namo bhagavate', and then the word 'varāha'."

"O Rūpa, Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, O Lord of that which is within; grant me the status of lordship of the earth at the end of the word 'pada', and cause it to be granted at the end [of the mantra]. This mantra, ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), consists of thirty-three syllables. || 54 ||
Its worship:

having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement of the *pīṭha-mantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava rites, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [limbs].
Salutation to the sage Bhārgava on the head;
salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Ādivarāha in the heart.
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*Namaḥ* to Ekadaṃṣṭra with both thumbs;
*Svāhā* to Vyomolkā with both index fingers.
To Tejo'dhipati with the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ;
to Viśvarūpa with the two ring fingers, huṃ;
to Mahādaṃṣṭra with the two little fingers, phaṭ.
The same applies to the heart-mantra and the others.
And thus it is said:
"The sage is declared to be Bhārgava, and the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh."
The wise have declared the deity of this mantra to be Varāha. "To Ekadaṃṣṭra" is said to be the heart; "to Vyomolkā" is remembered as the head;
"to Tejo'dhipati" is the tuft (śikhā); and "to Viśvarūpa" is the armor (varma).
One should arrange the five-limbed weapon-mantra for Mahādaṃṣṭra as follows.
The yantra for this [deity] is described in the *Prapañcasāra*:

"Having duly fashioned a mandala consisting of an eight-petaled lotus with a radiant pericarp, one should worship the Boar there—resplendent like a thousand suns—for the sake of attaining success. (57) (Figure 25)
Then the meditation:
from the feet to the knees, it resembles excellent gold;
from the region of the navel downwards, it has the luster of a pearl; from the region of the throat upwards, it resembles the rising sun.

I praise the primordial Boar, who possesses a dark-blue luster upon his head; who holds with his hands a chariot-wheel, a discus, a sword, a shield, the weapon called the mace, a spear, the gestures of generosity and fearlessness, and whose tusks gleam as they support the earth.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, and having performed the rites such as the placement of the conch and the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) as prescribed for Vaiṣṇavas,
one should again meditate [on the deity] and perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (pañca-puṣpāñjali-dāna).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*), one should begin [the main rite].

In the filaments—at the corners beginning with the southeast and in the cardinal directions (the four directions starting from the east)—one should offer salutation to the Heart-mantra of Ekadaṃṣṭra: *ekadaṃṣṭrāya hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
Svāhā to the head, the sky-meteor;
Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock, the lord of splendor;
Huṃ to the armor, the one of universal form.
In the four directions (in the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna): *mahādaṃṣṭrāya astrāya phaṭ*.
Outside of that, on the petals: *oṃ cakrāya namaḥ*, and likewise for the conch (*śaṅkha*) and the sword (*khaḍga*).
One should worship the shield, the mace, the spear, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness;
with these, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the incense offering up to the final dismissal.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa).
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with lotuses smeared with honey."
One should perform oblations with a tenth part of that [number], and worship Viṣṇu upon the pedestal. One should not recite the Viṣṇu-mantra at night;
and thus it is said:
"One should not recite a Vaiṣṇava mantra at night; however, there is no fault in doing so for a Śaiva or a Śākta mantra," according to the statement in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā.
Thus ends the section on Viṣṇu mantras. (60)
Now, regarding the Śiva-mantras:
she for whom Girijā performed penance with a specific aim, and the dust of whose lotus feet the wise revere;
I remember with a pure mind that moon-crested Lord, whose body is adorned by the king of serpents and who is the bestower of boons. || 1 ||
Now I shall declare the mantras of Maheśa, which bestow all prosperity—
those by means of which the sages of old swiftly attained union with Śiva.
Joined with the letter *ma* and the vowel *au*, its head adorned with the *bindu*, this mantra known as Prāsāda is proclaimed to be a wish-granting jewel for those who worship it. (3)
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa and other nyāsas upon the locations of the Mātṛkā.
Namely:
Aṃ, homage to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī! Homage everywhere!
Āṃ, to Ananta and Virajā; Iṃ, to Sūkṣma and Śālmalī; Īṃ, to Trimūrti and Lolākṣī; Uṃ, to Amareśvara and Vartulākṣī; Ūṃ, to Arghīśa and Dīrghaghoṇā; Ṛṃ, to Bhārabhūti and Sudīrghamukhī.
Ṛṃ to Atithīśa and Gomukhī; Ḷṃ to Sthāṇuka and Dīrghajihva; Ḷṃ to Hara and Kuṇḍodara; E to Jhiṇṭīśa and Ūrdhvamukhī; Aiṃ to Bhautikeśa and Vikṛtamukhī; Oṃ to Sadyojāta and Jvālāmukhī.
Oṃ, to Anugraheśvara and Ulkāmukhī; aṃ, to Akrūra and Suśrīmukhī; aḥ, to Mahāsena and Vidyāmukhī; kaṃ, to Krodhīśa and Sarvasiddhi-Mahākālī; khaṃ...
To Caṇḍeśa and Sarvasiddhi-Sarasvatī; Gaṃ, to Pañcāntaka and Gaurī; Ghaṃ, to Śivottama and Trailokyavidyā; Ṅaṃ, to Ekarudra and Mantraśakti; Caṃ, to Kūrma and Ātmaśakti; Chaṃ.

With *Eka-netra* and *Bhūtamātṛkā*, *Jaṃ* with *Caturānana* and *Lamborī*, *Jhaṃ* with *Abjeśa* and *Drāviṇī*, *Ñaṃ* with *Sarvanāgarī*, *Ṭaṃ* with *Someśa* and *Khecarī*, *Ṭhaṃ* with *Lāṅgalin* and *Mañjarī*, *Ḍaṃ*...
To Dārukarūpiṇī and [her consort], Ḍhaṃ to Arddhanārīśvara and Vīriṇī, Ṇaṃ to Umākānta and Kākodarī, Taṃ to Āṣāḍhi and Pūtanā, Thaṃ to Daṇḍi and Bhadrakālī, Daṃ to Adri and Yoginī, Dhaṃ...
*Ma* with *Mīnaśaṅkhinī*, *Naṃ* with *Meṣagarjinī*, *Paṃ* with *Lohitakālarātri*, *Phaṃ* with *Śikhikubjikā*, *Baṃ* with *Chagalaṇḍakapardinī*, *Bhaṃ* with *Dviraṇḍeśavajrā*, *Maṃ*...

To Mahākāla and Jayā; to Yaṃ, the essence of the skin, and Bālisumukheśvarī; to Raṃ, the essence of the blood, and Bhujaṅgeśa-Revatī; to Laṃ, the essence of the flesh, and Pinākīśa-Mādhavī; to Vaṃ, the essence of the fat—
To the two, Ātma-khaḍgī and Īśa-vāruṇī; śaṃ to the two, Asthy-ātmā and Baka-īśa-vāyavī; yaṃ to the two, Majjā-tmā and Śveta-rakṣo-vidāriṇī; saṃ...

ŚU with Śukra (Venus) as the self and Bhṛgu-Īśa-Sahajā; HAṂ with Prāṇa as the self, Nakulīśa, and Lakṣmī; LAṂ with Bīja as the self, Śiva, and Vyāpinī; KṢAṂ with Krodha as the self, Saṃvartaka, and Māyā.
In all cases, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed with the word *namaḥ* at the end.
According to the grammatical principle that "in a literary composition, dual and plural endings may optionally form a *dvandva* compound," this sentence is thus free from contradiction.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti,
Amareśvara, Arghīśa, Bhāratabhūti, Ātithīśa, Sthāṇuka, and Hara."
Jhiṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta,
Anugraheśvara, Akrūra, and Mahāsena are the sixteen forms corresponding to the vowels.
Following them are Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama.
Likewise, there are Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, and the four-faced one (Caturānana);
Abjeśa, Śarva, Someśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāruka; Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣāḍhin, and Daṇḍin.
There are Adri, Mīna, Meṣa, and Lohita; likewise Śikhī; Chagalaṇḍeśa and Dviraṇḍeśa, along with Mahākala and Vālī;
Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākīśa, Khaḍgī, and Bakas.
Śvetabhṛgvīśanakuḷi, Śiva, and Savarta—
these are declared to be the Rudras, bearing tridents and skull-bowls.
Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and Śālmalī are situated there; Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā are likewise mentioned;
as well as Sudīrghamukhī, the two Gomukhīs, and Dīrghajihvā.
Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvamukhī, and likewise Vikṛtamukhī;
Jvālāmukhī should be known after that, and Ulkāmukhī is recorded next; Suśrīmukhī and Vidyāmukhī—these are the powers of the vowels.
To Mahākalī-Sarasvatī, who is endowed with all supernatural powers (siddhis);
Gaurī is the lore of the three worlds; thereafter is Mantra-Śakti;
Ātma-Śakti is considered Bhūtamātā, as well as Lambodarī, Drāviṇī, and Nāgarī.
Furthermore, Khecarī, Cāpimañjarī,
Rūpiṇī, Vīriṇī, and then Kakodarī as well as Pūtanā;
there are the two yoginīs Bhadrakālī and Śaṅkhinī, as well as Garjinī and Kālarātri.
Kubjinī, Kapardinī, and Vajrā; Jayā, Sumukheśvarī, Revatī, and Mādhavī;
then Vāruṇī and Vāyavī are proclaimed, followed by Rakṣovidāriṇī.
And then there is Sahajā Lakṣmī, all-pervasive and endowed with Māyā;
these [goddesses] are seated upon the seats of Rudra’s lap, their forms crimson like vermilion, their lotus-like hands adorned with red lotuses and skull-cups. || 5 ||

Then, having performed the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) as described in the general manual of worship (sāmānyapūjāpaddhati), one should perform the placement of the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti). As follows:
Oṃ, salutation to Vāmā; likewise [salutation] to Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikariṇī, Balavikariṇī, Balapramathinī, and Sarvabhūtadamanī.
Having thus assigned these to the filaments starting from the east of the heart-lotus, [one should assign] Oṃ to Manonmanī in the center.
*Namaḥ*. Above that: *Oṃ namo bhagavate sakalaguṇātma-śaktiyuktāyānantāya yogapīṭhātmane namaḥ*.
And likewise in the Śāradā:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalapadā, and so forth; the one called Vikariṇī is proclaimed, then Balā and the others, followed by Vikariṇī, then Balapramathanī, and also Sarvabhūtadamanī.
Manonmanī is proclaimed as one of the seat-powers (pīṭhaśakti) of Śiva.
After [saying] "Salutation to the Blessed One" (namo bhagavate), one should then say "to the one who possesses all" (sakalādi);
thereafter, "to the one endowed with the powers of the qualities" (guṇādiśaktiyuktāya), and after that, "to Ananta."
The mantra beginning with "namaḥ" and ending with "antaḥ," namely *yogapīṭhātmane*, is for the seat.
Having subsequently conceived the form of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain upon that seat using this mantra, one should invoke Śiva there and worship him with the root mantra.
Then follows the Nyāsa of the Seer and so forth:
on the head, "Salutation to Vāmadeva, the Seer"; in the mouth, "Salutation to Paṅkti, the Metre"; in the heart, "Salutation to Sadāśiva, the Deity."
In the Śāradā:
the sage is Vāmadeva, the metre is Paṅkti, and the deity is Sadāśiva. || 6 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs:
*hāṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ* and so forth; likewise, *hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth.
One should perform the placement with the letter *ha* joined with the six long vowels.
As it has been said:
"The ritual of the six limbs is proclaimed by means of the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels."
Then, one should assign the five forms beginning with Īśāna to the thumbs and other fingers of both hands.
For example:
*hoṃ* to Īśāna, *namaḥ* on the two thumbs; *heṃ* to Tatpuruṣa, *namaḥ* on the two index fingers; *huṃ* to Aghora, *namaḥ* on the two middle fingers; *hiṃ* on the two ring fingers.
Salutation to Vāmadeva on the two little fingers; *haṃ*, salutation to Sadyojāta.
And likewise:
"The preceptor should assign the forms beginning with Īśāna to the thumb and the other fingers."

The one called Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, the one named Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta— these are placed in order from the inside outwards. They are joined with the five short vowels beginning with *o* in reverse order, combined with the element of space (*viyat*).
Furthermore, one should place those respective seed-syllables and so forth with those respective fingers.
Then, with those same fingers, one should place the five forms— beginning with "Hoṃ, obeisance to Īśāna"— upon the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet.

Then, one should install the respective forms with the corresponding fingers and seed-syllables (*bījas*) in the upward, eastern, southern, western, and northern faces. However, a Śūdra, having performed the ritual installation (*nyāsa*) up to this point, should then meditate, as he has no authority for anything beyond this.

Then, in the upward, eastern, southern, western, and northern faces of Īśāna, one should place the five kalās of Brahmā, beginning with the *ṛc* and starting with *praṇava*, ending with *namaḥ*. It is as follows:

Oṃ, Īśāna, Lord of all sciences; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Śaśinī. Īśvara, Lord of all beings; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Aṅgadā. Brahmādhipati, Lord of Brahman; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Brahmeṣṭadā.
May Śiva be auspicious to me. Oṃ, salutation to the digit (kalā) Marīcī.
Sadāśivoṃ, Oṃ, salutation to the digit Aṃśumālinī.
These are the four digits of Tatpuruṣa in his four faces: east, west, south, and north.
One should place [the mantras] as follows:
*oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe oṃ śāntyai kalāyai namaḥ*.
We meditate upon Mahādeva; Oṃ, salutation to the Kalā of Vidyā.
May Rudra inspire us; Oṃ, salutation to the Kalā of Pratiṣṭhā.
[May he] impel us; Oṃ, salutation to the Kalā of Nivṛtti.
Then, one should assign the eight digits (kalās) of Aghora to the heart, the neck, the two shoulders, the navel, the belly, the back,
and the chest, as follows:
Oṃ, to the non-terrible ones; Oṃ, obeisance to Umā, the digit of power.
Now, to the terrible ones; obeisance to Mohā, the digit of power. Oṃ, to the most terrible; obeisance to Kṣamā, the digit of power.
To the most terrible ones: Oṃ, salutation to the digit (kalā) Nidrā.
To all: Oṃ, salutation to the digit Vyādhi.
To all: Oṃ, salutation to the digit Mṛtyu.
Salutations to you! Oṃ, salutation to the digit (kalā) of Hunger. Salutation to those who possess the form of Rudra! Oṃ, salutation to the digit of Thirst.
Then, [one should worship] in the secret region, the scrotum, the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, and the two buttocks.
One should place the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva on the hips and on both sides.
For example: Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Ūrjā.
Salutation to Jyeṣṭha; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Rakṣā.
Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra; obeisance to Ratī, the digit (kalā). Oṃ, obeisance to Kalā; obeisance to Kapālinī, the digit. Kala, Oṃ, obeisance to Kāmā, the digit.
Salutation to Vikaraṇa; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Saṃyaminī.
Oṃ, salutation to the digit Krodhā (Kriyā);
salutation to Vikaraṇa; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Vṛddhi.
Bala: Oṃ, salutation to the digit (kalā) Sthirā.
Pramathana: Oṃ, salutation to the digit Rātri. Sarvabhūtadamana: Salutation; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Bhrāmaṇī.
Manas, oṃ, salutation to the digit Mohinī;
salutation to Unmanā, oṃ, salutation to the digit Jarā;
Manas, oṃ, salutation to the digit Mohinī.
"Salutation to Unmanā; Oṃ, salutation to Jarā, the Kalā.
Then, one should place the eight kalās of Sadyojāta on the two sides, the two breasts, the nose, the head, and the pair of arms.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; Oṃ, homage to the digit (kalā) Siddhi.
Homage indeed to Sadyojāta; Oṃ, homage to the digit Vṛddhi.
To Bhava, Oṃ, homage to the digit Mati.
In the state of non-existence: Oṃ, salutation to the digit Lakṣmī.
In the beginningless state of existence: Oṃ, salutation to the digit Medhā.
Worship me: Oṃ, salutation to the digit Prajñā.
Bhava! Oṃ, salutation to the digit (kalā) Prabhā; salutation to Udbhava; Oṃ, salutation to the digit Sudhā. || 8 ||
Then, one should assign the five *ṛc*s beginning with Īśāna to the five fingers:
*Oṃ īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmādhipatir brahmaṇo'dhipatir brahmā śivo me 'stu sadāśivaḥ*.
Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva;
may that Rudra inspire us.
Oṃ, from the non-terrible ones, and from the terrible ones, and from those more terrible than the terrible, from all sides, from all who are everything—
Salutations be unto you who possess the forms of Rudra!
Om, salutations to Vāmadeva, salutations to the Eldest, salutations to Rudra, salutations to Kalā,
salutations to Balavikaraṇa, salutations to Balapramathana, salutations to the Subduer of all beings.
Salutations to Manonmanā, salutations!
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta.
In existence, in non-existence, and in primordial existence, favor me; salutations to Bhavodbhava.
In this manner, one should place these *ṛc*s on the crown of the head, the face, the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
Thereafter, one should perform another placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
It is as follows:
Aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ, salutation to the heart, the All-Knowing One.
Amṛte tejojvālāmāline tṛptaye śikhibrahmaṇe, svāhā to the head, the Brahman who is the flame of light and nectar.
Jvalitaśikhiśikhāya anādibodhāya, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair, the beginningless awakening.
To the wielder of the vajra, whose hand holds the vajra, who is independent, and who is armor: *huṃ*.
To the three eyes, whose power is never diminished by others: *śauṃ cauṃ hauṃ vauṣaṭ*.
*Ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ*—to the weapon of infinite power: *phaṭ*.
And so it is said in the *Yāmala*:

"Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternally undiminished power, and infinite power—those who know the ritual rules call these the six limbs of the all-pervading Maheśvara. Thus.
Having performed the placement, one should meditate.
For example:

[I worship] the Lord who is adorned with five faces— white like a pearl, yellow like a cloud, white like a pearl, and the color of the hibiscus— and who possesses three eyes, wears a moon upon his crown, and has the radiance of ten million full moons.
I worship him who holds a trident, a hammer, a sword, a vajra, fire, a serpent-king, a bell, a goad, and a noose that removes fear, his limbs radiant with immeasurable ornaments.
Having meditated thus and worshipped mentally, one should perform the ritual placement of the *arghya* water.
In this context, there is a prohibition regarding the conch;
however, the lotus is praised everywhere except for the worship of Śiva and Sūrya. || 10 ||

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) as prescribed by the Śaiva tradition, and having meditated again and conceived the form (mūrti) with the root mantra, one should perform the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), and then begin the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇapūjā).
For example:
in the northeast, *oṃ īśānāya namaḥ*; in the east, *oṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*; in the south, *oṃ aghorāya namaḥ*; in the north, *oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*; in the west, *oṃ*.
Salutation to Sadyojāta.
In the corners beginning with the northeast: *Oṃ*, salutation to Nivṛtti; likewise to Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti.
Then, on the eight petals in the order starting from the east: *oṃ anantāya namaḥ*, and likewise for Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin.
Outside of that, in the order starting from the north: *oṃ umāyai namaḥ*, and likewise.

One should worship Caṇḍeśvara, Nandin, Mahābala, Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣa, Bhṛṅgarīṭa, and Skanda; outside of that, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as their weapons such as the thunderbolt, in order starting from the east.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 11 ||
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"Having meditated in this manner, one should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times with [offerings] soaked in honey."
One should perform oblations with flowers produced from the Karavīra tree, using a tenth part of that [number]. || 12 ||
The other mantra is Bhuvaneśa; [then] the Praṇava, "namaḥ śivāya," and again Bhuvaneśī—this is the eight-syllabled mantra. || 13 ||
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"The six-syllabled mantra is said to be restrained by Śakti; [next] is the eight-syllabled mantra.
Its worship is as follows:"

Having performed the seat-installation (*pīṭhanyāsa*), beginning with the morning rites and ending with the *pīṭhamantra* as prescribed for the day, one should perform the installation of the seers and so forth (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*).
[One should place: "Salutation to Vāmadeva, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the *paṅkti* metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; [salutation] to [the deity], on the heart."
Salutation to the deity Umāpati. || 14 ||
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*oṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the two thumbs); *naṃ tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā* (Naṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers).
Maṃ with the two middle fingers, Vaṣaṭ; Śiṃ with the two ring fingers, Huṃ;
Vāṃ with the two little fingers, Vauṣaṭ.
With the palms and backs of the hands: *phaṭ*.
Likewise for the heart and other [limbs]. (15)
Then the meditation:

I bow to him who has the luster of a bandhūka flower, who possesses three eyes, who bears a crescent moon, whose face is smiling, and who holds a trident, a skull-cup, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, with a beautiful laugh.

[He beheld] his beloved, whose left thigh was paralyzed, who held a beautiful red lotus shimmering in her palm, and whose body was embraced by Hanuman, she who wore glittering ornaments made of jewels.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the installation of the *arghya* water,

and having carried out the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) as prescribed in the Śaiva tradition, one should meditate again [on the deity] up to the point of the offering of the five handfuls of flowers beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā), one should begin as follows:
in the filaments— at the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna, in the center, and in the cardinal directions— [one should worship] with "Oṃ, to the Heart."
*namaḥ*, *naṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *maṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *śiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; *vāṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *yaṃ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*.
Then, in the directions starting from the east: *oṃ hṛllekhāyai namaḥ*, and likewise to Gaganā and Raktā.
To Karālikā and Mahocchuṣmā. Then, on the petals starting from the east, one should worship Vṛṣabha and the others:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha," and likewise to Kṣetrapāla, Caṇḍeśvara, and Durgā.
To Kārttikeya, to Nandin, to the destroyer of obstacles, and to the commander-in-chief;
thereafter, as before, one should worship Umā and the others upon the petals.
Outside of that, the Mothers beginning with Brahmyā are to be worshipped.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other weapons.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 16 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of fourteen hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and its tenth part according to the prescribed rule."
One should perform the oblation with the best fuel-sticks of *āragvadha*, soaked in honey;
*āragvadha* is [also known as] *śoṇālu*. (17)
Another mantra is the eight-syllable mantra: *Tāra* (Oṃ), *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), *Prāsāda* (Hūṃ), and *Namaḥ Śivāya*.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
The Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīṃ), Viyat (Ha), the Bindu (M), and the Anusvāra (Ṃ),
joined with these five syllables, is considered the eight-syllabled mantra.

The worship of this [deity] is as follows: having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement of the *pīṭha* as prescribed in the Śaiva tradition, one should perform the previously mentioned placements of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, along with the hand and limb placements (*karāṅganyāsa*). || 19 ||
Then, the meditation:
I bow to the Lord, the color of vermilion, whose beautiful moon-ornament shines upon his jeweled crown;
whose eye rises upon his forehead; whose lotus-face is smiling; and who is adorned with divine ornaments and unguents.

Of my beloved, who placed her hand upon her left thigh while holding a crimson water-lily, and whose palm rested upon the rounded, elevated peak of her breast as she held a sacrificial ladle against the edge of the altar-slab. || 20 ||
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings,
having performed the rites from the placement of the *arghya* water up to the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*),

and having performed the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañca-puṣpāñjali-dāna*), [one should perform] the worship of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*).
One should perform [the rite].
Having worshipped the limbs and so forth as before, one should worship Ananta and the others on the petals, and Umā and the others at the tips of the petals.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other ritual implements.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the offering of incense and ending with the dismissal of the deities.
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
And so it is said:
"The best among those who know mantras should recite this mantra eight hundred thousand times;
he should then perform a fire sacrifice with a thousand oblations of milk-rice soaked in clarified butter. (21)

The Mṛtyuñjaya Mantra: Tāra (Om), Sthirā (S), together with the ear (R) and the moon (U), followed by Bhṛgu (Bha) conjoined with emission (H). This three-syllabled mantra is declared to be the essence of Mṛtyuñjaya.
The letter *ja* is Sthira; the letter *u* is Karṇa; and the letter *sa* is Bhṛgu. || 22 ||
Its worship:
having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the *pīṭhanyāsa* as prescribed for Śiva, one should perform the *ṛṣinyāsa* and the other ritual placements.
Salutation to the sage Kahola at the head;
salutation to the goddess Gāyatrī meter at the mouth;
salutation to the deity Mahādeva, the Conqueror of Death, at the heart.
And thus:
the seer is Kahola; the goddess and so forth is declared to be the Gāyatrī meter;
and Mahādeva, the Conqueror of Death, is proclaimed as its deity. (23)
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *sāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*sīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *sūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*.
*Saīm* to the two ring fingers, *Huṃ*;
*Sauṃ* to the two little fingers, *Vauṣaṭ*;
*Saḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands, *Phaṭ*.
In this manner, one should perform [the ritual] in the heart and other [limbs] with the letter *sa* endowed with the six long vowels.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"One should perform the ritual of the limbs for the mantra with the letter *bhṛgu* (sa) joined with the long vowels. (24)
Then the meditation:
[He is] with eyes like the moon, sun, and fire; a smiling face; seated within two lotuses;
his hands graced by the mudrā, a noose, a deer, and a rosary; and possessing the luster of the moon.

One should meditate upon Paśupati, the conqueror of death, whose body is bathed in nectar flowing from ten million moons, who is radiant with ornaments such as necklaces, and who deludes the entire universe with his splendor.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) beginning with the placement of the *arghya* water, and having meditated again and performed the worship of the pedestal beginning with the placement of the *arghya*,
and having meditated once more, [one performs the rites] from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*).
Having performed the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā), one should act as follows:
[placing] *sāṃ* for the heart, with *namaḥ*, in the filaments, in the intermediate directions beginning with the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.
Having worshipped the six limbs with these and other [mantras], one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajras and so forth, outside of that.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the incense offering up to the dismissal. || 25 ||
The preliminary practice for this consists of three hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:

"The wise one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and with a mind of great clarity, he should perform the fire-oblation ten thousand times with pieces of Amṛtā mixed with pure milk and clarified butter. (25ka)
Now follows another mantra for conquering death: having extracted "Mṛtyuñjaya," one should utter "Pālaya" twice;
having pronounced "Mṛtyuñjaya" again, one should likewise recite it in reverse order.
This other mantra, named Mṛtyuñjaya, consists of twelve syllables;
one should perform all the rites, such as meditation and worship, just as before.
Another mantra:
First the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the word "Hṛdayam," followed by the word "Bhagavate" ending in the dative case (Ṅe),
then "Dakṣiṇāmūrtim," and one should utter "Mahyam Medhām."
Bestow [this mantra]; ending with two *ṭha*s, this mantra consists of twenty-two syllables. || 27 ||

Its worship is as follows: having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement of the *pīṭha-mantra* as prescribed in the Śaiva tradition, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [components].
On the head, salutation to the four-faced Seer (Ṛṣi).
On the mouth, salutation to the goddess Gāyatrī Metre (Chandas). On the heart, salutation to the deity Dakṣiṇāmūrti. || 28 ||
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *oṃ āṃ oṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*oṃ īṃ oṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
Oṃ ūṃ oṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers; oṃ aiṃ oṃ, huṃ to the two ring fingers; oṃ auṃ oṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers.
Oṃ aḥ oṃ, phaṭ with both palms and backs of the hands. Likewise for the heart and other [limbs].
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
One should fashion the six limbs with the six long vowels conjoined with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*),
or alternatively, one may fashion them sequentially with the words arising from the mantra.
And so it is said in the *Mānasollāsa*:

One should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) according to the inclination of one's mind, using three, four, six, or four and three protective mantra-syllables as they are divided.
Then the meditation:
[one should visualize] a banyan tree of great height, radiant with ruby fruits,
and adorned with various forms consisting of emerald leaves.
Adorned with hanging ornaments made of the nine great jewels,
one should contemplate the Leader of the World seated at the foot of the banyan tree,
with a complexion like crystal or silver.

I worship Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who holds a rosary of pearls, a jar of nectar, the gesture of knowledge (vidyājñānamudrā), and a serpent around his arm in his lotus-like hands; who has the moon as his crest-jewel, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with various ornaments. || 30 ||
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings,
having performed the rites from the placement of the *arghya* up to the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) as taught in the Śaiva tradition, and having meditated again,
one should perform the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*).
One should perform the armor-offering (*āvāraṇapūjā*).

One should worship the six limbs with the mantras "Oṃ Āṃ Oṃ, homage to the heart," and so forth, in the filaments, in the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.
On the petals, starting from the east and so forth: *oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*; likewise for Brahmā, Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, Śuka, and Vyāsa.
Outside of that, starting from the east and so forth: Siddha, Gandharva, Yogīndra, and Vidyādhara.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense and so forth until the dismissal of the deities.
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said:
"Remaining established in the vow of celibacy, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire with lotuses mixed with ghee, numbering one-tenth of that amount. (31)
Another mantra,
consisting of the letters *agni* (ra), *saṃvartaka* (ha), *āditya* (ra), *anila* (ya), and the sixth vowel (*u*) with a bindu (*m*),
is known as the Cintāmaṇi; it is the seed-syllable that bestows all prosperity.
The meaning of this is as follows:
Agni is the letter *ra*; Saṃvartaka is the letter *kṣa*; Āditya is the letter *ma*; *ra* is the letter *ra*;
Anila is the letter *ya*; *au* is its own form; and the sixth is the vowel *ū*. || 32 ||

Its worship is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having installed the seat (pīṭha) ending with the mantra according to the Śaiva tradition, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and the other [limbs].
Salutation to the sage Kaśyapa on the head;
salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre in the mouth;
salutation to the deity Ardhanārīśvara in the heart. || 33 ||
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *raṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*kaṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
Yaṃ with the two middle fingers;
maṃ with the two ring fingers;
raṃ with the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ.
With the two hands placed upon the palms, *phaṭ*.
Likewise for the heart and other [limbs].
And so it is stated in the *Nibandha*:
One should perform the six limb-protections (aṅgas) in sequence with the six consonants beginning with *ra*, followed by *phaṭ*.
Then the meditation:
[He is] beautiful with blue coral, possessing three shimmering eyes,
and holding in his hands a noose, a red lotus, a skull-cup, and a trident.
I bow to that form which possesses the jewel of the Lord of the Half-Mother (Śiva), with ornaments distributed [upon it], and a crown bound with the crescent moon.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the *arghya* water.
Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) as taught in the Śaiva tradition, and having meditated again,
one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*).
One should begin the offering to the enclosure (āvaraṇapūjā).
Namely:
in the filaments, in the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions, [one should offer] "Raṃ, homage to the heart."
One should worship with these and other [mantras].
Then, on the petals as before, one should worship Vṛṣabha and the others, and at the tips of the petals, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Indrāṇī.
One should worship Cāmuṇḍā and Mahālakṣmī;

having worshipped Indra and the other deities, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons, outside of that, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense until the dismissal. || 35 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*), contemplating in this manner, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times."
One should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains sprinkled with honey.
Another mantra is:
the letter *pā* (pa) with *ra* (repha) mounted upon it, followed by the first seed-syllable (*a*) with the *tāra* (om);
then the letter *dhā* (dha) with *ra* (repha) mounted upon it, conjoined with the fourth vowel (*i*).
The second [syllable] should be *vindumān* (possessing a bindu), and the third is *sargī* (possessing a visarga) ending in *ṭ*.
In the *Śāradā*:
"First, [the syllable] *lohita* (red) with *agnyāsana* (the seat of fire), and again *vindumān* with *satyām* (truth)."
The second [syllable] resides in the seed-syllable of fire (ra), is long, and is adorned by the moon of peace (the anusvāra).

The third is the plough-bearer (la) with the visarga; this mantra, endowed with these three seed-syllables, has Nīlakaṇṭha as its essence and is the supreme remover of the two types of poison. || 37 ||

The worship of this [deity] is as follows: having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the *pīṭhanyāsa* as prescribed in the Śaiva tradition, one should perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*.
Salutation to Aruṇa Ṛṣi on the head;
salutation to Anuṣṭubh Chandas on the face; salutation to the deity Nīlakaṇṭha on the heart. || 38 ||
Then follow the ritual placements on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), as follows: *hara hara svāhā* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*.
Svāhā to Kapardin; svāhā to the two index fingers. Svāhā to Nīlakaṇṭha; vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers.
Huṃ phaṭ to the consumption of the Kālakūṭa poison; huṃ to the two ring fingers.
"To the blue-throated one, svāhā! To the two little fingers, phaṭ!
Thus it is for the heart and the other [limbs].
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
The two syllables *hara* followed by the fire-born wife (*svāhā*) are proclaimed as the Heart mantra;
*kapardine* followed by the two syllables *ṭha* is declared as the Head mantra;
and *nīlakaṇṭhāya* followed by the pair of syllables *ṭha* is recited as the Tuft mantra.
At the end of the word *kālakūṭa*, the term *viṣabhakṣaṇam* joined with the feminine suffix *ṅī* [is used];
*huṃ phaṭ* is declared by the wise to be the armor (*kavaca*) for the one who has a blue throat (*nīlakaṇṭhin*).
The learned know these five limbs of the mantra to end with *svāhā*.
Then follows the placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*):
*proṃ namaḥ* on the head, *nrīṃ namaḥ* on the throat, and *ṭhaṃ namaḥ* on the heart.
And likewise:
One should place the three seed-syllables in sequence upon the crown of the head, the throat, and the heart-lotus;
then, becoming composed, one should meditate upon Nīlakaṇṭha. (39)
Then comes the meditation:
[He] possesses the splendor of ten thousand rising suns; his matted locks are illuminated by the crescent moon; he has the lords of serpents as his crest-ornament;
and he holds a rosary, a trident, and a skull-cup in his hands.
I worship the beautiful Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, who holds a khaṭvāṅga staff, who possesses three eyes and five radiant faces, who is clothed in a tiger skin, and whose abode is the lotus.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, having performed the placement of the *arghya* water,

and having carried out the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) as taught in the Śaiva tradition, one should meditate again, perform the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*), and then commence the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).

One should worship [the deity] with "Hara Hara Svāhā, obeisance to the Heart," and so forth, in the filaments at the corners beginning with Agni, in the center, and in the cardinal directions. Thereafter,
one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 40 ||
The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, and then perform ten percent of that number [of oblations] with ghee."
One should properly offer the oblation into the well-consecrated bearer of the sacrificial fire.
The other mantra is the Praṇava (Om), followed by "Hṛn Nīlakaṇṭhāya," which is another eight-syllable mantra. || 1 ||
In the Kalpa:
"Tāra" (Oṃ), then "Hṛn" (Namaḥ), and "Nīlakaṇṭhāya"—this is the supreme eight-syllable mantra. || 2 ||
All its worship and so forth are as before; the distinction, however, is that Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the metre (chandas), and Nīlakaṇṭha is the deity (devatā). || 3 ||
Now, another mantra:

the heart (hṛdayam), followed by va, the witness (sākṣi), ending with la, joined with the infinite (ananta) and the wind (marut)—this is declared to be the five-syllabled mantra; when preceded by the salutation (tāra), it becomes six syllables.

Its worship consists of completing the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the *pīṭhamantra* as prescribed for Śiva, and then performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
On the head, salutation to Vāmadeva, the seer;
on the mouth, salutation to Paṅkti, the meter; in the heart, salutation to Īśāna, the deity. || 5 ||
Then follows the placement of the forms (mūrttinyāsa): on the two index fingers, *naṃ* to Tatpuruṣa, obeisance;
on the two middle fingers, *maṃ* to Aghora, obeisance.
On the two little fingers: *śiṃ* to Sadyojāta, obeisance.
On the two ring fingers: *vāṃ* to Vāmadeva, obeisance. On the two thumbs: *yaṃ* to Īśāna, obeisance.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"They are known as Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Īśāna;
one should install these five forms, beginning with the letters of the mantra, in their proper order."
Furthermore, one should place them on the index finger, the middle finger, the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb;
likewise, one should place them on the face, the heart, the two feet, the secret organ, and the head.
In this manner, one should place them on the eastern, southern, western, northern, and central faces.
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *oṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*,
*naṃ tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*, and so forth.
The same applies to the heart and the other limbs.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"The preceptor should perform the six-limbed ritual of the mantra with six syllables."
Then follows the placement of the *golaka* [syllables]:
*oṃ namaḥ* at the heart; *naṃ namaḥ* at the mouth; *maṃ namaḥ* and *śiṃ namaḥ* on the two shoulders; *vāṃ namaḥ* and *yaṃ namaḥ* on the two thighs.
Thus [one should place them] on the throat, the navel, both sides, the back, the heart, the head, the face, the two eyes, and the two nostrils;
likewise on the joints of the hands and feet, including the tips.
Thus [one places them] on the head, face, heart, belly, and on the two thighs and two feet.
Thus, in the heart and face, [they hold] the axe, deer, gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting gesture.
Thus, on the face, shoulders, heart, feet, thighs, and belly.
Then, once again, one should place those five forms on the head, the forehead, the belly, the heart, and the secret organ.
Then one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*):
*Oṃ, salutation to the Being, whose essence is the nectar of the light-linga,
whose limbs are illuminated by the shadow of the body of the fourfold form, O Source.*
With this, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa). || 7 ||
Then comes meditation: one should constantly meditate upon Maheśa, who resembles a mountain of silver, adorned with the beautiful crescent moon,
his limbs radiant with jeweled ornaments, holding an axe, a deer, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and full of serenity.

Seated upon a lotus, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals, wearing a tiger skin, the primordial source of the universe, the seed of the universe, the remover of all fears, five-faced and three-eyed.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual placement of the *arghya* water.
Then, having performed the worship of the seat (pīṭha) as taught in the Śaiva tradition, and having meditated again,
one should perform the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), and then begin the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇapūjā).
For example:
having worshipped the five forms beginning with Īśāna as before upon the pericarp (karṇikā), one should worship the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti upon the filaments (keśara) as before.

Then, in the corners beginning with the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions, [one should place]: Oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ, Naṃ śirase svāhā, Maṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ, Śiṃ kavacāya huṃ, Vāṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ, Yaṃ astrāya phaṭ.
Thus one should worship.
Then, as before, one should worship Ananta and the others.
Then, in the sequence beginning from the north, one should worship Umā and the others, moving counter-clockwise.
Then one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements.
Then one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the incense offering and ending with the dismissal. || 9 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of thirty-six lakh recitations.
There should be thirty-six thousand oblations with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
And so it is said:
One initiated according to the Śaiva path should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should likewise offer oblations of auspicious milk-rice for as many thousands of times.
Here, by the word "tattva," the thirty-six principles (tattvas) are meant, because they are internal. || 10 ||
The mantra ending in *mantra* is *arghīśa*; that which stands at the peak of fire (*vahniśikhara*) and resides within the letter *la* is declared to be *dānda*.
This *caṇḍamantra*, ending in *phaṭ*, is said to consist of three syllables. || 11 ||
Its worship is as follows: having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the *pīṭhanyāsa* as prescribed in the Śaiva tradition, one should perform the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*.
For example: "Salutation to the sage Trita on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre on the face; salutation to the deity Caṇḍeśvara on the heart."
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"For this [mantra], the sage is declared to be Trita; the meter is cited as Anuṣṭubh;
Caṇḍeśvara is the deity," and so forth. || 12 ||
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *dīpta phaṭ*, salutation (*namaḥ*) to both thumbs;
*jvala phaṭ*, *svāhā* to both index fingers.
Jvālinī phaṭ to the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ; Jñeya phaṭ to the two ring fingers, huṃ;
Hana phaṭ to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ.
*Sarvajvālini phaṭ* [to the palms and backs of the hands] *phaṭ*.
Likewise for the heart and other limbs.

And so it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "One should perform the ritual of the limbs (*aṅga*) with [the mantras] 'Dīptā', 'Jvalā', 'Jvālinī', together with 'Jñeya' and 'Hana', joined with all the 'Jvālinīs' and ending with 'Phaṭ'. (13)
Then comes the meditation:
I meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara in my heart, with a red body, three eyes, and adorned with red garments.
He bears a ṭaṅka, a trident, a crystal rosary, and a water-pot,
and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual placement of the arghya water.
Then, having performed the worship of the *pīṭha* as taught in the Śaiva tradition, and having mentally projected the form (*mūrti*) with the seed-syllable *ṭhaṃ*,

one should meditate again and commence the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*), beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the offering of five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*).
Namely:
the first enclosure consists of the limbs, the second of the Mothers, the third of Indra and the other gods,
and the fourth of the Vajras and the other [weapons].
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 15 ||
The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times per syllable, and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that."
"With pure sesame and rice grains combined with the three sweets"— thus end the Śiva-mantras.
Now, the Kṣetrapāla mantra is given in the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*:
"Kṣauṃ" is the seed-syllable; "to the field-protector" (kṣetrapālāya), followed by "namaḥ," constitutes the mantra.
Alternatively, this mantra may begin with the *praṇava* (oṃ).
And likewise:
the final letter of the alphabet joined with the nasal bindu is the heart-mantra for Kṣetrapāla;
preceded by the Tāra (Oṃ), this consists of eight syllables.
Thus has the [mantra] of Kṣetrapāla been declared. || 17 ||
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:

having performed the morning rites up to the end of the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should install the seat (pīṭha) conceived as Dharma and the other [qualities], and then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages and so forth.

For example: its Brahman is the *ṛṣi*, the *anuṣṭubh* is the *chandas*, Kṣetrapāla is the *devatā*, *kṣauṃ* is the *bīja*, and *ātman* is the *śakti*; one should perform the *aṅganyāsa* with the *bīja* joined with the six long vowels. || 18 ||
Then comes the meditation: [one should visualize the deity] wearing shining, fierce matted locks, possessing three eyes, with the luster of blue collyrium and the like,
blazing with garments and garlands of red flowers, and holding a mace and a skull-cup in his staff-like arms.
I perpetually revere the Lord Śrī Kṣetrapāla, who wears white serpent-earrings and is formidable with the mingling of the sounds of bells, waist-bands, and tinkling ornaments;
having thus meditated and worshipped him mentally, one should perform the ritual preparation of the *arghya* offering.

Having performed the worship of the conceptualized seat (pīṭha) beginning with Dharma and so forth, and having meditated again, and having performed the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), one should begin the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
It is as follows:

The first enclosure consists of the [eight] limbs; the second, of the eight [deities]: Analākṣa, Agnikeśa, Karāla, Ghaṇṭārava, Mahākrodha, Piśitāśana, Piṅgalākṣa, and Ūrdhvakeśa; and the third, of Indra and the other [world-protectors].
The fourth [initiation] is performed with the vajra and other implements;
thereafter, one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the incense offering and ending with the dismissal. || 19 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (japa).
There is a fire offering (homa) of one-tenth that number using sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with clarified butter (ājya).
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with caru mixed with ghee amounting to one-tenth of that number; thereafter, one should worship Kṣetreśa.
In the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*, however, it is stated:
"This mantra is devoid of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
Its preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of ten thousand recitations. (21)
