Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the courtyard of his house at night, and having worshipped the deity together with his retinue there, he should offer the oblation (*bali*) three times into the skull-cup held in the hand of the deity while reciting the *balimantra*.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the attendants by their respective names. || 22 ||
The mantra for the *bali* offering is as follows: *ehy ehi viduṣi saru suru bhañjaya bhañjaya tarjaya tarjaya vighna vighna mahābhairava kṣetrapāla baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*.
And thus:
first there should be two *ehi*s, then two *viduṣī*s,
followed by two *bhajja*s, and again two *tarjaja*s.
Then, [one should worship] the pair of feet of Vighna, followed by Mahābhairava,
the two Kṣetrapālas who accept the bali offering, and Pāvakasundarī.
Or else: "Come, come! Turu turu! Suru suru! Jambha jambha! Strike, strike! Destroy the obstacle, destroy it! O Mahābali Kṣetrapāla, seize, seize! Svāhā! Thus.
This ritual of the bali offering wards off all planetary afflictions and brings about victory and prosperity. || 23 ||
One should also offer a bali-oblation with a large morsel accompanied by side-dishes.
As for the fruit: "The Kṣetrapāla, satisfied by the offering of the bali, bestows [blessings]."
Beauty, intelligence, strength, health, splendor, nourishment, fame, and prosperity.
Now, the mantra of Vaṭukabhairava:
[it consists of] "vaṭukāya" in the dative case, followed by the word "āpaduddhāraṇa" (the deliverer from calamity) in the dative case,
joined with two instances of "kuru," and ending with "vaṭuka" in the dative case.
The twenty-one syllables are encapsulated by the *hṛllekhā* mantra accompanied by the word "Śabda.
Thus it is stated in the Nibandha:
"One should extract the name Vaṭuka in the dative case (*ṅe’ntam*), followed by 'Āpaduddharaṇa' (the remover of calamities)."
Furthermore, one should extract two *kurus* ending in *ṅe* and ending with *vaṭuka*;
this great mantra (*mahāmanu*), consisting of twenty-one syllables, is conjoined with Śakti. (25)
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:
having performed the morning rites up to the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa).
It is as follows:
Having performed the placement [of mantras] upon the body from *dharma* up to *anaiśvarya*, one should perform the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth:
"Salutation to Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the Seer, on the head; salutation to Gāyatrī, the Metre, on the mouth;
salutation to Vaṭukabhairava, the Deity, on the heart. (26)
Then follows the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa):
*hroṃ voṃ* to Īśāna, *namaḥ* on the two thumbs;
*hreṃ veṃ* to Tatpuruṣa, *namaḥ* on the two index fingers.
Hrūṃ vuṃ, obeisance to Aghora, on the two middle fingers; hriṃ viṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, on the two ring fingers;
hraḥ vaḥ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, on the two little fingers.
Furthermore, one should place those respective forms, preceded by their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), upon the head, face, heart, genitals, and feet with those respective fingers;
likewise, one should place them in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western directions.
And likewise, in the *Nibandha*: "One should place the forms on the fingers, the body, and the face as before,
preceded by the seed-syllables of the Śaktis enriched with the five short vowels beginning with 'a' (a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ) and the syllable 'va'."
One should apply [the letters] enriched with the five short vowels to Īśāna and the other [faces]. || 27 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs:
*oṃ hrāṃ vāṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, and so forth;
*oṃ hrāṃ vāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
One should perform [the rite] with two seed-syllables endowed with the six long vowels.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha: "In that same way, by means of the letter *va* conjoined with the Power (*śakti*) possessing the six long vowels."
One should conceive of the limbs, beginning with the syllable Om, as being endowed with birth.
Then comes meditation:
his meditation is said to be threefold, according to the divisions of *sāttvika* and so forth.
Among these, the *sāttvika* is as follows:
I bow to the Child, who resembles crystal, whose face is radiant with earrings,
adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels such as tinkling bells and anklets;
whose form is luminous, whose countenance is pure, who is most gracious, three-eyed, and who holds [objects] with his two lotus-hands.
Vaṭuka, who incessantly holds a trident and a staff; || 29 ||

An example of the *rājasa* [type]: "The three-eyed one, resembling the rising sun, with red unguents and garlands, smiling-faced, granting boons, holding a skull, the gesture of fearlessness, and a trident in his hands."

I always meditate upon the God who removes all fear, whose neck is blue, who is adorned with hundreds of magnificent ornaments, whose crest is radiant with the cool-rayed moon, and who is clothed in garments as red as the bandhūka flower. 30.
An example of the *tāmasa* [meditation] is as follows:
"One should meditate upon Maheśa, who has the splendor of a blue mountain, who wears a crescent moon and a garland of skulls,
who is clothed in the directions (naked), who has tawny eyes, and who holds a hand-drum, a goad, a sword, a trident, and the gesture of fearlessness."
Holding a serpent, a bell, and a skull with his lotus-like hands,
possessing fearsome fangs, adorned with serpents as ornaments, three-eyed, and enriched with tinkling jeweled bells and anklets; || 31 ||
This is declared to be sattvic meditation, which destroys untimely death,
generates longevity and health, and bestows the fruit of liberation.

Rājasa meditation is unmanifested, yet it bestows the attainment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth; tāmasa meditation subdues enemies and removes the afflictions caused by malevolent spells, spirits, and diseases.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual placement of the arghya water.
The yantra for its worship is as follows:
upon a pedestal fashioned from dharma, adharma, and so forth, adorned with a lotus, situated within a triangle inside a hexagon, and beautified by a lotus in the center of the void. (Figure 26)
Then, having conceived the form with the root mantra and meditated upon it as before, one should perform the invocation and the subsequent rites.
In that regard, the sequence is as follows:
invocation with the *sadyojāta* mantra beginning with the root [mantra];
installation with the *vāmadeva* mantra beginning with the root [mantra].
Proximity is effected by the Mūla-mantra; confinement by the Aghora-mantra;
and the display of the Yoni-mudrā by the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.
The specific distinction is that the salutation is performed with the Īśāna mantra.
One should worship Īśāna and the others in the pericarp, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate corners.
This is the first enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Then, one should worship Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, upon the petals of the lotus in the sky.
They are as follows:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava,
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Sahāra— these are the eight Bhairavas.
With these eight, the second enclosure is formed. || 37 ||
Then, one should worship the six limbs in the six corners, starting from the east, with "Oṃ hrāṃ vāṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth. || 38 ||

Then, starting from the east, one should worship the sons of the goddesses Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī, Hākinī, and Mālinī; this is the third enclosure. In the eight directions, one should sacrifice to the sons of Umā, the sons of Rudra, and the sons of the Mothers on the right.
One should worship the sons of the upward-facing goddesses above and the sons of the downward-facing goddesses below;
this is the fourth enclosure (*caturthāvaraṇa*).
And so it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
Outside of that, one should worship these from the east up to the northeast:
first the sons of Ḍākinīs, then the sons of Rākiṇīs,
after that the sons of Lākinīs, and likewise the sons of Kākinīs.
One should place the sons of Śākinī, then again the sons of Hākinī,
followed by the sons of Mālinī, and thereafter the sons of the gods; likewise,
one should place the sons of Umā, Rudra, and the Mothers on the right side.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the thirteen groups of sons as follows: "Those with upward faces [grant] sons above; those with downward faces [grant] sons below. Thus [he worships]. (39)
Outside of that, on the eight petals, one should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in the form of vaṭukas.

Outside of that, in the east: *oṃ brahmāṇīputrāya namaḥ*; likewise in the northeast (*īśāna*): *māheśvarīputrāya*; in the north (*uttara*): *vaiṣṇavīputrāya*; in the northwest (*anila*): *kaumārīputrāya*.
In the west, to the son of Indrāṇī; in the southwest, to the son of Mahālakṣmī; in the south, to the son of Vārāhī; in the southeast, to the son of Cāmuṇḍā—this is the fifth enclosure.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:

Then one should worship the son of Brahmāṇī in the east, the son of Māheśī in the northeast, the son of Vaiṣṇavī in the north, the son of Kaumārī in the northwest, and again the son of Indrāṇī in the west.
Thereafter, one should worship the son of Mahālakṣmī in the western direction;
the son of Vārāhī in the south; and the son of Cāmuṇḍā in the southeast. Outside of that, in the ten directions, [one should worship] Hetuka, Tripurāntaka, Vetāla, and Vahnijihva.
One should worship Kālāntaka, Karāla, Ekapāda, Bhīmarūpa, Acala, and Hāṭakeśvara. This is the sixth enclosure.

Then, one should worship the lords of the yogis (yogīśas), together with their yoginīs, situated in the directions starting from Īśāna up to Nirṛti, who reside in the worlds of Sakala, Īśvara, Bhūmi, Antarīkṣa, and Svarloka. As follows:
Salutation to the divine Lord of Yogins accompanied by Yoginīs.
Likewise, salutation to the Lord of Yogins of the intermediate space accompanied by Yoginīs.
Salutation to the Lord of Yogins dwelling on earth accompanied by Yoginīs.
This is the seventh enclosure. || 40 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of reciting [the mantra] twenty-one hundred thousand times.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with ten percent of that amount, using oblations soaked in the three sweets (trimadhura).
And so it is said:
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
then he should perform oblations with sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets (trimadhura) ten times that number.
Now, regarding the offering of the *bali*:
having first propitiated Vighna and Durgā, one should present the *bali*.
It consists of cooked rice, minced meat, clarified butter, parched grain flour, and sugar.
Having prepared a morsel mixed with jaggery, sugarcane juice, cakes, and honey,
and having worshipped the deity according to the previously mentioned method,
one should offer an oblation (bali) to him at night with red sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings.
Or else:
having slain the unborn goat with its limbs complete, as previously described,
one should [visualize] the entire army of enemies at the time of offering the oblation.
One of refined intellect should offer [the oblation] to Vaṭuka as a bali-offering.
The noble-minded one should perform the *vidarbha* (interlocking) ritual using the name of Śakra and the *bali* mantra:
"O dog, together with your own pack and accompanied by dogs, consume day after day the blood and flesh of the enemy faction."
This bali-mantra has been declared, which bestows victory upon all.
Satisfied by this offering, Vaṭuka, with a wrathful mind, shall divide the entire enemy host along with their provisions among his own attendants.
When this is done, the enemy army is destroyed; of this there is no doubt. (45)
Then Bhairava [spoke]:
"The dust of whose lotus feet is worshipped by the hosts of immortals, and through union with whom the Supreme Lord became Paraśiva..."
Victorious is that Śāmbhavī, the sole mother of the world, who through her threefold form extends creation, preservation, and dissolution. 46.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
May the inconceivable splendor of the Triple City (Tripura)—which destroys the darkness of ignorance, delivers one from the ocean of saṃsāra, and is the seed of bliss—descend [upon us]. 47.
Now I shall declare the Great Vidyā, which is extremely well-guarded;
by knowing which, a man becomes the sovereign of all the hosts of Siddhas. (48)
Now, the mantras of Tripurabhairavī.
Now, regarding the threefold nature of Tripurā, according to the divisions of Bālā, Bhairavī, and Sundarī;
and thus it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
The goddess Tripurā is threefold and is celebrated as the triple power (triśakti). Now, the *Prapañcasāra* states her etymological derivation:
"Because she exists beyond the creation of the three forms (trimūrti), because she is superior (parābhava), and because she consists of the three (trayomayī), the Goddess is indeed Para."
Because she fills even the three worlds, the name "Tripurā" belongs primarily to Ambikā;
and so it is said in the Vārāhītantra:
"In ancient times, she was worshipped by the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa."
"O Goddess, the name 'Tripurā' has always been proclaimed for you by the gods. (49)
In the *Śāradā*:
"The elemental [syllable] situated in the sky (viyat), the Bhr̥gu (2), and the fire (3), topped with a bindu;
[the syllable] situated in the sky, that same [elemental], the center (1), and the fire (3), possessed of the left eye (1) and a bindu."
The mantra situated in space (Ā), the wind (Y), and fire (R), possessing the crescent moon of emanation (Ū), is the five-peak Vidyā, the knowable Tripurabhairavī.
The first peak is Vāgbhava; the second is Kāmarāja.
And the third is the Śaktikūṭa, which is said to consist of three seed-syllables (bījas).
The meaning of this is:
Śiva, Candra, Vahni, and Vāgbhava;
[and] Śiva, Candra, Kāma, Pṛthvī, Vahni, together with the fourth vowel and the bindu.
The letter Śiva (Ś), the Moon (A), the letter Repha (R), the fourteenth vowel (AU), the Bindu, and the Visarga. || 49ka ||
The worship of this [goddess] is as follows:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the placement of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa).
In this regard, there is a specific distinction.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] according to the previously stated sequence, beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with *hrīṃ jñānātmane namaḥ*, one should place [the following mantras] on the filaments of the heart-lotus starting from the east: *oṃ icchāyai namaḥ*, and likewise to Jñānā, Kriyā, Kāminī, Kāmadāyinī, Ratī, and Ratipriyā.
To Nandā; in the center, to Manonmanī; above that, to Aiṃ Parā, Aparā, and Parāparā; and to Hsrauḥ Sadāśiva-Mahāpreta-Padmāsana, [I offer] salutation.

Having thus performed the placement of the pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśakti) and the mantra of the pedestal (pīṭhamantra), one should perform the placement of the seer and the other [limbs] (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
For example:
"Obeisance to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the head; obeisance to the Paṅkti metre in the mouth;
obeisance to the deity Tripurabhairavī in the heart; obeisance to the seed-syllable Vāgbhava in the secret place."
Salutation to *namaḥ* at the feet; salutation to the third power (*tārtīya-śakti*) at the [thighs]; salutation to the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*), the *kīlaka*, at all the limbs.
As stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
The sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; one should place him on the head.
The metre is to be known as Paṅkti; having placed it on the mouth, one should place the deity Tripureśānī on the heart. Vāgbhava is said to be the seed-syllable.
The seed-syllable of Śakti is Śakti herself, and the Kāmabīja is the *kīlaka*.
Then, from the navel down to the feet: *hsraiṃ namaḥ*;
from the heart up to the navel: *hsaklrīṃ namaḥ*; from the head down to the heart: *hsrauṃ*.
One should place the first seed-syllable, *namaḥ*, on the right hand, the second on the left hand,
and the third on both hands. Then, one should place the three seed-syllables respectively upon the head, the *mūlādhāra*, and the heart.
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"The best of mantra-knowers should place the Vāgbhava [syllable] from the navel down to the feet;
he should properly place the Kāmabīja from the heart down to the navel."
Then, one should place the third [syllable] from the head down to the region of the heart;
the first and second [syllables] on the two hands, and the third on both [feet].
One should again place the three seed-syllables in sequence upon the foundation of the head and the heart.
Then follows the placement of the nine sources (navayoninyāsa): the first seed-syllable on the right ear, the second seed-syllable on the left ear, and the third seed-syllable on the chin.
In this manner, [one should worship] on the two cheeks, the face, the two eyes, the nose, the two shoulders, the abdomen, the two elbows,
the belly, the two knees, the tip of the penis, the feet, the private parts, the two sides, the heart-lotus, the two breasts, and the throat.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"One should perform the deposition (nyāsa) consisting of the nine wombs by means of the three seed-syllables in sequence:
[on] the two ears, the chin, again on the two cheeks, and then on the face."
Having placed [the syllables] on the two eyes, the nose, the two shoulders, and again on the abdomen; then on the two elbows, the two sides of the belly, the two knees, the crown of the head,
the feet, the private region, the two flanks, and the lotus of the heart.
One should place three seed-syllables on the two breasts and in the region of the throat.
Then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Rati and the others:
*aiṃ* to Rati, salutation at the root-center (*mūladhāra*); *klīṃ* to Prīti, salutation at the heart;
*sauḥ* to Manobhavā, salutation between the eyebrows; again, *sauḥ* to Amṛteśī, salutation between the eyebrows.

*Hṛdi klīṃ yogeśyai namaḥ*, *mūlādhāre aiṃ viśvayonyai namaḥ*. And likewise, in the *Nibandha*: "One should worship Rati at the base (*mūla*), Prīti in the heart (*hṛd*), and Manobhavā between the eyebrows."
One should install these three seed-syllables (*bījas*) in reverse order in these locations:
Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, and Viśvayoni, respectively. Having performed the installation with the seed-syllables in reverse order, one should then perform the installation of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*).
Now, the ritual placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa):
on the head, *shrīm*—salutation to Īśāna, the mind-born; on the face, *shrem*—salutation to Tatpuruṣa, the dolphin-bannered one; on the heart, *shrūm*—salutation to Aghora, the youthful Kandarpa.
*Namaḥ*, at the secret place: *Śrīṃ vāmadevamanmathāya namaḥ*; at the feet:
*Shraṃ sadyojātakāmadevāya namaḥ*.
[One should worship] Īśāna, Manobhava, and the others in the single face directed upward, and in the eastern, southern, northern, and western faces.
One should install the five forms preceded by their respective seed-syllables (bīja).
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
"Everything beginning with its own seed-syllable, ending with 'namas' for Īśāna, [should be placed] on the head."
The knower of the Self should assign this Puruṣa-Makaradhvaja to the mouth;
then Aghora, known as Kumāra, and Kandarpa within that;
and in the secret region, he should duly assign Vāmadeva and Manmatha.
Then, one should place Sadyojāta and Kāmadeva at the two feet;
and upon the faces— namely the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western— one should assign them as before,
situated in the order of Bhṛgu, Vyoman, and Agni.
The seed-syllable of these is proclaimed to be enriched with the five short vowels beginning with 'a' (satya-ādi).
Then follows the placement of the arrows (*bāṇanyāsa*):
*drāṃ* to Drāviṇī, *namaḥ* on the two thumbs;
*drīṃ* to Kṣobhiṇī, *namaḥ* on the two index fingers.
*Klīṃ* to Vaśīkaraṇī, salutation to the middle fingers; *Blūṃ* to Ākarṣiṇī, salutation to the ring fingers;
*Saḥ* to Sammohinī, salutation to the little fingers.
And so it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Supreme Goddess, one should place the five arrows in sequence upon the fingers of the hand, from the thumb to the little finger in order. (54)
Then, one should perform the placement of Kāma (Kāmanya-sa) in those locations in due order, as follows:
*hrīṃ* salutation to Kāma; *klīṃ* salutation to Manmatha; *aiṃ* salutation to Kandarpa.
*Namaḥ*, *blūṃ* to Makaradhvaja, *namaḥ*; *strīṃ* to Mīnaketana, *namaḥ*.
Then, one should place the previously mentioned arrows and the [five] Kāmas upon the head, feet, face, secret parts, and heart.
Likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:
"Having extracted the two letters ending in 'tha' situated in fire (ra) in sequence,
it is adorned by the face (u), the eye (i), and the left [eye] (ī)."

These two arrows have been proclaimed: the first is *mādana* situated on the earth (the letter *ma*), enriched with the vowel *ī* and the bindu, existing in the form of sound (*na*), O fair-faced one;
the second is the end of the *pha*-group (the letter *ba*), mounted upon Indra (the letter *a*), and adorned with the left ear (the letter *u*).
O beloved, the Moon is joined with the Bindu and Nāda and possesses the letter of creation (S).
O Maheśānī, O Pārvatī, hear the names of the five arrows:
Drāvaṇa (Melting), Kṣobhaṇa (Agitating), Vaśya (Subjugating), and that known as Ākarṣaṇa (Attracting).
Likewise, O Supreme Goddess, the names for Unmāda are applied in sequence;
however, in all instances of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the usage is in the feminine gender.
And so it is stated in the *Nibandha*:
One should place Drāviṇī, preceded by *drāṃ*, on the head; Kṣobhaṇī, preceded by *drīṃ*, on the feet;
Vaśīkaraṇī, preceded by *klīṃ*, on the mouth;
and Ākarṣaṇī, preceded by the seed-syllable *blūṃ* and joined with the letter *sa* (the end of creation) and the syllable *bhr̥gu* (ma), on the heart.
This placement of the arrows (*bāṇanyāsa*) has thus been described, beginning with *sammohanī* in due order.
In this context, *unmāda* and *sammohana* are synonymous.
The *kāmas* (desires) are to be understood as being in that very same place; hear now their seed-syllables (*bījas*).
O Parameśvarī, [the seed-syllable] of the Supreme (Parā) with the middle arrow, and Vāgbhava;
then, O Dear One, the fourth arrow and the female seed-syllable (Strībīja) in sequence—these, O Goddess, are the five desires (Pañcakāma). Listen to their names, O Beloved!
O Maheśānī, those known as Kāma, Anmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja, with Mīnaketu as the fifth, are proclaimed; O Goddess, one should then place these five Kāmas in the locations of the arrows.
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*hsrāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*hsrīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
Hsraṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers;
hsraiṃ, huṃ to the two ring fingers;
hsrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers.
"Hsraḥ phaṭ with both palms and backs of the hands;
likewise for the heart and other limbs.
The ritual of the limbs for the mantra is performed with the first seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels. (56)
Then follows the Subhagā-nyāsa:
on the forehead, *aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ*, obeisance to Subhagā; between the eyebrows, *aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ*, obeisance to Bhagā.
On the face: Aiṃ Klīṃ Blūṃ Strīṃ Saḥ, obeisance to Bhagasarpiṇī.
On the necklace: Aiṃ Klīṃ Blūṃ Strīṃ Saḥ, obeisance to Bhagamālinī.
On the throat: Aiṃ Klīṃ Blūṃ Strīṃ Saḥ, obeisance to Anaṅgā.

In the heart: *aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ*—salutation to Anaṅgakusumā. At the navel: *aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ*—salutation to Anaṅgamekhalā. At the base of the genitals: *aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ*—salutation to Anaṅgamadanā.
And likewise in the Nibandha: "In the forehead, between the eyebrows, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, and the foundation [of the feet],
there are the five Tārās beginning with Subhagā."
The fortunate goddesses should be installed by the practitioner according to the ritual procedure:
Bhagā, then Bhagasarpiṇī, and after that the supreme Bhagamālinī;
furthermore, Anaṅgā, Anaṅgakuṣumā, and then Anaṅgamekhalā.
All [the goddesses] are Anaṅgamadanā, overwhelmed by the confusion of intoxication;
these five are proclaimed with their seed-syllables: Blūṃ, Strīṃ, Saḥ, and Tārā.
Then follows the placement of the ornaments (*bhūṣaṇanyāsa*).
It is as follows:
on the head, *aṃ namaḥ*.
Āṃ, salutation to the forehead;
iṃ īṃ, to the two eyebrows; uṃ ūṃ, to the two ears.
Ṛ ṝṃ on the two eyes; Ḷṃ on the nose;
ḹṃ and Eṃ on the two cheeks.
Aiṃ Oṃ on the two lips; Auṃ on the lower teeth; Aṃ on the upper teeth.
Aḥ at the mouth; Kaṃ at the chin; Khaṃ at the throat.
Gaṃ at the throat; ghaṃ and ṅaṃ at the two sides; caṃ and chaṃ at the pair of breasts.
Jaṃ and jhaṃ at the two armpits;
ñaṃ and ṭaṃ at the two elbows; ṭhaṃ and ḍaṃ at the two hands.
Ḍhaṃ and ṇaṃ on the back of the hands; taṃ at the navel; thaṃ at the secret place.
Daṃ ghaṃ on the two thighs; naṃ paṃ on the two knees; phaṃ baṃ on the two shanks; bhaṃ maṃ on the two buttocks.
Yaṃ on the two palms;
raṃ on the two big toes;
vaṃ on the waist-belt.
Laṃ at the neck; laṃ at the bracelets; śaṃ at the heart.
KṢAṂ at the secret place; ṢAṂ at the two ears; SAṂ at the two cheeks.
At the head, [one places] *haṃ*. One should place [the mantras] everywhere ending with *namaḥ*.
And likewise, in another tantra:
One should place [the consonants] on the head, the forehead, the eyebrows, the two ears, the pair of eyes, and the nose.
One should place the vowels on the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, and the mouth;
and [the remaining letters] on the chin, the throat, the neck, the two sides, and the pair of breasts.
Then on the two armpits, the two shoulders, the hands, and the region of their backs;
then on the navel, the private parts, and again on the thighs, knees, and shanks;
then on the two buttocks, the two palms, and finally on the two big toes of the feet.
With a concentrated mind, one should place the letters from *ka* to *va* in these locations:
at the waist, then on the neck, on the wrists, in the heart, and in the private parts;
[and] in the ears, the cheeks, the head, and on the eyebrows, the eyes, and the teeth.
The best of teachers should thus place these eight [deities]. Then, having formed the three-part mudrā, he should meditate as follows:

I bow to the Goddess who holds with her lotus-like hands a garland of skulls possessing the splendor of a thousand rising suns, a stream of blood as red as saffron, a rosary, the Vidyā-mantra, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon; she who possesses the beauty of a throbbing red lotus and has three eyes.
"I bow to her who wears a crown of jewels like the full moon and possesses a gentle smile.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.

Then, having worshipped from Ādhāraśakti up to "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Self of Knowledge," one worships in the filaments starting from the east and in the center: Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, followed by Kāminī and Kāmadāyinī.

Ratī, Ratipriyā, Nandā, Nandinī, and Manonmanī—these should be worshipped with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. Then: *Aiṃ parāyai aparāyai parāparāyai hsauḥ sadāśiva-mahāpreta*.
"Salutation to Padmāsana.
Having thus worshipped, one should worship the lineages of gurus mentioned in the Śrīvidyā within the space between the eastern yoni and the central yoni.

In the *Nibandha*, [the mantra is]: Vāgbhava (AIM), Lohita (RAI), Śrīkaṇṭha (LOHITA), Anala (VA), Dīrghavān (YĀ), Parā (PAŚCĀT), Aparā (YĀ), HSAUḤ; then Sadāśiva-Mahāpreta in the dative case (ṄE’NTA), Padmāsana, and Namaḥ.
With this mantra, one should offer a seat to the lineage of the venerable gurus.
One should worship within the space between the eastern and central yonis, and then perform the visualization.
Having invoked the deity into that form with five *praṇavas*, one should worship it.
One should worship with a concentrated mind according to the procedure taught in the Āgamas.
Tārā, Vākśakti, Kamalā, HSKHPHREM, and HS AUḤ are remembered [as the mantras]. In the event of inability to do so, however: OṂ GURUBHYO NAMAḤ, OṂ GURUPĀDUKĀBHYO NAMAḤ, OṂ...

Salutations to the supreme gurus; Oṃ, salutations to the sandals of the supreme gurus; Oṃ, salutations to the higher-lower gurus; Oṃ, salutations to the sandals of the higher-lower gurus; Oṃ, salutations to the preceptor gurus; Oṃ, salutations to the sandals of the preceptor gurus; Oṃ.
Salutations to the teachers; Oṃ, salutations to the sandals of the teachers. || 60 ||
Regarding its worship diagram, it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
"Then one should draw a *bhūgṛha* (earth-palace) provided with an eight-petalled lotus, a pericarp enriched with nine triangles, and endowed with four gates. (Figure 27)
Then, having conceived the form of the Goddess in the *binducakra* with the mantra *aiṃ hrīṃ hskhphreṃ hsauḥ*,
and having meditated upon the Goddess as before using the *trikhaṇḍamudrā*,
one should invoke her: *Oṃ, O Queen of Gods, who are easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by Your retinue!*
"Remain perfectly steadfast as long as I worship you, O Reality.
Having invoked the deity into that form with five *praṇavas*,
[the mantras] Tārā, Vākśakti, Kamalā, HSKHPHREṂ, and HSAUḤ are remembered [as the seed-syllables].
Having thus performed the rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the offering of five handfuls of flowers, one should commence the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
Namely:
in the goddess's left corner, *aiṃ* to Rati, *namaḥ*;
in the right corner, *klīṃ* to Prīti, *namaḥ*.
In the southeast corner: *sauḥ* to Manobhavā, obeisance.
Then, one should worship with the previously mentioned limb-mantras upon the filaments in the corners starting from the southeast, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions.
And so it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"The worship of the limbs is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center.
Then, in the north: *drāṃ* obeisance to Drāviṇī; *drīṃ* obeisance to Kṣobhiṇī; [and] in the south..."
*Klīṃ* to Vaśīkaraṇī, obeisance; *Blūṃ* to Ākarṣaṇī, obeisance.
In front, *Saḥ* to Sammohinī, obeisance.
Then one should worship the five desires (*pañcakāmān*).
For example:
in the north, *hrīṃ* to Kāma, *klīṃ* to Manmatha;
in the south, *aiṃ* to Kandarpa, *blūṃ* to Makaradhvaja.
At the beginning [of the mantra], [one should worship] the woman for the one whose banner is the fish;
*namaḥ* is everywhere.
And likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:
O Goddess, there are two in the northern direction and two in the southern direction;
one at the front—thus one should worship the five arrows in due order.
Likewise, O Goddess, one should worship the five desires just like the arrows.
And likewise in that very same place:
"The five objects of desire, the supreme seed-syllable, the central arrow, and the Vāgbhava [syllable], O Supreme Goddess;
then the fourth arrow and the female seed-syllable, in due order, O Beloved."
O Goddess, my beloved, hear these names of the five objects of desire:
they are known as Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makaradhvaja, and, O Great Sovereign,
the fifth is proclaimed as Mīnaketu.
Then, in the eight birthplaces (yoni) starting from the east in order: *aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ*—*namaḥ* to Subhagā;
likewise, *aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ*—[namaḥ] to Bhagā.
Aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ, to Bhagasarpiṇī; aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ, to Bhagamālinī;
aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ, to Anaṅgā.
Aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ, to Anaṅgakusumā; aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ, to Anaṅgamekhalā;
aiṃ klīṃ blūṃ strīṃ saḥ, to Anaṅgamadanā.
Homage everywhere!
Then, on the eight petals in the order starting from the east and so forth: *oṃ asitāṅgabrāhmībhyāṃ namaḥ*;
likewise, *oṃ rudramāheśvarībhyām*, *oṃ caṇḍakaumārībhyām*, *oṃ*...
To Krodha-Vaiṣṇavī, Oṃ Unmatta-Vārāhī, Oṃ Kapālīndrāṇī, Oṃ Bhīṣaṇa-Cāmuṇḍā, and Oṃ Saṃhāra-Mahālakṣmī.
And likewise, in the Nibandha:
"One should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Subhagā, within the eight wombs;
these Mothers, seated upon the lap of Bhairava, are overwhelmed by the intoxication of their amorous play."
One should worship [the deities] on the eight petals duly with flowers and other offerings.
Then, having worshipped Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other implements, outside of that, one should complete the ritual from the incense offering up to the final dismissal.
However, after the food offering (naivedya), the fourfold bali as described in the Śrīvidyā tradition should be presented here. || 62 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of ten lakhs of recitations;
the fire-oblation (homa), however, should be performed with palāśa flowers twelve thousand times.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
Having received initiation, one who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one million times according to the principles;
he should offer oblations with flowers born from the Brahma-tree (udumbara) ten thousand times for each solar day.
Now, regarding the bestower of prosperity, Bhairavī says in the Jñānārṇava: "Just as this Bālā Tripurā is, so too is Tripurabhairavī."
O you of pure mind, hear now the [mantra] named Sampatpradā (Bestower of Prosperity):
Śiva and Candra situated in Vahni, followed by Vāgbhava;
likewise, O Goddess, Kāmabīja joined with Śiva and Candra thereafter.
O beloved, listen to the third [syllable], enriched by the earth-seed (la), fire (ra), and the end of fire (va).
O Maheśānī, one should join Śiva (ha) and Fire (ra) with the Śakti-seed (ai). O Parameśānī, having omitted the *sarga* (ḥ) of Kumārī, it becomes the *bindu* (m).
The goddess Tripurābhairavī is considered the bestower of great prosperity.
The meaning of this is: if Tripurābhairavī is devoid of the *visarga*, she bestows prosperity. || 64 ||
In another Tantra:
"O beautiful goddess, in that third seed-syllable which bestows prosperity, one should discard the *sarga* (the visarga) and then insert the *bindu*. (65)
Her [meditation] is as follows:
She has the luster of a thousand slightly copper-colored suns; her matted hair is adorned with a shimmering crescent moon and pearls variegated by various gems sparkling from her crown.
Abounding in mud of flowing blood, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
enriched by the beauty of three eyes, endowed with a face like the full moon,
and possessing full, elevated breasts shining with strings of pearl necklaces.
One should meditate upon the Eternal One (Nityā), who is clothed in red garments, whose form is intoxicated with youth,
who holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right hand,
bestowing boons and granting great prosperity.
The ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth are as before. || 66 ||
Regarding the limb-mantras, however, there is this distinction:
the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs is performed with the three seed-syllables repeated twice.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] is three hundred thousand recitations.
As stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The best of practitioners should perform the worship and other rites for this [goddess] just as for Bālā."
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount.
In another tantra:
"O you of virtuous vows, all rites such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship are performed just as for a virgin;
the best of practitioners should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishment."

According to this statement, some maintain that there should be a preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), because [the mantra] is an accomplished science (*siddhavidyā*). || 69 ||
Now, in the Jñānārṇava, it says: "Know Kauleśabhairavī to be like Sampatpradābhairavī."
O Goddess of gods, O Pārvatī, that very [seed-syllable] beginning with *hasa* exists within the three seed-syllables;
thus, there should be the *saharādyā* [mantra], as well as meditation, worship, and so forth.
The meaning of this is as follows:
If it begins with the letter 'sa' on the third peak, then she becomes Kauleśabhairavī. || 70 ||
Her worship, meditation, and so forth should be understood to be like those of Sampatpradā Bhairavī. || 71 ||
Now, Bhairavī, the bestower of all accomplishments,
says in the Jñānārṇava:
"In this very Vidyā, [the syllables] at the beginning and end are devoid of the letter *ra*."
Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, this [form] bestows all accomplishments by its very name;
it grants prosperity like Bhairavī, and its meditation, worship, and so forth are as follows.
Its meaning is:

If Kauleśa-Bhairavī is devoid of the letter *ra* at the beginning and the end, then she becomes Bhairavī, the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*); her meditation, worship, and so forth, however, are like those that grant prosperity. 72.
Now, regarding Bhayavidhvaṃsinī-Bhairavī and Sampatpradā-Bhairavī: if [the mantra] is devoid of the letter *ra* at the beginning and the end, then it becomes Bhayavidhvaṃsinī-Bhairavī.
Likewise, because it is seen in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti [Upaniṣad], worship and other rites grant prosperity. || 73 ||
Now, from the *Jñānārṇava* regarding Caitanyabhairavī:
"Having uttered the seed-syllable Vāgbhava, conjoined with the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."

O Maheśānī, one should extract the second seed-syllable as Sakalā Bhuvaneśānī; it consists of the soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa) situated in fire (the letter Ra), adorned with the vowel of Indra (the letter E), and enriched by the visarga. This is the Vidyā known as Trailokyamātṛkā. 74.
The meaning of this is as follows:
first, "conjoined with the twelve vowels of Candra and Śiva, enriched with Bindu and Nāda";
second, "Candra, Kāma, Pṛthvī, and Mahāmāyā"; [and third], "the seed-syllable of Candra, Śiva, and Vahni."
The third [syllable] is joined with the fourteen vowels and enriched with the visarga. || 75 ||
The worship diagram for her is described in the Jñānārṇava:
"O fair-faced one, one should draw the mandala in this manner: a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square with four gates. (Figure 28)
The worship of this [deity] is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having completed the ritual up to "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Self of Knowledge" for Ādhāraśakti and the others, one proceeds in order from the east of the heart-lotus.

In the filaments: *oṃ vāmāyai namaḥ*, and likewise *jyeṣṭhāyai*, *raudryai*, *ambikāyai*, *icchāyai*, *jñānāyai*, *kriyāyai*, *kubjikāyai*, *citrāyai*, *viṣaghnikāyai*, *bhūcaryai*, *ānandāyai*. In the center: *hsauḥ sadāśivamahāpretapadmāsanāya*.
Salutation!

These are the powers of the sacred seats (pīṭhaśaktis)—namely Sampatpradā, Bālā, Kaulīśī, and the bestower of all perfections (Siddhis) of the Vidyās—because they are mentioned in the Jñānārṇava. || 77 ||
Then follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth: "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer, on the head;
salutation to the *paṅkti* metre, on the mouth."
Salutation to the deity Caitanyabhairavī in the heart. || 78 ||
Then, for the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): having uttered the first seed-syllable, "Salutation to both thumbs" (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*).
Having uttered the second seed-syllable, "Svāhā to both index fingers" (*tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*).
Having uttered the third seed-syllable, [one offers] *vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers;
again, having uttered the first seed-syllable, *huṃ* with the two ring fingers;
and having uttered the second seed-syllable, *vauṣaṭ* with the two little fingers.
Having uttered the third seed-syllable, [one says] "phaṭ" with the palms and backs of the hands;
likewise for the heart and other [limbs].
And so it is stated in that very same [text]:
By repeating [the mantra] twice, one performs the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), which is the protection of all limbs.
Then follows the meditation (*dhyāna*):
[She who] possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns and is adorned with various ornaments.
She wears a crescent moon upon the crown of her head, is clothed in red garments,
and holds a noose and a goad; she is the eternal goddess who carries a skull-cup in her left hand,
is enriched by the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and possesses full, elevated, and firm breasts.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch, carry out the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), and then worship the pedestal powers such as Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā, as well as the mantra of the pedestal.
Then, having worshipped the lineages of gurus mentioned by Bhairavī and meditated once more,
one should perform the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali),
and then begin the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā). || 80 ||
Namely:
having uttered the first seed-syllable in the southeast, "to the heart, namaḥ";
having uttered the second seed-syllable in the northeast, "to the head, svāhā."
In the southwest (Nairṛta), having uttered the third seed-syllable, [say] "to the crest-lock, Vaṣaṭ.
In the northwest (Vāyu) corner, again having uttered the first seed-syllable, [say] "to the armor, Huṃ.
In the center, having uttered the second seed-syllable, [say] "to the three eyes, Vauṣaṭ," in the four directions.
Having uttered the third seed-syllable, *astrāya phaṭ*,
and having worshipped Rati and the others as before, [one should worship] in front with *oṃ vasantāya namaḥ*, on the left with *oṃ kāmadevāya namaḥ*, and on the right with *oṃ cāpāya namaḥ*.
Then, as before, one should worship the arrows.
Then, in the hexagon, starting from the east, [one should worship] with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Ḍākinī";
likewise to Rākiṇī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī.
One should worship with [the mantra] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, on the eight petals, starting from the east, one should worship the previously mentioned Aṅgakusumā and others.
On the tips of the petals, starting from the east, [one should worship]: *oṃ parabhṛtāya namaḥ*, *ebhaṃ sārasāya*, and *śukāya*.
To the one named Megha, or to Megha; to the outer corner of the eye, to the play of the eyebrows, to the *hāva* gesture, and to the *bhāva* emotion.
Then, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons.
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings.
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
Thus it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
One should recite the mantra a number of times equal to the target count, and so forth. || 81 ||
Now, in the *Jñānārṇava*, it is said: "And Kāmeśvarī,
consisting of eleven Rudras, is situated upon the eastern lion-throne."
Two seed-syllables of this very vidyā have been proclaimed;
at its end, O Supreme Goddess, are "nityaklinne madadrave. Of this very [vidyā], the third is the syllable of Rudra, the Supreme Sovereign.
All [rites] such as worship and meditation are just as before, as if they were consciousness itself. O fair-faced one, there is a specific instruction regarding the triangles; I shall explain it:
in the front triangle, in due order, are Nityā, Kilanā, and Madadravā.
Thereafter, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure for the sake of attaining all perfections.
Now, in the Jñānārṇava, regarding Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī:
Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Jīje, Lākinī, Kākinī— this is the pair.
O beautiful goddess, having extracted the two seed-syllables of Śākinī and Hākinī,
one should write the third seed-syllable, O Goddess, joined with the first vowel *ai*, adorned with the second vowel *ī*, and endowed with the vowel of the enemy (*u*).
O daughter of the mountain, the third [syllable] is pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and kalā;
some say the third seed-syllable is accompanied by the visarga.
In another tantra:
"One should draw the seed-syllable *kṣmā* (the delighter of the earth) upon the thigh, and here the auspicious (*śiva*) syllable in three ways;
then, in sequence, adorn it with the sun (*arka*), *māyā*, and *śakra*."
The first pair is endowed with the bindu and nāda, while the last is possessed of the visarga.
I shall describe her meditation, which cuts through all beings:
the Goddess who possesses the radiance of the rising sun, resembling the hibiscus flower;
she is adorned with garlands of severed heads and wears a garment as bright as the rising sun.
She possesses full and elevated breasts shaped like golden jars;
she holds a noose, a goad, a book, and likewise a rosary—this is the ellipsis. || 85 ||
O Supreme Goddess, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating [the mantra] twice, I shall describe her yantra: one should draw a triangle and enclose it within its own enclosure;
then, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus outside, and beyond that, a twelve-petalled one.
One should draw the mandala as four-cornered with four gates (see Figure 29).
O Goddess Śivā, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure as before;
O Goddess, one should worship the triangle consisting of the triad beginning with Rati.
One should worship the Ḍākinīs and others in the hexagon;
thereafter, the pair beginning with Brāhmī on the eight petals;
thereafter, the pair beginning with Vāmā as the pedestal-energies (pīṭhaśakti) of Bālā on the twelve petals, in due order.
O Supreme Goddess, in the square one should worship the world-protectors with their weapons;
by this very procedure, one should worship Bhairavī, who is known as Nityā.
Now,
in the *Jñānārṇava* [it is said]:
"Of this very Vidyā, the six syllables are situated in their proper sequence."
In the mature stage, this knowledge, when practiced in reverse, bestows both enjoyment and liberation;
one should perform all its rites, such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship, as previously described.
Now, in the Rudrabhairavī-jñānārṇava:
[The mantra consists of] Śiva (H), Candra (S), and Madanānta (K), followed by Pānta (PH) conjoined with Vahni (R).
O Dear One, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] is distinct from the Śakti and enriched with Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā;
it belongs to Bhairavī for the bestowal of prosperity. That very same [syllable] is the Kāmarāja [seed-syllable], as well as the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva and of the Great Lion Throne.
O Great Goddess, this Vidyā cannot be fully described.
Its meaning is as follows:
it is conjoined with the fire residing within the moon-gem of Śiva, distinguished by the eleventh vowel.
The Vāgbhava seed-syllable is endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*.

The Kāmarāja seed-syllable is distinguished by Śiva (ha), Candra (sa), Kāma (ka), Pṛthvī (la), and the fourth vowel (ī), and is endowed with *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*. The Preta seed-syllable is the Śakti-peak (*kūṭa*).
The third [chapter]. || 89 ||
The yantra for its worship is as follows:
a triangle, a circle, a circle with an eight-petaled lotus, a circle, and an earth-mandala, and so forth. (Figure 30)
Her worship:
having performed the rites from the morning duties up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the deposition on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa) as in the case of Caitanyabhairavī.
For example: having performed the placement (nyāsa) beginning with the power of the support (ādhāra-śakti) and ending with "hrīṃ, obeisance to the self of knowledge" (jñānātmane namaḥ),
one should then, in the order starting from the east, [place] "oṃ, obeisance to Vāmā," and likewise to Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Kālī.

Having installed the pedestal powers (pīṭhaśakti) as follows— *kalavikariṇyai*, *balapramathinyai*, *sarvabhūtadamanyai*, and in the center, *oṃ manonmanyai*— one should then install the pedestal mantra (*pīṭhamanu*).
Here, the pedestal mantra is:
Aghore Aiṃ Ghore Hrīṃ, to all those who are more terrible than the most terrible in every respect, Obeisance to those whose forms are Rudra! Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.
And likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:
After "Aghore" comes Vāgbhava; in "Ghore," however, is Bhuvaneśvarī;
[then] "Sarvataḥ sarvasarvebhyaḥ"; in "Ghora-ghoratare" is Ramā; one should write the three seed-syllables of the Goddess: "Namo 'stu rudra-rūpebhyaḥ."
And this vidyā, O beloved, has been declared with thirty-three syllables.
Then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer and so forth:
on the head, "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the Seer";
in the mouth, "Salutation to Paṅkti, the Metre."
In the heart, salutation to the deity Rudrabhairavī. || 92 ||
Then follow the ritual placements on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): having first uttered the seed-syllable, "Salutation to both thumbs" (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*).
Having uttered the second seed-syllable, "Svāhā to both index fingers" (*tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*).
Having uttered the third seed-syllable, [one offers] *vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers;
again, having uttered the first seed-syllable, *huṃ* with the two ring fingers;
and having uttered the second seed-syllable, *vauṣaṭ* with the two little fingers.
Having uttered the third seed-syllable, [one says] "phaṭ" with both palms and backs of the hands;
likewise for the heart and other limbs. 93.
Then the meditation:
[One should visualize her] possessing the splendor of a thousand rising suns, with the moon as her crest-jewel, three-eyed,
beautiful with various ornaments, and the destroyer of all enemies.
[One should meditate on] the Goddess, who is adorned with a garland of blood-dripping severed heads and clad in red garments,
[holding] in sequence a trident, a hand-drum, a sword, a shield,
a Pināka bow, arrows, and a pair consisting of a noose and a goad.
And a book and a rosary, seated upon the throne of Śiva.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings as before, one should perform the installation of the conch. || 94 ||
Then, having performed the worship of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) as described in the *Caitanyabhairavī*,

and having worshipped the seat with the seat-mantra mentioned in this mantra-text, one should meditate again and perform the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*).
One should begin the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā).
For example:
having first uttered the seed-syllable in the southeast corner, [one says] "homage to the heart" (hṛdayāya namaḥ).
Having uttered the second seed-syllable in the northeast, [one says] "to the head, svāhā.
Having uttered the third seed-syllable in the southwest, [one says] "to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ.
Again, having uttered the first seed-syllable in the northwest, [one says] "to the armor, hūm."
Then, having again uttered the second seed-syllable in the center, [one says] "vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
Then, having again uttered the third seed-syllable in the four directions, [one says] "phaṭ to the weapon" (astra).
Thereafter, having worshipped Ratnajā and the others within the triangle, one worships Anaṅgakusumā and the others at the base of the petals.
One should worship.

Having worshipped Asitāṅga, Brāhmī, and the others in the petals starting from the east, one should worship Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons, within the house of the earth.
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings. || 95 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"The knower of mantras, the best among those who know mantras, having worshipped [the deity] one hundred thousand times, [should recite] the mantra."
Because of this statement. || 96 ||
Then Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī said with waves of wisdom:
"O Goddess of the Gods, [the mantra] begins with *hasa* and the first *vāgbhava*, and ends with *hasaka*."
The seed-syllable *bhūḥ* is the first; *Bhuvaneśānī* is extracted as the second seed-syllable.
O Maheśānī, Śiva and Candra are Bhuvaneśa and Bhairavī.
And likewise, in the Tripurārṇava:
"The three Haṃsas are mounted upon the dental *sa*, differentiated by the vowels of the Vasus (8), the oceans (4), and the Paṅkti (5)."
The first [syllable] has a bindu, the last has a visarga, and the middle one is joined with Virañci, Indra, Hara, and Agni.
Its meaning is as follows:
"Śiva, Candra, and Vāgbhava" constitutes the first seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The second seed-syllable is Śivacandrakāmapṛthivīmahāmāyā.
The third seed-syllable is Śivacandra, which is the fourteenth vowel (au) with the visarga (ḥ).
The worship diagram (pūjāyantra) for this goddess should be understood to be like that of Caitanyabhairavī. || 97 ||

As for the worship: having performed the rites from the morning duties up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and having performed the placement of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa) as stated in the Caitanyabhairava, one should perform the placement of the seers and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
For example:
"On the head, salutation to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
on the mouth, salutation to the Paṅkti metre."
Salutation to the deity Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī in the heart. || 98 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs.
Thus it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs of the mantra using the middle [syllable] accompanied by the six long vowels."
With that middle seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels, one performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs.
As follows:
*Hsklhrāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*.
In this manner, one should perform the placement [of mantras] with "Hsklhrīṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers," and so forth;
likewise for the heart and other limbs. || 99 ||
Then comes the meditation:
[one should visualize her] resembling the javā flower, like the pomegranate blossom,
possessing a crescent moon and a mass of matted hair, three-eyed, and clad in red garments.
I take refuge in the auspicious Goddess, who is beautiful without ornaments, possessing full and high, firm breasts, and holding the noose, goad, boon-granting gesture, and fear-dispelling gesture.
Everything else should be performed as in the case of Caitanyabhairavī. || 100 ||
Another distinction of Bhuvaneśī and another distinction of Bhuvaneśī from Bhairavī are now described:
O Goddess, she who begins with the letter *sa* is indeed that very one; at that time, she is Sakaleśvarī.
All [practices] such as meditation and worship for this [deity] are as before.
If she is Sahādyā, the Sovereign of All, then meditation, worship, and so forth are as before. (1)
Now, the mantra of Tripurābālā is given in the Śāradā-tantra:
"The first [syllable] is the lower lip (va) with the bindu; [the second is] that which resides in Brahmā and Indra (la), joined with the moon (u)."
The second [manu] is said to be Manu, enriched by the creation of Bhṛgu; the third is proclaimed as Tārtīya. This [power] is renowned as Bālā, the subduer of the three worlds.
Its meaning is as follows:
The Vāgbhava, the Kāmabīja, and the Candrabīja, together with the Visarga and joined with the fourteenth vowel. || 2 ||
Her worship and so forth are like those of Tripurābhairavī, because it has been stated in the Śāradā-tantra;
however, a specific distinction is mentioned in the Jñānārṇava.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) and other such rites should be performed with this very seed-syllable alone;
as it is said:
"O Goddess, one should perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence by repeating [the mantra] twice. (3)
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of reciting [the mantra] three hundred thousand times.
And so it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: "One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables; the fire-oblation (*havana*) should be one-tenth of that."

One should likewise perform the libation (tarpaṇa), and thus one shall become a partaker of all good fortune; for other [mantras], there is a hundred-thousand-fold recitation (lakṣajapa), as stated in the Śrīvidyā [tradition]. || 4 ||
Another mantra from the Jñānārṇava: Having uttered the sound of the Sun (Ra), which consists of the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.

Ending in a vowel, situated on the earth (la), and endowed with the fourth vowel (au); pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and kalā; followed by the imperishable Bhṛgu (m) along with the vowel of Śakra (e)—this is considered the three-syllabled Vidyā.
The *bindu* is imperishable (*avyaya*).
It is likewise stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"This [vowel] ends with the *visarga* and the *bindu*, and is said to consist of seven [parts]. (5)
This is because this knowledge (*vidyā*) is introduced in the *Sārasamuccaya* and other works for the purpose of awakening from the curse.
For example:
"I have thus declared this origin of the root of the *vidyā*; it should always be known by those who desire accomplishment (*siddhi*)."
"By whomsoever this primordial Vidyā was cursed by the Goddess in the past, by him it shall become lifeless.
Thus [ends verse] 6.
Also in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"O devoted wife, this Vidyā which was cursed by you as a maiden has now been rendered void by the first [syllable] and paralyzed by the middle one."
However, because it is corrupted by the final [syllable], that vidyā does not succeed.

Nor should it be argued that the vidyā mentioned in the Śāradā[tantra] would likewise be cursed; for that [vidyā] is subject to cursing only when it is composed of the *bindu* as described in the Jñānārṇava. || 7 ||
Regarding the removal of the curse, the Muṇḍamālā Tantra states:
"The Vidyā was installed by me solely in the form of Śiva and solely in the form of Śakti."
Therefore, the letters *ha* and *sa* are [present] in the *vāgbhava*, the *kāmarāja*, and the third seed-syllable;
for it is seen thus in the *Sārasamuccaya* which is about to be described. (8)
In the *Tripurāsāra* as well: "For this very reason, Śambhu deposited the seed-syllable of Śiva-Śakti above those two preceding seed-syllables;
his own *kula* above the other, and the Fire (the letter Ra) in the middle and below from that point onward."
That became Arjitā;
after the middle seed-syllable, in the middle-lower [position]. || 9 ||
In the Rudrayāmala it is also said:
"O Goddess, the first is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmabīja, and the third is Śaktibīja, which should always be conjoined with Śiva. (10)
This is declared to be the Bālā [Vidyā], which is free from all defects.
One should place the initial seed-syllable in the middle and the middle syllable at the beginning;
he who thus recites the mantra shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds.
One should place the final [syllable] of the sādhya in the middle, and the middle one at the beginning.
Having done this, one should recite the mantra and obtain all accomplishments. || 11 ||
Another mantra from the Śrīkrama:
one should recite the Vāgbhava seed-syllable ending with the letter *ī*, which is the seed-syllable of Kledinī.
One should recite the Śakti joined with the vowel *au*, followed by the Visarga beneath it;
this seed-syllable (*bīja*), surmounted by the Bindu, Nāda, and Śikhā, is most difficult to obtain. 12.
O Goddess, these three seed-syllables—*sauḥ*, *klīṃ*, and thereafter [the third]—this is the five-syllabled Vidyā said to be difficult to obtain on earth. (13)
Another mantra is given in that very same place:

"O Goddess, the wise one should recite the three seed-syllables of Bālā preceded by *haṃsa*, or ending with *haṃsa*, O highly fortunate lady, for the purification of defects such as sleep and the like. (14)
In this very place:
O Great Goddess, the seed-syllable of the noose consists of the Śakti and Śiva [syllables] together with Fire,
joined with the twelfth vowel, and adorned with Nāda and Bindu.
I shall proclaim the Kāmarāja mantra: the syllable *hrīṃ*, which consists of Śakti and Śiva;
followed by *mādana* (the letter *ma*), the seed-syllable of Indra (*la*), and the left eye of Fire (*ra*) endowed with a bindu (*ṃ*).

O Great Goddess, the Śaktikūṭa is the syllable *kroṃ*, which possesses both Śakti and Śiva; it is joined with the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*) and endowed with the Nāda, Bindu, and Sarga. O Ambikā, listen now to the sixteen-syllabled Vidyā consisting of fourteen letters.
After that, the Haṃsa-bīja and the Ṣoḍaśī have been described by me. || 15 ||
Now, regarding the nine-peaked *bālā*:
in that very place it is said, "O Goddess, the three seed-syllables of *bālā* constitute the three peaks; this is the nine-syllabled [mantra]."
O Goddess, the three peaks of Vyomaka constitute the nine-peaked Bhairavī.
Another mantra in the Śrīkrama is as follows:
"O Goddess, Śiva and Śakti, together with the Seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja) endowed with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā, are declared to be Vāgbhava. O Dear One, now hear Kāmarāja."

The peak syllable (kūṭa), exceedingly difficult to attain, is endowed with Śiva, Śakti, Mādana, Indra, Vahni, and Māyā, and is pervaded by Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā. Śiva and Candra, ending with Satya, are joined with Sarga, Bindu, and Kalā.
This nine-syllabled Bālā is free from all defects.
Its meaning is as follows:
Śiva, Candra, and Vāgbhava constitute the first [part].
The second [syllable] is joined with Śiva (H), the moon (A), Kāma (I), earth (L), fire (R), the fourth vowel (Ī), and the bindu;
the third is joined with Śiva (H), the moon (A), the fourteenth vowel (AU), the bindu, and the visarga. || 17 ||
Another [tradition] begins with Candra;
and so it is stated in the Tripurāsāra:
"If the Bhairavīya [system] taught by the teachers begins with Akula, it should begin with Kula."
That very [vidyā] which bestows swift results on earth is called a *vidyā*, yet it must be kept strictly secret from the ranks of the uninitiated (*paśu*).
Another mantra is found in the *Tripurāsāra*:
The eighth [syllable] of Śiva alone is the first seed-syllable; the eighth seed-syllable of Bhaga is the other.
The supreme Śiva at the end—these three syllables counted together constitute the Saṅketavidyā, which is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
The meaning of this is as follows:

The *bālā* [mantra] is of three kinds: ending with the *bindu*, ending with the *bindu* and *visarga*, and ending with the *visarga*. Here, he extracts the one ending with the *bindu*: "the eighth from Śiva" is the vowel *ai*; "the eighth from Śiva called Sammohana" [is the same].

Śiva is the letter *ū*; its eighth is *ai*. [The term] "only the dot" (*kevalaṃ binduḥ*) refers to the *anusvāra*, based on the etymology: "what rolls (*valate*) upon the head (*ka*). That which is joined with this is [the seed-syllable], because it belongs to the *arśa-ādi* class [of words ending in the suffix *matup*]. By this, the first seed-syllable is the *Vāgbhava* seed.
*Bhaga* is the letter *e*; its eighth preceding seed-syllable is *i*, which is the second.

Thus, having placed [the first] on the head, the third seed-syllable is *au*, which follows *o* at the end of that; this alone constitutes the triad of seed-syllables distinguished by the *bindu* and *nāda*.
Another mantra is given in that same place: Śakti, Śiva, and the seed-syllable of Fire (Ra) with the twelve vowels and the bindu;
Śakti, Maheśa, Kāma, Indra, Fire, Moon, and Māyā.
Śakti, Śiva, Vahni, the vowel *u*, and the visarga—this seed-syllable (bīja), joined with Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā, is thus proclaimed. 20.
The procedures for these [deities], such as the mechanical diagrams (yantra), meditation, and worship, are like those of Bhairavī.
As for the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa), it consists of one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa), since that is how it is seen in the Śrīkrama and other texts. || 21 ||
The illuminating vidyā for these [mantras] is found in the Śrīkrama:
"O Maheśānī, [the syllable] 'vada' twice, followed by 'vāgvādini'. This is the eight-syllabled vidyā; one should employ it at the beginning of the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable]. (22)
"O Goddess of gods, [you who are] moist and dripping, grant me then great liberation!
Having uttered Kāmarāja, the Praṇava follows immediately thereafter."
Afterward, perform the Mahāmokṣa and likewise utter the Śaktikūṭa;
one should recite it first and then recite it again seven times in succession.

Now follows Annapūrṇā-Bhairavī: the Tāra (Om), Bhuvaneśānī (Hrīm), the Śrī-bīja (Śrīm), and the Kāma-bīja (Klīm); then the word "Māheśvari" following "O Bhagavatī" at the end of the heart-mantra (Hrīm).
The pair of syllables "annapūrṇe" constitutes this twenty-syllable vidyā.
And so it is said in the Kalpa:
"O Goddess, when the seed-syllable of desire is absent and preceded by the Śrī-bīja, this nineteen-syllabled mantra, O Goddess, bestows an abundance of wealth and grain. (25)
The procedure for her worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the *pīṭhanyāsa* as described in the general manual of worship, one should place [the mantras] in the filaments starting from the east: *oṃ vāmāyai namaḥ*, and likewise *jyeṣṭhāyai* and *raudryai*.
To Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī; in the center, to Manonmanī.
Near her: Oṃ, to Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityā, Vilāsinī.
One should worship Dogdhrī in the northeast, Aghorā in the southeast, and Maṅgalā in the center; everywhere, one should worship with the mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Above that, [one offers] *hsauḥ sadāśivamahāpretapadmāsanāya namaḥ*. (26)
Then follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer and so forth:
*namaḥ* to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; *namaḥ* to the *paṅkti* metre (*chandas*), on the mouth;
*namaḥ* to the deity Annapūrṇeśvarī Bhairavī, on the heart; and *namaḥ* to the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, on the private parts.
*Namaḥ* at the feet; *śrīṃ śaktaye namaḥ*; on all limbs, *klīṃ kīlakāya namaḥ*.
And likewise, in the *Jñānārṇava*:
The seed-syllable (bīja) is Bhuvaneśānī, the Śrī-bīja is said to be the Power (śakti), and the Kīlaka is the Kāma-bīja; such is the beginning [of the procedure]. || 27 ||
Then follow the ritual placements (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs:
"hrāṃ to the two thumbs, salutation," and so forth; likewise for the heart and other parts with "hrāṃ to the heart, salutation," and so forth.
And likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Maheśānī, [one should perform] the six limbs of Bhuvaneśī with [the seed-syllable] conjoined with the six long vowels," and so forth. (28)
Then follows the placement of the steps: on the head, *oṃ namaḥ*;
on the eyes, *hrīṃ namaḥ* and *śrīṃ namaḥ*.
At the two ears: *klīṃ* obeisance, obeisance, obeisance.
At the two nostrils: obeisance to the Blessed One, obeisance to Māheśvarī.
At the mouth: obeisance to Annapūrṇā.
*Guhye svāhā namaḥ*. Again, perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the secret place up to the crown of the head.
As stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
One, one again, and one; then one more, and then two;
four, four, and likewise two—O Pārvatī, O Goddess of the Gods, one should place these syllables upon the nine gates.
One should place the nine steps, beginning with the secret place (guhya) and ending at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Then, having placed the four seed-syllables in the *brahmarandhra*, the mouth, the heart, and the *mūlādhāra*,
one should place the remaining syllables— ending everywhere with "namas"— in the five locations of the space between the eyebrows, the nose, the throat, the navel, and the *liṅga*.

It is said in that very same place: "Having placed the four seed-syllables in sequence in the *brahmarandhra*, the mouth, the heart, and the *mūlādhāra*, one should place the others in the remaining [locations]."

O Goddess, one should place the [syllables] beginning with *namaḥ* in the five locations— the middle of the eyebrows, the nose, the throat, the navel, and the genitals— in the same sequence as before. Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*).
Namely:
possessing a radiance like the color of molten gold, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
her crown blazing with the luster of nine jewels, and reddish-brown like saffron.
She is clothed in variegated garments, possesses fish-like eyes, and has three eyes;
her full and elevated breasts have the form of golden jars.
He is white as the luster of cow’s milk, five-faced, and has three eyes.
Having seen Śambhu with a serene countenance, adorned by his blue throat, possessing matted locks,
decorated with shimmering serpents, resembling a kunda flower,
dancing incessantly and full of joy, [one attains] the supreme state consisting of bliss.
Having thus meditated upon her— whose face is joyful and whose eyes are tremulous, whose hips are adorned with a girdle,
who is eternally devoted to the giving of food, and who is embellished by the goddesses Earth and Fortune—
and having worshipped her mentally, one should perform the ritual installation of the conch.
The yantra for its worship:
one should draw a triangle, then a four-petaled lotus, followed by an eight-petaled lotus, then a sixteen-petaled lotus, and finally the earth-circle with four gates. (Figure 31)

Then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*), having meditated again, and having performed the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*), one should begin the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
In the pericarp (*karṇikā*), in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, as well as in the cardinal points, [one should worship] with *hrāṃ* for the heart.
One should worship with "namaḥ" and so forth. Then, at the front of the triangle, one should worship Śiva with: "Oṃ hauṃ namaḥ śivāya namaḥ.
In the northwest corner [of the triangle], [one should worship] with: "Oṃ namo bhagavate varāharūpāya bhurbhūvaḥsvaḥpataye."
"Grant me the status of a sovereign; cause [the Lord] to grant it, svāhā!
With this mantra, one should worship Varāha.
Thus it is stated in the Jñānārṇava.
Having first uttered the word *oṃ namaḥ*, then the word *bhagavate*,

then [the word] *varāharūpāya*, and likewise *bhūrbhūvaḥsvaḥpataye* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), one should say: "Grant me the state of being a lord of the earth (*bhūpatitvam*) and cause it to be given."
O fair-faced one, the mantra of Varāha is conjoined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-syllable *svāhā*).
In the southern corner, one should worship Nārāyaṇa with the mantra: *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*.
Then, to the south and north, [one should worship] with: *oṃ glauṃ śrīṃ annaṃ me dehi annādhipataye*.
One should worship Bhūmi and Śrī with the mantra "mamānnaṃ pradāpaya svāhā śrīṃ glauṃ.
Then, on the four petals, beginning from the front, one should worship with "oṃ paravidyāyai namaḥ hrīṃ."
Salutation to Bhuvaneśvarī, Śrīṃ; salutation to Kamalā, Klīṃ; salutation to Subhagā.
And likewise, in the Jñānārṇava:

O auspicious lady, one should worship Paravidyā with the syllable *Tāra* (Om), Bhuvaneśī with its own essence (*tadātmanā*), Kamalā with *Ramā*, and Subhagā with *Kāma*. On the eight petals, starting from the west, one should worship the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī.
In the sixteen petals, starting from the east: *naṃ* to Amṛtā Annapūrṇā, *moṃ* to Madanā Annapūrṇā, likewise *bhaṃ* to Tuṣṭi, *gaṃ* to Puṣṭi,
*vaṃ* to Prīti, *tiṃ* to Rati, *māṃ* to Hrī (*Kriyā*), *heṃ* to Śrī, *śvaṃ*...

One should worship these [deities] ending with the word *annapūrṇā* and ending with *namaḥ*: *riṃ* for Sudhā, *aṃ* for Rātri, *nnaṃ* for Jyotsnā, *pūṃ* for Haimavatī, *irṇe* for Chāyā, *svāṃ* for Paurṇamāsī, and *hāṃ* for Amāvasyā.
And so it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"The remaining syllables should be worshipped as those designated by the term 'Annapūrṇā' at the end;
thereafter, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the square."
In that very place:
one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in sequence within the square;
then, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense and so forth up to the dismissal. || 33ka ||
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"Having meditated in this manner, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind."
Immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations of food mixed with clarified butter, numbering one-tenth of that [total].
Thus end the Bhairavī mantras.
Now follow the Śrīvidyā mantras; therein is Meru.
Jñāna, Arṇava, Bhūmi, Candra, Śiva, Māyā, Śakti, Kṛṣṇa, Adhvamādana,
Ardha-candra, and Bindu— these nine syllables are said to be Meru.
The mantras of Mahātripurasundarī originate from Meru. || 35 ||
"Sakalā" is Bhuvaneśānī; the seed-syllable of Kāmeśī has been extracted.
By means of this, O fair-faced one, I shall declare all the Vidyās.
This fourth letter is at the end of Śakti, situated in the middle of "kala," O beautiful-eyed one.
The Vāgbhava [syllable], enriched with five colors, is then called Kāmarāja.
O fish-eyed one, O auspicious lady, this six-syllabled Kāmarāja mantra, enriched by Śiva and the Moon, is a means of intoxication that deludes all.
O lady of excellent hips, the seed-syllable of Śakti, preceded by the Moon (the letter *u*), is the deluder of all;
it consists of four syllables, while Tripurā consists of three syllables.
O Goddess of the gods, by worshipping this [Vidyā], Kāma becomes beautiful in all his limbs;
O Goddess, he becomes Kāmarāja. This Vidyā is the very form of Brahman.
The meaning of this is as follows:
*śakti* is the letter *e*; *tūrya* is the letter *ī*. Thus, the *vāgbhava-kūṭa* consists of the letters *ka*, *e*, *ī*, *la*, and *mahāmāyā*. || 36 ||

Śiva is the letter *ha*, and the Moon is the letter *sa*; therefore, *ha-sa-ka-ha-la-mahāmāyā* constitutes the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa*. The Moon is the letter *sa*; therefore, *sa-ka-la-mahāmāyā* [constitutes the *Śakti-kūṭa*].
The Śakti-kūṭa. Thus, by means of these three kūṭas, this is the Kāmarāja-vidyā. || 36ka ||
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme [mantra] named Lopāmudrā;
it is the Śakti and the fourth [digit] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, O beautiful one."
Having abandoned [the previous state], Lopāmudrā, enriched by Śiva and the Moon at the beginning, is revealed.

The meaning of this is as follows: having removed the letters *e* and *ī* from the *vāgbhava* [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, one should place the letter *ha* and the letter *sa* at the beginning.
The rest is the same; this [mantra] was worshipped by Agastya.
We shall explain the difference between these two later. || 37 ||
Another mantra:
O fair-faced one, I shall explain the extraction of the Vidyā of the one known as Kāmarāja, situated between Śakti and Mādana, by means of the Vāgbhava syllable.
The first part, Vāgbhava, should begin with Śiva; the second, Kāmarāja, should begin with Śivā; and the third, Vidya, should begin with Candra. This is the Vidyā worshipped by Manu.
Its meaning is as follows:
Then *kāma* (the letter *ka*), then *śiva* (the letter *ha*), then the letter *e*, and then the triad beginning with the letter *ī*—this constitutes the *vāgbhava* peak (*kūṭa*).
The middle peak begins with *śiva* (the letter *ha*), and the third peak begins with *candra* (the letter *sa*).
And so it is stated in the *Candrapīṭha*:
*Ka-śi-vau*, *bhaga-tūrye*, and *kṣamā-māya* constitute the Vāgbhava-kūṭa; *śiva-kāmau*, *bhagaṃ*, and *tūryaṃ* with the letter *la* constitute the Śakti-kūṭa.
This [mantra], when combined, is honored by all the Āmnāyas. (38)

O Goddess, this Vidyā, worshipped by Candra, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it consists of the syllable *Vāgbhava* preceded by the Moon (*A*), with *Śiva* (*Ha*) in the middle, and the *Mādana* (*Ka*) and *Śakti-bīja* (*Hrīṃ*) in the *Kāmarāja*, followed by the Face (*Aiṃ*).
The meaning of this is: the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable of this [mantra] is the *vāgbhava* of the *Kāmarāja-vidyā*, which begins with the letters *sa* and *ha*.

First the letter *sa*, then the letter *ha*, then *mādana* (the letter *ka*), then *śiva* (the letter *i*), then the letter *e*, then the letter *ī*, then the letter *la*, and then *mahāmāyā* (the letter *ī*); this is the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*.
The *vāgbhava-kūṭa* of this [vidyā] is itself the *śakti-kūṭa*; this is the vidyā worshipped by Candra. (39)
The first [syllable] is *hasa* (ha-sa), preceded by *śiva* (the letter *ha*) and situated in the middle with *saha* (sa-ha).
The second is *mādana* (ma) within the *kāmarāja*. Now hear the third, O Pārvatī: it is the *śakti-bīja* (ai) preceded by *hasa* (ha-sa), worshipped by Kuvera.
The meaning of this is as follows: if the Vāgbhava [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja is preceded by *hasa*, then that is its Vāgbhava.
Then Śiva and Candra, then Kāma, then Śiva, then the letter E, then the letter Ī, then the letter L, and then Mahāmāyā—this is the Kāmarāja-kūṭa.
Its Śakti-kūṭa is indeed the Vāgbhava-kūṭa; she is the one worshipped by Kubera. || 40 ||
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the third [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, together with the first [syllable], constitutes the Śakti-bīja; this is the Vidyā honored by Agastya.
Its meaning is as follows:
Whatever is the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, that very same is the Kāmarāja peak-syllable here as well;
the Śakti peak-syllable, however, begins with "sa," such is the remainder [of the statement].
But this second one is Lopāmudrā. || 41 ||
In the *Vāgbhava* [syllable] of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, abandon the *mādana*.
Having joined the moon (*candra*) in that very place, and thereafter in the *Kāmarāja*, having removed the moon from the mouth, one should place it there; this is the Vidyā worshipped by Nandin.
The meaning of this is as follows:
in the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, one should omit "Kāma" from the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] and substitute "Candra";
furthermore, in the Kāmarāja [portion], one should omit "Candra" at the end of "Śiva" and place "Candra" at the beginning.
One should perform [the rite]. The rest is the same. || 42 ||
O Goddess, having removed the third vowel from the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja,
place it below the moon within the seed-syllable of Śakti;
by that means, the peak-syllable (kūṭa) of Śakti consists of the moon, the Indra-vowel, Kāma, and Mahāmāyā.
This is the Vidyā worshipped by Indra;
the rest is the same. 43.
O Maheśvarī, in the second vidyā known as Lopāmudrā,
one should place that very same [seed-syllable] at the beginning of the Kāmarāja [part], omitting Bhṛgu;
the fourth [syllable] is without Śiva, while in the third [part], Śiva is complete.
And in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā: "Between the first *sa* and the last *sa*, what is that which is worshipped by the Sun?
The meaning of this is as follows:
In the second Lopaāmudrā, having removed the letter *sa* from below the letter *ha* in the *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, one should place that [letter *ha*] at the beginning and discard the second *ha*.
In the third *kūṭa*, one should place the letter *ka* above the final letter *sa*.
