This knowledge is honored by the Sun. || 45 ||
O beautiful goddess, having written Lopāmudrā as the second [syllable],
and having written that same one again situated in the fourth and fifth positions,
one should utter them by leaving out Bhuvaneśānī and pronouncing them as a single unit.
The great vidyā of four peaks was worshipped by Śaṅkara.
Its meaning is as follows:
having written the second [syllable], Lopāmudrā, and having written that very same one again, [one proceeds].
Having set aside Bhuvaneśī who resides in the fourth and fifth peaks, one should utter [the mantra] in a single recitation;
as for that recitation, having first uttered the three peaks, [one says]: *kāmaikāratūryendra śambhu*.
One should utter Śaśāṅka, Kandarpa, Śivendra, Candra, Śivacandra, Kandarpendra, and Mahāmāyā. (46)
O Goddess, one should then write Lopāmudrā again;
and the Nandikeśvara-vidyā shall be the Vaiṣṇavī consisting of six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭā).
The meaning of this is as follows:
Furthermore, by the force of the word "again" (punaḥ), the meaning is that the second [line] is for Lopāmudrā;
the author of the *Tantrakaumudī* says this is because of the context (*prakrama*).
However, in reality, having written Agastya’s two-fold vidyā, it is said to be "worshipped by Nandin."
From the words of Dakṣiṇāmūrti:
"O Varānanā, O Bhuvaneśānī, O Maheśvarī, divide into two parts that Vidyā known as Kāmarāja which resides within its three peaks."
Devoid of the *bindu* and devoid of the *nāda*, it becomes that which was worshipped by Durvāsas. || 47 ||
And in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti*:
"In the place of Māyā, one should write the pair of syllables 'ha' and 'ri' in sequence.
The meaning of this is as follows:
One should utter [the mantra] by dividing Trikūṭasthabhuvaneśvarī into two parts and removing the *nāda* and *bindu*.
Thus are the twelve divisions.
Regarding the fifteenth seed-syllable among the seeds, the *Navaratneśvarī* states: "O Goddess, [the sequence] is with Māyā (hrīṃ), Śrī (śrīṃ), and Madana (klīṃ); likewise with Śrī, Māyā, and Madana;
Madana with Māyā and Śrī; and Śrī with Madana and Māyā."

O Supreme Goddess, Madana has been declared as Māyā, and Śrī is said to be Tripurā, who is of the nature of the seed-syllables and is proclaimed as the destroyer of death. Thus ends the fifteenth [verse]. 48.
Now, regarding the technical [definition] of the sixteenth [digit] in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The end of the moon and the end of the sun, together with Indra and the others, separately."

O Goddess, who are the manifest embodiment of Brahman, one should join [the mantra] at the beginning of the Vidyā with the left eye, enriched by the Bindu and Nāda, consisting of the digits (kalās) of the Universal Mother.
All the *bhedas* with three peaks (*trikūṭāḥ*) indeed become five-peaked (*pañcakūṭāḥ*).
The *Vaiṣṇavī* should have eight peaks (*vasukūṭā*), and the *Śāṅkarī* should be six-peaked (*ṣaṭkūṭā*).
The meaning of this is as follows:
The letter *ha* is the end of *candra*; the letter *śa* is the end of *varuṇa*; the letter *ra* is at the beginning of *śakra*;
and the letter *ī* is the left eye.
"At the beginning of the Vidyā" refers to the beginning of the twelve Vidyās previously mentioned. || 49 ||
O Goddess, when you are adorned with the beginning of the Vedas and consist of the power of Śiva,
all her divisions are six-peaked, O Supreme Lady;
Vaiṣṇavī is nine-peaked, while Śāṅkarī is seven-peaked.
The meaning of this is as follows:
it consists of Śiva and Śakti and possesses the two previously mentioned seed-syllables (bījas); it is "headed by the Vedas," meaning the Praṇava (Om) is adorned at its beginning. || 50 ||
Now, O beloved, the three divisions of the Great Sixteen have been told; listen to the Mahāvidyā.
O auspicious one, the first two seed-syllables are indeed in reverse order.
O Supreme Goddess, having uttered [the first seed-syllable], one should then extract the others;
O Lady of Excellent Limbs, the Virgin Tripureśvarī is inward-facing.
One should worship her encased within these five seed-syllables.
O Supreme Goddess, this sixteen-syllable vidyā consists of six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭā).
Indeed, O Auspicious One, all [the other] three-peaked [vidyās] consist of sixteen syllables;
the Vaiṣṇavī has nineteen syllables, and the Śaivī has seventeen syllables.

The meaning of this is as follows: the first two seed-syllables consist of Māyā and Ramā; their reversed order means that Ramā comes first and Māyā afterwards, while the Kāma-bīja is situated in the middle, at the beginning, in the mouth.
Of whichever maiden [this applies]:
by means of these five seed-syllables, the [mantra] consisting of six peaks, seven peaks,
or nine peaks is "sampuṭitā," meaning it is made like a casket (sampuṭavat).
Therefore, the meaning is that it is encapsulated by both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order.
Some, however, say it is encapsulated only in direct order; that is not correct, because it contradicts all the tantras. || 51 ||
And likewise, in the Yoginītantra:
"The seed-syllable of Śrī, Māyā, Smara, Yoni-Śakti, Tāra, Māyā, Kamalā, and then Vidyā;
with the seed-syllables beginning with Śakti in reverse order, this is that Śrīṣoḍaśī, as proclaimed by Śiva. (52)
And so it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: Śrī, Māyā, Madana, Vāṇī, Parā, Tāra, Śivapriyā,
Haripriyā, Trikūṭā, that supreme Vāṇī, and Manobhava.
Māyā, Lakṣmī, Mahāvidyā, Śrīvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Parā;
and in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti [mantra], the wise one should write the second pair of vowels in reverse order.
Having turned the child inward, one should then draw [the syllables].
One should write the *tāra* (oṃ), then *māyā* (hrīṃ), then *lakṣmī* (śrīṃ), and likewise the three *kūṭas*. O Supreme Goddess, one should enclose the one called *ramā* with the *kalā*.
"By *kalā*" means by the five *kalās*, beginning with *Śakti*, mentioned previously.
"Named *Ramā*" refers to that which consists of the six *kūṭas* beginning with the *praṇava*, as mentioned before. Even if the reading were "named *Umā*," the meaning would be the same. || 54 ||
However, some who read "bālayā" instead of "kalayā" in that place state that the Supreme Goddess (parameśvarī) is encapsulated by the "bālayā" mantra, which is inward-facing;
they say [the sequence] is "ramā" (śrīṃ), "Supreme Goddess" (parameśvarī), and "hrīṃ."
Therefore, some say that on the northern petal one should utter "klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ," but that is not correct,
because they do not understand the meaning of the term *sampuṭa* (encasement).
In the *Navaratneśvara*:

"One should first utter the mantra, then immediately the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and again the mantra at the end in reverse order; that is known as the 'encased' (*sampuṭa*) [mantra]."
Thus, because it would result in the fallacy of non-sequential connection (*ananvaya*) due to the definition of the *saṃpuṭa* [arrangement], and because it contradicts all the tantras. || 56 ||
And so it is stated in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*:
"Place Śrī, Māyā, Madana, and Vāṇī at the beginning;
place the source of the Vedas, Bhuvaneśānī, and the three-peaked Śrībīja."
One should enclose the six peaks with the first five syllables.
And in the Māyātantra:
"Lakṣmī, Parā, joined with Madana and Yoni, Śakti, Tāra, Parā, and Kamalā."
The root-vidyā;
and the venerable King of Mantras of the Supreme Deity is proclaimed as being taught in a manner reversed from that of Śakti and the others.
By this, the view that [the mantra] is encapsulated by the five seed-syllables in direct order (anuloma) should be rejected. || 57 ||
In the Śruti, however, it is said: "Ramā, Māyā, Tāra, Parā, Lakṣmī, Kumārikā, Vidyā, Vyastā, Bālā, Śrī, and Parā."

The meaning of "vyasta" (separated) is that it is dispersed or inverted; thus, "kumārī" (the maiden) should be understood here as being inward-turned (*antarmukhī*). Following the maiden, there is a connection with the three seed-syllables beginning with *Tārā*, by virtue of the internal consistency of the Tantra and the authority of the *Traipurī* scripture.
And thus:
*Śrī*, *Māyā*, *Madhya*, *Ādi*, and *Bālikā*; followed by *Tāra*, *Māyā*, *Śrīvidyā*, and the five seeds beginning with *Parā* at the end. || 58 ||
Regarding the reading "and Śrīparā," it does not mean that only Bālā is divided [into parts] as Śrīparā;
rather, it is a statement of the essential nature of the sixteen seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Vidyā,
since there is no mention of them being taught according to a sequential order.
By this [logic], the views that Śrī-Māyā-Tāra, Māyā-Śrī-Bālā, and the three peaks (trikūṭa) are arranged separately as Bālā-Ramā-Māyā are also to be rejected.
In the *Kulāmṛta*: the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Śakti, the seed-syllable of Kāma, and the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava;
the seed-syllable situated at the end of Bālā, and after that, the Praṇava.

O Supreme Goddess, having placed the seed-syllable of Śakti, Ramā, and Vidyā— or Lopāmudrā, Kāmarāja, or the supreme Trikūṭā— and then again, O beautiful one, having placed the five seed-syllables beginning with 'A', [one should proceed].
Having arranged the supreme sixteenfold [mantra] in the reverse order, [one should proceed].
And in the Yāmala: "Lakṣmī, Parā, Madana, Vāgbhava, Śakti-bīja, Tāra, and Bhūti-kamala— these constitute the Mūla-vidyā."
And the three *kūṭas* are applied in reverse order;
these are well-known here in the tradition as the "Glorious Sixteen Syllables.
The three *kūṭas* belong to Bālā and the others, starting with *Ka*.
By the word "and" (ca), one should include Ramā and Māyā as well. || 61 ||
In the Nibandha:

[The mantra consists of] the letter ending in *sa* (śa) joined with the seventh letter preceded by *śiva* (ha), ending with *sūkṣmā* (ḷ) joined with the eighth (ṭha); then the Goddess (ī), the right arm (pha), Indra’s eye (la), and Kāma (ka) marked with *kalā* (anusvāra).

The teeth [are represented by] the letter *ta* facing upwards, joined with the remaining tooth [the letter *tha*], and the living soul (*jīva*) is endowed with the mouth [the letter *u*]. Thus, the fivefold seed-syllable is proclaimed as the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims.
One should then utter the syllable *ra*, which begins with the object of knowledge (*vedya*), possesses the three qualities (*triguṇā*), and is served by Kāma; then again, Lopāmudrā.
Then, by means of the fivefold [mantras] in reverse order,
this Śrī, who is higher than the highest, bestows the accomplishment of all aims; she is the most essential of the essential,
the supreme source of the origin of the entire world.
She is of the nature of Brahman, consisting of all qualities yet devoid of qualities, free from phenomenal expansion;
she is the direct cow of plenty, whose form is bliss found by the hosts of gods and demons.
The meaning of this is as follows:
*sānta* refers to the letter *ṣa*, because it has *sa* as its final (*anta*); *sāntānta* refers to the letter *śa*, because it has that [letter *ṣa*] as its final;
*śiva* refers to the letter *ha*; and its "seventh preceding" is the letter *ra*.
The letter *ī* is the end of the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the nasal dot (*anusvāra*) is its end; by that, the seed-syllable *ramā*.
The Goddess is *māyā*. The right arm is the letter *ka*, Śakra is the letter *la*, and the eye is their union.
Kāma is the bindu; Kalā is Kāmakalā, the letter *ī*; by these, the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) is formed.
The end of the teeth is the letter *ai*; above it is the mouth, and above the mouth is the bindu; by these, the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*) is formed.
The letter *sa* is the individual soul (*jīva*), the letter *au* is the remaining tooth, and the visarga is the mouth; thus, it is the seed-syllable of Parā.
The beginning of the Vedas is the *praṇava*.
Māyā consists of the three qualities (guṇas). || 62 ||
He states another variation in the *Kubjikātantra*: "Parā, Kamalā, Kāma, Vāgbhava, and Śakti;
then Tāra, Śakti, and Kamalā—one should then join these as the three peaks (*trikūṭa*)."
One should install Śakti and the others in reverse order; this is the supreme Mahāṣoḍhī.
O Great Goddess, a yogin or a king may recite this vidyā;
it bestows enjoyment and liberation, and at the end, it grants absolute isolation (kaivalya).
O Bhuvaneśānī, she who begins with *parā* should be known as Bhuvanasundarī;
the Great Vidyā beginning with *kamala* should be known as Kamalāsundarī;
and the Great Vidyā beginning with *kāma* should be understood as Kāmasundarī.
The Great Vidyā beginning with Vāgbhava is considered the supreme Vāksundarī.
The great vidyā beginning with Śakti is to be known as Śaktisundarī;
the great vidyā beginning with Tārā is to be known as Tārasundarī. || 64 ||

The first Vidyā is Ānandasundarī, which is hidden in form; O Goddess of the Gods, it is especially combined with Kāmarāja and Lopāmudrā. By reversing the first four syllables, there arises the Mahāṣoḍaśī mantra.
In the Yoginītantra:
the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Śakti, the seed-syllable of Kāma, and Vāgbhava;
the seed-syllable situated at the end of Bālā, and thereafter the Praṇava.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the seed-syllable of Śakti and Ramā;
or else Lopāmudrā, Kāmarāja, Bhairavī, or Parā.
Having placed these, O beautiful one, one should again place the first five seed-syllables.
When combined in reverse order, these sixteen are difficult to find on earth.
Having recited the mantra of the fourth [syllable] one hundred thousand times, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhīśvara);
the grammatical connection is that this occurs after having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the five seed-syllables in reverse order.
In the Jñānārṇava:
"Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues,
this sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā could never be fully described."
Vaikharī, being of the nature of the expressed object, is incapable of describing its qualities;
since the reality is beyond syllables (*nirakṣara*), Parā alone is the cause therein.
Indeed, those who have become silent perceive through Madhyamā, which exists in the intermediate state.
For she is the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman, bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Goddess of gods, by a single utterance [of her name], one gains the merit of ten million Vājapeya sacrifices,
thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices, and likewise the merit of circumambulating the entire earth.
O Goddess of gods, the pilgrimages to Kāśī and other sacred sites, numbering three and a half crores, do not equal this; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O Girijā, if even a single utterance [of this] is so, how much more so the absolute Brahman?
This sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā must never be revealed.
O auspicious Pārvatī, you must guard this [teaching] as you would your own private parts.
The Sixteenth [Chapter] on the Garland of Seeds,
from the Rudrayāmala: Having written the seed-syllable of Śrī and likewise the Kumārikā.
The seed-syllable of Śrī, Māyā, Kāma, Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā;
then Parā, Kāma, the seed-syllable of Vāk, Māyā, and the seed-syllable of Śrī—
this is the sixteenfold garland of seed-syllables, hidden in all the Tantras.
The kingdom may be given, the head may be given, but the sixteen-fold seed (the bride) must not be given away.
In the *Brahmayāmala*: "First, Lakṣmī and Parā, and likewise Kumārikā;
then the Śrī-bīja, the Parā-bīja, Kāma, and Vāgbhava."
One should write the *parā* and the *śrībālā* in reverse order;
at the end, one should place the *parā* and the *śrī*. Thus, the complete Vidyā, in which the *bālā* is preeminent, has been told to you; it is hidden in all the scriptures. (68)
In another tantra, he states another mantra:
"The first is the power Kuṇḍalinī; from her come the subsequent powers.
O Goddess, one should place the beloved of Govinda between those two."
Then, one should place the seed-syllable of Manmatha, followed by the first [syllable] of Bāla;

then, O Goddess, one should insert the face of the four Vedas into the mouths of Hṛllekhā and Rāma. Thereafter, O Goddess, one should assign Lopāmudrā, who consists of three peaks, or else the supreme [form].
O beautiful one, having first placed the five primordial seed-syllables, this sixteen-fold [vidyā] is indeed well-guarded; yet, O Goddess, out of affection it has been revealed. (69)
O Goddess, her incomparable majesty cannot be described even by hundreds of millions of tongues, let alone by five mouths.
Even one's most beloved—sons, wife, wealth, and so forth—should be given;
a kingdom may be given, even one's head may be given, but the sixteen-syllable mantra must never be given away.

In another way, the *Siddhayāmala* states regarding the sixteenth [syllable]: "O Dear One, at the beginning of all [the mantras] are: Kāma, Māyā, Ramā, Bālā, Trikūṭā, Strī, Bhaga, Aṅkuśa, Kālī, Kāmakalā, Kūrca, and the Praṇava."
This is the venerable Mahāṣoḍhī, who is renowned throughout the three worlds;
she is the knowledge that destroys death through wisdom and is saluted by all the Āmnāyas.
O Dear One, she is described at the beginning of the Saptalakṣa-Mahāvidyātantra and other scriptures.
Whatever sciences there are that have become the essence of essences and are well-guarded—what is the use of saying more here? Among them, the sixteenth is indeed the essence;
it has been revealed, O Great Goddess, as you have asked for it again and again.
In the Rudrayāmala:
"By joining Śiva at the end of the Earth [letter] with the Vāgbhava of Lopāmudrā,
and placing the letter *Sa* at the beginning of the Kāmarāja, there is the sixteen-syllable mantra of Lopāmudrā."
There is no knowledge equal to this within the domain of the ocean of learning.
In that very same [text]:

"The Queen of Vidyās, consisting of sixteen syllables, is auspicious, composed of the unity of Consciousness and Brahman; she resides in the *vāgbhava* [syllable], for she is beautiful through her connection with the infinite."
One should apply the seed-syllable of Śiva at the end of Lopāmudrā and Vāgbhava;
likewise, the seventeen-syllable mantra consists of the seed-syllable of Śakti preceded by Lopāmudrā.
If, at the end of the Śaktikūṭa of Lopāmudrā, it is joined with the Haṃsa seed-syllable,
then that is the seventeenth Vidyā, which is the direct embodiment of knowledge.
By the mere remembrance of her, one becomes Śiva and not otherwise; he becomes the lord of the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, a manifest Indra upon earth. || 75 ||
In that very context, the eighteen-syllable mantra is as follows, concerning Lopāmudrā: "One should join the lower [vowel] conjoined with the bindu at the beginning of the Vāgbhava;
the Mādana at the beginning of the Kāmarāja; and [the same] at the beginning of the third [Bīja], O Maheśvarī."
O Goddess, Bhṛgu, accompanied by Sarga and joined with Manu—this eighteen-syllable Śrīvidyā is indeed difficult to obtain on earth;
O Goddess, through the grace of the venerable Guru, it bestows eternal perfection. (76)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and ten thousand times, O fair-faced one, the eighteen-syllable lore of the Great Goddess Lopāmudrā should thereafter be propitiated;
otherwise, one incurs a curse and one's lineage perishes.
This Vidyā bestows all that is auspicious, destroys all obstacles,
grants all prosperity,
O Goddess, and brings about all blessings.
A knowledge such as this is exceedingly difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
In that very same [text]:
"In the case of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, however, the Vāgbhava [syllable] is placed at the beginning of the Vāgbhava;
the Bhuvaneśī [syllable] is in the Kāmarāja, and the Śrībīja is preceded by the Śakti. This is the eighteenth."
She is declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments, the direct giver of enjoyment and liberation, and the provider of the goals of human existence. || 79 ||
A science such as this is exceedingly difficult to find even throughout the three worlds;
it does not exist, it does not exist, it truly does not exist—I tell you the truth, the absolute truth. (80)
Another mantra:
having first extracted the Praṇava, then indeed Kulasundarī,
the syllable of desire (Kāma), the letter of power (Śakti), and then Indra and Hara.
Having extracted Bhuvaṇeśī in reverse order, then the Bālikā;
then the Praṇava with the Visarga, and then Kulasundarī. Having extracted Lopāmudrā and Vāgbhava in reverse order, then the Bālikā.
O Śivā, one should then place the Praṇava with the Visarga, followed by Kulasundarī; in the middle portion of the Śakti-kūṭa, one should join the letter Ha,
and there the reverse Bālikā along with the Brahma-syllable (Oṃ) and the Visarga.
Thus, this is the glorious supreme Vidyā, absolute and bestowing liberation.
What on earth cannot be accomplished by merely reciting it one hundred thousand times?
By the mere remembrance of it, one becomes Śiva; it is not otherwise.
Kulasundarī is the young maiden;
Brahmārṇa is the Praṇava (Om). || 81 ||
In the *Yoginījālaṃdhara*, concerning the *vidyā* of Kāmarāja:
"By means of the sequence of the three peaks beginning with the seed-syllables of Vāṅmāra and Śakti,
there arises the eighteen-syllable [mantra] known by the name Tripurāmālinī."
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is prescribed with fifty thousand recitations of the mantra. || 82 ||
In the Śrīkrama:
O Goddess of the Gods, hear that Vidyā, which is endowed with Kāma and Indra,
joined with the fourth vowel through the differentiation of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā.
She is the Mahāśrīsundarī Vidyā, the Great Tripurasundarī. || 83 ||
In the syllable *ka*, everything has arisen, bestowing both desire and absolute liberation;
in the syllable *la*, there is all-encompassing sovereignty; and in the syllable *ī*, it grants all spiritual accomplishments.
Thus, O blessed one, these three seeds constitute the essential compendium of the Vidyās. One should employ the Vāgbhava and Kāmarāja as the Śakti;
when uttered as a single syllable, it is declared to be the pure Brahmavidyā itself.
The *Kuloḍḍīśa* states the distinction between Kāmarāja and Lopāmudrā:
"Sundarī, being differentiated by the primordial [syllables] known as Śrī, Parā, Vāgbhava, Īśvarī, Tāra, and Manmatha, becomes sixfold. (86)
Likewise, in these two, in the first [mantra], there is Kāma, Māyā, and the Śrībīja; [in the second] there is Māyā, Śrī, and the Kāmabīja; thus the eighteen-syllable [mantra] is of three kinds.
And so it is stated in the Kuloḍḍīśa:
Kāma-māyā-ramā-pūrva (Kāma-Māyā-Ramā first), Māyā-Lakṣmī-Smara,
and Ramā-Māyā-Kāma— these are the three types of the eight-syllable mantra.
"Smara, Yoni, and Lakṣmī—this triad is within your mind, O Primordial One," thus it was propounded by the venerable teacher Bhagavatpāda. || 87 ||
Regarding the Śakti-Kāmarāja mantra in the Śrīkrama:
O Supreme Goddess, [the mantra consists of] the Māyā-bīja, then Jhiṇṭī, Kāma, Śakra, and Viyat in sequence,
marked by Jātavedas with the human limb (nṛgāṅka).
This is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, and the preceding one is the Kāmarāja.
In that very place is the seed-syllable of Śakti; she is proclaimed as Sundarī.
Here too, as before, there is the conjunction with the seed-syllable. Māyā is the vowel *ī*.
The *jhiṇṭī* flower is the letter *e*. || 88 ||
Again, he states the Śakti: "Then this Bhaga, followed by Māyā, Brahmā, Śakra, and Hara joined with Agni,
conjoined with the left eye, and adorned with Nāda and Bindu."
This is declared to be the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], with the Kāma-śakti as before;
the syllable *e* is Bhaga. Here too, the conjunction of seed-syllables is as previously described. || 89 ||
In this regard, there is a distinction:
O fair-faced goddess, when one bestows the seed-syllable of Brahmā upon the three peaks,
the first is Sundarī, O Goddess, and the second is Brahmasundarī.
O Maheśānī, in the Śaktikūṭa, she is considered Anantasundarī;
this is the sixteen-syllable Vidyā shown according to different traditions. (90)
Another mantra:
At the end of Trikūṭa is the seed-syllable Haṃsa, adorned with the Bindu and the Visarga;
this, conjoined with Śrī and Prāṇa, is the liberator from poverty and suffering. (91)
As for Śakti-Lopāmudrā:
Śakti, Maheśa, and Kāma, followed by the seed-syllable of Indra;
after that, Mahāmāyā—out of affection for you, I shall speak [this].
As before, the two syllables called Kāmaśakti are of the nature of being unfastened;
thus is the Great Vidyā of the Śākta tradition joined with the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya).
The *śakti* is the letter *sa*; as before, it is like the *vidyā* of Kāmarāja.
Here too, as previously, there is a conjunction of seed-syllables (*bīja*). || 92 ||
Another mantra:
the seed-syllable of Śiva, Śakti, Soma, and Mādana [Kāma], together with Purandara [Indra];
joined with Vyoman [Ha] and Vahni [Ra], and the vowel of the fourth state (Ū) with the Bindu.
As before, one should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti from Kāmarāja;
O Maheśānī, this Vidyā cannot be fully described.
Śakti is the letter *sa*; Soma is the letter *sa*.
As before, it is like the Kāmarāja-vidyā;
here too, as before, there is the conjunction of the seed-syllables (*bīja*). || 93 ||
Śiva-śakti, Bhuvaneśī, the supreme seed-syllable Vāgbhava,
Kāma, Vyoma, O Goddess, and Mahāmāyā following that;
then Soma, Vyoma, and Mahāmāyā— this is proclaimed as the nine-syllabled [mantra].
O Goddess, this is the power of Rudra, the leader indeed in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya).
Another mantra:
Mādana (ma), Gotrabhid (sa), Sāsta (ra), endowed with the left eye (ī) and the moon (bindu);
joined with Nāda and Bindu, it is thus declared, O Supreme Goddess. (95)
Brahmā, Gaganam, Śakra, Nakulīśa, and likewise Anala—
by means of Māyā, Bindu, and Sanāda, one should extract Kāmarāja.
Śakti, Mādana, Śakra, Hara, and Vahni, combined with Māyā and pervaded by Nāda and Bindu— this is declared to be the mantra that grants all desires.
O Great Goddess, this eleven-syllable Vidyā has thus been declared.
Another mantra:
Mādana, Pañcavaktra, Lohitā, Rudrayoginī,
Purandara, Mahāmāyā, and the supreme seed-syllable Vāgbhava.
As before, O Goddess, one should extract the beautiful Sundarī known as Kāmaśakti;
the syllable *kṣa* is Lohitā, and the syllable *ma* is Rudrayoginī.
As before, it is like Kāmarāja and Vidyā. || 97 ||

O Supreme Goddess, one should extract the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] as Bhṛgu (b), Īśa (i), Gaganam (ha), ending with Kāla (kṣa), Indra (r), and Maheśvara (au), enriched by the left eye (ī), fire (r), and the bindu (m). One should extract the Kāmarāja and Śakti-kūṭas in the same manner as before.
The Lord of Bhṛgu is the letter *sa*; the end of *ha* is the letter *kṣa*; and Time is the letter *ma*.
As before, [the mantra] is *kāmarājavidyāvat*.
This sequence applies everywhere. || 98 ||
Another mantra:
Viṣṇu, then Īśa, then the letter at the end of Ha (Kṣa), then Kāleśa, then Pṛthivī, then Bhuvaneśī; after that, Vāgbhava has been declared to you.
O Dear One, Kāmarāja and Śaktikūṭa have been described as before;
Viṣṇu is Īśa, the letter *ha* joined with *a*, and Kāleśa is the letter *ma*.
The *Śrīkrama* declares the *Subhagodayā* Vidyā as follows:
"Śakti, Svayambhū, Śambhu, Śakra,
Bhuvaneśvarī, Śiva, Mādana, Rudra, Indra, and Mahāmāyā— beyond these [is the final syllable]."
From that [arise] Kāma, Śiva, Brahmā, Indra, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
But this, O Supreme Goddess, is Sundarī Subhagodayā;
at the end of Trikūṭā, the seed-syllable Haṃsa then becomes the seventeenth.
The seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja), Vijayā, Māyā, Brahmā, Śakra, and Pārvatī;
the Mānmatha, the Śiva-śakti, the Mādana, Hara, and Indraka.
After that, Mahāmāyā; then Śakti, Manu, and Sasargaka;
Candra, Prajāpati, and Śakra; and after that, the supreme Mahāmāyā.
The eighteen-syllable Vidyā is Mahātripurasundarī; when joined with the *haṃsa* at the very end, it then becomes the twelve-syllable [Vidyā]. (1)
The Goddess said:
"Speech, creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and the inexpressible—these are the five beauties.
O Lord, O God, tell me of them, if it pleases your mind. (2)
Īśvara said:
Śiva, Mādana, Indra, Śakti, and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, Śakti, and Mahāmāyā, who is beyond that.
In the "Moon of Intoxication" (the letter *ma*) is Śakti-Śiva; at the end of that is Mahāmāyā.
Śakti is the letter *sa*. This is the terminology. (3)
Śiva, Candra, as well as Kāma, Śakra, and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Śiva and Indra, Kāma and Rudra, and Candra and Parameśvarī.
Śakti, Kāma, Śakra, and Mahāmāyā beyond that—this is the creation. || 4 ||
Śiva and Indra, Kāma and Śakti, and beyond that Mahāmāyā;
then Kāma and Candra, Maheśa and Indra, and Śakti and Pārvatī.
Brahmā, Maheśvara, Śakti, Śakra, and Bhuvaneśvarī—this is the state of persistence. || 5 ||
Śiva and Indra, Kāma and Śakti, and beyond them the Supreme Goddess;
Śiva and Śakti, Mādana and Indra, and Śiva with Vahni, Indu, and Māyā.
Śiva, Śakti, Ka, La, Ha, Vahni, Māyā, and Indu adorned with Bhū—this is the withdrawal (saṃhṛti). || 6 ||
Śakra, Brahmā, and the seed-syllable of the Moon; after that, Mahāmāyā;
then Vāgbhava has been declared—now hear Kāmarāja.
Śakti, Śiva, Mādana, and Indra; beyond them is the Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī). Śiva, Śakti, Soma, Śūnya, Brahmā, and Maheśvarī.
This is the Nirākhyā;
the letter Ha is void. || 7 ||
The Goddess said: O Lord, tell me of Svapnāvatī and Madhumatī;
now I wish to hear this, if you have compassion for me. (8)
Īśvara said:
Śiva, Mādana, and Śakra; Śakti and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Maheśa, Brahmā, and Haṃsa; and Indra and Bhuvaneśvarī as well.
Maheśa, Śakti, Kāma, Purandara, and likewise Viyat;
joined with Agni, Māyā, and Kalā, and adorned with Nāda and Bindu.
Haṃsa is the letter *ha*;
Māyā-kalā is the letter *ī*.
This is known as Svapnāvatī, which is the fifteenth kalā.
This is Svapnavatī. || 9 ||
Brahmā, Maheśa, Indra, Śakti, and Bhuvaneśvarī;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Śakra, and beyond them, the Supreme Goddess.
Mādana, Soma, Candra, Śakra, and Parameśvarī; Marut is the letter *ya*. This is known as Madhumatī, concealed in all the tantras.
This is the honey-sweet one. 10.
In the Śrīkrama, the Kāmakeśvarī-vidyā alone is recited according to the sequence of the Trikūṭa;
for Saubhāgyā, it is with the Trikūṭa, while for the fifth [Vidyā], it is the Pañcakūṭa.
Tripurā, who is the Great Vidyā fashioned from eleven syllables, is the knowledge more essential than the essential; she is declared to consist of eleven syllables.
Now the fifth: O Goddess, one should extract the seed-syllable Vāgbhava after [placing] Kāma, Viṣṇu, Śakti, Māyā, and Indra, followed by Mahāmāyā.
"Joined with Viṣṇu" means joined with the letter *a*. "Śakti" is the letter *e*; "Māyā" is the letter *ī*. || 12 ||
Then, in the Kali age, [there is] the sky-moon (viyat-candra), followed by the nakuli-fire (nakuli-vahni);
joined with the vowel of Māyā and endowed with the digits of Nāda and Bindu— this is the first peak-syllable (kūṭa) of Kāmarāja, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
The sky (viyat) joined with Viṣṇu (ya), Kāma (ka), Haṃsa (ha), and then Sakra (sa); after that,
Mahāmāyā (hrīṃ), which is thereafter called Svapnāvatī.
This is the second seed-syllable of Kāmarāja;
"haṃsa" refers to the letter *ha*. || 14 ||

One should extract the seed-syllable of Mādana, then the seed-syllable of Śiva, followed by the seed-syllable of Vāyu, and after that, the seed-syllable of Indra; thereafter, one should extract Mahāmāyā.
Thus ends the third peak.
This is Madhumatī. 15.
Then one should apply the seed-syllable of Śiva, Kāma, Indra, and the Goddess;
thereafter, one should extract Mahāmāyā and subsequently the Śakti-kūṭa.
The goddess is the letter *sa*. || 16 ||
In the Kuloḍḍīśa:
"The first peak-syllable is Vāgbhava, and the fifth is Śaktikūṭa;
O Goddess, the three middle peak-syllables are the enchanting Kāmarāja."
The fifth vidyā, which brings about auspiciousness throughout the three worlds, has been declared. || 17 ||
The Lord said: Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, to the Śaktikūṭa, which is very difficult to obtain.
The first peak-syllable is Vāgbhava, and the Kāmarāja is the third peak-syllable.
Out of special affection for you, O Maheśānī, I shall explain the Śaktikūṭa:
first Jīva and Prāṇa, and immediately after that, Mādana.
Then follows the seed-syllable *Indra*, and fifth is *Bhuvaneśī*;
thus is the *Śakti-kūṭa*.
*Jīva* is the letter *sa*, and *Prāṇa* is the letter *ha*. || 18 ||
Alternatively, O Goddess of the lords of gods, for Saubhāgyā, there is the Vāgbhava [Kūṭa],
the Kāmarāja [Kūṭa], and the Śakti-bīja, each consisting of three peaks (kūṭas), as before.
Whether it be the *kūṭa* beginning with the left eye (*vāmanetra*) or the *kūṭa* beginning with the vulva (*bhaga*),
this Vidyā destroys enemies, bestows accomplishment, and is free from all defects.
*Bhaga* is the letter *e*.
By this, the fifth [syllable] is eightfold through the division of the *vāgbhava-śakti-kūṭa*. || 19 ||
In the *Yāmala*: "The fifth knowledge (*vidyā*) is twofold; the supreme consists of five times five syllables (*pañcapañcākṣarī*).
In the middle is the six-syllabled one, and the power (*śakti*) is four-syllabled."
"Six" means the central peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of Kāmarāja-vidyā; "the peak-syllable of Śakti" means the peak-syllable of the Śakti of Kāmarāja.
This [vow] is fourfold due to the division of the Vāgbhava and Kūṭa [mantras]. || 20 ||
Of these two, which are established as being eightfold and fourfold respectively,
the third peak of Kāmarāja is located in that very place.
O Great Goddess, one should contemplate Kāmarāja, followed by the seed-syllable of Śiva; below that, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable of Haṃsa and then the seed-syllable of Indra.
After that, Mahāmāyā is the peak (kūṭa), which is extremely difficult to attain;
this too is eightfold as before, while the other is fourfold.

And so it is stated in the *Tattvabodha*: "The supreme [vowel] 'a' is the Śakra (Indra) in the space of desire, whose form is not established by any external configuration. Thus, the supreme [vowel] is the letter *sa*.
Mahāmāyā is that which possesses form created by configuration. || 22 ||
And so it is stated in the Tantra:
"O Great Goddess, [one should write] the seed-syllable of Kāma, then the seed-syllable of Śambhu;
below that, the seed-syllable of the Moon, and then one should write the seed-syllable of Earth."
And at its end is the Mahāmāyā-peak, which is extremely difficult to obtain.
This [Mahāmāyā] is eightfold as before, while the other is fourfold; therefore, the fifth [syllable] consists of thirty-six forms.
In the Śrīkrama:
"O fair-faced one, hear now the life-force (prāṇa) of these very vidyās:
one should apply Ramā, Māyā, and the Haṃsa-bīja at the beginning of the Vāgbhava [syllable]."
O Great Goddess, at the end of Śakti, one should place Haṃsa, Māyā, and Ramā; O Mistress of the Gods, joined with these, one should perform the recitation of the Vidyā.
And the recitation (*japa*) is to be performed exactly seven times, as it is seen in the *Dīpanī*;
"of these" refers to the vidyās mentioned previously in the *Śrīkrama*. (24)
Regarding the fifth [mantra], the distinction is as follows:
one should apply the seed-syllable *Ramā*, *Māyā*, and *Haṃsa* at the beginning of the *Vāgbhava* [syllable];
but at the end of the *Śakti*, O Maheśānī, one should likewise place *Haṃsa*, *Māyā*, and *Ramā*.
O Goddess, in the three [syllables] of Kāmarāja, the letter *ka* is joined with *Śakra*;
it is endowed with *Māyā*, the *bindu*, and *Īśvara*, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. (25)
First, one should apply this at the beginning of the *kāmakūṭa*:
the letter "va" (the last of the vowels), joined with fire (the letter "ra") and adorned with the left eye (the vowel "ī").
The seed-syllable of Śrī, conjoined with Nāda and Bindu, has been proclaimed;
O beautiful one, one should then recite the second, which is Kāmarāja.

The sky (ha) conjoined with fire (ra), adorned with the left eye (ī), and joined with the sound (nāda) and the point (bindu), is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Māyā (hrīṃ). One should also recite Madhumatī, which bestows the fruits of all desires. (25ka)
Now, the illuminator (dīpanī):
Having recited the Tāra, Lakṣmī, the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), Manmatha, and Bhuvaneśvarī, one should thereafter utter that which is called the Vāgbhava. (26)
Having then recited the Praṇava, Bhuvaneśānī, Ramā, Kāma, Vāgbhava, and Kāmarāja, one becomes the agitator of the three worlds.
O Great Goddess, being composed in meditation, one should there recite the syllable Oṃ, the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāk), Ramā, and Manmatha, together with Māyā and Svapnāvatī. (28)
Having then recited the Praṇava, the syllable Kāma (Klīm), Ramā (Śrīm), Bhuvaneśvarī, Madhumatī, Māyā (Hrīm), Śrīm, and the Kūrca-bīja (Phreṃ); || 29 ||
O Goddess of the gods, preceded by the Praṇava and encapsulated by the Haṃsa-bīja—
having uttered this seed-syllable, one should then recite the Śakti-kūṭa.
This, however, is the illuminating vidyā, the ajapā, whose form is breath.
The Japanese [tradition], however, states:
"One should recite at the beginning and recite afterwards seven times in succession;
one should also perform the *dīpanī* (illumination) for the *vidyās* beginning with Kāmarāja."
O Goddess of the Gods, in the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti-kūṭas, the illuminator of the Vāgbhava and Śakti-kūṭas should be understood here as being like the fifth [vowel]. 31.
Furthermore, in the *Kāmakūṭa*:
"The Praṇava, Bhuvaneśānī, Ramā, Kāma, Vāgbhava, and Dīpanī."
In every case, there is a connection with the vowels within the *kūṭa*. || 32 ||
And likewise, with reference to the Saubhāgyavidyā and others, it is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"By the distinction of vowels and consonants, she is divided into thirty-seven parts;
by the division into thirty-seven, she takes the form of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*)."
And this Vidyā, whose nature transcends the [lower] principles (tattva), is always to be meditated upon.
Likewise, the group of ten Śrīkaṇṭhas is indeed the designator of the Unmanifest (avyakta). O Goddess, that supreme eleventh [Śrīkaṇṭha] resides within the vital breath (prāṇa). 33.
Now, the Śrīyantra:

as follows—the point (bindu), the triangle (trikoṇa), and the eight-petaled lotus (aṣṭakoṇa); this triad is the wheel of withdrawal (saṃhāracakra). Then the ten-spoked and the fourteen-spoked [wheels].
These three constitute the wheel of persistence.
It consists of eight lotuses, sixteen petals, three circles, and is adorned with three arches;
it is endowed with four gates and is of the nature of emanation.
As it is said in the *Yāmala*: [Figure 32]
The King of Śrīcakras is proclaimed as consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, an octagon, two decagons, an eight-petaled lotus,
a sixteen-petaled lotus, three circles, and three square enclosures.
For the Supreme Deity, one should draw the Cakrarāja with vermilion, saffron, and so forth;
or one may have it fashioned by engraving upon gold, silver, the five precious gems, crystal, copper, or similar materials. || 34 ||
In the Śrīkrama:
"If anyone proceeds with this yantra without having drawn a perfectly level line or without having painted a perfectly symmetrical face, I take everything away from him. (35)
O Goddess, if one does not worship her wherever she resides,
his breaking of the fast occurs with nothing but her flesh and blood.
"Act with such diligence that the animal does not see [the writing];
for if by chance it should be written somewhere in front of the animal, my own limbs will surely be injured here by one of sinful intent. (37)
Likewise, in the Bhūtabhairava:
"O Maheśānī, if one should arrange filaments within this yantra,
the Bhairavas, together with the Yoginīs, will inflict violence upon them."
According to this statement, there are no filaments here. || 38 ||
The practitioner should never mark the yantra at night;
if the yantra is marked through negligence, a curse occurs instantly.
There, O Goddess, one should always dwell among Aparājitā flowers, Karavīras, and Javās; there, in that yantra, is my worship.
Likewise, in the *Svacchandabhairava*:
"One should fashion a very beautiful diagram (*yantra*) measuring one cubit on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*);
it may be constructed out of gems and other materials according to one's desire."
One tola, two tolas, three tolas, or four tolas;
having made [an image] exceeding this, a man will certainly become liable for penance. || 41 ||
Having filled [the vessel] with menstrual blood, one should worship the Śrīcakra on the ground;
all obstacles perish and that which is desired is attained. (42)
One-tenth part for gold, twelve for copper, and sixteen for silver;
these shall be the proportions for these three metals.
Whoever indeed worships in this wheel shall obtain good fortune;
he becomes the master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, without delay. (43)
O beloved, whether the sacrifice is fashioned with corals,
or with rubies, or with sapphires, or with lapis lazuli, or with crystal, or even with emeralds;
One certainly obtains wealth, sons, as well as a wife and fame;
copper is said to bestow luster, while gold destroys enemies.
One made of silver bestows security, and one of crystal grants all accomplishments; this should be understood as true for every such yantra. || 44 ||
Now, regarding the expiation for the destruction of the Śrīcakra: O Dear One, if the Yantra is burnt, cracked, or stolen by a thief,
one should perform a fast for one day without indolence.
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times, preceded by fire-oblations (homa) and libations (tarpaṇa).
Having satisfied the guru with true devotion, one should also feed the brahmins.
Having recited it one hundred thousand times, one should perform a fire-oblation consisting of one-tenth of that number, and a libation consisting of one-tenth of that [oblation].
One should perform [the recitation] one hundred thousand times;
some say ten million times. || 45 ||
If a mortal ever renders a [sacred object] marked with signs defiled by cracks and the like,
or breaks it, death will certainly befall him.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should cast it into the king of holy fords, or into the best of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, or into the ocean; otherwise, one shall incur suffering.
But this refers only to the case of a mechanical device (yantra). || 46 ||
Now, the majesty of the water from the feet of the Śrīcakra:
[The merit of bathing] in the Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, Narmadā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Gomatī, Gaṅgādvāra, Gayā, Prayāga, Badarī, Vārāṇasī, and the Sindhu rivers...

The water from the feet of the Śrīcakra bestows the fruit of ten million billion holy immersions in sacred fords such as the Revā, Setu, and Sarasvatī, within the interior of the vessel of the universe. (47)

Now, the fruit of beholding the Śrīcakra: Whatever fruit one might obtain by duly performing a hundred sacrifices, that same fruit one attains by beholding and worshipping the Śrīcakra. (48) [The Sixteen Mothers]
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing a great gift (mahādāna), that same fruit one attains by performing the vision of the Śrīcakra. 49.
Whatever fruit one obtains by bathing in thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas),
that same fruit one obtains through devotion by performing the viewing of the Śrīcakra.
Now, the *Saṃkṣepa-Śrīvidyā-paddhati*:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the ritual placement of the sages and other elements (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*).
For example: for this Tripurasundarī mantra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas),
Tripurasundarī is the deity (devatā), Vāgbhava is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Kāmarāja is the pin (kīlaka).
The third [seed-syllable] is Śakti; its application is for the sake of accomplishing the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
Thus it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The seed is Vāgbhava, Śakti is the third, and Kīlaka follows thereafter."
Then follows the deposition of the seed-syllables (bīja) of Kāmarāja and Meśānī.
Namely:
on the head, "Obeisance to the seer Dakṣiṇāmūrti";
on the mouth, "Obeisance to the Paṅkti metre."
Salutation to the deity Tripurasundarī in the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable Vāgbhava in the secret place; salutation to the power Tārtīyī at the feet.
Salutation to Kāmarāja, the Kīlaka, on all limbs; likewise, with the Samayāṅka: salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the [Kīlaka] of the Tripurasundarī mantra.
Homage to the Seer; homage to the Paṅkti metre on the head.
Salutation to the goddess Tripurasundarī in the mouth; salutation in the heart. || 51 ||
Regarding the essential nature of Vāgbhava and the others in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti [Tantra]: "Great mantras issue forth like sparks from a great fire;
in the same way, O Dear One, the letters of the Mātṛkā have issued forth from Vāgbhava."
For this very reason, that itself is called her seed-syllable (bīja) Vāgbhava. || 52 ||
The Mother of the Universe, manifesting as a woman in the form of a man,
O Goddess of the Gods, pierces the three worlds with great delusion;
therefore, O Goddess, she who is proud of her auspicious fortune protects the entire world by means of that very piercing.
Therefore, this is called power (śakti). || 53 ||
Now, the placement (nyāsa) of Vaśinī and the others is as follows:
aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ ravaluṃ, salutation to Vaśinī, the goddess of speech, at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ kalahrīṃ, salutation to Kāmeśvarī Vāgdevatā on the forehead.
Caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ navalīṃ, salutation to Modinī Vāgdevatā.
Between the eyebrows:
*ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ yalūṃ*, salutation to Vimalāvāgdevatā at the throat.
Taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ jaṃ— salutation to the goddess of speech Aruṇā in the heart. Paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ ha sa la va yūṃ— salutation to the victorious goddess of speech Jayinī at the navel.
Yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ jhaṃ marayūṃ, salutation to the Goddess of Speech Sarveśvarī at the *mūlādhāra*.
Śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ kṣamarīṃ, salutation to the Goddess of Speech Kaulinī.
On all limbs.
And so it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"At the end of the *a*-group, one should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) conjoined with fire (*ra*), the letter *pha*, and earth (*la*)."

O beloved, O Goddess of excellent vows, one should worship Vaśinī, the deity of speech, who is adorned with an ornament on her left ear and who consists of the Bindu and the end of the Nāda; O Maheśānī, at the end of the Ka-group is the supreme seed-syllable *kalahrīṃ*.

Having uttered Kāmeśvarī, one should then worship Vāgdevī. At the end of the *ca*-group [consonants], one should worship Modinī, who is adorned with the fourth vowel [au], the letter *dh*, the letter *ph*, and the letter *kṣa*, and is embellished by the nasal sound (*nāda*) and the bindu. 54.

O Maheśvarī, at the end of the *ṭa*-group [of consonants] is the seed-syllable of Vāyu preceded by Earth (Bha), enriched with the left ear (U), the moon (bindu), and the nasal drop (bindu); this is Vimalā, the sovereign of speech. At the end of the *ta*-group is Ja, followed by Earth (Bha) and adorned with the left eye (I).
One should worship the Seed-syllable, accompanied by the Bindu and Nāda, as well as the goddess Vāgdevī, who is crimson in hue.
At the end of the labial class (pa-varga), it is joined with space, moon, earth, water, and wind;
it is conjoined with the vowel *ū*, and endowed with the bindu, nāda, and kalā.
O Goddess praised by heroes, one should worship the victorious deity of speech,
which is composed of the letter at the end of the *ya*-group, the letter *ja*, the letter *ka*, the letter *la*, and the letter *ra*, combined with the wind (*va*).
One should worship Sarveśī, who is enriched by the beauty of the moon upon her left ear,
situated in the letter *kṣa* followed by *va* and *ha*, and encircled by the fourth vowel (*ī*).
One should worship Kaulinī speech, which is pervaded by the digits of Nāda and Bindu;
O Great Goddess, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, one should perform the placement [of mantras] at the end of the *śa*-group.

One should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) with the eight groups of consonants at the locations of the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, throat, heart, navel, the foundation (ādhāra), and the assembly (vyūha).
Then follow the nyāsa of the hands and limbs: *aṃ* to the two middle fingers, salutation;
*āṃ* to the two ring fingers, salutation.
Sauḥ, salutation to the two little fingers.
Aḥ, salutation to the two thumbs. Āṃ, salutation to the two index fingers.
Sauḥ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands. Likewise: Aiṃ, salutation to the heart; Klīṃ, svāhā to the head.
Sauḥ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā).
Aiṃ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca).
Klīṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya).
Sauḥ, Phaṭ to the weapon-mantra. Then, having performed the pervasive projection with the root mantra, one should meditate. || 55 ||
"I take refuge in the Auspicious One (Śivā), who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, four arms, and three eyes, and who holds a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow.
Having meditated thus and worshipped her with mental offerings, one should contemplate: "I am Bliss."
One should perform the installation of the conch shell. || 56 ||
For example:
having drawn a triangle in the middle of a hexagon to one's left in front of the Śrīcakra, and having placed a tripod there, one should worship the hexagon with the root mantra.

Then, having washed the conch with "Phaṭ," having placed perfumes, flowers, and so forth therein, and having filled it with water while reciting the root mantra, one should worship the mandala and other elements.
[One should worship] with "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās" upon the tripod; and "Aṃ... [upon the conch].
"Oṃ, salutation to the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās," [recited] over the conch; "Uṃ, salutation to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen kalās," [recited] over the water.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha:
With three parts of the *praṇava*, [one should visualize] the orbs of Fire, Sun, and Moon; then:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters!"
Thus, having invoked the sacred water (tīrtha) from the solar disc and veiled it with "Hūṃ," one should worship it with the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga).
Then, having displayed the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā) and recited the root mantra eight times, that water—
Having poured a little water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel into another, one should sprinkle oneself and the articles of worship with that water.
Having placed the vessels for the *pādya* and other offerings to its south, one should begin the worship of the seat (*āsana*).
For example: above the yantra, [one should say] "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," and likewise to Prakṛti,
Kūrma, Ananta, Pṛthivī, Rasāmbudhi, and Ratnadvīpa.
To Nandanodyāna, to Ratnamaṇḍapa, to Kalpavṛkṣa, to Maṇivedikā, and to Ratnasiṃhāsana;
in each case, one should worship with [mantras] beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ.
Upon the seat (pīṭha), on the Vaindava-cakra, [one offers] "Oṃ hsoḥ, obeisance to the great corpse-seat of Sadāśiva. Then,
having conceptualized the form (mūrti) with the mantra "hsraiṃ, hasakl rīṃ, hsauṃ" upon the Vaindava, and having formed the Tri-khaṇḍā mudrā, one should meditate once more.
Drawing forth the radiant [light] through the nostril, he brings it into the handful of flowers, reciting: "Oṃ!
O Supreme Goddess, who dwells within the great lotus forest, whose form is the bliss of the cause, who is intent on the welfare of all beings, Mother, come, come hither!"

Having thus established [the deity] in the image and performed worship with offerings according to one's capacity, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 58 ||
Having uttered the Vāgbhava-kūṭa in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, [one says] "Hṛdayāya namaḥ"; having uttered the Kāmarāja[-kūṭa], "Śirase svāhā";
having uttered the Śakti-kūṭa, "Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ"; and again, having uttered the Vāgbhava[-kūṭa]...
*Hūṃ* for the armor; having uttered *Kāmarāja*, *Vauṣaṭ* for the three eyes;
having uttered *Śaktikūṭa*, *Phaṭ* for the weapon.
And likewise in the *Jñānārṇava*:
Then one should perform the limb-enclosure (*aṅgāvaraṇa*) originating from the *Śrīvidyā* mantra.
Thereafter, one should worship the lineage of gurus in the center of the middle triangle within the [mandala].
As follows:

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the gurus; likewise, Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the sandals of the gurus; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the supreme gurus; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the sandals of the supreme gurus; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ...
Salutation to the supreme and subordinate gurus; aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the supreme preceptor-gurus;
aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the sandals of the supreme preceptor-gurus; aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the teachers; aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, salutation to the sandals of the teachers.
In all cases, one should worship preceded by the three seed-syllables: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.
Then, on the first line of the square: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the eight Siddhis beginning with Aṇimā; obeisance!
Thus, on the middle line: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the śrī-pādukā of the eight goddesses beginning with Brahmāṇī; obeisance. On the inner line: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ...
I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and the other mudrās; obeisance!
In every instance of the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa), the term "venerable sandals" (śrīpādukā) is to be employed.
And so it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
Having first uttered the word *śrīpada*, one should extract the word *pādukā*;
thereafter, one should worship the deities of the limbs with the words *pūjayāmi* and *namaḥ*.
At the tip of the wheel: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Tripurācakranāyikā; obeisance!
Here, in this Trailokyamohana Caturasra-cakra presided over by Tripurācakranāyikā, these—

"May Aṇimā and the other Prakaṭa Yoginīs, together with their Śaktis, weapons, retinues, and vehicles, be honored and gratified. With these words, he should offer the arghya water to the Root Goddess. || 59 ||
The etymological derivation of the term *Tripurā* is found in the *Vārāhī*:
"In ancient times, she was worshipped by the thirty deities beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
therefore, the name 'Tripurā' was proclaimed even by the gods. (60)
The libation (*tarpaṇa*), however, is performed with the *tattvamudrā* formed by the left hand.
And so it is stated in the *Svatantre*:
"O Pārvatī, by joining the thumb and ring finger with the left hand..."
One should satisfy the beautiful goddess and the oceans together with their vehicles. || 61 ||
Then, upon the sixteen petals: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the sixteen Nityā-kalās beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī; *namaḥ*.
At the tip of the wheel: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Tripureśī, the Sovereign of the *Śrīcakra*; obeisance!
Now, in the sixteen-petaled wheel (*ṣoḍaśadala-cakra*) which fulfills all desires:

These Guptayoginīs, beginning with Kāmakarṣiṇī, presided over by Tripureśī, the Mistress of the Cakra, together with their Śaktis (samudrās), and so forth—this one should offer again to the Root Goddess (Mūladevī).
Then, on the eight petals: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, [to] the eight goddesses beginning with Anaṅgakusumā.
I worship the venerable sandals; obeisance!
At the tip of the wheel: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the Mistress of the Wheel of Tripurasundarī; obeisance!

Here, upon the eight-petalled wheel that causes universal agitation and is presided over by the Mistress of the Tripurasundarī-cakra, these Guptatarayoginīs beginning with Anaṅgakusumā, together with their mudrās and so forth, one should offer to the Root Goddess.
Then, on the fourteen-spoked wheel: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the fourteen goddesses beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī; *namaḥ*.
At the front of the wheel: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the *śrīpādukā* of Tripuravāsinī, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakranāyikā*).
I worship; salutations!
Here, in this fourteen-spoked wheel that bestows all prosperity and is presided over by the Mistress of the Wheel, Tripuravāsinī, these [deities]:
One should offer to the Root Goddess [the worship] beginning with "The powers such as Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, the Yoginīs of the Tradition, along with their mudrās," and so forth.
In the outer ten-spoked wheel: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the venerable sandals of the goddess Sarvasiddhipradā.
I worship; salutations!
At the tip of the wheel: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Tripurā, the Mistress of the Śrīcakra; salutations!
Here, in this outer ten-spoked wheel which accomplishes all aims and is presided over by the Mistress of the Tripurā-cakra,
these goddesses beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā, together with the Kula-kaulinī Yoginī and their seals (mudrās), and so forth, one should offer to the Root Goddess.
In the eighteenth-spoked wheel: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the goddess Sarvajñā and the others; obeisance!
At the front of the wheel: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of Tripuramālinī, the sovereign of the wheel.
I worship; obeisance!
Here, within this protective ten-spoked wheel (*daśāracakra*) presided over by the sovereign of the *Tripuramālinī* wheel, are these goddesses beginning with Sarvajñā.
One should offer [the oblation] to the Root Goddess with the mantra beginning "The Yoginīs of the secret pride are the Mudrās," and so forth.
On the eight-spoked wheel: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the venerable sandals of the eight goddesses of speech, Vaśinī and the rest; *namaḥ*.
At the tip of the wheel: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the Mistress of the Wheel of the Siddhas of Tripura; obeisance!
Here, in the eight-spoked wheel that removes all diseases and passions.

One should offer [the oblation] to the Root Goddess, beginning with: "These secret yoginīs, Vaśinī and the others, presided over by the Mistress of the Wheel of the Siddhas of Tripura, together with their retinues," and so forth.
There, in the intermediate triangle, one should worship the six root limbs (mūla-ṣaḍaṅga).
Then, in the front corner: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the sandals of the venerable Kāmeśvarī Nityā; obeisance.
In the right corner: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, [I worship] the sandals of the venerable Vajreśvarī Nityā.
I worship; salutations!
In the left corner: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of the Nityā Bhagamālinī; salutations!
At the tip of the discus: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Tripurāmbikā; obeisance! || 62 ||
Here, within this triangular wheel (*triśracakra*) that bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*),
whose interior is adorned with an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a goad,
and which is presided over by Tripurāmbikā, the mistress of the wheel— these [goddesses] beginning with Kāmeśvarī [are situated].
One should offer [the oblation] to the Mūladevī with the mantra beginning "The Yoginīs of the secret and the most secret, together with their mudrās," and so forth.
Then, in the center of the *bindu*, one should worship with: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the eternal Śrī Mahātripurasundarī; obeisance!"
Thus, one should worship three times.
On the left: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Yonimudrā; *namaḥ*.
At the front of the *cakra*: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, [I worship] the *śrīpādukā* of Tripurabhairavī, the Mistress of the *cakra*.
I worship; obeisance!

Here, in this Bindu-cakra, which consists of universal bliss, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, and which is presided over by Tripurabhairavī, the mistress of the cakra—these are the Yoginīs who are the sovereigns of all cakras.
"May the oceans, together with their weapons, vehicles, and retinues, be honored and gratified"—with these words, one should offer [the oblation] to the Root Goddess. || 62ka ||
Then one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings.
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is stated in the Vāmakeśvaratantra:

Staying there, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, assuming the very form of the Goddess herself. O fair-faced one, one should perform the oblation with *kiṃśuka* flowers, or with safflower (*kusumbha*) blossoms mixed with the three sweets, using ten parts [of the former] for every one part [of the latter].
Now, the specific ritual manual for Śrīvidyā is as follows:
having risen during the Brāhmī-muhūrta, discarded one's sleep, and cast off the garments worn at night, [one should contemplate] the Guru.

Having meditated upon [the deity] in the form described above, [one should recite]: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasakhaphreṃ hasakṣamalavarayūṃ sahakṣalavarayīṃ hsauḥ śrī amukānandanāthaśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, if the Guru is female.
Having recollected, "I worship the Śrīpādukā of Amuśakti Ambā," one should worship with mental perfumes and other offerings as follows:

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Laṃ, I offer fragrance consisting of the element of earth; salutations. [Thus with the two little fingers. Likewise: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Haṃ, I offer flowers consisting of the element of space.
*Namaḥ*—thus with both thumbs.
*Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ yaṃ*, I offer incense consisting of the wind element; *namaḥ*.
Thus, with the two index fingers:
*Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Raṃ*, I offer the lamp whose nature is fire; *namaḥ*.
Thus, with the two middle fingers.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vaṃ, I offer this food-offering (naivedya) consisting of nectar; obeisance. [With these words, using the two ring fingers. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ, I offer betel-leaf (tāmbūla); obeisance.
Thus, with palms joined in *añjali*, [one offers] betel.
As stated in the *Viśuddheśvara*:
"Having meditated in this manner, one should again worship [the deity] with offerings consisting of the five elements."
The principle of smell and the earth element are associated with the application of the little finger.
One should offer the great flower consisting of sound by joining the first finger;
the incense consisting of wind by joining the two index fingers; and the great lamp consisting of fire-form by joining the two middle fingers.
In the act of salutation with joined palms, or in the offering of betel, the Vāgbhava [syllable] is traditionally prescribed.
In every case, one should join [the mantra] with a salutation at the end of its respective seed-syllable (*svasvabīja*).
The first finger is the *vṛddhā* (thumb). "At the end of its respective seed-syllable" means at the end of the seed-syllable of each respective element. 64.
Then, having displayed the *yoni-añjali-mudrā* and paid homage, one should perform the praise beginning with "akhaṇḍamaṇḍalākāram" and so forth.
The remainder should be performed according to the sequence stated in the general ritual manual for worship (*sāmānyapūjāpaddhati*). || 65 ||
Now, the special bathing ritual for Śrīvidyā:
having performed the Vedic bath, having performed the sipping of water (ācamana), and having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga),
one should invoke the sacred waters from the solar orb using the syllable *kroṃ* and the goad-mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*).
Having uttered the seed-syllable of the power of the root-vidyā, having cast the yoni-mudrā into that water,
and having displayed the dhenu and yoni mudrās, one should consecrate it ten times with the root-vāgbhava-bīja, [visualizing] the Goddess situated in the midst of the waters of bliss-nectar.
Having reflected thus, having consecrated [the water] seven times with the root-mantra,
and having sprinkled oneself seven times with the root-mantra while perceiving it as a stream of nectar issuing from the lotus of her mouth, [one should do so] again twenty-one times.

Reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should immerse oneself three times in that water by means of the stream of nectar flowing from beneath the lotus-feet of the Goddess; then, having risen, one should perform an ablution (*abhiṣeka*) upon the head seven or three times with the *yonimudrā*. Having likewise performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and reached the bank, [one should remain] on ground free from defects.

Having put on two garments, having applied the *tripuṇḍra*— consisting of three lines in the form of a half-moon— with pure sacrificial ashes consecrated by the root mantra, having remembered the venerable Guru as before, and having performed the ritual actions up to the *tāntrika-aghamaṣaṇa*, [he performs] the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
One should perform [it]. || 66 ||
It is as follows:
having performed the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and having drawn [the deity] from the solar orb with the *tīrtha* and *aṅkuśa* mudrās while reciting the mantra "Kroṃ," then—
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Śakti, one should cast [the offering] with the yoni-mudrā;
then, one should display the dhenu-mudrā and the yoni-mudrā there.
Having consecrated the deity with the root *vāgbhava* seed-syllable,
one should contemplate her as standing in the midst of the waters of the nectar of bliss.
O Goddess, the consecration with the root-vidyā should be performed seven times.
With a stream of nectar issuing from the lotus-face of the Goddess,
one should recite the mantra seven times and sprinkle one's own body.
Immediately thereafter, the practitioner should recite the vidyā twenty-one times.
Having submerged himself beneath the lotus-feet of the Goddess and emerged,
he should likewise perform an aspersion upon his head with the yoni-mudrā, O Goddess.
Or likewise, the foremost of practitioners should sprinkle it twenty-one times.
Then, having reached the bank, one should perform the ritual acts as desired;
immediately thereafter, one should put on two appropriate garments.

Having sipped water (ācamana) and facing the east, one should apply the sacred ash (bhasma) consecrated with the root mantra (mūlamantra) to the surface of the forehead as before, and then meditate upon the venerable Guru (śrīguru).
"Salutation to the supreme deity dwelling within the solar orb.
Having taken the *arghya* water in his joined palms, he should offer it three times with the *gāyatrī*.
Thereafter, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra to the Goddess according to one's capacity.
Having sipped water for the sake of satiation and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma),
the practitioner [should worship] the Vasus, the Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas, and then the Aṅgirasas; thereafter the gods, the cows, and then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the planets as well.

One should offer libations to Lopāmudrā, Mahālyā, and Anasūyā with the Ṛṣitīrtha; then, one should satisfy the constellations, the zodiac signs, and the yogas, along with the Karaṇas in their proper order, ending with the word "svāhā" (the wife of Agni) on the fourth day, using the Devatīrtha.
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, and those named Gautama and Agastya; as well as the Agniṣvāttas and Barhiṣads— his own ancestors according to the lineage of the Pitṛs.
One should offer libations three times with words ending in "ṅe" and those ending in "hṛt," using the Pitṛ-tīrtha.
One should satisfy Bhairavas, Kṣetrapālas, the host of Kumārīs and Yoginīs, spirits, and all living beings; let these be satisfied. Then, one should satisfy the Goddess. (75)
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"One who is pure should perform the libation (tarpaṇa), preceded by the gods, sages, and ancestors. (76)

Having visualized a triangle, a circle, and a square within that water, one should satisfy Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka on the left and right sides of the circle respectively; then, in the space between the triangle, circle, and square,
one should satisfy the lineage of gurus to be described hereafter, starting from Īśāna and ending at Vāyu.
Then, having gratified [the deity] in the center of the triangle with the Sādhya- and Siddha-āsana mantras to be described hereafter,

and having invoked the Blessed Lady into the water, one should gratify her three times with a stream of supreme nectar according to the previously mentioned sequence; and in the triangles, [one should worship] the triad of goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī.
Having gratified [the deity] with the samaya-vidyā to be described hereafter.
One should satisfy the deities of the limbs at the corners of the square.
Then follows the libation for the deities of the enclosures.
Then, having offered the *arghya* to the Sun and performed the ritual salutation with the mantra "Haṃsaḥ so 'ham," [one should proceed].
Having discharged the sacred water (tīrtha) into the solar disc, one should proceed to the place of sacrifice with speech restrained.
Regarding the place of sacrifice, the *Kālīkulasaṃbhava* states:
"For those with few desires, a forest is beneficial for worship in order to attain success;
for those free from desire who seek liberation, constant worship at home is recommended."
Even in the home of sages, chief ascetics, initiated ones, or twice-born brahmins, performing sacrifice with juices derived from plants, trees, or sugarcane is recommended.
In the Kulārṇava:
"Seated comfortably on a pleasant seat in a solitary, secluded, and beautiful place free from disturbances, facing either east or north—at the beginning there... (79).
Worship of the Sun: As it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "One should first worship Āditya, who is directly manifest as the witness of the world;
otherwise, there will be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (80)
Also in the Bṛhatstavarāja:

"Having performed the ritual bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), the libations (tarpaṇa), and the worship of the Sun according to the rules, I worship the fifth [digit] here for the sake of attaining purity. || 81 ||
Then, having gone to the door of the house, [one should recite]: *oṃ ātmatattvāya svāhā* | *oṃ vidyātattvāya svāhā* | *oṃ śivatattvāya svāhā* |
Having thus performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and prepared the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*), one should perform the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*).
It is as follows:
having sprinkled the door with the *bālā* mantra, [one worships] on the right and left sides, above and below, with "Aiṃ."
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gāṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Duṃ, salutation to Durgā.
Likewise, Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vāṃ, salutation to Vaṭuka.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kṣāṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Dvāraśrī. Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutation to Dehalī.
Then, entering the house with the left foot leading, [he should offer oblations] in the corners beginning with the southeast: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati";
likewise, "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Duṃ, obeisance to Durgā."
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vāṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kṣāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla.
In the center: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the Jewel Pavilion (Ratnamaṇḍapa).
In the directions: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Kāmadeva and Rati; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Vasanta and Prīti; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī.
In the *Somabhujagāvalī*:
"Sarasvatī, Śrī, Māyā, and Durgā immediately after her."
Then one should worship Bhadrakālī, Svasti, Svāhā the auspicious-maker, Gaurī, Lokadhātrī, and likewise Vāgīśvarī; these one should worship. || 82 ||
Then, one should offer three handfuls of flowers while reciting: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to Dīpanātha, who is joined with the twelve red Śaktis.
(From the Viśvasāra).
"O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountains, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet.
Having thus propitiated her: "O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu."

"And you, hold me always and make my seat pure. Having thus established the seat, one should then, with the Astra-mantra, dispel terrestrial obstacles by striking the ground three times with the left heel, and [dispel] those moving in the atmosphere with water empowered by the Astra-mantra.
Having dispelled divine obstacles with a glance from the sharp gaze fixed upon the venerable Bālā,
and having taken white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, and flowers, one should drive away the obstacles by reciting "aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ apasarpantu te bhūtāḥ" and so forth.
Then, in the southwest: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* obeisance to Brahmā; *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* obeisance to the Lord of the Site (*vāstvadhipati*);
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* obeisance to the Lotus-Throne of the Support-Power (*ādhāraśakti-kamalāsana*)—thus [is] the seat.

Having performed worship and sat down there, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). Although the *Kalpasūtra* prescribes the purification of the elements by performing the drying, burning, and flooding [of the body] through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) consisting of air, fire, and water, [one should do so] three times.

Regarding the phrase "one should perform breath control" (*prāṇān āyamyet*), nevertheless, it should be understood that breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) occurs after the ritual placement of the *mātṛkās* (*mātṛkānyāsa*).
And so it is stated in another tantra:
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa).
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the other placements (nyāsas).
Then, having performed the placement of the Mātṛkās ending with the breath-control, [one should perform] the placement of the seers and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
One should perform it. || 83 ||
Namely:
on the head, salutation to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
on the mouth, salutation to the Paṅkti metre.
Salutation to the deity Śrī Tripurasundarī in the heart; salutation to the Vāgbīja in the secret place;
salutation to the Śakti-kūṭa, the Śakti, in the two feet.
"Salutation to Kāmarāja, the stake (kīlaka), on all limbs.
In another Tantra:
"One should place the Seer (ṛṣi) in the region of the head, and the Metre (chandas) in the lotus of the mouth."
One should place the deity in the heart, the seed-syllable (bīja) in the secret region, the power (śakti) in the two feet, and the wedge (kīlaka) upon all the limbs. 84.
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs,
as follows:
*aṃ* to the two middle fingers, *namaḥ*.
Āṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers; Sauḥ, salutation to the two little fingers;
Aṃ, salutation to the two thumbs.
Āṃ, salutation to the two index fingers;
Sauḥ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
And likewise:
Having uttered this seed-syllable twice, one should perform the purification of the hands— on the middle and other fingers, as well as on the palms and the backs—
with the mantras joined with the fourth [vowel] (au) individually for each. 85.
Then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the [five] kalās beginning with Nivṛtti:
*krāṃ* to Nivṛtti, salutation to the secret place;
*krīṃ* to Pratiṣṭhā, salutation to the heart.
Aiṃ, salutation to Vidyā at the throat. Hauṃ, salutation to Śānti between the eyebrows.
Hrauṃ, salutation to Amṛtā at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
And so, having described the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) in the *Kulāmṛta*:
"Then this practitioner, possessing a divine body, becomes a recipient of swift accomplishment; there is no doubt in this matter. I shall now proclaim those ritual depositions (*nyāsa*)."

One should place Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Amṛtā in the secret place, the heart, the throat, the middle of the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). [The syllables] joined with the fire of desire (Kāma), two by two, are endowed with the mouth and the left eye.

The speech-syllable (Vāṇī), joined with the human-organ (Visarga) and the two voids (Vyoma), and below the second [void] there is Fire; thus, O Maheśvarī, there are five. Indeed, all these—the half-moon, the moon, and the Visargas—are in their proper sequence.
O Supreme Goddess, one should first perform the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*).
Then, having uttered the *Bālā* mantra, "O Mahātripurasundarī, protect me, protect me," one should place the joined palms at the heart.
Again, one should perform the binding of the directions with the mantra: *aiṃ klauṃ sauḥ astrāya phaṭ*.
And likewise: "First, the three seed-syllables of Bālā, followed by Mahātripurasundarī."
Saying "Protect yourself! Protect yourself!", one should perform protection while touching the heart;
likewise, one should then perform the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra and its mudrā.
Then, at the end of the Bālā-mantra, one should say "Oṃ amṛtārṇavāsanāya namaḥ" at the feet.
"Obeisance to Tripureśvarī, seated upon the lotus of the boat at the end of Bāla"—
thus [one should worship] on the two knees.
And so it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
O Tripureśvarī, one should first place the great mantra beginning with the words "amṛtārṇava" for the seat (āsana); thereafter, at the end of the Bālā-mantra,
one should place "namo potāmbujāsanāya" upon the knees.
"Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, obeisance to the seat of the goddess Tripurasundarī," [this is recited] on the two thighs.
And likewise: having uttered "Tripura," followed by the word "Sundarī" at the end—[namely, Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Tripurasundarī].

One should place the mantra *ṅe'ntaṃ devyāsanam* (the seat of the Goddess ending in *ṅe*) followed by *namaḥ* upon the two thighs. Then, with *haiṃ hklīṃ hsauḥ tripuravāsinīcakrāsanāya namaḥ*, one should place it upon the two buttocks.
[Then] *hsaiṃ ha sa klīṃ hsauḥ*.
"Obeisance to Tripurāśrī, the seat of all mantras," thus at the secret place.
"Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Bleṃ, obeisance to Tripuramālinī, the seat of the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished," thus at the region of the navel.
"Hsraiṃ Hsaklīṃ Hsrauḥ, salutation to the throne-seat of the power (śakti) on the couch of Tripurāmbā"— thus [one should place it] on one's own chest,
at the end of the seed-syllables of the three-peaked vidyās.
Salutation to Śrī Mahātripurabhairavī, seated upon the great corpse of Sadāśiva on a lotus throne, at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
And likewise, in the Yāmala:
One should place [the seed-syllables] *haiṃ*, *hklīṃ*, and *hsauḥ* followed by "Tripuravāsinī" and "Cakrāsanāya namaḥ" upon the two buttocks.
Then, one should place *hsaiṃ*, *hsaklīṃ*, and *hsauḥ* followed by the word "Tripurāśrī."
At the end of the seat for all mantras, one should place "namo guhye.
Then one should give "hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ bleṃ" and "tripuramalinī," along with the "sādhyasiddhāsana" ending in "ṅe," and place it in the region of the navel.

At the end of *hsaiṃ ha sa klīṃ hsraurante*, followed by *tripurāmbāpada* and *paryaṅkaśaktipīṭhāsanāya namaḥ*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the chest. At the end of the seed-syllables of the three-peaked Vidyā (*trikūṭavidyā*), [one recites] *mahātripurabhairavī*.
With the mantra "Obeisance to Padmāsana from the station of the great preta Sadāśiva," one should thus place [the deity] in the location of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 86 ||
Now, the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa):
Aiṃ, to the heart of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, the power of omniscience, salutation!
Klīṃ, to the head of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, the power of eternal contentment, svāhā!
Sauḥ! To the Śikhā of the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, the primordial power of consciousness, Vaṣaṭ! Aiṃ! To the Kavaca of the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, the independent power, Huṃ!
