One should perform the *nīrājana* (waving of lights).
And so it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Therefore, one should perform the *ārātrika* for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals."
O Parameśvarī, on a vessel made of gold, silver, or bronze,
one should draw a beautiful nine-pointed yantra with saffron.
O Śivā, having prepared a *caru* offering in the form of the moon, one should place it upon the head in the center of that [vessel].
Having placed one lamp in the center, [he should place] eight lamps in the eight corners—
lamps made of barley, wheat, mung beans, and other grains, mixed with sugar,
filled with ghee, and beautified by the splendor of cups set upon them.
O Maheśānī, having consecrated it with mantras,
thereafter one should write the Śrī-bīja and the Parā-bīja, O lady of excellent complexion;
and afterwards, O beloved, the letters ga, sa, ma, pa, la, and indra (ya) should be placed in order.

Joined with the left ear (the letter *v*), and adorned with the resonance (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*), these are the five seed-syllables, O beautiful one; they are the five jewels. By reversing the order of the first seed-syllable, this is the nine-syllabled mantra of Ratneśī.
Then, having uttered the root mantra:
"O Auspicious Goddess, Mistress of the entire wheel of wheels, O Navātmikā! Accept this ārātrika, O Goddess, for my success."
Then one should display the wheel mudrā (cakramudrā).
O Great Goddess, one should display the wheel mudrā during the ārātrika rite. Then, one should complete the ritual up to the conclusion of the dismissal (visarjana).
Thus ends the section on Śrīvidyā, the forty-first.
Now, regarding the mantras of Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, I shall declare the mantra of Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, which bestows the fruit of all desires;
by the mere grace of whom a human being becomes Sadāśiva.
One without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth becomes wealthy; he attains poetic skill and great scholarship—of this there is no doubt. (2)
In the *Viśasāra* and the *Yāmala*:
"Lakṣmī, Lajjā, then Māyā, and the twelfth vowel;
two Vajravairocanīs, two Māyās, followed by *phaṭ* and joined with *svāhā*. (3)
If the first [mantra] begins with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ), then Śrī becomes manifest in every direction.
By the first seed-syllable of Lajjā (Hrīṃ), women are brought under one's control.
And by the first seed-syllable of Māyā (Hūṃ), there is the destruction of great sins.
The first seed-syllable, consisting of twelve measures (mātrās), is the bestower of liberation.
O Goddess, Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Samrāṭ is proclaimed [as the meter].

O Goddess, Chinnamastā is remembered as the deity; the seed-syllable (bīja) is the pair of *kūrca* syllables (*huṃ*), and *svāhā* is the power (śakti). The application (viniyoga) is stated for the sake of one’s desired goal.
In this context, the word "shame" (lajjā) refers to the supreme seed-syllable of desire (kāma).
And so it is said:
"In this matter, O Goddess, the seed-syllable of desire is expanded upon the plane of modesty (*lajjāpada*).
This should be known as the *Mahākālamata*, the extraction of the mantra that brings auspiciousness."
In the reading *pūrvamāyāpadeti*, the meaning is that it is the seed-syllable of shame (*lajjābīja*) preceding the *māyā* [syllable].
And so it is said:
By the term "Māyā" at the beginning, the seed-syllable of modesty (hrīṃ) is intended; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *Tāpinī* and other texts.
And so it is said:
"The wise man should recite [the mantra] beginning with Kāma, or beginning with Vāgbhava, or beginning with Māyā."
Or one may recite the Lakṣmī-vidyā and other mantras that bestow the fruits of the four aims of life;
furthermore, according to the opinion of other sages, the word "māyā" occurs everywhere [in these mantras] as the "kūrca" syllable (hūṃ).

In that very place, the vomited [letter] conjoined with fire (Ra) and endowed with the *rativindu* (Anusvāra) is declared to be this seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, which bestows the accomplishment of all desires and aims.
[Furthermore,] it is joined with the left eye (I), fire (Ra), and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Śiva is declared to be the seed-syllable of Laḍḍā (Lajjā).
Having first extracted Īśāna, which is the seed-syllable of the Enemy of Tripura, adorned with the nasal sound (nāda) and the bindu,
and having arranged it on all sides with the left ear (the letter *u*), the wise here worship that Māyā.
The seed-syllable Vāgbhava is said to consist of the twelve vowels, adorned with the *nāda* and the *bindu*, for the sake of purifying all speech;
thus it is stated in the explanation of the four seed-syllables of the mantra.
But let it be correct. || 7 ||
In the Bhairava doctrine, however, Māyā is indeed Bhuvaneśvarī herself.
Lakṣmī resides in the first seed-syllable, and Manobhava (Kāmadeva) resides in the seed-syllable of Lajjā;
in this third [syllable], the Goddess always dwells, destroying even the greatest of sins.
In the fourth syllable, however, resides Guṇātītā, who bestows the knowledge of liberation.
In the letter *va* is Varuṇa himself, while in the letter *ja* is the Lord of the Gods (Indra).
In the letter *ra* is the god Hutāśana (Fire), and in the letter *va* is the Lord of the Earth (Vāsuki).
In the letter Ai is the goddess Tripurā; in the letter Re is Tripurasundarī;
O Goddess, Trailokyavijayā is always established in the letter Au.
In the syllable *ca*, the Goddess [is present]; in the syllable *na*, Vināyaka;
in the syllable *ī*, Kamalā herself; and in the syllable *ye*, Sarasvatī.
In the pair of *māyās* (the two *hrīṃ*s), the Goddess is always united with Prakṛti.
Vaikharī resides in the syllable *phaṭ*, Kusumāyudha in the syllable *svā*, and Rati in the syllable *hā*; such is the collection of mantras, according to the commentary. || 8ka ||
Now follows the procedure for worship:
having performed the morning duties and so forth, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (mantrācamana) as follows:
Having drunk water with the three syllables *lakṣmī*, *māyā*, and *kūrca*,
the practitioner should wipe his lips with the *vāgbhava* syllable and wipe them twice with the two *māyā* syllables.
He should wash his hands with the *kūrca* syllable and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with these mantras.

By touching the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, heart, head, and shoulders with the syllables of the venerable *Māyākūrca*, *Vāk*, *Kāma*, and *Tripuṭā*, as well as with the *Kāmakalā* and the *Aṅkuśa*, one becomes Śambhu in an instant.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in this manner, one beholds Chinnamastā after a year.
Then, having performed the ritual up to the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Thereafter, one should perform the sixfold mantra-deposition which brings the three worlds under control,
using the Śrī-bālā, Tripuṭā, Yoni, Prāsāda, and Praṇava mantras.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet upon their respective locations using these seed-syllables (*bīja*), namely: *kā*, *lī*, *vadhva*, *ṅkuśaiḥ*, *kāmakalā*, *kūrcāstrakaiḥ*, followed by the syllables of the sixteen-syllable mantra, each consisting of eight and ten syllables respectively. One should place them individually with these seeds.
This sixfold seed-syllable is indeed proclaimed to be of the nature of Brahman.
Indeed, by performing this ritual placement (nyāsa), they all become possessed of vajra-bodies; endowed with all sovereign powers, they are liberated while living for ten years. || 11 ||
Then one should perform the Nyāsa of the Seers and so forth:

for this mantra, Bhairava is the Seer (ṛṣi), Samrāṭ is the Metre (chandas), Chinnamastā is the Deity (devatā), the two *hūṃ*s are the Seed-syllables (bīja), and *svāhā* is the Power (śakti); its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals.
For example: "Homage to Bhairava, the seer (ṛṣi), on the head;
homage to the sovereign meter (samrāṭ-chandas), on the mouth."
In the heart: *namaḥ* to the deity Chinnamastā;
in the secret place: *namaḥ* to the seed-syllable *hūṃ hūṃ*; at the feet: *namaḥ* to the power (*śakti*) *svāhā*. || 12 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs: "Oṃ āṃ, svāhā to the sword for the heart," [is performed] on the little finger;
"Oṃ īṃ, svāhā to the excellent sword for the head," [is performed] on the ring finger and the sacred finger (the middle finger).
Oṃ ūṃ suvajrāya śikhāyai svāhā—thus on the two middle fingers. Oṃ aiṃ pāśāya kavacāya svāhā—thus on the two index fingers. Oṃ auṃ kroṃ netratrayāya svāhā—thus on the two thumbs.
Oṃ aḥ surakṣā-surakṣāyāstrāya phaṭ. Thus [one recites] over the palms and backs of the hands;
likewise over the heart and other [limbs].
As it is stated in the Bhairavatantra:
"One should first utter the letter 'A', marked on its head with a bindu;
then, for the younger [mantra], it is joined with 'khaḍgāya hṛdayāya svāhā'."
Then, O Goddess, one should utter the syllable *ī*, which has a radiance equal to ten million moons;
thereafter, for the sake of the limbs of bliss (*sukhaṅga*), one should utter [the mantra] ending with "to the head" (*śirase*);
then, joined with *svāhā*, it should be recited while the fingers are held in the purifying gesture (*pavitrāṅguli*).
Then the syllable *ū* should be uttered, its head marked with a *bindu*.
After that, "to the excellent Vajra" (*suvajrāya*) should be uttered, and immediately thereafter "to the crest-lock" (*śikhāyai*).
Then, ending with *svāhā*, one should perform the placement upon the middle finger.
Thereafter, one should place the goddess Mātrādvādaśikā;
having uttered "pāśāya," one should then say "kavacāya," and subsequently place the mantra ending in "svāhā" upon the index finger.
O Goddess, following the syllable *auṃ*, one should place the *aṅkuśa* (the goad) immediately thereafter;
ending with *svāhā*, this is for the three eyes on the two thumbs of both hands.
Then, the letter *a* ending in the *visarga* and joined with the letters of protection (*surakṣākṣara*).
Following that, one should place the mantra "asurakṣāya saṃyuktam astrāya" conjoined with the syllable *kaḍ* upon both hands. This is the measure for the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
In the heart, at the head, at the crest-lock, in the armor, and in the circle of the eyes;
and as far as the weapon-mantra, in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, in due order— thus is the statement of Bhairava in the *Triśaktitantra*.

"One should utter the Praṇava first, followed by the letter 'Ā' joined with the Bindu"—from such statements, the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs is to be performed conjoined with the Praṇava. (13)
Then, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) three times using the root mantra, from the head down to the feet, or from the feet up to the head.
Then comes meditation:
one should meditate on a pure, blooming, white lotus at one's own navel;
in the center of that lotus calyx is the mandala of the fiercely radiant one (the sun).
Resembling the Javā flower and similar to the red Bandhūka,
it is adorned with a circle of the source (yoni-maṇḍala) marked by the lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas;
and in its center is that Great Goddess, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
She holds Chinnamastā in her left hand, who herself holds her own severed head.
With her mouth wide open, terrifying, and licking with her fierce tongue,
she was drinking a stream of blood flowing from her own throat;
her mass of hair was disheveled and adorned with various flowers.
In her right hand she holds a curved knife, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
she is naked, most formidable, and stands in the pratyālīḍha posture;
the goddess wears a necklace of bones and has a serpent as her sacred thread.

The practitioners of mantra should always meditate upon Rati and Manobhava seated for the sake of sexual pleasure— Rati, eternally sixteen years of age with full and elevated breasts— intent upon inverted coitus.
The Ḍākinī is joined with Varṇinī through the union of left and right;
she is drinking the stream of blood gushing from the neck of the goddess.
Varṇinī is red, gentle, with loose hair and naked.
Holding a skull and a knife in her left and right hands respectively,
adorned with a snake as a sacred thread, she appears as if composed of blazing radiance;
divine, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, and embellished with various ornaments.
[He should visualize] a Ḍākinī standing on his left side, eternally twelve years of age, adorned with a garland of bones, resembling the fire of the end of an aeon and the sun,
with matted hair like lightning, three eyes, and rows of teeth like a flight of cranes.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, possessing full and elevated breasts,
the Great Goddess— most formidable, with disheveled hair and naked—
licking her great tongue and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
With her left and right hands joined, she holds a skull-cup and a chopper;
she performs the drinking of the stream of blood flowing from the neck of the Goddess.
She is exceedingly terrifying due to the skull-cup held in her hand, which is itself fearsome.
The wise practitioner should meditate upon that Goddess being served by these two, drinking [the nectar] with that mouth; the word "with" (tena) implies "with the mouth.
And thus it is said:

"Likewise, he holds in his left arm his own head, complete with its skull, filled with streams of blood, with its tongue lolling out, and most terrifying"— such is the reading in the Bhairavatantra. (15ka)

The necessity of meditation is stated in the Tantra: "If one should worship after having meditated upon Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā in this manner, the Goddess, having immediately severed his head, drinks his blood. (16)
This is its worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*).
In that very [text] it says:
"One should make the eastern petal white, and the one in the southeast red in color."
To the south [one should draw] black, then yellow, white, red, and white-black;
thereafter, one should make the pericarp (karṇikā) yellow, situated in the center of that.
In the middle of that, one should indeed fashion the mandala of the fiercely radiant one (the Sun).
The lines of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas* are respectively red, white, and black;
having then placed two *māyās* accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*,
one should construct an outer enclosure for that wheel, surrounded by a rampart.
First red, then black, white, and yellow in due order;
endowed with four gates and presided over by the Kṣetrapālas—such is the worship yantra of this [goddess]. || 17 ||
Alternatively:
First, one should draw a triangle, and in its center, three mandalas;
in their center, one should place the yoni, provided with three gates.
Furthermore, one should draw an outer eight-petaled lotus and three earth-mandalas;
in the center, within a triangle, one should write the *kūrca* seed-syllable accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*. (Figure 33)
And furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall explain the sequence:
one should meditate on a lotus within one's own navel, resembling a circle of the sun.
The ascetic should meditate there in the center upon the Great Goddess Chinnamastā, who is joined with the wheel of the womb (yonicakra), rests upon the three qualities (guṇas),
has the form of a lamp-flame, and abides in non-duality.
Accompanied by the *yonimudrā*, with the eye situated in the heart—this is what should be meditated upon; listen now to this for both ascetics and householders. (18)
For example:
within the center of one's own body, [one should contemplate] the lotus of the navel,
which is unstained, devoid of qualities, subtle, and radiant like the crescent moon.
Having meditated thus upon her who is accessible only through samādhi, who is enveloped by the three qualities (guṇas),
who transcends the kalās and transcends the guṇas, and who bestows liberation alone;
and having worshipped her with mental offerings as one would Tara, one should perform the installation of the conch.
One should perform it. || 19 ||
Then follows the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā):
to Ādhāraśakti, to Prakṛti, to Kūrma, to Ananta, to Pṛthivī,
to the Ocean of Milk, to Ratnadvīpa, to the Kalpavṛkṣa, and beneath that.

To the golden lion-throne; to the bulb of bliss, the stalk of consciousness; to the lotus consisting of all the principles (tattvas); *saṃ* to the quality of goodness (*sattva*), *raṃ* to the quality of passion (*rajas*), *taṃ* to the quality of darkness (*tamas*); *āṃ* to the Self (*ātman*), *aṃ* to the inner Self (*antarātman*), *paṃ* to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), *hrīṃ* to the Self of knowledge (*jñānātman*).
Homage everywhere;
in the center of the lotus, to Rati and Kāma. || 20 ||
In the Bhairava system, however,
the man who knows the mantra should worship the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (Kūrma), and thereafter the King of Serpents (Nāgarāja), as well as the Lotus Stem and the Lotus.
The mandala is square; one should worship the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas), as well as Rati and Kāma, and then perform the worship of Śakti.
Thus, over Rati and Kāma, [the mantra] is: *vajravairocanīye dehi dehi ehi ehi gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*.
"Grant me success, grant it! Slay my enemies, slay them! Karālike hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!"—this is the *pīṭha-mantra*.
One should perform worship everywhere with [the mantra] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, having meditated again, one should invoke [the deity]. || 21 ||

Just as in the *Sarvasiddhivarṇinī*, the *Sarvasiddhiḍākinī*, and the *Vajravairocanī* [tantras], one should invoke her by reciting that mantra again, saying: "Come here! Stay here! Be present here! Be firmly established here! and with the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ kroṃ haṃsaḥ*.

Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the vital breaths) and having applied the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantra "Oṃ Āṃ, svāhā to the heart of the sword," and so forth, one should perform worship according to one's capacity and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*).
For example: *vajravairocanīye dehi dehi ehi ehi gṛhṇa gṛhṇa imaṃ baliṃ mama siddhiṃ dehi dehi mama śatrūn māraya māraya karālike hūṃ phaṭ*!
With the mantra "svāhā," [he should offer]. || 22 ||
Then, on the right side of the Goddess, [worship] "Oṃ, obeisance to Varṇinī"; on the left, "Oṃ, obeisance to Ḍākinī.
Having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the body of the Goddess, [worship] "Oṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhanidhi" on the right.
*Namaḥ*. To the left: *Oṃ Padmanidhaye Namaḥ*. One should worship Lakṣmī, Lajjā, Māyā, and Vāṇī in the cardinal directions beginning with the east.
In the intermediate directions, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara.
In the center, [worship] Sadāśiva. Everywhere, one should worship with [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "namaḥ.
Then, having offered five handfuls of flowers, one should worship the enclosures (āvaraṇas).

Having worshipped the six limbs with "Oṃ Āṃ, svāhā to the sword-heart," and so forth, in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in the center, one should worship on the eight petals in order starting from the east: "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Kālī," and likewise to Varṇinī and Ḍākinī.
One should worship Bhairavī, Mahābhairavī, Indrākṣī, Piṅgākṣī, and Saṃhāriṇī everywhere with mantras beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "namaḥ. || 23 ||
For example:
one should [worship] Kālī by her various names— Varṇinī, Ḍākinī,
Bhairavī preceded by "Mahā-", and thereafter Bhairavī.
Then, one should worship Indrākṣī, Sapiṅgākṣī, and Saṃhārakāriṇī on the petals starting from the east, in due order,
reciting the seed-syllable of Lajjā (hrīṃ) preceded by Oṃ and followed by Namaḥ.
In the center of the lotus: *huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
To Svāhā, *namaḥ*. To the Samrāṭ meter, *namaḥ*, on the right of the Goddess.
To the north of the Goddess, [offer] salutation to all the castes (sarvavarṇa). Again, to the south, salutation to the Seed-syllable and the Power (bījaśakti).
On the tips of the petals, in order starting from the east, [salutation] to Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and Kaumārī.

One should worship Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī everywhere with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. Then, at the gates in the four directions: oṃ karālāya namaḥ.
Oṃ to Vikarāla, likewise to Atikarāla, and to Mahākarāla.
As it is said in the Bhairavī:
"At the eastern gate Karāla and Vikarāla, and at the southern [gate]..."
In the west is Karāla, and in the north is Mahākarāla.
Thereafter, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal of the incense and other offerings.
Regarding the dismissal, however, this is the specific distinction:
Having displayed the *saṃhāramudrā* and placed [the breath] upon the joined palms through the left nostril,
she is mounted upon the *yonimudrā*, blazing like the flame of a lamp,
and gradually waning like the moon during the dark fortnight.
Having recited this mantra, one should cause [the deity] to enter Caṇḍaraśmi.
The mantra is as follows:
"O Goddess, you who dwell on the mountain upon the earth at the northern peak!"
O Goddess, born from the womb of Brahmā, enter into my interior.
The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa), because it is a perfected vidyā. || 25 ||
Regarding the offering of the *bali* in the Bhairavīya [tradition], it is said:
"The *bali* should be offered at night with fish, meat, liquor, and so forth;
or else with sweet things such as honey-wine, according to one's means. (26)
The mantra, however, should be recited as follows: first, one should utter the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by "Sarvasiddhiprade" (O Bestower of All Siddhis);
then, in the case of Varṇinī, "Sarvasiddhiprade" should be spoken thereafter.
Then the name of the ḍākinī should be uttered, followed by the names of the goddesses;
then "Come! Come! should be said, and immediately after that, "This offering (bali)! Then, having said "Take! Take!", one should immediately thereafter say "My success (siddhi)!"
"Dehi dehi māye," followed by "phaṭ svāhā," is declared to be the mantra for the bali offering; when worshipped, O Queen of the Gods, it is thus honored. (27)
Another mantra:
Bhuvaneśī, the Kāma-bīja, the Kūrca-bīja, and the Vāgbhava;
then Bhuvaneśī, the Kūrca-bīja, and the Vāgbhava.
And then follows: Vajravairocanīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. || 28 ||
The procedure for its worship is as follows:
the rites of ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth, should be performed as in the case of the Ṣoḍaśī. || 29 ||
Hṛllekhā, Mādana, Lakṣmī, Vāgbhava, and Kūrca,
ending with Astra— this is the Mahāvidyā known as Chinnamastā.
Indeed, no science equal to this exists even within the three worlds.
This six-syllabled mantra directly bestows liberation; there is no doubt about this. O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe its meditation:
she always stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, holding a severed head and a chopper-knife.

One should meditate upon her who is clothed in the directions, joyfully drinking the stream of nectar from the blood of her own headless trunk; whose crest-jewel is bound by a serpent, who possesses three eyes, and is adorned with a blue lotus held in her heart; who stands firmly upon the God of Love (Manobhava) as he is absorbed in passion for Rati, and who resembles the color of a Java flower.
In her right hand, she holds a razor and a skull-bowl with hair hanging loose;
born of the quality of passion (rajas), she is named Varṇinī;
and from the severed headless trunk of the Goddess, she joyfully drinks the stream of blood falling down.
She whose crest-jewel is bound by a serpent should always be meditated upon by the gods and those who know the Manu-mantra;
she holds a black body in her left hand, as well as a sword and a skull-cup,
stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, and joyfully drinks the blood dripping from a headless trunk.
This very one, who at the time of dissolution is capable of devouring the entire universe, is the power of darkness (tāmasī);
she too is the Goddess higher than the highest, known by the name Parā Ḍākinī. Thus is the visualization.
All her worship and so forth should be performed like that of the Ṣoḍaśī. || 31 ||
Another mantra:
Tāraṃ, the two Lañjās, Vajravairocanīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
For this one as well, all [practices] such as meditation and worship should be performed as in the case of the Ṣoḍaśī. || 32 ||

O Dear One, that which is joined with the *sūtra* (the sky) and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda* is the single-syllabled Great Vidyā, which brings the three worlds under its control. The *sūtra* is the long vowel *ū*.
This great vidyā, ending with *ṭha* and *ṭha*, causes the delusion of the three worlds;
beginning with *tā* and ending with *rā*, it bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
And for Vajravairocanī, there is the pair of mantras *kūrcam* with *phaṭ ṭhaṭhaḥ*.
This great vidyā, beginning with Tārā, is the remover of all splendor;
it is the vidyā that attracts the three worlds and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
One should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, just as on the sixteenth day. || 34 ||
Now he speaks in praise of the sixteen-fold Vidyā:
"Likewise, with every effort, the sixteen-fold [Vidyā] is to be worshipped by all;
beginning with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, it alone bestows all sovereignty. (35)
When preceded by *lajjā* (hrīṃ), she is supreme, attracting the women of heaven and the nāgas;
when preceded by *kūrca* (huṃ), she destroys the great sins of all living beings. When the Goddess is preceded by *vāgbhava* (aiṃ), she bestows the state of being the Lord of Speech.
This sixteenfold knowledge, however, is to be known as consisting of seventeen syllables. (37)
Enclosed by the seed-syllable *śrī*, that [vidyā] always increases prosperity;
enclosed by *lajjā*, this supreme vidyā is the attractor of the three worlds. (38)
Enclosed by the *kūrca* [bīja], she removes the sins of all sinners;
and when enclosed by the *vāgbīja*, she bestows the state of being a Lord of Speech. (39)
"O Dear One, this fourteen-fold knowledge consists of seventeen syllables.
With Tārā at the beginning, there is another sixteen-syllable [mantra], which becomes seventeen-syllabled.
This knowledge is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), which always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (40)
One should utter Kamalā, Bhuvaneśānī, the Kūrca-bīja, Sarasvatī,
and Vajravairocanīye as the initial seed-syllables;
then Phaṭ Svāhā— the supreme Great Vidyā consisting of eighteen syllables.
O Goddess, these nineteen syllables beginning with Tārā constitute the very nature of the Brahmavidyā; they are the auspicious Vidyottamā, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (41)
The first [syllable] shall consist of the letters *randhra* (0), *candra* (1), and *akṣi* (2), encased by *lakṣmī* (Śrī) and so forth;
this Great Vidyā is fourfold and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
Just as it begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), it always grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (42)
Another mantra:
I shall proclaim another vidyā; listen attentively!
*Hṛllekhā-kūrca-vāgbīja-vajra-vairocanīye hūṃ!*
*Astraṃ svāhā*. This fourteen-syllable Great Vidyā is considered the bestower of all sovereignty and the enchantress of all. (43)
Then [one should utter] Bhuvaneśī, the three *tattvas*, the *vāgbīja*, and the *praṇava*;
then "Vajravairocanīye," "phaṭ," and likewise the supreme "svāhā.
This fourteen-syllable mantra bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
This is the knowledge, the great knowledge that destroys birth and death. || 44 ||
In another tantra:
Ramā, Kāma, and likewise Lajjā, Vāgbhava, and the Vajra-word;
for the purpose of enchantment, the mantra of the pair of Lajjās, conjoined with Svāhā.
This is declared to be that sixteenth [digit], which bestows the fruit of all desires.
All these auspicious sciences, the most essential of the essential, have been declared.
Bhairava is their seer (ṛṣi), while I am known by the name Krodhabhūpati;
Samrāṭ is the meter (chanda) and Chinnamastā is proclaimed as the deity (devatā).
O beautiful one, with the six long vowels preceded by the Praṇava (Om),
and beginning with Khaḍga and ending with Ṭhaṭha, one should fashion the six limbs.
They are free from faults such as those of women; they are well-perfected by gods and asuras.
Among all castes and in all stages of life, as well as among the lowest castes, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Those sciences, such as the Prāṇavāda and others, which have not been prescribed for Śūdras and the like—
there is this specific distinction regarding them: if a woman should practice this [vidyā],
she certainly becomes a Ḍākinī and is born among the Ḍākinīs.
"May she be like a perfected yoginī who is bereft of husband and bereft of son"—thus I have told you the entire secret reality, O beloved.
Out of a wave of great affection and devotion, I am your slave, O beloved. 48.
For these [deities], the meditation, worship, and so forth should be performed as in the case of the Ṣoḍaśī. || 49 ||

At the navel is a pure lotus; above that is a lotus and the mandala of the fierce-rayed sun. In its center, within a triangle, is the praiseworthy Chinnamastā, who assumes a triple body, the sole essence of saṃsāra, the mother of the three worlds, and rich with the arising of Dharma and Kāma.
I bow to that Yoginī, whose form is wisdom, who removes all fears, and who is the mudrā of yoga.
Thus ends the section on Chinnamastā.
Now begins the section on Śyāmā:
In the Bhairavatantra, it is said: "I shall now declare the great vidyās of Kālikā, which are very difficult to obtain."
By the mere knowledge of which a man becomes liberated while yet living. || 1 ||

In this [practice], there is no need for the purification of thoughts, nor is there any fault regarding friends and the like; there is no great exertion, nor considerations of proper and improper time; there is no great expenditure of wealth, nor is there any physical suffering. || 2 ||
The practitioner who meditates upon her, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires, holds in his hand every accomplishment at all times; of this there is no doubt. (3)
In his assembly, speech consisting of both prose and verse arises;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants are rendered lusterless. (4)

Even kings become servants; what then of other people? One becomes capable of bringing day and night under one's control, and in the end, that man attains the state of a Gaṇa of the Goddess, which is difficult to obtain.
Now, the mantras of Śyāmā;
therein, in the Kālītantra: [The mantra consists of] three *kāma*s (the syllable *ka*) situated in fire (*ra*), adorned with Rati and the Bindu.
Then one should utter the pair of *kūrca* syllables, followed by the pair of *lajjā* syllables;
then, on the right, the syllable *kālile*, and one should recite the preceding seed-syllables (*bīja*s).
At the end, one should place the consort of Fire (*vahnivadhū*); this is proclaimed as the Queen of Vidyās (*vidyārājñī*).
The *Yāmalatantra* states the meaning of the letter *ma*: "Because of its nature as water due to the letter *ka*, she alone bestows liberation;
through union with the syllable of fire (*ja*), she is auspicious and composed of all splendor. (7)
O Goddess of the gods, she brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution through the three Māyās;
and because the *bindus* are devoid of fruit, she bestows the fruit of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
That Śāmbhavī consists of three seed-syllables and is solely the power of consciousness-knowledge;
by means of the two sound-seed-syllables alone, she awakens the mass of sounds.
By the two seed-syllables of *lajjā*, she brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
by the word of invocation alone, she always makes her presence manifest;
with the *svāhā* [mantra], she is the Mother of the worlds, the destroyer of all sins. (10)
The procedure for her worship is as follows:
having performed the morning rites and so forth, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (mantrācamana) as follows:
Having drunk with the three [mantras] beginning with *Kālikā*, one should perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) with those beginning with *Kālī*;
having wiped the lips twice with two [mantras], one should wash the hands with one [mantra].
Having sipped water (ācamya) in this manner—touching the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, and arms in succession—one becomes Kālī; after one year, she beholds her.
*Kaṃ* means the head.
As follows:
one should rinse the mouth three times with "krīṃ.
Then, with "oṃ kālyai namaḥ" and "oṃ kapālinyai namaḥ," one should wipe the lips twice.
One should wash the hands with "Oṃ kulvāyai namaḥ";
[wash] the mouth with "Oṃ kurukulvāyai namaḥ";
and [wash] the right nostril with "Oṃ virodhinyai namaḥ."
Oṃ, salutation to Vipracittā—thus on the left nostril. Oṃ, salutation to Ugrā; Oṃ, salutation to Ugraprabhā—thus on the two eyes.
Oṃ, salutation to Dīptā; Oṃ, salutation to Nīlā—thus on the two ears.
Oṃ, salutation to Ghanā—thus at the navel.
Oṃ, salutation to Balākā—thus at the chest. Oṃ, salutation to Mātrā—thus at the head.
Oṃ, obeisance to Mudrā; Oṃ, obeisance to Mitā—thus on the two shoulders.
This is the mantra for sipping water (ācamana). 11ka.
Then, having performed the ritual up to the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform breath control (praṇāyāma) according to the rules using the seed-syllable of Māyā. || 12 ||
Then follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
As follows:
for this mantra, Bhairava is the seer, *uṣṇik* is the meter, Dakṣiṇakālikā is the deity, and *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable.
The seed-syllable is *hūṃ*, the power (*śakti*) is *krīṃ*, and the pin (*kīlaka*) is for the sake of accomplishing the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*); such is the application (*viniyoga*).
And so it is stated in the *Kālīkrama*:
The *kīlaka* and the first seed-syllable bestow the fruits of the four aims of human life.
[One should recite: "Salutation to Bhairava, the seer (*ṛṣi*), upon the head;
salutation to the *uṣṇih* meter, upon the mouth."
Salutation to the deity Dakṣiṇakālikā in the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable Hrīṃ in the secret place; salutation to the Śakti Hūṃ at the feet.
On all limbs: *krīṃ* to the Kīlaka, salutation. || 13 ||
Then follow the ritual placements (nyāsa) on the limbs and the hands.
As it is stated in the Kālītantra: "The ritual placements on the limbs and the hands are now described according to the rule."
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Uṣṇik is cited as its meter (chanda). The deity is said to be Kālikā, while the seed-syllable (bīja) is La-jjā.
The first seed-syllable shall be the pin (kīlaka), which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
The *śakti* [syllable] is the *kūrca* seed-syllable; it is Aniruddha-Sarasvatī.
The application is for the sake of poetic composition, as indicated by the words "it should be," and so forth.
By means of that *māyā*, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
One should fashion it with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and endowed with the six long vowels,
according to the *Vīratantra*.
Or one may arrange it with the first [syllables] of the long hexad and the first [syllables] of the vital breath (prāṇa),
as follows: Oṃ hrāṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ.
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers. Oṃ hūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers. Oṃ hraiṃ, huṃ to the two ring fingers.
Oṃ hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers.
Oṃ hraḥ, phaṭ to the palms and backs of the hands.
Thus [the mantras are applied] to the heart and other [limbs].
Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the heart, and so forth;
or alternatively, with "Oṃ krāṃ, salutation to the two thumbs," and so forth. || 14 ||
Then follows the deposition of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*): *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ namaḥ* at the heart;
*eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ namaḥ* on the right arm.
*Ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ namaḥ* on the left arm;
*Ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ namaḥ* [on the right arm].
On the right foot: *maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ*. On the left foot: [the same].
According to the opinion of Virūpākṣa, this placement (nyāsa) includes the nasal bindu.
As it is stated in the Vīra-tantra:
"One should place *aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ vai* in the heart," and so forth.
Furthermore, in the Kālītantra, it is without the nasal bindu (*nirbindu*).
As it says:
"A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ—[one] should touch the heart with these," and so forth.
However, one should place these phonemes either with the nasal bindu or without the bindu; according to the Bhairavīya statement accepted by the Teacher, both are indeed appropriate. || 15 ||
Now follows the sixteen-fold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*).
As it is stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"Having performed the placement of the pure *mātṛkā*, one should perform the *mātṛkā* enclosed by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*)."
The best of practitioners should place the *tāra* (om) encased by the *mātṛkā*;
that [tāra] encased by the *śrībīja* (hrīṃ), and that [bīja] encased by the *mātṛkā*.
One should place the Goddess encased by *kāma* (klīm), and *kāma* itself encased by her.
One should place the Goddess encapsulated by Śakti, and Śakti encapsulated by her;
having again placed the *krīṃ* and the pair [of syllables], as well as *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* as before;
and the Goddess encapsulated by the Mūla-mantra, and the mantra itself encapsulated by her.
Having performed the placement of the mantra according to the rules in both forward and reverse order,
one should subsequently perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) one hundred and eight times with the root mantra,
as follows:
Oṃ aṃ oṃ—thus is the *tāra* encased by the *mātṛkā*.
Thus is that [the *tāra*] encased by the *śrībīja*.
The *śrībīja* is encased by that [the *tāra*].
Thus, the Mātṛkā is encapsulated by Kāma; Kāma is encapsulated by the Mātṛkā. Likewise, the Mātṛkā is encapsulated by Śakti.
One should place the Śakti enclosed by the Mātṛkā.
Likewise, one should place the *krīṃ* and the pair, as well as *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*, as before;
then one should place the Mātṛkā enclosed by that, and that [mantra] enclosed by the Mātṛkā.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā encased by the mantra, and the mantra encased by that [Mātṛkā],

and again the mantra alone in both direct and reverse order in the positions of the Mātṛkā, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra one hundred and eight times. || 16 ||
This nyāsa should also be performed for Tārā. Thus has the sixfold limb-nyāsa (aṅgaṣoḍhā) of Guptadurgā been proclaimed;
it is likewise [to be applied] for Tārā, Kālikā, Unmukhī, and Parā.
When this excellent Nyāsa is performed, all sin is utterly destroyed. || 17 ||
Then follows the Nyāsa of the Principles (Tattva).
As follows:
having divided the root [mantra] into three parts, at the end of the first part: *oṃ ātmatattvāya*.
With "svāhā," [the offering] extends from the feet up to the navel.
At the end of the second section, with "oṃ vidyātattvāya svāhā," it extends from the navel up to the heart.
At the end of the third section, with "oṃ śivatattvāya svāhā," it extends from the heart up to Śiva.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa).
As it is stated in the *Svatantra*:
"At the end of the three sections of the root-vidyā, preceded by the *praṇava* and according to the rule..."
One should perform the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) with the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
Now, the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*).
As it is stated in the *Kumārīkalpa*:
"In the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), between the eyebrows, on the forehead, and in the region of the navel..."
One should sequentially place the seven seed-syllables in the secret place, the mouth, and all the limbs. They are as follows:
the first seed-syllable is in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The second seed-syllable is at the center of the eyebrows;
the third seed-syllable is on the forehead;
the fourth seed-syllable is at the navel.
The fifth seed-syllable is in the secret place;
the sixth seed-syllable is in the mouth;
the seventh seed-syllable is in all the limbs.
These three are optional rites. || 19 ||
Then, having performed the pervasion seven times with the root mantra and having displayed the mudrā according to the rule, one should meditate. || 20 ||
As it is said in the Kālitantra: "Kālī is fierce, with a terrifying face, her hair loose, four-armed, divine,
and adorned with a garland of severed heads."
Her left upper and lower lotus-hands hold a sword with its blade recently severed,
while her right upper and lower hands grant fearlessness and boons;
she has the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise naked.
She was smeared with blood dripping from the rows of skulls suspended around her neck;
she was terrifying with pairs of corpses used as her ear-ornaments;
she possessed formidable fangs and a gaping mouth, and her breasts were full and elevated.
She wears a girdle fashioned from the joined hands of corpses, her face is smiling,
and her countenance is made radiant by streams of blood trickling from both corners of her mouth.
She who utters a terrible roar, who is exceedingly fierce, and who dwells in the abode of the cremation ground;
she who is endowed with three eyes shaped like the orb of the rising sun;
she who is jagged-toothed, and whose mass of hair hangs down loosely over her right shoulder.
She is seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a Śava,
surrounded on the four sides by Śivās of terrible roar,
and together with Mahākāla, she is intent upon the inverted act of love.

One should thus meditate upon Kālī, who possesses a face serene with happiness and a lotus-face smiling with joy, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires; she who is adorned with two corpses as her earrings, who has terrible arrows as her ornaments, and who has a corpse as her ear-ornament.

Adorned with a left ear-ornament consisting of the wing of a bird, and having made an ear-pendant from two young snakes whose venom had departed—thus [is she described]; for both readings are seen [in the tradition]. 21ka.
In the *Svatantra-tantra*, regarding the intermediate dhyāna:
one should meditate on the auspicious Goddess, who resembles a mountain of collyrium, with a formidable face,
adorned with a garland of severed heads, with disheveled hair, and a smiling countenance.
Seated upon the lotus-heart of Mahākāla,

she possesses full breasts and is intent on inverted sexual union; she has terrible fangs, is adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread, and wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament along with [the severed] heads.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with a garland of severed heads, she has a girdle formed by thousands of corpses in her hands and is clothed in the directions as her garment;
she shines brilliantly with thousands of crores of Śivas and Yoginīs.
Her lotus-face is filled with blood, and she is intoxicated by drinking the [blood] from the center;
her eyes are fire, sun, and moon, and her face quivers with redness.
She wears earrings fashioned from the two young snakes that have been stripped of their skin.
She is smeared with blood dripping from the garland of severed heads suspended around her neck;
she stands in the midst of the cremation fire, worshipped by Brahmā and Keśava;
her lotus-like hands hold a freshly severed head, a sword, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual placement of the *arghya* water.
Namely:

having drawn a triangle containing the syllable *hūṃ* upon the ground to one's left, and having placed the vessel for the *arghya* offering there, one should fill a conch or similar vessel with pure water and so forth while reciting the root mantra.

Having offered perfumes and other articles, one should invoke the sacred waters with the mantra beginning "oṃ gaṅge ca," and then [worship] the base (ādhāra) with "maṃ namo vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane" and the conch (śaṅkha) with "aṃ namo sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane. Then "uṃ..."

Having worshipped the water with "Oṃ, salutation to the lunar maṇḍala, whose essence consists of sixteen digits," one should [worship] the heart and other limbs with "Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the heart; Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head; Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft; Oṃ hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor" in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu.
At the top: *oṃ hrauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; in the four directions: *oṃ hraḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*.

Having worshipped thus, having covered it above with the fish-mudrā (*matsyamudrā*), having recited the root mantra ten times, having rendered it nectar with the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*), and having protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), [one should employ] the *bhūtinī* and *yoni* mudrās.

Having displayed it and poured a little of that water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, he should sprinkle himself and the articles of worship with that water using the root mantra, and then begin the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*). || 23 ||
The worship yantra for this [deity] is as follows:
first, having written a bindu, her own seed-syllable (bīja), and Bhuvaneśī, then a triangle, outside of that four triangles, a circle, an eight-petalled lotus, and again a circle.
One should draw an underground chamber consisting of four doors (Figure 34-ka).
This has been stated in the Kālītantra:
First, having drawn a triangle, one should draw another triangle outside of it;
then the practitioner of mantra should indeed draw three excellent triangles.
Then, having drawn a circle, one should thereafter draw an eight-petaled lotus.
Having drawn a circle according to the rules, one should draw a single outer square (bhūpura).
Likewise, in the Kumārīkalpa it is said:
"In the center, however, is the circle of the bindu (vaidava-cakra), adorned with the seed-syllable of Māyā. (24)
Now, regarding the specific support, it is stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "In a copper vessel, or in a skull made from the wood of a cremation ground,
or on a Saturday or Tuesday, or upon a corpse that has arisen [there]."
The discus should be fashioned according to the prescribed rite from gold, silver, or iron.
The Tantra describes another yantra: "A hexagon by means of Śakti and Agni, and a ninefold [lotus] by means of the Śaktis;
on an eight-petaled lotus, with the Earth [square] provided with four gates. (Figure 34-kha)
Then follows the worship of the seat (*pīṭhapūjā*).
According to the *Kumārīkalpa*:
"Thereafter, one should perform the worship of the seat, beginning with the worship of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*)."
One should likewise meditate upon Prakṛti, Kamaṭha, Śeṣa, and the Earth;
the Ocean of Nectar, Maṇidvīpa, and the House of Cintāmaṇi;
the cremation ground, the Pārijāta tree, and at its base, the jeweled altar.
Upon that jewel, the best of practitioners should place a pedestal.
In the four directions, he should place the sages, the gods, and the Śivas with their skulls, as well as Dharma and Adharma, and so forth, [reciting]: *Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Self of Knowledge*.
Having worshipped thus up to this point, one should worship [the goddesses] in the filaments (keśara) in the order starting from the east:
Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Kāminī, Kāmadāyinī,
Ratī, Ratipriyā, Nandā, and Manonmanī in the center.
One should perform worship everywhere with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Above that: *hsauḥ sadāśivamahāpretapadmāsanāya namaḥ*.
To the north of the seat (*pīṭha*) is the worship of the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṃkti*).
Then, having meditated once more and brought a handful of flowers, one should invoke [the deity] into the form fashioned by the root mantra:
"Oṃ! O Goddess of gods, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue, until I shall worship you..."
Remain perfectly steady for that duration.
Then, having uttered the root mantra: "O Goddess [Name], come here, come here; stay here, stay here; be firmly restrained here; be present here."

Then, having veiled [the object] with the syllable *hūṃ*, having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkṛtya*) with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), having rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*, and having made it supreme with the *paramīkaraṇamudrā*, one should display the *bhūtinī*, *ākarṣiṇī*, and *yonimudrās*, and perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
One should worship with the root mantra, using water for the feet and other offerings. || 28 ||
The sequence therein is as follows:
first, having uttered the root mantra, [one says] "This water for the feet (pādya) is for such-and-such deity, namaḥ. Likewise, "This water for honor (arghya), svāhā."
This is the water for sipping; *svadhā*. I present the water for bathing. Again, this is the water for sipping; *svadhā*.
This is the fragrance, *namaḥ*.
These are the flowers, *vauṣaṭ*.
Then, having offered five handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, one should offer incense and lamps.
Reciting "vanaspati" and so forth, and having uttered the root mantra, [one says]: "This incense, obeisance!
As for the lamp mantra:
"The great lamp, well-illuminating, which dispels darkness everywhere."
"May this lamp, a light both internal and external, be accepted.
Reciting the root mantra: 'This lamp, obeisance' (eṣa dīpo namaḥ).
Then, having worshipped the bell with: 'Oṃ jayadhvani mantramātaḥ svāhā'."
Playing [the instrument] with the left hand, having offered incense at a low level, one should offer the lamp up to the limit of one's vision.
Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, one should offer whatever food offering (naivedya) is available.
One should give. || 29 ||

Then one should perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*). Having received the command by saying, "O Śrī Amukī Devī, I worship your enclosure," [one worships] at the filaments in the corners starting from the southeast with: *oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
In the northeast: Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head. In the southwest: Oṃ hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
In the northwest: Oṃ hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor.
In front: Oṃ hrauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
In the four directions: Oṃ hraḥ, phaṭ to the weapon.
Then, outside on the hexagon: Oṃ, obeisance to Kālī.
One should worship everywhere with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namas*.
Thus: to Kapālinī, Kulvā, Kurukulvā, Virodhinī, and Vipracittā.
In the first triangle: to Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, and Dīptā.
In the second triangle: Oṃ to Nīlā, likewise to Ghanā, and to Valākā.
In the third triangle: likewise to Mātrā, to Mudrā, and to Mitā.
And thus it is said:
The wise one should worship Kālī, Kapālinī, Kulvā, Kurukulvā, Virodhinī, and Vipracittā in the outer hexagon; and Ugrā, Ugraprabhā,
and Dīptā within the triangle in its center.
One should worship Nīlā, Ghanā, and Balākā in the central triangle;
one should worship Mātrā, Mudrā, and Mitā in the other three [triangles].
Thus it is said.
All of them are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, and adorned with garlands of severed heads;
they brandish the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) with their left hands and possess pure smiles.
They are naked, have laughing faces, and are adorned by their respective mounts.
Having meditated thus, one should worship.
Then, on the eight petals, in order starting from the east, [one should offer salutations] with: *oṃ brāhmyai namaḥ*, and likewise to Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, and Aparājitā.
To Vārāhī, to Nārasiṃhī—
one should worship these with perfumes and other offerings. In the leaf-vessel, one should worship the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga.
Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, one should worship Mahākāla to the right of the Goddess with water for the feet and other offerings. || 30 ||
His meditation is as follows:
one should worship Mahākāla to the right of the Goddess; he is smoke-colored, holding a staff and a khaṭvāṅga, with a face terrifying due to its fangs, and [appearing as] a child.
His waist was covered with a tiger skin; he was pot-bellied and wore red garments.
He had three eyes and hair standing on end, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
With the crescent moon shining upon his mass of matted locks, he was fierce and resembled a blazing fire.
And so it is stated in the *Kumārīkalpa*:
"One should worship Mahākāla on the right side of the Goddess, [reciting]:
HŪṂ KṢRAUṂ YĀṂ RĀṂ LĀṂ VĀṂ ĀṂ KROṂ Mahākālabhairava."
"Destroy, destroy all obstacles! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!

Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings by means of this mantra, and having gratified [the deity] three times with libations, one should worship the Goddess with the five "thieves" (pañcāpacoraiḥ) using the root mantra. || 32 ||
And so it is stated in the Kālītantra:
"One should worship Mahākāla with effort, and afterwards one should fully honor the Goddess.
[Also] in the Kālīkalpa:
Having extracted the armor-mantra *kṣrauṃ*, followed by *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ āṃ kroṃ*,
then "O Mahākālabhairava, destroy all obstacles," and having spoken again "destroy," one should extract *māyā* (hrīṃ) and *lakṣmī* (śrīṃ).
A mantra joined with *phaṭ* and *svāhā* accomplishes all purposes. || 33 ||
Then one should worship the weapon of the Goddess.
And so it is said in the *Kālīhṛdaya*:
"One should worship the sword and the severed head in the upper-left, upper-right, and lower hands of the Goddess."
One should worship the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and boon-granting (*vara*) on the upper and lower parts of the Goddess’s right hand.

Then, having meditated upon the Goddess and recited the mantra as much as one is able, one should offer the recitation into the Goddess’s left hand with the verse beginning "Beyond the secret" (*guhyātītyādi*) and perform the self-offering (*ātmasamarpaṇa*).

And likewise, in the *Svatantra*: "Then again, having worshipped the Root Goddess with mudrās, libations, and offerings, and having performed the recitation and prostrated, one should dismiss her into the heart."
Then, having offered praise, performed circumambulation, and prostrated with the eight limbs, one should recite the armor (*kavaca*) named *Śrījaganmaṅgala*.
Then, having dissolved the deities of the enclosure into the limbs of the Goddess, [one should dismiss them] with the *saṃhāramudrā*, [saying]: "O Goddess Amukī..."
Having dismissed [the deity] with the words "Forgive me," one should cause that splendor to ascend into one's own heart along with the flower, using the mantra:
"O Goddess, on the northern peak, dwelling upon the mountain on earth;
O Goddess born from the womb of Brahmā, go within me. (34)

Then, having offered a portion of that *naivedya* in the northeastern direction with the words, "Salutation to the outcaste woman who eats leavings (*ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī*"), having given the remainder to those one desires, having partaken of a little for oneself, having drunk the water used for washing the feet, and having placed the *nirmālya* upon one's head, one may wander about as one pleases. || 35 ||
Then, having placed the mechanical ointment in the left hand and having written the *māyā* seed-syllable with the little finger of the right hand, one should apply it as a *tilaka*.
And thus:
Having applied the medicinal paste to the yantra on the left [hand], and having drawn the *māyā* (the letter *ī*) with the little finger of the right hand,
the practitioner should apply a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with this mantra:
*Oṃ yaṃ yaṃ spṛśāmi pādābhyāṃ yo māṃ paśyati cakṣuṣā*.
Let that very king and his wicked bandits go into servitude!
And at the time of recitation, the tongue should be smeared with camphor.
Thus it is said:

"According to the statement in the Viśvasāra, 'The tongue should always be rich with camphor during the rite of recitation,' this [use of camphor] applies only to recitation performed for specific desires (kāmya-japa). || 36 ||
Then, having held a flower and sandalwood consecrated one hundred and eight times with the root mantra, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control;
becoming endowed with all perfections, one will become Bhairava within a year. || 37 ||
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of two hundred thousand recitations.
Thus it is stated in the *Kālītantra*:
"The practitioner of the mantra, pure and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times during the day."
At night, with his mouth full of betel, he should perform the recitation on his bed for one hundred thousand times.
Regarding the procedure, the *Svatantrotantra* states:
"During the day, having become pure and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), a man should perform the recitation for one hundred thousand times."
Then, O Beloved, one should perform oblations with sacrificial offerings ten times that amount.

Regarding this, Nīlasārasvata states the duration for the ancillary practice (*aṅga*): "One who eats sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and remains pure by day should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
likewise, being impure at night, one should recite it one hundred thousand times in that same manner."
The mantra-practitioner should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth [of the recitations], and should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) and perform consecrations (*abhiṣeka*);
so say the traditionalists.
However, in reality, according to the *Kumārīkalpa*:
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day while remaining pure;
at night, with the mouth full of betel, one should recite it one hundred thousand times on a bed.
Having thus recited the mantra two hundred thousand times, the knower of mantras, O Goddess, should perform ten thousand *homa* offerings according to the division of day and night.
Therefore, having recited one hundred thousand times during the day, he should perform the *homa* as its tenth part; at night—
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times at night, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number; such is the secret meaning.
Regarding the time for night recitation, the *Muṇḍamālā* states: "When the first watch has passed, until the end of the third watch, one should perform the recitation during the night;
however, one should not recite during the remainder of the night."
According to the opinion of Pūrṇānanda, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa).
Here it should be understood, O Brahmins, that for Brahmins, the puraścaraṇa is accomplished by merely one hundred thousand recitations during the daytime.
And so it is said in the Phetkārīya: "For all twice-born castes, the daytime vidhi is prescribed here;
for Śūdras, it is likewise declared that the possession [of the deity] at night yields great fruit. (41)
Also in the *Kālīrahasya*:

"A pure twice-born man should recite the mantra exactly one hundred thousand times during the day alone; according to the opinion of Pūrṇānanda, that constitutes the *puraścaraṇa* for a hundred-thousand recitation, whereas the view found in various *tantras* is considered doubtful."
From the observation of two hundred thousand [recitations], it is established that the *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished by exactly two hundred thousand;
and elsewhere:
"One should recite the mantra only during the day, and never at night."
For Śyāmā, the feeding of Brahmins as a limb of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should be performed with food ending in sacrificial oblations (haviṣya). || 42 ||
And so it is stated in the Viśvasāra:
"One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and remaining pure during the day;
thereafter, O Dear One, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial food ten times that number."
One should satisfy Pārvatī with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) equal to one-tenth of that [amount],
or with honey, O Supreme Goddess, or with water mixed with sugar. And one should consecrate the Goddess with waters equal to one-tenth of the libation (tarpaṇa).
One should devotedly feed twice-born brahmins with sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*) equal to one-tenth of that [number].

The practitioner of the mantra, knowing the *Kālī-mantra*, should bestow a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the preceptor. O Dear One, the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the *pāśava* [tradition] has been told; now hear that for the *vīra* [tradition].

At night, with his mouth full of betel, having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times while prostrating upon his bed with a concentrated mind, the practitioner of mantra should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the prepared fire according to the *Kālīkūlārṇava*.
With a composed mind, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the animal-like rite (*pāśava-kalpa*).
Having received [the teaching on] Kālikā of divine form from the mouth of a divine guru,
the practitioner (*sādhaka*), as a mantra-reciter, should always recite it one hundred thousand times according to the heroic rite (*vīra-kalpa*).
In the *Viśvasāra*:
"One should recite [the mantra] for one hundred thousand times day and night with supreme devotion," as stated in the *Kumārīkalpa*.
One who knows the mantra should recite it one hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day with purity;
at night, with his mouth full of betel, he should recite it another hundred thousand times on his bed.
Having thus recited two hundred thousand times, the knower of the mantra should perform the ten-fold subsidiary rites (daśāṃśa).
Because of this statement, [some claim] that there is a specialized preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of two hundred thousand [recitations].
That is not so, because it contradicts the previously cited statements.
The intent of this statement lies in the two types of *puraścaraṇa*. (42ka)

Now, the divisions of the mantra: The first letter of the [consonant] group, joined with fire (the letter *ra*) and adorned with the *rati* (the letter *i*) and the *bindu* (the nasal dot), is the single-syllabled great mantra that bestows the fruit of all desires. || 43 ||
But she who consists of the three qualities (triguṇā) especially awakens one to all the scriptures. || 44 ||
The procedure for the worship of these two is as follows:

having performed the morning rites up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), having assigned the previously mentioned seers, meters, and deities, having performed the assignment of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), and [performed] the assignments of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa).
One should perform [the assignment] as follows: Oṃ krāṃ, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ).
Oṃ krīṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers, and so forth;
likewise, Oṃ krāṃ, obeisance to the heart, and so forth. || 45 ||
And so it is said in the Vīra-tantra:

"The preceptor should fashion the six limbs of this mantra by joining the first [syllable] with the long [vowel] and the six [consonants], preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), and conjoined with the [six] classes [of phonemes]."
Everything else should be performed as before. || 46 ||
The meditation on the Single Syllable (*ekākṣara*) is described in the *Siddheśvaratantra*:
[She is] mounted upon a corpse, most terrifying, with formidable fangs, bestowing boons,
endowed with a laugh, three-eyed, and holding a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands.

One should meditate upon the Goddess who has disheveled hair and a lolling tongue, repeatedly drinking blood, endowed with four arms, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (47)
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for these two consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
Thus it is stated in the *Siddheśvaratantra*:
"Having meditated in this manner, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule."
The most excellent practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rule of one-tenth of that [number]. || 48 ||
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:

"Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day and remaining pure; likewise, one devoted to great purity should recite it one hundred thousand times at night. (49)
By the mere recitation [of the mantra] at night, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall become the bestower of success. || 50 ||
Another mantra is found in the Kālītantra:
"O lotus-faced one, listen as I proclaim the jewel of knowledge (vidyāratna)."

One should extract the seven seed-syllables according to the sequence of dissolution: two *māyās* (the letter *ī*), the pair of *kūrca*s (*ha-ha*), ending with *indrā* (*la*), the three *mādanas* (*ka-kha-ga*), and *māyā* joined with two *bindus* and *īśvara* (*ī*). This is the word "Kālike" for the right [hand]. Thus one should extract the seven seeds.
The mantra of Kālikā, beginning with Tārā, should be known as consisting of twenty-one syllables;
"aindra" (the vicinity of Indra) refers to the letter *ra*. || 51 ||
And likewise in the Tantra:
"O Maheśānī, there are three Kāmas and two Krodhas at the end of Vahni, conjoined with Rati and endowed with the Bindu; these constitute the two words of address."
The seven seed-syllables, preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with Svāhā, are joined with the [five] withdrawals (saṃhāra). || 52 ||
Thus he states clearly here. And so:
"The *praṇava*, the two *māyās*, the two *kūrca*s, and the three of one's own seed-syllables [are placed] in Dakṣiṇakālikā."
The three seed-syllables of herself,
two *kūrca* syllables, and two *māyā* syllables constitute the twenty-one syllables [of this mantra].
Her worship and other rites should be performed according to the *dakṣiṇā* ritual.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations, as it is so stated in the Tantras;
the fire-oblation (homa), however, is one-tenth of that amount. || 53 ||
In the Viśvasāra:
"O Goddess of Gods, this king of mantras consists of twenty-three syllables ending with *svāhā*;
without the *praṇava*, it becomes twenty-two syllables."
The twenty-one-syllable mantra beginning with "mauḥ" and excluding "svāhā" is the granter of desires;
the twenty-syllable Mahāvidyā is likewise devoid of "svāhā" and the syllable "oṃ.
One should perform all rites, such as meditation and worship, according to the procedure for the Dakṣiṇā-mantra.
In the Bhairavatantra:
"O Goddess, the two seed-syllables of Kāma and the long *hūṃ*—this three-syllabled great vidyā is known as Cāmuṇḍā-Kālikā. (55)
In the Tantra: Now I shall proclaim the great vidyā, the perfected vidyā arising from me,
known as Kālīhṛdaya, which was formerly taught by Bhairava.
By the power of her knowledge, I perceive the three worlds. || 56 ||
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable Hṛllekhā;
having extracted the seed-syllable Rati, conjoined with the fifth vowel and joined with two Ṭha-s, she is proclaimed as the Queen of Vidyās.
The seed-syllable of Rati is one's own seed-syllable.
And so it is said in the Cāmuṇḍātantra:
"May Kālikā, who consists of twenty-two syllables and begins with Rati, protect [us]."
Thus, because of the exposition of the *kavaca* (armor) located in the *Cāmuṇḍā-tantra*:

"Therefore, [the mantra consists of] the *praṇava*, the *māyā*-seed, one's own seed, the fifth letter 'pa', the *bhaga* which is the letter 'e', and the beloved of fire (*vahnivallabhā*) [the letter 'ra']. (57)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth.

For example: for this mantra, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandas*), Siddhakālī Brahmarūpā Bhuvaneśvarī is the deity (*devatā*), the seed-syllable of oneself is the seed (*bīja*), and the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*) is the power (*śakti*).
The placement of the syllables (varṇanyāsa) and the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) are performed as in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti ritual.
As for the meditation:

she has three eyes, her limbs are drenched by the nectar-essence flowing from the crescent moon split by a sword; with her right hand she drinks blood dripping from a skull-cup, and her hair is loose.

Clad in the directions as her garment, girt with a golden belt, and adorned with a jeweled crown and other ornaments; with a blazing tongue, possessing the luster of a blue lotus, and with her feet kissed by earrings shining like the sun and moon—having meditated thus, everything should be performed as on the right side. 59.
The *puraścaraṇa* consists of twenty-one thousand recitations.
As it is stated in the *Kālītantra*:
"One should recite twenty thousand three hundred and one times."
The knower of mantras should perform the fire oblation with soft flowers using one-tenth of that [number].
Another mantra is found in the Viśvasāra: first the root seed-syllable, then Māyā, and after that the seed-syllable of Lañjā.
This great vidyā was spoken by Mahākāla to Mahākālī. || 61 ||
The first letter of the class [ka], conjoined with fire [ra] and endowed with the pleasure-point [ī];
these three constitute Vahni-vallabhā. 62.
The three seed-syllables of oneself, followed by *phaṭ* and the beloved of Fire (*svāhā*). || 63 ||
One's own three seed-syllables, the *kūrca* mantra, the *lajjā* (shame) mantra, again those same [three], and the beloved of Fire (the *svāhā*). (64)
The Vāgbhava syllable, *namaḥ*, and the root seed-syllable; again that same [syllable], followed by *Kālikāyai* and *Vahnivallabhā*.
The procedure for their worship is as follows:

having performed the morning rites up to the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement of the seer and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa). For example: Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer, Paṅkti is the meter, and Kālikā is the deity.
On the head, salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer;
on the mouth, salutation to Paṅkti, the metre;
on the heart, salutation to Kālikā, the deity. || 66 ||
Then the meditation:
[the goddess] has four arms and is black in color, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
she holds a sword in her right hand and two blue lotuses.
Holding a scythe and a skull-bowl in her left hands in succession,
she herself bears a single matted lock of hair that reaches toward the heavens;
she wears a garland of severed heads upon her head and another around her neck.
Wearing a serpent-necklace upon her chest, with blood-red eyes,
clad in black garments and a tiger-skin around her waist,
she places her left foot upon the heart of a corpse and her right foot [upon the other].

Having dissolved [the corpse] upon the back of a lion, she herself— leaping up, accompanied by loud laughter, joined with most terrible roars, and extremely fearsome— licks the corpse. Having meditated thus, one should perform everything else according to the procedure for the southern [direction].
For all the previously mentioned mantras, the ritual procedure must be performed with the offering of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 67 ||

The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of two hundred thousand recitations; for other [mantras], it consists of one hundred thousand recitations corresponding to the number of syllables in the mantra. || 68 ||
The two seed-syllables of one's own [name], the two *māyās*, "dakṣiṇakālike," and the beloved of fire (svāhā). || 69 ||
Nijaṃ kūrcam, lajjā, dakṣiṇe kālike phaṭ. || 70 ||
The two root-seeds, the two *kūrca*s, the two *lajjā*s, followed by "O Kālikā" on the right, and the six previous seeds, ending with the beloved of Fire (Svāhā). (71)
The procedure for their worship is as follows:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth.
For these [mantras], Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer, Paṅkti is the meter, and Dakṣiṇakālikā is the deity.
The deity [is as before]; everything else is accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 72 ||
The seed-syllable of oneself is Vahnivallabhā;
Bhairava is its seer (ṛṣi). || 73 ||
The two seed-syllables of one's own [name], the two *kūrca* syllables, the pair of *lajjā* syllables, and the beloved of Fire (the *svāhā*). || 74 ||
One's own seed-syllable, the *kūrca* (huṃ), the *lajjā* (hrīṃ), and the beloved of fire (svāhā).
For this [mantra], Pañcavaktra is the seer (*ṛṣi*). || 75 ||
The three roots, the two kūrca-s, the two lajjā-s, and the beloved of fire (svāhā). || 76 ||
The root seed-syllable is "Kālike" on the right, followed by the beloved of fire (the syllable Ra).
One's own seed-syllable, the two *kūrca* syllables, *māyā*, again those [same syllables], and the beloved of Fire (the *svāhā* syllable). 78.
The two roots, the two *kūrca*s, the two *lajjā*s, and again those very same ones, followed by the beloved of Fire (*vahnivallabhā*).

One's own three seed-syllables, two *lajjā*s, two *kūrca*s, again those same [syllables], the beloved of Fire (Svāhā), the Heart, the Vāgbhava, the two root-mantras, "Kālikāyai," and two *ṭha*s. || 81 ||
Hṛdayaṃ pāśadvayaṃ aṅkuśadvayaṃ phaṭ svāhā kālike kūrcam.
The seers and other details for these [mantras], as well as their worship and so forth, are accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa). || 83 ||
The extent of these vidyās is stated in the Viśvasāra:
"Now I shall describe the five-syllabled mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Having extracted Prajāpati (the syllable *pra*), then [place] it mounted upon fire (*ra*), O beloved."
Combined with the fourth vowel, adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*,
these three seed-syllables (*bīja*) in their proper sequence, followed at the end by Vahnisundarī—
this five-syllabled Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) was proclaimed by the Lotus-born One.
I shall now declare the six-syllabled Mahākālī; listen, O Pārvatī!

Having extracted the three seed-syllables (bījas), one should extract the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra). This vidyā, ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā), is said to be the Enchantress of the Three Worlds.
O Supreme Goddess, the eight-syllabled Great Vidyā is now described:
the wise one [should recite] three seed-syllables in sequence, followed again by three seed-syllables;
this Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is said to bestow the fruits of the four aims of life.
O Supreme Goddess, the eleven-syllable Vidyā is now described: first is Vāgbhava (AIM), followed by Hṛdaya (HŪM), then Prajāpati (L) mounted upon Fire (R) and conjoined with the fourth vowel (Ī),
adorned with the Bindu and Nāda.
Then, having doubled that [syllable] and placed the word *Kālikā* ending in the dative case (*-ai*),
the eleven-syllable Vidyā ending in *svāhā* has been declared, O Dear One.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the Seer (*ṛṣi*) and Paṅkti is stated to be the Metre (*chandas*).
The deity Kālikā is remembered as the power (śakti) higher than the highest.
The eleven-syllable mantra of Kālikā is extremely difficult to obtain.
One should recite this mantra two hundred thousand times for the rite of preliminary purification (puraścaraṇa).
For others, one hundred thousand recitations of their respective syllables have been prescribed by the Lotus-born One;
"others" refers to those such as the aforementioned Pañcākṣarī and so forth.
Her visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
"Four-armed, dark-complexioned," and so forth. || 84 ||
Then the root-seed (mūlabīja), then Māyā, then the seed of modesty (lajjābīja);
then "Dakṣiṇe Kālike," and at the end of that, Vahnisundarī.
This eleven-syllable Kālī bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. 85.
The ten-syllable Great Vidyā bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
The armor-mantra begins with the root-seeds, followed by Bhuvaneśvarī at its end, and "Dakṣiṇe Kālike" at the conclusion; thus it is proclaimed to end with the weapon-mantra (astra). (86)
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā consisting of twenty syllables,
by the mere grace of which one becomes a lord of the earth and cities.
One should utter the two root-seeds, and thereafter one should speak the two *kūrca* [syllables].
Having extracted the two *lajjās*, there are two words ending in *saṃbuddhi*;
likewise, as before, there are six seed-syllables (*bījas*), and at the end is *vahnisundarī*. (87)
The seer (ṛṣi) is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the meter (chandas) is declared to be Paṅkti;
and the deity (devatā) is said by the wise to be Kālī, preceded by the South. 88.
Now I shall proclaim another Vidyā, the Mistress of the Three Worlds.
Having extracted her own seed-syllable, the beautiful goddess of fire (Svāhā) follows at its end.
Bhairava is declared to be its Seer (Ṛṣi), as is consistent with all Tantras. (89)

The eight-syllabled mantra which has been proclaimed and kept secret in all the Tantras consists of two of one's own seed-syllables, two *kūrca* syllables, and two *lajjā* syllables, followed by *svāhā*. This Vidyā is said to bestow the fruits of all desires. (90)
The syllable *nija*, *kūrca*, likewise *lajjā*, and at its end *vahnisundarī*—this is the five-syllabled Great Vidyā; the sage is remembered as Pañcavaktra. || 91 ||
O lotus-faced one, listen to the nine-syllable Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā):
it consists of one's own three seed-syllables, followed by a pair of *kūrca* syllables, and then a pair of *lajjā* syllables;
this knowledge, ending with *svāhā*, is declared to be the bestower of all prosperity. (92)
Now I shall proclaim another knowledge-mantra (vidyā), that nine-syllabled one:

having extracted the root seed-syllable (mūlabīja) followed by two words ending in "Sambuddha" (Omniscient One), this mantra is said to end with "svāhā"; it causes the destruction of all enemies. (93)
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen to the eight-syllable mantra.
One should extract one's own seed-syllable, then the *kūrca* (the "tuft" syllable), and then *māyā*. Extracting those again, ending with *svāhā*, it bestows liberation.
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra] endowed with ten principles:
first the two roots, then the pair of *kūrca*s, and thereafter the two *lajjā*s.
Furthermore, at the end of those very seed-syllables (bījas), there is the fourteen-syllable Vidyā known as Vahnisundarī, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Having extracted the three Brahmās (A, U, Ma) joined with the fire of passion (Ra),
and then the two "beards" of Lajjā (Śrīṃ) conjoined with Nāda and Bindu;
having again extracted them in sequence, the mantra ends with the wife of Fire (Svāhā).
This sixteen-fold Vidyā has been fully described; it is like a wish-fulfilling tree.
In the Māyātantra:
"O Goddess, [the mantra consists of] the Heart [seed-syllable], the Vāgbhava [syllable], followed by the pair of one's own seed-syllables;
then, having uttered the word 'Kālikāyai', at its end is Vahnisundarī. (97)
In another tantra:
