"Namas, the noose and goad twice, phaṭ svāhā, Kāli Kālike! This fifteen-syllable mantra of Kālī has a long *tanucchada* (armour). || 98 ||
O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, their worship should be performed with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
one should perform a recitation (japa) numbering one hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). || 99 ||
The yantra for their worship is described in the Kālītantra:
"First, having inscribed a triangle, one should place another triangle outside of it;
then the practitioner of mantra should indeed draw three excellent triangles."
Then, having drawn a circle, one should draw an eight-petalled [lotus];
having drawn a circle according to the rule, one should draw a single outer square (*bhūpura*).
(From the *Kumārīkalpa*)
In the center, however, is the Vaindava-cakra, adorned with the seed-syllable and Māyā.
Now, regarding Guhyakālī,
the Viśvasāra states: "Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the Vidyā that bestows all fruits."

The Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) Guhyakālī, who directly bestows the fourfold aims of life, destroys great sins, grants all perfections, is eternal, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is exceedingly difficult to attain even within the three worlds. (1)
Having first placed the group beginning with Indra (the letter *i*) along with the *rativindu* (the nasal *m*),
and having then tripled it,
one should extract the syllable of Īśāna (*ha*) joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), and endowed with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
Then, having doubled that [syllable], one should extract the two *īśāna* syllables (*ha* and *sa*),
joined with the left eye (*i*) and fire (*ra*), and endowed with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
Having uttered "O Kālikā" in its [the mantra's] own form, or otherwise, one should speak it in the southern [form].
Then, one should apply the seven seed-syllables (bījas) according to the previous sequence;
this Vidyā, ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), is declared to be the Enchantress of the Three Worlds (Trailokyamohinī).
Alternatively, the mantra is "O Guhyakālike" with two seed-syllables, or "O Dakṣiṇakālike. || 2 ||
Then follows the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), then the *kūrca* (HŪM), and at the end of that, Bhuvaneśvarī.
In the secret [part], "Kālike," and likewise there shall be two seed-syllables.
This Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, has been declared; it is hidden in all the Tantras.
This, however, is declared to be the *Ṣoḍaśī* [yantra], which bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*). (The *Guhyakālī* and other yantras, Figure 35).
Its meaning is as follows:
First one's own seed-syllable, then the *kūrca* (hūṃ), then *māyā* (hrīṃ), then two words of address;
then two of one's own seed-syllables, two *kūrca*s, two *māyā*s, and the beloved of fire (svāhā).
Having omitted two *kāma*-seed-syllables (klīṃ), this becomes the fourteenth *vidyā*.
The words "of this mantra" are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 3 ||

The seven-seed mantra was previously taught; furthermore, O Kālikā, at the end of the secret [mantra], the Vidyā ending in *svāhā* is declared, which is concealed in all Tantras. This too consists of fourteen syllables.
If one omits the word consisting of her name and so forth, then on the right side there are fifteen syllables.
And thus:
"Having uttered the word on the right side, it shall consist of fifteen syllables. (4)
Likewise:
having abandoned the seed-syllable of desire, [there is] the sixteen-syllabled [mantra]. (4)
By this, due to the absence of the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) in the sixteen-syllable vidyā, it becomes fifteen syllables long. || 5 ||
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Kāma, one should place two words ending in "Sambuddhi" (Oṃ);
then, one should again place Kāma at the end of that, followed by the consort of Vahni (Ratī).
This is declared to be the nine-syllabled vidyā of Guhyakālī.
By addressing the word "pada" in the south, there shall be the ten-syllable vidyā.
The worship of these [goddesses] is performed right there. One should perform the group of nyāsas as before and worship Śivā as before;
one should recite the vidyā as before, for everything is indeed just as before.
One should arrange the offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) as previously described. || 7 ||
The mantra for the bali offering is: *Ehyehi jaganmātar jagatāṃ janani gṛhṇa gṛhṇa mama baliṃ siddhiṃ dehi dehi śatrukṣayaṃ kuru kuru hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ phaṭ oṃ*.
*Kālikāyai namaḥ phaṭ svāhā*.
Alternatively, this is the *bali* mantra for Guhyakālī:
*Ehyehi guhyakāli mama baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa mama śatrūn nāśaya*.
Destroy! Devour! Devour! Flash! Flash! Cut! Cut! Grant success! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!
Likewise, this is the mantra for the seat:
Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Guhyakālī, belonging to the great preta Sadāśiva. || 9 ||
The Mantras of Bhadrakālī:
O Pārvatī, listen as the Vidyās of Bhadrakālī and others are described.
One should worship every seed-syllable, beginning with the Kāma-bīja, both before and after [the mantra].
One should likewise join Bhadrakālī, ending in the vocative case (ṅe), in the midst of the seed-syllable.
This supreme Vidyā, consisting of twenty-four syllables, is said to end with Svāhā.
This auspicious Vidyā, Bhadrakālī, bestows the four aims of human life. || 10 ||
Having extracted the seven seeds, and likewise [the syllable] *śmaśānakāli*,
then again the seed in the same sequence ending with *svāhā*— this twenty-one-fold Vidyā is considered the *Śmaśānakālikā*, which bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). (11)
First one should utter the seed-syllables, and after that the word "Mahākālī.
At the end of that are the seven seed-syllables ending with "svāhā," which bestows all accomplishments.
This twenty-syllable great vidyā of Mahākālī is thus proclaimed. (12)
The worship and recitation for these [deities] should be accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
The specific detail is that one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the thunderbolt and the other weapons, within the *bhūpura*.
At the four gates of the *bhūpura*, starting from the east, one should offer: "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva; Oṃ..."
One should worship with "Salutation to Sūrya" and "Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa.
For instance:
[one should worship] the world-protectors (lokapālas) within the earth-pavilion (bhūgṛha), and their weapons outside of that.
And on the *bhūpura*, the wise practitioner should worship in sequence in the four directions;
thereafter, he should worship Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, and Gaṇeśa.
The worship diagram (pūjā-yantra):
a triangle, a hexagon, and a beautiful nine-sided figure;
three circles, and an eight-petaled lotus provided with filaments.

Mounted upon three squares of earth and adorned with the circle of the yoni, this is declared to have fifteen spokes; it is proclaimed in all the Tantras. "Trikoṇam" means having the form of a triangle. (Figure 35)
As for the meditation:
one should visualize the goddess Mahāmeghaprabhā, clad in black garments,
with a flickering tongue, terrible fangs, sunken eyes, and a laughing face.
Adorned with a necklace of serpent-creepers, having the crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
she draws up toward the heavens her single mass of matted hair which itself licks all things;
her body is encircled by a sacred thread of serpents, and she sits upon a bed of serpents.
[She is] Guhyakālikā, who possesses a forest garland joined with fifty skulls, has a large belly,
and has Ananta with a thousand hoods above her head;
she is encircled by the hoods of serpents in the four directions.
Her left bracelet was adorned by Takṣaka, the king of serpents;
her right bracelet was fashioned by Ananta, the king of nāgas;
and she wore jeweled anklets with a girdle and necklace fashioned by a nāga.
On the left is that which is of the nature of Śiva, fashioned in the form of a calf;
one should meditate upon the Goddess as having two arms, wearing a sacred thread made of serpents,
and adorned with earrings and ornaments fashioned from human bodies.
With a serene countenance and gentle appearance, she is adorned with the nine precious gems.
She is served by hosts of sages such as Nārada;
she is enchanting to Śiva, exceedingly formidable with her loud laughter, and the bestower of the desired objects of practitioners.
She bears a single matted lock of hair that, it is implied, reaches up to touch the sky.
"She bears the infinite [serpent] upon her head"—this is the ellipsis.
"Guhyā" (the secret one) is an elliptical designation. 15ka.
Thus ends the section on Śyāmā.
Now, the mantras of Tārā:
Now I shall proclaim the mantras of Tāriṇī, which bestow all accomplishments;
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner becomes liberated while living.
One obtains pure poetry that unfolds without restraint;
one attains scholarship in all sciences and becomes a lord of wealth through riches. (2)
At the royal gate, in the assembly hall, in disputes, and in legal proceedings—everywhere he attains victory like another Bṛhaspati. (3)

Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one takes the letter *ta* conjoined with fire (*ra*), and further conjoined with Māyā, the Bindu, and Īśa (*ha*); this is the second seed-syllable extracted.
The third shall be the Kūrca seed-syllable (*Hūṃ*), followed by the syllable *phaṭ*.
But one whose mantra is fully perfected is endowed with the five rays;
"five rays" means the five syllables. || 4 ||
Likewise:
because she bestows speech through her divine play, she is Nīlasarasvatī;
because she saves [beings], she is always Tārā, the bestower of blissful liberation.
Because she delivers from fierce calamities, she is celebrated as Ugratārā. || 5 ||
In the *Tārārṇava*: "Since the lore propitiated by Vasiṣṭha does not yield fruit quickly,
for that reason a most terrible curse was pronounced even by that sage."
From that time forward, this knowledge has not been fruitful for anyone.
He states the removal of the curse:
"The seed-syllable of the Moon (caṃ) is joined above the seed-syllable situated within *trapā* (hrīṃ);
from that time forth, this Vidyā has been illustrious like a bride."
This knowledge is the bearer of fruit for all sciences; it is victorious for those who desire victory. It is the knowledge that destroys poison and bestows immortality.
Merely by knowing this mantra, one becomes a conqueror upon the earth. (7)
In the *Ekavīrākalpa*:
"The seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjā*), the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū*), the seed-syllable of the tuft (*kūrca*), and likewise *phaṭ*.
Thus is the five-syllabled mantra (*vidyā*) that reveals the five elements."
The seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū*) is *strīṃ*.
Thus it is said in the Viśvasāra:
"O Maheśānī, the *satarī* is proclaimed to be the seed-syllable of the bride. (8)

Likewise, in the Ekavīrākalpa: "The seed-syllable of the bride (vadhūbīja) is said to be the sixteenth consonant (kṣa), adorned with the fire (ra), the left eye (ī), and the bindu (ṃ), mounted upon the moon-seed (sa)."
The moon is the letter *sa*. || 9 ||
In the Nīlatantra: "This Tārā and others possess five colors, as does Nīlasarasvatī;
she consists of all languages, is pure, and is saluted by all the Āmnāyas. (10)
In the *Tārārṇava*:
"Having extracted the one following *aṇu* (the letter *i*), and thereafter the one following *māyā* (the letter *ī*),
mounted upon the fifth of *pa* (the letter *pha*), it is proclaimed as having five rays."

After that, the single-syllable mantra situated in the midst of the *jīvanī* follows; then, O Goddess, one should bestow the weapon-mantra (*astra*) known as *ugradarpa*. With the syllable *strīṃ*, there is everywhere the removal of curses. || 11 ||
Regarding the five-syllabled mantra, it is stated in the Tantra: "When the Vidyā begins with the seed-syllable Śrī, then Śrī is present in every direction.
Indeed, this same Great Vidyā, when preceded by Māyā, grants all desired objects."

When this Vidyā begins with the Vāgbhava syllable, it bestows the status of Lord of Speech; when it consists of a single matted lock (Eka-jaṭā) preceded by Tāra, it grants great liberation to the virtuous. When devoid of the Astra-mantra and consisting of three syllables, it is Mahānīla-sarasvatī.
This is declared as Kullukā, hidden in all tantras;
it is the Māyā situated within the Jīvanī.
As it is stated in the *Saṅketacandrodaya*:
"Hṛllekhā, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhuvanā, Devīśvarī, Hrīṃ, Mahāmāyā, she who dwells in the midst of life, the sustainer of the three worlds, the Supreme Lady, the Transcendent."
This has come down through tradition and been attained in many ways due to differences of opinion;
this is the Pañcākṣarī. 13.
He says that very thing: "The five-syllabled Ekajaṭā is Maheśvarī in the absence of Tārā;
but when preceded by Tārā, O Goddess, she becomes the illustrious Nīlasarasvatī."
Ugratārā, the three-syllabled [Vidyā], Mahānīlasarasvatī, and indeed Ekajaṭā herself, because she is the primordial nature (prakṛti), [are the deities] of other Vidyās as well. || 14 ||
The place for the practice of these vidyās is stated in the *Nīlatantra* and the *Mahāphetkārīya*:
"In a solitary liṅga, or in a cremation ground, or in an empty house, or at a crossroads;
upon a corpse, or on a skull, or in water that does not reach the neck."
Whether on the field of battle, in a vehicle, on dry land, or in a solitary forest—
staying there, the yogi should accomplish the Vidyā who is the sovereign of the three worlds.
In that very place:
"Where one does not perceive another linga within a radius of five krośas, that alone is declared to be a linga; there, the highest siddhi is attained. (16)
Also elsewhere—in a thicket, on a mountain, or in a desolate place, at a crossroads, in a temple, or in an empty, secluded, and solitary dwelling. (17)
Also in the Vīra-tantra:
"If a dull-witted person recites [the mantra] in an empty house, a cremation ground, at a solitary linga,
by a pond, within the Ganges, on a mountain, or anywhere pure and clean, provided he is always endowed with devotion,"

The Lord of the world’s creation, who knows the meaning of all scriptures, shall, through the illustrious Nīlabāṇī-vidyā, become a preeminent yogi at the end of his body and attain the state of supreme bliss, the nirvāṇa of Brahman. || 18 ||
Now, regarding the sipping of water (ācamana) for Tārā,
the Bhairavatantra states: "Having sipped with the three variations of Tārā, one should wash the hands with Māyā."
Having wiped the lips twice with the *strīṃ* and *hūṃ* [mantras], one should wash the hands with *phaṭ* syllables.
Having touched the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, head,
and arms with Vairocana and the other [deities], one is liberated from all sins.
Having sipped water and become Bhairava, one beholds her after a year through the various forms of Tārā—namely, the different forms of Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī. (19)
Vairocana and the others, however, are: Vairocana, Śaṅkhapāṇḍava, Padmanābha, Amitābha, named Māmaka, Tāvaka, (Pāṇḍara and Asitābha), Padmāntaka, and Yamāntaka.
Vighnāntaka and Narāntaka;
these [names] are preceded by the fourth vowel (ū) and the Praṇava (Oṃ), and end with "namaḥ. || 20 ||
Now follows the ritual procedure for her worship:

having completed the morning duties up to the bath, one goes to the place of sacrifice and consecrates the water with the mantra *oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, using that water for the purpose of worship.

Having performed [the preliminary rites] and having cast a small portion into another body of water, one should wash both hands and feet with that very water while reciting: *oṃ hrīḥ viśuddhasarvapāpāni śamaya aśeṣavikalpam apanaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having placed *kulakuśa* grass, gold, and silver respectively upon the index finger and the ring finger, and having sipped water with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, one should contemplate the seat (*pīṭha*).
The specific procedure is stated in the *Kumārītantra*: "O Goddess of the Gods,
having risen from the water after bathing, having put on two garments,
and having applied the sectarian mark (*tilaka*) according to one's family tradition, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)."
Likewise:
O Maheśvarī, having taken a conch with water in one's hand and gone to the door,
one should wash one's hands and feet according to the method that will be described.
In the Matsyasūkta:
"Tāraṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" is the consecration of the water.
Likewise:
At the end of *tāram* and *lajjāviśuddhā*, and indeed at the end of all *pāni*,
one should utter the word *vikalpa* at the end of *śamayā* and at the end of *svaśeṣā*.
*apanayānte dharma phaṭ svāhā* for the purification of the path;
*tāram māyā ca vahnijāyā* is remembered as the mantra for sipping water (*ācamana*). These are the *kulakuśas*.
Gold and silver are prescribed for rites such as recitation (japa) and worship;
they are said to perform the functions of *kuśa* grass, yet wild *kuśa* grasses are not truly *kuśa*.
Silver should be worn on the index finger, and gold should be worn on the ring finger.
As for the seat:
having visualized a cremation ground there, one should remember a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) therein;
at its root is a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems.
Richly adorned with various ornaments and graced by sages and gods,
it was surrounded on all sides by auspicious female spirits rejoicing in flesh and bones;
and in the four directions, it was decorated with corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, charcoal, and bones.
In the center of that, one should visualize the deity through the yoga of meditation as previously described.
Having meditated thus, one should bind the topknot while reciting: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

"Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"— by sprinkling water with this, one should purify the ground. "Oṃ sarvān vighnānutsāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"— with this, by casting unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while forming the *nārāca-mudrā*, one should dispel the three kinds of obstacles.
One should clear away [obstacles] from the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms.

Having consecrated the ground with "Oṃ pavitravajrabhūme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should spread out seats such as cushions made of soft wool or other suitable materials for the practice, and then [recite] "Oṃ āḥ."

Having worshipped that [mandala] with flowers and other offerings while reciting "surekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should sit there according to the sequence beginning with the svastika. || 21 ||
Thus it is said in the *Matasyasūkta*:
"Seated upon soft and gentle woolen blankets or upon a grass mat, one may accomplish the highest perfection."

The *Śrīkrama* states the characteristics of the "tender" (*komala*) and other [types of corpses]: "From the interval of five years until death, [the corpse of] a child who has not yet received the top-knot ceremony (*acūḍaka*);
from six months until ten months prior [to death]."
A child who has died while still in the womb, or up to the eighth month of gestation—
this is called "tender" (komala) when placed upon a seat or upon kusha grass.
And so it is stated in the Nīlatantra:
A boy who has undergone the *cūḍā* ceremony but whose *upanayana* initiation has not yet been performed—
if he dies in his fifth year, they know him as *komala*.
"In the fifth year" means when the fifth year is completed.
He states the measurement of the seat:
"One should prepare a square seat measuring one cubit or two cubits on all sides; once it is purified, one should then perform the cleansing and the worship."
The seat may also be the skin of a black antelope, a tiger, or other such animals.
As it is stated in the Tantra:
"The skin of a black antelope or a leopard, with the head intact," and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "on the seats" (*viṣṭareṣu*) and so forth:
having fashioned a *vaṭuka* from a hundred blades of *kuśa* grass, one should perform the consecration of the breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for the corpse therein as follows:

One should perform the mantra: *oṃkāram āḥ surekhe vajrarekhe*, followed by *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* upon the corpse-seat (*śavāsana*) of the maṇḍala. Having sat down in the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), one should likewise worship the seat itself.
One should draw a mandala that is square and has four doors.
Then, one should tie a protective knot at the end of the cloth with the mantra: *oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
With *oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should purify body, speech, and mind through pervasion. With *oṃ puṣpaketurājārhate śatāya samyaksambuddhāya oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpabhūṣite*.
One should consecrate the flower with the mantra *puṣpacayāvakīrṇe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, upon a seat made of gold or other materials, smeared with yellow orpiment, saffron, and so forth, [one should recite]: *oṃ āḥ surekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
By means of the mantra, one should draw the yantra consisting of an inverted triangle, within which is an eight-petaled lotus, surrounded by a circle and a square provided with four gates.
One should write the syllables of the mantra on the petals of the lotus, starting from the eastern petal. (Figure 36)

And so it is said in the *Kulacuḍāmaṇi*: "Then, having carefully constructed the pedestal with the very essence of the family (*kularasa*), [one should recite]: 'Āḥ, O one of beautiful lines, O one of adamantine lines! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā.'"
Having drawn an eight-petaled,
beautiful, square mandala with four gates using this mantra— with *kularasa* and *svayambhūrasa*— one should thus delineate the mandala. (21 kha)
Regarding the method of writing the syllables, the *Phetkārīya* states:
"Then, having prepared a soft seat, one should draw an eight-petaled circle with sandalwood paste; one should then write the *māyā* [syllable] on the eastern petal."
One should write the seed-syllable *pha* in the second [position], *u* in the north, and *ṭa* in the west;
one should write the seed-syllable *tāra* (om) in the center, and then perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
In the second [position], that is, the south, one writes *tāra*, because Tārā is associated with the *praṇava* (the syllable *hūṃ*).

The syllable *ṭaṃ* is in the western part, the *kūrca* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) at the edge of the petals, and two *bhūpura*s (circles) [are drawn] outside; this is according to the statement of Bhairavī. Some maintain that there is a lotus accompanied by a hexagon in the center.
As it has been said:
"One should likewise draw the yantra with a lotus situated within a hexagon, followed by two earth-mandalas (circles),
and then a square with four doors."
The writing of the seed-syllable is as before. || 22 ||
In the *Nīlatantra* as well, he describes a special yantra for those seeking the grace of Sarasvatī:
"The sky (0) and the moon (1), followed by the sixty-fourth letter (Ṭha), with filaments shimmering from pairs of vowels,
petals shining with the unfolding of the consonant groups, and entirely encircled by the abode of the earth (La)."

This supreme yantra of the Blue-Body Lord, shining with the excellent colors of the Moon and the Lord of Stars (the Sun) and beautified by its triangles, is declared to bestow the accomplishment of all aims. 23.
Or, having drawn the yantra in this manner, one should worship the pīṭha.
And likewise, in the Kumārīkalpa:
Then, having placed the arghya vessel, one should worship the gatekeepers:
Gaṇeśa preceded by the seed-syllable *gaṃ*, likewise Vaṭuka preceded by *vāṃ*,
Kṣetrapāla preceded by *kṣāṃ*, and Yoginī preceded by *yāṃ*.
The wise one should worship [the deities] in the east, west, south, and north; everywhere, one should worship with [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "namaḥ. || 24 ||
In the Tantra:
"All of them are enriched by the vowels and long vowels, preceded by the seed-syllables of the Śaktis.
For example:

At the eastern door of the pedestal: Oṃ hrīṃ gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa; at the south of the pedestal: Oṃ hrīṃ vāṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka; at the west of the pedestal: Oṃ hrīṃ kṣāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla.
To the north of the pedestal: Oṃ hrīṃ yāṃ, obeisance to the Yoginīs. In the center: Oṃ, obeisance to the cremation ground; Oṃ, obeisance to the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
At its base: obeisance to the jewel-pedestal (maṇipīṭha).
Thus, homage to the various ornaments;
to the various sages; to the various gods;
and to the jackals rejoicing in the abundant flesh and bones.
From the corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, charcoal, and bones in the four directions;

then, in the eight petals beginning with the fire [direction], [one should worship]: *oṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ*, and likewise for Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi; in the center, *hsauḥ*.
Salutation to Sadāśiva, the great preta, seated upon the lotus throne.
As it is stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*: "Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, and likewise Prīti."
Fame, Peace, Contentment, and Nourishment— these are the eight powers;
they are declared to be the six powers of the goddess Nīlasarasvatī in the Vīratantra.
In the midst of that, one should worship the vehicle of the Goddess, which is indeed a corpse. || 25 ||
Then one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
It is as follows:
having placed both hands palms-upward upon one's own lap, by means of the mantra "Haṃsa," [one should awaken] the *Kulakuṇḍalinī*.

Having joined the individual soul with the twenty-four principles in reverse order through the path of the *suṣumṇā* into the Supreme Self, the Supreme Śiva, who resides in the head, one should meditate on the syllable *hrīṃ*,
red in color, at the navel, while performing sixteen recitations of it during the inhalation (*pūraka*).

Having completely incinerated the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) with the fire produced from that [syllable], one should contemplate a yellow-colored syllable *strīṃ* in the heart; then, by means of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), through the recitation of that [syllable] sixty-four times,
one should disperse the ashes with the wind produced therefrom, and [contemplate] a white-colored syllable *hūṃ*.

Having visualized [the deity] at the head, one should bathe that entire body— which has become free from all suffering— with the nectar produced by the thirty-two-fold recitation performed during the exhalation (recaka), thereby flooding the bones with that nectar.
And thus says the Śruti:
"The thirty-six principles constitute the body.
Therefore, one should contemplate the Self as free from suffering and stainless, through its non-difference from the Deity.

In that all-pervading water, one should meditate on a red lotus arising from the syllable *āḥ*, and upon it, a white lotus arising from the syllable *ṭāṃ*; and upon that, a blue-colored *hūṃ* syllable; and above that, one should meditate on a flaying knife adorned with the syllable *hūṃ*. || 26 ||
Having meditated upon the deity above that, one should establish the vital breaths by reciting "ĀṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ SVĀHĀ" eleven times and then meditate.
As it is said in the Phetkārīya:
Having meditated on the syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ), red in color, at the navel,
one should then contemplate the white body consisting of karma as being consumed by the fire produced from it.
Then, [one should meditate on] the syllable *strīṃ* (strīṃ), yellowish in appearance, at the heart, and by the wind arising from it...
Having scattered the ashes, one should then contemplate on the forehead the *kūrca* mantra,
which has the color of snow; having flooded those bones with the nectar arising from it,
one should then contemplate oneself [as being so drenched].
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), which is free from all suffering, stainless, and composed of the deity,
one should contemplate the universe as empty;
[one should contemplate] the self as untainted, devoid of qualities, pure, and composed of the deity.
Then, one should meditate on a red lotus arising from the syllable *āḥ* in the intermediate space;
furthermore, one should meditate on a white lotus above that, arising from the syllable *ṭāṃ*;
and above that, one should again meditate on the syllable *hūṃ*, which has the appearance of blue.
Then one should visualize a flaying knife born from the syllable *hūṃ*, adorned with the seed-syllable;
upon that flaying knife, one should meditate on oneself as being composed of Tāriṇī. (26a)
She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, fierce, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
she is short-statured, pot-bellied, and terrifying, with a tiger skin wrapped around her waist;
endowed with the bloom of fresh youth, she is adorned with the five mudrās.
Four-armed, with a protruding tongue, most formidable, and bestowing boons;
her two right arms are equipped with a sword and a chisel,
and she is endowed with a pair of left hands holding a skull-cup and a blue lotus.
One should meditate on her with a single tawny, fierce matted lock, adorned at the crown of her head by Akṣobhya;
she is adorned with three eyes shaped like the orb of the rising sun,
situated in the midst of a blazing funeral pyre, possessing terrible fangs, and appearing formidable.
Her face is smiling with intense passion, and she is adorned with the ornaments of women;
she stands upon a white lotus within the waters that pervade the universe. Akṣobhya, assuming the form of a three-bodied serpent, rests upon the head of the Goddess.
"Adorned with the five mudrās" means that she is decorated with five skulls joined by four bands of white bone on the forehead;
as stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "She is beautified by five skulls joined by bands of white bone."
The venerable Śaṅkarācārya has also said: "She who wears upon her forehead a variegated garland of bones, and bears a formidable skull accompanied by five [elements]. || 27 ||
Then follows *prāṇāyāma*: having recited the root mantra four times while holding the left nostril, one should fill the air.
Thereafter, holding both nostrils, one should retain the breath (*kumbhaka*) sixteen times.
Thereafter, one should exhale through the right nostril with a cycle of eight counts.

Then, filling again through the right and retaining the breath (kumbhaka), one should exhale through the left. Again, filling through the left and retaining the breath, one should exhale through the right.
Thus, there are three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 28 ||
Then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth:
"Homage to the seer Akṣobhya on the head;
homage to the Vṛhatī metre on the mouth."
Salutation to the glorious Ekajaṭā in the heart;
salutation to the seed-syllable HŪṂ at the mūlādhāra; salutation to the Śakti PHAṬ at the feet.
Having pronounced the remaining syllables, [one says]: "Salutation to the Kīlaka in all limbs.
And likewise in the Vīratantra:
"Akṣobhya is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], and Bṛhatī is declared to be its meter (chandas)."
The goddess Nīlasarasvatī is concealed within the three worlds;
the seed-syllable HŪṂ is her mantra-power, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life. (29)
Then follows the placement of the Mātṛkās as taught in the Kālītantra.
As it has been said:
"As it is with Kālī, so it is with Nīlā; one should place the Mātṛkās according to that sequence."
Namely: aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ namo hṛdi;
eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ namo dakṣabhuje.
Ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ namo on the left arm;
ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ namo.
On the right calf: maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ; on the left calf: [the same]. || 30 ||
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *hrāṃ akhilavāgrūpiṇyai aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *hrīṃ akhaṇḍavāgrūpiṇyai tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*.
Hrūṃ, to her whose form is the speech of Brahmā, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers; hraiṃ, to her whose form is the speech of Viṣṇu, hūṃ to the two ring fingers;
hrauṃ, to her whose form is the speech of Rudra, vauṣaṭ to the two little fingers.
HRAḤ SARVAVĀGRŪPIṆYAI KARATALAPṚṢṬHĀBHYĀM PHAṬ.
In this same manner, [the mantra is applied] to the heart and other [limbs].
The regulation of the fingers has already been explained previously.
Now, regarding the side of Nīlasarasvatī,
it is stated accordingly in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
"Having uttered [the mantra] whose form is the entirety of speech, one should say 'namas' to the heart."
"Vāgrūpiṇī" is for the head; "Vahnivallabhā," having uttered "Brahmavāgrūpiṇī," is for the crest-lock with "Vaṣaṭ";
and having pronounced "Viṣṇuvāgrūpiṇī," one should utter "Hūṃ" for the armor.
One should also say "to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ" for the one whose form is the speech of Rudra;
then, having said "whose form is all speech," one should remember "to the weapon, phaṭ."
At the end of the seed-syllable containing the six long vowels, one should join the name ending in the dative case (ṅe).
This, however, pertains to the tradition of Nīlasarasvatī;
elsewhere, it is: *hrāṃ ekajaṭāyai aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
Hrīṃ tāriṇyai, svāhā to the two index fingers; hrūṃ vajrodake, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers;
hraiṃ ugrajaṭe, hūṃ to the two ring fingers.
Hrauṃ mahāpratisare, with the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ!
Hraḥ piṅgograikajaṭe, with the palms and backs of the hands, phaṭ!
Thus [the mantras are applied] to the heart and other [limbs].
And likewise, concerning Ekajaṭā, it is stated in the Nīlatantra: "At the end of the seed-syllable, 'Ekajaṭāyai' is proclaimed as the heart-mantra;
'Tāriṇyai' is likewise for the head, and 'Vajrodake' is for the topknot."
The armor (kavaca) is assigned to Ugrajaṭā, and likewise the great Pratisarā;
similarly, Piṅgograikajaṭā is proclaimed as the eye (netra), and the weapon (astra).
At the end of the seed-syllables containing the six long vowels, one should append the name ending in the dative case (ṅe). (31ka)
Since they were not mentioned here, the *pīṭhanyāsa* and *mātṛkānyāsa* have not been written down.
And so it is said in the *Phetkārīya*:
"A wise person should perform exactly what is stated here; he should not introduce anything else."
Therefore, one who desires the fruits [of practice] should perform the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa) of Tārā.
(32) I shall proclaim the sixfold [placement] of Tārā, which is hidden in all tantras, which pacifies all obstacles, and which destroys all sins. (33)
It eternally pacifies great poverty, bestows all prosperity,
grants all desires, and confers universal sovereignty.
To a disciple who is endowed with devotion, humble, high-souled, generous, of noble birth, and devoted to pure conduct; (35)
Having performed it in this manner, O Goddess of gods, one should reveal it to the practitioner.
"Otherwise, there would be a loss of spiritual attainment"; thus was the command issued by the Śaṅkaras. || 37 ||
The first placement is with the Rudras; the second is considered to be with the Planets (Grahas);
the third should be with the World-Protectors (Lokapālas); the fourth is with Śiva’s Power (Śakti);
the fifth should be with the Tārā-mantras and so forth; and the sixth is said to be with the Sacred Seats (Pīṭhas).
Together with that one, the Rudras are proclaimed to be fifty.

O Goddess, the wise one should sequentially perform the placement (nyāsa) using the letters of the Mātṛkā joined with the Bindu, preceded by the three-syllable seed-mantra, ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), and concluding with *namaḥ*. This three-syllabled Tāriṇī is said to be the destroyer of the bonds of worldly existence.

Having meditated for a long time with a concentrated mind upon Tāriṇī— blue in color, three-eyed, seated upon a corpse, wearing various ornaments, and adorned with Akṣobhya upon her crown— [one should proceed]. 39.
Now follows the Rudranyāsa: Hrīṃ Stroṃ Hrūṃ Aṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭheśa; with these and other such [syllables], one should perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās.
Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ āṃ, obeisance to Ananteśa; hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ iṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣmeśa; hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ īṃ, obeisance to Trimūrtīśa; hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ uṃ, obeisance to Amareśa.

Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ ūṃ, obeisance to Arghīśa. Likewise: 3 ṛṃ, obeisance to Bhārabhūtīśa; 3 ṝṃ, obeisance to Atithīśa; 3 ḷṃ, obeisance to Sthāṇukeśa; 3 ḹṃ, obeisance to Hareśa; 3 eṃ, obeisance to Jhiṇṭīśa; 3 aiṃ...
To Bhautikeśa, 3; Oṃ Sadyojāteśa, 3; Auṃ Anugraheśa, 3; Aṃ Akrūreśa, 3; Aḥ Mahāseneśa, 3; Kaṃ Krodhīśa, 3; Khaṃ Caṇḍeśa, 3; Gaṃ Pañcāntakeśa, 3; Ghaṃ Śivottameśa, 3.
Ṅaṃ to Ekarudreśa, 3 caṃ to Kūrmeśa, 3 chaṃ to Ekanetreśa, 3 jaṃ to Caturānaneśa, 3 jhaṃ to Ajeśa, 3 ñaṃ to Sarveśa, 3 ṭaṃ to Someśa, 3 ṭhaṃ to Lāṅgalīśa, 3 ḍaṃ to Dārukeśa, 3 ḍhaṃ...
To Arddhanārīśvareśa, 3 ṇaṃ to Umākānteśa, 3 taṃ to Āṣāḍhīśa, 3 thaṃ to Daṇḍīśa, 3 daṃ to Adrīśa, 3 dhaṃ to Mīneśa, 3 naṃ to Meṣeśa, 3 paṃ to Lohiteśa, 3 phaṃ to Śikhīśa.
3 BAṂ to Chagalaṇḍeśa; 3 BHAṂ to Dviraṇḍeśa; 3 MAṂ to Mahākāleśa; 3 YAṂ to Bālīka; 3 RAṂ to Bhujaṅgeśa; 3 LAṂ to Pinākīśa; 3 VAṂ to Khaḍgīśa; 3 ŚAṂ to Vakeśa; 3 YAṂ.
To Śveteśa, 3; to Bhṛgvīśa, 3; to Nakulīśa, 3; to Śiveśa, 3; to Saṃvartakeśa, 3. Thus ends the Rudra-nyāsa. || 40 ||
Now, the placement of the planets (*grahanyāsa*): One should place the red Sun in the heart with the vowels preceded by the three syllables.
One should place the white Moon between the eyebrows with the *avagaṇa*.
One should place the red Maṅgala with the *ka*-group in the three eyes;
likewise, one should place the dark-blue Budha with the *ca*-group in the heart-mandala;
and [one should place] the yellow Bṛhaspati with the *ṭa*-group in the hollow of the throat.
One should then place Śukra, white in appearance, with the *tavarga* in the region of the throat;
Śanaiścara, blue in color, with the *pavarga* in the region of the navel;
and Rāhu, smoke-colored, with the *yavarga* in the mouth.
And at the two lakṣas in the region of the anus, O fair-faced one, [one should worship] the smoke-colored Ketu.
The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: having meditated upon a red-colored sun at the heart, [one recites] *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ aṃ* (sixteen times) and *sūryāya namaḥ*.
Having meditated on the white-colored Soma between the eyebrows: 3 yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ somāya namaḥ. Having meditated on the red-colored Maṅgala at the three eyes: 3 kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ.
Salutation to Maṅgala.

Having meditated upon Budha, dark in color, in the heart-mandala: *caṃ* 5, salutation to Budha. Having meditated upon Bṛhaspati, yellow in color, in the throat-pit: *ṭaṃ* 5, [salutation] to Bṛhaspati.

Homage! Having visualized the white planet Venus in the region of the throat: *taṃ 5*, homage to Venus (*śukrāya namaḥ*). Having visualized the blue-colored Saturn (*śanaiścara*) in the region of the navel: *paṃ 5*, [homage] to Saturn (*śanaiścarāya*).
Homage!
Having meditated on Rāhu, smoke-colored, in the mouth: 3 yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ, homage to Rāhu.
Having meditated on the smoke-colored Ketu in the anus, [one recites]: "Laṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to Ketu.
Thus ends the placement of the planets (grahanyāsa). 41 ka.
Now, the placement of the world-protectors (lokapālanyāsa): One should place Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, Vibhu,
and Īśāna upon one's own head and in the eight directions in successive order.
One should place Ananta below and Brahmā above; then,

one should perform the placement upon the head and in the eight directions, as well as below and above, using the eight groups of consonants preceded by the three-syllable [mantra] and the short and long vowels— this is the meaning.
The ritual application there is as follows: *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ aṃ āṃ kaṃ 5 indrāya namaḥ*.
The word *namaḥ* is used everywhere.
3 iṃ īṃ caṃ 5 to Agni;
3 uṃ ūṃ ṭaṃ 5 to Yama;
3 ṛṃ ṝṃ taṃ 5 to Nairṛta.
3 ḷṃ ḹṃ paṃ 5 to Varuṇa;
eṃ aiṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ to Vāyu;
3 oṃ auṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ to Kubera.
3 aṃ aḥ laṃ kṣaṃ to Īśāna; 3 to Ananta below; 3 to Brahmā above.
Thus ends the ritual assignment (nyāsa) of the world-protectors (lokapāla). || 42 ||
Now, the ritual placement of Śiva and Śakti (Śiva-śakti-nyāsa): Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; beyond that, O Goddess, is Paraśiva—these are proclaimed as the six Śivas. || 43 ||
One should place Brahmā together with Ḍākinī at the Mūlādhāra;
in all cases, having uttered the three-syllable mantra, [one should assign] the letters from *va* to *sa*, accompanied by the bindu.
Having likewise assigned the wheel called Svādhiṣṭhāna along with Viṣṇu and the letter Ā, as well as the letters from va to la,
one should then assign [the letters] at the Maṇipūraka in the navel.
One should place Rudra together with the letters from Ḍa to Pha, as well as Lākinī; and in the Anāhata [cakra], one should place Īśvara together with the letters from Ka to Tha, as well as Kākinī.
Then, in the great cakra called Viśuddha, which is conjoined with the sixteen vowels,
one should install Sadāśiva and Śākinī as before.
O Goddess of the gods, one should install the supreme Śiva, whose form is Brahman, accompanied by Hākinī and endowed with the letters Ha and Kṣa, in the Ājñā-cakra. (48)
Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*):
At the *mūlādhāra*, [one recites] *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ*, [and says] "Salutation to Brahmā together with the *Ḍākinī*."
In the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra]: 3 vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ; obeisance to Viṣṇu together with Rākiṇī.
In the Maṇipūra [cakra]: 3 ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ.
Salutation to Rudra accompanied by Lākinī.
In Anāhata: 3 kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ; salutation to Īśvara accompanied by Kākinī.
To the one named Viśuddha, 3 aṃ 16, together with Śākinī, obeisance to Sadāśiva.
To the Ajñā-cakra, 3 haṃ kṣaṃ, together with Hākinī, obeisance to Paraśiva.
Thus ends the Śiva-Śakti Nyāsa. || 49 ||
Now, the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with Tārā:
Tārā, Ugrā, Mahogrā, Vajrā, Kālī,
Sarasvatī, Kāmeśvarī, and Cāmuṇḍā— these eight are considered to be Tāriṇī.
First, having uttered the syllable of Tāriṇī at the beginning, one should then sequentially assign [the mantras] starting with *tara*,
preceded by meditation, ending in the dative case (*ṅe*) and followed by *namaḥ*, adorned with the eight groups of vowels and the nasal drop (*bindu*).
One should place [the seed-syllables] at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), on the forehead, between the eyebrows, in the cavity of the throat,
in the heart, at the region of the navel, in the generative organ, and in the foundation (ādhāra).
The application is as follows:

At the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra): *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ aṃ* (16 times), *namaḥ* to Tārā. At the forehead: *3 kaṃ* (5 times), *namaḥ* to Ugrā. Between the eyebrows: *3 caṃ* (5 times), *namaḥ* to Mahogrā.
At the hollow of the throat: Oṃ 3 Ṭaṃ 5, obeisance to Vajrā. At the heart: Oṃ 3 Taṃ 5, obeisance to Kālī. At the region of the navel: Oṃ 3 Paṃ 5, obeisance to Sarasvatī.
At the *liṅga*: 3 yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ, obeisance to Kāmeśvarī.
At the *mūlādhāra*: 3 śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ, obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā.
Thus ends the Tārā-nyāsa. || 50 ||
Now, the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa):
Kāmarūpa at the mūlādhāra, likewise Jālandhara in the heart,
the one called Pūrṇagiri on the forehead, and Uḍḍīyāna above that.
One should designate Vārāṇasī between the eyebrows, Māyāvatī within the three eyes as they blaze, Madhupurī at the circumference of the face,
Ayodhyā in the region of the navel, and Kāñcī at the hips.
These ten principal seats (pīṭhas) are known in their sequence;
one should install them in order, ending with "namaḥ," differentiated by short and long vowels.
Now, the ritual application (prayoga):
At the *mūlādhāra*: *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ aṃ āṃ kaṃ 5*, obeisance to the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Kāmarūpa. At the heart: [3] *iṃ īṃ caṃ*, obeisance to the sacred seat of Jālandhara.
On the forehead: 3 uṃ ūṃ ṭaṃ 5, salutation to Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha.
Above the forehead: 3 ṛṃ ṝṃ taṃ 5, salutation to Uḍḍīyāna-pīṭha.
Between the eyebrows: 3 ḷṃ ḹṃ paṃ 5, salutation to Vārāṇasī-pīṭha.
At the three eyes (3): *eṃ aiṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*, salutation to the seat of Jvalantī (*jvalantīpīṭhāya namaḥ*).
At the circle of the face (3): *oṃ auṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ*, salutation to the seat of Māyāvatī (*māyāvatīpīṭhāya namaḥ*).
At the throat (3): *aṃ aḥ laṃ kṣaṃ*, salutation to the seat of Madhupurī (*madhupurīpīṭhāya namaḥ*).
At the region of the navel: 3. Salutation to Ayodhyā-pīṭha.
At the hips: 3. Salutation to Kāñcī-pīṭha. || 51 ||
Thus, the sixteenfold [mantra] of Tārā, which bestows all accomplishments, has been fully explained;
by the grace of this ritual placement (nyāsa), one becomes Akṣobhya among all living beings.
Thus ends the Tāroṣoḍā in the Rudrayāmala. Another method [is found] in the Kālītantra:
Having interspersed them with the mantra, one should place the Mātṛkā in six ways;
O lady of excellent hips, this is proclaimed as the Tārā-ṣoḍhā (the sixfold placement of Tārā), performed both in direct and reverse order.
When this excellent Nyāsa is performed, all sin is destroyed;
he becomes worthy of worship by the Yoginīs—he is not a mere mortal, but a god. (54)
O Maheśānī, he whom those whose forms are encapsulated by the six syllables bow down to shall immediately become short-lived; the deity trembles with fear.
For him, there is no one worthy of worship in the worlds, not even his own father or mother, who shine as his foremost kin.
As it is said in another Tantra:
"One should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the emission-vowel (visarga) accompanied by the process of emanation; one should place the vowel 'i' ending in the bindu with the process of withdrawal.
One should place the letters beginning with 'ḍa' accompanied by the bindu and the emission-vowel according to the path of maintenance. (56)

The withdrawal of the withdrawal, the nourishment of the sons of creation, and the placement of peace for the sake of maintenance; therefore, it is considered that the ritual action is threefold. (57)
They say that this ritual of placement (nyāsa) is prescribed for the Maskarins and Vaikhānasas as ending with reabsorption (saṃhāra);
for householders (gṛhamedhin), it ends with maintenance (sthiti); and for those belonging to the [other] orders (varṇin), it ends with emanation (sṛṣṭi). || 58 ||

Some teachers say that for a householder endowed with dispassion, [the stages] end with withdrawal (saṃhāra); for one who has known the Innate (sahajāna), they reside in forest-dwelling; and for seekers of knowledge, there is creation (sṛṣṭi). 59.
By this, it should be performed according to the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭi), maintenance (sthiti), and withdrawal (saṃhṛti).
The phrase "and in six ways" means by the reverse order of emanation, maintenance, and so forth.
Emanation consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
Stability consists of the letters from Ḍa to Tha;
dissolution consists of the letters from Kṣa to A. || 60 ||
Now, the internal sixfold [division].
It is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Listen, O Goddess, beloved; I shall proclaim the secret sixfold [division] of the seasons."
This [method] for the purification of the body of the minister is not to be disclosed anywhere;
the *praṇava* (oṃ) is enclosed by the letters of the *mātṛkā* at the locus of the *mātṛkā*. 61.
O Pārvatī, one should place the syllable enclosed by that very [seed] right there;
likewise, O Goddess, the Māyā-bīja should be deposited with effort. (62)
Likewise, one should place the seed-syllable of the bride with a well-concentrated mind;
and likewise, O Goddess, the seed-syllable of the *kūrca* should be placed in its entirety.
And having likewise deposited the entire weapon-mantra immediately thereafter,
O Goddess, this Guhya-ṣoḍhā must never be disclosed. Even if there is no worship nor recitation of mantras, it must necessarily be performed every day.
Alternatively, the Kālī-Ṣoḍhā should be performed.
As it is stated in the Yāmala:
"The Guhya-Ṣoḍhā should always be practiced for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra of Tāriṇī."
Or else, O Goddess, there is neither worship nor recitation of the Sixfold Kālī.

Then, having recited the root mantra, one should perform the three pervasive placements (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*): from the head down to the feet and from the feet up to the head; and from the heart down to the mouth and from the mouth up to the heart.
Alternatively, one may perform the pervasive placement seven or five times with the root mantra encased by the *praṇava*.
One should perform it.
As stated in the Phetkārīya:
"Having encased it with the syllable *oṃ*, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the mantra. (66)
Then follows the placement of the *arghya* (offering water).
As follows:
having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square on one's left, [place] the vessel with its base (*sādhāra*) therein.

Having placed the vessel and filled it with water and other substances using the root-vidyā, having empowered the water with the water-mantra, and having cast red sandalwood, bilva leaves, and so forth into it,
one should [offer] to the Arghya in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in the center and the cardinal points, [reciting]: *hrīṃ akhilavāgrūpiṇyai*.
Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*) with "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth, or alternatively with "Hrāṃ Ekajaṭāyai" and so forth,
one should cover the *arghya* vessel with the *matsya-mudrā* and recite the root mantra ten times.
And thus it is said in the *Kālītantra*:
One should recite the vidyā ten times for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.
Then, having protected it with the Astra-mantra and displayed the Dhenu-mudrā, one should visualize that water as consisting of light,
pour a little into the prokṣaṇī vessel, and [sprinkle] oneself with that water.
Having sprinkled the articles of worship, one should begin the worship;
or else, immediately after the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
And so it is stated in the *Phetkārīya*:
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should carry out the installation of the water-offering (arghya) and other requisites.
Having then performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth.
Then, having fashioned a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should meditate upon the deity as non-different from oneself. || 67 ||
As follows: Parā, who stands with her foot placed in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon the heart of a corpse, whose terrible *aṭṭahāsa* laughter resounds,
who holds a sword, a blue lotus, a flaying knife, and a skull-cup in her hands, and who arises from the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*.

Dwarfish, with large blue eyes and joined by a single matted lock of hair containing tawny snakes, the fierce Tārā herself, having cast her lethargy into the skull-bowl, destroys the three worlds. 68.

Having meditated thus, and having visualized the *mātṛkā* yantra within a handful of flowers as red as the rays of the sun mingled with *dūrvā* grass, unhusked grains, and red sandalwood held in the hand,
[one should contemplate] from the heart [the goddess] consisting of the splendor of the root mantra, composed of pure gnosis and consciousness.
Having reached the Supreme Śiva within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the head by means of piercing the six cakras,
and having come to rest in that ocean of nectar through the continuous performance of the ritual action (kriyā-samabhivyāhāra).

Having brought that [deity], who has become one with that nectar and consists of consciousness and bliss, from the flowing nostril-passage, one should invoke her into the form fashioned by the root mantra.
And so it is said in another tantra:
Having brought the Goddess through the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
one should meditate on her as she flows out through the nostril while remaining within one's own joined palms;
then, having placed her upon the flower, one should deposit that flower upon the image or other representation.
Oṃ! O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue:
as long as I worship you, remain steadfast.
Having performed the rites of invocation and so forth according to the previously mentioned sequence, [one should display] the five mudrās, beginning with the yoni-mudrā.
One should show [the mudrās] together with their seed-syllables. One should display the five mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) mudrā.
Thus it is said in the Bhairavīya.
These, however, are to be sought in the section on mudrās. || 69 ||

Having performed the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) with *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ svāhā*, one should worship with either the sixteen or five offerings, reciting the root mantra followed by: *śrīmadekajaṭe vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The procedure for this is as follows: first the root mantra, then having uttered this mantra, [one says] "this substance, obeisance to such-and-such deity."
And likewise, in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "Having uttered 'O Śrīmadekajaṭā,' and [the word] 'accept the vajra-flower' (*vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha*),
one should perform the worship after pronouncing [the mantra] beginning with Tārā and ending with the fire-born wife (the *svāhā*)."
The meaning is: *tāra* (oṃ), *kūrca* (hrīṃ), followed by that [mantra], ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*, and concluding with *vahnijāyā* (svāhā).
In a certain ancient ritual manual, it is stated: *oṃ bhagavatyekajaṭe hrīṃ*.
O you whose body is the pure Dharma, pacify all evils, remove all conceptual constructions, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Homage to the Lotus!
*Oṃ tāriṇi hrīṃ*, this is the water for sipping, *svadhā*.
Oṃ hrīṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare, this arghya, svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ kapālike, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), svadhā! Śrīmadekajaṭe, this water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya) with fragrant water, namaḥ!
The distinction between incense and flowers is as follows:
Oṃ, O Supreme Goddess, out of compassion, accept this supreme fragrance which completely fills the quarters with the scent of supreme bliss.
O Śrīmadekajaṭā, this is the fragrance; obeisance!
Likewise: Oṃ, O Supreme Goddess, please accept this flower, born of the fourth forest, enchanting with its various qualities, and possessing the fragrance of bliss.
This composition of words is approved by the masters of the Vidyādharas. || 70 ||
In the *Tāriṇīnirṇaya*: "The Praṇava, then 'O Blessed One, O Ekajaṭā,' then Māyā;
thereafter, from the body of pure dharma, [the word] 'all sins' follows."

"Śamaya sarvavikalpān apanaya hūṃ phaṭ" is the mantra for the head. O Goddess, this is the mantra for the water for the feet; now hear the mantra for the water for rinsing the mouth: "Tāraṃ vajriṇi māyā," that is, the *tāra* (oṃ), then *vajriṇi*, then *māyā*, followed by the *tāra* and then *māyā* again.
"Maṇidhari vajriṇī" is the mantra for Mahāpratisarā;
"Māyā" is the mantra for Kapālinī during the honey-mixture offering, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Then, having displayed the Yoni-mudrā, O Goddess, command the attendants of the Blessed One.
One should perform worship after making the request, "I worship.
It is as follows:
one should worship the six limbs in the filaments—specifically in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions.
For example: Hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart of Ekajaṭā;
Hrīṃ, svāhā to the head of Tāriṇī.
HŪṂ VAJRODAKE ŚIKHĀYAI VAṢAṬ | HRAIṂ UGRAJAṬE KAVACĀYA HUṂ | HRAUṂ MAHĀPRATISARE NETRATRAYĀYA VAUṢAṬ |
In the four directions: *hraḥ piṅgograikajaṭe astrāya phaṭ*.
On the side of Nīlasarasvatī, however, one should worship the six limbs with *hrīṃ akhilavāgrūpiṇyai hṛdayāya namaḥ* and so forth, and place the Akṣobhya-vajra-flower upon the head of the Goddess.
One should worship Akṣobhya with the mantra: *pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, to the north of the pedestal, from the northwest to the northeast, one should worship the lineage of gurus as follows:
"Ūrdhvakeśānandanātha, accept the vajra-flower! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Thus it is stated in the Phetkārīya: "With the mantra 'Accept the vajra-flower! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā'..."
There is no doubt that they differ only in name while being identical in their single mantra.
With this mantra, one should worship all the retinues.
Thus [one worships] Vyomakeśānandanātha, Nīlakaṇṭhānandanātha, and so forth.
One should worship Vṛṣadhvaja and Ānandanātha; these are the Divyaughas. [Then] Vasiṣṭhānandanātha, Kūrmanātha, and Ānandanātha.
One should worship Mīnanāthānandanātha, Maheśvarānandanātha, and Harināthānandanātha;
these are the Siddhaughas.
Likewise, Mother Tārāvatī, Mother Bhānumatī, Mother Jayā, Mother Vidyā, Mother Mahodarī, Sukhānandanātha, Parānandanātha,
Pārijātānandanātha, and Kuleśvarānandanātha.
One should worship Virūpākṣa, Ānandanātha, and Pheravī Ambā;
these belong to the Mānavaugha. 70 ka.
And so it is said in the Tārātantra:
"Now I shall describe the gurus of Tārā, who bestow both seen and unseen fruits:
Ūrdhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Vṛṣadhvaja."
The divine lineages bestow accomplishments, O child; now hear the lineages of the Siddhas according to their true nature:
Vasiṣṭha, Kūrmanātha, Mīnanātha, Maheśvara, and Harinātha. Now hear the human lineages; I shall speak of their gurus.
Tārāvatī, Bhānumatī, Jayā, Vidyā, Mahodarī; Sukhānanda, Parānanda, Pārijāta,
Kuleśvara, Virūpākṣa, and Phera— thus has the Tāriṇī-kula been described.
The gurus, ending with the word Ānandanātha, bestow all accomplishments. Women who are in the form of gurus are proclaimed as ending with the word Ambā.
If one is unable [to worship the full assembly], one should worship Akṣobhya alone.
"One must certainly worship the deity situated upon my crown," according to the words of the Goddess in the *Phetkārīya*.
Then, [one worships] on the petals starting from the east:
Mahākālī, Rudrāṇī, Umā, and likewise Bhīmā;
Ghorā, Bhrāmarī, and Mahārātri as the seventh;
Bhairavī is declared the eighth—one should worship these Yoginīs.
Then, one should worship Vairocana, Śaṅkhapāṇḍava, Padmanābha, and Ansitābha on the four petals starting from the east in counter-clockwise order.
On the petals in the corners beginning with the southeast, one should worship Nāma, Kamaka, Pāṇḍava, and Tāraka.
In the four gates starting from the east, one should worship Padmāntaka, Yamāntaka, Vighnāntaka, and Narāntaka in clockwise order with the mantra "vajrapuṣpa" and so forth.
And likewise, it is said in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
The practitioner of mantra should worship Vairocana, Śaṅkha, Pāṇḍava, Padmanābhaka,
and Asitābha in the four petals starting from the direction of Indra; likewise, he should worship Nāmaka, Māmaka, Pāṇḍava, and Tāraka.
One should worship [the deities] in the four corners beginning with the southeast (vahni) using their respective mantras in sequence.
As stated in the *Nīlatantra*:
"One should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) precisely by way of counter-clockwise rotation."
Having worshipped Vighnāntaka at the eastern gate and so forth, one should then worship Padmāntaka, Yamāntaka, and Narakāntaka. (70kha)
Then follows the offering of the *bali*.
As it is stated in the *Phetkārīya*:
"At the end of worship and at the beginning of a meal, one should cause the *bali* to be given with the mantra. (71)
The procedure there is as follows:
having drawn a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square on one's left, and having worshipped it with flowers,
one places upon it a vessel together with its base, filled with the prescribed sacrificial offerings.
Holding it with the left thumb and ring finger, recite: *oṃ hrīṃ ekajaṭe mahāyakṣādhipataye mayopanītaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya mama sarvaśāntiṃ kuru kuru paravidyāmākṛṣyākṛṣya truṭ*.
Having recited "truṭa chindhi chindhi sarvajagadvaśamānaya hrīṃ svāhā" three times, one should offer the bali-oblation. || 72 ||
Thus it is stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"Having worshipped in this manner, one should draw the pervasive mandala on the left;
one should worship it with flowers after placing the vessel there."
"Having placed the substance deposited in the vessel, the best of practitioners should diligently offer the bali-oblation with the thumb and the ring finger.
Thus it is said.
And so it is stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
"Having first extracted the *praṇava* (oṃ), and after that the *hṛllekhā* (hrīṃ),
one should utter the word 'ekajaṭe' at the end of the phrase, followed by the word 'mahā'."

Having addressed the Lord of Yakṣas with the word *adhipa*, and having uttered the word *dama* from the position [of the mantra], one should say *pada* and then *upanītam*. Having spoken the word *padam* twice, saying "accept the offering" (*baliṃ gṛhṇa*), and having likewise spoken it twice as "cause to accept" (*gṛhṇāpaya*), one should then utter the entire sequence beginning with my word (*mama*).
Recite "śāntiṃ kuru" (grant peace), followed by "paravidyām" (the supreme knowledge).

Then say "dvidhākṛṣya" (having drawn [it] twofold), and likewise "truṭa chindhi" (cut asunder) twice. Then, from the word "sarvādi" (beginning with all), recite "jagadvaśamānaya" (bring the world under control).

The mantra joined with *māyā* (Hrīṃ) and *svāhā* is prescribed for the rite of the bali offering. Thereafter, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times, either in secret, aloud (*nigadena*), in a whisper (*upāṃśunā*), or mentally (*mānasena*).
And so it is said:
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times according to the number of one's lifespans;
or again, O Goddess, one should recite it a thousand times during the rite of daily worship.
If one is unable, one should not recite less than twenty times.
And likewise:
one should recite [the mantra] a thousand, a hundred, or twenty times with the secret rosary. (74)
In that regard, the secret of recitation (*japarahasya*) is as follows:
having visualized the pervasion of the three seed-syllables in the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and *maṇipūraka* respectively— blazing like ten million flashes of lightning and mutually interwoven.
Having meditated upon the syllable *phaṭ*, which consists of all splendor and is the essence of rest, within the heart, one should utter it.
Thus, in the Nīlatantra:
"I shall explain the meditation on the mantra, which bestows omniscience through recitation."
O Great Goddess, since even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified through mantra and meditation,
one should contemplate the *hṛllekhā* at the root-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
and the second [syllable] of yellow color in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
One should meditate on the seed-syllable of the beard (*kūrca-bīja*), resembling a cloud and possessing great luster, at the navel;
and the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astra-bīja*), with a radiance like the fire of time (*kālāgni*), at the heart.
One should then contemplate the entire Vidyā from the root-base (*mūla*) up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Having thus recited according to one's capacity that [mantra] which resembles ten million suns and has been previously beheld by yogis, one should complete the ritual actions beginning with the dedication of the recitation and ending with the dismissal (visarjana). || 75 ||
The procedure for the offering of the recitation (*japasamarpaṇa*) is stated in the *Phetkārīya*:
"Then, with the water of the *arghya* offering, the wise one should offer the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess by means of the mantras that are more secret than the secret. (76)
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said: "Having performed [the preliminary rites] in this manner, one who eats sacrificial food (*haviṣyāśī*) should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind.
Furthermore:
Taking up the *rahasyamālā*, one should constantly recite it one hundred thousand times.
As stated in the *Rahasyamālā*:
"Success is achieved instantaneously by means of the rosary known as the Great Conch (*mahāśaṅkha*).
A rosary fashioned from fifty beads bestows all accomplishments."
Likewise:
"Success is achieved by one's beloved with a rosary called the *mahāśaṅkha*;
in the absence of a *mahāśaṅkha*, a crystal rosary should be used."
And so it is said:
"If one is unable even with a great conch shell, one should perform the recitation with a crystal rosary. (78)
Regarding the *mahāśaṅkha*, another tantra states:
"A rosary fashioned from a fragment of a human forehead bone is a *mahāśaṅkha* rosary; it is beloved for the recitation of the *Tārā* mantra."

The bone situated between the ears and the eyes is proclaimed as the *mahāśaṅkha*. One should know that which has been touched by *tulasī*, cow dung, or even a drop of Gaṅgā water to be untouchable, as are the *śālagrāma* stones and the like.
Knowledge of the *kullukā* is essential among the *tārā* mantras.
Thus it is said in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"The person who recites a great mantra without knowing the *kullukā*..."
He meets his death, or else he becomes insane. || 79 ||
In the Māyātantra:
"Having written the Kullukā on a birch-bark leaf, one should wear it upon the head;
one will certainly be victorious at the royal gate and in the assembly. (80)
Having recited [the mantra] as thus instructed, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number;
likewise, the libation (tarpaṇa), the consecration (abhiṣeka), and the feeding of Brahmins should each be a tenth part.
And one should satisfy the supreme goddess; the manner of doing so is stated here.
And likewise, in the *Siddhasārasvata*:

"Having first performed the recitation (*japa*) in this manner, the practitioner should offer oblations (*homa*) with ten parts of black stones smeared with clarified butter; and with one-tenth of that [number], he should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (83)
In that very same [text]:

"Having first performed the recitation (japa) in this manner, the mantra-practitioner should then offer oblations with ten parts of black stones (asitopala) soaked in clarified butter, or else he should offer oblations with bilva fruits."
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with pure scented waters mixed with the liquid of black aloe-wood; the method for doing so is stated here.

Having invoked [the deity] in the water according to the rules, and having gratified the Goddess and her attendants individually with water-offerings such as the *pādya* and others, in accordance with the prescribed rites; 85.
Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*):
Having worshipped his own self with the thought that it is the Goddess, the supreme practitioner should pour water upon his head while thinking, "I am sprinkling [her] with water. (86)
Now, the divisions of the mantra:
in the *Ekavīrākalpa*:
"One should write the letter Kha joined with the *kūrca* [hūṃ], as well as the *raudra* and the *traiguṇya*."
This great Vidyā, which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis), is considered to belong to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa through their respective powers in sequential order. Its meaning is as follows:
*Kha* is the nature of space itself, but it is not the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśabīja*).
Thus, it is said in the *Tantra*:
"Having extracted that which is known as *ṛddhi*, it is adorned with the *bindu* and the *nāda*."

The Raudra-prāsāda mantra consists of the three qualities (traiguṇya), the Praṇava; the power of Brahmā is the Vāgbhava-bīja; the power of Viṣṇu is the Ramā-bīja; and the power of Maheśa is the Bhuvaneśī-bīja.
The method for meditation and worship of Tāriṇī shall be as previously described. [The Praṇava...]
*Bhuvaneśvarīm*, *hāṃ*, the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*hūṃ*), *namas tārāyai*, "rescue me, rescue me from all that is difficult to cross," the two *praṇavas* (*oṃ oṃ*), and the *vahnijāyā* (*svāhā*).
And likewise, in the *Nīlatantra*:

Having first extracted the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should extract the seed-syllable *hṛllekhā*. Then, one should extract the *kūrca* seed-syllable, which consists of the letter *ga* joined with the final letter [ha], adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, followed by the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the word *tārāyai*.
"O you who cross over all that is difficult to cross, save me, save me!"—then again, "tāra" twice followed by "vahnijāyā" (svāhā). This mantra is the celestial wish-fulfilling tree.
One should perform all rites, such as meditation and worship, as previously described. || 88 ||
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of four hundred thousand recitations.
As it is stated in that very same source:
"Indeed, by four hundred thousand recitations of this, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained. (89)
In the *Māyātantra*,
the Blessed One said:
"Tārā, Ugrā, Mahogrā, Vajrā, Kālī, and Sarasvatī."
Kāmeśvarī and Bhadrakālī—these eight are remembered as the Tāriṇīs. || 90 ||
He states their mantra:
"The life-force (ajīva) situated in the aspirate consonants, joined with the vowel of the Veda,
surmounted by the Nāda and Bindu, and endowed with the ray of reality (tattvaraśmi)."
Kapila is situated at the left ear, rich with resonance (nāda) and topped by the bindu;
likewise, the end of the side and the end of ña are proclaimed as the end of the arrow (śa). 91.

The second mantra extracted is the Māyā-kavaca beginning with *mā* (92). It should be known that the third is reversed (*viparīta*) in three ways, while the fourth begins with *kūrca* (93). The fifth is proclaimed as beginning with *māyā* and ending with *kavaca* (94). The sixth is situated within *māyā*.
The seventh [syllable] ends in the accusative case, and the eighth is the armor (kavaca);
with one in the middle, there are eight variations.
The meaning of this is as follows:
the letter *u* is the *repha*; the letter *ha* is the *ajīva*; the *nigama-svara* is the letter *ī*;
the *tattva-raśmi* is the seed-syllable of *vadhū*; the letter *ha* is *kapila*; and the letter *pa* is *pārśva*.
Its end is the letter *pha*; the end of *ña* is the letter *ṭa*; that which ends in *śara* (sibilants) ends in *phaṭ*. Thus, the five-syllabled *prakṛti* is formed.
By the phrase "from the middle and so forth," [the mantra] is *vadhūrmāyā kūrcaṃ phaṭ*.
"Reversed" means that here there is a reversal of the initial and final seed-syllables (*bīja*). Thus, *kūrca*, *vadhū*, *māyā*, *phaṭ*.
[Alternatively: *kūrca* is *kūrca*, *māyā* is *vadhū*, and *phaṭ*.
Regarding "māyādi":
by that, *māyā* is the bride (*vadhū*) and *phaṭ* is the *kūrca*;
thus, *māyā* is the bride and *phaṭ* is the *kūrca*.
With "the second," there is *māyā*, *kūrca*, *vadhū*, and *phaṭ*;
with "the eighth," there is *vadhū*, *kūrca*, *māyā*, and *phaṭ*.
The seer is Aṣṭaka, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and likewise the deity is Maheśānī, the consort of Śambhu; one should employ her in the four aims of human life. 98.
One should recite the mantra for a period of time characterized by its specific duration, according to the method thus described. || 99 ||
One should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, as previously described. || 100 ||
This is the distinction of the three-syllable mantra alone: where there are not *phaṭ* and *au*, there indeed [the rule does not apply].
In recitation (*japya*), it should be known as the three-syllable mantra; in ritual placement (*nyāsa*), everything is established [within it].
Another mantra:
The *praṇava* is in the *tāra*, and in the *tāra* is that which is beloved of Fire (*vahnivallabhā*).
As it is stated in the *Gāndharva*:
"Having first extracted the *praṇava*, [one places] 'in the *tāra*' and likewise 'in the *tāra*'."
This mantra, "tattā svāhā," is declared to consist of ten syllables. || 2 ||
Her meditation is described in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"She is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, and two-armed, holding a boon-granting gesture and a lotus;
she is surrounded by [attendants] of many colors and many forms."
One should meditate upon her with a smiling face, adorned with smiling pearls,
her pair of lotus feet placed upon jeweled sandals.
His worship and other rites should be performed as previously described.
As for the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it consists of ten hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).
That has been stated in that very same source:
The wise practitioner should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times according to the rules and in accordance with the prescribed ritual;
the mantrin should then perform a fire oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number of red flowers smeared with clarified butter.
Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśānī, Praṇava, again Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśvarī, Phaṭ, Svāhā.
This has been stated in the Mātṛkārṇava:

Vāgbhava, Kuladevī, Tāraka, Vāgbhava, and Hṛllekhā, ending with the Astra-mantra and culminating in Vahnijāyā (Svāhā), is the mantra; this eight-syllabled mantra is declared to be the unsurpassed mantra of Vedamātā. Its five limbs [are as follows].
One should fashion the weapon [mantra] with the five seed-syllables of the mantra;
having performed the placement (nyāsa) with the remaining syllables, the person becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
One should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, just as before.
In the Matsyasūkta:
Having first extracted the Praṇava, [one should utter] "Padme" and likewise "Yugme";
then one should say "Mahāpadme," "Padme," and thereafter the word "Padmāvati."
"Māye svāhā"—this mantra is declared to consist of seventeen syllables.
As previously indicated, he who performs the recitation of this [mantra] at midnight at a crossroads shall likewise become a poet as swift as Adrutakavi.
Haṃsaḥ, Praṇava, Māyā, Vadhūbīja, Kūrcabīja, and Haṃsa.
As it is stated in the Svacchandasaṃgraha:
"O Maheśānī, [the seed-syllable] of Śiva, and after that, the seed-syllable of Śakti."

The first syllable of the Veda (OM) joined with the Bindu and Sarga (visarga), followed by Māyā (Hrīṃ) and Strī (Śrīṃ) at the end of the seed-syllables of the consonant groups; this is declared to be the Haṃsa-bīja. This eight-syllabled Vidyā is said to be difficult to obtain on earth. 9.
This five-syllabled vidyā, which begins and ends with *hiṃsā* and brings great prosperity,
has been proclaimed solely through your grace and out of affection for you.
One should perform the recitation, worship, and other rites for these two just as one does for the five-syllabled mantra.
In another tantra:
"The pair of *lajjā*, the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū*), and then the long *tanucchada* (armor);
following *sāre* and *svataḥ*—this other four-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed."
If at its end there is the syllable *phaṭ*, the mantra becomes five-syllabled. || 11 ||
Likewise:
the seed-syllables of Tāra, Śakti, and Vadhū, followed at the end by the long *tanucchada* (armor), then the *astra* (weapon) and finally *agnivadhū*; this becomes the seven-syllable mantra.

This [method] has been taught for the mere mantras, as well as for the long armor-mantra; furthermore, there is another method consisting of three syllables, wherein the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū) is encapsulated. || 12 ||
The secret preliminary practice (*rahasyapuraścaraṇa*).
As it is said:
"O Lord, please explain the preliminary practice for those who are incapable."
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described in another manner. || 13 ||
On a Tuesday or a Saturday, having procured a human skull and mixed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), especially with sandalwood and other substances,
one should bury it in the ground to a depth of half a cubit in a grove or forest.
If on that day, during the night, the practitioner recites it one thousand times while alone, he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
having brought a corpse, it is buried by that same door;
from that day until that [same] day, one performs one hundred and eight [recitations].
He shall become the lord of all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 16 ||
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
on the eighth, the [twelfth] *nakṣatra*, and the fourteenth— on both of these two [lunar days]—
beginning from sunrise until [sunset].
Having recited [the mantra] for as long as it takes until sunrise, one shall become free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments. || 17 ||
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
specifically during the autumn season, from the fourth to the ninth lunar day,
having worshipped with devotion, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times at night.
One should recite [the mantra] alone in a solitary place, specifically in a dark chamber;
from the eighth day until the ninth, one should be devoted to fasting.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:

Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the next eighth day of the dark fortnight, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is prescribed to be performed with a recitation (japa) numbering one thousand. 19.
Having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, during the great festival ending on the ninth day, one should especially perform worship on the night of the eighth and ninth days.
On the tenth day, one should perform the breaking of the fast with fish, meat, and other such foods;
devoted to a spirit of devotion, one should daily recite [the mantra] six thousand times.
O Maheśānī, beginning from the fourteenth day until the next fourteenth day, if one recites [the mantra] during that time, it is considered *puraścaraṇa*;
indeed, by mere recitation alone, the mantras become perfected.
O Maheśānī, having performed the recitation from the time the sun rises until the sun has set, that is considered the *puraścaraṇa*. || 23 ||
Now, regarding the practice of hero-siddhi (*vīrasādhana*), it is stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"On the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights..."
One should especially accomplish the *vīrasādhana* during the dark fortnight. O beautiful goddess, when half a watch or a full watch has passed,
one should take a corpse or go to a funeral pyre as one pleases.
The practitioner of mantra, devoted to the meditation on mantra, should accomplish his own welfare. || 25 ||
One must certainly not feel fear, and one should avoid laughter there;
one should not look at the fourteenth lunar day, but should instead practice the mantra itself.
Now, the materials for worship:

food with meat, jaggery, goat, liquor, milk-rice, flour-cakes, and various fruits as the food offering (*naivedya*), prepared according to the prescriptions of their respective *kalpas*. [The place of meditation...]
Having summoned his friends, who hold weapons in their hands and are endowed with all necessary qualities, he himself, free from fear, should accomplish the task.
And so it is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

"For the purpose of the bali offering, there should be meat with rice, molasses, goat, as well as honey, flour-cakes, *paramānna*, milk, roots, and likewise fruits—these seven vessels. (29) *Saptapātraṃ*...
Having performed the bali offering in four vessels in the four directions,
one should always place three vessels in the center with this mantra:
[to] the Guru, or the brother, or likewise to Brāhmaṇas of virtuous vows.
And for the sake of protection, one should station others as well at some distance.
The characteristic of the funeral pyre is as follows:
the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) pyre is to be grasped, but not one conditioned by formative forces (saṃskāra).
