When obtained even from outcasts and the like, it bestows success solely and swiftly. (31)
Now, the definition of the qualified candidate is as follows:
"One who possesses great strength, great intelligence, and great courage; who is pure, highly lucid, compassionate, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. (32)
Then, having prepared the general water-offering (arghya) and preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana), one should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) as follows:
"Oṃ, etc. I, [Name], of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious [Name] Devaśarman, desiring the accomplishment of such-and-such mantra, shall perform the *sādhana* of the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should be adorned with garments, ornaments, jewelry, and the like.
Facing the eastern direction; "sprinkling on the sacrificial grounds with the root mantra ending in the weapon [mantra]" means with the root mantra ending in the syllable *phaṭ*.
Having meditated upon the dust of the Guru’s feet, as well as Gaṇeśa,
Vaṭuka, the Yoginī, and the Mātṛkās, beginning with the left foot;
and likewise:
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and the others, and having protected oneself with the Astra-mantra; for it is said:
"The knower of mantras should effect protection for himself by means of the Astra-mantra."
Then one should cast three handfuls of flowers onto the funeral pyre.
As it is stated in the Vāratantra:
"And whatever gods and terrifying rākṣasas are stationed here..."
Piśācas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and the qualities of Apsarases;
Yoginīs, Mātṛs, Bhūtas, and all the women who move through the sky—
may they grant success here and likewise be my protectors.
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should offer three handfuls of flowers.
One should worship Bhairava Kālabhairava as the Lord of the Cremation Ground (Śmaśānādhipati) in the west;

thereafter, one should worship Mahākāla in the four cardinal directions beginning with the east. Following that, one should worship the Seed-syllable of Sound (Śabdabīja), and after that, the Lord of the Cremation Ground.
"O Lord, accept this final offering of food mixed with meat;
thereafter, accept, accept! O pair [of deities], remove all obstacles, then grant me success and bestow [your blessing] accompanied by the *svāhā*."
The first bali offering is declared with the mantra beginning with *praṇava*.
After *māyā* (hrīṃ), *bhairava*, and subsequently *bhayānaka*,
one should offer the second bali on the right, having extracted it as before.
(2) For the deity of the western direction, one should perform the ritual with the syllable *praṇava* at the beginning;
at the end of the word *śava* and the end of the word *kāla*, the word *bhairava* follows, and then *śmaśānādhipa*. In this manner, as before, one should offer [the oblation] in the north.
(3) And at the end of *hūm*, one should recite as before after Mahākāla:
"O Lord of the Cremation Ground. One should offer the *bali* as before.
(4) The knower of mantras should subsequently present the *bali* with water for the feet and other offerings.
For example: having worshipped the Lord of the Cemetery with the five types of offerings, one should present the bali offering with this mantra.
Namely:
Oṃ hūṃ! O Lord of the Cremation Ground, take, take, take this offering of food with meat;
cause it to be taken; ward off obstacles; grant me accomplishment!
Svāhā!
Then, having worshipped Bhairava as before, [one offers] in the south: "Hrīṃ! O Bhairava, Terrifying One! This food-offering with meat," and so forth.
Then, having worshipped Kālabhairava in the west with: "Hūṃ! O Kālabhairava, Lord of the cremation ground, this offering of food mixed with meat," and so forth;
and having honored Mahākāla in the north with: "Hūṃ! O Mahākāla, Lord of the cremation ground, this..."
"Obeisance to the one whose strength is food mixed with meat," and so forth.
Then, one should offer three supreme oblations (*bali*) in the midst of the funeral pyre, [reciting]:
"O Kālarātri! O Mahākālī! O Kālikā of terrible sound!"
"Accept this offering, O Mother; grant me supreme accomplishment.
Having given the offering to Kālikā, one should cause it to be given to the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha).
At the end of the word [Kālikā] and at the end of the word [Bhūtanātha], one should also say "Lord of the Cremation Ground" (Śmaśānādhipa).
One should cause the supreme bali offering to be given with the mantra beginning with *praṇava*.
At the end of the word [for the deity], one should add "to all the lords of the gaṇas" (*sarvagaṇanāthebhyaḥ*) and then "to the presiding lord" (*adhipāya*).
Having offered this at the head of the cremation ground, one should extract [the mantra] as before.

O beautiful one, having offered the *bali* with the mantra beginning with *Tārā*, and having performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and with water, one should then place a yellow cloth. Upon that, either on birch bark or a *vaṭa* leaf, one should place the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamaṇtra*).
Having spread out a seat upon that [ground] and then assumed the *vīrāsana* posture,
one should perform protection in the directions with the *vīrārdana* mantra.
Its meaning is as follows:

Having sprinkled the bones from the cremation ground and other materials with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having written the pīṭha-mantra prescribed for each respective ritual on birch bark or similar material, one should spread out a seat such as a tiger skin thereon, and sit upon it in the manner of the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
One should perform protection in the four directions with the mantra "vīrārdana. || 34 ||
The mantra for the subduing of heroes is as follows: *hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ kālike ghoradaṃṣṭre pracaṇḍe caṇḍanāyike dānavān dāraya hana hana śavaśarīre mahāvighnaṃ chedaya chedaya*.
"SVĀHĀ HŪM PHAṬ.
With this, one should consecrate a clod of earth and cast it in the ten directions;
in the midst of that, the god Bhairava is not overcome by obstacles.
In the *Nīlatantra*:
"Then, O Goddess, two *kūrca* syllables, followed by a pair of *māyā*s;
then *Kālike*, *Ghoradaṃṣṭre*, *Pracaṇḍe*, and *Caṇḍanāyike*."
Having said "dāraya" (tear asunder) the dānavas, [one says] "hana" (slay) twice again;
then, for the corpse-body, "chedaya" (cut) twice again for the great obstacle;
ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), followed by the armor (*varma*) and the weapon (*astra*) mantras, this is considered the mantra for the subduing of heroes. (34ka)
O Goddess, if through negligence the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear,
he will not be overcome if he is protected by those various groups of friends.
Having fashioned a lamp-wick from white *arkapuṣpa*, camphor, and the cotton of white *vātyālaka*, and having placed a lamp therein,
one should worship the weapon-mantra with "Obeisance to the Weapon of the Goddesses" (*devyastrebhyo namaḥ*) and bury the burning lamp beneath.
And so it is said:
Having placed a lamp there with a wick made of cotton from the arka, indu, sita, vāṭyāla, and tūla plants, one should worship the Astra-mantra therein.
When that great lamp is overcome by obstacles,
one should bury the family-lamp beneath it with the weapon-mantra.

Then, having performed the entire network of nyāsas, such as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth, as prescribed in that ritual manual (kalpa), and having fully worshipped the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should recite the mantra of the formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
As for the formal resolve:

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) beginning with "Today," etc., as follows: "I, of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious Amudevaśarman, desiring the perfection of such-and-such a mantra, shall perform the recitation (*japa*) of such-and-such a mantra for such-and-such a number of times"; he should then recite the mantra preceded by the visualization of the deity.
And so it is said:
"One should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites according to the specific injunctions of each respective ritual manual;
then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of either the sixfold mantra or the *tāraka*, one should worship, being intent upon the meditation on the mantra."
Having become thus, one should mutter the mantra with undistracted mind. || 37 ||
The Japanese tradition, however, states: "If it be a single-syllable mantra, one should recite it one thousand times;
for a two-syllable mantra, it should be eight thousand; and for a three-syllable mantra, it should be fifty thousand."

Thereafter, however, the knower of mantras should perform one thousand and eight recitations of the *Gajāntaka* mantra, beginning at night and continuing until sunrise. "Gajāntaka" here means one thousand and eight. || 38 ||
If unbearable fear arises, one should bind the ears and eyes with a cloth.
Then, until midnight, if nothing whatsoever is perceived,
one should scatter mustard seeds while reciting that very mantra known as Jayadurgā.
The mantra of Jayadurgā is: Oṃ durge durge rakṣaṇi svāhā.
Oṃ, you are sesame, whose deity is Soma; you are the essence of the cow-sacrifice, the cause of satisfaction.
"You are the giver of heaven to the ancestors, the protector of mortals like me,
and the bringer of peace amidst obstacles caused by bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas. Having recited this, one should scatter sesame seeds in the four directions, beginning with the northeast (īśāna).
Then, having gone seven steps, he should lie down right there;
having worshipped the deity again, he should perform the recitation of mantras. || 39 ||
Then, if [the deity] should say, "Choose a boon," one should cause [the deity] to swear an oath of truth.
And so it is said:
When told, "Choose a boon," the practitioner, with a steady mind—
And having caused the truth to be uttered, he should choose an excellent boon. || 40 ||
Having first offered the *bali* at the beginning of the recitation (*japa*), one should offer the *bali* afterwards as well;
whether at the end of the recitation or during its course, when the words "Give!
Give! are uttered, then too one should present the *bali*, whether it be a buffalo or even a goat.
And the bali offering with a cake made of barley flour. || 41 ||
When he requests an offering of a man or even an elephant, he should say, "I will give it on another day," and having accepted the request, he should go to his own home. (42)
On the following day, one should then offer human figures made of flour;
by "flour" is meant that produced from barley grain. || 43 ||
And so it is said in another tantra:
"Alternatively, one should strike [the effigy] made of barley flour or likewise of rice flour, according to the rite, with the Candrahāsa [sword], using its respective mantra. (44)
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer a bali-oblation to the deity according to the prescribed rite,
having taken either a buffalo, a goat, or even a boar."
With a joyful mind, he should go home together with his own friends. Then he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
O Goddess, having completed the practice, he should give a sacrificial fee according to his means.
One should offer it to the guru, or to the guru’s son, or to his wife. || 45 ||
Now, regarding the means of attaining power (*śavasādhana*):
therein, the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* states the rule for the location:
"In an empty house, on a riverbank, on a mountain, or even in a secluded place."
At the root of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, or in a forest area near such places. || 46 ||
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
on Tuesday, and during the dark of night, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.
Māṣa-bean rice for the sake of the bali offering, as well as incense, lamps, and so forth;
sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and mustard seeds should be placed there with great care. 48.
Then, having gone to one of the previously mentioned locations and prepared the general *arghya*,
facing east and uttering the syllable *phaṭ* at the end of the root mantra, he should sprinkle the sacrificial ground (*yāgabhūmi*) and worship the Guru,
Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, and the Yoginīs in the four directions, starting from the east.

Having performed worship and having written the previously mentioned *vīrārdana* mantra on the ground, one should offer three handfuls of flowers according to the previously stated sequence beginning with "ye cātra," and after prostrating,
one should offer the bali-oblation to the lords of the cremation grounds (*śmaśānādhipati*) in the same manner as before.

Having performed the binding of the topknot with the Aghora mantra, and having placed the hand on the heart at the end of the Sudarśana mantra while reciting "protect me, protect me" (ātmānaṃ rakṣa rakṣa), one should perform self-protection.
The Aghora and Sudarśana mantras are as follows:

Oṃ hrīṃ sphura sphura, prasphura prasphura, O you of terrible and most terrible form, caṭa caṭa, pracaṭa pracaṭa, kaha kaha, vama vama, bindha bindha, slay, slay, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ sahasrāre hūṃ phaṭ! || 49 ||
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the network of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*) according to the previously mentioned sequence,

and having scattered mustard seeds in all directions with the *Jayadurgā* mantra and scattered sesame seeds with the mantra "Tilo 'si," one should go to the vicinity of the prescribed corpse. || 50 ||
As prescribed in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"One pierced by a staff, pierced by a stake, pierced by a sword, one dead in water,
pierced by lightning, bitten by a snake, an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), and one who is possessed."
He was youthful, handsome, brave, radiant, and undaunted in battle;
he stood facing those engaged in combat, utterly devoid of any desire to flee. || 51 ||
In the Bhairavatantra it is also said:
"A corpse pierced by a staff or the like, or one overcome [by disease] and dead in water, should be brought;
one should not take a corpse that has died of its own accord."

One should carry away a corpse that is under the control of a woman, one who has fallen from his caste, one who is untouchable, one devoid of moral conduct, one who is naked, one with indistinct gender marks, one afflicted by leprosy, or one broken by old age; however, one should not carry away a corpse that died during a famine, nor one that has been left for a night.
One should avoid such women of this kind in every respect. || 52 ||
Also in the Kālītantra:
"Having abandoned the cow-dung of a Brāhmaṇa, one should accomplish the Vīrasādhana;
in the primary Vīrasādhana, great corpses are recommended."
They are praised for those who perform minor applications, for the sake of attaining all accomplishments. || 53 ||
Having spoken thus, one should take hold of the corpse and bring it to the place of worship with the root mantra.
Having gone near it, one should sprinkle the corpse with "Oṃ Phaṭ," offer three handfuls of flowers with "Oṃ Hūṃ Mātṛkāyai Namaḥ Phaṭ," touch the corpse, and prostrate.
As it is stated in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
"One should perform the sprinkling of the corpse with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) preceded by the Praṇava:
'Oṃ Hūṃ Mṛtakāya Namaḥ Phaṭ'."
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should prostrate while preceded by physical touch.
The mantra for prostration is as follows:
"O Vīreśa, supreme bliss, bliss of Śiva, Lord of the Kula!
O Śaṅkara, whose form is that of Ānandabhairava, who rests upon the couch of the Goddess!"
"I am the Hero (I am Śiva); I take refuge in you; arise for the worship of Caṇḍikā!
With this mantra for the corpse, he should prostrate and wash the corpse.
Having washed it with fragrant water using the mantra "Oṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to the deceased," [he should proceed].
Having bathed [the corpse], having lifted the water away with a cloth, having perfumed it with incense, and having anointed the corpse with sandalwood and other substances,
one should take hold of the waist of the corpse and bring it to the place of worship.
As it is stated in the Kālītantra: "One should utter the mantra beginning with the syllable *tāra* (om), followed by the word *śabda*, and ending with *namo mṛtakāya*.
This is the mantra for bathing the corpse," and so forth.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"O Goddess of Gods, if one who is smeared with red [substances] fumigates [the object] with incense, draws upon it with perfumes and the like, and then eats [it], he becomes a Kula practitioner. (55)
Then, having prepared a bed of *kuśa* grass with its head toward the east, one should place the corpse upon it.
As it is stated in that very same source:
"Having prepared a bed of *kuśa* grass, one should place the corpse there."
Then, having placed cardamom, cloves, camphor, jasmine, catechu,
and fresh ginger into his mouth along with betel leaf, the wise and disciplined practitioner should turn the corpse face down and smear its back with sandalwood paste.
Having fashioned a square area extending from the base of the arms to the waist,
one should draw a lotus in the center with eight petals and four gates;
then, according to the specific ritual injunctions for each [deity], one should write the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) in the middle.

Then, with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ*, one should write the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*) as prescribed in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*), and upon that, place a seat such as a woolen rug (*kambala*).
As stated in another tantra:
Having gone into the presence of the corpse, he should hold [the bone] at his waist.
If it should cause him distress, he should spit upon the corpse;
then, having performed a washing again, he should bring it back to the place of recitation.

Then, having placed twelve-finger-length sacrificial wood-pieces in the ten directions as before, and having worshipped the ten deities beginning with Indra, one should offer a *bali* oblation consisting of meat and rice.
As it is said in another Tantra:
"Having placed sacrificial wood pieces measuring twelve finger-breadths in the cardinal directions, one should worship there the deities beginning with Indra in their proper sequence. (56 ka)
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:

"Oṃ lāṃ, obeisance to Indra, lord of the gods, whose vehicle is Airāvata, who holds a vajra in his hand, together with his attendants and his retinue. Having thus worshipped him with water for the feet and other offerings, [one should proceed].
One should offer the bali-oblation.
Having inscribed the seed-syllable for Indra, followed by "to the Lord of the Gods," then "accept this bali," then the pair "gṛhṇa-yugma," and then "make [them] accept the pair" (gṛhṇāpaya yugam).
Having warded off obstacles, grant success, [ending with] the two *ṭha*s.
With this mantra, one should first offer a bali consisting of meat;
having performed the respective names and so forth, one should bring the bali as before.
Then, for all the world-protectors, the most excellent practitioner [should offer]:
Oṃ lāṃ! To Indra, lord of the gods, accept this offering, accept it, cause it to be accepted; having warded off obstacles, grant me success, svāhā!
This is the offering of black-gram porridge: Oṃ lāṃ, svāhā to Indra!
Oṃ rāṃ, salutation to Agni, the lord of splendor, whose vehicle is a ram, who is accompanied by his retinue, who holds a spear in his hand, and who is equipped with weapons!
Having thus worshipped, one should offer the *bali* with the mantra: *oṃ rāṃ agnaye tejo'dhipataye*, and so forth.

Having worshipped with *oṃ yāṃ yāmāya pretādhipataye daṇḍahastāya mahiṣavāhanāya sāyudhāya*, and so forth, one should offer the *bali* to Yama, the lord of the *pretas*, with *oṃ yāṃ yamāya pretādhipataye baliṃ*.
One should offer [the oblation].

Having worshipped with "Oṃ Kṣāṃ! To Nirṛti, the lord of the Rakṣas, who holds a sword in his hand, together with his vehicle and retinue," and so forth, [one recites]: "Oṃ Kṣāṃ! To Nirṛti, the lord of the Rakṣas..."
One should offer the *bali* with these and other [mantras].

Having worshipped [Varuṇa] with "Oṃ vāṃ, to Varuṇa, lord of the waters, who holds a noose in his hand, whose vehicle is a makara, who is equipped with weapons," and so forth, [one recites]: "Oṃ vāṃ, to Varuṇa, lord of the waters..."
One should offer the *bali* with these and other [mantras].
Having worshipped with "Oṃ yāṃ vāyave prāṇādhipataye hariṇavāhanāyāṃkuśahastāya" and so forth, one offers the *bali* with "Oṃ yāṃ vāyave prāṇādhipataye" and so forth.

One should give [the offering]. Having worshipped with "Oṃ, to Kubera, lord of the Yakṣas, mace-handed, mounted on a man, together with your retinue," and so forth, one should offer the *bali* with "Oṃ, to Kubera, lord of the Yakṣas," and so forth.
One should give [the offering].

Having worshipped as before with "Oṃ hāṃ, to Īśāna, the lord of beings, who holds a trident in his hand, whose vehicle is a bull, together with his retinue," and so forth, [one offers] "Oṃ hāṃ, to Īśāna."

One should offer the *bali* with the mantra beginning "To the Lord of Beings" (*bhūtādhipataye*). Between Indra and Īśāna, one should worship with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ! To Brahmā, the Lord of Progeny, whose vehicle is the swan, who holds a lotus in his hand, together with his retinue," and so forth; then, Oṃ...

One should offer the *bali* with the mantra beginning: "Āṃ, to Brahmā, the lord of progeny, whose vehicle is the swan," and so forth, in the space between Nairṛta and Varuṇa. Having worshipped with the mantra beginning: "Oṃ, aṃ, to Ananta, the lord of *nāgas*, who holds a discus in his hand, whose vehicle is a chariot, together with his retinue," and so forth, [one offers] "Oṃ, aṃ, to Ananta."
Having performed worship with the mantra beginning "To the Lord of Nāgas, together with his weapons," and so forth, one should offer the *bali* offering.
Thereafter, one should offer the *bali* to all spirits (*sarvabhūta*),
using meat-containing food in every instance.
Then, one should cause the presiding deities to remember the bali offering; thereafter,
one should also give instructions to the sixty-four Yoginīs and the Ḍākinīs.
Then, having placed the materials for worship nearby and the assistant practitioner at a distance,

one should worship the corpse by reciting the root mantra followed by *hrīṃ phaṭ śavāsanāya namaḥ*. Having uttered the root mantra ending in *hrīṃ phaṭ*, one should sit upon the corpse in the manner of mounting a horse.
Having placed *kuśa* grass under the soles of his feet, having spread out the hair of the corpse, and having tied it into a topknot (*juṭikā*),
he should pay homage to the Guru and the deity Gaṇapati; then, having performed *prāṇāyāma* and the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*),
he should cast clods of earth in the ten directions with the *Vīrārdana* mantra as before.
He should make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa):

"Today, etc., I, of such-and-such lineage, the venerable Amudevaśarmā, desiring the vision of such-and-such deity, shall perform the recitation (japa) of such-and-such mantra for such-and-such a number of times."

Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should worship the seat with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti-kamalāsana*). Then, having placed the vessel for the offering water (*arghyapātra*) and other items to one's left near the corpse, and having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) upon the head of the corpse, [one should proceed] with the sixteen utterances and the ten ritual services (*daśopacāra*).
Having worshipped the Goddess with the five types of offerings (pañcopacāra), one should satisfy the Goddess at the mouth of the corpse with perfumes and other substances.
Then, rising from the corpse and going before it, one should recite the mantra.
Oṃ, be subject to me, O Lord of Gods; grant, grant me the accomplishment of the heroes, O illustrious one, you who have taken refuge in the supreme goal!
Then, having bound the feet of the corpse with a silk thread, one should bind them firmly with the root mantra.
Oṃ! Be under my control, O Lord of Gods, you who are the abode that grants the accomplishments of heroes!
O Terrible One, you who cause the fear of the timid to vanish, O Deliverer from Saṃsāra, O Compassionate One!
Protect me, O Lord of the Gods of gods, Sovereign over the lords of heroes!
By this [instruction], one should draw a triangular yantra at the base of the corpse's feet.
Then, having sat upon the corpse, having extended both hands to the sides,
having placed *kuśa* grass over them, and having set one's own feet there, one should again perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], having visualized the Guru upon his head, having meditated on the Goddess in his heart, having joined his lips together, and having become silent with the rosary prepared, he should recite the mantra, free from fear.
Here, the recitation should be performed according to the sequence for the practice in the cremation ground. || 58 ||
If nothing is perceived until midnight, then, having performed the scattering of mustard seeds and sesame as before and the walking seven steps, one should perform the recitation;
when fear arises, one should chant thus: || 58 ka ||
"There is no fear from one with trembling skin; when fear arises, one should speak thus:
'Whatever you request as an offering, elephants and the like must be given.
I shall give it on another day; tell me your name.'"

Having spoken thus in Sanskrit, one should again recite [the mantra] fearlessly; if she then speaks sweetly, one should likewise speak sweetly. Then, having caused her to swear an oath of truth, one should thereafter request a boon.
If he does not grant the truth or does not bestow the boon,
then the wise one should again recite with a one-pointed mind.
The meaning of this is as follows:

If, at the time of recitation, one desires an elephant or similar object by means of traveling through the sky, then one should say, "I shall give it on another day; tell me your name in my place," and then recite again.
If he pronounces his own name sweetly, then one should say, "Make it true that you are so-and-so."
When the truth has been established, one should request a boon.
If at any time he does not act according to the truth or does not grant the boon,
then one should recite [the mantra] again.
And so it is said:
"When the truth has been established and the boon obtained, one should abandon the recitation of mantras and the like;
knowing that the fruit has arisen, one should then release the tuft of hair."
Having washed and positioned the corpse, one should release the foot-bindings;
having released the foot-wheel, one should cast the ritual materials into the water.
Having placed the corpse either in the water or in a pit, one should perform a ritual bath.
Then, having gone to his own home, he should offer the *bali* on the following day. The *bali-mantra* is as follows:
"O those for whom I am the sacrificer, may they accept this *bali* tonight."
Then, having given away horses, elephant-like men,
and boars made of flour as requested, one should subsequently observe a fast.
Then, on the following day, having performed his daily rites, he should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and feed twenty-five Brahmins as well.
For example:
On the following day, having performed the daily rites, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
then, one should feed twenty-five Brahmins there.
Or, having gradually reduced [the fast] by seven or five days up to ten days,
one should then bathe, eat, and reside in an excellent place.
If there were no food to be eaten by the Brahmins, then [the king] would fall into poverty;
if he were to become impoverished because of that, then the Goddess becomes enraged.
Therefore, one should guard [the food] for three nights, or six nights, or even nine nights. (64)

If one approaches the bed of a woman, then one should predict illness; by hearing music, one becomes deaf, and from seeing a dance, one becomes blind. If one speaks during the day, then one will suffer from muteness for fifteen days. (65) [Fifteen days]
As long as the deity remains within the body,
one should not accept scents or flowers once they have gone outside;
at that time, having discarded the garment, one should take up another cloth.
One should never engage in the censuring of cows or brāhmaṇas, nor should one ever touch a wicked person, an outcast, or a eunuch. || 67 ||
Being pure, he should touch gods, cows, Brahmins, and others every day;
and in the morning, at the conclusion of his daily rites, he should drink water infused with bilva leaves.
Then, having bathed in the Gaṅgā when the sixteenth day has arrived,
one should recite the mantra ending with "svāhā" and the word "namaḥ" at the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa).
In this manner, after three hundred [recitations], one should satiate the gods with water.
For one who is devoid of bathing and libations, there can be no propitiation of the Deity;
by this injunction, the practitioner attains perfection. Having enjoyed excellent pleasures in this world, at the end of his enjoyment, he goes to the abode of Hari.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should perform the rite for ensuring the ritual's flawlessness (acchidrāvadhāraṇa). || 69 ||
Thus ends the means for achieving power (*śavasādhana*). Now follow the mantras of Caṇḍograśūlapāṇi and the various divisions of the *vidyās*.
In the *Kubjikātantra*:
"One should extract the Praṇava (Oṃ), then Māyā (Hrīṃ), and the Kūrca-bīja (Hūṃ);
followed by 'śivāya' ending with Phaṭ—this is the great mantra of Caṇḍogra."
And the mantra of Caṇḍograśūlapāṇi accomplishes all purposes.
Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], Gāyatrī the metre (chandas), Māyā the seed-syllable (bīja), and Caṇḍogra is declared to be the deity.
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is performed with the seed-syllable preceded by Om and endowed with the six long vowels.
As for the meditation:
[one should visualize the deity] resembling pure crystal, with four arms and a crown;
holding a trident and a skull-cup in the right hands, and a noose and a goad in the left.
Pervaded by the essence of the drinking of wine, it grants the desired objects of the practitioner. || 72 ||
Having meditated upon and worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should mutter the mantra five thousand times;
then, in a consecrated fire, one should offer oblations with red lotuses in the measure of a tenth part.
Now, the ritual application here is as follows:
By offering oblations with [substances] smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one attains poetic skill and becomes a possessor of wealth;
by the homa of red lotuses, one shall obtain great prosperity. || 73 ||
By means of an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa), one destroys enemies without delay;
by an oblation of safflower oil (kusumbha-taila), one slays foes—of this there is no doubt. (75)
By the oblation of *karavīra* flowers, the paralysis of speech (*vāka-stambha*) certainly arises;
by the oblation of white lotuses, one may delude the entire world. One should worship the root mantra in the center of an eight-petaled lotus with six corners.
With a purely pure disposition, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite [the mantra] during the day. || 77 ||
By the mere performance of its preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), one is not defiled by obstacles;
by the mere recitation of this very mantra, one shall obtain all accomplishments (siddhi). || 78 ||
(Caṇḍograśūlapāṇiyantra, Figure 38).
Thus ends the section on Caṇḍograśūlapāṇi;
now follows the Mātaṅgī mantra.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra:
Now I shall describe the Great Goddess Mātaṅgī, who bestows all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis). Merely by worshipping her, one obtains perfection of speech (vāksiddhi) without delay. (79)
Then follows the Praṇava, Māyā, the Kāmabīja, and the Kūrca; then Mātaṅgī joined with the syllable *ṅe*, and the Astra-mantra ending with the Vahnijāyā (Svāhā)—this is the mantra. (80)
The sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the Virāṭ metre is proclaimed;
the goddess Mātaṅgī is the deity, the bestower of all accomplishments. (81)
The practitioner of mantra, being composed, should perform the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa);
he should fashion these with the seed-syllable preceded by the Praṇava and endowed with the six long vowels.
The diagram for this is as follows: one should draw a beautiful diagram consisting of a six-pointed star and an eight-petaled lotus;
there, the knower of mantras should perform worship with hibiscus flowers.
With a well-composed mind, one should worship the eight Śaktis upon the eight petals:
Rati, Prīti, Manobhavā, Kriyā, Śraddhā,
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Madanālasā.
Having thus worshipped the eight powers (*aṣṭa-śakti*) and provided with offerings,
the practitioner, with a steady mind, should then meditate upon the Supreme Goddess (*parā-devī*). (Illustration 38) It is as follows:

She has a dark-complexioned body, wears the moon as her crest-jewel, and possesses three eyes; she is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and holds in her staff-like arms a sword, a shield, a noose, and a goad. (84)
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess with delightful perfumes and flowers,
one should offer milk-rice mixed with sugar as an oblation to the Great Goddess.
During the period of preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), one should recite the mantra six thousand times.

The practitioner, together with his Śaktis, should offer oblations of clarified butter along with sugar and honey, using fuel-sticks made from the wood of the Brahma-tree (udumbara), for one-tenth of that number. Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraskriyā), he should carry out the ritual application (prayoga).
At a crossroads, in a cremation ground, or at the center of a lunar phase,
the practitioner of mantras should offer fish, meat, milk-rice, and guggulu incense;
this should always be performed during the night yoga, and the adept should remain full of devotion.
Thus, by the mere practice of this application, poetry is surely produced. One may certainly effect the paralyzing of fire, the paralyzing of water, and the paralyzing of speech.
The practitioner of mantra conquers his enemies, just as Tārkṣya [conquers] the race of serpents.
In the sciences, in debate, and in poetry, he was like a second Bṛhaspati. || 87 ||
By this very procedure, Mātaṅgī becomes the bestower of perfection;
indeed, having come to that house, Kubera himself bestows wealth.
One should not worship the Supreme Deity without fish and without meat. 88.
Now, the mantras of Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī:
Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī, the fair-faced goddess, the great Piśācinī; the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjābīja), ṭhaṃḥ ṭhaṃḥ ṭhaṃḥ.
As it is stated in the Phetkāriṇī:
"Having uttered the word *ucchiṣṭa* and likewise *cāṇḍālinī*,
one should thereafter proclaim the goddess Sumukhī immediately following that."
After [the mantra of] Mahāpiśācinī, then the seed-syllable of Lajjā (hrīṃ),
followed by three syllables *ṭha* conjoined with the *nāda* and *bindu*,
and finally with the *visarga*, O Great Goddess; this bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Another mantra: *ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli mātaṅgi sarvavaśaṅkari namaḥ svāhā*.
This has been stated in another tantra: "Alternatively, one should utter the words *ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli mātaṅgi*."
Then, at the end, the beloved of the fire of the heart [the syllable *hrīṃ*] brings everything under control;
this mantra of nineteen syllables shall grant all desired objects. (90)
Another mantra, from the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*: Vāgbhava, Māyā, Kāma, Sauḥ, Aiṃ;
O Jyeṣṭhamātaṅgī, I bow to you; O Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī, O Subduer of the Three Worlds!
Svāhā!
O Maheśānī, this is the supreme Vidyā endowed with the syllable Hūṃ.
This Vidyā is a Great Vidyā that removes all sins.
It bestows happiness, liberation, and the fortune of sovereignty;
whatever perfection one prays for, one shall obtain it by force.
And I shall proclaim the ritual procedure; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!
O Goddess, immediately after eating, even if the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) has not been performed, the practitioner should first offer the bali-oblation with the root mantra.
Then, having meditated upon that goddess, one should recite the mantra for the sake of attaining the desired success; one should also offer a bali-oblation with the remains [of the meal]. || 92 ||
And thus:
there is no requirement for sacred bathing sites nor for constellations, nor even for the ritual placement of mantras on the limbs;
there is no obstacle from the faults of women, nor impurity, nor any restrictive observance.
He in whom this mantra abides is not afflicted by obstacles. || 93 ||
As for the meditation:
[one should visualize her] seated upon a corpse, clothed in red garments,
adorned with red ornaments, and decorated with a necklace of *guñjā* seeds.

The best of mantra-knowers should meditate upon her as a sixteen-year-old maiden with full and elevated breasts, holding a skull and a chisel in her hands, the supreme embodiment of light, through the union of the left and right [channels]. (94)
Having offered the bali-oblation with the remnants [of food], one should recite [the mantra] with the mind fixed upon it.
One who desires success must perform the recitation with the remnants;
for one reciting while using the remnants, all perfections arise. || 95 ||
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall proclaim that which bestows fruit:
the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
Having fashioned a square mandala on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) on all sides...

O Goddess, the practitioner should worship the maṇḍala with the root mantra. Then, having recited the root mantra and the mantra "Salutation to the Maṇḍala," and having meditated upon the deity in the form of fire, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
And so it is said: Then,
having composed his mind upon the Goddess who is established in the form of fire,
and having meditated on the Goddess, he should perform the homa with curd, white mustard seeds, and rice grains.
By performing one thousand oblations, even a king shall become subject to one's will.
One should perform an oblation for the Goddess with the flesh of a cat;
he attains the supreme Vidyā that brings all scriptures under its control.
One should perform a fire-oblation with goat meat combined with honey according to the procedure of one thousand [recitations]; thereby, the supernatural powers (siddhis) of the lineage are attained.
One who desires knowledge should perform oblations with milk-rice mixed with sugar;
indeed, for him the fourteen branches of learning will surely manifest immediately. (97)
One who, being composed in mind, offers bilva leaves smeared with the three sweets for one month,
even a barren woman obtains an excellent son who lives a long life. Having offered karkandhu flowers together with goat’s blood, [one attains the same].
O Goddess, for the unfortunate woman, you forcibly bestow auspicious good fortune. || 99 ||
O Great Goddess, by performing a fire-oblation with honey and milk-rice using the garment of a menstruating woman, one may bring the three worlds under one's control.
Thus, O Goddess, this [mantra] which destroys all sins has been declared;
by the recitation of the mantra, O Goddess, it destroys all sins. Having abandoned the defilement of impurity, he who is pure shall certainly recite it. || 1 ||
Although no preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this has been mentioned, nevertheless, a recitation (japa) of one thousand and eight times is required;
it should be understood that the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites are to be performed with a tenth part of that number.
And so it is said:
"Regarding those for which no number has been stated by the wise for recitation (japa) and oblation (homa),
the number for both recitation and oblation shall be eight thousand," because of this statement.
The traditional teaching (sampradāya) holds that [the number of recitations] is eight thousand or one thousand and eight;
however, the authors of the commentaries maintain that because these [mantras] are perfected vidyās, there is no preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) required for them. || 2 ||
Now, the mantras of Dhūmāvatī according to the Phetkāriṇī:
"The seed-syllable of Dhūmāvatī consists of the two letters *da* and *ta*, followed by the lord of the *argha* (the letter *i*), and ending with the bindu; it is the second *ṭha* (*pha*)."
The mantra of Dhūmāvatī is proclaimed as that which effects the subjugation of enemies.
The worship of this [goddess] is as follows:

having performed the morning rites and so forth, and having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement of the seers and other factors (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
For example: "Homage to the seer Pippalāda on the head; homage to the Nivṛt metre in the mouth; homage to the deity Dhūmāvatī in the heart. (4)
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs:
*dhāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *dhīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*, and so forth.
Likewise: *dhāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth. || 5 ||
Then comes the meditation:
she is discolored, fickle, angry, tall, and clad in soiled garments;
her hair is discolored, she is harsh, a widow, and has sparse teeth.
Mounted upon a chariot with a crow as its banner, with pendulous breasts, a winnowing basket in her hand,
and exceedingly harsh eyes; shaking her hand while endowed with boons,
she has an elongated nose, is intensely crooked, and possesses a sidelong gaze.
Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, she is a source of fear and fond of quarreling; she has sparse teeth and gaps between her teeth.

For the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), the practitioner of mantra, devoted to fasting, should recite [the mantra] day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in an empty house,
a cremation ground, or a forest, remaining silent and restrained. He should recite it one hundred thousand times.
Wearing wet garments and with his hair tied up, during the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), he should write the mantra upon a piece of cloth; having placed Śiva thereon, he should worship him.
And thus it is said:

Having taken hold of Śiva by means of the name of the enemy, one should mutter the mantra; within five hundred repetitions, the enemy is seized by fever. Peace from the fever may be attained through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or even with milk.
Then, having worshipped as before with the fivefold offerings, one should perform the recitation. || 7 ||

Having done so with the mantra, including the name of the enemy, on a leaf from a *yāminī* tree in the forest, the destruction of the enemy occurs through ten thousand recitations (*japa*). Having burnt a crow in the cremation fire and taking its ashes, they should be consecrated with the mantra.

The immediate eradication of enemies who are hostile occurs when [the mantra] is consecrated thus and cast in the eight directions one hundred and eight times; this is the meaning of "one should cast it in the eight directions. (7ka)
Having prepared an image of Śiva with cremation-ground ashes, one should place it upon that [base].
One should worship it during the dark fortnight, unobstructed by adversaries.
Incense made from buffalo milk should be offered, as well as whatever else brings about the downfall of Indra.
Having assumed the form of a buffalo in a dream, one should destroy the enemy;
with this mantra, one should scatter that ash in the enemy's dwelling.
One will certainly cause the enemies to be eradicated; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Having fashioned a linga from the ashes of a cremation ground, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings.
Addressing it as "O Blessed One," while mentally contemplating the ritual action,
one should combine the leaves of the neem tree and the crow's wing and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should offer incense while reciting the name of the person to be acted upon; this will instantly cause enmity among enemies.
The meaning of this is:
having combined the leaves of the *nimba* and the crow-palm (*kākacchada*) trees, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over them, and with that—
"By means of this substance, cause [so-and-so] to hate, cause to hate! Having uttered the root mantra, one should offer incense.
And thus it is said:
Peace shall always be attained by offering oblations of milk into the fire of funeral wood.
Likewise, Kālikā in the form of a vulture comes and slays the enemy by means of incense made from menstrual blood; peace is achieved through incense made from the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*).
With the incense of *varāhakarṇa*, one may destroy a woman in the form of a sow;
with the incense of *aśvattha* leaves, peace is attained and not otherwise.
Peace from all malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*) arises through the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
O Goddess of gods, having pierced a stake made from the wood of a milk-tree with either milk or the three sweets (madhuratrika),
one should engrave the syllables of the name with the mantra; then, having recited it and written [the name] upon two pieces of cloth, one should bury them to effect the eradication of enemies.

One should offer a *bali* to the twice-born with an oblation sprinkled with the dust from his two feet; having muttered that [mantra] over the ashes of a funeral pyre and fixed them at the enemy's house, their expulsion occurs—such is the ritual application (*prayoga*). || 9 ||
Now, for the mantra of Bhadrakālī:
having extracted the seed-syllable of Prāsāda (Hrīm), one should extract the word "Kālī";
then, having uttered the word "Mahākālīm," [one should utter] the pair "Kili" thereafter.
This great mantra of Bhadrakālī ends with "astra" and "agnipriyā."
Having propitiated [the deity], one should recite the mantra daily; one should perform one hundred and eight recitations (*japa*).
A rosary (*japamālā*) should be prepared with one hundred and eight beads.
This Great Goddess, Bhadrakālī, the dispeller of fear, should be meditated upon.

"Having propitiated" means that, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should worship the Śiva-liṅga with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). || 11 ||

As for meditation: [One should visualize] Koṭarākṣarī, emaciated by hunger, her face soiled with filth, her hair disheveled, weeping and saying, "I am not yet satiated; I shall make this entire world into a single morsel."
Holding in her two hands a pair of nooses resembling blazing flames of fire, with teeth like the fruit of the *jambu* tree, may Bhadrakālī protect me and dispel all fear. 12.
One should perform the mere ritual application that effects the subjugation of enemies.
This goddess, the Great Goddess, is the one who brings about the suppression of foes;
she should be meditated upon according to one's desire, bestowing the attainment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.

Some say that its preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth are like those for the Dakṣiṇakālī mantra; however, in reality, the *puraścaraṇa* consists of one thousand and eight recitations (*japa*). || 14 ||
Now, the mantra of Ucchiṣṭagaṇeśa:
Oṃ hastipiśāci likhe ṭha ṭha. In another tantra:
Having first uttered the word *hastipada*, then the word *piśācī*,
followed by *devarāja* with the eye (*sanetra*) and the beloved [syllable] endowed with the sound of Īśa;
this mantra, ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*) and preceded by the *tāra* (Oṃ), grants all desires.

Some say that "gaṃ" should be placed in the position of the *praṇava*; however, according to the *Tattvabodha*, it is "gaṃ" at the beginning, [the syllables] being "likhe," "agnivanitā," and "gaṃ. 15.
Likewise:
This mantra, which is the very essence, should not be given to just anyone;
it is a secret revealed in all the scriptures with the intent for their welfare. (16)
And so it is said:
"Neither the lunar day nor the asterism, nor even fasting, is prescribed; the mantra grants the fruit of all desires through contemplation according to one's wish. (17)
The procedure for its worship is as follows:
having performed the morning rites up to the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
One should say: "Salutation to the seer Sudhīra on the head; salutation to the Nivṛt-gāyatrī metre on the mouth; [salutation] to [the deity] on the heart."
Salutation to the deity Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs with the Praṇava, one should meditate. || 18 ||
As for the meditation (*dhyāna*):
one should visualize Gaṇeśa with a red form, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing red garments, possessing three eyes, and seated upon a red lotus throne.
One should visualize Mahākāla with four arms and two tusks, his face smiling;
holding a desired object in his right hand and a tusk in the hand below it,
with a noose and goad in his other two hands, and his head encircled by a mass of matted locks.

Having meditated thus upon [the deity] who is enriched by the crescent moon on the forehead and adorned with all ornaments, one should worship [him] on the head with flowers held in the hand while reciting the root mantra,
and then begin the external worship.

(Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should worship it. Therein, first having established the *arghya* with the root mantra and having recited the root mantra ten times, having sprinkled oneself and the articles of worship with that water, and having meditated again, [one should worship] in the center of the eight-petaled lotus.
One should install [the deity].
Then, having worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), one should [offer] into the petals starting from the east and so forth: "Oṃ vakratuṇḍāya svāhā."
Thus: svāhā to Ekadanta; to Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighneśa, Gajavaktra, Vināyaka, Gaṇapati; and in the center, to Hastimukha. In every case, the mantra ends with svāhā.

Having worshipped the deity again three times, performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity and offered it, and having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) in the form of a sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should give the *bali* with the mantra: "Oṃ, to Ucchiṣṭagaṇeśa Mahākāla, this is the *bali*, obeisance. Then, one should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) and so forth.
Furthermore, those desiring special fruits should offer the *bali* with the mantra: *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hrūṃ svāhā*.
Then, having cast a single flower toward the southern direction, one should dismiss [the deity] with the words, "Forgive me. || 20 ||
(Plate 39: The Ucchiṣṭagaṇeśa Yantra) The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of sixteen thousand recitations (*japa*).
And so it is said:
Beginning from the fourth day of the dark fortnight until the fourth day of the bright fortnight,
a woman, preceded by the observance of restraints, should daily recite the mantra one thousand times;
she should daily bathe [the deity] with honey, and offer as sacrificial food molasses and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having eaten one’s leftovers, one should daily recite [the mantra], thinking: "I am always the beloved Gaṇeśa.
Having fashioned an image with white chalk or red sandalwood, and having installed it the size of a thumb in the presence of a twice-born, a fire, and a preceptor, [one should worship].
Having recited [the mantra] sixteen thousand times, one will certainly become a master of the mantra (*siddhamantra*).

"With a woman" (*yoṣit*) means that one should approach a woman preceded by the prescribed rules; it does not mean a rule of renunciation, because such a thing would be irrelevant, improper, and because of the observation [in the text]: "one who has not sipped water" (*anācānta*). || 21 ||
"Having become impure by being left-over (ucchiṣṭa), one should perform recitation and worship;
it will not succeed if one is not left-over; therefore, one should act in this manner.
This is also because of the statement from another Tantra.
According to some, there is no ritual worship; one should perform recitation mentally.
According to others, there is no placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa); one should contemplate what was previously stated: "I am Gaṇeśa."
Having stayed in a solitary forest at dawn, one should recite the mantra with one's mouth stained by the remnants of betel-leaf smeared with red sandalwood paste;
according to some authorities, one may recite it in all circumstances while adorned with all ornaments.
According to the opinion of Anyamata, one worships and chews a sweetmeat (modaka); according to Bhṛgumata, one eats fruit;
and according to Vibhīṣaṇamata, one offers meat as a sacrificial oblation and eats that very same thing.
Now, the specific application:
at the king’s gate, likewise in the forest, in an assembly, in a gathering of clans, in a dispute,
in legal proceedings, in battle, or in the peril of enemies.
Whether on a boat, in the forest, at a gambling match, or likewise in calamity;
in a village fire, when beset by thieves, or in danger from lions, tigers, and the like—
by the mere remembrance of the Lord, everything indeed shall flee away.
All that perishes quickly, just as darkness is dispelled by the sun. || 23 ||
Likewise:
Gaṇeśāna, who grants the fruits of one's desires when properly worshipped with offerings, was propitiated by the wise King of Yakṣas immediately after his meal.
Having thus established the expenditure, he attained mastery over that wealth. || 24 ||
By performing a fire-oblation with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga, consecrated with the root mantra one hundred and eight times, the practitioner of mantras certainly attains good fortune.
Likewise:
one should bury a consecrated stake made from the bone of a monkey in the house of someone; for that person, there will be supreme eradication.
If one should dig in the street of someone whose trade is buying and selling, that person's commerce will be ruined;
if one buries it in a tavern, that liquor will become spoiled; but if one buries it in a courtesan’s house, she will not find a patron.
One should bury it in the girl's house; then marriage will certainly take place. || 28 ||
If one buries a consecrated stake made from human bone in someone's house, that person's death is certain. (29)
It is the consensus of all that health shall be restored once [the obstacle] has been extracted;
by reciting the mantra one thousand times in the name of whomever, that person shall come under one's control.
By performing five thousand homas, one shall obtain an excellent woman;
by performing ten thousand homas, a king shall immediately come under one's control.
By one hundred thousand recitations, he becomes a king; by two hundred thousand, he gains the ranks of kings;
and by one million, his entire kingdom is brought under his control in every way.
Through ten million recitations, there is no doubt that one attains the great siddhis such as aṇimā;
one becomes eternally a sky-walker (khecarī) and omniscience arises. (33)
If one writes down the mantra and wears it on the head or the neck, good fortune and complete protection will certainly be attained therein. (34)
Now, the mantra of Dhanada: O Goddess,
one should first extract the syllable *tu* joined with the *bindu*, then the seed-syllable of Lajjā (*hrīṃ*),
then the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī (*śrīṃ*), followed by the vocative address "O beloved of Rati."
Ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), this is declared to be the most excellent of the best king of mantras. || 35 ||
In another tantra:
Having extracted the fourth [vowel] joined with the bindu, the Praṇava of Lakṣmī,
and the seed-syllable of Māyā, together with the awakening and Ratipriyā.
This supreme among the best of king-mantras is said to end with the wife of Fire (svāhā).
This mantra, approved by Kubera, consists of the Lakṣmī-praṇava and the Śrī-bīja.
Its worship is as follows:
having performed the morning rites up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer and so forth.
One should say: "Salutation to Kubera, the seer, on the head; salutation to Paṅkti, the meter, on the mouth."
Salutation to the deity Hṛddhanadā. || 37 ||
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs: "hrāṃ to the two thumbs, svāhā," and so forth;
likewise for the heart and other parts. || 38 ||
Then comes the meditation:
[She is] with the luster of the interior of saffron, possessing a touch of youthful bloom,
with arms as tender as lotus stalks, and adorned with armlets upon her limbs.
Her two lotus-feet are adorned with anklets that shimmer like the tips of a balance-beam;
she is embellished with a necklace of rubies, a crown, earrings, and other ornaments;
her eyes are like blue lotuses, and she is graced by her slightly budding breasts.

One should meditate upon the goddess who bestows wealth, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne within a golden enclosure at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), wearing red garments and red unguents, and holding a revolving lotus in her two hands.
Having meditated thus and performed worship with mental offerings, one should begin the external worship.
The worship diagram (pūjāyantra):
One should draw a wheel consisting of nine triangles upon the pericarp;
having drawn a lotus with petals in the cardinal directions, one should draw a square on the outside.
Having drawn vajras in the corners, one should inscribe the seed-syllable in the center. (Figure 40) Then, the placement of the *arghya* vessel:
having washed the vessel with "phaṭ," having filled it with water by means of "namaḥ," [one should place] there [the syllable] with the *praṇava*.

Having cast fragrant flowers [into the water], having invoked the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) ten times over it; then, having poured a little of that water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should sprinkle oneself and the ritual implements three times with that water while reciting the root mantra.

Having performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) beginning with "Ādhāraśaktyai" and ending with "Hrīṃ Jñānātmane Namaḥ," and having worshipped in the center with "Oṃ Padmāsanāya Namaḥ," one should again meditate, invoke [the deity], and worship with the five services (pañcopacāra). || 41 ||

Then, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should worship with the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mantra beginning with "hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" in the filaments— at the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions. Then, on the petals starting from the east, [one worships] "oṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ," and likewise "padmāyai" and "padmālayāyai."
One should worship the Goddess again in the center, offering oblations to Śrī, Haripriyā, Tārā, Kamalā, Cañcalā, Ajā, and Lolā.
Then, having recited the mantra according to one's capacity and offered the recitation (japa), one should dismiss her with the words, "Forgive me. || 41ka ||
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
"One should recite with a rosary made of beads such as gems and the like."
When one hundred thousand recitations have been performed, one should perform the *puraścaryā* for the attainment of the mantra's power.
In whatever manner the practitioner performs the most captivating applications,
if one recites [the mantra] eight thousand times at night for seven days,
by this alone the ritual procedure beginning with the *puraścaraṇa* becomes perfectly accomplished. (43)

O Goddess, what here is difficult for a human being to accomplish if he should strive? Whether having eaten or not having eaten, by offering milk-rice (pāyasa), or even ten times over, or without performing purification, or while wearing tattered clothes— [all this is easily achieved].
O Goddess, he who remembers that Vidyā is not overcome by miseries of poverty.
One should worship Kāmadeva daily with devotion by the side of the Goddess;
through that, there is great pleasure for the Goddess, and she grants one's desired object. (45)
And at the conclusion of the worship, the goddess Dhaneśvarī arrives at night;
having bestowed [her gifts] and cast off all her ornaments, she goes to her own abode. (46)
O Maheśānī, having bestowed abundant wealth and fulfilled the desires of the practitioner, that auspicious woman becomes submissive.
Or else, O Great Goddess, an anointing with sandalwood paste should always be given to him with devotion for the perpetual pacification of poverty. (48)
Worship should be performed for the Great Goddess, who is anointed with sandalwood paste;
and an offering of food should be presented daily for the pacification of poverty. (49)
The yakṣiṇī herself said: "Whatever man remembers me, for him I shall effect the abandonment of poverty, acting like a maidservant. (50)
A preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of one thousand [recitations] performed seven times is desired;
likewise, a fire-oblation (homa) with clarified butter, sugar, and honey, consisting of a tenth part [of the recitation],
should also be performed for the immediate pacification of poverty.
The worship of the Great Goddess should be performed upon a surface anointed with sandalwood paste;
likewise, a very beautiful mandala should be fashioned within a copper vessel.
In that regard, the wise person should perform worship of the Goddess in this manner;
for how could there be any fear of poverty for him, since he shall become a lord of ten million? (53)
The placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement of hands (karanyāsa), as well as the deities belonging to her body,
are always performed for her worship and other rites according to the opinion of Kubera.
Now, the mantra of Śmaśānakālī from the Kālītantra:
first Vāṇī, then Māyā, then Lakṣmī, and after that the Kāmabīja.
In the *Kālikā* [mantra], one should write the four seed-syllables in the form of a *saṃpuṭa*;
O Goddess, this eleven-syllable [mantra] bestows the four aims of human life. (Śmaśānakālī Yantra, Figure 41)
Its yantra is as follows:
a circle with eight petals, outside of which is the surface of the earth;
it is provided with four gates, and one should draw the root-mantra in the center.
One should draw the eight groups of consonants, beginning with the *ka*-group,

upon the eight petals; on the pericarp (*dharaṇī*), one should draw the first group of four, and within each of those four [sub-petals], from east to north, one should worship the Goddess in the center.
The sequence of worship:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and other elements.
Salutation to the sage Bhṛgu on the head; salutation to the Nivṛt meter in the mouth; salutation to the deity Śmaśānakālikā in the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Vāk in the private parts;
salutation to the power Hrīṃ at the feet; salutation to the wedge of the Kāma-bīja in all limbs.

Then, the ritual assignments of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *aiṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *śrīṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *klīṃ* to the two ring fingers, *hūṃ*; [and] *kālike*.
With the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*.
*Klīṃ*, ending with the primordial *vāgbhava* [syllable], with the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*. Thus for the heart and the other limbs. || 58 ||
Then the meditation:
[one should visualize] the Goddess, who resembles a mountain of collyrium, dwelling in a cremation ground,
with red eyes and loose hair, possessing pure flesh and being exceedingly terrifying.
I bow to the auspicious Śivā, who has tawny eyes, who holds in her left hand a skull-cup filled with wine and flesh,
and in her right hand a freshly severed head;
whose face is ever smiling, and who is constantly intent upon chewing raw meat.
Her limbs were adorned with various ornaments, yet she was naked and perpetually intoxicated by spirits.

Having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra] for the Goddess, especially in a cremation ground; or even at home, a householder may perform the great worship at night, especially while naked, with offerings of fish, meat, and fine food.
As for the worship:

having meditated and performed mental worship, one should perform the ritual placement of the *arghya* water. Having meditated again and worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should worship Brāhmī and the others upon the leaves.
Outside of that, one should worship Bhairavas such as Asitāṅga and the others.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this [mantra] consists of eleven lakhs of recitations.
And so it is said:
"One should recite the mantra one lakh times according to its syllables, and should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that. (62)
Another mantra is found in that very same place: "Having written the seed-syllable of Kāma, one should write 'to Kālikā';
ending with 'namas', O Goddess of Gods, this seven-syllabled mantra is supreme."
The six-limbed [rite] for the goddess Kālikā is as follows; everything else is as before.
"For the goddess Kālikā" means by means of her own seed-syllable (bīja). || 63 ||
The mantra of Bagalāmukhī:
As it is stated in another tantra:
"I shall fully explain the Brahmāstra, which produces immediate conviction."
For the benefit of practitioners and for the immobilization of enemies, by the mere remembrance of whom even the wind becomes still. (64)
First the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the firm Māyā (Hrīṃ), and then "Bagalāmukhi. At the end of that, [the words] "of all the wicked" (sarvaduṣṭānām), then the word "speech" (vācam),
then the word "mouth" (mukham), then "paralyze" (stambhaya), and then the two words "pin the tongue" (jihvāṃ kīlaya).
One should then draw a firm *māyā* for the destruction of the intellect (*buddhi*).
One should further write the syllable *oṃ* and the word *svāhā* at the end.
This thirty-six-syllabled *vidyā* bestows all prosperity.
In the *sthiramāyā*, [the seed-syllable] is *hlīṃ*. And so it is said: "The *māyā* joined with Indra (L) and devoid of Vahni (R) is proclaimed as *sthiramāyā*. (65)
In another tantra: [The mantra] is Vahnihīnendrayuṅmāyā Bagalāmukhi, joined with "sarva.
Having uttered "the speech of the wicked," one should recite "paralyze their mouth" (mukhaṃ stambhaya).
"Kīlaya jihvām," then "vināśaya," and one should utter the word "padam.
Then follows the seed-syllable (bīja) and then the *tāra* (Oṃ), ending with the wife of fire (Svāhā).
This thirty-four-syllable mantra of Bagalāmukhī begins with the *tāra*.
This is also another mantra. || 66 ||
The worship of these two is as follows:
having performed the morning rites up to the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth. As follows:

Salutation to the sage Nārada on the head; salutation to the Tṛṣṭubh metre on the mouth; salutation to the deity Bagalāmukhī on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Hlīṃ on the private parts; salutation to the power Svāhā on the feet.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa): Nārada as the Ṛṣi upon the head of this [deity], the Triṣṭubh metre in its mouth, and the goddess Śrī-Bagalāmukhī in the heart.
The seed-syllable *hlīṃ* is in the secret region, and the power *svāhā* is in the two feet.
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *oṃ hlīṃ aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, *bagalāmukhi tarjanībhyāṃ svāhā*,
*sarvaduṣṭānāṃ madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ*, *vācaṃ mukhaṃ stambhaya*.
With the two ring fingers, *huṃ*; with the two little fingers, *jihvāṃ kīlaya kīlaya vauṣaṭ*;
with the palms and backs of the hands, *buddhiṃ vināśaya hlīṃ oṃ svāhā phaṭ*.
Thus [it is applied] to the heart and other [limbs].
And so it is said in the *Divyatantra*:

"One should perform the ritual placement (*karāṅganyāsa*) on the fingers and palms with the syllables arising from the mantra, specifically those consisting of two, five, five, seven, and the remainder. (68)

Then, at the end of the root mantra, [recite]: "I worship the venerable sandals of Bagalāmukhī, the pervader of the Ātmatattva," at the Mūlādhāra. At the end of the root mantra, [recite]: "I worship the venerable sandals of Bagalāmukhī, the pervader of the Vidyātattva."
At the head: "I worship the venerable sandals of Bagalāmukhī, who pervades all principles (sarvatattvavyāpinī)," at the end of the root mantra; [and] thus on all limbs.
And likewise: on the crown of the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the two cheeks,
the two nostrils, the two lips, the perimeter of the mouth, the right shoulder, and the elbow.
One should then place [the mantras] again on the wrists, at the base of the fingers, on the throat, the breasts, the heart,
the navel, the hips, the private region, the left shoulder, the elbow,
and likewise on the wrists and the base of the fingers.
Having sequentially assigned the syllables of the mantra to the right and left thighs, knees, ankles, and the bases of the toes, one should meditate according to the prescribed rule.
Then the meditation:
[one should visualize her] seated upon a lion throne on a jewel-encrusted altar within a jeweled pavilion above an ocean of nectar in the center, possessing a deep yellow complexion.
I meditate upon the Goddess, whose limbs are adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands,
who holds a mallet to the tongue of her enemy;
with her left hand, she seizes the tip of the tongue while crushing her foes.
And with the blow of the mace in her right hand, I bow to her who is adorned with yellow garments and possesses two arms;
having meditated thus and worshipped her mentally, one should begin the external worship.
Therein, first is the placement of the *arghya* (offering water).
As follows:
having prepared a square measuring eight finger-breadths, [one should place it] in the corners starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and in the directions starting from the east.

Having worshipped with flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and red sandalwood while reciting "glauṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ," and having performed the gift of the elephant, one should fill the arghya vessel with that [elephant-essence] or with honey.
Then, having worshipped three times with the root mantra (mūlavidyā), one should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Then, having displayed the Dhenu-yoni-mudrā, one should sprinkle oneself and the ritual implements with that water. || 71 ||
Its yantra is as follows:
a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a surrounding square enclosure (bhūpura).
Then, having uttered the root mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Throne of the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti)," thus...
Salutation to the lotus-throne of Śakti.
Then, having meditated as before and invoked [the deity] upon the seat, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Thereafter, having displayed the mudrās, one should worship a maṇḍala in front with the six limbs.

Then, having consecrated [the offering] with the root mantra and displayed the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās, one should cast three drops (*bindu*) into the mouth using the principles (*tattva*) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva; then, by joining the index finger and thumb, one should satisfy Bagalāmukhī along with her limbs and retinue. || 73 ||
Then, having worshipped according to the available ritual offerings (*upacāra*), one should begin the worship of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
In the six corners: in the east, *oṃ subhagāyai namaḥ*; likewise, in the southeast, to Bhagasarpiṇī;
in the northeast, to Bhagavahā; in the west, to Bhagasiddhā; in the southwest, [to Bhaganandā].

To Bhaganipātinī in the southeast, and to Bhagamālinī in the northwest. Then, on the petals of the eight-petaled lotus, the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped at the tips of the petals:
Oṃ, salutation to Jayā; likewise to Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, and Stambhinī.
To Jambhinī, Mohinī, and Ākarṣiṇī.
Then, at the doors, [one should offer] "Oṃ, obeisance to Bhairava.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as the vajra and the other weapons.
Then, having offered incense and other offerings, performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, displayed the trident mudrā (*triśūlamudrā*),
and presented three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should display the womb mudrā (*yonimudrā*) to the Goddess. Thereafter, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to Bhairava.
Then, one should complete the ritual actions ending with the dismissal [of the deities]. || 73ka ||
(Bagalāmukhī Yantra, Figure 42).
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
And so it is said:
Clad in yellow garments and facing the east,
one should recite my mantra one hundred thousand times using a rosary of turmeric knots,
constantly devoted to celibacy, self-restrained, and intent on meditation.
One should also perform the oblation with priyaṅgu flowers and yellow blossoms.
In the second mantra, all [procedures] such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) are as before.
As for the visualization (*dhyāna*):
[she is] deep and intoxicated with passion, possessing a luster equal to the brilliance of gold.
One should visualize the goddess with four arms and three eyes, seated upon a lotus throne;
holding a mallet in her right hand and a noose and a tongue in her left,
she wears yellow garments and possesses firm, full breasts.
Adorned with golden earrings, wearing a yellow crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
and decorated with yellow ornaments, she was seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.
Now, the ritual application:
it effects the paralysis of speech and the destruction of the intellect of the wicked;
during the practice of recitation and fire-offerings, one should also recite the mantra ten thousand times.
One should offer oblations of salt mixed with turmeric and yellow orpiment at night;
one will thus paralyze the enemy armies—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (77)
Alternatively, one should perform oblations with yellow flowers smeared with the three sweets;
this practice brings about the realization of all rites of immobilization (stambhana). || 78 ||
As for the yantra: one should write the two *oṃ*s facing each other with their heads pointing upward and downward;
the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is placed in the center, and outside of that, the three syllables.

One should write the third letter of the second group, adorned with a bindu and joined with the fourteenth vowel, situated upon the earth (the letter *la*). This should be encircled by the letter *ṭha*, and outside of it, a four-cornered enclosure should be drawn.
One should draw eight vajras joined to the lines of those corners with empty spaces;
on both sides of the central line of the trident are the seed-syllables of the Earth (Pṛthivī).
Furthermore, in all eight corners and outside of them, one should write Vagalā.
Or else, one should encircle the sphere of the Mātṛkās within the air-element and the earth-element in eight ways; thereafter, it should be bound on the outside by the stable *māyā* [syllable],
using the *aṅkuśa* seed-syllable whose feet are joined with the *nāda*.
One should draw [the diagram] as before, encircling it,
and afterwards draw Vagalamukhī upon a cloth or a stone slab using turmeric, datura, and orpiment;
having thus drawn it for the purpose of divine paralyzing or the paralyzing of the mouth, one should firmly step upon it.
In a dispute, having drawn the yantra on birch bark with those very same materials,
one should take clay from the wheel of a potter as it is spinning in reverse and then have a bull fashioned from it.
Having placed the yantra upon it and smeared it with lacquer,
one should fix it on his nose; then, having placed a yellow cord in his own house,
he should daily worship that four-cornered [yantra] with yellow offerings.
The mouth of even Vācaspati [the Lord of Speech] becomes paralyzed when he is wicked. (Figure 43:
The Bagalāmukhī Dhāraṇayantra from the Viśvasāra)
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Vidyā, Dhūmāvatī,
Bagalā, Siddhividyā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalātmikā.
These ten Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the perfected sciences (siddhavidyās). || 80 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the Tantrasāra composed by Kṛṣṇānanda Bhaṭṭācārya.
Now begins the third chapter: the Karṇapiśācī mantra.

As it has been stated in another Tantra: "The letter *a* situated in the ears, mouth, eyes, and red lotus is Ananta; the letter *i* is Bhuvaneśī, joined with the word 'past and future' and followed by the wife of Fire (the syllable *svāhā*)."
This mantra beginning with "Tārā" was practiced by Vyāsa through one hundred thousand recitations; by means of devotion to Paiśācika, one certainly attains omniscience before long. || 1 ||
Another mantra:
"Kaha-yugma, Kālike, likewise gṛhṇa-yugma, Piṇḍa, Piśāci, Svāhā"—this, O Dear One, is said to contain the letters of the king (Nṛpa). 2.
As for the meditation (*dhyāna*):
[one should visualize her] as black, with red eyes, three-eyed, short-statured, and pot-bellied;
with a tongue as crimson as the *bandhūka* flower, her hands displaying the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), and with her face upturned.

We bow to that Paiśācī goddess, who has smoke and flames for matted hair, whose two hands sport with a skull-cup, who is restless, all-knowing, and who makes her dwelling upon the heart of a corpse. || 3 ||
Now, the worship:

At night, specifically at midnight, having placed the Piśācikī [mantra] upon the heart and having offered the "burnt fish" (dagdhamīna) oblation, one should worship her at night and perform the recitation.
"Oṃ karṇapiśāci, take, take this offering of a burnt fish; grant me success, grant it! Svāhā!"—with these words, one should present the offering of a burnt fish. || 5 ||
"O Goddess of gods, make whatever there is—red sandalwood, bandhūka, javā flowers, and so forth—into nectar; [saying] 'svāhā,' one should sprinkle them with water."
Having recited [the mantra] a certain number of times in the forenoon, and having eaten a single meal free of meat at midday, one should likewise recite it that same number of times during the night.
Nothing else should be consumed, except for betel leaves and the like.
The libation (tarpaṇa) shall be one-tenth of the recitation (japa).
"Oṃ, I offer libations to Karṇapiśācī, hrīṃ svāhā.
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of one hundred thousand [recitations] in this sequence, [one should perform] one-tenth [of that].
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
In its absence, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) ten times the number of oblations, one should pray for a boon.
Having written the root mantra with red sandalwood paste upon the yantra, one should worship the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) above it. || 7 ||
Now, the characteristics of accomplishment are described:
