from hearing the sound of the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth in the sky, or from seeing the appearance of long flames of fire, one should know that accomplishment will occur and act accordingly. || 8 ||
Another mantra:
*Oṃ hrīḥ karṇapiśāci me karṇe kathaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having applied lamp-oil to one's feet, one should recite this a hundred thousand times at night.
Thereupon, he becomes omniscient; for him, there is no need for worship or meditative concentration.
Likewise:
*Tāraṃ kāmabījaṃ jayādevi svāhā*. For this [mantra] as well, there is an absence of the assignment of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth; one should first recite it one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*).
Having struck down a house-lizard and worshipped Jayādevī upon it according to one's ability, one should recite the mantra until she comes back to life; then, success is attained.
As for that success: when a question regarding the mind and so forth is posed, she appears, and then everything [is revealed] on her back.
One perceives the past, the future, and so forth. || 10 ||
Now, the mantras of Mañjughoṣa:
May the glorious Mañjughoṣa be victorious—he who destroys the darkness of the flood of dullness, who ferries beings across the ocean of saṃsāra, and who brings happiness to practitioners. (11)
In that regard, the *Āgamottara* states:
"Having extracted the beginning of the *mātṛkā*, one should extract the seed-syllable of fire (*ra*).
Then, one should extract the left portion known as the 'tortoise' (*kūrma*), and thereafter extract the 'cloud' (*megha*)."
Then one should form Mīneśa (the letter *i*) joined with the moon of the left eye (the vowel *u*). This six-syllable mantra of Mañjughoṣa was proclaimed by Śambhu:
the first letter of the Mātṛkā (*a*), the fourth semi-vowel (*ya*), and the Tortoise (*ca*).
The letter *la* is the lord of Aries, and the letter *dha* is the lord of Pisces;
these are said to be the illuminators (*dīpanī*), while the root mantra is now being told.
O Dear One, the goad (aṅkuśa), the seed-syllable of power (śakti), and then the seed-syllable of Ramā—
this mantra consisting of these three seed-syllables destroys the darkness of the flood of dullness.
O Dear One, [then] the seed-syllable of power, the seed-syllable of Ramā, and then the seed-syllable of desire (kāma).
This Vidyā, consisting of the three castes, is declared to be the bearer of the Vedas. || 13 ||
The syllable *ha* mounted upon fire (*ra*), adorned by the moon of the left eye (*i*), is declared to be this *Sarvajñavidyā*, whose essence is the single ear (*ekarṇa*), O Dear One. (14)

Whether it be a *siddha*, *sādhya*, or *susiddha* mantra, or even one that is an enemy to the practitioner, at that time, through devotion, the mantra shall become a bestower of auspiciousness and a giver of wisdom. This applies during midday, while in water, while eating, and likewise while using a vessel.
Having drawn a *yantra* resembling a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) upon cow dung in a foreign land, during sexual union, at the vulva of a beautiful woman, in a cow-pen, or at night on a cow’s skull,
one should inscribe the mantra-syllables three times, both upwards and downwards.
The most excellent practitioner should write [this] with effort using a sandalwood stylus. || 16 ||
For the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should especially draw the yantra (or mantra) upon ox-hide;
by doing so, one is eternally victorious in water, becomes a lord (*maheśvara*) in matters of food, becomes eloquent on cow-dung, and attains omniscience in a cow-pen.
In Kuce he was always a retainer of the Vedas, and in Gomunda he was a great poet. || 17 ||
Having combined cow’s urine, the root of the *badarī* tree, sandalwood, and earth,
and having recited the mantra over it eight times, one should always apply it as a *tilaka*.
Having paid homage to the most excellent and supreme one, one should pray with devotion.
And having obtained that boon from him, one should indeed dwell according to one's pleasure.

There shall be no worship of other deities, no ritual bathing, and no utterance of the *praṇava*. One should not clean the teeth with the hem of one's garment or with salt. One must not discard the garment worn at night, nor should one ever remain impure.
Having thus applied diligent effort and learned [this] from the mouth of the Guru, the wise one shall become a lord among poets in one month; indeed, in two months he shall become a sovereign;
and in three months, that mortal shall become an expert in all the scriptures. (19)
One desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring wealth obtains abundant wealth;
and one desiring long life and health shall attain all their desires. (Illustration 44) Thereafter, the ritual placement of hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) follows.
*Kṣāṃ śāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*.
Likewise for the heart and other [limbs].
And so it is stated in the Tantra:
O beloved, two colors have been described: Saṃvartaka and Vakeśa.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using these two, which possess the six long vowels.
Saṃvartaka is the letter *kṣa*.
Śakāra has disheveled hair. || 1 ||
Meditation: [One should visualize] the Youthful One (Kumāra), white as the moon, holding a sword and a book in his hands, most beautiful and exceedingly peaceful, adorned with five topknots.
I bow to Mañjughoṣa, whose face is preeminent and exceedingly broad, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, and who is skilled at burning away evil intellects. || 2 ||

Then one should perform the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā), beginning with the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) and so forth. Immediately thereafter, one should provide a seat for the pedestal (pīṭhāsana) using spirits, ghosts, and the like.
[One offers] water for the feet (pādya) saying, "Salutation to the giver of knowledge," and likewise, "To the maker of the intellect, mine."

For the destruction of dullness, there should be fragrance; indeed, the wise one should offer the water of honor (arghya) to the Lord of the Yakṣas with the words "Bestower of all Siddhis," and then offer flowers.
Then, having taken a *kundapuṣpa* flower, one should worship the Bhairavas:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, the one known as Unmatta, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra is recorded as the eighth.
Then, having offered incense and other offerings, one should scatter flowers. With those flowers, one should especially worship the eight Yakṣiṇīs:
Surādisundarī and immediately after her, Manohāriṇī.
Kanakāvatī, Kāmeśvarī, Rativaryā,
Padminī, Naṭī, and thereafter Anurāgiṇī—
these are the Yoginīs of worship, preceded by the seed-syllable *hṛllekhā*.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should mutter the mantra six hundred thousand times;
and with kunda flowers smeared with ghee, one should offer eleven hundred oblations into a kindled fire in a forest or at the abode of the ancestors.
Thus, the practitioner who has accomplished the mantra shall become a great lord of yogis.
In the *Kukkuṭeśvaratantra*:
Pārvatī questioned Śaṅkara, the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, the Supreme Lord, as he sat comfortably upon the summit of Mount Meru. (7)
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, regarding Mañjughoṣa— who bestows desired objects in this world according to all the scriptures and traditions— please speak of him to me.
What more need be said? By reciting this especially, men attain the state of poetic inspiration. This mantra grants all desires and likewise bestows the perfection of the mind;
it fulfills the wishes of devotees like another wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the great mantra that brings happiness to practitioners;
by knowing which, even one of dull intellect generally becomes equal to Vācaspati.

This mantra, when accompanied by the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), the placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and the external placement (vahirnyāsa), bestows success through recitation alone, even without fire offerings, worship, and the like. || 11 ||
Whether the practitioner recites it himself or causes it to be recited according to the prescribed rite, he attains omniscience; this is the truth, the very truth, O Pārvatī. 12.
One should recite the mantra until the face of Kārttikeya appears;
he shall then become highly eminent in all scriptures, equal to Bṛhaspati. (13)
Śrī Pārvatī said: Who is the Ṛṣi here, what is the Chandas, and which deity is worshipped here?
Or who is to be meditated upon here? Tell me all that, O you who are kind to your devotees. (14)
Īśvara said: The sage named Vṛhadāraṇyaka and the Virāṭ meter are indeed that very one known as Mañjughoṣa, who grants liberation through the gift of devotion. 15.
Having meditated upon the form of Bhairava, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
then the mantra bestows liberation—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (16)
I shall now describe the meditation upon the great-souled Bhairava;
listen as I speak of how one should meditate and then recite the mantra. (17)
O Maheśānī, desiring their welfare, I shall describe the meditations—sāttvika, rājasa, and immediately thereafter tāmasa—in due order. (18)
Having meditated upon the form that grants immediate accomplishment, one should perform sattvic recitation;
it bestows success upon practitioners and grants whatever is desired by devotees. (19)
O Goddess, this extraction of mantras is difficult even for the three worlds to obtain;
it is not to be revealed, being a supreme secret, and must not be given to just anyone.

O Dear One, I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra, more secret than the secret; this six-syllabled mantra, consisting of the forms of Viṣṇu, Agni, Pāśin, and the Moon joined with the vowel *u*, has arisen for the happiness of the worlds.
It bestows omniscience and eloquence in the assembly; for one devoted to the knowledge of Vedānta, it shall be a granter of wealth.
If the practitioner, subsisting on offerings of food, recites the first mantra ten thousand times, he becomes like another Bṛhaspati in person.
If a man performs the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for only one month, even from his mouth shall issue speech that flows with aesthetic flavor (rasa).
By practicing continuously for three months, he becomes a poet; of this there is no doubt. (23)
One should first write the mantra upon a cow skull, on a cow’s back, on a discus, or even on cow dung; having written the mantra on the yantra, one should then recite the mantra again.
Having first performed meditation alone and contemplated for a long time,
the wise one should go to a secluded place and recite my mantra while facing downward.
Beginning from the full moon day, having worshipped with one hundred and eight flowers of the kunda plant, one should recite the mantra at a crossroads.
Having performed the ascension of the three skulls at midnight with hair loosened, one who knows the ritual procedure should indeed recite [the mantra] for just six months;
he becomes a speaker equal to Bṛhaspati—of this there is no need for doubt. (27)
A single shaven head of a dog, one of a jackal, and one of a bull—this is known as the "Three-Shaven" (Trimuṇḍa), which brings happiness to practitioners. || 28 ||
Having placed a cow’s skull as the seat, a dog’s skull on the left,
and a jackal’s skull on the right, one should perform the worship.

One should clearly draw a yantra there in the shape of a half-moon, resembling the young crescent moon; therein, one should perform worship with *kunda* flowers using the lotus-hand of the left [hand] during the ritual practice of erotic love, such as recitation (*japa*) and other forms of worship. (Figure 45)
To the south,
having visualized [the deity] white as the rays of the full moon’s cool beams, seated upon the summit of a bull at the edge of a crossroads. || 31 ||
Having intentionally mounted the heads of a dog and a jackal, the practitioner, having performed the recitation as much as desired with *kunda* flowers,
[visualizes] a wheel even larger than that, measuring one *rasa* (six) *koṇas* (squares), fashioned from cowhide.
With fresh saffron and gorocanā. || 32 ||
Having fashioned [the image] according to the prescribed rite in a solitary cremation ground, one should worship with fresh *palāśa* leaves grown in the forest;
having meditated upon the white Child amidst the full mandala and the cool-rayed moon.
Holding an excellent sword in his hand. || 33 ||
One should mutter [the mantra] over a naked person whose mass of hair is disheveled, who is richly endowed with excellent books, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals and red like blood—
having carefully taken oil from the house of a dead man at night with the hand-petal. (34)

Having offered that very golden flower which she had bent down, he chants his prayers at will before her; then, having anointed her feet with the nectar of his speech at the foot of a *akiṃśuka* or *akṣoḍa* tree, [he continues]. (35)
Relying on only three skulls during the night, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity on the full moon day;
standing at the foot of a *lakucha* tree, mounted upon a single skull alone, one should meditate at midnight upon [the deity] white as the rays of the moon.
If even a dull-witted person recites this mantra three hundred thousand times, he becomes directly like Bṛhaspati in this world; there is no wonder in this.

He who, having eaten and remaining at the foot of a plantain tree with the remnants of his meal, sits upon a seat fashioned from strewn flowers and performs worship by means of a single rising breath— he too is invincible in this world.
Vākpati shall be the Lord (Īśvara). || 37 ||
Having cleansed his tongue with his own lotus-like hands and having worshipped [the Lord] in the assembly hall with hundreds of rāsnā flowers,
whoever indeed recites [this mantra] a full hundred thousand times daily shall conquer the Lord; how much more so the Lord of Speech himself?
It is wonderful! || 38 ||
Having stood upon the wooden block of a washerman at the hour of midnight, even on a full moon night, if one recites [the mantra] while holding a sword for a full month—
or even more swiftly— [the result] emerges from his mouth.
Her voice sounding like nectar. || 39 ||
Even for one who uses karañja wood for cleaning the teeth, the words of Bṛhaspati are certainly easily obtained.
The wise mantra-practitioner should diligently offer oblations with sesame oil, *kunda*, white water-lilies, and flowers; thus he shall attain all accomplishments.

Having applied a tilaka-mark upon the surface of his forehead with roots of the *bhānumūla* plant dyed with the juice of madder and clouds, mixed with his own blood and equal parts of *kuṣṭha*, he remains engaged in recitation for the sake of awakening to the Vidyā.
He shall be a master of the nine sciences. || 42 ||
In the Bhairavatantra as well:
"O beloved, listen to the stainless mantra known as Mañjughoṣa, which bestows wealth and lineage, is delightful, and grants omniscience and eloquence. (43)
It is the root of faultless poetry and bestows creative intuition in all matters. || 44 ||
The Goddess said: O Blessed Lord, husband of Girijā, please tell me what is appropriate:
who is that Mañjughoṣa, of what nature is he, and indeed, what is his ritual practice?
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to my words; no hesitation should be felt here.
That god who is Mañjughoṣa is myself, O Goddess—of this there is no doubt. (46)
"I alone am Śaṅkara, O Goddess, who myself assume various forms;
now hear from me the truth regarding my ritual practice. (47)
The six-syllabled mantra is the essence that instantly destroys evil-mindedness;
its recitation, up to a hundred thousand repetitions, is truly desired by the gods.
O Goddess, by reciting [this] for three fortnights, a person becomes eloquent; he shall possess the state of a skilled poet and a creative intuition that conquers the entire world. (49)
Whether he be learned or unlearned, whoever recites this for three months becomes wise;
and whoever recites it for six months becomes all-knowing with an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
O Goddess, all perfections are truly attained within a year.
His food is the excrement of men; his sacrificial offering is the impurity of the eyes;
one should offer him water for the feet with urine; and his fragrance is that which arises from the wood of the khadira tree.
The leaves and flowers of the *āraṇyaka* tree are certainly [suitable];
they declare that the seeds of cotton with roots of castor oil plants (*eraṇḍa*) are worthy of honor (*arghya*).
By means of the stalks of the *tuṇḍakī*, there shall be water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*). (51)
O Great Goddess, I shall describe the meditation that bestows all accomplishments:
[one should meditate upon] the Youth with five topknots, as white as the moon, holding in his hands a sword, a book, and a limb, exceedingly beautiful and supremely tranquil.
I bow to Mañjughoṣa, whose excellent face is exceedingly broad, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, and who is skilled at burning away evil intellect. || 52 ||
I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra through the instruction on salutation;
listen, O highly fortunate goddess, for it bestows immediate fruit in the Kali age. (53)

I bow to that beneficial Lord Mañjughoṣa; I pay homage to him who is the essence of all mantras, the embodiment of subjugation, stainless, beyond qualities yet the essence of all that possesses qualities, and the granter of all desires. (54)
I bow to Ravīśa, the supreme essence, praised by the gods beginning with Brahmā; he who is red, endowed with the quality of rajas, and possesses a melodious voice. || 55 ||
I bow to him who is not known by speech nor skilled in physical action; to him who is peaceful, free from darkness, and clad in yellow robes.
The gods fell at his feet for the sake of victory over the Daityas;
the individual soul (jīva) falls at his feet for the sake of awakening—I bow to him.
I bow to Mañjughoṣa, whose true nature even the gods do not know by virtue of his being, who is joyful and the essence of all things. (58)

I bow to that bestower of welfare, who is the Lord of Intellect and the Lord of the Universe, who is the cause of realization and so forth, who is both with parts and yet partless, and who is beyond all fruit.
The seer (ṛṣi) should be Kaṇva, the metre (chandas) Paṅkti, and the limbs (aṅgas) consist of six syllables;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability so that the preceptor may be satisfied.
Success is certainly attained simply by pleasing the guru.
O Pārvatī, one’s father must not be made the guru in the rite of initiation;
for as long as the son remains miserable, the father shall go to hell. (61)
Now, the ritual manual (kalpa) of Tāriṇī from the Tāriṇītantra: The Lord said, "Listen, O Daughter of the Mountain, to [the practice] which is supreme and destroys dullness."
Knowledge, which yields the fruit of the four aims of life, bestows all accomplishments.
The first letter of the class [ka], joined with fire [ra] and adorned with the left eye [ī],
combined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, bestows the eight *siddhis*.
Furthermore, O Goddess, it is the four-faced one, adorned with the letter *la*.

O beloved, the great seed-syllable (mahābīja), which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life, is marked by the fourth vowel and the crescent moon. Then, having uttered the word "Kṛṣṇa," the word "Devī" is thereafter remembered.
Then one should give the syllable *hrīṃ*, and thereafter extract the one preceded by *kha* (the letter *kh*),
adorned with the vowel *ī*, the letter *r*, and the letter *m*. Then, having uttered the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], one should extract this mantra.
The nine-syllable mantra of Daurvārī has thus been proclaimed.
This very Mahāvidyā is difficult to obtain both in heaven and in the mortal world.
The Goddess is the bestower of the eight supernatural powers and the giver of the fruits of the four aims of human life.
A science like this has never existed, nor will there ever be; a mantra like this has never existed, nor will there ever be; and an accomplishment like this has never existed, nor will there ever be.
O Goddess, what indeed does he not achieve who attains this Vidyā?
Before long, he obtains speech that delights in both prose and verse;
through the mere knowledge of this Vidyā, he quickly becomes a swift poet.
Without prosody, without grammar, and without practice, O Pārvatī— || 66 ||
Even for a poet, without knowledge, without effort, and without discourse, the state of being a poet arises on the tongue, fashioned by the power of aesthetic relish (rasa). 67.
Regarding the procedure for worship therein:
first, taking water, the washing of the feet is prescribed;
having sipped water twice and tied the topknot, one then performs the purification of the ground. (68)
Having performed the expulsion of obstacles, one should then purify the flowers;
O Goddess of Gods, having purified both hands with the Astra-mantra immediately thereafter.
Having bowed to the gurus and Gaṇapati, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
The seed-syllable Vāgbhava, which bestows all perfections, resides in the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
by the powerful flames arising from it, the body is incinerated by the wise. (70)
Having cleared away that heap of ashes with the wind produced by the syllable *hrīṃ*,
and having moistened those bones with the nectar produced from the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) on the forehead,
one should then proceed once they have become solidified.
Then, having meditated upon the Self as being untainted, devoid of qualities, pure, consisting of the deity,
and completely liberated from all sins,
the practitioner should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) through the purification of the body. || 71 ||
One should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the first root-seed syllable;
thereafter, O Goddess, listen to the mantra-installation (mantranyāsa) which bestows the perfection of mantra.
Śaṅkara is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Bṛhatī is said to be the meter (chandas), Tāriṇī is declared to be the deity (devatā), and the syllable Hrīṃ is called the seed-syllable (bīja).
Vāgbhava is said to be the power (śakti); thus one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the seer and the other attributes.
The ritual application (prayoga) is as follows:
Salutation to the sage Śaṅkara on the head;
salutation to the Bṛhatī metre in the mouth.
Salutation to the deity Tāriṇī in the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Hrīṃ in the private parts; salutation to Vāgbhava-śakti in the feet. || 73 ||
Then, the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*):
*krīṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *klīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*;
*kṛṣṇadevi* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *hrīṃ* to the two ring fingers, *huṃ*.
*Krīṃ* to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*; *aiṃ* to the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
In this manner, [one should perform the assignment] at the heart and other limbs. Likewise, one should fashion the six limbs by means of the seed-syllables. (74)
O Goddess, one should first place Dharma and the others; then one should place Adharma and the others.
One should place these in sequence, one above the other, in the center.
Then, having uttered the word "Kalpavṛkṣa" (the wish-fulfilling tree), one should contemplate the jewel-throne (maṇipīṭha).
Having uttered the word *śava*, one should then place a skull-cup above it;
O Goddess, one should place a funeral pyre provided with fire in the four directions.
Then, within the eight petals of the heart-lotus, one should place the eight Śaktis.
Durgā, Jayā, Medhā, Vijayā, Suprabhā, Kālī, Gaurī, and Śivā—these are remembered as the eight Śaktis. (75)
Then, the wise practitioner should install the five wombs (pañcayoni) within his own body:
first, he should install Yonivīrā on the right side at the hairline;
then, he should install Yoniviśvā on the left side at the hairline.
O Goddess, one should place the form of the Yoni at the root of the nose according to its divisions;
the Yonikāmā and Yonihārā on the right and left eyes;
and the form of the Yoni on the lip for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
And at the corners of the mouth, O Goddess, according to the distinction of right and left,
the supreme practitioner should place the Great Goddess; thereafter, he should place her as the Yoni-chāyā, the Yoni-kāmā, and the one whose form is the Yoni.
O fair-faced one,

the wise man should meditate upon Yonicintā, Yoninityā, and that which has the form of the Yoni at the left armpit and in the heart; he should always remember the locus of the Yoni at the breasts and in the region of the navel.
The wise one should install [the goddesses] Yonisiddhā, Yonividdhā, and Yonirūpā;
these are remembered by the discerning as ending in the dative case and concluding with "namas.
Then, with a steady mind, he should meditate upon the Goddess within the seat of his own body.
He describes the meditation:
[One should visualize her] as black, pot-bellied, and terrifying, adorned with serpent-earrings;
with a red face and a lolling tongue, she wears red garments around her waist.
O Goddess of gods, she has full and elevated breasts, is fierce, and is encircled by a great serpent; she stands upon a corpse, and above that, upon a skull-cup;
she is intent on meditation at the tip of her nose, most formidable, and the bestower of boons.

The goddess has four arms and long hair; with her upper right arm she holds a single lotus, and in her upper left hand she holds a drinking vessel. In her lower right and left hands, she displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

[He beheld] the Goddess Sadāśivā, who dwells on the mountain, who bestows all supernatural powers, who is eternal, and who is endowed with three eyes; she was drinking a stream of blood from a drinking vessel, and she had a serpent as her sacred thread.
She has a long nose, long shanks, long limbs, and a long tongue;
she is endowed with three eyes, distinguished as the moon, the sun, and fire.
The Goddess who destroys enemies, most formidable, bestower of boons,
with a tiger skin bound upon her head, illuminating the three worlds;
she who brings happiness to practitioners and strikes fear into all the worlds.
Thus I bow down to the Great Goddess Tāriṇī who is of such a nature;
having meditated thus and worshipped her with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual installation of the conch as in the case of Tārā. || 77ka ||
The worship diagram for her is as follows:
O Goddess of Devas, having fashioned the diagram, one should place it in the center of the mantra;
then, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus using red sandalwood paste.
Outside of that, the best of practitioners should draw eight petals;
then, he should draw a pair of fire-mandalas in the center of the yantra.
O Goddess, he should then write the first seed-syllable on the eastern petal.
The second [syllable] is on the southern petal, the third on the western petal, and on the northern petal, O Goddess, one should then write "phaṭ" and the goddess Vāṇī;
it is provided with four gates and endowed with eight vajras. || 78 ||
There, having worshipped the pedestal with the previously mentioned mantra and having meditated as before,
one should invoke Maheśānī there and worship her while reciting the mantra.
O Goddess of Devas, having worshipped Pārvatī with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), [one should proceed].
One should worship Kṣetrapāla, Bhairava, Gaṇanātha, and Mahāntaka— this quartet— at the four doors. O Goddess,
having worshipped these on the eight petals starting from the east, the practitioner [should proceed].
O Goddess, [the first is] Anaṅgamanmathā; Laghimā is Madanāturā;
then Anaṅgakusumā, O Devi, and likewise Aṣṭakarṇikā;
then Kapālikā, O Mistress of the Gods, and likewise the eight Yoginīs.
Likewise, one should worship the attendants upon the sixteen petals:
there, Sukhadā (the Giver of Happiness), Mokṣadā (the Giver of Liberation), Bhuktidā (the Giver of Enjoyment), and Bhogadā (the Giver of Pleasures);
then Muktidā (the Giver of Release), Siddhidā (the Giver of Accomplishment), Kāmadā (the Giver of Desires), and Dhanadā (the Giver of Wealth).

Then, one should worship at the eastern gate the goddess who bestows security, who bestows auspiciousness, the giver of boons, the giver of the self, as well as the giver of yoga, the giver of enjoyment, the giver of devotion, the giver of all perfections, and the eight perfections beginning with *aṇimā*.
O Goddess, one should worship the ten kalās of Fire at the southern gate;
O Queen of the Gods, one should worship the kalās of the Moon at the western gate; and likewise, O Goddess, one should worship the kalās of the Sun at the northern gate.

O Goddess, one should worship with the six-limbed rite, and thereafter worship the weapons. O Mistress of the God of Gods, these [mantras] are declared to end in the dative case; O Great Goddess, they are said to end in "namaḥ" and bestow all accomplishments.
With many kinds of flowers, smeared with red sandalwood paste, O Great Goddess, and with red flowers endowed with various fragrances; || 79 ||
Likewise with bilva leaves and fragrances, especially with javā flowers,
white and red palāśa flowers, karavīras, and marūvaka flowers;
with bilva blossoms, kunda flowers, and auspicious cloves.

O Great Goddess, one should worship Nityatāriṇī with Aparājitā flowers, Campaka, and Keśara; likewise, one should worship her with Mālatī and Vakula flowers, along with dūrvā grass and forest blossoms.

Having thus worshipped with Kadamba flowers, white blossoms, saffron, and likewise golden [flowers], O Maheśvarī, one who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times using these materials. (79-ka)
Now begins the Sarasvata-kalpa.
Narada said:
"O Lord of Gods, by what means may the arising of knowledge occur for men?"
But tell me that illumination of Vedic knowledge, O Lord of the World. (80)
Brahmā said: Excellent, excellent! You have asked that which brings benefit to the worlds.
This very same thing was asked by me of Viṣṇu in the past, at the beginning of the Kalpa.
O Brahmin, that which was spoken by him with a serene inner self, in the very form of the word "Brahman," that I shall relate to you with diligence.
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, to my supreme secret ritual manual of Sarasvatī, by the mere knowledge of which the removal of dullness occurs. (83)
One becomes an omniscient illuminator of all scriptures before long;
indeed, through practice, one's speech becomes truly wonderful.
The gods attained pervasiveness, Bṛhaspati attained lordship over speech,
and even the sage Dvaipāyana became the Vedavyāsa after knowing him.
I shall now proclaim the extraction of the mantra along with the worship of its limbs and enclosures:
[the syllable] Ananta (Ha) joined with the Bindu (M), adorned at the end of the left cheek (U).
One who recites it twelve hundred thousand times shall become a master of speech, even if previously mute. (86)
The wise practitioner should meditate upon a pure lotus with ten petals at the navel;
in its center, the mantra-knower should contemplate for a long time the triad of mandalas.
He should then meditate upon the jewel-throne, which is white in color and composed of moonlight.
Above that, one should then meditate upon the goddess Vāgīśvarī.
The Goddess, possessing the splendor of a pearl and radiating a web of moonlight,
white and adorned with a crescent moon,
wears a pearl necklace and holds in her two right hands the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyā*) and a rosary of beads.
Holding with her two left hands a divine jar filled with nectar and a sacred book, she possesses full, swelling breasts;
she is slender at the waist, translucent, and adorned with various jewels.
Having meditated thus upon [the deity] as non-different from oneself, one should then worship them in sequence. || 88 ||
With the first [syllable] joined with the long vowel, one should perform the [placement of] limbs on the two hands;
likewise, one should perform the ritual of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) in the heart and other locations using the seed-syllable.
Furthermore, the instructor [should place them] between the eyebrows, at the navel, and in the secret place.
One should again place the seed-syllable on the physical body and then perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*).
One should perform the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*) upon the body for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.
Having diligently worshipped the seat that has been proclaimed as belonging to the Mātṛkā, one should proceed.
One should prepare a seat with a lotus of colors and fashion the form [of the deity] by means of the root mantra;
then, having invoked her, one should worship the goddess Vāgīśvarī within that [form]. (89)
The first circle of deities should be worshipped with the limbs (aṅgas), and the second with the powers (śaktis).
Having worshipped the Brahmāṇīs and others according to the rule upon the tips of the petals,
the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped outside, and their weapons outside of them.
In this manner, the practitioner of mantras, always devoted to recitation and worship, should perform the full adoration.
A eloquent person certainly attains the power of poetry by means of twelve hundred thousand [recitations].
Having chanted a thousand times in the morning, one should drink [a decoction] of *brāhmī* combined with *vacā*;
thus, the wise one does not forget even the Vedas and Āgamas that have been heard.
Standing in water reaching up to the neck, one should meditate upon the Goddess within the orb of the sun—
resembling a mass of light, accompanied by her retinue,
holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands, and bearing a mudrā and a book.

Having conquered his senses for six months by means of the *sahasramāna* [practice] in Japan, and having attained the formidable perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*), he shall become the foremost among poets. (92)
Now I shall describe the supreme practice that destroys dullness:
having risen at the end of the night, being pure and composed,
one should contemplate oneself and the Guru with a state of pure devotion.
One should contemplate that entire world pervaded by a mass of light emanating from that.
Having awakened with the power (śakti) the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, who resides asleep at the mūlādhāra, one should pierce the cakras in succession;
then, having led her to the Supreme Śiva, one should cause her to reach the abode of Soma.
Having pierced through the upper knot and conquered the one whose nature is like a lamp— the supreme self who shines forth by means of her own power in the form of the seed-syllable—
one should then meditate upon her as being of the nature of the Śabdabrahman, unwavering.
Then, one should contemplate the body as pervaded by a mass of that light.
If one recites [the mantra] daily for a thousand times for a full year,
then that practitioner of mantra becomes like another Vācaspati.
One becomes a knower of the meanings of various treatises such as prosody, poetics, and logic;
moreover, through the power of knowledge, one's poetic skill and erudition become preeminent. (94)
Now I shall further explain a yoga that is very difficult to find on earth:
one should contemplate [the goddess] situated in the navel-cakra, gentle and red in appearance,
with hips bound by a silken cloth and adorned with red ornaments.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon the divine goddess holding a noose and a goad, and bestowing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she fulfills all heart's desires with her nectar-showering glance.
Having meditated thus, a person should then recite the mantra one hundred thousand times as prescribed.
The twice-born should perform a *homa* oblation with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Then, he should satisfy the Goddess with ghee mixed with milk.
He should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), along with curd and flour soaked in honey.
By performing the ritual procedure in this manner, one shall indeed become Vaiśravaṇa in person. || 96 ||
By offering oblations of *siddhārtha* seeds mixed with the three sweets, one brings the world under control;
by a lotus-oblation, one shall obtain great and exalted prosperity. (96)
O Goddess, for this Heart-Vidyā there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult to obtain;
it has been taught out of affection, yet it must not be given to just anyone. (97)
This secret has been told to you, along with the cause of the origin of the Vidyā;
it was given to us by Viṣṇu, and by me to you, O best of the twice-born. (98)

When a practitioner who has mastered the mantra places his hand upon the head of even a child and touches him, by the grace of the perfected lore, that child too shall utter unimpeded divine speech consisting of prose and verse. (99)
Thus ends the Sārasvata chapter of the Svāyambhuva-mātṛkā-tantra. The Ritual Manual of Kātyāyanī:
The Blessed One said:
"O Pārvatī, you have asked about a most secret mantra;
O Goddess of pure smiles, I shall tell it to you out of devotion. (100)
O Goddess, when Kātyāyanī becomes pleased, she then bestows poetic talent, incomparable sovereignty, and the supreme state. || 1 ||
O beloved, there occurs the attraction of women, as well as the killing and expulsion of enemies, and likewise the subjugation of kings.
I shall tell you all of that; receive my words with devotion.
First, hear the great mantra beginning with *vāgbhava* and ending with *namaḥ*:
it is *śiva* seated upon fire (*ra*), followed by the letter *va*, adorned with the *bindu* and the *śānti*.
The letter *ca* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and endowed with the fourteenth vowel, followed by the suffix *-ṅe* and the word *Caṇḍikā*, is declared to be the ten-syllabled mantra. (3)
Known as Cintāmaṇi, it is meditated upon even today by Māyā and others.
The deity is Caṇḍikā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the sage is Kapila.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and thereafter perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number.
One should worship on the seat as instructed by one's mother; the ritual of the limbs (aṅga) is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable (bīja).
Having first worshipped the limbs, the worship of the weapon (śastra) follows thereafter.
Then the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) are to be worshipped, and their weapons outside of them.
Furthermore, these goddesses—Ḍākinī, Yoginī, Khecarī, and Śākinī—are to be worshipped in the cardinal directions; they are well-perfected and bestowers of fruits.
Then the meditation:
[One should meditate on her] whose thighs are adorned by the lotus of her right foot,
and who is fully crushing the demon Mahiṣāsura with the tip of her left foot.
She is exceedingly serene, with a beautiful countenance and endowed with three lovely eyes;
she is adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, matted locks, and a crown;
she wears variegated silken garments and is embellished with the crescent moon.
The Goddess, possessing the splendor of ten million moons, holds with her graceful arms a sword, a shield, and vajras, as well as a trident, an arrow, a bow, a noose, a conch, a bell, and a lotus.

Constantly praised by the gods who have gathered in the heavens and by the world-protectors and others standing in the sky, while rejoicing— by meditating upon the Goddess in this manner, one becomes a preeminent man.
As Rāma is among the Kṣatriyas, as Purandara is among the gods, as Tārkṣya is among the serpents, and as Śani is among those of cruel deeds; || 7 ||
Just as among birds the hawk is the strongest, so too is he who knows the mantra;
this supreme secret has been told by me in brief. (8)
Now listen, O beloved, to the procedure for recitation and fire-offerings.
O Goddess, if this mantra is contemplated in the presence of an assembly,
it is seen by the disputants as resembling ten million suns.
O Great Goddess, they flee from there in an instant out of sheer terror.
One should begin the recitation on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina;
having performed it one thousand times every single day until reaching the ninth day of the bright fortnight,
one should take up a victorious sword and worship it according to the prescribed ritual.
Having offered the bali-oblation at midnight, one should perform the procession in the morning.
Upon reaching the battlefield, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times;
O Goddess, upon seeing that person, agitation arises in the heart of the enemy.
O Great Goddess, considering Yama to have arrived with his messengers, the lords of men flee; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (11)
Wearing white garments, observing silence, and established in the vow of celibacy,
one should meditate upon the Great Goddess who is white in complexion and adorned with white ornaments; then,
one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day for one month according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered three thousand oblations of *mālatī*, *bakula*, and *kunda* flowers combined with honey, the practitioner of mantras becomes a lord of speech before long.
O Goddess, one easily and swiftly composes clear poetry;
or one performs recitation daily for hundreds of years.
Even a barren woman obtains a son possessing the prowess of Kārttikeya.
She may become unfortunate to her husband, or she may become fortunate and exceedingly charming. || 13 ||
Having reflected upon the form previously described, and having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, or ten thousand times thereafter,
one attains the power of hearing by offering oblations of blue lotuses or white lotuses.

Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of severed heads, Mahākālī— whose terrifying eyes were round and red, and who sportively devoured the asuras with her tongue— was like another Kālarātri.

One who is firm in mind and established in the vow, having meditated thus upon the Goddess who agitates the entire world— including the gods, asuras, and mountains— should recite her mantra three hundred times for seven days at a cremation ground or a crossroads; he who recites it with self-restraint will achieve his goal.
O Goddess, he shall certainly destroy his enemies. || 15 ||
By this very procedure, one should offer a bali-oblation at a crossroads,
having concentrated the mind and fashioned a figure (puṇḍī) from burnt fish and blood-stained food;
and having visualized [the deity] whomsoever, one should cause raw meat smeared with turmeric to be offered.
Within seven days, the enemy will undoubtedly reach the abode of Yama;
neither Hari nor even Śaṅkara is able to protect him anywhere.
The mantra for the bali offering is as follows: First, the pair of Umā’s seed-syllables, then the pair of Cāmuṇḍā’s seed-syllables;
having uttered the words "Kālikāli," one should then say "khādaya" twice.
One should say "subjugate" (*vaśīkuru*) and then repeat "O Great Being" (*mahāsattva*).
After pronouncing the wife of Fire (*vahnijāyā*, i.e., *svāhā*), this is the auspicious *bali* mantra.
[It consists of] the seed-syllable of Umā, the seed-syllable of Hṛllekhā, the seed-syllable of Cāmuṇḍā, and the seed-syllable of Śyāmā. (17)
Having donned the skin of a black antelope and sat down in his own courtyard, he,
being composed in mind, contemplated himself in a terrible form on a Tuesday and even on censured lunar days.
Having taken the worshipped sword at midnight, one should offer an oblation;
and one should give the blood from its stroke to the Goddess according to the ritual.
One's body shall become incapable of being cut or pierced by enemies; of this there is no doubt. || 18 ||
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrīṃ),
then the word "Kātyāyanī" in the dative case (Kātyāyanyai), and then "Vahnerbhāryā" (the wife of Fire)—
this is the eight-syllabled Great Vidyā that bestows the fruits of all desires.
One should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship, as previously described.
Thus ends the Kātyāyanī-kalpa. || 19 ||
Now, the mantras of Durgā:
In the Viśvasāra [Tantra]:
"Now I shall declare the mantra of Durgā; listen, O lotus-faced one."
By the mere grace of whom one becomes Gaṅgādhara himself. || 20 ||
Having extracted the seed-syllable ending in *tha*, adorned with the left ear [the letter *u*],
and joined with the moon-drop (*bindu*), this seed-syllable is exceedingly rare;
it directly bestows the four aims of life and destroys even the greatest of sins.
O beloved, there is no knowledge equal to the single-syllable [mantra] in the three worlds.
O Great Goddess, even without perfumes, without flowers, without preliminary fire-offerings, and without exertions, it bestows success through mere recitation alone.
O Goddess, Nārada is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra;
Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas), and the Goddess of the World (Jagaddhātrī) is the deity (devatā).
Bestowing the four aims of human life, Durgā is established within all living beings. 23.
That great vidyā is manifold; listen to it, O Gaṇeśvarī.
One should recite the vidyā beginning with the *kūrca* mantra, or at its end, the *vahnisundarī*;
or the wise one should recite the vidyā beginning with *lajjā*, or ending with *phaṭ*.

Or one should again recite [the mantra] joined with the seed-syllable of the bride (vadhū-bīja) and ending with *svāhā*. Or, for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*), one should recite the *vidyā* beginning with *lakṣmī*. Or one may recite it beginning with the *vāgbhava* syllable, or again recite it beginning with the *praṇava*.
The wise man should recite either beginning with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) or ending with PHAṬ;
this three-syllabled Vidyā was proclaimed by Brahmā in ancient times.
O Pārvatī, one should place one's own seed-syllables (bījas), joined with long vowels,
upon one's own body in the heart and other locations as before. One should perform the group of nyāsas as before and carry out the ritual actions as before.
One should practice the Kālī-vidyā and chant the vidyā day and night.
O Goddess, twelve hundred thousand recitations are declared as the *puraścaraṇa*;
one should chant with supreme devotion to Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, according to the proper place, the proper time, and the prescribed rules of conduct. (26)
One should worship Durgā, the remover of misfortune, with supreme devotion using fish, meat, well-prepared cakes, and the flesh of deer, rabbits, and porcupines.

One should worship the Supreme Goddess with Svayambhū flowers, white fragrant blossoms, Javā, Alaktaka, and Sindūra, combined with red sandalwood, various kinds of meat, and diverse ritual substances.
One should worship with crows, parrots, buffaloes, goats, mongooses, men, as well as elephants, camels, donkeys, and vultures according to this rite;
then great accomplishment shall come to pass— no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
As for the meditation:
one should visualize the Great Goddess as having four arms, seated upon the shoulders of a lion, adorned with various ornaments, and wearing a sacred thread made of a serpent.
She is endowed with two left hands holding a conch and a bow,
while her right hands bear a discus and five arrows;
she is clothed in red garments, and her body is like the rising sun.
She was attended by hosts of sages such as Nārada, the beautiful goddess of worldly existence,
whose lotus-stalk-like navel was encircled by the three folds of skin;
she sat upon a lion-throne on an island composed of jewels.
One should meditate upon her, the mistress of worldly existence, as seated upon a fully blossomed lotus.
O beloved of Hara, listen as I describe the Durgā-yantro:
one should first draw a triangle provided with nine corners;
it should be fashioned together with three circles and endowed with eight petals.
It should be made with three lines and joined by the Rudra-mandala and the Bhupura;
having leveled it, one should draw it according to this prescribed method.
The wheel, endowed with various weapons and accompanied by mantras, should be inscribed.
There, one should worship that Goddess who is the form of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti).
One should worship Durgā, seated upon a lotus and resting on the back of a lion.
The powers (śaktis), beginning with Prabhā, are to be worshipped with perfumes and other offerings within the nine-cornered [mandala].
Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, Nandinī,
Suprabhā, Vijayā, and Sarvasiddhidā— these are the nine Śaktis.
One should worship Hrīṃ and the others with water scented with sandalwood;
having first uttered the syllable Oṃ and immediately thereafter the syllable Hrīṃ,
one should worship them in sequence according to their respective names in the dative case, O Dear One.

O Daughter of the Mountain, one should worship the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, joined to the left and right of the Goddess with supreme devotion using red sandalwood and other offerings; one should always perform the offering of the *arghya* at the conclusion of the worship.

Furthermore, the limbs (*aṅga*) are to be worshipped again in the corners of the petals; the Mothers, equipped with weapons such as the vajra, [are worshipped] in the earth-fortress (*bhūpura*), as are the world-protectors (*lokapālaka*). (Illustration 47).
Thus end the mantras of Durgā.
Now, regarding the mantras of Viśālākṣī,
in the Ādiyāmala,
the Lord said: "Having first extracted the fixed syllable (Oṃ), one should extract the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ)."
One should extract the mantra ending with the word *viśālākṣī* in the dative case (*viśālākṣyai*) and ending with *hṛt* (namaḥ).
O Śivā, this eight-syllabled great lore (*mahāvidyā*) bestows the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*).
O beloved, this lore, difficult to obtain in the three worlds, has been told here incidentally.
O Maheśānī, Sadāśiva, the Great Lord, is its seer; Paṅkti is said to be its meter; Viśālākṣī is its deity;
the Śakti is declared to be the Praṇava, and the seed-syllable is the Bīja of Lajjā.
Its application is proclaimed to be in the pursuit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 35 ||
The placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) are now described according to rule.
One should perform them with the seed-syllable (bīja) preceded by the Praṇava and endowed with the six long vowels.
The formula is: "Oṃ hrāṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth. (36)
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should meditate upon the supreme goddess Śivā.
One should meditate upon the goddess Viśālākṣī, who has the luster of molten gold,
who possesses two arms, and who is the fierce Caṇḍī bearing a sword and a shield.
Beautiful with various ornaments, wearing red garments, auspicious,
eternally sixteen years of age, with a serene countenance and three eyes,
she is lovely with a garland of severed heads and possesses full, elevated breasts.
Upon the corpse, one should meditate on the Great Goddess, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
the goddess who brings about the destruction of enemies, the bestower of the practitioner’s desired objects,
the mother of all good fortune, and the granter of great prosperity.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Great Goddess with ritual offerings.
During the period of *puraścaraṇa*, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra one million times.
Then, having invoked [the deity] into the center of the *yantra*, he should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Thereafter, he should draw a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a circle.
One should draw a mandala that is square and has four gates;
there, having invoked the Goddess who is beautiful with all auspiciousness,
one should worship her according to the ritual rules— she who has large eyes and a large face.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess within the triangle, one should then worship the Mothers in sequence:
Paṅkajākṣī, Virūpākṣī, Raktākṣī, Sulocanā,
Ekanetrā, Dvinetrā, Koṭarākṣī, and Trilocanā.
These eight Yoginīs, who are the embodiments of the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi), are to be worshipped as Maheśānī at the tips of the petals in the sequence starting from the west;
one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) upon the great goddess in the square.
And outside of that, one should worship Vajra and the others for the sake of good fortune;
then, having recited [the mantra] according to one's capacity, one should perform the remaining rites as before. || 38 ||
(The Viśālākṣī Yantra, Figure 48).
Now, the mantras of Gaurī according to the Tantra:
"Hrīṃ Gaurī Rudradayite Yogeśvari Savarṃ Phaṭ"—this sixteen-syllable mantra, ending with the two ṭha-sounds (svāhā), has been proclaimed by the wise. (39)
The worship of this [goddess] is as follows:
having completed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth.
For example:
"Salutation to Parvatarṣi on the head;
salutation to Gāyatrī metre on the face."
In the heart: *namaḥ* to the deity Śrī Gaurī.
Then, the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs:
*hrāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*, and so forth.
Hrāṃ, salutation to the heart, and so forth. || 40 ||
Then, for meditation: I always worship that Gaurī, who possesses a golden luster, who holds in her hands a mirror, collyrium, a noose, and a goad, and who is adorned with every ornament.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, and having performed the rites beginning with the placement of the conch up to the worship of the seat (pīṭha), one should again meditate, invoke, and worship the Goddess. || 41 ||
Then, one should worship the six limbs in the corners starting with the southeast (Agni) using "hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth.
On the petals, starting from the east, [one should worship] "oṃ subhagāyai namaḥ," and likewise Rati, Kāminī, and Kāmadāyinī.
One should worship the noose, the goad, the mirror, and the collyrium-rod.
Outside of that, one should worship Indra and the other deities, as well as the vajra and the other implements.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the incense offering up to the dismissal. || 42 ||
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*).
An oblation (*homa*) of clarified butter (*ājya*) should be performed in the tenth part of that number.
And so it is said:
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), he should perform oblations with clarified butter (ājya) numbering one-tenth of that amount.

As for the results: whatever—be it perfumes, flowers, collyrium, food, sandalwood, or the like—is given to anyone after being consecrated with the root mantra, that person certainly becomes submissive. || 44 ||
Just as at night, having written the name of a beloved woman between her left thighs with turmeric,
and covering it with his left hand while reciting [the mantra] a hundred or a thousand times, he draws that woman under his control.
This worship and so forth brings about good fortune, subjugation, and all forms of prosperity. || 45 ||
Now, the mantra of Brahmaśrī:

it is found in the *Mantradevaprakāśinī* as follows: "Hṛllekhā, preceded by salutation, [is] Brahmaśrī; O resplendent one, O you who are worshipped by kings, O victorious one, O unconquered one, O Gaurī!"
O Gāndhārī, subduer of the three worlds, subduer of all people, subduer of all women and men, [you who are] fierce in fair combat! Hrīṃ Svāhā! || 46 ||
And the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*O radiant one, worshipped by kings, homage with the two thumbs!
O victorious one, most victorious one, Gaurī, Gāndhārī, svāhā with the two index fingers!*
O Subduer of the Three Worlds, *vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers;
O Subduer of All Worlds, *hūṃ* with the two ring fingers;
O Subduer of All Men and Women, *vauṣaṭ* with the two little fingers.
*Hrīṃ svāhā astrāya phaṭ* in the midst of the most terrible roar of the great battle;
*namaḥ* to the heart, O resplendent one, O you who are worshipped by kings!
*Svāhā* to the head, O victorious one, O further victorious one, O Gaurī, O Gāndhārī!
Obeisance to the subduer of the three worlds, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock; obeisance to the subduer of all worlds, *huṃ* to the armor;
obeisance to the subduer of all women and men, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
Hrīṃ svāhā! To the weapon of the terrible roar of fierce combat, phaṭ! || 47 ||
Then the meditation:
[She] has a crown formed by the rays of a full moon, her beautiful lotus-hands hold a noose and a goad, and her limbs are as red as the bandhujīva flower.
May Pārvatī—venerated by hosts of immortals, possessing three eyes, and adorned with vermilion, garments, and flowers—grant you prosperity.
Her limbs are the guardians of the world (Lokapālas), and her [other] parts are the Mother-goddesses (Mātṛkās); thus there are three enclosures. 48.
The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of ten thousand recitations (japa).
A homa sacrifice with milk-rice (pāyasa) should be performed at one-tenth that number.
Alternatively, for three days, one may perform it with sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with the three sweets (madhutraya), or with parched grain flour (lavarṇa).
A thousand-fold oblation brings swift subjugation.
Having worshipped the Goddess situated within the solar disc at dawn and reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one becomes the subduer of the three worlds. (49)
Now, the mantra of Rājamukhī consists of forty-two syllables and is explained in detail in the context of the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
As follows:
Oṃ rājamukhi, homage to the heart.
Vaśyamukhi hrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to the head.
Devī devi, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
O Great Goddess, *huṃ* for the armor!
O Goddess supreme among goddesses, *vaṣaṭ* for the three eyes!
Subjugate the faces of all people, subjugate them, *svāhā*! *phaṭ* for the weapon!

Just as in the case of all the Śrīs, the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should be inserted at the beginning of the recitation and in all places where people reside. Thus ends verse 50.
Now, the mantra for Indra, as given in the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*: "Iṃ, [salutation] to Indra; this is the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*)."
Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter (*chandaḥ*), Indra is the deity (*devatā*), *iṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *āya* is the power (*śakti*).
The ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is performed with the seed-syllable as follows:
*iṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*, and so forth;
*iṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*, and so forth. || 51 ||
Then comes the meditation:

I bow to the Lord Indra, the sovereign of the guardians of the directions, who is yellow in color, possesses a thousand eyes, holds a vajra and a lotus in his hands, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Having meditated thus and invoked [the deity], one should worship. || 52 ||

Then, one should worship the six limbs with "Iṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth, in the corners beginning with the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions. Then, on the petals starting from the east, [one worships] "Kaṃ, obeisance to Kārttikeya," and likewise "Raṃ, obeisance to Agni."
Yaṃ for Yama, kṣaṃ for Nirṛti, vaṃ for Varuṇa, yaṃ for Vāyu, saṃ for Soma, and īṃ for Īśāna.
Thereafter, one should worship the thunderbolt and the other [emblems]. || 53 ||
The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa), followed by ten thousand oblations (ayutahoma) with clarified butter and sesame seeds. || 54 ||
Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*):
having placed a water-pot wrapped in nine cloths upon a lotus situated within a square,
and having filled it with scented water, one should worship Indra together with his retinue there, [reciting] a thousand [times].
By reciting [the mantra] and performing an ablution with that water, one who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom, and for others, supreme prosperity arises. || 55 ||
Now, the mantra of Garuḍa, as stated in the Nibandha:
Saṃvartaka joined with the two eyes (netra), followed by Tāra on the side, and Agnisundarī.
This is declared to be the Gāruḍa mantra, which destroys both types of poison. A person, remembering Garuḍa as their own self, should mutter this mantra;
by merely looking [at it], he shall destroy the poison arising from the race of serpents. (56)

The worship of this [deity] is as follows: having performed the morning rites and so forth, up to the placement of the *pīṭha-mantra* as prescribed for Vaiṣṇava rites, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other components.
For example: "Homage to the seer Rudra on the head; homage to the Paṅkti metre on the mouth; homage to the deity Pakṣīndra on the heart."
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable; Svāhā is the power. || 57 ||
Then, the placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): *jvala jvala mahāmate svāhā*—*namaḥ* to both thumbs;
*garuḍacūḍāmaṇe svāhā*—*svāhā* to both index fingers; *garuḍaśikhiśikhe*.
Svāhā to the two middle fingers; Vaṣaṭ! O Garuḍa, shatterer, shatterer, piercer, piercer, put to flight, put to flight, crush, svāhā to the two ring fingers;
Hūṃ! Oṃ, you who bear a fierce form, remover of all poisons, strike fear!
"Bhīṣaya svāhā" with the two little fingers, "vauṣaṭ"; "sarvaṃ daha daha bhasmīkuru svāhā" with the palms and backs of the hands, "phaṭ.
Thus [it is performed] for the heart and the other [limbs]. || 58 ||

Then, having assigned the syllables of the mantra to the thumbs through to the little fingers of both hands, one should assign the five syllables to the feet, the waist, the heart, the face, and the head.
Then the meditation:

[He is] situated upon a lotus consisting of the syllables of the pair of fires within the armor, possessing the first letter of the five elements; adorned with both ornaments and lacking ornaments, having the lords of serpents as his ornaments, granting the gestures of fearlessness and boons, with lotus-like eyes and a beautiful face.

"I worship the King of Birds, who has severed the fangs of the wicked serpents, who dispels all poison through his remembrance, who is the very life-force, the leader of life, whose body is revealed by the three Vedas, and who consists of nectar.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch.

Having worshipped the pedestal (pīṭha) ending with the mantra as taught by the Vaiṣṇavas, and having meditated upon it again and invoked [the deity], [one should worship] the two *repha*s situated in the middle of the syllable *huṃ*,
with the pericarp joined by the seed-syllables consisting of the letter *kṣa*, the vowel *ī*, and the bindu, and with eight filaments consisting of pairs of vowels.
One should worship the King of Birds upon the eight-petaled Mātṛkā-lotus, which is joined with the eight groups of consonants beginning with ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, and la. || 60 ||

The first enclosure consists of the [eight] limbs; the second of the eight nāgas—Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and Kulika; and the third of Indra and the other [guardians].
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of five hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).

Alternatively, for the sake of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times and the garland-mantra (mālāmantra) a thousand times for each syllable; then, a fire-offering (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number should be performed with black flowers smeared with ghee. || 61 ||
The *mālāmantra* is spoken as follows:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate garuḍāya kālāgnivarṇāya ehyehi kālānalalolajihvāya pātaya pātaya mohaya mohaya vidrāvaya vidrāvaya bhrama*.
Bhrama bhrāmaya bhrāmaya hana hana daha daha paca paca hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. || 62 ||

Having meditated upon that [lotus] in the midst of the ocean of milk as consisting of the previously mentioned syllables of the *mātṛkā*, having the nature of nectar, white in color, and having meditated upon a snake upon that lotus, one should place *raṃ* and *haṃ* on the head, face, heart, and navel of the bitten person.

Having visualized the four seed-syllables *ṭhaṃ vaṃ* as streaming with nectar, and having meditated upon Garuḍa— whose color is like a moonstone and who consists of ambrosia— above the head of the victim,
one [should sprinkle] the bitten person with a stream of nectar flowing from the conch filled with nectar held in his hand.

One should recite the mantra while meditating upon Garuḍa as he causes [the poison] to flow away. (Figure 49) By this mere meditation, the bitten person becomes free from poison, rises up, and shall live for a long time. || 63 ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Garuḍa, who has the form of Mahendra, whose form has the appearance of a mountain peak; withdraw, withdraw! release, release! move, move!
cause to fall, cause to fall! be poisonless, be poisonless! even poison is nectar.
"I designate this form as being like food, svāhā! Homage! Nala nala, vara vara, duna duna, kṣipa kṣipa, hara hara, svāhā!
By means of this Garuḍa mantra, the practitioner, having become Garuḍa, [empowers] that which has been consecrated.
Even stationary poison, when consumed, becomes nectar; how much more so food, drink, and the like?
Thus ends the mantra of Garuḍa.
Now follows the hymn to Garuḍa:
[I praise] Suparṇa, Vainateya, the enemy of serpents, and the terrifier of serpents.
The conqueror of Death, the dispeller of poison, the unconquered one, the one of universal form,
Garuḍa, the best of birds, Tārkṣya, the son of Kaśyapa—
these are the twelve names of the high-souled Garuḍa.
Whoever recites this upon rising in the morning, whether while bathing or lying down,
poison shall not overcome him, nor shall those who seek to harm him do so. In battle and in legal disputes, victory shall be his.
One attains liberation from bondage and indeed success on one's journey.
Thus ends the *Garuḍa-stotra*. 65.
Now, the ritual manual of Hanumān:
The Goddess said:
"The rites dedicated to Śiva, to Gaṇapati, to Śakti, and to Viṣṇu..."
The Saura practices and whatever other rites have been heard by me, O Lord of Gods, have all issued from your mouth. Now,
if it may be told, let some other practice belonging to the gods be explained.
Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess; I shall proclaim it—heed it with full attention.
This is the meritorious practice of Hanumān, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
This is the most secret [teaching] in the world, the supreme means for attaining swift success;
by its grace, Jayo became the conqueror of the three worlds.
I shall now describe its method of practice, which swiftly brings accomplishment to men. (67)
Immediately after that, for Hanumān, who is of the nature of Rudra, there is the armor-mantra "phaṭ," consisting of twelve syllables beginning with "viyat-sanarakaṃ.
I have declared this mantra; it must be guarded with great effort.
Out of affection for you and because of your devotion, O beautiful one, I am your servant.
This mantra was formerly given to Arjuna by Hari;
having performed the practice with victory, he conquered the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
On a riverbank, in a temple of Viṣṇu, in a solitary mountain, or in a forest,
one should accomplish the great sādhanā by fixing the mind in one-pointed concentration.
He describes the meditative absorption (dhyāna):
"Having uprooted the great mountain, he ran toward Rāvaṇa, crying out 'Stay!
Stay! O wicked one, O you who utter a terrible roar! in the midst of battle."
Red as liquid lac, fierce, resembling Yama the Destroyer at the end of time,
with blazing eyes like a flaming fire and a radiance equal to ten million suns,
he appeared in the form of Rudra, surrounded by the great goddesses led by Aṅgada.
Having thus meditated upon Hanumān in this form, whoever should recite the mantra, he shall become pleased after one hundred thousand recitations; I have told you the truth. (70)

For men, accomplishment is attained through meditation alone; of this there is no doubt. Having bathed at dawn on the bank of a river and seated upon a seat of *kuśa* grass, one should perform the entire practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with its six ancillaries using the root mantra.
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers and meditated upon Rāma together with Sītā,
one should then draw an eight-petaled lotus with its filaments upon a copper plate using a stylus rubbed with red sandalwood paste.
One should write the mantra within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and there invoke the Lord of Monkeys (*kapiprabhu*).
Having meditated upon Hanumān within the pericarp, beginning from his feet and so forth, one should then offer perfumes, flowers, and other articles with the root mantra. (Figure 50)
O Goddess, one should worship Sugrīva, Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Nala, Nīlaka, Jāmbavanta, Kumuda, and Keśarin on each petal, starting from the east in due order, with perfumes and sandalwood paste.
One should worship Pavana and Añjana on the right and left [sides].
Then, at the tips of the petals, one should offer eight handfuls of flowers to the monkeys.
Thereafter, the practitioner should indeed meditate upon the King of Mantras for as long as it takes to reach one hundred thousand recitations.
Having reached the day of the completion of one hundred thousand recitations,
one should perform a great worship with a one-pointed mind and heart toward that son of the Wind-god;
one should perform the recitation day and night until his manifestation occurs.
Considering the practitioner to be very firm, the Son of the Wind (Hanumān) then becomes well-pleased and proceeds before the practitioner.
Having granted the desired boon to the practitioner, the Lord of Monkeys departed;
and having obtained the boon, the sovereign of practitioners may dwell in his own happiness. (73)
"This meritorious sādhana is indeed difficult even for the gods to obtain;
out of affection for you, O Pārvatī, I have explained it to you, for you are devoted to me.
Thus ends the Hanūmat-sādhana from the Garuḍa-tantra, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. 74.
Now, the Heroic Accomplishment (*vīrasādhana*):
the extremely secret *vīrasādhana* of Hanumān is being written.
Having risen during the *brāhmī* hour and performed his daily obligatory rites, the twice-born [practitioner]...
Then, having gone to a river and bathed, one should invoke the sacred site (tīrtha) eightfold;
thereafter, having recited the root mantra, one should sprinkle [the water] as many times as the number of the sun (twelve).

Then, having put on two garments and sat down on the bank of the Gaṅgā or on a mountain, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs with the formulas: "Hāṃ, salutation to the two thumbs," "Hāṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth. || 76 ||
Then follows *prāṇāyāma*: having uttered the letters beginning with *a*, one should fill the air through the left nostril;
having uttered the five groups of consonants (*pañcavarga*), one should retain the air (*kumbhaka*); and having uttered the letters beginning with *ya*...
One should exhale the breath through the right nostril.
Having done this three times and performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) with the syllables of the mantra, one should meditate.
In battle, one should meditate upon Hanumān, accompanied by ten million monkeys,
rushing forward to conquer Rāvaṇa after seeing him rise up in haste;
and [one should likewise meditate upon] the great hero Lakṣmaṇa fallen upon the ground of the battlefield.
Having generated wrath toward the Guru and seized the mountain that was his body, he caused the three worlds to tremble with cries of "Alas! Alas! and with arrogance;
pervading as far as the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), he assumed a terrifying form.
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] six thousand times. || 78 ||
Its mantra is as follows: having first uttered one's own seed-syllable, one should then speak "pavana" (wind);
then "nandana" should be given; and at the end, with the vocative case-ending "ṅe," one adds the beloved of fire (Svāhā).
This Daśārṇa Manu is declared to be a celestial tree for men. || 79 ||
One should recite [the mantra] throughout the day and night on the seventh day; then, having instilled great fear, she will certainly arrive when three parts of the night remain.
If the practitioner overcomes her illusion, he obtains his desired boon. [This is] the Vidyā.
Whether it be wealth, or even a kingdom, or the subjugation of enemies, one attains that very instant; this is the truth, the truth, most certainly so. || 81 ||
Thus ends the ritual manual of Hanumat.
Now follows the mantra of the poison-fire;
it consists of the nature of two *kha* letters joined with the visarga and the bindu. 82.
Now, the procedure for worship:
having performed the morning rites and so forth, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and the rest. As follows:
Salutation to Agni, the seer, on the head;
salutation to the Paṅkti meter, on the mouth;
salutation to Agni, the deity, on the heart.
At the secret place, obeisance to the seed-syllable Khaṃ;
at the two feet, obeisance to the power of the Bindu. || 83 ||
The ritual assignment (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs is performed using the letter *kha* joined with the six long vowels;
for meditation and worship, it is to be done like the Vaiśvānara mantra described by Śārada.

The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), followed by a fire-oblation (*homa*) of clarified butter (*ājya*) amounting to one-tenth of that number.

Having meditated upon a five-petalled white lotus on the palm of one's own left hand, one should contemplate the letter *kha* with the visarga (*visarga*) in its pericarp (*karṇikā*), and the [five] letters with the *anusvāra* on its five petals.
Having meditated on the syllable *kha* and visualized it as consisting of red-colored nectar, one should destroy all poison through that touch.
Having touched one afflicted by poison or disease with the hand thus prepared, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
It destroys all poisons of scorpions and the like, fevers, indigestion, erysipelas, toothaches, eye diseases, and all other types of pain. || 86 ||
Now, the mantra for neutralizing the venom of scorpions and other such creatures is as follows:
Oṃ sa va ha sphuḥ; oṃ hili mili cili hasphuḥ; oṃ hili hili cili cili hasphuḥ.
To Brahmā, phuḥ! To Viṣṇu, phuḥ! To Indra, phuḥ! To all the gods, sphuḥ!
These are the removers of scorpion venom.
*Oṃ geri ṭhaḥ*. This is the mantra that removes the poison of mice. || 87 ||

Oṃ saraṇe sphuḥ, oṃ asaraṇe sphuḥ, oṃ viṣaharaṇe sphuḥ. By reciting this mantra and scattering white mustard seeds, there is the destruction of mice. Thus ends the mantra for the destruction of mice. || 88 ||
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ oṃ svāhā garuḍa hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of Durgā, which removes the poison of spiders. || 89 ||
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Viṣṇu; move, move! strike, strike! hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! This is the mantra of Viṣṇu, which removes the poison of all species of insects. || 90 ||
Now, the Ārdrapaṭī [mantra]: Oṃ, Hṛdaya, Bhagavati Cāmuṇḍe, you who are clothed in red,
whose form and prowess are irresistible, for the sake of slaying [so-and-so], O bewildered one, [svāhā]— the beloved of Fire.
Covered with a wet red cloth, one should perform recitation facing south with arms raised on the bank of a river flowing to the ocean or on saline soil;
as long as the cloth dries, the life-force of the enemy dries away.
Thus ends the Ārdrapaṭī [chapter]. 91.
Now, the mantra of Śmaśānabhairavī: O Śmaśānabhairavī, consumer of human blood, flesh, and bones! Grant me success; fulfill my heart's desires! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! || 92 ||
Now, the mantra of Mahākālī:
Oṃ phreṃ phreṃ kroṃ kroṃ, seize the bound souls (paśu), hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
This application with the mantra of Śmaśānabhairavī is to be performed for as long as it takes in the case of a cruel rite.
Now follows the ritual application (prayoga) of the Mahākālī mantra;
in this case, no ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth need be performed.
And thus it is said:
There is no need for deliberation here regarding certain matters such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and purification (śuddhi). 94.
Then, in a black pitcher filled with black water,
one should worship Kālikā with black flowers in a cremation ground while facing south—
she who has five faces, is exceedingly fierce, and possesses three eyes in each face.

Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who holds in her right and left hands a spear, a trident, a bow, arrows, a sword, a shield, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who is adorned with many ornaments, the practitioner shall accomplish whatever goal resides in his mind. (95)
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā as the eighth—
these are stationed in the place of the water-jars, starting from the east and ending with the northeast.

The procedure there is as follows: having meditated upon the Goddess and worshipped her with the ritual services according to the rules, one should worship the eight powers beginning with Brāhmī in the sequence starting from the east. || 97 ||
Likewise:

one should offer oblations into a blazing fire in the sky while intent on uttering the names [of the enemies] for the purification of those foes; likewise, one should mutter the mantra of the Goddess.
With fuel-sticks of *picumarda*, as well as wood from the *vibhītaka* tree,
and with house-soot from a cremation ground, by means of an oblation of *vibhītaka* charcoal and the application of the *Kālī* mantra, one destroys an enemy within seven days. (98)
Uccāṭana (expulsion) should be performed in the afternoon, and likewise māraṇa (killing) at the junction of day and night;
standing in the southern direction, facing south toward the village or other location. || 99 ||
Now, the mantra of Jvālāmālinī:
Oṃ namo bhagavati jvālāmālini gṛdhragaṇaparivṛte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. The ritual application therein is as follows.
Therein is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*Oṃ namaḥ* is declared for the heart; *Bhagavatī* is remembered for the head;
*Jvālāmālinī* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*); and then *Gṛdhragaṇaparivṛte*.
One should assign the *varma* (armor), *svāhā*, and *astra* (weapon) mantras, joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), upon the body.
The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows:
*oṃ namo hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth. 100.
One should certainly recite the mantra without eating; through such recitation, one becomes victorious.
One should recite it eight thousand times for twenty-three days;
this daily practice bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*), of this there is no doubt.
Merely by recollecting [this], the mantra-practitioner shall destroy all enemies. || 1 ||
Another practice:
according to the Phetkārīya, [the mantra is] Oṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhāṃ ṭhiṃ ṭhīṃ ṭhuṃ ṭhūṃ ṭheṃ ṭhaiṃ ṭhoṃ ṭhauṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaḥ.
