"Seize so-and-so, seize! Hūṃ hūṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ!

With this mantra, one should empower a five-finger-long stake made of jackal bone a thousand times; then, if one buries it in the house of someone, or in a cremation ground by means of that person's name—
Or if one should bury it, he becomes insane. || 2 ||
Oṃ ḍaṃ ḍāṃ ḍiṃ ḍīṃ ḍuṃ ḍūṃ ḍeṃ ḍaiṃ ḍoṃ ḍauṃ ḍaṃ ḍaḥ,
seize, seize [the person named] so-and-so, hūṃ hūṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ!
With this mantra, one should prepare a ritual stake made of human bone measuring one span (vitasti) in length.

If one should bury [the substance] consecrated with a thousand recitations in someone's house, or bury it in a cremation ground while uttering someone's name, that person’s entire retinue shall perish. || 3 ||
When [the rite] has been performed, there is indeed peace.
The mantra for peace is as follows: Oṃ saḥ saṃ saṃ haḥ, may there be peace for [name], svāhā!
With this mantra, one should offer oblations of milk sprinkled with honey;
by that, peace is attained. || 4 ||
Oṃ ḍhaṃ ḍhāṃ ḍhiṃ ḍhīṃ ḍhuṃ ḍhūṃ ḍheṃ ḍhaiṃ ḍhoṃ ḍhauṃ ḍhaṃ ḍhaḥ, kill [so-and-so], kill! ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ!
By means of this mantra, one should prepare a thirteen-finger-long stake made from the bone of a donkey.
If one should bury [the substance] consecrated with a thousand recitations in someone's house, that person shall perish from fever. || 5 ||
Oṃ ṇaṃ ṇāṃ ṇiṃ ṇīṃ ṇuṃ ṇūṃ ṇeṃ ṇaiṃ ṇoṃ ṇauṃ ṇaṃ ṇaḥ.
With this [mantra], one should consecrate a six-finger-long stake made of *khadira* wood a thousand times; into whose house one buries it, or into whose name [it is buried] in a cremation ground...
Or he should bury it; that destroys all his food. || 6 ||
Now, the release from the bondage of fetters:

Oṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti! O Nirṛti of piercing splendor, by the knowledge of that which consists of you, may this bond given by Yama be loosened; having ascended to the highest heaven, let there be no enmity. 7.

Of this mantra for breaking the shackles, Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi), Nirṛti is the deity, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and its application (viniyoga) is for the removal of misfortunes such as imprisonment. || 8 ||
In this manner, the wise person should recite the mantra ten thousand times, including the ṛṣi and other components;
then one becomes liberated from bondage and calamity, and not otherwise.
Now, the *ciṭi* mantra: one should utter the *tāra* (oṃ), then two *ciṭis*, and after that, *cāṇḍāli*.
Then one should utter *mahadādyām*, and after that, *amukaṃ me*.
"Bring [them] under control! Ṭha-dvandva!"—this is declared to be the *ciṭi* mantra.
By this procedure, one shall bring kings under control within seven days. (10)
He states the procedure:
having written that [mantra] on a palm leaf, interlaced with the name of the person to be accomplished,
one should place it in water mixed with milk and boil it at night.
He becomes submissive and is brought under one's control; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. || 11 ||
Having written this on a palm leaf, one should bury it in the house of Bhadrakālī;
this is declared to be the practice for bringing all living beings under one's control.
Now, the Tryambaka mantra:
"We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity;
may he deliver us from death as a cucumber is released from its stem, [but not] from immortality. (13)

Vasiṣṭha is declared its sage (ṛṣi), and the Anuṣṭubh is said to be its meter (chandas). Tryambaka, the Lord of Pārvatī, is designated as its deity (devatā). And the ritual assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed by means of the divided syllables of the mantra. || 14 ||
In that regard, the ritual procedure is as follows:

having completed the rites beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and ending with the deposition on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa), one should perform the deposition of the seers and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
For example:
"Salutation to the sage Vasiṣṭha on the head; salutation to the Anuṣṭubh metre in the mouth; salutation to the deity Tryambaka in the heart."
The application is for the pacification of such-and-such a person. || 15 ||
Then follow the ritual placements on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*).
As follows:
"To Tryambaka, salutation with the two thumbs; 'We worship' (*yajāmahe*), with the two index fingers."

Svāhā to the middle fingers for the fragrant [incense] that increases nourishment; Vaṣaṭ to the ring fingers for [the mantra] "like a cucumber from its stem"; Huṃ to the little fingers for [the mantra] "may I be released from death"; Vauṣaṭ to the palms and backs of the hands for [the mantra] "may I not [be released] from immortality"; Phaṭ.
The same applies to the heart-mantra and the others.
As it is said:
"The heart is declared to consist of three syllables, and the head of four."
The crest (śikhā) is said to consist of eight syllables, and likewise the armor (kavaca) of nine syllables.
Similarly, the eye (netra) is formed by five syllables, and it is taught that the palm (karatala) consists of three syllables.
Thereafter, [these are assigned] to the eastern, western, southern, and northern faces.
Then, in the chest, throat, and face; next, in the navel, heart, back, and abdomen;
thereafter, within the genitals, anus, roots of the thighs, knees, and the pair of shanks;
and finally, in that pair of circles, the breasts, the sides, and the feet.
One should place the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the two hands, the two nostrils, and the head.
Then one should place the eleven syllables:

on the head, the pair of eyebrows, the eyes, the mouth, the two cheeks, again on the heart, the abdomen, and then on the private parts, the thighs, the knees, and the feet; thus one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa). || 17 ||
Then comes the visualization of the meditative absorption (dhyāna):

[one should visualize the deity] bathing his head with the nectar-fluids from two jars held in his hands, holding those two [jars] with two hands, and bearing the deer-skin and the rosary with two [other] hands.
I worship Lord Śiva, who is as beautiful as Kailāsa, who holds two nectar-pots placed upon his arms, who rests upon a clear lotus, who wears a crown of the new moon, and who possesses three eyes.
Having meditated thus and worshipped him with mental offerings, one should perform the ritual preparation of the *arghya* water.

Then, having performed the worship of the *pīṭha* as taught by Śiva, and having meditated once more, and having performed the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of the five handfuls of flowers (*pañcapuṣpāñjali*), one should begin the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
In the filaments [of the lotus] at the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions, one should offer: "To Tryambaka, *namaḥ* unto the heart."
With these and other [mantras], one should worship with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Then, on the eight petals: *oṃ arkāya namaḥ*, and likewise for Indu, Vasudhā, Jala, Vahni, Vāyu, Viyat, and Yajamāna. (19)
Outside of that, in the east and so forth,
are Ramā, Rākā, Prabhā, Jyotsnā, Pūrṇā, Pūṣā, Pūraṇī, and Sudhā. The mantra is as follows:
"Salutation to Ramā," and so forth.
Outside of that:
Viśvā, Vidyā, Sitā, Prajñā, Sārā, Sandhyā, Śivā, and Niśā.
Outside of that:
Ārdrā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Medhā, Kānti, Śānti, Dhṛti, Mati.
Outside of that:
One should worship Parā, Umā, Pāvanī, Padmā, Śāntā, Amoghā, Jayā, and Amalā.
Then, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense (dhūpa) until the final dismissal (visarjana). || 19-ka ||
The preparatory rite for this consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
And so it is said in the Śāradā-tilaka: "One who has conquered the senses should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times while meditating in this manner;
he should perform ten thousand oblations with ten substances saturated with clarified butter."
The wise know them to be Bilva, Palāśa, Khadira, and Vaṭa; sesame and mustard; milk from a cow, curd, and again Dūrvā grass. (20)
The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows:
on a Saturday or another day, one should touch the root of an *aśvattha* tree and recite [the mantra] one thousand times; and likewise:
Whoever recites [the mantra] while touching the root of the Aśvattha tree on a Saturday shall be directly liberated from death; what need is there for other trivial rites? (21)
Likewise:
having bathed, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times while facing the sun;
thus liberated from mental and physical ailments, one shall attain long life. || 22 ||
Every day, the practitioner of mantra should offer one hundred and eight oblations of dūrvā grass;
having conquered all diseases, he shall attain a long life.
One should offer fuel-sticks of the *vaṭa* tree for ten thousand oblations;
there will be an abundance of wealth and grain, and success is achieved in no time at all. || 24 ||

Now, regarding the *Amṛtasañjīvanī*: first the seed-syllable of the temple (*prāsādabīja*), followed by the death-destroying *tāraka*, and the *vyāhṛtis*; having uttered these, he who constantly recites the *tryambaka* mantra in a *sampuṭa* fashion according to the direct order (*anuloma*).
The three-syllable mantra for conquering death, which removes mortality:
Oṃ Jūṃ Saḥ. Through the recitation of this, all accomplishments (siddhi) arise. || 25 ||
Now, the science of reviving the dead (*mṛtasañjīvanī*) worshipped by Śukra consists of the first quarter of the *gāyatrī* and one quarter of the *tryambaka*,
as well as the second quarter of the *gāyatrī* and the second quarter of the *tryambaka*.
The third foot of the Gāyatrī is the remaining foot of the Tryambaka mantra.
The mantra is as follows:
*oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhim*.

We meditate upon that splendor of the Divine which increases prosperity; may He who impels our intellects deliver us from bondage, as a cucumber from its stalk, and release us from death into immortality. 26.
Dhyāna:
[He is] clear, seated upon a clear lotus; in his two hands rest two full jars, and in his two lotus-hands are two rosaries of deer-bone, as well as two pots that are eternally full.

May the Lord, possessing a body adorned with a multitude of pure ornaments, bestow prosperity upon you—he who, with two [hands], holds those two flowing [streams] over his head and bathes the crescent moon with nectars.
Having meditated thus and invoked him with the mantra: "Obeisance to Tryambaka, the Great Rudra."
One should worship [it].
From the recitation of this, all accomplishments arise. || 27 ||
Now, regarding attraction:
I shall describe in brief the methods of attraction, as they are seen in the Tripurātantra and as they are seen in the Bhūtaḍāmara. (28)
One should extract the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Manmatha, and the seed-syllable of Lajjā.
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the word "Tripurādevī," followed by the dual form of the name "Amukī," and then the word "ākarṣaya" twice; [this is the mantra].
Having extracted the mantra ending with "svāhā," one should recite it ten thousand times.
Having drawn a hexagon with red sandalwood and saffron,
the mantra-practitioner should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) endowed with the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*),
adorned with the nasal resonance (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*), by means of the vowels representing the six long states.
One should worship her with red flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, and other food offerings,
while meditating in one's mind upon the Goddess who has three eyes and the crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
whose form resembles the rays of the rising sun and whose body is as crimson as vermilion.
He holds a lotus in his right hand and a rosary in his left.
By the grace of this mantra, one can summon even Rambhā or Urvaśī; of this there is no doubt, so what need be said of mortal women here?
Having inscribed [the mantra] upon birch bark with saffron,
liquid lac, and a mixture of Kashmiri saffron, agallochum, musk, and yellow pigment (rocanā), combined with the blood from the ring finger, one should recite the mantra of Kamalākṣī.
Oṃ śrīṃ kamalākṣi, attract, attract [so-and-so], oṃ phaṭ!
One should first recite this mantra one thousand times;
thereafter, the wise practitioner should take it upon birch bark and fashion it into a pill.
One should wrap that very [clay]— which has been fashioned from the earth arising at the site of the target and encased in mud-paste—
with the heat of the sun's rays; then, having again coated it with the three pungent spices (trikaṭuka),
one should fashion a female image and place it within her belly.
The practitioner, having placed the pill in a vessel and [visualizing] an image in the form of the target (sādhya),
should face it in a solitary place at night; as long as the mind remains steady, he should recite the mantra while maintaining that very form.
...until she arrived, trembling and her form languid with passion. || 31 ||
Now, as for the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), therein is the mantra of Cāmuṇḍā:
*Tāraṃ cāmuṇḍe jaya cāmuṇḍe mohaya vaśamānaya amukaṃ svāhā*.
Dhyāna:

She has a beautiful face and is formidable with the tips of her fangs; she stands in dense darkness, her right hand hidden by a skull-topped staff (khaṭṭāṅga) as a thunderbolt, and holding a noose in her left hand at her head.
Dark-complexioned, with tawny hair, terrifying, draped in a tiger skin, and carrying a corpse—Cāmuṇḍā should always be meditated upon by practitioners during the rite of recitation. || 33 ||
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, the goddess Cāmuṇḍā— offered ten parts of *kiṃśuka* flowers into the midst of the fire—
quickly becomes the bestower of fruits to practitioners by her mere name.
Now, regarding the rite of inciting mutual enmity: when the two have met in battle, enraged by their equal fury,
the practitioner takes up the dust raised by the other's hooves.

Enmity arises from dust, and hostility toward an enemy is produced by striking; with a mixture of these, enmity between mutual foes is certainly established. One should draw [the diagram] using buffalo and horse dung along with cow urine.
The names of those two quickly brought about mutual enmity between them.
One should draw [the figure] on a cloth from a cremation ground using the blood of a buffalo or a horse;
for whomever the name is written, there shall be mutual enmity between them.
In the center of the six-cornered wheel, provided with the name of the enemy, I shall now fully declare the mantra known as Mahābhairava. (37)
Oṃ, homage to Mahābhairava, the dweller in the cremation ground! Create, create enmity between [Name] and [Name], hūṃ phaṭ!
One should write this mantra there; enmity will certainly arise. || 38 ||
I shall now describe another practice that is difficult to find on the surface of the earth;
by the mere knowledge of it, enmity among enemies is certainly produced. (39)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Śmaśānakālikā! Cause so-and-so to be split asunder, cause him to be split asunder;
slay, slay; cook, cook; churn, churn! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
With this king of mantras, the wise and disciplined practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having kindled a fire from the *khadira* wood,
and then again a fire from the cremation ground,
one should perform [the rite] ten thousand times in the fire-pit using neem leaves mixed with pungent oil, accompanied by sesame seeds, barley, and unbroken rice.
Meditating upon the goddess Kālikā, who possesses a luster like that of a sapphire,
whose complexion is as blue as the sky, who is the Great Fierce One who crushes both gods and demons,
who has three eyes, a great roar, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Holding a skull and a sword in her hands, she stands upon the moon and the sun;

she is surrounded by a net of arrows and encircled by the *preta* and *bhairava* spirits. Dwell­ing in the wilderness of the ancestors (*pitṛkāntara*), she is the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
One should offer oblations with various flowers, rice-balls, and goats,
having worshipped Maheśānī with a mind full of devotion; then,
taking that ash and consecrating it with mantras, one should wear it.
Whomever one should strike with that ash, hatred shall arise among men toward them.
Fire becomes cool, the sun falls to the earth,
the ocean dries up, and the moon falls— if these were to happen,
O Goddess, then the King of Yogas, so difficult to attain, would become false. (41)
The practitioner should fashion a six-cornered king of wheels inscribed with the names of the enemies; then, by means of the previously mentioned substances, he should effect their mutual hatred.
Oṃ drāṃ! O you who cause hatred, create mutual hatred between [Name] and [Name], create, create, svāhā!
One should write this mantra on the exterior of the yantra using the aforementioned materials.
They shall become mutually hostile; this is the yoga in the Kubjikā doctrine. (43)
Now, as for eradication (*uccāṭana*):
I shall describe the procedure for eradication as it is taught in the *Śrīmatottara*.
One should write the name on a neem leaf using the excrement of buffaloes and horses.
Oṃ, homage to Kākatuṇḍī, O white-faced one! Expel [the name], HŪṂ PHAṬ!
Having worshipped this mantra and having written it with the aforementioned substances, one should then offer as oblation everything situated in a neem tree or in a crow’s nest.
Having brought fire from a cremation ground kindled with *dhustūra* wood,

and having offered oblations into that fire with great oils or pungent substances while reciting the previously mentioned mantra, [one should offer] its leaf smeared with black mustard and pungent condiments.
Having worshipped Dhavalāmukhī with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra),
the knower of mantras should scatter that ash upon the enemy's mansion;
by means of a mind joined with meditation, the eradication of the enemy shall occur.
The Great Goddess is smoke-colored, three-eyed, and crowned with the moon;
she is endowed with a mass of matted hair, draped in a tiger skin,
has a slender body, and her lotus-like hands are adorned with a garland of bones and a flaying knife.
One should contemplate her in one's mind as having eyes like hollows, excellent fangs, and a belly resembling the netherworld (pātāla); in this manner, the expulsion of the enemy must be performed.
O Maheśvarī, this method of yoga has been proclaimed in the Vīra-tantra;
it must be guarded with effort and never revealed.
Likewise:
on a Sunday or a Saturday, one should take a human bone four finger-breadths long;
having engraved it with the initial letter of the night [of the week], one should cast it into the principal chamber.
Within seven days, it will effect the eradication of the enemy.
The mantra is:
*Hūṃ, perform the eradication of [Name], perform it, svāhā!*
HŪṂ [Name], slay, slay! SVĀHĀ. || 47 ||

*ripumala-rodhana*: Having dug up the *ripumala* (the enemy’s filth) and the scorpion, one should bury them in the ground. By the obstruction of the filth, the enemy dies; when it is extracted, it brings happiness.
The mantra is: Oṃ stambhini, paralyze, paralyze the impurity of [name], hūṃ phaṭ!
Now, the rite of exorcism (*abhicāra*): *Oṃ viruddhe rūpiṇi caṇḍike vairiṇam amukaṃ dehi dehi svāhā*.
Having thus consecrated the sword and recited the mantras of the sword, [one should employ] the sword.

Having worshipped the goat and so forth, and having consecrated it with the name of the enemy, saying "You are so-and-so," and having bound its mouth three times with a red thread, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the vital breaths) using the enemy’s name, [reciting]:
"Oṃ, this is that enemy who hates; him, in the form of this sacrificial animal..."

Having recited "Destroy, O Great Goddess! *Sphem sphem*! Devour, devour!", having placed a flower upon the head of the sacrificial offering (*bali*), having recited the *balimantra* and fully worshipped the offering, [one says]:
"Today, in the month of Āśvina, on the Mahānavamī day, I, of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious Amukadevaśarmā..."
"Destroy such-and-such an enemy! This goat or buffalo, dedicated to such-and-such a deity, I offer unto you, O Blessed Durgā!
Having thus relinquished [the animal], and having cut [it] with "Āṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ," and having recited the *bhūla* mantra, [he offers] this blood.
Having offered blood to the head with the mantra "Salutation to Durgā," one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the flesh of the eight limbs using the root mantra. || 49 ||
Now, the mantra for an easy delivery:
*Oṃ manmatha manmatha vāhi vāhi lambodara muñca muñca svāhā | Oṃ, the bonds are released and the fetters are released; the rays are released by the sun.*
"O Mārīca, you who are released from all fear, come, come! Svāhā!
Having consecrated water eight times with either of these [mantras], it should be drunk; thereafter, an easy delivery occurs. || 50 ||
Now, the method for invisibility:
with five wicks made from the fibers of the arka, śālmalī, kārpāsa, paṭṭa, and lotus, [one should perform the rite] upon five human skulls.
Lamps should be made with human oil, and soot should be collected from human skulls;
one should diligently collect these five [substances] as before in a temple of Śiva.
Then, one should bring those produced from the five locations together into a single whole.
Having consecrated the eyes with the mantra, one should apply collyrium; then one cannot be seen even by the gods. || 51 ||
The mantra is:
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ kāli kāli mahākāli māṃsaśoṇitaṃ khādaya khādaya devi mā paśyatu mānuṣeti hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
One should consecrate it with the mantra recited one thousand and eight times.
Then, having performed the consecration one thousand and eight times with the root mantra and applying that collyrium to the eyes, one becomes invisible to the three worlds. || 52 ||
Now, the practice of the Yoginīs; from the Bhūtaḍāmara:
"Therefore, I shall now fully explain the supreme practice of the Yoginīs."
Named the Accomplisher of All Aims, it bestows all perfections upon embodied beings;
this great vidyā is extremely secret and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (53)
O beloved, I shall describe the foremost among those goddesses, the beautiful one of the gods, by whose worship the Lord of Yakṣas became the master of wealth;
indeed, by worshipping her alone, a man attains sovereignty.
Then, having risen at dawn and performed the auspicious rites of bathing and so forth,
one should approach the temple and thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
At the end of the syllable Om, one should effect the binding of the directions with the mantra "Sahasrāra Hūṃ Phaṭ."
Then the knower of mantras should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra;
he should perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga) with Māyā and draw an eight-petalled lotus.
Upon that lotus, he should perform the placement of the Great Mantra (mahāmantra) and the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa).
Having invoked the goddesses of the sacred seats (pīṭha-devīs), one should meditate upon the Goddess who is dear to the world—
Gaurī, who resembles the full moon, who wears variegated garments,
whose breasts are full and lofty, who is beautiful, and who bestows fearlessness upon all.
Having meditated thus, one should offer auspicious water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings with the root mantra.
Having again presented incense, one should offer the food offering (naivedya) with the root mantra,
along with beautiful sandalwood paste, betel leaf, and camphor.
At the end of the *praṇava*, [he should say] "O Goddess of the World, O beautiful lady of the gods, come!
The wise man should recite this mantra three times a day, every day, one thousand times, while constantly meditating upon the Goddess, the consort of Fire.
At the end of the month, having performed a most beautiful offering and worship throughout the entire day, one should recite the mantra; at midnight, Sundarī arrives.
Considering the practitioner to be very firm, she goes to the practitioner’s abode;
then, being well-pleased and with a face always smiling, she stands before the practitioner.
Seeing the Goddess, the lord of practitioners should offer auspicious water for the feet and other honors.
Having offered excellent sandalwood and *sumanasa* flowers, one should state one's desired wish. || 56 ||
Whether it be his mother, sister, or wife, out of a spirit of devotion—
if she be his mother— she grants him wealth, most enchanting riches,
and even the sovereignty of the earth that he has prayed for, day after day. (57)
In this world, truth has been protected like a son; this truth is most certainly established. His sister gives him wealth and likewise divine garments;
bringing a celestial maiden and a Naga maiden day after day, she presents them to him.
Whatever one prays for, she grants it all day after day;
protected in this world like a brother by her fulfillment of every heart’s desire.
If that goddess were to become the enchanting wife of the practitioner,
he would be the supreme sovereign among all kings in this world, the best of practitioners.
Whatever has been, whatever is becoming, and whatever is yet to be— [all that belongs to him].
All of that he certainly offers to the foremost of practitioners. || 59 ||
Her movement is certain everywhere—in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld.
Whatever that Goddess bestows cannot be fully described;
the supreme practitioner enjoys union with her in such a manner.
Having abandoned going to another's wife, otherwise one certainly perishes. || 60 ||
Next, I shall describe another means of accomplishment created by Brahmā in ancient times.
Having approached the bank of a river, one should then perform the bathing and other rites.
As before, one should perform all the necessary actions and draw a mandala with sandalwood paste.
Having written one's own mantra there and performed the invocation, one should meditate upon the captivating woman:
she who has the eyes of a deer, a face like a lotus or the moon, lips red as the *bimba* fruit, and is anointed with the fragrance of sandalwood.

Having thus meditated upon the Goddess— who wears silken garments, has full breasts, is enchanting, youthful, eternally fulfilling desires, and is multiform— one should recite the mantra while offering incense of agaru, lamps, and other offerings.
One should [offer] perfumes, flower essences, betel leaves and the like, starting from the root. || 62 ||
O Tārā, O Māyā, go, O Manoharā, beloved of Agni!
With a serene mind, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times every day;
at the end of the month, having occupied the entire day, one should perform the supreme recitation.
Having understood that the practitioner is steadfast, she should recite the mantra until midnight.
Then, having approached the presence of the practitioner, being well-pleased and enchanting, she says:
"Choose a boon quickly, whatever dwells in your mind. (63)
The master practitioner, having meditated upon her, should joyfully worship her with water for the feet and other offerings;
he should likewise perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅga), and the rite of Māyā.

Having offered an oblation of fresh meat, one should worship with a concentrated mind using sandalwood water, flowers, and fruit that are pleasing to the mind. Then, being worshipped and gratified, she fulfills whatever is prayed for.
She gives a hundred gold pieces to the practitioner day after day;
he, however, spends them all, and as long as she remains, she will not give any more.
For him, approaching another's wife would not be called true;
there is no doubt that his movement becomes unimpeded. || 67 ||
This knowledge has been declared to you, which is well-guarded even by the gods and demons;
O Supreme Goddess, I am bound to you by my affection and devotion. 68.
Next, O beloved, I shall describe another means of accomplishment; listen with a focused mind.
Having gone to the foot of a banyan tree, the best of practitioners should worship the Goddess.
Then he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga), and the rite of Māyā. (69)
Having offered an oblation of fresh meat, one should worship her with a concentrated mind;
day after day, one should offer her the *arghya* of impure blood.
O beloved, having thus meditated upon the auspicious Goddess Pracaṇḍavadanā— who has lips like a ripe bimba fruit,
who wears red garments, who is youthful, and who bestows all desires—
the best of practitioners should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Having worshipped for seven days, one should perform the rites according to the rules on the eighth day;
one should worship day by day with body, mind, and speech.
*Tāra*, *māyā*, and likewise *kūrca*—these are for the rite of protection; outside of that, the great mantra is:
*āgaccha kanakānte vati svāhā*. Having offered a pleasing *bali* offering, one should recite the mantra until midnight. (72)
Perceiving the preeminent practitioner to be steadfast, she comes to the practitioner’s abode;
and the preeminent practitioner, having seen her, should then offer the arghya and other honors. (73)
Then, having abandoned clothing, ornaments, and other such things, she goes to her own abode along with her retinue, while her husband remains enjoying his desires. (74)
In this way, the wife should always act in accordance with the command of the practitioner;
the wise man, having set aside his own wife, should devote himself to her.
Kāmeśvarī:
Next, I shall describe Kāmeśvarī, who bestows the fruit of all desires. [The mantra is:
Oṃ, Bhuvaneśānī, āgaccha kāmeśvari (Oṃ, Bhuvaneśānī, come, O Kāmeśvarī). Then...
The wife of Vahni is Mahāmantra, who brings happiness to practitioners. || 76 ||
Having performed everything as previously described, one should fashion a well-adorned image with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*) upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf;
then, ascending the bed, one should recite the mantra with a single-minded focus.
The wise one, being well-composed, should recite [the mantra] one thousand times for one month;
he should also offer a lamp with ghee and honey to Kāmeśvarī,
who has a moon-like face and eyes like dancing wagtails.
Constantly meditating thus upon the beloved one, whose movement is restless and who is like an arrow of the flower-bowed god, one should recite the mantra; then she arrives at midnight.
Having seen the best of practitioners, she should say to him, "Give me your command.
Then, assuming the form of a woman, she should offer him water for his feet and other such services.
The goddess, being exceedingly pleased, shall always delight the practitioner with joy;
she shall always protect him like a husband with food, drink, and the enjoyment of pleasure. 79.
Having led [the devotee] away at night and bestowed upon him great sovereignty,
abundant wealth, garments, ornaments, and other articles, he certainly departs at dawn;
in this way, his success shall be daily through the power of assuming any form at will.
Ratisundarī: Then, having fashioned a doll upon a cloth, he meditated upon her form— golden-hued, fair-limbed, and adorned with every ornament.

Having thus meditated upon her— beautiful, with lotus-like eyes, and adorned with anklets, armlets, and necklaces— the practitioner, having offered excellent water for the feet (pādya) along with sandalwood,
flowers, and jasmine blossoms, should recite the mantra.
The practitioner should offer incense of *guggulu* and lamps while reciting the root mantra.
The mantra is as follows: *Tāraṃ*, *māyā*, then the words *gaccha ratisundarī*.
One should recite the mantra eight thousand times every day, using the wife of Vahni (the syllable *svāhā*) as the concluding word.
At the end of the month, for an entire day, one should perform auspicious rites such as worship;
likewise, [one should offer] a lamp of ghee, as well as incense, flowers, and betel-leaf.
The wise man should recite the mantra until the beautiful woman arrives.
Having recognized the firm and eminent practitioner, she certainly goes there at midnight.
Then one should worship her with devotion using a garland of jasmine flowers;
well-pleased, she shall satisfy the best of practitioners with delights and food.
Having become his wife, she grants him his desired boon;
yet, having cast off her ornaments and other finery, she certainly departs at dawn. In accordance with the practitioner's command, she goes forth day after day.
O Goddess, in a solitary wilderness, success shall be attained; of this there is no doubt.
One should abandon one's wife and worship him [the deity]; otherwise, one will certainly perish. 84.
Padminī:
Next, I shall describe another means of accomplishment in one's own home in the presence of Śiva:
[the mantra] beginning with the first letter of the Vedas, followed by Bhuvaneśī, and "āgaccha padminī vallabhā. (Come, O beloved Padminī.)
Then, having prepared the entire mandala with sandalwood paste as before, one should write the great mantra of Pāvaka and then the root mantra.
[One should visualize the goddess] seated on a lotus throne, dark-complexioned, and possessing full, elevated breasts.
Having thus meditated upon her who has delicate limbs, a smiling face, and eyes like the petals of a red lotus,
one should recite the mantra a thousand times day after day.
Upon reaching the full moon at the end of the month, one should always worship her according to the prescribed rites.
The practitioner should recite the mantra until midnight with firm practice;
having ascertained that all is auspicious, she goes to the abode of the practitioner. (85)
Having become his wife, that Padminī indeed accomplishes the practitioner's goals through various means—
through divine foods, ornaments, and the like— day after day. Protected by her husband in this world, she is always protected in heaven as well.
Having abandoned his wife, the lord of practitioners should always worship her, O Dear One. (86)
Naṭinī:
Thereafter, O beloved, I shall describe the Great Vidyā as it was known by the wise Viśvāmitra; having mastered which, the Vidyās Balā and Atibalā were accomplished. 87.
The mantra is as follows:
at the end of the Praṇava [Om], "Mahāmāyā Naṭinī Pāvakapriyā Mahāvidyā. This has been declared; it must be guarded with great effort. (88)
Having gone to the bank of the Aśoka tree, one should perform the ritual bath as before;
with a well-composed mind, one should perform everything using the root mantra. (89)
Having thus meditated upon Gaurī, who deludes the three worlds, who wears variegated garments,
who is adorned with diverse ornaments, who is beautiful, and who bears the attire of a dancer,
one should recite the mantra a thousand times day after day.
Having worshipped her with offerings of meat, the wise man should present incense and lamps; he should always give her perfume, sandalwood paste, and betel-leaf.
The best of practitioners should worship her with devotion for one month;
having reached the final day of the month, he should perform a great worship.
At midnight, O most excellent of practitioners, he should instill some fear [in the deity].
Considering the practitioner to be very firm, she goes to the practitioner's abode. || 92 ||
Then, with all her sciences (vidyās), she spoke with a slightly smiling face:
"Choose quickly a boon, whatever dwells in your mind.
Hearing that, the best of practitioners should contemplate it with his mind and intellect.
Having treated her as a mother, a sister, or even a wife with a spirit of affection, one should satisfy her with devotion; the actress is fully capable of doing so. (93)
If that goddess were his mother, she would joyfully protect him like a son;
she bestows a hundred gold pieces and the substance of spiritual accomplishment day after day.
If that sister brings and gives a maiden— a daughter of a god, a Naga maiden, or a princess— to the practitioner day after day,
he shall know all news of the past and the future. || 95 ||
Through offerings of food and other services, she grants him the enjoyment of his desires;
O beloved, she certainly gives him a hundred gold pieces constantly.
Whatever he wishes for, she gives all of that—of this there is no doubt.
Now, I shall proclaim the Madhumatī Mahāvidyā; listen with careful attention.
Having joyfully drawn the image of a woman upon a birch-bark leaf with saffron, [proceed].
Then, O Dear One, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth;
having performed the placement of the life-force (jīvanyāsa) and so forth, one with a tranquil mind should meditate there.
Having thus meditated upon her, who resembles pure crystal and is adorned with various ornaments—
decorated with anklets, necklaces, armlets, and jeweled earrings—
one should recite the mantra a thousand times day after day.
Beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should worship with flowers and other offerings;
one should joyfully perform worship at the three junctions of the day with the proper rites of incense and lamps. 99.
Having reached the full moon day, the best of practitioners should worship with perfumes and other offerings;
likewise, he should offer a lamp of ghee, incense, and delightful food offerings.
Both by night and by day, he should perform the recitation of mantras with a well-composed mind.
At the time of dawn, she will certainly come into the presence of the practitioner. || 100 ||

Having become cheerful of countenance, she should gratify Rati with foods; and repeatedly, with maidens adorned with jewels belonging to the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, she should please the lord of practitioners.
She certainly bestows divine substances such as those to be chewed and those to be sucked. || 1 ||
O beloved, whatever object exists in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld, it is truly brought and given according to the desire of the practitioner. || 2 ||
She always gives a hundred gold pieces to that practitioner day after day;
having granted the boon to the practitioner, she goes to her own abode.
By the grace of her boon, he certainly becomes long-lived, free from disease,
omniscient, handsome, illustrious, and all-pervading.
That lord of practitioners enjoyed himself with that goddess day after day.
The mantra is as follows: Tāra (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), then "Gaccha anurāgiṇi maithunapriye," followed by Vahnibhāryā (Svāhā). This is declared to be the mantra that bestows all accomplishments. || 5 ||
This [mantra], O beloved, is indeed honey-sweet and bestows all accomplishments;
for out of affection for you, this most secret of secrets has been proclaimed.
The determination of the time, vessel, location, and so forth for the *sādhana* of the Yoginī.
The Goddess said: "I have heard the meritorious *sādhana* of the Yakṣiṇīs, which bestows happiness."
At what time should it be performed, and by what rite, O Lord? Furthermore, who are the qualified persons? Tell me briefly, O Lord. (7)
The Lord said: In the spring, the wise man, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and having his senses subdued, should practice [the rite],
always intent on meditation and intensely eager for the vision of Him.
In a dense forest, in a wilderness, or especially in Kāmarūpa—having reached any one of these places, one should practice with a well-concentrated mind.
By this method, [the deity] will manifest directly; of this there is no doubt.
All the servants of the Goddess are also authorized here, as are those who hold supreme authority;
even without being a servant of Tārakabrahman, one is authorized here.
Thus ends the section on the practice of the Yoginīs. 10.
Now, the determination of the substratum of worship:
therein, in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], it is said:
"Water, fire, the heart, and the wheel are born from the field (kṣetra) of Viṣṇu."
And a yantra or an image is always the proper place for the worship of Hari.
In the Gautamīya [Tantra]:
"The worship of Hari must always be performed at Śālagrāma, on a gem, on a yantra, or within image-mandalas; however, it should not be performed upon bare ground alone. (12)
By the mere touch of a Śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million births are destroyed;
how much more so its worship, which brings about the presence of Hari? (13)
If, through the merits of many births, one should obtain the Kṛṣṇa stone marked with the sign of a cow’s hoof-print, one’s birth is brought to completion. By this,
the preeminence of even the stone in the worship of Viṣṇu is established.
For the mandala and so forth are common to all. || 14 ||
In the Yoginītantra:
"One should worship the Goddess in the form of a *liṅga*, and likewise in the form of a book;
one should worship Mahāmāyā in a maṇḍala, in a yantra, in images, and in water."
Or one should worship the Supreme Goddess as she resides within a stone. || 15 ||
In the *Kaulāvalī*: "Where the *aparājitā* flower and the *javā* flower are found;
where white or red *karavīra* flowers are present; or where the *droṇa* tree stands."
The Goddess should always reside there; the worship of Caṇḍikā is performed upon that yantra.
All of this [is done] even in the absence of a yantra. || 16 ||
And so it is said:
"The yantra is declared to consist of mantra, or the mantra itself is the deity.
Just as there is a distinction between the body and the self, so too is there a distinction between the yantra and the deity."
Likewise, one should first draw the yantra and the form of the deity.
Because it restrains all suffering arising from defects such as desire and anger, they call this a "yantra" (instrument/machine); when worshipped, the Divine is pleased within it.
"Without the yantra, the deity is not pleased.
Those who know the Tantras say that because it restrains suffering, it is called a 'yantra' (instrument of restraint).
Thus, the primacy of the yantra in worship is established. || 19 ||
Now, regarding the consecration of the yantra,
in the Vāmakeśvaratantra, Bhairavī said:
O Great God, by your grace I have heard about the schism of the *cakra*;
now I wish to hear the definitive rule for the rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O highly fortunate goddess, O Kaulinī who creates the universe,
to the determination of all the castes as part of the concluding rite (udyāpana) for that [observance].
Having bathed, the practitioner of mantra should form a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and perform the worship of the Guru.
Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with the Śiva-mantra,
the practitioner should cast the wheel (cakra) therein, accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having extracted that [liṅga], one should then place the discus in a golden vessel;
[one should worship it] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with milk, and with cool water,
as well as with fragrant sandalwood, musk, and saffron.
The wise practitioner should perform the rite of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in sequence with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar, interspersed with water and incense.
One should cause the supreme bathing of the Goddess to be performed with eight golden jars filled with water, or with those filled with decoctions.

Having completed the bath, one should place that goddess upon a golden pedestal. Having touched the yantra with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, one should consecrate it with the *gāyatrī*: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra inspire us."
One hundred and eight times, O Goddess, for the sake of attaining the state of divinity. || 24 ||
Then, having performed the purification of oneself, one should worship the deity with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Having invoked the Goddess there, one should worship her and perform the ritual placement of the life-force (jīvanyāsa).
One should always worship her with the sixteen types of offerings (upacāra) and the great mudrās (mahāmudrā) and so forth.
One should worship the Goddess there with fruits, betel leaves, and food offerings. || 25 ||
One should offer silk thread and the like, as well as garments and ornaments;
O Maheśvarī, one should also offer a mallet, a fly-whisk, and a bell, according to what is appropriate.
One who is intent on his own welfare should diligently offer all of this.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing all desired goals, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times;
having then performed the offering of the bali-oblation, one should prostrate before the King of Yantras.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the residual ghee into the fire;
if one is unable to perform the rite of homa, one should perform twice as much recitation.

Having brought a single cow adorned with golden horns and other ornaments, one should give it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor; thereafter follows the ritual dismissal (visarjana) of the Goddess.
In the *Tantrapradīpa*:
"O Īśvarī, one should install the yantra upon fruit, a wall, or a cloth;
it bestows wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, fame, and long life. (30)
Elsewhere it is also said:
"One should not place the yantra on a wall, nor on a cloth, nor likewise on a wooden board, O Goddess, for one who possesses a sense of 'mine' regarding sons, grandsons, home, and so forth. (31)
Now, the procedure for the consecration of the yantra:
having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*) and preceded by the recitation of the *svastivācana*, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*):
"Today, etc., I, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), the venerable Amukadevaśarmā, [for the sake of] such-and-such deity..."

Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the consecration of the yantra for the sake of [the deity's] pleasure," one should bring the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and, having empowered it one hundred and eight times with the mantra *haum*, place the yantra therein while reciting the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ).

Then, having lifted it up, one should place it in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials. Then, having bathed it with cool water, sandalwood, fragrant musk, and saffron, and having brought the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should utter "Hauṃ."
Having consecrated [the object] one hundred and eight times with the mantra and having purified it as before, one should bathe it.
The procedure therein is as follows:
first, having bathed it with milk, and then having bathed it again with water, [one offers] incense.
One should offer [these].
Likewise with curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar.
Then with milk, cool water (with fragrant sandalwood, musk, and saffron).
One should bathe [the image].
Then, one should bathe it with eight golden jars filled with water mixed with saffron and gorocanā.
In all cases, bathing is performed with the root mantra. || 33 ||

Then, having lifted the yantra and placed it in another vessel, one should touch the yantra with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass and recite: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra inspire us."
Having thus consecrated [the object] one hundred and eight times with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should perform the rite of vitalization (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
In the Viśvasāra-tantra:
"The deities of the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra are Brāhmaṇa and the others;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are proclaimed as its seers (ṛṣis)."
Then, at that time, one should recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the meters (chandas).
For this mantra of the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (ṛṣis);
the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are the meters; and Consciousness (caitanya) is the deity for the installation of the vital breaths.
The application [is as follows]. || 35 ||
Namely: Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hauṃ haṃsaḥ.
The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of such-and-such deity are here as its vital breaths; likewise, *ām* and so forth for such-and-such deity.

The life-force (jīva) is established here; likewise, "Ām" and so forth, all the senses of such-and-such deity; likewise, "Ām" and so forth, the speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths of such-and-such deity, having come here, may they remain happily for a long time—svāhā!
Having thus established the vital breaths (prāṇas), one should invoke the deity there and worship them with either the sixteen or the five services (upacāras). || 35-ka ||
And so it is stated in the Bhairavatantra:
"Having conceived the form with the root mantra, one should perform the placement of the life-force (jīvanyāsa).
[One should place] Māyā, ending with the noose and goad, and the seven letters beginning with *ya*, each accompanied by the bindu."
Viyat (the sky) conjoined with Satya (truth) and Indu (the moon)—at the end of that, one should utter "Haṃsa. Then one should say:
"Her vital breaths are here; her vital breaths are here; her life-force is established here.
Having uttered this again, one should indeed speak of all her sense organs once more.

And for her, having established the vital breaths with the mantra: "May speech, mind, sight, hearing, and smell also come here and remain happily for a long time— ṬHA ṬHA," one should then invoke the Goddess.

Then one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Then, having offered the silk thread and so forth, and having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times, if one is capable, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*).
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should offer the remnants of each oblation.

In the absence of the fire sacrifice, a double recitation of the mantra must be performed. Then, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should perform the rite for ensuring the ritual's flawlessness (acchidrāvadhāraṇa). || 37 ||
Thus ends the procedure for the consecration of the yantra.
Thus concludes the third chapter in the Tantrasāra composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya Śrī Kṛṣṇānanda Bhaṭṭācārya. 3.
The Fourth Chapter: Now, the Miscellaneous Section.
Regarding that, the prescription of directions for worship.
In the *Nāradīya* concerning Viṣṇu:

Having bathed, wearing white garments, and having sipped water (ācamana), facing the eastern direction and having taken his place on a pure seat, he should perform the ritual expulsion of obstructive spirits (*bhūtotsāraṇa*). || 1 ||
But in another commentary:
"The practitioner of mantra, having sat upon a seat facing either east or north, with his legs bound in the lotus posture (padmāsana), should be composed and have his senses subdued. (2)
Also in the *Sārasamuccaya*:
"Whether facing east or facing the direction of Kubera (the north), this is the rule for worship at night; there is no fixed restriction [regarding direction]. || 3 ||
And so says the Smṛti:
"One should always perform rites for the gods at night facing north;
likewise, being pure, one should always perform the worship of Śiva facing north. (4)
Now, regarding what is prescribed and prohibited in worship,
the *Yantratantraprakāśa* states:
"Likewise, two *liṅgas* as well as two *Gaṇeśas* should not be worshipped."
Likewise, one should not worship two Śaktis or two Sūryas in a single place. || 5 ||
There are two discs [of Viṣṇu] in Dvārakā and two Śālagrāma stones;
by the constant worship of these, a householder shall attain freedom from anxiety.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"Having combined fifteen hundred liṅgas, or otherwise, O Goddess, one should worship each individual one with bilva leaves. (7)
Even a householder may worship a single Pāśupata Liṅga fashioned from clay, stone, or other materials, as well as a single Śālagrāma stone.
In the *Yāmala*:
"One should not worship Viṣṇu with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), nor Vināyaka with *tulasī*;
one should not worship Durgā with *dūrvā* grass, nor the Sun with *bilva* leaves. (9)
The *unmatta* flower and the *arka* flower should always be avoided by the wise when [worshipping] Viṣṇu.
In the Gautamīya: "One should never take red sandalwood or red flowers;
one should not worship the Son of Devakī with bilva leaves or those blossoms. (11)
As for that which is stated in that very same source:
"The lotus, the two *karavīra* flowers, the two types of *tulasī*,
the *jāti*, the *ketaka*, the *nāgakeśara*, the *pāvantī*, the *kahlāra*, the *campaka*, and the *utpala*..."
The *nāndyāvarta*, the *yūthī*, the *mallikā*, the *navamallikā*,
the *kunda*, the *mandāraka*, the *saugandhika*, the *keśara*, the *kuruṇṭa*, the *aśoka*, the *sarja*, the *bilva*, and the *munipuṣpaka*.
One should worship with a leaf of the *āmalaka*, a pure leaf of the *karṇikāra*, or one born from the *palāśa* tree;
these or other flowers should be offered according to availability.
Thus, the rule regarding the *bilva* applies when the prescribed flowers are unavailable.
In another tantra:
For the goddesses, mandārava flowers are for Arka; likewise, tagara is for Āditya.
Red flowers are exceedingly dear to Gaṇeśa and to Sūrya.
For Śiva, one should offer jasmine, madantī, yūthī, bandhūka, and ketaka;
red javā, the two types of mālatī, and likewise ketakī at the three junctions of the day; as well as saffron, red water-lily, and the red hayāri.
Likewise:
A wise person should not offer to Śivā anything that has a pungent odor or no odor at all, that is defiled by worms, hair, and the like, or that has been brought wrapped in garments. (14)
One should not worship with buds, nor without *campaka* and lotuses;
nor should one worship Viṣṇu with dry leaves, flowers, or fruits, nor with those brought after bathing, nor with stale ones, nor with those obtained by begging, nor with black-colored ones.
One should avoid flowers that have blossomed on their own and those that have fallen to the ground by themselves;
one should especially avoid the *vṛhatī* flower and those that are scentless.
The phrase "blossomed on their own" means those caused to open by a person [themselves]. || 15 ||
One should never worship with flowers that have fewer than three petals.
One should avoid those that have fallen to the ground, those touched by the limbs [of others], and those defiled by hair, insects, and the like.
One should also strictly avoid the kumuda, the pāṭala, and the śirīṣa.
One should avoid flowers that have fallen to the ground, with the exception of the śephālī and the vakula.
Likewise:
[An image] made of bilva, khadira, or dhātrī leaves, as well as of tamāla or lotus, is not defiled even when it is cut or broken. (17)
In the Gautamīya [Tantra]:
One should avoid flowers that are soiled, touched by the ground, defiled by worms, hair, or the like, or those that have been stale when used for the worship of the deity.
The lotus and the āmalaka fruit remain pure for two days;
the tulasī and bilva leaves are always pure;
and the karavīra flowers are fit for one day, O ascetic. (18)
In the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess, one should not worship with flowers that have been stale, even if they are made of gold;
nor, O Supreme Lady, with flowers that have become *nirmālya* (remnants of an offering) or are defiled. (19)
Regarding Tripurā, in the Vārāhīya [Tantra] it is said:
"One should not worship with *palāśa* or *kāśa* flowers; one should avoid them from afar. Likewise, one should not use leaves from the *dhātrī* or *tamāla*, nor from the two types of *tulasī*."
From worshipping [it], sin indeed arises, and it also robs one of fortune through the planetary conjunctions (*lagna*).
Tulasī should always be avoided during the worship of Tripurā by the wise;
by merely smelling Tulasī, the beautiful goddess becomes enraged. (20)
In the *Kaulāvalī*:
"One who desires his own welfare should not offer red *arghya*, white *dūrvā* grass, blue-throated [saffron], or *kuruṇṭaka* flowers to Mahādevī. (21)
Also in the Yoginītantra, with reference to the Goddess:
"With a yellow jhiṇṭī flower, and with white tagara."

One should always avoid worship with the white *uḍra* flower and the *puṣpa*. One should not worship the Great Goddess with two types of *tulasī*, nor with flowers born of the *mandāra*, *kahlāra*, or *tamāla*, nor with those produced from *kuśa* or *kāśa* grass.
Likewise, with reference to all [trees]:
one should worship the Great Goddess with the flowers of the *bakula*, the *aśoka*, and the *arjuna* when they are without their stalks; however, one should avoid those that still have their stalks.

One should worship with *viṣṇukrāntā*, *javā*, *nāgakeśara*, *nāgavallabha*, *vandhūka*, and *mandāra* together with their stalks. One should not touch them with anything other than the hand, nor should one touch them once they have fallen to the ground.
One should worship the Śephālī and Bakula flowers even when they have fallen to the ground;
likewise, a Mālūra fruit that has fallen to the ground may be offered. Sandalwood is the wood for that [deity], while the root of the Bilva and the leaf of the Kadalī should be avoided.
Likewise: the bilva leaf, the mango leaf, the leaf of the tamāla and the āmalakī,
the kahlāra lily, the tulasī, the lotus, and the flower of the munipuṣpa.

O Śaṅkarī, that which has been kept overnight and whatever else consists of buds is acceptable; likewise, the leaf of the stainless Bilva and the leaf of Tulasī do not become defiled even if cut or broken, nor does the Jātī flower.
Likewise, in the Matsyasūkta, among the sciences such as astrology, it is said:
"The red *kokanada* lotus is the best flower, as are the *bandhūka*, the *śatapatra*, the *varvara*, the *advitara*, and the two kinds of *karṇikā*."
The *vaka*, *mandāra*, mango blossoms, and *karavīra* are praised; likewise the two types of *mallikā*, *jātī*, *kṣauma* flower,
*jayantikā*, *bilva* leaf, *kuruvaka*, *munipuṣpa*, and *keśara*.
One should worship with the leaves of vāsantī, dvita, kāśapuṣpa,
marūvaka, madana, lavaṅga, yūthī, and śephālikā,
as well as with fragrant white and red flowers.
With bilva fruits, maruvaka flowers, and so forth, excluding tulasī leaves.
Although it is said that "worship devoid of *tulasī* shall never take place," nevertheless, that restriction does not apply to the *Tripurā* and other such rites.
And so it is said:
"The worship of Sundarī, Bhairavī, Kālī, Brahmā, Vighna, and Vivasvat,
if performed without Tulasī, that worship shall be fruitless."
Thus, "not fruitless" means "fruitful.
Therefore, according to the previous statement, *tulasī* must always be avoided in the worship of Bhairavī and others;
however, in the worship of other [deities], there is no fault whether it is present or absent. || 26 ||
"One should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains" is intended as a prohibition of rice, which would otherwise be obtained by extension [of the rule] in the absence of flowers. || 27 ||
For it is said:
"O beautiful one, in the absence of flowers, the daily worship must be performed even with water, dūrvā grass, or rice,
due to the lack of flowers."
But it is not intended to prohibit the arghya and other such offerings. || 28 ||
And thus: "With fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass— this is declared to be the *arghya* for all the gods."
Thus, one should not worship Durgā with *dūrvā* grass, and so forth. || 29 ||
"O Goddess, there is never any worship here without *dūrvā* grass;
therefore, O Śivā, one should take *dūrvā*, which consists of all flowers," according to the statement in the *Śrīkramīya*. (30)
And so says Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"She is always to be worshipped with all flowers, whether prescribed or prohibited;
worship of all deities must be performed, for here devotion is the essential factor. (31)
Likewise, in another tantra:
"The worship of the Goddess should always be performed with both aquatic and terrestrial flowers,
whether they are prescribed or not, by one whose mind is endowed with devotion."
This, however, pertains to the case of extreme devotion when the prescribed flowers are unavailable. || 32 ||
Likewise, in the Kālītantra:
"With auspicious apāmārga and bhṛṅga [leaves], excluding tulasī... (33)
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"Dhustūra, Aśoka, Bakula, white Aparājitā, black Aparājitā," and so forth—such rules regarding flowers are to be understood. || 34 ||
Now, regarding the specific details of recitation (japa):
since recitation without its supporting structure (setu) is fruitless, that structure is now defined. || 35 ||
In that regard, the Kālikā Purāṇa states:
"The Praṇava is the bridge of the scriptures; the Praṇava is remembered as the essence of mantras.
That which is not preceded by the Oṃ-syllable flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart."
Just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant, even so the mantra of sacrificers, being without a dam, leaks away in an instant. (36)
That fourteenth vowel which is the bridge known as *au* is called the bridge for the Śūdras by means of the anusvāra and the nasal sound (*nāda*). || 37 ||
Now, the purification of the five limbs (*pañcāṅgaśuddhi*):
since worship is fruitless without the purification of the five limbs, it is now described.
Regarding this, the *Kulārṇava* states:
The purification of oneself, the place, the mantra, the ritual substance, and the deity is the fifth.
O Goddess, as long as one does not perform these, how can there be worship of the deity?
Without these five purifications, worship leads to malevolent magic (abhicāra).

Purification of the self is declared to be achieved through thorough bathing, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), as well as breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth, along with all the ritual depositions (nyāsa) such as those of the six limbs.
By means of sweeping, smearing with unguents, and so forth, [the site] is made as pure as the surface of a mirror;
it is adorned with canopies, incense, lamps, flowers, garlands, and the like, and with powders of five colors—this is declared to be the purification of the place (sthānaśuddhi). || 40 ||
Having interwoven the letters of the root mantra with the phonemes of the Mātṛkā in both direct and reverse order, repeating them twice, this is declared to be the purification of the mantra. (41)

Having consecrated the articles of worship with the root mantra and the weapon mantra according to the prescribed rule, one should display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā) and others; this is proclaimed as the purification of the substances.
Having established the Goddess upon the pedestal and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,

the knower of mantras— the wise one— should sprinkle the garlands and other offerings, as well as the incense and so forth, with water three times using the root mantra; this is declared to be the purification of the deity.
Having thus performed the fivefold purification, one should thereafter perform the worship.
Now, the means for the accomplishment of mantras:
as it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"If a mantra, though properly performed, does not bring about accomplishment..."
It must be performed again by that very same person; then success will certainly be attained. || 44 ||
If the mantra, having been performed again, does not become accomplished, it must be performed once more by that same person; then it will undoubtedly be accomplished. || 45 ||
Furthermore, if that mantra, though practiced, does not become perfected, then seven expedients spoken by Śaṅkara should be employed therein. || 46 ||
One should perform, in sequence, the acts of wandering, obstructing, subjugating, pressing, nourishing, and withering, ending with burning; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected.
One should perform the rotation with the seed-syllable of Vāyu and the threading according to the sequential method;
having written that mantra upon the yantra with realgar, camphor, and saffron,
one should write the threaded mantra with uśīra and sandalwood.
It should be written in the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water;
through worship, recitation, and burnt offerings, once it has been rotated, it becomes a bestower of success.
If, despite being thus whirled, it is not accomplished, one should perform its confinement (*rodhana*).
One should recite the mantra while encasing it with the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī.
Thus it becomes confined and perfected; if this does not happen, then subjugate it.
Lac-dye, sandalwood, costus, turmeric, madana, and realgar—
having inscribed the mantra with these substances upon a very beautiful birch-bark leaf, it should be worn around the neck; thereby success will be attained, or one may cause the enemy's oppression.
Having thoroughly recited the syllables through the yoga of the lower and upper [mantras],
one should likewise meditate upon the deity in her lower and upper form;
having written the Vidyā with "sun-milk" (cow's milk) and having stepped upon it with the foot.
With such a mantra, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed day after day;
then, one who is afflicted and overcome with shame shall become perfected (siddha), and thereafter one should nourish him.
One should join the three seed-syllables of the young girl at the beginning and the end;
having written the Vidyā with cow’s milk and honey, one should visualize it in the hand. Thus nourished, it becomes perfected; if not, one should perform the rite of drying.
One should interlace the mantra with two seed-syllables of Vāyu (Yam).
This vidyā, having been written with excellent ashes, should be worn around the neck.
If it is dried yet remains unaccomplished, it should be incinerated by means of the seed-syllable of Fire (Ram).
In the rite of burning, one should join each individual syllable among the mantras with the seed-syllable of Agni at the beginning and the end, as well as below and above;
having written the mantra with the oil of the Brahma-tree (Butea monosperma), one should wear it.
Then, as stated by Śaṅkara, the mantra becomes perfected at the region of the throat. (55)
Śiva said: Thus has this been fully told to you out of devotion alone.
One would attain fulfillment by means of even a single [verse]; how much more so by many, O lady of excellent vows? (56)
Now I shall further explain the cause for the accomplishment of mantras:

having encased the mantra within the *mātṛkā* (alphabet), the wise practitioner should recite it one hundred times in both forward and reverse order; at the end of that, he should recite the mantra alone.
One should perform this daily until the hundred thousand [recitations] are completed;
it has been stated by those who know the tantras that the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur. (57)
Now, the characteristic of accomplishment:
the effortless fulfillment of one's desires is the supreme characteristic of accomplishment.
Likewise, there is the removal of deaths and the vision of the deity;
its application is the effortless attainment of success, which is the supreme characteristic of accomplishment.
Entering another's body and likewise entering a city; ascending upwards in this manner, as well as movement through the cities of the moving and the unmoving;
the union with the Khecarī and listening to her teachings and so forth.
One should observe the cavities on the ground; this is the characteristic of the highest [grade].
There is renown, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, a very long life, and the supreme power of subjugating kings and their retinues.
In all places and throughout all worlds, he becomes a source of wonder and remains happy;
by his very sight, he removes diseases and likewise neutralizes poisons.
The practitioner effortlessly attains the fourfold types of scholarship.
Detachment, the desire for liberation, renunciation, mastery over all things, the practice of the eightfold yoga, the total abandonment of the desire for enjoyments,
compassion toward all beings, and the arising of qualities such as omniscience.
The perfection of such qualities as these is the characteristic of middling accomplishment. || 59 ||
Fame, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, long life,
affection from kings and their ministers, mastery over the world, great sovereignty, wealth, and the abundance of sons, wives, and other such riches.
The inferior accomplishments (siddhis) are said to be the first stage for practitioners;
however, he whose mantra is truly perfected is Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt.
The defects of mantras:
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra, Śaṅkara said:
"In former times, the Mahāvidyā Bhuvaneśī was indeed [attacked] by the King of the Gods."
Then, although the Great Vidyā had been propitiated, she became devoid of power. || 61 ||
The single-syllabled [mantra], though devoid of power, was made radiant by the *vāgbhava* [syllable].
That Vidyā known as *kāmarāja*, which was previously afflicted by the arrow of the Flower-Bowed One (Kāmadeva), was established by Bhuvaneśī. 62.
"O devoted wife, this Vidyā which has been cursed by you is the maiden [Tārā];
she is established by me solely as the form of Śiva and solely as the form of Śakti—this Vidyā Tārā, whose nature is like the moon. (63)
With reference to the Vidyās such as Bhairavī and others: she who is asleep, burnt, and pinned down is the very form of withdrawal (saṃhāra);
she who is intoxicated with passion, fainted, and deprived of power is paralyzed.
Severed, obstructed, and aged, she is seedless and devoid of power.
Likewise, in the Viśvasāra:
"Severed, obstructed, devoid of power, turned away, uttered [inappropriately],
deaf, eyeless, pinned, and likewise paralyzed."
Burnt, fallen, terrified, soiled, and insulted;
pierced, fast asleep, intoxicated with pride, and fainted;
robbed of his vigor, humiliated, and utterly ruined—the child once again.
Furthermore, [the types of] Kumāra, Yuvan, Prauḍha, Vṛddha, Nistriṃśaka,
Nirvīja, Siddhihīna, Manda, Kūṭa, Tathā, Niraṃśaka, Sattvahīna, Kekara, and Jīvahīnaka.
One who is smoky and embraced by smoke becomes deluded and afflicted by hunger;
one who is excessively proud becomes deprived of limbs; one who is said to be excessively angry becomes cruel and ashamed, as well as tranquil in mind.
One who has fallen from his position, one who is mutilated, and one who is devoid of affection are proclaimed [as unfit].
I shall now describe the characteristics of those who are excessively aged and those who are afflicted by disease.
That mantra whose beginning, middle, and end are said to contain the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Y),
whether conjoined or unjoined, and further pervaded by a vowel in three,
four, or even five ways, is designated as "Chinna" (the severed).

But that mantra which is marked by two *bhū* syllables at the beginning, middle, and end is known as "obstructed" (*ruddha*); it is devoid of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). || 67 ||
That mantra which is devoid of the three principles of Māyā, the Śrī-bīja,
and Rāva, and lacks the Śakti, is said to be powerless if it does not contain them in its middle.
The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) is in the mouth, Māyā (HRĪṂ) is on the head, and the goad (AṂKUŚA) likewise;
this is declared to be Parāṅmukha, the letter HA joined with the Bindu.
If the moon (the letter *u*) is absent from the beginning, the end, or the middle, that mantra is known as "deaf.
A five-syllabled mantra that is devoid of the letters *ra*, *ka*, and *u* should be understood as "blind"; it bestows suffering, grief, and disease. (70)
At the beginning, middle, and end [of the mantra] are the Haṃsa, the Prāsāda, and the Vāgbhava;
the letter *ha* with the *bindu* is the *jīva*, and the *rāva* yields four fruits.
That in which the word "I bow to Māyā" (*māyā namāmi*) is absent is *kīlita*.
That mantra in which there is one [syllable] in the middle and two at the head, yet neither the weapon (astra) nor Purandara (Indra) are present, is paralyzed and devoid of success.
If the fire and wind [seeds] are joined at the head of a mantra and are seen there seven times, they declare that mantra to be "burnt."
A mantra that appears with two, three, six, or eight missing syllables is said to be "fallen" (srasta); it is devoid of all spiritual accomplishments.
He in whose mouth there is neither *māyā* nor the *praṇava* according to the prescribed rule, whether it be *śiva*, *śakti*, or that which is called *bhīta*, is proclaimed as such. (75)
That mantra in which there are four *m* sounds at the beginning, middle, and end is indeed impure and accompanied by all obstacles. (76)

That mantra in the middle of which there is the letter *da*, or which has armor (*kavaca*) on its head in two parts, and in which the weapon (*astra*) resides, is declared to be "obscured" (*tiraskṛta*).
The two syllables *dyo* are in the heart and the head, while *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* are in the middle;
that very mantra, when thus differentiated, is free from all [other] scriptures.
That which consists of the three qualities (guṇas) and is devoid of the haṃsa is declared to be deep sleep (suṣupta). || 79 ||
Whether it be a mantra or a vidyā consisting of seventeen syllables,
beginning with five *phaṭ* sounds, that which is declared to be "intoxicated with pride" (*madonmatta*)—
if its weapon (*astra*) is situated in the middle, that mantra is "fainted" (*mūrcchita*). || 80 ||
A mantra whose constituent parts (aṅgas) have ceased [to function] is said to be one whose power has been stolen. || 81 ||
The mantra which consists of eighteen syllables, joined with the four [syllables] at the beginning, middle, and end, should be known as Bhīma. (82)
Or that mantra which consists of nineteen syllables, joined with the *tāra* (om),
enriched with the seeds of *hṛllekhā* and *aṅkuśa*, is declared to be *pradhvasta*.
A mantra of seven syllables is known as a child; one of eight syllables is known as a youth;
one of sixteen syllables is a young man; and a mantra of forty syllables is considered mature.
The thirty-syllable, the sixty-four-syllable, the hundred-syllable, and even the four-hundred-syllable mantra—this is proclaimed as the "Vṛddha" (the increased). || 85 ||
The sage of thirty syllables is said to be that which consists of nine syllables joined with the *dhruva*;
at its end is the heart-mantra, the head-mantra is in the middle,
and it lacks both the *śikhā* and *varma*, or possesses only the *vauṣaṭ* or *phaṭ* sounds.
Or, if it is devoid of the syllables of Śiva and Śakti, it is declared to be "seedless" (nirbīja). || 86 ||
In these positions, if the syllable *phaṭ* is seen in a mature form, that mantra will be devoid of success; likewise, a mantra consisting of ten syllables is considered weak. (87)

A single-syllable mantra is called a *kūṭa*; it alone is said to be partless (*niraṃśaka*). A two-syllable mantra is devoid of essence (*sattvahīna*), while a four-syllable one is "squint-eyed" (*kekara*). || 88 ||
A six-syllabled mantra devoid of the seed-syllable (jīva), a seven-and-a-half syllabled mantra,
and even one of twelve-and-a-half syllables is "smoky" (dhūmita) and thus censured.
Likewise, that which consists of twenty-one syllables with two and a half seeds, or twenty syllables, or thirty syllables, is known as the "embraced" (āliṅgita). || 90 ||

A mantra of twenty-two syllables is proclaimed to be "deluded" (mohita). A mantra of thirty-two syllables, as well as one of twenty-seven syllables, should be known as "afflicted by hunger" (kṣudhātta); likewise, one of twenty-four syllables is so designated. || 91 ||
A mantra consisting of eleven syllables, or twenty-five syllables, or twenty-three syllables is declared to be "haughty" (dṛpta). || 92 ||

The mantra may consist of twenty-six syllables, or likewise thirty-six syllables, or it may have twenty-nine syllables; indeed, it is that very same [mantra] even when deprived of its ancillaries (aṅga).
Whether it has twenty-eight syllables or thirty-one,
he should be known as excessively angry and censured in all ritual actions.
A mantra consisting of thirty syllables, or even thirty-three, should be known as excessively cruel; it is censured in all ritual activities.
Beginning from forty and continuing up to sixty-three,
that same number of mantras is declared to be designated as "with shame" (savrīḍa).
Those Ṛṣi-mantras that consist of sixty-five syllables have tranquil minds.
From sixty-five syllables up to ninety-nine,
all those mantras are said to be displaced from their proper positions and are not auspicious.
Those Ṛṣi-mantras that consist of thirteen syllables or fifteen syllables should all be known as deficient; likewise those of one hundred and fifty syllables.
Whether they number two hundred and ninety-two, or one less than that,
or even up to three hundred, they are proclaimed to be those who are devoid of affection (niḥsneha).
Beginning from four hundred syllables up to a thousand syllables, that mantra is considered excessively long and is devoid of all scriptural efficacy. || 100 ||
Mantras exceeding one thousand syllables are called *daṇḍakas* and are known as *pīḍitas*.
Mantras of two thousand syllables are divided into seven parts;
these mantras, existing in their respective forms, should be understood as being in the nature of hymns (*stotra*).
In the same way, the mantras must be understood by practitioners in all ritual acts.
If a wise person practices a mantra without recognizing these defects,
success will not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Now, the pacification of defects in mantras:
in that same [text], it is said:
"Those mantras described in various tantras as being defective—such as those that are 'severed' (chinnā) and so forth—"
They all attain perfection through the power of the syllables of the Mātṛkā. || 2 ||
Having encapsulated the mantra—and especially the vidyā—with the letters of the Mātṛkā, one should first recite it one hundred and eight times for the sake of attaining success;
then the mantra, as a great vidyā, shall grant the results as described. || 3 ||
Having encased it with the *mātṛkā* and placed the syllable in the center, one should then form the syllables of the mantra; this is the purification method approved by the Tantras.

Having bound that *yonimudrā* and contracted the foundational lotus (*ādhārapaṅkaja*), one should meditate on the syllables of the mantra arising from it as moving back and forth up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Then, having filled the breath, one should perform *kumbhaka*.
The practitioner of mantra should recite it one thousand times for the pacification of defects in the mantra.
Likewise:
having first cast illusion (māyā) or desire (kāma), or even prosperity (śrī), into these flawed leaves for the sake of freeing them from those defects— || 6 ||
Likewise:
even a wicked mantra is accomplished if it is encapsulated by the *tāra* (the syllable Om);
whatever mantra one may have devotion for, that very mantra is accomplished for him.
Likewise:
"The Praṇava, the Goddess Mātṛkā, and the Hṛllekhā—these are the three nectars.
Through the conjunction of these three nectars, even a corrupted mantra attains success. (8)
Now, regarding the rules for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*):
therein, the derivation of the word *kuṇḍa* is stated in the *Viśvasāra*, as cited in the *Sārāvalī*:
"O Goddess, on the earth (*kau*), a beautiful cavity (*vila*) is seen."

Therefore, the *kuṇḍa* has indeed been described for the benefit of practitioners; that is to say, it is a cavity or pit, distinguished by such features as a very beautiful girdle (*mekhalā*) and the womb (*yoni*). || 1 ||
In that regard, first is the determination of the house;
therein, first is the determination of the ground, as stated in the Gautamīya:
