One should perform the formal acquisition of the ground as far as the sacred precinct extends. || 2 ||
The ground that is white soil is proclaimed to be Brāhmī;
the red soil is Kṣatriyā, and the yellow is proclaimed to be Vaiśyā;
the black soil is Śūdrā—the earth is thus proclaimed to be fourfold.
A Brāhmaṇī brings about the accomplishment of all goals; a Kṣatriyā is considered to bestow sovereignty;
a Vaiśyā produces wealth and grain; but a Śūdrā would be censurable. || 3 ||
In the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*:

"First, one who is an expert in the science of architecture (*vāstuśāstra*) should examine the ground; then he should perform the removal of hidden obstacles (*śalya*) and so forth, or otherwise dig to a human depth. (4)
Having joined the site in the east, the northeast, or even the north,
the mantra-practitioner should, according to the divisions, mentally conceive the pavilion in that direction.
It should be nine cubits in measure, or seven cubits,
or five cubits in measure, square on all sides; however,
in the case of a single fire-pit, it should be five cubits.
It is stated in that very same work: "According to the system of a single pit, another [type of] house measuring five cubits should be made;
that single pit is recommended in the northern part of the house. (7)
For example:
"Then, in the northern direction, one should likewise construct a single quadrangular pit (kuṇḍa);
for the Lakṣahoma, however, one should do so in the middle of the house, as there is no defect [in doing so]."
Likewise, in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
"A wise man should construct a mandala in the northeast corner of the site,
measuring six, twelve, eight, or sixteen cubits on all sides."
It was provided with four gates and adorned with archways and other ornaments.
In the Nibandha:
"On that ground measured in three parts, one should prepare a square altar (vedi) of one cubit (aratni) in height for the sake of the mandala. (10)
Now, as a related topic, the nine pits (*kuṇḍas*):
regarding this, the *Śāradā-tantra* states: "In the pavilion previously described, the wise man [should divide] the area outside the altar into three parts."
Having divided the field, one should designate the directions starting from the east within the central portion.
In the eight directions, there are eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) of beautiful form, arranged in due order.
And likewise, in the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā,
the author describes the eightfold arrangement of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas): "The square, the yoni-shaped, the half-moon, the triangle, and the well-rounded circle."
They are hexagonal, lotus-shaped, and octagonal by name.
(Regarding the types of sacrificial pits, Figure 51:
The pit for the Preceptor (Ācāryakuṇḍa) should be in the center; those for Gaurīpati and Mahendra [should be on the sides].
One should mark out a piece of ground measuring one cubit (hasta) as before.
This sacrificial pit, however, is square on all sides and brings about auspiciousness. || 4 ||
The wise one should divide the square field into five parts;
he should place one part in front, measuring half of a half of the corner.

The knower of mantras should rotate [the cord] by that same measure, and likewise another pair of cords; then he should lay them down so that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) becomes shaped like a womb (yoni).
The wise one, an expert in the tantra, should divide the square field into ten parts;
he should discard one part each at the bottom and at the top.
Then, he should drop a chord-line at the front and, from that measurement, draw a circle.
This beautiful reservoir should be shaped like a half-moon. || 7 ||
According to Bhaṭṭa’s commentary, it is as if an arrow and bow were cast forward in front;
and thus:
"One should cause the string of the bow to fall at the tip, because of its being half the length of the arrow. (8)
When the field has been divided into four parts, one should place a single portion on each of the two sides; then, from that measurement,
the wise man should mark forward and draw three lines to form what is called a triangular *kuṇḍa*.
The wise man should place one part outwards upon the field, which consists of eighteen parts;
by that measurement he should rotate [the cord] to form a circle, which is declared to be the *kuṇḍa*.
One should divide the field into eight parts; by this measurement, one should place a single part on each side of the central line from the middle.
The best of mantra-knowers should draw four fish-designs on both sides;
then he should apply six lines, which is declared to be the hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having divided the square field into eighteen parts,
one should set aside one part on the outside and draw a circle with it.
One should fashion three circles for the pericarp and so forth on the outside;
this is declared to be the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*padmakuṇḍa*), which is enchanting to the eye.
The word "outside" (*bahiḥ*) here refers to the middle; the word *bahiḥ* expresses the sense of the center, as indeclinables have multiple meanings.
The teachers [hold that] it should be [drawn] with *tvādi*;
Bhaṭṭa [holds that] one should draw the circles of the pericarp and so forth, each further out than the last, otherwise there would be an excess in the measurement. || 14 ||
Having divided the square into eight parts, one should draw four circles:
the pericarp and filaments in the center, the petals in the third [circle], and their tips in the fourth; thus Bhaṭṭa says one should fashion the circles. (15)
One should divide the previously mentioned field into twenty-four parts;
having set aside one part on the outside, one should fashion a square. [This is done] by means of the measurement of half and half of the corner of the inner square.
One should fashion it from the corners of the external square;
one should drop eight threads toward each direction according to the rule.
This is indeed declared by those who know the tantras to be the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The depth of the excavation should indeed be equal to the width of the pit. Whatever the form of the pits, such shall be the form of the girdles (mekhalās).
There are three girdles for the pits, which [measure] one fist in size respectively.
Thus have the sacrificial pits been described; next, the sruk and sruva ladles shall be discussed.
The Guru should fashion the *sruva* ladle for the sacrifice according to the method that will be described hereafter, using one of the following:
*śrīparṇī*, *śiṃśapā*, or a milky-sap tree. (18)
Having taken [the cord], one should divide it by thirty-six [parts] to the extent of one cubit; "one cubit" means the length of an arm. || 19 ||
Likewise, Agastya says:
one should indeed fashion the *sruk* ladle for the purpose of oblation according to the measure of one's own arm;
the handle (*daṇḍa*) should consist of twenty parts, and the altar-base (*vedī*) should consist of eight of those parts.
The neck is measured by one part, and the face is measured by seven parts;
the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts of the altar-base (vedī). || 21 ||
The opening should be the size of the neck;
one should fashion a passage in the mouth with the measurement of the little finger for the exit of the clarified butter.
In the center of the altar, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned with one part;
outside of it, one should fashion a pit (avaṭa) on all sides with one part.
Its pit should be circular with three parts, and with half a part [of that] on the outside;
one should fashion petals all around with one part.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be around the mouth and the altar (vedī), measuring half a part on all sides.
At the base and the tip of the staff (daṇḍa), there should be two pot-like ornaments (kumbha), measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively.
The pair of gaṇḍīs should have equal proportions; this is declared to be the width (anāha) of the staff.
The back portion of the altar (vedī) should be six parts in width and shaped like a tortoise.
One should draw the face of a swan, an elephant, or a peacock;
the characteristic of the *sruk* ladle is said to be [the depiction] on the back part of its face.
One should fashion the *sruva* ladle with twenty-four parts;
the measurement of its handle is declared to be twenty-two parts.
With four parts, one should form the swelling [of the head] which holds the honey and ghee;
with two parts, one should draw the shape of a deer's footprint in the mud.
The *gaṇḍī* should be at the base and tip of the handle and adorned with a ring (*kaṅkaṇa*).
Thus has been declared the rule for the *sruva*, in accordance with all the tantras.
[In this context], *gaṇḍī* means the bowl, and *kaṅkaṇa* means the ring.
According to Bhāguri, the word *gaṇḍī* refers to both a bracelet and a water-pot. || 30 ||
In the absence of those two, however, Vasiṣṭha says:

"Then, for the rite of oblation, one should provide a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle upon two beautiful, flawless leaves of the *palāśa* tree, or, if space is limited, upon two leaves of the *aśvattha* tree. (31)
Now, the specific fruits of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*): according to the *Nibandha*,
the square pit is declared to bring about all accomplishments for men.
The Yonikuṇḍa bestows sons; it has the luster of a half-moon and grants auspiciousness.

A triangular pit brings about the destruction of enemies; a circular one is for rites of pacification (śāntika); for acts of cutting (cheda) and killing (māraṇa), the pit should be hexagonal; and a lotus-like pit is said to bestow vision and alleviate disease. It is declared that an eight-sided pit [is for these purposes].
Now, the determination of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the purpose of optional oblations (*kāmya-homa*):
as it is stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
"For the rites of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and likewise for health (*ārogya*), the sacrificial pit is square."
For attraction, it should be a triangle; likewise, for eradication, it should be circular; and for killing, practitioners should always employ a circular [diagram]. (34)
In another tantra:
"The fire-pit for nourishing rites is in the north; for pacifying rites and the like, it is in the west;
for eradication, the pit is in the northwest; and for killing, it should be in the south. (35)
And so it is said:
"For Brahmins, the [shape] should be square; for kings, it is desired to be circular;
for Vaiśyas, it has the appearance of a half-moon; and for Śūdras, it is declared to be triangular. (36)
Some Tantrikas desire that for all [deities] it be a square; O Maheśānī, one should accomplish all rites within a square.
Thus:
The square fire-pit (kuṇḍa) grants everything and is suitable for all types of officiants. || 37 ||
The rule regarding the measurement of the cubit for the construction of houses and other structures is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"Chariots and the like, swings, boats, and even carts..."
It must be made with the measuring finger (mānāṅgula), and never with any other. || 38 ||
Whatever measurements have been mentioned, such as the fist (muṣṭi) or the cubit (aratni),
must be performed by the patron (yajamāna) alone and never by anyone else.
Likewise:
"When the act of measuring has been mentioned but the measurer has not been specified, the sacrificer shall be the one who performs the measurement; such is the conclusion of the learned. (40)
Those who know the tantras understand a cubit (hasta) to be twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula) more [than that].
The measure of a finger (mānāṅgula) is declared to be the length of the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand of the artisan. 41.
In another tantra:
"The middle finger is measured by the transverse span of one's own thumb;
this is the 'thumb-measure' (pramāṇāṅguṣṭha), which is used for all rites according to others. (42)
Furthermore, in the absence of the patron (yajamāna):
one finger-breadth is formed by eight barley grains with their husks removed;
twenty-four such fingers joined together constitute a cubit (hasta) that is not too long. || 43 ||
Furthermore, according to the sequence of finger-breadths (vayaya):
the best [finger] is formed by eight of those barley-corns, the middle by seven barley-corns,
and the smallest is declared by the best of sages to be six barley-corns.
When a thousand oblations are to be offered, one should make the sacrificial pit one cubit in size;
for ten thousand, it should be two cubits, and for a hundred thousand oblations, four cubits.
For six cubits [in length], one hundred thousand oblations (lakṣa) are prescribed; for eight cubits, one million (daśalakṣaka);
and for ten cubits, indeed ten million (koṭi). Thus the measurement of the cubit is established. Beyond ten cubits, there is no sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the fire-oblation (homa) on this earth.
In the *Śāradā*:
"It is recorded as eight karas for ten million [repetitions]"; this should be understood according to the heaviness or lightness of the substance.
And so it is said:
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is prescribed for a *lakṣahoma* (one hundred thousand oblations).
This should also be understood to apply here to offerings of clarified butter (*ājya*), as well as to offerings of honey, ghee, dūrvā grass, karavīra flowers, and so forth.
Likewise:
they declare that for fifty oblations, the pit (kuṇḍa) should measure one fist;
for one hundred oblations, it should be one aratni; and for one thousand oblations, it should be one hasta.
For ten thousand oblations, a pit two cubits [in measure] is prescribed; for one hundred thousand, it is declared to be four cubits;
for one million, six cubits; and for ten million, eight cubits is traditionally taught.
In a pit measuring one cubit, one hundred thousand oblations are ordained.
One should increase it by hand up to ten lakhs. || 48 ||
Regarding the measurement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) starting from two cubits and so forth, it is stated in the Gautamīya: "Whatever diagonal cord (koṇasūtra) there may be of each preceding pit,
that is proclaimed to be the measurement for each subsequent pit."
One should construct a pit measuring two cubits according to the measurement of the ear-ornament (karṇasūtra); in all pits and in every case, one should increase the size according to this rule.

Regarding the specific details concerning the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the Gautamīya Tantra states: "Then the practitioner of mantras should dig the pit according to the injunctions of the scriptures,
carefully avoiding the body and the head-region of the serpent."
A blow to the head results in death; blows to the [other] lumps cause injury to those lumps; a blow to the tail brings about suffering; and a blow to the chest accomplishes all goals. (51)
The determination of the Nāga-head and so forth is as follows:
according to the measurement of the site (vāstu), the body indeed lies constantly on its left side;
having turned over upon the ground every three months, they call that the Vāstunāga.
The perfected ones. || 52 ||
In the months beginning with Bhādrapada, his head should face the north; in the three beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, his head faces the south.
Indeed, in the month of Phālguna and those following, his head faces west; and in the months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, his head faces the north.
The Naga. || 53 ||
The depth of the excavation should be equal to the width of the pit;
if the excavation is deeper than that, there will be illness, and if it is shallower, there will be loss of wealth. (54)
In the case of a curved pit, there is suffering; in one with a broken girdle, death;
in one devoid of a girdle, grief; and in one that is excessive in size, the loss of wealth. || 55 ||
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed without a vulva (yoni) is said to cause the ruin of one's wife;
a pit devoid of a neck-opening is said to cause the destruction of one's offspring. (56)
The first girdle is declared to be *sāttvika*, the second is remembered as *rājasa*, and the third is said to be *tāmasa*; such is the determination regarding the girdles. (57)
The three girdles of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be one fist in width;
their height and length should be known as measuring one and a half finger-breadths.
In a pit measuring one *aratni*, they [the lines] shall consist of three, two, or one finger-breadth;
in a pit measuring one cubit (*hasta*), they shall be four, three, or two finger-breadths.
In a two-cubit pit, those [lines] should be known as measuring sixty-four finger-breadths;
but in a four-cubit [pit], they should be known as measuring eighty-eight finger-breadths.
In a *kuṇḍa* measuring eight *rasas* (sixteen fingers), those [lines] shall be eight, six, and four fingers respectively;
in a *kuṇḍa* measuring eight *vasus* (sixteen fingers), they shall be twelve, eight, and four fingers;
in a *kuṇḍa* measuring ten *hastas*, they shall be fourteen, twelve, and ten fingers.
The wise should understand that the girdles are equal in width and height on all sides. || 62 ||
In front of the *hotṛ* priest, their source is above like an aśvattha leaf;
the inner part of the girdles should have a rim of one finger-breadth all around.

The wise man should gradually increase those [measures] for a pit of one cubit up to ten cubits; for others, the increments are distinct, according to half-finger-breadths. [This applies] from one cubit up to the end of one cubit.
Because it is observed that the navel and the womb have the same measure. || 64 ||
In the *Gautamīya*:

"At the first girdle, one who knows the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should fashion the vulva-shaped lip (*yonikuṇḍoṣṭhī*) in front of the Hotṛ priest; it should be like the lip of an elephant's trunk, possessing all the required features. (65)
The yoni of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one muṣṭi, one aratni, or one hasta is said to possess a length,
width, and height of six, four, and two aṅgulas respectively.
One should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth wide and slightly downward-facing;
in other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase the width of the yoni by one finger-breadth for each successive pit,
and one should also increase the tip of the yoni by the measure of two barley grains.
In the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*:
"The location situated outside the girdles is called the *sthalam* (platform). The stalk (*nāla*) commenced from the square platform is hollow in the middle."
The stalk should be thick at the base and slender at the tip, making it beautiful;
one should fashion it starting from the outer ground, outside the girdle.
Likewise:
starting from the base, the stalk should have a perforation in the middle of the yoni;
the term "with a perforation" (sarandhraka) is connected to both [ends]. || 69 ||
Thus it is stated in the Gautamīya:
"Beginning from the base, the stalk should extend to the middle of the yoni and have a perforation;
its tip is fine and its base is broad, and this stalk is intended to be perforated."
One should make an opening in the middle of the *yoni*; that is designated as the "receiver of the clarified butter" (*ājyagrāhin*).
"From the middle to the very center" is the meaning. || 70 ||
Likewise, Vasiṣṭha says: "Raised at the back like the trunk of an elephant, with a hollow in the middle"—
the meaning is that there is an opening in the middle of the girdle.
And likewise: "A wise man should make a hole above the second girdle, sufficient for placing the enclosing stick (paridhi) between the two girdles. (71)
As for the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*):

the enclosing sticks are a cubit (*bāhu*) in length, straight, with their bark intact, free from blemishes, three in number, and with unbroken tips; according to some, however, there are four in each direction.
The navel of fire-pits measuring one *muṣṭi*, one *ratni*,
or one *hasta* should be raised according to their respective dimensions and provided with four or three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In other pits, the wise man of noble intellect should increase the navel by a sequence of two barley-grains (*yava*) at each step.
In a vulva-shaped pit one should avoid the vulva, and in a lotus-shaped pit, the navel. Having divided the navel-region into three parts, one should fashion the pericarp in the center;
with two outer portions, one should arrange eight petals.

Regarding the rule for the *yoni* in the case of nine *kuṇḍas*, the *Siddhāntaśekhara* states: "In a *kuṇḍa* situated in the directions of Indra (East), Agni (Southeast), and Yama (South), the *yoni* is positioned facing north;
in the others, the *yoni* faces east; and in those of the East and Īśāna (Northeast), it is considered to face north."
In a concise fire-offering ritual,
one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit on all sides and raised by one finger-breadth;
then, taking the sacrificial ladle (sruva) in the right hand, one should take the oblation consisting of the three sweets.
Facing east, one should offer oblations at the end of the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā) with the palm turned downward;
one should append "namas" at the end [of the mantra] and likewise "dviṭha" (phaṭ) at the end of "svāhā. This rule is prescribed for all instances of worship and oblation.
"Ending with 'namas'" refers to the mantras of the Purāṇas. || 73 ||
And likewise, the Brahmapurāṇa states:
"One's own name, preceded by the syllable Oṃ and followed by a salutation,
when proclaimed for all sentient beings, is designated as a mantra."
For example:
"This is water for the feet; Oṃ, obeisance to Āditya.
This is the arghya offering; Oṃ, obeisance to Āditya," and so forth.
Having first mentioned the substances and so forth, one should subsequently mention the deities, according to the scriptural statement beginning with "surān" (the gods).
However, one should not say, "Oṃ, obeisance to Āditya; this is the *pādya* for Sūrya," and so on. || 74 ||

In the Tantric system, this rule does not apply; there may be a variation regarding the *arghya* and other offerings. A wise practitioner, with a mantra purified by the syllable *oṃ* and ending in *svāhā*, should offer oblations at the conclusion of the word *svāhā*, while meditating upon the deity of the mantra.
"By [the mantra] purified by the syllable Oṃ," and so forth; this too refers to the Vedic mantras.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [it being] another mantra.
Therefore, in a mantra that already ends with *svāhā*, another *svāhā* should not be uttered. || 75 ||
Having set aside five finger-breadths of the *sruva* ladle, it is held with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*. As it is said:
"Having left five finger-breadths on the outside, one should hold it with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*. (76)
Where the number of oblations is not mentioned, and where no number is specified for recitations and the like, there should be one hundred and eight or one thousand;
and when the substance of the offering is not specified, sesame and clarified butter are said to be the oblation.
Now, regarding the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*):
it has been stated in the *Somabhujagāvalī*:
"A mantra is not perfected if it is not recited, nor does it bestow fruit if it is not offered in sacrifice."
One does not obtain undesired objects of desire; therefore, one should worship the triad.
Through worship one obtains worship, and through recitation (japa) one attains accomplishment (siddhi)—of this there is no doubt.
And through the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one gains prosperity and finds all accomplishments.
In the *Nīlatantra* as well:
"I shall proclaim the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) by which one attains all goals;
having properly performed the ritual worship, one should carry out the procedure preceded by the offering of oblations (*bali*)."
Then the best of practitioners should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa); a Brāhmaṇa should also perform the bali-offering, the vaiśvadeva, and so forth. 79.

Having sprinkled [the site] with water for the guest-offering (arghya), one should draw three lines according to the rule. Having brought the fire in accordance with the ritual, and having recited the root mantra while saying "Salutation to the flesh-eaters," [one should place it] either in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon the altar (sthaṇḍila).
Or one may spread fire upon the ground with the three *vyāhṛtis*;

having offered oblations three times ending with *svāhā*, one should perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) oblation. Then, having invoked the Goddess with the root mantra, one should offer sixteen oblations.
Having offered oblations, having praised, and having paid homage, one should dismiss [the deity] into the lunar orb.
Regarding the specific procedure for Śyāmā and others:

one should offer eight oblations to the Bhairavas with auspicious sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, proceeding in order from the eastern direction; thereafter, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa).

Now, the procedure for the abbreviated fire-sacrifice (saṃkṣepahomaprayoga): [It is performed] either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), which has been consecrated by the rites of inspection and so forth. || 1 ||
And likewise:
"Beholding with the root mantra, striking with the Śara [weapon], sprinkling with that same [mantra] is taught, and sprinkling thoroughly with the Varma [mantra] is considered [the rule]. (2)
One should draw three lines with their tips pointing eastward and three with their tips pointing northward.
Then, having recited the root mantra and worshipped [the site] with "Oṃ, salutation to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa)," one should draw three lines each pointing eastward and three pointing northward.
Having worshipped Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara in the east-pointing [lines] in clockwise order,
one should worship Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu in the north-pointing [lines].
In the case of Sundarī, however, the application of the *ṣaṭtārī* (six-starred mantra) is used everywhere.
And the *ṣaṭtārī* is: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ brahmaṇe namaḥ*.
In this manner, one should perform the worship in sequence. || 4 ||
Likewise, in the *Brahmasaṃhitā*, in the section on fire-offerings (*homakāṇḍa*):
"Having constructed an altar in the northeast, measuring one cubit in width and height,
one should place the water-pot upon it according to the sequence of the prescribed procedure."
Then, having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rites,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the presence of the deity.

Then, having drawn a hexagon, a circle, and a triangle within the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), an eight-petalled lotus outside of that, and a square with four doors outside of that, one should offer handfuls of flowers upon it with the root mantra; however, in the case of the Sundarī [vidyā], one should use the Bālā [mantra]. || 6 ||
Then, having sprinkled everything with the *praṇava* (Om), one should worship the *yogapīṭha* of the fire.
As follows:
having worshipped the *ādhāraśakti* and the others upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*), [one should worship] in the four corners starting from the southeast with "Oṃ..."
Salutation to Dharma, and likewise to Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
In the directions starting from the east, [salutation] to Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya.
In the center: Oṃ to Ananta; likewise to Padma; and Aṃ to the Akarmaṇḍala.

Salutation to the one whose self consists of twelve digits; *oṃ*, salutation to the lunar maṇḍala whose self consists of sixteen digits; *raṃ*, salutation to the fiery maṇḍala whose self consists of twelve digits.
Then, in the filaments, starting from the east and including the center: *oṃ* salutation to Pītā (the Yellow One); likewise [salutation] to Śvetā (the White One).
Salutation to Aruṇā, salutation to Kṛṣṇā, to Dhūmrā, to Tīvrā, to Sphuliṅginī, to Rucirā, and to Jvālinī.
Then, [the mantra] *raṃ* for the seat of fire (*vahnyāsana*): salutation. || 7 ||

Then, having meditated thus: "Vāgīśvarī, with eyes like blue lotuses, has bathed after her menses and is united with Vāgīśvara," [one should recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ vāgīśvarāya namaḥ* and *oṃ hrīṃ vāgīśvaryai namaḥ*.
Having thus worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), one should bring forth the fire produced from a sun-crystal or the like, or from the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
In the case of the Sundarī-pakṣa, however, one should worship Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī.
In the Gautamīya:
One should fetch fire produced from stone, or that originating from Aruṇi, or that produced in the house of those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), or even that found in the forest. (9)
An offering received from a Brāhmaṇa who maintains no sacred fire yields only half the benefit;
from a mere Kṣatriya, the sacrificial fire grants a fourth part of the fruit;
and from a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the act of Homa becomes fruitless.
Therefore, with every effort, one should collect [the substance] freed from fire.
In another tantra: Or else, having brought fire from the house of a twice-born,
the practitioner should gaze upon it while it is consecrated with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Immediately thereafter, one should invoke Agni with the Astra-mantra;
then, using the root mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ," one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda).
Then: *oṃ* homage to the yoga-pīṭha of Vahni. In the four directions: *oṃ* homage to Vāmā;
likewise to Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā.

Then, having recited the root mantra and worshipped the pit with "Obeisance to the pit of such-and-such deity," one should meditate upon Vāgīśvarī in the form of that specific deity beneath it as being in her menses; then, having brought the fire as prescribed and consecrated it with the rites of inspection and so forth, [one should utter] "raṃ."

Therefore, having extracted the fire and recited the root mantra followed by *huṃ phaṭ kravyādebhyaḥ svāhā*, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*); then, having protected it with the fire-mantra, veiled it with *huṃ*, rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*, and lifted it up with both arms.

Having circled it three times above the vessel, with his knees touching the ground, he should cast this [substance] into the womb of the Goddess facing himself, perceiving it as the seed of Śiva. || 12 ||

Then, having worshipped with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of fire," and having infused consciousness with "Raṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire," one should ignite [the fire] with: "Oṃ cit piṅgala, slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! O Omniscient One, give your command! Svāhā!"
Then, one should worship with the verse: "I revere Agni, the blazing Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations;
the golden-hued, stainless, kindled one whose faces are on every side. (13)

Then, having assigned a name by saying, "O Agni, you are the name of such-and-such deity," one should worship with the *arghya* and other offerings while reciting: "Oṃ, Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here; O Red-eyed One, accomplish all rites, svāhā!
Then, one should offer salutation with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the seven tongues of Agni, beginning with Hiraṇyā."

Oṃ *sahasrārciṣe* hṛdayāya namaḥ, and so forth; obeisance to the six limbs of Agni (*agni-ṣaḍaṅga*). Oṃ to Agni Jātavedas and so forth; obeisance to the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*). Outside of that, Oṃ to the eight powers beginning with Brāhmī (*brāhmyādi-aṣṭaśakti*). Further outside, Oṃ to the eight treasures beginning with Padma (*padmādi-aṣṭanidhi*).
*Namaḥ*; outside of that, *oṃ indrādilokapālebhyo namaḥ*; outside of that, *oṃ vajrādyastrebhyo namaḥ*. || 14 ||
Then, having placed two kuśa leaves, each a span in length, into the midst of the clarified butter,
one should perform the oblation while meditating upon the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* in the left, right, and middle portions respectively.
Having taken clarified butter from the southern part with the *sruva* ladle, one should offer it into the right eye of the fire with the mantra: *oṃ agnaye svāhā*.
Likewise, having taken clarified butter from the northern part, one should offer it into the left eye with the mantra: *oṃ somāya svāhā*.
One should offer oblations.
Then, taking clarified butter from the middle portion, one should offer it into the eye on the forehead of the fire with the mantra: "Oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā."
Again, from the south, having taken clarified butter with "Oṃ namaḥ," [he offers it] into the mouth of the fire with "Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭikṛte svāhā. || 15 ||
Then follows the Mahāvyāhṛti-homa:
*oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*.
*Oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda, bring [the gods] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites.*

One should offer oblations three times with the mantra "svāhā. Then, having worshipped the deity in the fire according to the ritual seat (pīṭha) using the root mantra, one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter into its mouth while reciting the root mantra.
Having meditated upon the identity of oneself with the deity of fire,
one should offer eleven oblations with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
Then, [one should offer] "svāhā" to the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) of the root mantra, in this manner:
"Oṃ svāhā to the deities of the enclosure!

If one is capable, one should offer one oblation for each [deity]. Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the materials prescribed in the respective ritual manual (*kalpa*). || 16 ||

Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra, one should bring one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) into one's own heart by means of the withdrawal gesture (*saṃhāramudrā*), dismiss them with the words "Forgive me," give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and perform the formal closing of the ritual to ensure its flawlessness (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*).
Thus concludes the procedure for the abbreviated oblation (saṃkṣepahoma). || 17 ||
Now, the procedure for the Bṛhaddhoma:
the preceptor, having adorned himself, arrives at the door of the sacrificial pavilion, prepares the general *arghya* offering,
performs the worship of the door, enters the house, and [worships] the deity prescribed in the respective ritual manual.
Having performed worship and constructed an altar measuring one cubit in the northeast direction,
and having placed a water-pot upon it and worshipped it according to one's capacity, one should consecrate the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the rites of inspection and so forth.
This is stated in the *Homakāṇḍa* section of the *Brahmasaṃhitā*: "Having constructed an altar in the northeast, measuring one cubit in both width and height,
one should place the water-pot upon it according to the prescribed sequence."
There, one should worship the deity with ritual services according to the prescribed rules;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the presence of the deity.
Beholding with the root mantra and striking with the arrow-mantra are prescribed;
sprinkling with that same [mantra] and sprinkling again with *darbha* grass using the armor-mantra are prescribed;
having performed protection with the weapon-mantra, one should then commence the consecration (*saṃskāra*).
Then, having recited the root mantra, one should worship the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the formula: "Oṃ, obeisance to the pit. || 2 ||
In the case of Tārā and other deities, however, one should utter the name of each respective deity and say, "Salutation to the fire-pit" (*kuṇḍāya namaḥ*).
Then, one should draw three lines with their tips pointing eastward and three lines with their tips pointing northward in the center of the pit.
Thereafter, everything should be performed according to the sequence prescribed in the *Saṃkṣepahomapaddhati*.
In the Tantra: Or else, having brought fire from the house of a twice-born,
the practitioner should gaze upon it while it is consecrated with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Immediately thereafter, one should invoke Agni with the Astra-mantra;
then, using the root mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*).

Then, having consecrated the fire through the rites of inspection and so forth, and having meditated upon the unification of the terrestrial fire with the digestive fire (*audarya*) and the lunar fire (*vaindava*), one should bestow consciousness upon the fire by saying, "I invoke the consciousness of fire (*raṃ*)," and then consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the syllable *oṃ*.

Having rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenumudrā*, sprinkled it while reciting *phaṭ*, and veiled it with *hūṃ*, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting "Oṃ *raṃ* obeisance to the form of fire (*vahnimūrti*"); then, having circled it three times above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should remain with the knees touching the ground while uttering the *praṇava*.

With the thought that it is the seed of Śiva, one should cast this [seed] into the womb of the Goddess facing oneself. Then, having offered water for rinsing the mouth and other items to Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī, one should meditate upon the deity in the form of Fire held within the womb.
Afterwards, for the protection of the fetus, one should tie a darbha-grass bracelet.
One should kindle the fire with the mantra: "O Citpiṅgala, slay, slay! Cook, cook! Burn, burn! O Omniscient One, give your command, svāhā! (4)
Then, with palms joined in reverence:
"Oṃ, I pay homage to Agni, the blazing one, the Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations;
he who is golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and facing in all directions."
With this [verse], one should worship the fire. || 5 ||
Then, one should perform the placement of the tongues of fire (*vahner jihvānyāsa*) upon one's own body as follows:
at the *liṅga*, "Obeisance to Sarayū, the golden one" (*sarayūṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*).
Pāyau: Śarayūṃ, obeisance to Kanakā.
Mūrdhni: Śarayūṃ, obeisance to Raktā. Vaktre: Varayūṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā.
To the nose, *larayūṃ*, obeisance to Suprabhā; to the eyes, *rarayūṃ*, obeisance to Bahurūpā;
to all the limbs, *yarayūṃ*, obeisance to Atiraktā.
These [are for use] in the ritual of the sattvic sacrifice. || 6 ||

In rites for desired objects (*kāmyakarman*), however, together with the previously mentioned seed-syllable (*bīja*), [the flames] are Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, Bhadralohitā, Rohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā; these belong to the *rājasa* [nature]. In cruel rites (*krūrakarman*), however, together with the aforementioned seed-syllable, they are Viśvamūrtti and Sphuliṅginī.
Smoky-colored, swift as thought, red, formidable, black, and dark—this is the sequence of the Nyāsa.
It should be understood that everywhere it is to be performed according to the previous method, through the application of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the differentiation of ritual actions. || 7 ||

And so it is said in the Śāradā-tilaka: "In the genitals, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, [the letters] from *sa* to *ya*, joined with *vahni* (ra), *yārghīśa* (ha), and accompanied by the bindu, are to be placed everywhere."
The mantras of the fires for the tongues have been fully declared by the teachers of the seventeen [traditions].
Then, the placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) is as follows:
*sahasrārciṣe* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *svastipūrṇāya* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; [and] *dhūmavyāpine* [to the two ring fingers].
With the two ring fingers: *huṃ* to Saptajihva; with the two little fingers: *vauṣaṭ* to Dhanurdhara; with the palms and backs of the hands: *phaṭ*.
Likewise, for the heart and other limbs: *sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth. (9)
Then follows the ritual placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*), as follows:
on the head, *oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ*; on the right shoulder, *oṃ agnaye saptajihvāya namaḥ*; on the right side, *oṃ agnaye havyavāhanāya namaḥ*; on the right hip...

Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Aśvodaraja, on the penis; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Vaiśvānara, on the left hip; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Kaumāratejas, on the left side; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Viśvamukha, on the left shoulder; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Devamukha, on the left shoulder.
In all cases, the syllable *praṇava* comes first.
And so it is said:
"Then the preceptor should assign the eight forms of Jātavedas upon the head,
the two shoulders, the two sides, the two hips, the two sides of the waist, and the two upper arms."
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and he known as Havyavāhana;
another is named Aśvodaraja, and again the one called Vaiśvānara;
Kaumāratejas, Viśvamukha, and he remembered as Devamukha.
The forms of Fire (Vahni-mūrti) consist of Tārā and the others beginning with Agni-pada, ending with the word "namas. || 11 ||
Then, having prepared the seat for Fire with the mantra "Raṃ, obeisance to the seat of Fire," one should contemplate the Form there:
the beloved Śakti, holding aloft a svastika and the gesture of fearlessness with her long arms.
One should meditate upon Fire, which has the luster of the Japā flower, is seated upon a lotus, possesses three eyes, wears matted locks bound in a topknot, and is adorned with a crown. 12.
Then, having sprinkled the girdles with pure water by means of the young girl,
he should wrap them three times each around the girdle, covering the base with the tips of *darbha* grass that are hollow in the middle.
Then, having placed the enclosing sticks (paridhi) in the directions excluding the east, the deities beginning with Brahmā should be worshipped there in a clockwise direction. || 13 ||
Having again meditated upon the fire, one should invoke it onto that seat with this mantra and worship it with perfumes and other offerings:
*oṃ vaiśvānara jātaveda ihāvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmaṇi sādhaya*.

With "Svāhā, this is the water for the feet; O Agni, obeisance," and so forth in sequence, one should worship Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā on the girdle. In the center of the hexagon, [one worships] Sarayū with "Obeisance to Hiraṇyā" (Ṣarayūṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ) and [Sarayū] with "Obeisance to Kanakā" (Ṣarayūṃ kanakāyai).
Homage to Śarayū, the Red One; homage to Varayū, the Black One;
homage to Larayū, the Radiant One; homage to Rarayū, the Multiformed One; homage to Yarayū, the Exceedingly Red One.
The presiding deities of these [tongues] are stated in another tantra:
"The immortals (amartyas), ancestors (pitṛs), gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, piśācas,
and rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities of the seven tongues."
Thus, for the rites of desire (kāmya), [the mantra is] "O Sarayū, obeisance to Padmarāga," and so forth;
for the rites of wrath (krūra), [it is] "O Sarayū, obeisance to Viśvamūrti," and so forth. || 14 ||
As it says in the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*:
"Hiraṇyā, possessing the luster of sevenfold gold, is situated in the direction of the Trident-bearer (the North);
Kanakā, with the color of lapis lazuli, is established in the eastern direction."
Resembling the rising sun, the tongue is red and situated in the fire;
resembling black and blue clouds, she is stationed in the south-western direction;
and Suprabhā, with the luster of a ruby, is stationed in the western direction.
Exceedingly red with the luster of the Javā flower, she is situated in the northern direction;
she is manifold in form as described, stationed in the south and the north.

Then, in the filaments— at the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions— one should perform the placement [of mantras]: *oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā*,
*oṃ uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ dhūmavyāpine kavacāya huṃ*, *oṃ*.
To the seven-tongued one with three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *oṃ* to the bow-wielder, the weapon, *phaṭ*.
Then, on the petals starting from the east: *oṃ* obeisance to Agni Jātavedas; *oṃ* obeisance to Agni Saptajihva; *oṃ* obeisance to Agni Havyavāhana; *oṃ* obeisance to Agni Aśvodaraja.
*Namaḥ*, *oṃ agnaye vaiśvānarāya namaḥ*, *oṃ agnaye kaumāratejase namaḥ*,

*oṃ agnaye viśvamukhāya namaḥ*, *oṃ agnaye devamukhāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped the forms of Agni, who holds the *śakti* and the *svastika*, [one should worship] the world-protectors (*lokapālān*).
One should worship [them] in their respective directions. || 16 ||
Then, having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with both hands and turned them face downwards,

having heated them three times in the fire, and having taken *darbha* grass, having purified their tips, bases, and middles in due order, one should sprinkle them again with water using the right hand.
Having heated the darbha grass over the fire and cast it into the flames, he should place it within the kuśa grass on his own right side. || 17 ||

Then, having brought the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) toward oneself and purified it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, one should place the clarified butter into it and perform the respective purificatory rites such as *vīkṣaṇa* and so forth.
Then, having removed a coal from the north-western side, one should place the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) upon it with the mantra "namaḥ".
Then, having ignited a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter, one should deposit [the vessel] with this [mantra].

Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) over the clarified butter with a pair of blazing darbha blades while reciting the mantra "namaḥ," one should cast that pair of darbha blades into the fire. || 19 ||
Then, having shown burning darbha grass over the clarified butter while reciting the mantra "phaṭ," one should cast them into the fire.
Then, taking some clarified butter and again joining a charcoal back into the fire, one should touch water.

Holding two *darbha* blades, each the length of a span (*prādeśa*), with the thumb and ring finger of the right hand turned downwards and positioned above [the vessel], one should purify the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with the *astra* mantra; then, with the mantra "Namaḥ," one should perform the mixing of the liquid facing oneself using those two *kuśa* blades. || 20 ||
Then, having inserted a pair of darbha blades with a knot between them to the measure of a span (prādeśa),
one should divide them into two parts and contemplate them as the bright and dark fortnights.
Then, having meditated upon the iḍā nāḍī in the left, the piṅgalā in the right, and the suṣumnā in the middle;
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa). || 21 ||
For example:
with the mantra *namaḥ*, taking clarified butter from the southern part with the *sruva* ladle, one should offer it into the right eye of the fire with the mantra *oṃ agnaye svāhā*.
Similarly, taking clarified butter from the left side, one should offer it into the left eye of the fire with "Oṃ somāya svāhā.
Then, taking clarified butter from the middle part, one should offer it into the forehead-eye of the fire with "Oṃ agnīṣomābhyām..."
One should offer with "svāhā.
Then, taking clarified butter from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the mantra "namaḥ," one should offer it into the mouth of the fire with "oṃ agnaye sviṣṭikṛte svāhā."
In all cases, the remnants of the oblations are collected in another vessel. || 22 ||
Then follows the Mahāvyāhṛti-homa:
*oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*.
Then: *O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites.*
Having offered oblations three times with the word "svāhā," one should perform for the fire the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna). || 23 ||

Namely: the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), the birth-rite (jātakarma), the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa), the first outing (niṣkramaṇa), the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), and the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa).
The Upanayana, the Mahāvrata, the Upa-niṣad-bath, the Godāna, and that called Udvāha;
for cruel rites, ending with Māraṇa.
And so it is said:
In auspicious rites, the rites should end with marriage; in cruel rites, they should end with death.
In that regard, the sequence is as follows:
"Oṃ, I accomplish the impregnation (garbhādhāna) of Agni; svāhā!"—with this, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) in order for each respective rite. || 25 ||
In the case of Sundarī, however, one should offer each oblation with the mantra: "Oṃ, I prepare the conception for Agni; Aiṃ, obeisance. This is what is set forth in the Kalpasūtra. || 26 ||
At the naming ceremony, however, having worshipped Mūladevī for the purpose of bestowing that name,
one should likewise offer three oblations with the fifth Bāṇa-mantra. Immediately thereafter, one should perform the naming with the hymn "Kāmāgni" and the name "Hutāśana."
Then, having worshipped the two parents of the fire (Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī) and having united them with one's own self,
one should offer five fuel-sticks— held at their roots, tips, and middles and soaked in ghee— while meditating upon them mentally. || 27 ||

Then, having offered one oblation each to the tongues, limbs, and forms previously mentioned of the Fire, and having taken clarified butter four times with the *sruva* ladle and placed it in the *sruc* offering-spoon, and having covered it with the *sruva*, rising up, [he recites]: "Oṃ Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring hither [the gods]; O red-eyed one, [perform] all rites."
One should offer oblations with this mantra: "Sādhaya svāhā! Vauṣaṭ! || 28 ||
Then, one should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Vighneśvara as follows:
oṃ svāhā, oṃ śīṃ svāhā, oṃ śīṃ hrīṃ svāhā, oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ.
Svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada svāhā!
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, [grant success] to all people,
svāhā! Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ, to Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, [grant success] to all people for me.
"Bring under control, svāhā!
And likewise in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"O Goddess, with these ten [syllables] beginning with Tārā, joined one after another..."
One who belongs to the Gāṇapatya lineage should first offer ten oblations with the mantra of Manu.
Then, having worshipped the seat of the deity within the fire and contemplated her in the form of fire, one should worship her with the fivefold offerings and so forth. || 30 ||
In the case of Sundarī, however, having performed worship with the Ṣaḍānana mantra and the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra),

[one should offer] OṂ HRĪṂ ŚRĪṂ to the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of the circle of Yoginīs— the most secret of all secrets, the lineage of the most hidden oral tradition, O Kulakaulinī— O Womb, O Mystery, O Supreme Mystery, O Ultimate Mystery!
The distinction is that one thinks, "I am worshipping. || 31 ||
However, in the case of Tārā and others, one should worship Brāhmī and the rest, Lakṣmī and the rest, Indrā and the rest, and Vajrā and the rest; this is the distinction. || 32 ||
Then, one should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter into the mouth of the fire with the root mantra.
Then, having meditated upon the oneness of the fire, the deity, and oneself, one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
Then, one should offer individual oblations for each of the deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇadevatās) of that respective deity.
Thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the specific substances prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa) as intended.
It is as follows:
One should offer oblations on the tongue named Bahurūpā for all rites;
for she is Sāvitrī, known as Bahurūpikā, who [bestows] all accomplishments.
In the *Yāmala*: "In the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is the one named Hiraṇyā for the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*);
the one named Kanakā for immobilization (*stambhana*) and so forth; and the one named Raktā likewise for causing enmity (*dveṣaṇa*)."
The one named Kṛṣṇā is praised for killing; Suprabhā is for rites of pacification (śāntika);
the one called Atiraktā is for eradication (uccāṭana); and Bahurūpā bestows excellent accomplishment (siddhi).
Oṃ bhūr! To Agni, to the Earth, and to the Great One, svāhā! Oṃ bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu, to the Atmosphere, and to the Sky, and to the Great One, svāhā!
Oṃ svaḥ! To the Moon, to the Constellations, to the Directions, and to the Great One, svāhā!
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā to the Moon, to the constellations, to the directions, and to the Great One.
Regarding the rule for the fingers in a *kāmya* (optional) homa:
a person should perform oblations for the sake of pacification (*śānti*) by joining the index finger and the thumb;
for burning fevers and malevolent spells (*abhicāra*), one should use the mudrā of the ring finger and the thumb.
It is highly praised for inciting enmity, for eradication, and indeed for killing;
by means of the forefinger and the middle finger, there shall be the pacification of slaughter.
Likewise, it pertains to the body, intelligence, beauty, as well as states such as political wisdom and nourishment.
All acts of attraction, even those performed from afar,
indeed come to pass instantly through the joining of the index finger and the ring finger;
likewise for enchantment, subjugation, and the increase of affection.
All this is accomplished by means of the ring finger and the little finger;
likewise, enchantment, attraction, agitation,
and expulsion are achieved effortlessly through the union of the little finger, the middle finger, and the thumb.

Through oblations performed according to the prescribed rules, as well as through the application of ritual substances, and by the employment of mudrās and mantras, all mantras attain success. || 37 ||
Then, having placed the oblation materials into the *sruc* with the *sruva*, having covered them with that [ladle], and having positioned both near the navel,
one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantra beginning with "itaḥ pūrvam" and the root mantra, using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
Having withdrawn [the fire] into oneself and having again offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis,
one should offer a single oblation each to the tongues, limbs, and forms of Agni.

Then, as before, having sprinkled water upon the girdle (mekhalā) and joined the fire with oneself by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should cast the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) along with the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*) into the fire.
However, the specific rule for occasional rites (*naimittika-karma*) is that one should burn these [sticks].
One should not burn [the offerings] during the obligatory rite (*nitya-karma*).
Thus it is said in the *Śāradā*:
"The practitioner of mantra should burn them in the occasional rite (*naimittika*), but he should not burn these in the obligatory rite. (39)
Then one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
And so it is said in the *Jñānamālā*: "One should give ten thousand gold pieces for [the practice of] a hundred thousand [repetitions], and ten gold pieces for a hundred thousand."
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given just as it is in the case of a fire-oblation;
in its absence, the fee is to be understood as that which causes satisfaction to the Guru. || 40 ||
If it is the *homa* as a constituent part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), then after the *homa* for the principal deity and the deities of the retinue (*āvaraṇadevatā*),
one should perform one thousand and eight oblations for the deity with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, or with substances prescribed by the ritual manual (*kalpa*).
Or one should offer a hundred oblations. || 41 ||
Then, having brought the disciple— who has thoroughly cleansed his teeth and bathed— to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
and having beheld him with divine vision, the Guru, having united that [disciple's] consciousness within himself,
should perform the purification of the paths (adhvaviśodhana).
For example: touching the disciple’s foot with a bunch of *kuśa* grass, one should offer eight oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, reciting: *oṃ śodhayāmi kalādhvānaṃ svāhā*.
Having thus touched the anus (*pāyu*): *oṃ śodhayāmi tattvādhvānaṃ svāhā*.
Having touched the navel: *oṃ śodhayāmi bhuvanādhvānaṃ svāhā*.
Having touched the heart: *śodhayāmi varṇādhvanaṃ svāhā*.
Touching the forehead: *oṃ śodhayāmi padādhvānaṃ svāhā*.
Touching the head: *oṃ śodhayāmi mantrādhvānaṃ svāhā*.
In all cases, one should offer eight oblations.
Having thus withdrawn [the universe] sequentially into that Supreme Śiva, one should then generate it again in due order through the path of emanation by means of the respective oblations.
It is as follows:

The path of mantras [leads to] the path of words; the path of words [leads to] the path of phonemes; the path of phonemes [leads to] the path of worlds; the path of worlds [leads to] the path of principles; and the path of principles [leads to] the path of kalās.
One should offer oblations in this sequential order.
Then, beholding that disciple with divine vision, one should project the consciousness residing within oneself into the disciple.
Thereafter, having completed the ritual acts such as the offering of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *sruc* ladle, [one proceeds] according to the previously mentioned sequence.
One should cause the initiation (dīkṣā) to be performed. Thus ends the manual for the Great Homa (vṛhaddhomapaddhati). 42.
Now, the measurement of the substances for the oblation:
one *karṣa* of clarified butter is prescribed for the oblation, and one *śukti* of milk is likewise recorded;
the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are declared by the wise to be equal in measure to those.

An equal amount of honey, milk, and boiled rice is declared to be the measure of one *akṣa*; curd should be the measure of one *prasṛti*; parched grain (*lāja*) should be commensurate with a handful; flattened grain (*pṛthuka*) should be of that same measure, and likewise, the *śakti* grains are said to be so.

The measure for jaggery should be half a pala; sugar is likewise prescribed as such. The measure for the sacrificial porridge (caru) should be half a mouthful; sugarcane is prescribed up to the size of a joint.
One should prepare each leaf and flower, as well as the cakes, in this same manner.
They know that the plantain fruit and the orange are each offered as a single unit;
the citron is divided into four pieces, and the jackfruit is cut into ten. (43)
The wise know that coconuts should be cut into eight pieces;
the wood-apple fruit is made into three parts, and the wood-apple is cut into two.
For the fire-oblation, the cucumber fruit is said to be cut into three pieces.
Other fruits should be unbroken; the fuel sticks should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, and guḍūcī should be four finger-breadths long. Rice should be one handful in measure, as should mung beans, black gram, and barley.
The rice grains should be half that amount; the kodrava grains should be measured by a handful (muṣṭi).
The wheat and red lotuses are prescribed at the measure of a handful.
The sesame seeds should be the size of a culluka, and the mustard seeds should be of that same measure.
Salt should be the measure of a śukti, and black peppers twenty in number;
*pura* (guggulu) should be the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*), and asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*) is recorded as being equal to that.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron—each the size of a tamarind seed—have been prescribed by the teachers. (43-ka)
The preceptor should meditate on Vaiśvānara as standing during the oblations of kindled fuel,
as reclining during the oblations of clarified butter, and as seated during all other matters.
A wise man should offer oblations into the interior of the fire in all ritual acts.
It is taught that if an oblation is offered into the ear, disease will arise; if into the eye, blindness is proclaimed;
if into the nose, mental anguish; and if into the head, there is doubt regarding wealth. (45)
Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, here is the nose;
where there is a small flame, that is the eye; where there are embers, there is the head;
and where the blazing flame is, that is the tongue of Jātavedas (the fire-god). || 46 ||
Resembling gold, vermilion, the morning sun, saffron, and honey—
such is proclaimed to be the auspicious color of Suvarṇaretas.
A fire that brings auspiciousness has a sound like that of a kettledrum, a rain-cloud, or a lordly elephant;
it resembles the fragrance of jasmine, campaka, punnāga, pāṭala, and yūthikā flowers; and it is like the scent of the padma, indīvara, and kahlāra lotuses, as well as ghee and guggulu resin.
The experts in the Tantras have stated that the auspicious fragrance belongs to the purifier (fire). || 48 ||
The flames of the fire, free from flickering, moving clockwise, and resembling umbrellas, bestow happiness upon the sacrificer and especially upon his kingdom. (49)
Smoke as white as jasmine or a conch is declared to bring auspiciousness for the fire;
black smoke, the color of a black path, shall destroy the sacrificer.
Smoke resembling the sound of a crow swiftly destroys the kingdom.
A sound from fire that resembles its own natural resonance brings about total destruction;
a foul odor from the sacrificial fire will bring suffering to the sacrificer. (50)

A severed or circular crest (śikhā) brings about death and the depletion of wealth. Smoke resembling the wings of a parrot or having a luster like that of a pigeon causes the loss of horses and cattle before long.
In the event of such defects, for the sake of expiation,
the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
Thus ends the section on fire-offerings (*homa*).
Now, the definition of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) as stated in the *Śāradā*:
"I shall now correctly explain the definition of the six rites in this tantra."
In accordance with all tantras, it bestows the accomplishment of the fruits of practice. || 1 ||
The wise proclaim the six rites (ṣatkarma) as ending with killing: pacification, subjugation, immobilization, then inciting enmity, expulsion, and finally, killing. || 2 ||
The removal of diseases, malevolent spells, seizures, and so forth is declared to be *śānti* (pacification).
Bringing all people under one's influence is declared to be *vaśya* (subjugation). (3)
The obstruction of the activity of all [beings] is declared to be "stambhana" (paralysis);
causing mutual hatred among those who are affectionate is considered "vidveṣaṇa" (inciting enmity). || 4 ||
Uccāṭana is proclaimed to be the expulsion from one's own country and so forth;
Māraṇa is declared to be the taking away of the life-force of living beings.
One should accomplish the rites after having understood one's own deity, as well as the directions, time, and other factors. || 5 ||
Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī are declared to be the deities of the six rites; one should worship them at the beginning of each rite in their respective order.

Kālī and Bhadrakālī [are assigned to the intermediate directions]. The directions are considered to belong to Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni. Starting from sunrise, they correspond in sequence to ten *ghaṭikās*.
The seasons, beginning with spring, occur day after day;
they are known as spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season. (7)
In this context, the *ghaṭikās* are *daṇḍas*. Alternatively: midnight is the autumn season (*śaratkāla*), and the dawn is the winter (*hemanta*);
the forenoon (*pūrvāhna*) would be spring (*vasanta*), and midday (*madhyāhna*) is indeed summer (*grīṣma*).
The rainy season is the afternoon; the winter is said to be the evening.
Alternatively:
"At the conjunction of the *ūṣā* [dawn], it is winter; at daybreak, the arrival of the cool season (*śiśira*);
at half a watch, it would be spring; and at the arrival of midday, summer."
And in the fourth watch, when the sun has set, the period known as the rains and autumn [occurs]. || 9 ||

The winter season is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), spring for rites of subjugation (vaśya); the cool season (śiśira) is to be known for rites of immobilization (stambhana), and summer is said to be for rites of creating enmity (vidveṣa). The rainy season is to be known for rites of eradication (uccāṭana), and autumn for rites of killing (māraṇa).
Now, the rule for lunar days: The fifth, second, third, and likewise the seventh [lunar days],
when conjoined with the weekdays of Mercury (Budha) and Jupiter (Ijya), are to be known as suitable for rites of pacification (śāntikarma).
The sixth, the fourth, and the thirteenth lunar days joined with Jupiter and the Moon;
the ninth, as well as the eighth and the ninth, are recommended for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika);
likewise, the tenth and the eleventh, when conjoined with Sunday or Friday.
For the rite of attraction, the new moon, the ninth day,
the first day of the lunar fortnight, and the full moon when the sun is weak should be known as the appropriate times for the act of hatred.
Likewise, the fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight, as well as Sundays,
are auspicious lunar days for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), especially during the evening twilight (pradoṣa).
The fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight, as well as the new moon day,
when joined with the days of Saturn and Mars, are recommended for rites of killing.
The fifth lunar day joined with Wednesday or Monday, the tenth white (waxing) lunar day,
and the full moon— these are to be known as the auspicious dates for the rite of immobilization (stambhana).

One should perform auspicious deeds when there is the rising of auspicious planets and during auspicious ascendants; one should perform acts of killing during the Riktā lunar days, on a Sunday, and during the Mṛtyu yoga.
In the Cāmuṇḍā Tantra:
one should recite facing east for subjugation (vaśya), facing south for malevolent rites (abhicāraka);
one should know that facing west results in immobilization (stambhana), and facing north brings about pacification (śāntika). || 16 ||
Furthermore, attraction is in the southeast; likewise, killing is in the southwest.
Uprooting is in the northwest, while the northeast bestows liberation.
Similarly, for malevolent sorcery (abhicāra), the ground should be sloped toward the south. 17.
The garment is said to be red, and the crown is remembered as red;
the ornaments are made of copper, and with the left hand, one performs the worship and other rites.
For the purpose of killing, a rope made specifically from human sinew is prescribed;
or, having fashioned a rosary from the tooth of a donkey that died in battle,
it should be recited by one desiring the slaughter of enemies.

For the rite of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should recite [the mantra] using broken elephant-tusk jewels strung on a thread made from the hair of the person to be acted upon. Having prepared a rosary from the teeth of a horse, one should recite it while gazing at it for the rites of inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*).
Now, the description of the postures and so forth:
The wise declare that the postures are called Padma (Lotus), Svastika, Vikaṭa, Kukkuta (Cock), Vajra, and Bhadraka. (20)
Having assumed the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) by placing the hands between the knees and the thighs and resting them on the ground, one establishes the *kukkuṭāsana* situated in the void;
other [postures] are to be described. 21.

The six mudrās are to be known in sequence as those called the lotus, the noose, and the mace; and those named the pestle, the thunderbolt, and the sword, for the rites of pacification and so forth. (22)
Water is prescribed for pacification (śānti) in the Moon [mandala]; fire is declared for subjugation (vaśya);
earth is praised for immobilization (stambhana); space is proclaimed for causing enmity (vidveṣa);
wind is remembered for eradication (uccāṭana), and again, fire is remembered for killing (māraṇa). || 23 ||
During the respective emergence of each element, the practitioner of firm resolve, joined with the corresponding mandala,
should perform that specific rite.
The syllables of the Moon, Water, Earth, Sky, Wind, and Fire are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for the six rites (*ṣatkarma*), respectively. (25)
Grathana, vidarbha, sampuṭa, rodhana, yoga, and pallava— these are the arrangements for the six types of ritual actions.
One should separate the letters of the name with the mantra according to the prescribed rule;
one should know that this method of stringing [the letters] is highly commended for rites of pacification (śāntika).

One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between two syllables of the mantra; this is to be known as *vidarbha* by practitioners for the rite of subjugation.
The mantra should be at the beginning and at the end of the name; this is known as the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa).
This is declared by those who know the mantras to be recommended for the rite of immobilization (stambhana).

The mantra should be placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name; this is considered "obstruction" (rodhana), and it is praised as the most excellent method among the rites for inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa).
The name should be at the end of the mantra; this yoga is considered for expulsion (uccāṭana).
The mantra should be at the end of the name; this pallava is considered for killing (māraṇa). || 31 ||
White, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored are proclaimed as the colors of the deities mentioned in the mantras for the six types of ritual actions.
The substances for writing mantras are sandalwood, gorocana, turmeric, house-soot,
charcoal from a funeral pyre, the eight poisons used for killing,
the fire of a hawk's nest, salt, bile, and the juice of the *dhustūra* plant is auspicious.
House-soot, the three pungents, and the eight poisons are thus declared.
Having correctly understood the mudrās of Time and the other [deities], the wise one should employ the six rites for the sake of attaining the results as described. (34)
In the Kulārṇava:
"Vaṣaṭ is prescribed for expulsion (uccāṭana), and Hūṃ Phaṭ at the end for killing (māraṇa);
Namaḥ is prescribed for immobilization (stambhana), and Svāhā for rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika). (35)
One should employ "svāhā" at the end of the mantra during the fire-oblation (homa) and the satiation (tarpaṇa), and "namaḥ" during the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship (pūjana);
the practitioner should apply these according to the established rule at the time of recitation (japa).
This is the meaning.
Having joined these respective ritual acts at the end of the mantra during the time of recitation (*japa*), one should recite the mantra.
This rule does not apply to fire offerings (*homa*) and the like;
thus some say, "In *homa*, [this] is not [the case]."
That is not so;
one should recite "svāhā" and "namaḥ" during the fire-rite (agnikārya), and likewise in all acts of worship.

One should employ *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* in sequence for the rites of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśa*), hatred (*dveṣa*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*).
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), torment (*santāpa*), and fever (*jvara*), *svāhā* is prescribed.
The wise should employ *namaḥ* for the pacification of anger, for tranquility, and for bestowing affection;
*vauṣaṭ* for enchantment, stimulation, nourishment, and the conquest of death;
and *huṃ* for the destruction of affection, as well as for killing and cutting.

In rites of eradication (uccāṭana) and inciting enmity (vidveṣa), *vauṣaṭ* is used; in the performance of paralysis (stambhana), *vaṣaṭ* is used. In matters concerning the kindling of mantras and regarding gain or loss, *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed.
Because of this specific statement, this same rule applies even in the case of fire-offerings (*homa*). || 36 ||
Regarding the rules for vessels and other materials when writing mantras for rites such as *śāntika* (pacification), it is stated in that very [text]:
"For *śāntika*, [use] silver or copper; for *vaśyaka* (subjugation), birch bark;
for all purposes, gold; and for *krūra* (cruel) rites, the shroud of a corpse. (37)
The three fragrances are prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), while the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are for subjugation (vaśyaka).
For all activities, there should be eight fragrances, and for fierce rites (krūra), the eight poisons.

For rites of pacification (*śāntika*), the pen should be made of *dūrvā* grass; for subjugation (*vaśya*) and similar rites, it should be a peacock’s tail feather. All rites may be performed with gold, but for cruel rites, it should be a crow’s tail feather.
In houses there should be the Śāṅkara [mudrā], and the Caṇkā [mudrā] must be in the house; all [mudrās] are in the temple, and the Krūra-karma [mudrā] is in the cremation ground.
Now, the arising of the elements:
the movement of earth is downward like a staff; that of both its layers is also [downward];
that of water is upward; and that of fire is upward; while that of wind is horizontal.
The movement [of the breath] through the center of the sky is known as the arising of the elements.
Upon the arising of the earth, the knower of the Self should perform the rites of immobilization and subjugation;
during the time of water and fire, one should perform the rites of pacification and nourishment.
The Maruts [are] for killing and so forth, as well as for the expulsion of adversaries;
they are praised for the destruction of poison and the like, and at the rising of the sky. (41)
Now, the mandalas of the elements: that of space is circular, marked with six dots;
that of the wind is triangular, endowed with a svastika; that of fire is joined with a half-moon.
The wise know that the mandalas are a lotus for water, a square with a vajra for earth, and they have the same luster as their respective elements;
they say they are colored by their own colors and also surrounded by their own names.
The sky is clear, the wind is black, fire is red, water is transparent, and the earth is yellow, and so forth. || 43 ||
Another ritual application is stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, accompanied by meditation and ritual placement (*nyāsa*),
for the purpose of pacifying defects in the ritual procedure and as a means for self-protection."
If he does not obtain the fruit [of his labor], he shall incur the curse of the deities.
As for the statement:

"One should not perform the rite of killing; if one should perform it, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times," that refers specifically to the performance of an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*).
Now, regarding the hymns and armor-protective mantras (*kavaca*) in the Vārāhī-tantra: having first recited the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), one should recite the hymn or the *saṃhitā*.
"And one should place the Praṇava at the beginning," so said the Primeval Being.
Thus it should be understood in all cases; otherwise, it would be fruitless. (45)
Now, first, the hymn to Bhuvaneśvarī; the Lord said:
Now [I shall describe] her who consists of bliss, who is directly the very nature of the Śabdabrahman.
I praise Ambikā, the cause of the universe, for the sake of attaining all perfections.
Having praised Speech, the primordial mother of the lotus-born Brahmā, the bestower of bodies upon Viṣṇu and Śiva, and the cause of the creation,
maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds;
O Mother, I purify you.

O Daughter of the Mountain King, you alone are indeed the cause of the possession of power by the God who is the enemy of Manmatha, even though he has assumed the forms of earth, water, fire, the best of winds, the Hotṛ priest, the moon, and the sun.
O Mother, I understand that very reason for the preeminence of the triple-streamed river, worshipped by all the gods:
it is because she is constantly purified by the pollen of the lotus-feet of Śambhu within his matted locks.
That which is a transformation. || 4 ||
The lord of the night-lilies gladdens the lily, and the sun gladdens the lotus, but neither can gladden the other;
thus, each sovereign rules over the delight of only one. You, however, cause the entire universe to rejoice.
By one's own vision. || 5 ||
Even now you possess the fresh youth of all the worlds;
though the daughter of the King of Mountains, you are exceedingly tender.
Even as a mother, you have not been seen by the three [gods]; O Gaurī, you are to be meditated upon, yet you are not on the path of the mind.
You are established. || 6 ||
Having attained after a long time this birth among humans which is so difficult to obtain, and having further acquired proficiency in their own senses,
those who do not worship you, O Mother of the worlds, are like those who have climbed to the very top of a ladder only to let it fall.
They fall again. || 7 ||
O Bhavānī, those who, being full of longing, worship you with sandalwood paste mixed with camphor powder and cool water, and with flowers of exquisite fragrance— [they indeed attain their desires].
Indeed, they are renowned as the ground of all worlds without exception. || 8 ||
Having entered the central position in the first lotus, resembling a sleeping serpent-king, she fashioned the universe; then,
bearing the shimmering grace of a circle of lightning-streaks, she burst open five lotuses.
Forbearing. || 9 ||

O Mother, Consort of Maheśvara, those whose bodies have been sprinkled along that path by the nectar-essence flowing from You shall never again enter a womb; may they never fail to manifest within their hearts.
Those who possess a womb. || 10 ||
I bring to mind with my mind your face, beautiful with its dangling earrings; your full breast-slopes and slender, rounded waist; and your hand, elegantly marked with a rosary and a water-pot.
The form of Gaurī. || 11 ||
Having established themselves in yoga, having conquered the sixfold group of enemies, and having restrained the collection of the senses within a serene mind,
they behold her who has a beautiful face and whose hands are enriched with the noose, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā.
O Bhuvaneśvarī, the yogis [meditate upon] you. || 12 ||
Resembling refined gold, being consecrated by four elephants with jars of nectar held aloft,
and bearing two beautiful lotuses in your two hands— you, Padmā, are indeed you yourself, possessing both the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.

O Goddess, you are she who, having mounted the king of beasts with your vine-like arms— eight in number, bearing fierce and diverse weapons— and possessing the luster of a blade of durva grass, surpass the wings of the enemies of the immortals.
O Bhavānī, O Durgā! || 14 ||
Her face was beautified by the spray of water from the summer heat; she wore a string of necklace fashioned from *guñjā* berries;
clad in yellow silk, she possessed a dark luster, appearing like the languor of the God of Love at the onset of passion.
I repeatedly remember the young Pulinda woman. || 15 ||
