May the youth, equipped with armor, wearing a breastplate, carrying a sword, and bearing a bow and arrows, [protect me].
May Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, protect us by fulfilling our heart's desire. || 24 ||
May Nṛsiṃha be before me, and the one whose banner is Garuḍa behind me; and on my two sides may Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa stand, bearing bows and arrows.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, the hero, the powerful one followed by Lakṣmaṇa;
the descendant of Kakutstha, the perfect Person, the son of Kauśalyā, the best of the Raghus. || 26 ||
He is the one to be known through the Vedānta, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Ancient One, the Supreme Person;
the Beloved of Jānakī, the Glorious One, whose prowess is immeasurable. || 27 ||
I bow to that best of the Raghus, who has the archer Lakṣmaṇa at his right, the auspicious Jānakī at his left, and Māruti in front of him.
Again and again I bow to Śrī Rāma, the remover of calamities, the bestower of all prosperity, who is delightful through his virtues. || 29 ||
Whoever, my devotee, should constantly recite these names of mine, he obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. (30)
Thus ends the Śrī Rāma-kavaca, named Vajrapañjara, composed by the venerable Vasiṣṭha and the illustrious Budhakauśika, within the Padma Purāṇa authored by Vedavyāsa.
Now begins the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Stotra:
Be gracious to me, O Blessed One, whose self is blunted by ignorance;
[grant] supreme devotion, which is colored by the pollen of the lotus-feet of You. (1)
O Unborn One, be gracious, O Blessed One, whose cage is immeasurable splendor!
O Immeasurable One, be gracious, O Destroyer of our suffering, O Supreme Person! (2)
O self-knowing one, be gracious; O blissful self, free from all ailment!
O you whose essence is inconceivable, O soul of the universe, O Supreme Lord, be gracious! (3)
Be gracious, O Exalted One, among the exalted; be gracious, O Auspicious One, who brings peace;
be gracious, O You of profound virtues, O You of deep majesty and great splendor! (4)
Be gracious, O Unmanifest One, vast expanse beyond the reach of the expansive!
Be gracious to those whose nature is exceedingly tender; be gracious to those who travel to the very end.
O Lord of all, you who are greater than the greatest of gurus, be gracious to embodied beings, O Ananta!
Victory to you, Mādhava, whose nature is beyond illusion; victory to you, the eternal bearer of the conch!
Victory, O glorious holder of the conch! Victory, O delighter of Nandaka!
Victory, O wielder of the discus and mace! Victory, O God Janārdana! 7.
Victory to you, whose head is crowned by a diadem set with the finest jewels!
Victory to you, who are reddened by the rays of the sun obstructed by the shadow of the Lord of Birds! 8.
Salutations to you, O enemy of Naraka; salutations to you, O slayer of Madhu;
salutations to you, O one with playful side-glances; salutations to you, O destroyer of Naraka.
Salutations to the Lord who removes sin; salutations to the dispeller of all fears.
Salutations to you who have gathered all souls within yourself; salutations to you who bear the Kaustubha gem.
Salutations to you who transcend the eye; salutations to you, the remover of fear. Salutations to you of diverse forms; salutations to you who surpass the path of the Vedas.

Salutations to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who, through his manifestation as the three forms, is the cause of heaven, maintenance, and dissolution; he who is victorious over the enemies of the thirty gods.
To the one who shatters the circle of enemies with his own wheel, the wielder of the discus, the kinsman of the wheel;
to the Universal One, worthy of universal homage, who conforms to all beings. || 13 ||
Homage be to the one meditated upon by yogis; homage be to the one whose form is the inner self.
Homage to you, the giver of liberation, who is dear to the devotion of your devotees. 14.
Worship, oblation, ritual action, meditation, and finally prostration—O Lord of Gods, may all my actions become an adoration unto you. (15)

Thus, the mantra-practitioner who is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu through the distinctions of sacrifice, recitation, and ritual adoration, and whose actions are centered in the heart, shall indeed, after a long time,
attain all desires and have Kṛṣṇa as his inner self.
One attains the supreme liberation, which is free from birth and death. || 16 ||

I bow to the leader of Gokula, who is surrounded by cows and cowherds, who is the protector of the cows, the bestower of cattle upon the cows, and who is praised by the cowherds and thousands of cows.
One should propitiate the Lord of the World, who is identical with the world, the Supreme Person, by means of this hymn of praise for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Thus ends the *Kṛṣṇastotra*. Now begins the *Gopālastotra*.
Nārada said:
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, who takes the form of a cowherd, the delighter of the cowherd girls, dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like blue lotuses. || 1 ||
His hair was dark blue and curly, bound with peacock feathers that quivered;
he was adorned with a forest garland fastened with *kadamba* flowers.
His golden earrings, set with clusters of gems, shimmered as they swayed; his chest was illuminated by a magnificent necklace of large, lustrous pearls.
His body was radiant with golden armlets, anklets, and a crown;
his mass of garments fluttered, stirred by the gentle breeze.
With the sweet sounds of the flute placed between his lovely lips, he repeatedly enchanted the hearts of the radiant cowherd girls. || 5 ||
He was like a bee drinking the nectar from the lotus-faces of the cowherd girls,
agitating their minds with his smiling sidelong glances.
It was filled with cowherd women whose bodies were blooming with youth, who were closely embracing one another,
and who were adorned with various garments and ornaments.
In one place, eager for the playful sport of sporting in the waters of the Kālindī, which were dark as crushed collyrium,
he was challenging the cowherds to battle and addressing the herds of cows;
[all this] in a spot served by cool breezes mingled with the waters of the Kālindī.
He was staying somewhere in Vṛndāvana, in the shade of a Kadamba tree.
He was seated upon a jeweled throne resting against a mountain of jewels,
situated within a golden pavilion located at the center of a wish-fulfilling tree.
On the beautiful Govardhana mountain, whose quarters were made fragrant by the scent of spring blossoms, He stood, longing for the delight of the rāsa dance. || 11 ||
With the excellent mountain held as a parasol upon the palm of his left hand,
he released a dense downpour of pearls, both broken and unbroken, like a mass of rain-clouds.
It was constantly gazed upon by the cowherd communities with their faces upturned and accompanied by their calves, amidst the great splendor of flute music and the sounds of the *huṃ* chants.
It was graced by cowherds who followed only Kṛṣṇa, acting under the influence of his movements, with staffs and nooses raised in their hands.

The Supreme Being beyond the supreme was being praised by Nārada and other foremost sages, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, with words exceedingly affectionate and full of love.
The man who thus reflects upon the God and praises Him with devotion at the three junctions of the day—He, being pleased with him, grants his desired boon. (16)
He becomes a favorite of the king, dear to all people, attains stable prosperity, and certainly becomes an eloquent speaker. (17)
Thus ends the *Śrīgopālastotra* in the *Gautamīya Tantra*. Now begins the *Śrīkṛṣṇakavaca*.
Pulastya said:
O Blessed One, Knower of all Dharmas, please graciously tell us, O Lord, that armor which has been proclaimed, named "The Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds. || 1 ||
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O best of Brahmins, I shall proclaim this most wonderful armor (kavaca), which was formerly spoken out of compassion by Nārāyaṇa to Brahmā.
This was told to me by Brahmā; out of great affection, I shall tell it to you—this most secret reality, which is the embodiment of the multitude of Brahman-mantras.
By retaining and reciting which, Brahmā unfailingly expands the creation;
by retaining and reciting which, Mahālakṣmī protects the three worlds.
Through recitation and retention, Śambhu is the destroyer who knows all principles;
and Durgā is the mother of the three worlds, [the slayer] of the great asuras such as Mahiṣa.
Since he slew those arrogant ones merely by reciting and retaining [this mantra],
so too may Indra and all others attain supreme sovereignty.
This armor is extremely secret; one should not speak of it anywhere.
One should reveal it only to a disciple who is endowed with devotion and to a spiritual practitioner (sādhaka).
By giving this armor of the Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds to a deceitful disciple of another, one shall meet with death; [it was revealed] by Prajāpati. || 8 ||
The seer is Gāyatrī, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Nārāyaṇa himself;
its application is proclaimed to be for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 9 ||
May the Praṇava protect my head, and "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" protect my forehead; may the eight-syllabled mantra, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, protect the pair of my eyes.
May *klīṃ*, the single-syllable mantra that deludes all, protect the pair of ears;
may *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* always protect the nose, and *govindāya* the tongue. (11)
"May the eighteen-syllable great mantra, *gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*, protect my face; may the ten-syllable [mantra] protect my throat. (12)

*gopījanapadaṃ vallabhāya svāhā* protects the two arms; *klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ śyāmalāṅgāya namaḥ*, the ten-syllable mantra, protects the shoulders. *klīṃ kṛṣṇa klīṃ* may protect the hands; *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* may protect the limbs born of the body.
O Bhuvaneśānī, *klīṃ* is my heart, and *kṛṣṇāya* is my hands and breasts. (14)
May the mantra ending in "gopālāya agnijāyā" (svāhā) always protect the pair of bellies; may this supreme mantra, "klīṃ kṛṣṇāya," always protect the pair of sides. || 15 ||
May the mantra "Kṛṣṇa Govindaka," beginning with "Smara" and ending with the dative suffix (ṅe), protect [the heart];
may the eight-syllabled mantra protect the navel, and may the two-syllabled "Kṛṣṇa" protect [the belly].
May *klīṃ kṛṣṇakaṅkālaṃ klīṃ* protect the back; may *kṛṣṇāya dviṭhāntakaḥ* [protect] the two thighs.
May *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇaṭhadvayam* always protect the two shanks. (17)
May the seven-syllable [mantra] protect the thighs, and may the thirteen-syllable [mantra] protect [the rest].
Then, from the word *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, follows the word *gopījanavallabha*. (18)
"Bhāya svāhā" protects the anus; "klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sa" is the ten-syllabled mantra.
And "hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ" is the ten-syllabled mantra that protects the two knees.

May the thirteen-syllable mantra protect the shanks; [may] the eighteen-syllable mantra preceded by *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*, as well as the twenty-syllable one, [protect them], bearing the discus and other weapons. (20)
May the powerful leader of Dvārakā always protect all my limbs;
thereafter, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva. (21)
May this twelve-syllable mantra beginning with Tārā always protect me in the east;
likewise, the ten-syllable mantra is Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, and the sixteen-syllable one is Klīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ.
May Viṣṇu, armed with the mace and other weapons, protect me in the direction of Agni;
may the ten-syllabled mantra "hrīṃ śrīṃ" always protect me in the south.
"Tāro namo bhagavate rukmiṇīvallabhāya ca svāhā"—may this sixteen-syllable mantra protect [the practitioner] in the south-western direction. (24)
Klīṃ, salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa; may Varuṇa protect me.
This eighteen-syllable mantra ending with Kāma (Hrīṃ) shall always protect me in the northwest.
Śrīṃ, the mantra for Kṛṣṇa, the master of Māyā and desire, Govinda, consisting of twelve syllables and ending with two Ṭha-sounds—may Viṣṇu always protect me in the North. (26)
Vāgbhava (aiṃ), Kāmakṛṣṇāya, Hrīṃ, Govindāya, and thereafter Śrīṃ; at the end of Gopījanavallabha, Bhāryāyāḥ Svāhā, and then Karau. (27)
May the twenty-two-syllable mantra always protect me in the northeast;
it is He who performs the divine dance in the midst of the hoods of Kāliya. || 28 ||
I bow to the son of Devakī, the King of Dance, the Infallible One;
may the thirty-two-syllable mantra also protect me from below at all times. (29)
We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon the one whose arrows are flowers;
may that bodiless one (Anaṅga) inspire us—may he protect me from above. || 30 ||
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you this armor (kavaca), which is the embodiment of a multitude of Brahma-mantras, named "The Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds," and whose form is that of Brahmā.
This was previously told by Brahmā and heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa;
out of affection for you, I have related it, but it must not be spoken to anyone.

Having prostrated before the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should then recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) once, twice, or as much as one knows; for that mantra is indeed composed of all austerity.
The teacher is indeed authoritative regarding all mantras; there is no doubt in this matter.
One hundred and eight recitations are prescribed as the rule for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of this mantra. || 34 ||
Having performed the oblation and so forth with a tenth part [of the total], one will certainly accomplish that;
if one's armor (kavaca) is perfected, one becomes Viṣṇu himself.
Through the performance of the *puraścaryā* rite, he shall attain the perfection of mantras;
having cast aside all rivalry, Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall dwell with him forever. (36)
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers, one should recite [the mantra] once with the root mantra;
one shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand years of worship. || 37 ||
If one writes [this] on birch bark, places it within a pill, and wears it either around the neck or on the right arm, he too is Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, whatever great gifts there may be, as well as circumambulating the entire earth—[all these are equal to this]. (39)
Therefore, those [other mantras] do not equal even a sixteenth part of this [mantra] from a single recitation;
by the grace of the Kavaca, a man becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 40 ||
"Agitate the three worlds"—by thinking thus, one becomes the conqueror of the three worlds.
He who worships Puruṣottama without knowing this armor [of mantras] [is ineffective]. 41.
Even if recited a hundred lakhs of times, the mantra does not succeed for him.
Thus ends the Śrīkṛṣṇakavaca, named Trailokyamaṅgala, in the Sanatkumāra-tantra. Now follows the Nṛsiṃhakavaca.
Nārada said: O Lord of the hosts of gods beginning with Indra, O Lord of the world,
O Master worthy of worship, tell me, O Lord, the armor (kavaca) of Mahāviṣṇu in his form as Nṛsiṃha.
"By the recitation of which a wise man shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
Brahmā said:
"Listen, O Nārada, best of sons, rich in asceticism; I shall speak."
The armor of Narasiṃha, known as Trailokyavijaya.
By reciting it, one becomes eloquent and a conqueror of the three worlds;
for, my child, by its recitation and retention, I myself have become the creator of the worlds.
Lakṣmī protects the three worlds, and Maheśvara is the destroyer;
by reciting and retaining this, even the gods became lords of the directions.
I shall declare the mantra of Brahmā, which wards off delusion and other such obstacles;
by its grace, Durvāsas became the conqueror of the three worlds.

The teacher of this armor (*kavaca*) of Trailokyavijaya, which is to be recited and retained, is Krodhabhairava; Prajāpati is its seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī, and the all-pervading Lord Nṛsiṃha is its deity. (6)
May the great mantra, the seed-syllable *kṣrauṃ*, moon-colored, protect my head. || 7 ||
Oṃ, I bow to the fierce, heroic, great Viṣṇu, the blazing one whose face is turned in every direction; to Nṛsiṃha, the terrifying yet auspicious one, the death of death itself. || 8 ||
May the thirty-two-syllable mantra, the king of mantras that is like a celestial tree, protect my throat with the syllable *dhruvaṃ kṣrauṃ*, and may it protect my eyes with the words *bhagavate*. (9)
May Narasiṃha, garlanded with flames, protect the ears;
and likewise may he with blazing fangs and fiery eyes protect the nose.
And for the sake of destroying all rākṣasas, likewise for the sake of the welfare of all beings,
and for the destruction of all fevers, [utter] the two words "daha daha."
Protect, protect! O armor-mantra, svāhā! May it protect my face.
Salutation to Rāmacandra, preceded by Tārā; may it protect my heart. (12)
Klīṃ shall protect the pair of sides; then the syllable Om (Tāra) and the word Namaḥ;
Nārāyaṇāya protects the navel; and Āṃ Hrīṃ Krauṃ Kṣrauṃ Huṃ Phaṭ [protect the rest]. || 13 ||
May the six-syllable mantra protect the waist; may the word *oṃ namo bhagavate* protect the back; may *vāsudevāya* protect the two thighs; and may *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* protect the two shanks.
May the supreme mantra *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* always protect the knees;
may *klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ śyāmalāṅgāya namaḥ* protect both feet. || 15 ||
"KṢRAUṂ NṚSIṂHĀYA KṢRAUṂ—may this always protect all my limbs.
Thus, O child, I have told you that which embodies the entire multitude of mantras.
Out of affection for you, I have disclosed this; it must not be told to anyone.
Having performed worship of the Guru, one should then receive the armor (kavaca).
Having become endowed with all merit, one shall become endowed with all perfections;
the performance of one hundred and eight recitations is prescribed as the rule for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā). || 18 ||
Having performed the oblations and other rites with a tenth part [of the total], the best of practitioners, his armor perfected, becomes a meritorious soul resembling the god of love. (19)
Then, having aroused competition [between them], Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall dwell in his home;
therefore, having offered eight handfuls of flowers, one should recite [the mantra] once with the root-mantra alone.
One would obtain the fruit of worship for thousands of years if one were to write [this] on birch bark,
place it in a pill within gold, and wear it.
On the neck or on the right arm, one becomes Narasiṃha himself;
for a woman, it is on the left arm, and for a man, on the right hand.
One who wears this meritorious armor shall become endowed with all perfections;
even a woman who has borne only one child or one whose children have died shall [attain success]. || 23 ||
A woman barren of children or one whose sons have perished shall become possessed of many sons;
by the grace of this armor-mantra (kavaca), a man becomes liberated while yet living. || 24 ||
Thus he truly agitates the three worlds and becomes the conqueror of the three worlds;
so too do the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and those who are dānavas.
Upon seeing it, they certainly flee from one country to another;
indeed, abandoning that very region where the armor remains—whether in a house or in a village—they depart to a great distance. (26)
Thus ends the *Nṛsiṃhakavaca*, named *Trailokyamaṅgala*, from the *Brahmasaṃhitā*.
Now begins the *Śivastotra*.
Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, who dwells within all beings, whose forms are Earth, Fire, Water, Wind, Ether, Agni, Indra, Moon, and Sun. || 1 ||
Salutations again and again to the eternal, great, and supersensuous Śruti, who has made her abode within the Vedas and from whom the Vedas are born. || 2 ||
Salutations be to you, Śambhu, who is indefinable through the distinctions of gross and subtle; salutations to Bhava, the destroyer of the suffering born of worldly existence. || 3 ||
Salutations again and again to the All-Knowing One, who has transcended the path of logic, who bestows the fruits of ascetic penances, and who is generous in granting the four aims of human life.
Salutations again and again to the Great One, who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; who has dispelled all fear; who is the object of meditation for yogis; and who is beyond all attributes.
Salutations to the Soul of the Universe, the inconceivable one, whose crest is the shimmering moon; to the destroyer of the pride of Kandarpa, the slayer of Time. || 6 ||
Salutations again and again to him who dwells amidst those who consume poison, who has approached the bull-like shoulders [of Śiva], and whose matted locks are bound together like a river’s banks.
Salutations again and again to the pure one, whose nature is purity, the inner self of the pure, the end-maker of the city [of the body], the full, he whose name is merit.

Salutations again and again to the one who bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation upon his own devotees, who is himself without abode yet is the dwelling place for all, and who is praised by the entire world in the scriptures.
Salutations again and again to the three-eyed one, who is the fundamental source of the triple form;
salutations again and again to the destroyer of rebirth, whose nature is the abode of the three luminous realms.
Salutations again and again to Him whose feet are reddened by the rays from the crest-jewels of the gods and asuras; to the Beloved who has given half of His own body to His beloved.
With this hymn of praise during worship, one should gratify the Lord of the World—the omniscient Supreme Lord who, through devotion, bestows both devotion and liberation. (12)
For him, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that remains unattainable;
what worldly fruit could there be [greater than this], for liberation itself is held in his hand. (13)
Thus ends the hymn to Śiva.
Now follows the armor (kavaca) of Śiva.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, worshipped by all traditions! O God, you have told me everything, yet the armor (kavaca) has not been revealed.
O Lord, if you have affection for me, reveal to me the armor (kavaca) of the mantra known as Prāsāda, which provides protection from all [dangers].
The Blessed Lord said:
Vāmadeva is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra-armour of the temple;
Paṅkti is the metre (chandas), O Goddess of the Gods, and Sadāśiva is the deity here.
And its application is proclaimed for the accomplishment of the practitioner's desired goal. || 3 ||
Oṃ, may Sadāśiva, known as Prāsāda, always protect my head. || 4 ||
May Maheśvara, whose nature consists of six syllables, speak to me;
may the eight-syllabled mantra, restrained by Śakti, ever protect my eyes.
May the Blessed One, whose nature consists of five syllables, protect my two arms;
may Mṛtyuñjaya, whose nature consists of three seed-syllables, always protect my life.
May the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, seated at the foot of the banyan tree and assuming the form of the thirty-six syllables, protect me always from all sides. (7)
May Rudra, consisting of twenty-two syllables, protect my belly;
may Nīlakaṇṭha, whose self consists of three syllables, always protect my throat.
May Hara, the wish-fulfilling gem in the form of a seed-syllable, who is the Lord Half-Female, the bestower of all prosperity, always protect my private parts. || 9 ||
May Maheśvara, whose nature is the single syllable and who is of the form of the peak-mantra (kūṭa), along with Mārtaṇḍabhairavī, eternally protect my feet. 10.
May the destroyer of Tripura, known as Tumburu, whose nature is that of a great seed-syllable and who is the lord of the thirty gods, always protect me on the field of battle. (11)
May Īśāna protect my upward head at all times;
may Tatpuruṣa, the Lord of the Mountain, protect me in the southern direction.
May Mahādeva, known as Aghora, protect me in the east; may Mahādeva always protect me in the west;
and may he who bears the form of Sadyojāta always protect me in the north.
O Goddess, he who recites this protective armor (*kavaca*), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, at the time of dawn, shall attain his desired fruit. (14)
The best of practitioners who recites this armor-mantra at the time of worship will certainly become endowed with fame, prosperity, beauty, intelligence, and long life. (15)
The practitioner who wears this armor, which is the very nature of my thought-form, upon his neck,
attains victory in battle, in gambling, and in debate.
The practitioner who wears this armor on his right arm will bring gods, humans, and gandharvas under his control; of this there is no doubt. || 17 ||
O Goddess of the gods, for him who wears this armor upon his head with a disciplined mind, the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, reside in his hand.
This vidyā, wrapped in a white cloth, [should be written] on birch bark.
Having placed it within a silver vessel, the wise man should preserve it.
Having attained great fortune, he shall at the end of his life become an inhabitant of my own body.
This must never be given to just anyone, nor should it ever be disclosed.
One should reveal it to a disciple who is endowed with devotion and to a practitioner;
otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment. This is the truth, O beautiful one. (21)
Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, this auspicious armor has been told;
it must not be given to anyone, O Blessed One, if one desires one's own welfare.
O Great Goddess, whoever worships with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings this armor-mantra uttered from my own mouth, by him all the gods are worshipped; of this there is no doubt. (23)
Thus ends the Śrī Sadāśiva Kavaca in the Bhairava Tantra. Now begins the Vaṭukabhairava Stotra:
[I bow] to the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa.
Pārvatī questioned Śaṅkara, the Supreme Lord.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, [please reveal] that mantra among all the scriptures and traditions which delivers men from calamity and bestows all spiritual perfections.
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, this has been desired by me;
specifically, it is the accomplishment of peace and nourishment for kings.
O Lord of Gods, you should deign to tell me that which increases my joy, accompanied by the placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), the hands (karanyāsa), and the seed-syllables (bījanyāsa).
The Blessed One said: Listen, O Goddess, to the great mantra which is the cause of deliverance from calamity, the pacifier of all suffering, and the destroyer of all enemies. (5)
O beloved, this king of mantras destroys diseases such as epilepsy and especially fevers by its mere recollection.
O beloved, out of affection I shall tell you this mantra, the essence of all things, which destroys the fears of the lords of the planets and increases happiness.
I shall specifically declare this mantra which bestows all desired objects, grants kingship and enjoyments to men, and delivers one from calamities. (8)
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should extract the Praṇava of the Goddess;
then [the word] "Vaṭukāya" and subsequently "Āpaduddharaṇāya."
Then, after that, one should again cast two *kuru*s for Vaṭuka;
O Dear One, having extracted the *praṇava* of the Goddess, this is the extraction of the mantra.
O Goddess, this retention of mantras is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds;
this mantra, endowed with all powers, must not be disclosed.
Merely by the recollection of this mantra, ghosts, spirits, and piśācas flee,
afflicted by fear, just as living beings flee from Rudra at the onset of the Kali age.
Whether one recites it, causes it to be recited, or honors the book,
there shall be no fear of fire or thieves, nor likewise any fear of the planets or kings.

He shall have no fear of pestilence and shall be happy everywhere; through the worship of even this book, he shall constantly possess long life, health, sovereignty, and the prosperity of sons, grandsons, and other riches. (14)
Śrī Pārvatī said: "O Lord, this one known as Bhairava, who is considered the deliverer from calamity,
and this supreme Bhairava-kalpa have been described by you."
His names number in the thousands, tens of thousands, and even millions;
having extracted their very essence, please recite those one hundred and eight names.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The practitioner who recites this, which destroys all evils,
attains all desires as well as spiritual perfection."
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim [the teaching] of the great-souled Bhairava.
In this world, the supreme one hundred and eight names of the Deliverer from Calamity [should be recited].
O Goddess, it removes all sins, is meritorious, wards off all calamities, grants all desires and goals, and brings happiness to practitioners. || 19 ||
First, with a concentrated mind, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs of the body:
placing Bhairava on the head, Bhīmadarśana on the forehead,
Bhūtāśraya on the eyes, and Tīkṣṇadarśana on the mouth.
One should place Kṣetrapa between the ears and Kṣetrapāla in the heart;
one named Kṣetra at the region of the navel, and Sarvāghanāśana on the hips.
Having placed the three-eyed one on the thighs, one should place Raktapāṇika on the shanks.
One should place the Lord of the Gods of gods on the two feet, and Vaṭuka on all the limbs.
Having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should thereafter, with a single-minded focus, recite the supreme hymn known as the *Nāmāṣṭaśataka*.
Regarding this *Nāmāṣṭaśataka*, the meter is stated to be *anuṣṭubh*.
The sage is proclaimed by the virtuous to be named Vṛhadāraṇyaka, and the deity is said to be Vaṭukabhairava;
the application is declared to be for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. || 21 ||
Bhairava, Lord of Beings, the Soul of Beings, the Creator of Beings;
Bestower of the Field, Protector of the Field, Knower of the Field, Warrior, and the Cosmic Manifestation. || 1 ||
Dwelling in cremation grounds, a consumer of flesh, a consumer of skull-bowls, and the ender of sacrifices;
a drinker of blood, a taker of life, perfected, the giver of perfection, and served by the perfected ones. || 2 ||
Karāla, the subduer of Time (Kāla), whose body is composed of Kalās and Kāṣṭhās, the Seer (Kavi);
he who has three eyes, many eyes, and likewise tawny eyes. || 3 ||

He who holds a trident in his hand, he who holds a sword in his hand, Kaṅkālī, Dhūmralocana, the fearless one, Bhairava, the terrible one, the protector of beings, and the lord of the Yoginīs. || 4 ||
The giver of wealth and the taker of wealth, the bestower of riches and possessed of brilliant luster;
the destroyer of serpents and having serpents for hair, he whose hair is the sky and who bears a skull.
He is Time, the wearer of a garland of skulls, the desirable one, and the treasury of arts;
he is the three-eyed, the flaming-eyed, the bearer of the triple-flamed fire, and the protector of the three worlds.
The child with three eyes is peaceful, beloved by peaceful people;
he is Vaṭuka, the Lord of Vaṭukas, and the bearer of the excellent khaṭvāṅga staff.
The overseer of beings, Paśupati, the mendicant, the attendant, the rogue, the sky-clad one, Śauri, Hariṇa, and Pāṇḍulocana. || 8 ||

He is the profoundly peaceful one, the bestower of peace, the pure, the benefactor Śaṅkara, the beloved kinsman, the lord of the eight forms and the treasures, the eye of knowledge, and the embodiment of darkness.
He who has eight supports, who is joined with serpents, who is the moon, the bearer of poison, and Śiva;
who is the sustainer of the earth, the lord of the mountains, the king of the world, and whose very nature is the earth. || 10 ||
Wearing a skeleton, shaven-headed, and possessing a serpent as a sacred thread;
likewise, he is the one who causes yawning, delusion, paralysis, killing, and agitation.
His body resembles pure blue collyrium, and he is adorned with a shaven head;
his soul is one who enjoys the offerings of children, and he is a lover whose prowess is desire itself.
The remover of all transgressions, the one difficult to traverse, frequented by wicked spirits;
Kālī, the treasury of arts, the beloved, the subduer of passionate women, and the self-controlled; the bestower of all accomplishments, the physician, the sovereign, and the powerful. || 13 ||
O Goddess, I have told you this secret of the great-souled Bhairava, consisting of one hundred and eight names, which grants all desires. 14.
Whoever recites this supreme hymn of one hundred and eight names shall have no misfortune whatsoever, nor any fear of diseases. (15)
A person never encounters any fear from enemies anywhere. || 16 ||
One should recite this hymn with undistracted mind, free from fear of sins, in times of danger from pestilence, danger from kings, and likewise in danger arising from thieves or fire. (17)
In the event of a most terrible portent, or fear born of a painful dream,
or in the face of a most dreadful imprisonment, one should recite this hymn with a concentrated mind.
All [calamities] reach pacification through the recitation of the Bhairava [mantra];
eleven thousand repetitions are prescribed for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). || 19 ||
O Goddess, that man who recites this three times a day for a year without weariness shall attain his desired success, even if it be difficult for a human being to achieve.
One who desires land shall obtain the earth by reciting it for six months;
furthermore, a king desiring the destruction of his enemies should recite it for eight months.
By reciting it three times at night, one certainly destroys all enemies;
by reciting it at night for three months, one shall bring even a king under one's control.
Any man who desires wealth, who desires a son, or who desires a wife,
should recite this three times, or likewise once, at night.
One shall obtain wealth, sons, as well as a wife; of this there is no doubt. || 24 ||
O Goddess, one who is afraid shall be liberated from fear; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Whatever desires one may long for, one attains them constantly. (25)
This secret is not to be disclosed; it must not be given to just anyone.
One should bestow this meritorious hymn, which grants the fruit of all desires, upon one who is of noble birth, tranquil, upright, and free from hypocrisy. (26)
I shall describe the meditation upon the Lord, by meditating upon which a person should recite [the mantra]:
resembling pure crystal, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns,
with eight arms, three eyes, four arms, and two arms.
The god who has a serpent for a girdle and hair the color of fire.
[He saw] Kumārīśa, naked and of great strength, known as Vaṭuka, who likewise held a skull-topped staff, a sword, a noose, and a trident. || 28 ||
Holding a ḍamaru drum, a skull-cup, the gesture of granting boons, and likewise a serpent;
resembling a dark blue cloud and possessing the luster of a mass of black collyrium. (29)
With a face made terrifying by its fangs, adorned with anklets and armlets,
endowed with its own natural color, and accompanied by dogs.
Having meditated, one should recite [the mantra] with great joy; thus one shall obtain all desires. || 31 ||
Oṃ! Victorious is Vaṭukanātha, the bestower of spiritual accomplishments, who holds a skull-cup in his hand, wears earrings, carries a staff, is dark blue like the twilight,
has a serpent as his sacred thread,
and dispels obstacles during the performance of sacrificial rites.
For practitioners. || 32 ||
Having heard this, the Goddess Maheśvarī herself was filled with joy, and she then [revealed] the supreme eight hundred names for Bhairava.
Thus ends the *Vacukabhairavastavarāja* from the *Āpaduddhārakalpa* within the *Viśvasāra*.
Now follows the *Bhairavīstotra*: "O Tripurā, I shall praise you with this hymn for the attainment of my desired fruit."
By means of which men attain that fortune (lakṣmī) which is worshipped by the gods as they proceed [to their goal]. || 1 ||
Even Brahmā and the other gods do not know her subtle form— the beginningless embodiment of the world— through even hundreds of Vedic hymns;
therefore, we praise her gross form, which has the luster of fresh saffron and resembles a beautiful young creeper.
She who has become the mother of the entirety of all speech.

I bow to you, who possess the brilliance of a thousand suns suddenly risen, whose hands bear the marks of the knowledge-gesture, the rosary, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness;
whose lotus-face is adorned with three blue-lotus eyes, and who are radiant with a necklace of large pearls.
We worship the Three Cities. || 2 ||

Do those whose minds are agitated by mutual strife and quarreling know that [the Lord], who is radiant with streams of vermilion, bowed by the weight of His breasts, and attainable only as the fruit of merit accumulated in previous births?
O Mother, those of dull intellect [cannot grasp] Your true nature. || 3 ||
The sages declare you to be gross, while the Vedas describe you as subtle; others call you the abode of all speech,
O Bhavānī, while yet others say you are the root of the worlds.
We consider him to be an ocean of boundless compassion. || 4 ||
They meditate upon you in their hearts— adorned with a crescent moon, white as the autumnal moon, consisting of fifty syllables,
holding a book, a rosary, a jar of nectar, and the gesture of exposition.
Holding [objects] with her lotus-like hands, she has three eyes. || 5 ||
O Mother, Śambhu has half his body joined with you; Viṣṇu has his body embraced by Kamalā;
and Padmodbhava is also your abode, the dwelling place of Speech—yet they perform their respective functions in the world.
O Tripurā, you alone are she. || 6 ||

I meditate upon you, the Supreme Goddess, who consists entirely of consciousness, residing in my heart; you who utter the four states beginning with the "Supreme" (Para) as they are established in their respective stages, relying upon the organs of speech such as the throat.
I never forget it at any time. || 7 ||
Having restrained the vital breath and conquered the six internal enemies,
O Mother, those of steady intellect meditate upon Your form at the crown of their heads— Your form adorned with the crescent moon as its crest-ornament.
The wise man [attains] a friend like the rising sun.
"Having obtained half the body of the enemy of Mantha (Śiva), you bring about the creation of the worlds"—such is the Vedic proclamation.
O Daughter of the Mountain, O sole Mother of the universe, this is true; for were it not so, there would be no stability for the entire world.
O Mother, having performed worship with flowers from the celestial trees upon your throne in the caves of the Golden Mountain,
the wives of the Siddhas sing together.
Their lotus-eyes were reddened by the taste of wine sipped by the kinnarīs. || 10 ||

I worship within my heart the Goddess, whose body possesses the playful splendor of lightning, who bears supreme beauty as she departs from her own abode for the capital city of Śiva, and who causes the lotuses of the suṣumnā path to blossom.
Her limbs are sprinkled with the supreme nectar. || 11 ||
O Mother, I take refuge in you, the source of bliss, the abode of the Vedas, whose body is pure consciousness,
whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu, and who are the dwelling place for the birth of all good fortune.
In Tripura, as it truly is. || 12 ||
She who, in the form of the Moon, creates the world that arises from word and meaning;
she who, by her own power, sustains it again in the form of the Sun; and she who, as the nature of Fire, withdraws all that at the end of the age—that Śāradā, one should never [forget] in the mind.
I forget. || 13 ||

O Daughter of the King of Mountains, people worship you in many ways— as Nārāyaṇī, as the one who carries across the ocean of hell, as Gaurī, as the quencher of weariness, as Sarasvatī, as the bestower of knowledge, and as she who is adorned with three eyes.
Those men who praise the Mother of the World with these twelve verses in sequence shall attain perfection of speech and obtain prosperity after reaching her own presence.
Thus ends the Bhairavīstavarāja in the Bhairavītantra. Now follows the Bhairavīkavaca.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
All the sciences to be mastered have been heard and acquired by me;
now I wish to hear that armor which was previously mentioned. || 1 ||
The one named Trailokyavijaya, the warder-off of weapons and missiles—O Lord, who other than you is capable of showing such compassion? (2)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Pārvatī, O beautiful one, my beloved as my own life; I shall proclaim the armor of weapons and missiles named *Trailokyavijaya*, which is the very embodiment of mantra.
Having recited and retained this, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds;
for by holding it, Madhusūdana slew all the Daityas. || 4 ||
Brahmā expands the creation by holding him who is the bestower of desired objects;
so too does Kubera, the lord of wealth, and Vāsava, the sovereign of the thirty gods. || 5 ||
By whose grace I am the Lord, the all-pervading conqueror of the three worlds;
this [knowledge] must never be given to the disciples of others nor to those who are not practitioners.
Having given this even to one's own sons, let alone others, one shall attain death [only after fulfilling its power].
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is indeed the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor (kavaca) of Bhairavī.
The Virāṭ meter, the goddess Jagaddhātrī Bālabhairavī, and the application for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are proclaimed. || 8 ||

The first [syllable] is the lower lip (A) with a dot (M), Kāma (E) joined with Śaktīśa (AU) and the Moon (I), and Bhṛgu (S) joined with the vowel of Manu (U); this is the emission consisting of the three seed-syllables. || 9 ||
May this Bālā protect my head, she who is endowed with ten million *bindu-nādas*;
and may Kumārī protect my forehead, she who is the maiden devoid of creation (*sarga*).
May the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja) protect the two eyes, and may it always protect the pair of ears;
may the seed-syllable of Desire (Kāmabīja) always protect the pair of nostrils.
May Bālā, the bestower of Sarasvatī and of pure luster, protect my tongue;
may she protect my throat with "hasaiṃ," my shoulders with "hasakalarīṃ," and my arms with "hasaur."
May Pañcamī Bhairavī protect the hands; may Hasaraiṃ always protect [them].
May Hasakalarī protect the heart; may she protect the chest; may Hasaroḥ protect the breasts. (13)
May the goddess Bhairavī, whose form is consciousness, protect me;
may *hasraiṃ* always protect my two sides, and may *hasakalarīṃ* always [protect them]. (14)
May Bhairavī, who is difficult to find on earth, protect my belly and waist;
may the Seed-Vidyā "Aiṃ Īṃ Oṃ" always protect the middle region of my body. 15.
May *hasaiṃ* always protect my back, and likewise may *hasakalarīṃ* protect my navel;
may *hasauḥ*, the six-armed Bhairavī, protect the region of my hips. 16.
May HASARAIṂ protect my two thighs; may HASAKALARĪ always protect me;
may HASAUḤ protect the region of my secret parts; and may Bhairavī protect my knees. (17)
May she who bestows prosperity always protect [me]; may *hasaiṃ* protect the shanks, and *hasarīṃ* the feet;
may *hasauḥ* protect the entire body; may Bhairavī protect me at all times. 18.
May HASAIṂ protect me in the east; may HASAKALARĪ protect me in the southeast;
may HASAUḤ, stationed in the Bhairavī-cakra, protect me in the south.
Hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ māṃ—may Cakrabhairavī always protect me in the southwest;
hasaiṃ hasakalahrīṃ hasarauḥ—may Bhairavī protect me in the west.
Kṛīṃ kṛīṃ kṛīṃ: may she protect in the northwest; hūṃ hūṃ:
may she always protect in the north; hrīṃ hrīṃ: may she always protect in the northeast; O Kālikā, protect in the south! (21)
May the previously mentioned seed-syllables protect me from above,
and may Kālikā, the wielder of the sword, protect me from below in the cardinal and intermediate directions— svāhā!
Oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ phaṭ! May that Tārā protect me always everywhere—in battle, in the forest, in a fortress, and in waters difficult to cross because of the waves. (23)
"May she who holds a sword and a dagger, and who is fierce, always protect me.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this great armor, most excellent among the excellent, known as the *Trailokyavijaya*, which is supremely wonderful. (24)
Whoever, having become purified, should recite this, shall obtain the fruit of worship;
having cast aside all rivalry, Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall then dwell in his home.
He who is afraid of enemies, or timid in battle; or fearful in the forest, or in the midst of water;
or in debate before an assembly due to an opponent, or from the wrath of a king, or from a multitude of planetary portents;
or fearful of a fierce wind, or of a calamity, or even from the anger of a guru that is difficult to appease.
Having worshipped the Goddess, he who recites this at the three junctions of the day shall become equal to Maheśa and victorious.
If one writes this armor named Trailokyavijaya, spoken from my own mouth, upon birch bark and wears it as a pill placed within gold, [he shall be protected]. (27)
Whether worn on the neck or the right arm, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
having reached his body, weapons become like flowers. (28)
Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī shall dwell happily in his house;
yet he who recites the supreme Bhairavī mantra without knowing this armor (kavaca) [shall not attain such results].
If a child recites this vidyā, or if a poor person recites it, he shall meet with death.
Thus ends the *Bhairavī-kavaca*, named *Trailokyavijaya*, from the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord.
Now begins the *Śrīvidyā-stotra*.

O Mother, did not those possessed of devotion and full of knowledge perform at the root of your lotus feet services that were like auspicious showers of rain filled with nectar, serving as the auspicious lamps for Lakṣmī’s own choice of a husband? || 1 ||
O Mother, lotus-eyed one dwelling in the waters, this alone is truly desirable:
the presence of your form—which is like a blooming red lotus and drenched in supreme nectar—within your acts of worship. || 2 ||
How many indeed are there whose power is but slightly sullied— Brahmā and the others who are overwhelmed by dissolution day after day?
O Mother, he alone remains with steady perfection who performs even a single prostration at your feet.
He performs [it]. || 3 ||
O Tripurasundarī, having once obtained your sidelong glance— which arises from the splendor blossoming with compassion—
those who possess devotion to you, made beautiful by the state of passion, bring others into a state of enchantment.
Young women, even throughout the three worlds. || 4 ||
O Mother Tripura, dweller in the triangular abode, three-eyed goddess, the gods chant your very name as the syllable *hrīṃ*.
Upon remembering you, the hosts of Vama abandon their fear and sport together in the Nandana grove.
By the world-protectors. || 5 ||
O Mother, if this half of your body were not for my consolation, how could the cruel force of the poison,
rising up to my very throat, not have been fully lethal?
Of that which is eternally cooled by being immersed in the nectar of immortality.
O Goddess, prostration at your two lotus-like feet produces omniscience and eloquence in the assembly;
moreover, it brings forth a shimmering, radiant crown, a brilliant parasol, and two great fly-whisks.
He gives the earth. || 7 ||

O Mother, Tripurasundarī, look upon me, the protectorless one, who am filled with devotion toward You alone; look upon me with Your side-long glances, which are oceans of compassion that grant all desired objects like wish-fulfilling trees.
One whose view has increased. || 8 ||
Alas, others indeed direct their minds toward and offer devotion even to base deities;
O Goddess, I alone remember you with my mind, and I bow to you alone as my refuge, O Mother.
You alone. || 9 ||
O Tripurasundarī, although there exist hundreds of thousands of glances from Your eyes, look upon me somehow;
for surely no person equal to me— a sole vessel of compassion— has ever been born, nor will one ever be.
Or it is born. || 10 ||
O Dwellers of Tripura, what indeed is difficult to obtain here for those who daily chant your name as "Hrīṃ Hrīṃ"?
Madhumatī herself serves those who are worthy of honor— the garlands, the crowns, and the rutting elephants.
Lakṣmī. || 11 ||
O lotus-eyed Mother, may my prostrations— which bring about prosperity, delight all the senses, are skilled in bestowing universal sovereignty,
and are intent on removing all evils— constantly attend to me alone.
Not another. || 12 ||

Victorious is that [Goddess] who holds the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow, and the flower-arrows, acting as the witness for you— the Lord Khaṇḍaparaśu, the Supreme Bhairava, whose dance is fashioned by the dissolution of the cosmic ages.
The form is one. || 13 ||
O Mother, may this supreme form of yours, red as thick saffron paste, always be fixed [within me];
a form arisen in the triangle, adorned with a radiant crown and an ornament of a digit of the moon.
Anointed with the supreme nectar. || 14 ||
O Mother, that knower of mantras who daily recites this hymn before you— kindled by the great mantra encapsulated by three *hrīṃ*s—
comes under the sway of kings, and prosperity and eloquence remain with him for a long time.
His fame, laden with a weight of stainless eloquent sayings, endures for a long time. || 15 ||
Thus ends the Śrīvidyāstotra.
Now, the *Kiṅkiṇī-stotra*:
O Mother of all beings, what suffering does not perish when you are remembered? O Lotus of the lineage, what fame is not attained when you are worshipped?
What kind of happiness, O Goddess praised by the best of gods, is not obtained when you are lauded? What kind of yoga does the mind not expand upon when it takes you as its object? || 1 ||
When remembered, you destroy the fear of worldly existence; when worshipped, O bringer of auspiciousness, you are honored.
When praised, O Goddess, source of compassion, you grant one's desires. (2)

Salutations to You, O Mother, who are the ocean of the awakening of supreme bliss, whose nature is radiant splendor, whose lotus-feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels of the hosts of gods, and who are the mere Great Being that is the repose of consciousness. 3.
O Eternal One, you are the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world; through your desire to act, you consist of the three qualities (guṇas).
O Supreme Goddess, for my sake— who am devoted and constantly engaged in Your worship— You have assumed a divine form for the benefit of all living beings.
O Goddess worshipped by the thirty [gods], grant me success in this world and the next;
O Śivā, protect me, who am a vessel withered by the three types of suffering.
I speak of nothing else, I hear nothing else, I think of nothing else; I remember nothing else, I worship nothing else, nor do I take refuge in anything else.
Having abandoned everything with devotion, O Goddess, protect me out of your compassion, O Mother!
Grant me success! || 7 ||
Whether through ignorance, negligence, or a deficiency in the ritual means, whatever is deficient or excessive—all that you should forgive. (8)
O Goddess, whose body is compassion, please forgive all of that out of mercy— whatever was deficient in materials, deficient in ritual action, or devoid of faith and mantras.
Whatever action I perform, whether it be great or even small, all of that must be forgiven by you, O Mother of the World; here I join my palms in supplication. (10)
Thus ends the Kiṅkiṇī-stotra.
Now, the Śrīvidyā-kavaca. The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, who increases the devotion of your devotees!
It has been indicated; please tell me the armor (kavaca) of the Great Goddess.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the armor (kavaca), which is the embodiment of mantras;
it is not to be disclosed, supremely secret, and bestows the accomplishment of all desired objects.
O Goddess, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi) of the armor-mantra (kavaca); Paṅkti is declared to be the meter (chandas), and the deity is Tripurasundarī;
its application (viniyoga) is for the accomplishment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
O Goddess of the Suras, there are the Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and Śakti seeds.
May Vāgbhava protect my head, and likewise may Kāmarāja protect my heart.
May the seed-syllable of Śakti always protect me at the navel, the secret place, and the feet;
may Bālā, with "Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ," protect my face for the attainment of all perfections.
May *hasaiṃ*, *hasakalarīṃ*, and *hasauḥ* protect Bhairavī from the region of the throat; may Sundarī protect the region of the navel, and may Kāmakalā always protect the head.
May Mahātripurasundarī protect me in the space between my eyebrows and nose; may Subhagā protect me on the forehead, and Bhagā from the region of the throat.
May Bhagodayā protect [me] in the heart, Bhagasarpiṇī in the belly, Bhagamālā in the region of the navel, and Manobhavā in the generative organ. 8.
May the auspicious Mahādevī, the sovereign of the kings of kings, protect [me] in the secret place;
may Jagadambikā, whose form is consciousness, protect [me] in the two feet.
Nārāyaṇī, who brings auspiciousness in all limbs and in every undertaking,
and likewise Brahmāṇī and Vaiṣṇavī— may they protect me in the east and the south.
May Vārāhī protect [me] in the west, and Maheśvarī in the north;
may Kaumārī protect in the southeast, and Mahālakṣmī in the southwest.
May Cāmuṇḍā protect [me] in the northwest; may Indrāṇī protect in the northeast.
May Mahāmāyā protect in the water; may Sarvamaṅgalā protect on the earth.
May Varadā protect in the sky; may Bhuvaneśvarī protect everywhere in the world.
This armor of the Goddess is difficult to obtain even for the gods;
one should recite it, having risen at dawn, pure and with a restrained mind.
For him there shall be no mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor shall there be fear anywhere;
likewise, he shall have no fear of pestilence nor fear of sins.
One shall not fall under the power of poverty, nor shall one remain under the power of death;
one shall go to the city of Śiva, O Goddess—I tell you the truth, the absolute truth. (15)
O Dear One, he who recites the Śrīvidyā without knowing this armor does not obtain its fruit; instead, he shall suffer the stroke of a weapon.
Thus ends the Śrīvidyā-kavaca in the Siddhayāmala. Now begins the Mahātripurasundarī-kavaca.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, who bestows grace upon the worlds; O Mahādeva, by your favor, many mantras have been heard by me in various ways. (1)
O Lord, I have heard from you, O Master, about various means of accomplishment (sādhana), as well as the extraction of ritual pegs (kīlaka) and the removal of defects such as curses.
The armor (kavaca) of the Goddess Rājarājeśvarī has been indicated by me;
O Lord, I desire to hear it from you, so please tell it to me.
The Lord said: "O Goddess, you have been restrained by me again and again hundreds of thousands of times; yet, O beloved, due to the nature of women, you ask me once more."
This armor is an absolute secret that bestows the fruit of all desires;
O Goddess of the gods, I shall tell it for your pleasure—listen to it.

Of this armor-mantra (kavaca) of the sixteen-fold knowledge (ṣoḍaśī-vidyā) of the Sovereign Queen of the Kings of Queens, the Illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, Mahādeva is the seer (ṛṣi), the Prastārapaṅkti is the meter (chandas), the Sovereign Queen of the Kings,
the Illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the accomplishment of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha). || 6 ||
May Bhairavī protect me in the east; may Bālā protect me in the south;
may Mālinī protect me in the west; and may Trāsinī protect me in the north.
May Mahādevī Mahātripurasundarī protect [me] above;
may Deveśī, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla, protect [me] below.
May Vāgbhava protect my foundation; likewise, may Kāmarāja protect my heart;
and may Ḍāmara, the granter of all desires, eternally protect my head. (9)
May the Blessed Goddess Mahāvidyā, the Supreme Sovereign, protect me always at the aperture of Brahmā, in all my limbs, and in every location of the body's openings. 10.
Aiṃ Klīṃ may protect my forehead; Hrīṃ Blūṃ Saḥ may protect my two eyes;
Drāṃ Draīṃ Drāṃ Drīṃ may protect my nose and ears, as well as my chin;
Sauḥ may protect my throat, and Sahrīṃ may protect my heart and the region of my navel. || 11 ||
May *kalahrīṃ klīṃ strīṃ* protect my secret place; may *sahrīṃ* protect my feet;
may *sahahrīṃ* protect me everywhere; and may *saklīṃ* protect my joints. || 12 ||
In the water, on land, in the sky, in the cardinal directions, and likewise in the royal palace—
may Tvaritā protect me with *hūṃ kṣe māṃ*, together with *hrīṃ* and *klīṃ*, she who is born of the mind.
May Haṃsā protect me; may Mahādevī, the supreme partless deity, Vijayā, Maṅgalā, Dūtī, Kalyāṇī, Bhagamālinī, Jvālā, Mālinī, and Nityā—the auspicious Śivā—protect me at all times. (14)
Thus, O Goddess, this armor, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, has been declared by me out of affection for you; it must be guarded with great effort. (15)
This is the supreme secret, dear one, more hidden than the hidden;
it is auspicious, bestowing wealth, fame, long life, enjoyment, and liberation. (16)
O Goddess, O Śivā, it destroys the evil dreams of men, brings men and women under one's control, effects attraction, and performs the rites of immobilization and eradication.
Without knowing this armor-mantra, whoever worships Śivā, the Queen of the Queens of Kings, along with the hosts of Yoginīs, will be devoured by them; of this there is no doubt. (18)
O Śaṅkarī, he shall never attain success in mantra;
in this world, he shall suffer poverty, disease, suffering, and fear,
and in the next world, having gone to hell, he shall enter the womb of a beast.
Therefore, one should practice this constantly; from that, one shall become qualified.
Whoever recites this highly meritorious armor-mantra (kavaca), which has issued from my own mouth, according to the prescribed rite before the ritual of worship,
shall enjoy auspiciousness, prosperity, and delights, and finally attain the state of the Goddess.
That, moreover, occurs at the time of death. || 20 ||
Thus ends the Kavaca (Armor) of the Sixteen-Syllable Vidyā of Tripurasundarī in the Kulānanda Saṃhitā.
Now begins the Stotra of Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā.
At the navel is a pure lotus, red like a shimmering bandhūka flower;
within its center is a radiant solar disc, and therein is the great yoni-cakra. In its midst is Pradyumna, engaged in inverted sexual union with his beloved standing behind him.
Śivā, whose essential nature is a splendor shining like ten million rising suns. || 1 ||

In her left hand she holds a severed head, and in her other hand a great knife; she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, with garments reaching to the ends of the quarters and her mass of hair disheveled;
drinking the stream of blood gushing from her own severed head, she is the Supreme Goddess.
She shines with three eyes that gleam with a radiance equal to the rising sun.

[He beholds] his own power (ātma-śakti) in the form of a woman (varṇinī), red in color with reddish hair, naked, of fierce appearance, adorned with bones, holding a gleaming knife in her lotus-like hand, and loudly feeding [her]— other than with her left [hand]— with many thick streams of flowing blood.
The Yoginī Yoganidrā, with one leg extended in the *pratyālīḍha* posture and eyes reddened with passion. || 3 ||
Clad in the directions as her garment, with disheveled hair, possessing a form as terrible as a mass of clouds at the time of universal dissolution,
she is fierce; her fangs are formidable, and the tips of her flickering tongues flash from the cavity of her mouth and belly, which are difficult to behold.

She whose pair of eyes flicker like lightning, who is terrifying with the serpent gliding upon the slope of her heart, and who possesses a beautiful form—she who instantly increases the Ḍākinī with the blood flowing from her own severed throat. || 4 ||

Her inconceivable form is meditated upon day after day, without ceasing, by the foremost of yogis who know the Self— by Brahmā, Īśāna, Acyuta, and others, whose magnificent lotus-feet have been placed upon their heads.

With my mind, I meditate upon Chinnamastā— the essence of saṃsāra, the mother of the three worlds, the most praiseworthy, the beloved, the bestower of desired objects, and the remover of the impurities of the Kali age—
she who assumes a threefold form to effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.

I meditate with my mind upon that primordial Prakṛti, for the complete attainment of all goals— she who is the transformation of the three qualities (guṇas) of the world, and from whom Brahmā, Acyuta, and the Trident-bearer (Śiva) arise;
she whose pair of smiling lotus feet the immortals enjoy as their great gain.
I am devoted to the yoga-worship of liquor, meat, and the wives of others;
I am honored by the undertaking of the various dispositions of many kinds of people; I am detached from the common folk; I am established in Bhairavī; I am devoted to the feet of the Guru.
I am Bhairava; I am Śiva. || 7 ||
This hymn, which bestows all accomplishments and directly destroys even the greatest sins, was spoken by Brahmā in ancient times; it is of great merit. (8)
O Goddess, whether one recites this upon rising in the morning or even while in the presence of the Goddess, for such a person there shall be success that grants all desired aims.
Wealth, grain, a son, a wife, a horse, an elephant, the earth,
and great knowledge— one shall certainly attain these eight perfections.

Upon her feet—which are adorned with tiger skins, beautified by their own calves, lovely, possessing hanging bellies, short, and blessed with indescribable joints; which are decorated with rows of severed heads;
and which hold a knife with the luster of jasmine, wonderful and graceful, as well as the state of primordial wisdom—[I bow].
O Mother, compassionate toward your devotees, O Mahāmāyā, let there be salutation unto you! || 11 ||
Thus ends the hymn to Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā.
Now follows the armor (kavaca) of Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of my life, those various mantras of Acchinnamastā which were spoken by you, my protector, and kept well-guarded, have now been heard and mastered by me.
Now I desire to hear the armor (kavaca) previously mentioned;
O Lord, let the armor named Trailokyavijaya be told.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess of gods, you who are saluted by all the deities; I shall proclaim the armor known as Trailokyavijaya, which deludes the entire universe.
Consisting of all vidyās and directly bestowing victory over gods and asuras,
by its retention and recitation, the Lord, the all-pervading one, becomes a conqueror of the three worlds.
O Goddess of the gods, because of its retention and recitation, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Rudra become the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the worlds.
This should not be given to the disciples of others, nor especially to those who lack devotion;
it should be given to a devoted disciple who is dearer to one than even one's own life.
Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi) of the armor (kavaca) of the Goddess Chinnamastā;
the meter is Virāṭ, and the deity is Chinnamastakā.
The application for Trailokyavijaya and for liberation has been proclaimed.
May the syllable HŪṂ protect my head—Chinnamastā, who possesses the splendor of power.
May the three-syllabled mantra *hrāṃ hrūṃ aiṃ* protect the forehead, and may she who is clothed in the directions (*digambarī*) protect the face.
May *śrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ aiṃ* protect the two eyes, as does she who bears a garland of severed heads.
May that Vidyā, beginning and ending with the Praṇava, protect the pair of Śrutis forever:
*vajravairocanīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, preceded by the Dhruva.
May she who holds a severed head and a chopper protect the nose:
Śrī-māyā-kūrca-vāg-bījaiḥ vajra-vairocanīye hūṃ. (11)
HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ! This is the sixteen-syllable great vidyā, whose form is that of Brahmā;
she is clad in bark garments at her side, joyfully making [the practitioner] drink a stream of blood.
May Chinnamastā, together with her own Śakti, protect my face at all times—she who holds a severed head and a sword, who is red in hue, and who grants the desires of the practitioner. (13)
May she, together with Varṇinī and Ḍākinī, protect me from all sides; may Ramā and the others protect my tongue, and may Lajjā and the others protect my throat.
May the Vidya beginning with *kūrca* protect the heart; may the Vidya beginning with *vāk* protect the pair of breasts; and may the Sureśvarī, the Vidyā encased by *ramā*, protect the two sides. 15.
May she who is encircled by Māyā protect me at the region of the navel;
may the goddess who is encircled by Kūrca always protect me at the region of the back. 16.
May she, encased by the seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja) and accompanied by her Śakti, protect the center.
O Vajravairocanīye, HŪṂ! May the Sovereign (Īśvarī), with the Kūrca and Vāgbīja syllables, [protect you]. || 17 ||
HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ! May Chinnamastā, the Great Vidyā whose radiance is equal to ten million suns, together with her Śakti, ever protect my two thighs. 18.
Hrīṃ hrūṃ Varṇinī [protects] the knees; śrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ and Ḍākinī [protect] the feet.
May she who abides in all vidyās and is eternal always protect all my limbs. (19)
May the Yoginī Ekaliṅgā protect me in the east;
may Ḍākinī protect me in the southeast, and may Śrī Mahābhairavī protect me in the south.
May Bhairavī protect [her] constantly in the southwest;
may Indrākṣī protect in the west; and may Asitāṅgī protect in the northwest and in the north.
May Saṃhāriṇī, always accompanied by her instrument (the axe), protect the northeast corner;
thus may these eight Śaktis, together with their instruments, protect the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Kṛīṃ kṛīṃ kṛīṃ: may she protect me in the east; hūṃ hūṃ: may she protect me in the southeast;
hrīṃ hrīṃ: may she protect me in the south; and may Kālikā protect me in the south.
May *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protect me in the southwest, and may *hrūṃ hrūṃ* protect me in the west;
may *hūṃ hūṃ* protect me in the northwest, and may *svāhā* always protect me in the north. (24)
May Mahākālī, holding a sword in her hand, protect [me] forever in the northeast corner.
Tāra, Māyā, Vadhū, Kūrca, and Phaṭ—this is the Great Mantra (mahāmanu). || 25 ||
May Tārā, bearing a sword and a chisel, always protect the upper region;
and may the virtuous Ekajaṭā, with the syllables *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, protect me in the netherworld (*pātāla*);
and may Mahānīlasarasvatī, together with Tārā, protect me from the sky.
Thus has been told to you the armor (kavaca) of the Goddess, which is the embodiment of mantra;
by wearing and reciting it, Bhīma became known as the Bhairava named Krodha.
He himself becomes the creator and destroyer of the lords of gods, asuras, and sages;
by his command, Madhumatī goes to the presence of each practitioner.
The Ḍākinīs beginning with Bhūtinī and the sky-faring Yakṣiṇīs and others receive his command by the grace of that armor-mantra.
This very supreme Brahma-armor, uttered from my own mouth,
one should recite once after having worshipped the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings, using the root mantra alone.
One shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for a year by writing this [mantra] on birch bark and placing it within a pill set in gold. (31)
If one, restrained in speech, should wear it on the right arm or around the neck,
having become endowed with all sovereign powers, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
Lakṣmī shall dwell in his home and Vāṇī in his lotus-like face;
even weapons such as the Brahmāstra become harmless upon his body.
He who worships Chinnamastā without knowing this account will also meet death swiftly by the stroke of a weapon. || 34 ||
Thus ends the *Chinnamastā-kavaca* in the *Bhairava-tantra*. Now begins the *Śyāmā-stotra*:
The seed-syllable [HRĪM] is formed by the letter *ma* (the middle of the vowels), devoid of its own vowel, joined with the moon (*i*) and the left eye (*ī*).
O Mother, for those who recite this hymn to the destroyer of Tripura three times,
words— both prose and verse— spontaneously flow forth from the cavity of their mouths,
as they attain all perfections, shining with a luster as beautiful as a dark rain-cloud.
O Great Goddess, if a person of dull intellect, with a mind fixed on duality, should ever recite even once this other seed-mantra of Maheśa— namely Īśāna, encircled by the moon and the left ear—
he shall conquer the Lord of Speech and Dhanada for a long time.
While the crescent-moon-crested Lord, who wears the most terrible Rāva as his ear-ornament, prevails, he causes the multitude of lotus-eyed women to swoon with longing for food.

O Kālikā with disheveled hair, those who mutter your seed-syllable— the Lord (Īśa) situated in Vaiśvānara, joined with the left eye of the moon-bearer (Śiva)— as well as your other pair [of syllables],
slay their enemies and bring even the three worlds under their control.
"O Kālikā, whose face bears two streams of blood from the pair of corners of her mouth! || 3 ||

O Mother Kālikā, who removes the sins of the world, those who recite this name of Yours, or who maintain this power of Your mantra— [to them You grant] a sword in the upper left palm, a severed head below it, and likewise the gestures of fearlessness and boon in the right hand.
Of these, eight are held in the hands of Tryambaka, who has revealed his face; they are his supernatural powers (siddhis). || 4 ||

O Mother, Consort of the Destroyer of Smara, those who recite the mantra beginning with the first letter of the [first] group situated in fire (ra), followed by the three letters encircled by the moon (u-u-u), then the two Kūrca-bījas (huṃ-huṃ), the pair of Lañjās (strī-strī), and finally the two syllables "smi-ta" joined beneath "tvad," while meditating upon Your true nature— they [attain liberation].
Those whose eyes are like the petals of the lotus that serves as the stage for Lakṣmī’s dance become masters of their own form at will. || 5 ||
Whether individually, in pairs, or even all three together, they recite while constantly meditating upon the supreme seed-syllable, which is utterly secret, joined with Your name. For them,
Kamalā dwells within the lotus of their eyes, and Vāgdevī resides in the orb of the moon that is their face.
[She is] endowed with a divine garland of skulls, a neck exceedingly radiant, and full breasts. || 6 ||

I bow to you, who have the multitude of arms of the lifeless as your girdle, whose hips are radiant, who are clothed in the directions, who are the creator of the three worlds, and who possess three eyes;
you who are engaged in amorous play with Mahākāla upon a bed of corpses in a cremation ground, resting on the heart of a dead body.
Even one of dull intellect becomes a poet by meditating upon the Mother. || 7 ||

They always meditate upon you, the youthful consort of Hara, who have entered the cremation ground— filled with auspicious yet terrible heaps of corpses and collections of skulls and bones— and who remains there contented, sporting intensely in amorous union above it.
Nowhere do they suffer any humiliation. || 8 ||
O Mother, what more shall we say? We are dull-witted; neither the Creator, nor Īśvara, nor even Hari knows Your supreme nature.
Nevertheless, O Dark One, our devotion to You makes us loquacious; this must be forgiven.
Indeed, anger toward animals is appropriate. || 9 ||
If a devotee, at night, recites your mantra while attached to a young woman who possesses full, swelling breasts and hips, even if he is naked,
meditating on you with disheveled hair, she and all others will come under his control.
The poet who has attained perfection lives for a very long time on this earth. || 10 ||
If one recites [the mantra] in the reverse order while always contemplating you as the supreme Great Kāla in the act of love,
then for that wise man wandering upon the surface of the earth, [you] will become submissive in his lotus-hand.
The multitudes of Siddhis, the consorts of Śiva. || 11 ||
O Mother, Blessed One, you give birth to the cycle of existence, you protect the entire world beginning with the earth,
and at the time of dissolution, you withdraw it all; therefore, you are indeed the Creator, the Lord of the three worlds, the Consort of Śrī, and, alas, the Great Lord himself.
Why should I praise you, who are everything? || 12 ||
Many hosts of gods serve the consort of Hara, yet they are deluded at heart; O Mother, they do not know Your supreme nature at all.
I have taken refuge in You, the primordial one who is worshipped by the wise, such as Hari, Hara, and Viriñci.
She was spontaneously intent upon the great bliss of the essence of passion.
The earth, the water, the pure fire, the wind, and the sky—you alone are the auspicious Kali, the beloved of Śiva, the all-encompassing.
What praise can be offered to you, O Mother? Out of your compassion, may you be gracious toward me who have no other refuge.
May there be no further birth for me in existence. || 14 ||

O Mahākālī, staying in a cremation ground, composed, with matted hair, wearing a garment of directions, and reciting your mantra one thousand times with flowers whose potency has been shed by the sun,
he who is absorbed in meditation upon you may wander at will.
He becomes a sovereign ruler of the earth. || 15 ||
If one takes a flower whose vitality has been drained by sweeping in the house, roots and all,
at midday on a Tuesday and offers it upon a funeral pyre while reciting the mantra even once with love, he shall always travel mounted upon an elephant.
The sovereign of the earth was a preeminent and virtuous poet. || 16 ||
If a devotee, meditating again and again upon the temple of the Flower-Bowed God (Kāmadeva), which is filled with its own blossoms, recites your mantra before him,
he will eventually become like a lord of the Gandharva hosts, a river for the nectar of poetry.
Absorbed in the supreme state, he becomes manifest. || 17 ||
On the seat of the fifteen-spoked wheel, upon the heart of a corpse and a *śiva*, she whose face is smiling,
who is intensely bound by the beauty of the essence of passion with Mahākāla—
whosoever, himself devoted to the bliss of love at night, should meditate upon you; [He shall attain the supreme state.]
O Mother, he would be the destroyer of Smara (Kāma). || 18 ||

May all perfections be attained by those virtuous ones dwelling among mortals who offer you as an oblation for worship even the flesh of a lizard, a bone, a fruit, a cat, or further, a camel, a goat, a sheep, a man, a buffalo, or even a goat.
On every step, something unprecedented comes forth. || 19 ||
The self-controlled practitioner, intent on consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya), should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day,
skillful in meditating upon the pair of your feet, O Mother; furthermore, at night, naked and engaged in the pleasure of sexual union, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
On the surface of the earth, he was equal to the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva).
O Mother, whoever recites this hymn called *Manusamuddhāraṇajanu-svarūpa*, which includes the ritual procedure for worshipping Your pair of lotus feet—
whether at midnight or during the time of worship— even their mere prattle [shall bear fruit].
The nectar-like essence of poetry flows forth. || 21 ||
A multitude of fawn-eyed women follows him, trembling with love; even the lord of the earth, a rival to Kubera, is under his sway;
and his enemy, by the mere play of his pastimes, casts himself into prison—may he live long as one liberated while yet alive.
He becomes one who is devoted to the True Being in every birth. || 22 ||
Thus ends the Śyāmāstotra composed by Mahākāla.
Now follows her armor (kavaca).
Bhairavī said:
O Lord, the worship of Kālī has been heard, as well as its various dispositions, O Master;
now I wish to hear the armor (kavaca) previously mentioned. || 1 ||
You alone are indeed the creator, the protector, and the destroyer;
you alone are my refuge, O Lord—protect me from this peril of suffering.
Bhairava said:
Listen to the secret, O Bhairavī, beloved of my life;
I shall declare the armor named Śrījaganmaṅgala, which is the very embodiment of mantra.
By reciting and retaining it, one may delude the three worlds in an instant;
even Nārāyaṇa, having held it, became a woman before Maheśvara. || 4 ||
Having seized the Lord of Yoga, the best of the Raghus brought him to agitation,
and he indeed slew the night-stalkers such as Rāvaṇa, who were arrogant because of the boons they had received.
By whose grace even the Lord, the all-pervading conqueror of the three worlds,
became the lord of wealth, Kubera, and even the lord of the gods, the husband of Śacī.
For thus, O beloved, all the gods who are lords of all supernatural powers [are subject to it];
moreover, Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor-verse (kavaca) known as the Śrījaganmaṅgala.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Kālikā, and she is said to be on the right. || 8 ||
Its application is proclaimed for enchanting the worlds, for overcoming the wicked, for the attainment of worldly enjoyment and liberation, and indeed for the attraction of women. || 9 ||
Oṃ, may Kālikā protect my head; the supreme single-syllable mantra Krīṃ, and Kālikā, the bearer of the sword, [protect] my forehead with Krīṃ Krīṃ Krīṃ. || 10 ||
Hūṃ hūṃ, may she protect my pair of eyes; hrīṃ hrīṃ, may she protect my two ears. O Maheśvarī, may Kālikā protect my pair of nostrils on the right.
KṚĪM KṚĪM KṚĪM may protect the tongue; HRŪM HRŪM may protect the cheeks;
HRĪM HRĪM SVĀHĀ, she whose form is her own essence, may protect the entire face. 12.
The twenty-two-syllable Mahāvidyā, Kālī, who holds a sword and a severed head, may she protect me on all sides with her entire body. 13.
May the three-syllabled mantra *krīṃ hūṃ krīṃ* protect my heart; may Cāmuṇḍā protect it.
May *aiṃ hūṃ oṃ aiṃ* protect my pair of breasts, and *hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā* protect the region of the nape of the neck.
May the great eight-syllabled vidyā, together with the hand-attributes, protect my two arms;
may the six-syllabled mantra—krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ—protect my hands.
KṚĪṂ protects the navel and the middle region; may Kālikā protect [the area] on the right. KṚĪṂ SVĀHĀ protects the back; that ten-syllabled mantra is Kālikā. (16)
"Kṛīṃ! May my secret always be protected; obeisance then to Kālikā.
This seven-syllabled great vidyā is concealed in all tantras. (17)
Hrīṃ hrīṃ, may Kālikā protect [me] on the right; hūṃ hūṃ, may she protect both hips.
Oṃ kālī daśākṣarī vidyā svāhā, may this ten-syllable mantra protect the pair of my thighs.
Oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ me svāhā—may Kālikā always protect [me] at the knees.
This is the Heart-Vidyā of Kālī, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. || 19 ||
KṚĪṂ HRĪṂ HRĪṂ may she protect my right ankle; may Kālikā protect [it].
KṚĪṂ HŪṂ HRĪṂ SVĀHĀ—may this fourteen-syllable mantra protect my feet.
May Kālī, who bears a sword and a severed head, the bestower of boons and the remover of fear, protect every limb on all sides with all her vidyās. 21.
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, Vipracittā, as well as Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, Dīptā, and Ghanatviṣā. || 22 ||
