Nīlā, Ghanā, Bālākā, Mātrā, and Mudrāmitā—these are all my [consorts], bearing swords and adorned with garlands of severed heads. (23)
May Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, and Aparājitā protect me in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (24)
May Vārāhī and Nārasiṃhī, and all those adorned with immeasurable ornaments, protect me in every direction with their own weapons, in whatever manner may be fitting. (25)
Thus has been narrated to you this divine armor, most wonderful by name, the auspiciousness of the entire world, which embodies the flood of great vidyās.
O Brahmin, one should perform the worship of the Guru according to the rules and then recite this armor-mantra (kavaca), which attracts the three worlds, as uttered from my own mouth. (27)
One may recite this armor-mantra (kavaca) three times, once, or even throughout one's entire life; by repeating it fifty times, one shall become the conqueror of the three worlds.
By the grace of this armor-mantra, one truly agitates the three worlds;
within a month, one becomes a great poet and shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should offer a handful of flowers to Kālikā once with the root mantra alone;
one shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for a hundred thousand years.
If one should wear this written on birch bark or placed within gold— whether worn on the crest-lock, on the right arm, or around the neck— (it shall grant protection).

Through his wrath he may delude the three worlds, and in an instant he may pulverize the three worlds; endowed with splendor, he shall become a treasury of various sciences for the sake of his sons and kinsmen.
Furthermore, weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others meet their destruction by the mere touch of her body; and whatever woman is barren or whose children have died [is likewise restored]. (33)
By wearing this armor on the neck or on the left arm, a woman will surely have many children who survive; of this there is no doubt. (34)
This should not be given to the disciples of others, and especially not to those who lack devotion;
it should be given to disciples endowed with devotion, otherwise one will meet with death.
Having aroused a rivalry in the abode of Kamalā and Vāgdevī—his own mouth—he certainly dwells there, maintaining his steadfastness until the end of his grandson's lineage. (36)
If one recites the Kālī-dakṣiṇā mantra without knowing this armor (kavaca), even after reciting it a hundred thousand times,
his mantra will not be perfected;
he will suffer the blow of weapons and shall soon meet his death.
Thus ends the Śyāmā-kavaca in the Kālī-kalpa, within the Bhairava-tantra, from the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
Now follows the Tārā-stotra.

O Mother Nīlasarasvatī, bestower of the wealth of good fortune upon those who bow to you, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon the heart of a corpse, with a smiling lotus-face, eyes like full-blown blue lotuses,
three eyes, and holding a flaying knife, a skull-cup, a lotus, and a sword— [I salute you].
You alone are my refuge; I take shelter in you, the Sovereign Lady. || 1 ||

O Mistress of speech, O wish-fulfilling creeper of devotion, O Sovereign of the accomplishment of all aims, O Bestower of success in all matters concerning the composition of prose, Prakrit, and verse!
You who are endowed with three eyes like blue lotuses, O ocean of the waters of compassion!
Out of compassion, sprinkle those like us with the nectar that increases good fortune. || 2 ||
O you whose body is filled with a multitude of dwarf-like pride, radiant in the guise of a serpent and others, adorned with bells shaken upon a beautiful waist girt with a tiger-skin,
and dripping with dust from a recently severed [limb]—
O terrifying one, who is beautiful with a garland of human skulls and rows of knotted hair from two rubbed-together heads, destroy my fear! 3.

O you who consist of the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, marked by the illusory body, the limbs of passion, the form of a woman, the *vindu*, and the half-moon—you alone, whose essence is mantra, are the refuge for one such as me. O Mother, your form is fashioned from the three abodes; it is gross, subtle, and supreme, yet it brings no pain.
How can I possibly take refuge in her who has somehow come within the range of my perception? || 4 ||
By serving your lotus feet, those of meritorious deeds attain union with her,

whose nature is equal to the illustrious Supreme Lord, the three-eyed Śiva, Brahmā, and others; for you, O Mother, are the one who brings down even the gods headed by Indra, whose bodies are so intent on drowning in the ocean of saṃsāra.
For why would one of dull intellect serve those who are themselves deluded regarding the service of the feet? || 5 ||
O Mother, those gods whose crowns are marked by the seal of the pollen from your two lotus feet have entered your lap without fear, victorious in the battle for conquest;
while others, bearing the rivalry that "I am a god in this world, there is no one equal to me," remain outside.
Just as the moon and sun inevitably meet their own destruction when they become equal [in strength].
By the mere remembrance of your name,
the hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and yakṣas, as well as the lords of the nāgas,
the foremost of the daityas and dānavas, the sky-dwellers, animals such as tigers, and the ḍākinīs, become intent on fleeing and are unable even to look at you.
And O Mother, when the Destroyer is enraged, he destroys human beings on the surface of the earth in an instant.

O Mother, O lady of excellent limbs, by serving your feet, those various powers— prosperity, the hosts of Siddhas, the Siddhas beginning with the Pādukā, the paralyzing of enemies, the paralyzing of elephant herds, and even enchantment— truly become accomplished for men; indeed, there is no weariness.
O beloved, even a person of small intellect becomes a master of speech here through the power of love. || 8 ||
The man who, being devoted, pure, and self-restrained, recites this meritorious *Tārāṣṭaka* in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, [attains the supreme goal].
One obtains poetic skill and learning, becoming a knower of the meaning of all scriptures;
having attained imperishable fortune and enjoyed pleasures as desired,
one attains fame, splendor, freedom from disease, and the state of being beloved by all.
Having attained renown in the worlds as well, one shall obtain liberation at the end.
Thus ends the Tārāṣṭaka in the Nīlatantra. Now follows the Tārākavaca. The Lord said:
Indeed, this knowledge that liberates from the greatest fear is to be kept secret within the Koṭi-tantras;
listen now to her divine armor, which grants all desires.

For the Tārākavaca: Akṣobhya is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the Blessed Lady Tārā is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is in recitation for the attainment of success in all mantras.
May the Praṇava protect my head—Maheśvarī, whose form is Brahman.
May Maheśvarī, in the form of the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, protect [me] on the forehead. || 2 ||
May the syllable *strīṃ*, Maheśvarī in the form of modesty, always reside in my mouth;
may the syllable *hūṃ*, bearing the form of the power (śakti) of Bhavānī, protect my heart. (3)
May Phaṭkāra protect all my limbs, bestowing the fruit of all accomplishments;
may Kharvā, the Goddess of the gods who removes fear, protect me on both cheeks. (4)
May the great goddess Lambodarī always protect me with her pair of shoulders;
may the goddess, the beloved of Śiva, who is clothed in a tiger skin, protect my waist.
May the Great Goddess, whose breasts are full and uplifted, protect [us] at both flanks;
and may she, whose eyes are red and round, always protect us at the region of the waist.
May Lalajjihvā, the Mistress of the World, always protect me at the navel;
may the goddess Karālāsyā, the beloved of Hara, always protect me at the linga.
May Piṅgograikajaṭā, the destroyer of obstacles, protect [me] at the shanks;
may the Goddess Maheśvarī, holding a skull-bowl, protect [me] at the circle of the knees. (8)
May she who is blue in color always protect my knees at all times;
may the Goddess, wearing serpent-earrings, protect the pair of my feet thereafter. || 9 ||
May the Goddess, wearing a necklace of serpents, protect every limb at all times;
may the Goddess, wearing serpent-bracelets, protect from the intermediate regions. || 10 ||
May the four-armed goddess, the destroyer of enemies, always protect me while walking;
may the great goddess, sword in hand, always protect me at the time of hearing. 11.
May the Goddess who wears blue garments and destroys obstacles protect me;
may she, with a knife in her hand, always protect me from enemies in the midst of a dispute. 12.
May the Goddess, assuming the form of Brahmā, protect me always in battle;
may the Goddess, wearing serpent-bracelets, protect me always at the time of eating. 13.
May the great goddess Śavakarṇā protect [me] always on the bed;
may the goddess Vīrāsanadharā protect [me] always during sleep. (14)
May the Goddess, bearing bow and arrow, protect me amidst the multitude of obstacles;
may the Goddess, whose waist is adorned with serpents, protect me in all undertakings. 15.
May the Goddess, bearing severed heads, protect [me] always in the forest;
may the Goddess, stationed in the midst of the funeral pyre, protect [me] always during the act of slaying. || 16 ||
May the Goddess who wears a leopard skin, who bestows sons, wives, wealth, and so forth, and who is adorned with ornaments—the beloved of Hara—protect me. 17.
"Protect, protect! O Great Goddess, who is the form of the seed-syllable, accompanied by 'hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ', may you always protect [me] in the mountain forest retreats. (18)
Maṇidharā, Vajriṇī, and likewise the goddess Mahāpratisarā; protect, protect, hūṃ hūṃ! Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā! Maheśvarī! 19.
May she who is worthy of King Puṣpaketu protect me always in the forest;
Oṃ hrīṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ phaṭ—she who grants all desires in the wilderness. 20.
Oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe, may Maheśvarī protect my sons;
hūṃ svāhā, may she, joined with power, always protect my wife. || 21 ||
Oṃ āṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! May Maheśānī, the beloved of Hara, protect me in gambling.
Oṃ hrīṃ! May the Goddess who dispels all obstacles always protect me from obstacles. (22)
Oṃ, O pure vajra-ground, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
May the Goddess, the destroyer of all obstacles, protect me upon the earth. 23.
Oṃ āḥ surekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—may the goddess named Lākinī protect me in the netherworld (pātāla). 24.
May the Great Goddess in the form of Śakti, whose essence is the syllable Hrīṃ, protect me in the east;
may the Great Goddess in the form of a bride, whose essence is the syllable Strīṃ, protect me, O Queen of the Gods. (25)
May the Great Goddess, whose nature is *hūṃ* and who possesses a wrathful form, protect me;
may Mahāmāyā, whose nature is *phaṭ*, always protect me in the north. (26)

May the Goddess, whose nature is the syllable *phaṭ* and who is the consort of Hara, protect me in the west; may the Queen of Gods, whose nature is the syllable *hūṃ* and who is the daughter of the Mountain, protect me in the center. (27)
May she who is blue in color and ever consists of the Vāgbhava syllable protect me everywhere;
may Bhavānī, the bestower of all sovereignty, protect me in my home. (28)
May the Goddess Sarasvatī, who delights in the gift of knowledge, protect my mouth—[and me] in scripture, in debate, in battle, in water, and on treacherous mountains. 29.
May Durgā, who is of terrifying form and the dispeller of fear, always protect me in the cremation ground; may the formidable one protect me in the dreadful abode of spirits and ghosts.
O Great Goddess, may Śivadūtī protect me eternally everywhere.
As for the majesty of this armor, I am unable to describe it even in hundreds of years.
O Goddess, I am able to describe the fruit that arises from this for one's sons, wives, kinsmen, and throughout every land at all times. (32)
He for whom there is no fear shall be honored by kings;
whether pure or impure, this armor grants all desires.
O Maheśānī, by reciting or remembering this, a mortal becomes free from suffering and grief, and certainly becomes a supreme poet in all scriptures. (34)
A mortal becomes a master of all speech, a lord of wealth who holds the world in his power;
in battle, at dice, and in debate, victory shall be certain for him there. (35)
The mortal man, endowed with sons and grandsons, becomes an enjoyer of all women;
his enemies become his servants, and he is always beloved by everyone. (36)
The proud become humble, the disputant falters at the mere sight [of her], death comes under her control, and the lords of the earth become her servants. (37)
All this has been recounted as an incidental discourse; this armor grants all desires.
By reciting or remembering it, a mortal becomes capable of both inflicting curses and bestowing grace.
He shall become a sovereign lord of oceans of blissful multitudes, a preeminent poet, a master of all speech, a subduer of the world, and forever happy. (39)
Having obtained the grace of the Guru and acquired the well-guarded lore—even therein, O Goddess, the armor is difficult to find within the three worlds. (40)
The Guru is the god Hara himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara;
for him who worships them without making any distinction between them, spiritual perfection is not far off.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, the practices of mantra have been described as before;
one should likewise contemplate the light at the navel and the face above the heart.
O Maheśānī, the king, a great lord of speech, possesses sovereignty and the skill of a great poet; he should always engage in the company of women.
A mortal who delights in the fivefold conduct becomes a Siddha, and not otherwise;
a mortal who is joined with Śakti becomes a Siddha, and not otherwise. || 44 ||
O Goddess, upon seeing that practitioner, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all those who are gods, asuras, and humans, become filled with shame. (45)
O Goddess, those deities who bestow success in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld always praise that supreme practitioner upon seeing him.
And all those gods who are of the nature of obstacles, whether in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld, always praise that supreme practitioner upon seeing him. (47)
Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess, fully proclaimed by me;
it is the direct embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 48.
Having approached and propitiated the primordial Guru, whoever— whether free from delusion or pride, or even joined with dullness— takes up this support of the wish-fulfilling tree,
that person becomes perfected on earth and reaches the further shore of all suffering and calamities; Death itself becomes his friend.
O Goddess, the misfortunes of that king shall also quickly perish.
Upon reaching his body, weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others indeed become like garlands and flowers on earth, bringing only happiness.
Prosperity remains firm in his home, and the Goddess of Speech surely dwells in his mouth. (50)
The man who worships Tārā without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca) will certainly become short-lived, destitute, and foolish; of this there is no doubt. || 51 ||
Whoever, having written it, should wear it on the neck, on the head, or on the arm,
for him there shall be the accomplishment of all aims, whatever resides in his mind.
O Maheśānī, being composed in mind, one should write the mantra with gorocanā and saffron, or with red sandalwood, or with lac.
On the eighth day, on a Tuesday, or likewise on the fourteenth day,
O Goddess of the gods, one should, with a concentrated mind, draw the yantra at the time of twilight.
Especially under the asterisms of Maghā, Śravaṇā, or Revatī, when the moon has entered the sign of Leo and the sun is situated in Cancer. (55)
When Jupiter has entered the sign of Pisces and Saturn is situated in Scorpio,
whoever, facing north, writes [this] and wears it— || 56 ||
Whether in a cremation ground, in the wilderness, or especially in an empty house,
he who draws the yantra at night shall attain unwavering success.
O Maheśvarī, one should have the mantra written on a birch leaf by a guru;
he who wears it with devotion through the yoga of meditation and concentration [shall attain success]. || 58 ||
Success will be his before long; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 59 ||
Thus ends the Ugratārā-kavaca in the venerable Rudrayāmala Tantra. Now begins the Tārā-kavaca named Trailokyamohana. The Goddess said:
O Lord, the worship of Tārā and all the vidyās have been heard from you;
now I desire to hear the armor (kavaca), which is the embodiment of the mantra. (1)
O Lord, please reveal out of compassion that which was previously indicated to me— the one named Trailokyamohana, the warder-off of all calamities.
Bhairava said:
O beloved of my life, worshipped by gods, dānavas, and vidyādharas,
listen to the supreme armor (kavaca) named Trailokyamohana.
O Goddess, it consists of all vidyās; it is eternally composed of all mantras.
O Goddess, it provides all protection and bestows all vidyās.
Even Vedavyāsa became omniscient by holding and reciting it;
by holding and reciting it, the Lord Īśvara became the conqueror of the three worlds;
and so too did Kubera, the lord of wealth, and Śacīpati, the lord of the gods.
Because of constant recitation and retention, all the lords of the directions, being endowed with all perfections, shall attain every sovereignty. || 5 ||
O Sovereign of the Gods, by his grace I am the lord of the Bhairavas; through his wrath, I am known among the gods as the formidable master of anger.
One should not give it to the disciples of others, but should give it only to one's own disciples;
even to sons who are not devoted, for by giving it to them, one meets with death.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this armor-mantra (kavaca) that fascinates the three worlds is Śiva;
its meter (chandas) is Virāṭ, and its deity (devatā) is proclaimed to be the noble Tārā.
Its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the four aims of life and for the acquisition of knowledge. || 8 ||
Oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ may my head protect; hūṃ phaṭ may it protect my forehead;
may Tārā, whose mantra consists of five and a half syllables, protect the pair of my eyes. (9)
Oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ, may Śrūtī protect [me], and may she protect the nose;
may Tārā, adorned with a severed head, protect the face through the six-syllabled mantra.
Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ: may she protect my face; may Maheśvarī protect my tongue.
Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ: may that Nīlasarasvatī also protect my throat.
May she who takes the form of the single-syllable *Tāra* protect my two shoulders constantly;
may she who takes the form of the single-syllable seed-mantra *Hūṃ* always protect my throat.
Aiṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ—may Tārā protect my two arms;
śrīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ—may Śrītārā protect my two breasts. || 13 ||
Hrīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ—may Tārā protect my heart;
hūṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ—may the seed-syllable of Tārā always protect my back. (14)
Klīṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ—may she who is the embodiment of desire protect the two sides;
oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ namaḥ—may the Great Six-Syllabled One protect [me]. 15.
Aiṃ Sauḥ Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Phaṭ Svāhā—may this protect the region of the waist at all times.
This eight-syllabled Great Vidyā is the manifest embodiment of Brahman itself.
Khaṃ Hūṃ Hauṃ Oṃ Aiṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Sā—may she always protect the secret region.
And the seven-syllabled mantra of Ugratārā is the very nature of the root-vidyā. || 16 ||

Oṃ hrīṃ hāṃ hūṃ namas tārāyai, followed by all the words [of the mantra]; then the word "tāraya" for that which is difficult to cross, then "tāraya," then two *praṇavas* (oṃ), and finally "svāhā"—may this Great Vidyā always protect my knees. (17)
Aiṃ Sauḥ Oṃ Aiṃ Klīṃ Phaṭ Svāhā—may Parātmikā protect my shanks.
Oṃ Hrīṃ Strīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Tārā Haṃsa-ādyantā Navākṣarī;
may Mahogratārā, the Great Goddess, protect my feet eternally. (18)
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsauḥ Shauḥ, speak, speak, O Goddess of Speech!
The three Kāma-bījas constitute the very form of Nīlasarasvatī. Aiṃ Aiṃ Aiṃ, kāhi kāhi, kalarīṃ svāhā—[recite this] always.
May Tārā, consisting of thirty-four letters, protect my entire body. || 19 ||
May the ten-syllable root-vidyā—Indra, Vāmā, Akṣi, Yuk, Pṛthvī, Sarasvatī, the beloved of Anala, and those beginning and ending with Kūrca—protect me from above. (20)
Tārā, Māyā, Vadhū, Kūrca, Kālī, and then Kāmakalā; Ugratārā, Bhaga, Kāma, Parā, Lakṣmī, Śivā, and Aṅkuśa— this,
I have now declared to you, is the Mahāṣoḍaśī of the Goddess Tārā.
By receiving this according to the prescribed rule, one leads death itself onto the path of death.
This knowledge was kept secret by me in the Tantras, Ādis, and Yāmalas;
now, O beloved, it has been told to you as an ancillary part of the armor (kavaca).
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this supreme armor, more secret than the secret, named Trailokyamohana, which is the very embodiment of mantra. (23)

O auspicious lady, this armor (kavaca) which has issued from my mouth consists solely of the knowledge of Brahman and is of the nature of Brahman itself; it also consists of the knowledge of mantras. If one worships the Guru according to the prescribed rites and recites this armor, [one attains the goal].
Whether three times or once, according to his knowledge, he becomes Bhairava at that very moment.
Freed from all sins, he shall uplift ten million members of his lineage;
he shall be a guru and qualified for all vidyās, as well as for japa and other rites. || 25 ||
One hundred and eight repetitions of this are prescribed as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
By reciting it one hundred and eight times, one becomes a lord of cities upon the earth;
such a hero may wander through the three worlds like Guha, the Lord of the Gaṇas. || 26 ||
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, shall flow like the current of the Gaṅgā.
Then, having offered eight handfuls of flowers with the root mantra itself, he shall obtain the fruit of five thousand years of worship. (27)
If one writes [this mantra] on birch bark, places it inside a pill, and wears it—
on the right arm if a man, or likewise on the left arm if a woman—
that woman will have many sons, and that man will possess wealth and sons.
Having become the lord of all accomplishments, one shall roam about like Bhairava. || 28 ||

O Bhairavī, upon reaching his body, weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others become like garlands of flowers and grant him happiness; Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall certainly dwell in his home for a long time.
That base person who worships Tārā without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca) will certainly become short-lived, impoverished, and foolish; of this there is no doubt. (30)
Thus ends the Tārākavaca, named Trailokyamohana, from the Tārākalpa within the Bhairavī-Bhairava Saṃvāda.
Now follows the Bagalāmukhī Stotra.
I meditate upon Bagalāmukhī, whose beautiful cheeks are radiant with swinging golden earrings,
whose face possesses a moon-like orb with the luster of a shining golden campaka flower,
who has struck down her enemies with her mace, and whose flickering tongue moves restlessly.
She who paralyzes speech, mind, and face. || 1 ||
I bow to her who sits upon a corpse-throne in a mandala of beautiful, blooming red lotuses in the midst of the ocean of nectar; she who has cast down her enemies with the crown of her lion-throne,
who is golden-hued, who crushes the tongues of her foes with her hands, and whose mace whirls in motion.
All calamities suddenly and immediately depart from him who meditates thus upon her who bears [the world] in this manner.
O Goddess, the practitioner of mantra, having placed handfuls of yellow flowers with devotion in his left hand for the sake of worshipping your lotus feet, recites the mantra of beautiful syllables.

Then, intent on the meditation of the seat (pīṭha), one should, by means of breath-retention (kumbhaka), recollect the seed-syllable of the Earth; instantly, there shall arise dullness in the speech and heart of that enemy-faced one. || 3 ||
O Śrīnitye, when restrained by your minister, the disputant falls silent, the king becomes a pauper, fire becomes cold, the wrathful becomes tranquil, the wicked man acts like a virtuous one,
the swift pursuer limps, the arrogant becomes humble, and even the all-knowing becomes dull-witted.
O Bagalāmukhī, I offer salutations to you; I worship you every day. || 4 ||
Your mantra is sufficient for crushing adversaries; your hymn is pure; your yantra is a restraint upon disputants and is victorious over the three worlds—wondrous indeed is it!
O Mother, that living being who possesses the charming name "Śrī Bagalāmukhī" upon his lips [is truly blessed].
By the mere utterance of your name in an assembly, the mouths of disputants shall become paralyzed. || 5 ||
It is the subduer of the wicked, the pacifier of fierce obstacles, the dispeller of poverty,
and the queller of the fear of kings; it draws the hearts of fawn-eyed women and is the sole abode of good fortune for my eyes— its gaze filled with compassion.
O Mother, may your form, which brings death to Death itself, appear before me!
O Mother, shatter the faces of my adversaries; bind their tongues;
nail down the intellect of the Daityas and gods; paralyze their fierce course!
O fair-limbed Goddess clad in yellow raiment, crush the enemies with your sharp mace!
O Bagalā, full of compassion at this very moment, remove the flood of obstacles for those who bow to you. || 7 ||

O Mother Bhairavī, Bhadrakālī, Vijayā, Vārāhī, O refuge of the universe, Śrīvidyā, Samayā, Maheśī, Bagalā, Kāmeśī, Rāmā, Ramā; O Mātaṅgī, O Tripurā, O you who are higher than the highest, O bestower of heaven and liberation— I am your servant.
O Sovereign of the Universe, I have come to you for refuge; out of compassion, protect me! 8.
In a violent conflict, amidst a band of thieves, at the time of striking with weapons, in captivity, in the midst of disease,

in a debate on spells or in a verbal dispute, when the king is enraged, during the time of a divine portent, or in the night; whether for subjugation or for paralyzing, at the time of slaying an enemy, or in a solitary place or among people— [in all these, one should employ this].
Whether walking or standing, if a steadfast person recites this three times a day, he shall swiftly attain Śiva.
Whoever constantly recites this purifying hymn of the Goddess here with devotion, having likewise worn this yantra upon their arm, hand, or neck during battle—
whether they be kings, enemies, elephants blinded by rut, serpents, lions, or other such creatures— they shall indeed go [to their destruction].
The hosts of enemies are utterly deluded; Fortune is stable, and the supernatural powers are perfected.
You are the supreme knowledge, the mother of the three worlds, the destroyer of the flood of obstacles, the attractor of women, and the bestower of infatuation upon the minds of men;
you are the performer of paralyzing and expelling rites, and the bestower of delusion upon the minds of beasts.
The mantra beginning with Brahmā, [starting] from the tongue and the throat, is victorious like Bhairavī. || 11 ||

Knowledge, fortune, eternal good luck, long life, and the attainment of all imperial sovereignty through sons and grandsons; honor, enjoyment, subjugation [of others], health, and happiness have been obtained.
By that person on this very ground. || 12 ||
O Supreme Goddess, please accept this armor of recitation which has been performed for the purpose of subduing the wicked; salutations be unto you! (13)
Known as the Brahmāstra, it is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
it should be given to one who is devoted to the guru, but it must not be given to just anyone.
One should meditate upon that Bagalāmukhī, who is clad in yellow garments, has two arms and three eyes, possesses a tender body, and holds a stone mallet in her hand;
reciting this at morning and midday shall grant the accomplishment of one's goals. (15)
Thus ends the Śrī-Bagalāmukhī-stotra in the Rudrayāmala Tantra. Now begins the Mātaṅgī-kavaca. The Illustrious Goddess said:
Excellent, excellent, O Mahādeva! O Lord of the Gods, please speak the divine armor (kavaca) of Mātaṅgī, which bestows all perfections upon human beings.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious *mātaṅgī-kavaca*.
It must be kept secret, O Great Goddess; observing silence, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).

For this armor-mantra (kavaca) of Śrīmātaṅgī, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandas), Mātaṅgī is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the four aims of human life.
Oṃ: May Mātaṅginī protect my head, and may Bhuvaneśī protect my eyes.
May Tripurā sever the pair of my ears with her speech. || 3 ||
May Mahāmāyā protect my throat, and likewise Māheśvarī my heart;
may Tripurā protect my two sides, and Kāmeśvarī my anus.
Likewise, Caṇḍī is on the two thighs, Ratipriyā on the two shanks,
Mahāmāyā on the pair of feet, and Kuleśvarī on all the limbs.
May Vaiṣṇavī always protect both the limbs and the minor members;
may she who is established under the name Mātaṅgī always protect the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head).
May that Mahāpiśācinī always protect [him] on the forehead;
may the goddess Sumukhī protect the two eyes, and may she protect the nose.
May Mahāpiśācinī always protect me from behind;
may Lajjā, holding a broom in her hand, protect my teeth and lips.
O Great Goddess, may the three *ṭha* syllables, together with the *visarga*, protect the chin and the region of the throat, as well as the heart, at all times.
May the restless Lolā protect my navel; may Kālikā protect my eyes;
may Cāmuṇḍā protect my belly, and likewise may Kātyāyanī protect my generative organ.
May Ugratārā protect the anus; may Ambikā protect the feet;
may Śarvāṇī protect the arms; and may Caṇḍabhūṣaṇā protect the heart.
May Mātṛkā protect [him] on the tongue; may Puṣṭikā protect him in the east;
may Vijayā guard him in the south; may Medhā protect him in the west.
May Śraddhā protect in the southwest; may Lakṣmaṇā guard in the northwest;
and may the goddess Mātaṅgī, the performer of auspicious deeds, protect in the northeast. (13)
May the Queen of the Gods protect [me] in the southeast, and may Bagalā protect me in the north;
may the Great Goddess, who acts for the welfare of the gods, protect me from above.
May Vaśinī, who possesses universal forms, protect me eternally in the netherworld (pātāla).
Then [the mantra consists of] the Praṇava, Māyā, the Kāmabīja, and the Kūrca. || 15 ||
The mantra of Mātaṅginī, ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā) and preceded by the syllable ṅe, consists of eleven and a half syllables; may she protect me always everywhere. 16.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this supreme armor named Trailokyamaṅgala, which is more secret than the secret and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (17)
Whoever recites this constantly becomes an abode of prosperity;
he shall attain supreme and incomparable sovereignty—of this there is no doubt. || 18 ||
If one worships the Guru according to the prescribed rites and recites this armor-verse (kavaca),
one will certainly attain sovereignty, the state of being a great poet, and perfection of speech.
A Mātaṅgī woman shall always perform auspicious rites for him;
[so too shall] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and those gods who are the best of the Suras. (20)
O Goddess, upon seeing that practitioner, the Brahma-rākṣasas, Vetālas, Grahas, and other classes of spirits become filled with shame. || 21 ||
Whoever wears this armor will certainly attain all perfections;
even kings shall become his servants, and he shall accomplish the six ritual acts.
He becomes successful everywhere; what is the use of further prolixity?
Whatever man should worship Mātaṅgī without knowing this armor (kavaca), [he gains nothing]. || 23 ||

One will certainly become short-lived, destitute, and foolish; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one should always practice devotion toward the Guru and maintain a firm resolve regarding the armor-mantra (kavaca). || 24 ||
To him, the goddess Mātaṅginī bestows all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis). || 25 ||
Thus ends the armor of Mātaṅginī, which bestows the fruit of speed, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Nandyāvarta;
thus concludes the fourth chapter.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Tantrasāra* composed by the Great Preceptor Śrī Kṛṣṇānanda Bhaṭṭācārya.
The Fifth Chapter.
Now, as a supplementary topic, the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) and so forth are defined.
Next are the sixty-four ritual offerings.
The mantras for all the offerings should be preceded by the three *tāras* (oṃ āḥ hūṃ) and should end with "I prepare (*kalpayāmi namaḥ*)."
For example: 1. *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I offer water for the feet; *namaḥ*. 2. Likewise, I offer the *arghya* (water of honor); *namaḥ*. 3. [The same].
In this sequence and so forth;
likewise, in the Siddhayāmala:
"Having placed the threefold Tārā at the beginning, [one should utter] Bhuvaneśvarī for the sake of the one to whom something is to be given."
I perform the visualization; thereafter, this is the rule for the ritual offerings (upacāra). || 1 ||
4. Seating upon a throne; 5. Anointing with fragrant oil; 6.
Entry into the bathing hall.
Seating upon a jeweled pedestal in the bathing pavilion (8);
divine bath-powder for massage (9);
bathing with warm water (10).
11. The consecration by bathing with the waters of all sacred fords contained within a golden pitcher; 12. Polishing with a washed cloth;
13. Dressing in a dawn-colored silk garment.
14. A red silk upper garment;
15. Entry into the pavilion for the unguent; 16. Seating upon the jeweled throne for the unguent.
Anointing all the limbs with divine fragrances such as sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, musk, camphor, musk-pouch, and yellow pigment (rocanā) [17];
and for the mass of hair, incense of black agallochum along with jasmine, mālatī, jātī, campaka, and śatāśoka flowers.
Adorned with garlands of flowers from the *patra*, *pūga*, *kuhara*, *upunnāga*, *kahlāra*, *yuthī*, and *sarvavartu* trees (18);
the entry into the pavilion of ornaments (19).
Seated upon a jeweled pedestal adorned with ornaments (20);
a crown of nine gems (21);
a crescent moon (22).
Sīmantasindūra (23),
Tilakaratna (24), and Kālāñjana (25).
26. A pair of ear-lobes; 27. An ornament for the nose;
28. Lac-dye for the lips.
29. The ornament of interlacing; 30. The golden variegated foot-pattern; 31. The great foot-pattern.
The Muktāvalī (32), the Ekāvalī (33),
and the Devacchandaka (34).
The fourfold pair of armlets (35), the series of bracelets (36),
and the series of finger-rings (37).
The girdle-string for the waist (kāñcīdāmakaṭīsūtra) 38;
the ornament called śobhā 39; and the anklet (pādakaṭaka) 2.
40. A jeweled anklet; 41. A toe-ring for the foot; 42.
A noose in one hand.
In one hand is a goad (44);
in the other hands are a lotus, a sugarcane bow (45),
and in another hand, flower-arrows (46).
47. [The worship of] the glorious ruby sandals;
48. the mounting of the lion-throne together with the deities of the enclosures who are attired like herself;
49. the sitting upon the couch of Kāmeśvara.
A cup for drinking nectar (50);
water for sipping (51);
camphor pills (52).
53. The laughter of the play of blissful exaltation; 54. The auspicious *ārātrika* lamp-offering; 55. The white parasol.
A pair of chowries (56),
a mirror (57),
and a palm-leaf fan (58).
Fragrance 59 | Flower 60 | Incense 61 |
62. A lamp; 63. An offering of food; 64. For the purpose of drink.
One should again offer water for sipping (ācamanīya), betel (tāmbūla), and a prostration (namaskāra).
In the absence of these services, these mantras are to be recited.
As it is said in the Navaratneśvara:
In the absence of the sixty-four types of offerings, the practitioner with a steady mind should recite that mantra; he shall obtain that very same fruit. (2-ka)
Now, the eighteen modes of service: the seat, welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering,
water for sipping, bathing, clothing, the sacred thread, and all kinds of ornaments.

One should perform the worship of the Mantra with the eighteen services (upacāras): perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food, libations, garlands, ointments, as well as prostration and dismissal. || 3 ||
Now, the sixteen modes of service:
water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), bathing, clothing, and ornaments;
then fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, food offerings (naivedya), and again water for sipping.
One should employ betel, worship, hymns of praise, libations, and prostrations;
these are the sixteen services to be utilized in the ritual worship.
Now, the ten services (daśopacāra):

water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and again water for sipping; then the services beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya)—these are the ten services in their proper order.
Now, the fivefold offerings: perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offering;
having obtained the unbroken fruit [of these], one certainly attains liberation. (6)
Now, regarding the determination of the time when gems, pearls, and other materials become *nirmālya* (discarded offerings),
the *Yoginītantra* states: "Those gems, pearls, and gold that have indeed been bestowed by the Deity..."
Nor should one offer faded flower-garlands, nor likewise a copper vessel for twelve years.
O Maheśvarī, merely by the offering of a fine cloth, a garment, and food for six months, as well as sweetmeats and kṛsara, [the goal is attained] in half a watch of the day.
Silken cloth [is prescribed] for three months, and the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) is remembered as mine;
likewise, food should be served while it is still warm, as should the finest rice-milk (paramānna).
O Pārvatī, the head and blood [are obtained] in a day and night;
O Śaṅkarī, curd, milk, and clarified butter in a muhūrta, and [the rest] in a watch (yāma).
The *karavīra* flower is [pure] for a day and night; likewise is the *bilva* leaf.
The red *javā* flower and the *mādhya* flower remain as *nirmālya* (used) for one and a half watches (*yāmaka*).
O Maheśānī, by merely offering a garland of karavīra, lotus, and bilvaka flowers, or betel leaf, for even half a watch (yāmārddha), [the fruit is attained]. || 12 ||
O beloved, one should not offer withered flowers, nor pomegranate, nor bilva fruit;
however, one should diligently employ fragrant flowers and plantain.
Now, the mantras for the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) of Tripurasundarī:
"O Mother, please accept this [seat] offered to you, which is washed by streams of water reddened with rising sandalwood and saffron, and fashioned from various priceless gems and corals."

O Mother Sundarī, O wish-fulfilling creeper for your devotees, I respectfully worship your glorious sandals, which are devoutly rubbed on all sides by the lotus-hands of the celestial beauties. || 1 ||

Having taken this great, stainless oil— which is worshipped by the Lord of the Gods and other deities, which is fashioned from a mass of shimmering gold, which is radiant with beautiful luster, and which possesses the fragrance of campaka and ketakī flowers— along with the lion-throne, the hosts of gods [approached].
O Ambikā, please accept this fragrant unguent respectfully offered by a young woman. || 2 ||
Afterwards, O Goddess, wife of Śambhu, O Śrīsundarī, take for the most part a stainless *dhātrī* fruit, which is thoroughly filled with a collection of fragrant substances;
then, having cleansed your hair with a comb, bathe in the stream of the Mandākinī.
May it be radiant with fragrance for your delight, O Śrīsundarī. || 3 ||

O Bestower of Boons, accept this pure and fresh musk, radiant with a great fragrance, shining with an abundance of sandalwood, saffron, and agallochum, held in the lotus-like hand of the beloved of the Lord of Wine.
At the venerable feet of Tripurasundarī. || 4 ||
And this most excellent [mountain], held by the lotus-hands of the beloved consorts of the Gandharvas, gods, and Kinnaras, tawny with saffron,
and blazing with the gift of the radiant beauty of the shimmering orb of the sun, O Mother—
O Śrīsundarī, may this stainless garment spread [its beauty] for your delight. || 5 ||
In her pair of ears, earrings fashioned of gold; on her lotus-hands, rings; on the expanse of her hips, a bow with its string;
on her two feet, anklets; a necklace upon her chest; and on her two hands, bracelets jingling with a resonant sound—all these are placed [upon her].
Let him be praised, who daily bestows joy by placing his crown upon [his] head. || 6 ||
Upon her neck, a beautiful necklace of radiant gems held a mass of lovely luster; on the surface of her forehead, vermilion bore the seal of beauty;
her eyes, with pupils shining like royal lotuses, possessed the splendor of the petals of a brilliant blue lotus—[all] fashioned from that divine medicine.
May the illustrious Śāmbhavī compose [this] at the feet of the Illustrious One. || 7 ||

O Tripurasundarī, accept this mirror, fashioned from corals and intended for the destruction of sins, which arose from the milk-ocean churned by Mount Mandara and is as radiant as the rays of the moon; look upon Your face with it at Your glorious feet.
He dwells within a lotus that brings delight,
bathed by streams of musk, sandalwood, agallochum, and nectar,
and made fragrant with blossoming campaka, pāṭala, and other sweet-smelling substances.
O Ambika, accept with joy this pure water offered by the celestial hosts, poured from a multitude of great jeweled jars resting upon the heads of the divine women. 9.
With flowers such as the *kahlāra*, *utpala*, *nāgakeśara*, *saroja*, *ākhya*, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *kairava*, and *ketaka*, as well as the *raktāśvamāra* and others—
with a profusion of fragrant garlands and a stream of various essences— [The Lord] was worshipped.
I worship the Blessed One, Śrīsundarī, who dwells within the copper-colored lotus. 10.
This incense— composed of the powders of *māṃsī*, guggulu, sandalwood, and aguru, along with camphor, *śaileya*, and saffron mixed with honey and blended with clarified butter—
was prepared for the pleasure [of the deity] in a jeweled vessel within the abode of fragrance.
Composed by Surakāminī for your delight, O Śrīsundarī. 11.

O Tripurasundarī, may your lamp shine forth— constructed by celestial nymphs, filled with ghee, possessing a radiant jewel-wick that flickers like liquid oil, destroying the great darkness, resting within a golden cup, and provided with a wick made of fragrant aloe-wood.
O Goddess, you are a lamp for the sake of joy. || 12 ||

The food offering (naivedya) consists of pure, delicious rice cooked with *śāli* grains, suffused with the fragrance of jasmine (*jātīsaurabha*), accompanied by side dishes (*vyañjana*) seasoned with asafoetida, black pepper, cumin, and other aromatic ingredients;
and with cooked foods including milk-rice (*pāyasa*), honey, curd, and clarified butter.
Composed by Surakāminī for your delight, O Śrīsundarī. 13.
Take this [betel], radiant with cloves in bud, abundant with betel leaves, tender with nutmeg,
and rich with camphor and areca nuts; filled with the sweetness of nectar and placed within a beautiful jeweled vessel, accept it upon your lotus-like face.
With a betel-roll shimmering with a little camphor. || 14 ||
Accept this [garland], beautiful as the moonlight shimmering from the autumn moon, possessing the lovely splendor of pearls from the rippling river of amorous play,
and radiant with fragments of stalks shining like fresh gold.
O Mahātripurasundarī, the great, manifest parasol. || 15 ||
O Mother, may this white chowrie— resembling the moon and jasmine, dispelling the distress of perspiration, and perpetually waved by beautiful women— expand your joy;
it is instantly [grasped] in the hearts of Agastya, Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, Śuka, Vyāsa, and others, as well as Vālmīki.
May the sound of the Vedas, even while being performed, bestow blessings.

May she, being celebrated with the sounds of flutes, mṛdaṅgas, conchs, and kettledrums by her own celestial maidens amidst the clamor [of the assembly], be for your pleasure in the art of the Vidyādhara dance. 17.

O Goddess, for one whose conduct is permeated by the rasa of devotion, if even a single moment of joy is obtained from any source whatsoever, that alone is a true fruit; it cannot be attained here even in ten million lifetimes. 18.
Whoever praises the Supreme Deity with these sixteen verses arranged as ritual offerings shall obtain their fruit.
Now, regarding the greatness of the rudrākṣa in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The man who [wears it] on the crest-lock, on the hands, on the neck, and also on the ears..."
Whoever wears the rudrākṣa with devotion shall attain the world of Śiva. || 1 ||
A wise person should wear a nine-faced rudrākṣa on the left arm,
and likewise, one with fourteen faces upon the crest-lock (śikhā).
Śiva with one face directly removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
he grants invincibility and causes the suppression of fire when facing the current [of a river]. || 3 ||
The two-faced [form] is Hara-Gaurī, which effects the destruction of sins such as cow-slaughter;
the three-faced [form] is Agni, which destroys the heap of sins arising from three births.
Brahmā himself, with four faces, removes the sin of killing a human being;
but Kālāgni, with five faces, removes the sins of approaching those who should not be approached and of looking at forbidden things.
Guha, who possesses six faces, directly removes the sin of foeticide;
Ananta, who possesses seven faces, is always the destroyer of the sin of stealing gold.
Vināyaka has eight faces and is the destroyer of all falsehood;
Bhairava has nine faces and brings about union with Śiva.
Viṣṇu is remembered as having ten faces, the destroyer of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas;
Rudra has eleven faces and bestows the fruits of various sacrifices.
The Sun shall have twelve faces, bestowing the fruit of all sacrifices;
Kāma shall have thirteen mouths, bestowing the fruit of all desires.
Śrīkaṇṭha has fourteen faces and is the supreme one who effects the upliftment of the lineage;
Rudrākṣas that are flawless and well-ripened are prescribed for wearing.
Now, regarding the consecration of the rudrākṣa:

at the time of bathing, one should employ the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); likewise, during the installation of the rudrākṣa, one should use the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara). || 11 ||
And one should likewise employ the Tryambaka and other mantras there:
Oṃ, we worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity;
may he deliver us from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality.
Likewise: Oṃ hauṃ aghore hauṃ ghore hūṃ ghoratare oṃ hraiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ sarvataḥ sarvasarvebhyo namaste rudrarūpiṇe hūṃ hūṃ.
O best of the twice-born, by means of this mantra as well, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the rudrākṣa according to the rules; thereby one obtains a fruit even greater than that.
After that, endowed with devotion, one should wear it with one's own specific mantra.
Then, the mantras in sequence are:
Oṃ oṃ bhṛśaṃ namaḥ | 1 | Oṃ oṃ namaḥ | 2 |
Oṃ oṃ namaḥ | 3 | Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ | 4 | Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ | 5 |
Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ. 6. Oṃ oṃ hūṃ hūṃ namaḥ. 7. Oṃ saṃ hūṃ namaḥ. 8.
Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ | 9 | Oṃ haṃ namaḥ | 10 | Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ | 11 |
Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ. 12. Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣauṃ namaḥ. 13.
Oṃ namo namaḥ. 14. || 13 ||
O Guha, if even a dog dies while a rudrākṣa is situated upon its body, it too attains the state of Rudra; how much more so, then, for human beings?
Whatever merit a man performs while wearing a rosary of twenty-seven rudrākṣas upon his body, all that becomes ten millionfold. || 15 ||
Rudra becomes pleased with him who gives Rudrākṣas made of earth to the twice-born on the six-faced mountain, and he bestows his own abode upon him. || 16 ||
The man on earth who wears a rudrākṣa without the mantra goes to terrible hells for as long as fourteen Indras endure. || 17 ||
Thus ends the majesty of the rudrākṣa.
Now, the description of the deities, mantras, and so forth regarding the consecration (saṃskāra) of rudrākṣas by another method, as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: Kārtikeya said:
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, and fourteen. (18)
And who is the presiding deity here for these faces, O Śaṅkara?
Tell me truly what their respective qualities are. (19)
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the truth according to the sequence for each and every face.
Śiva with a single face directly removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The two-faced [form], along with the God and Goddess, certainly destroys the sin of cow-slaughter;
the three-faced one is Dahanah himself and removes even the murder of a Brahmin.
Brahmā himself, with four faces, removes the sin of killing a human being;
Rudra himself, with five faces, known by the name Kālāgni,
[removes the sins] from approaching those who should not be approached and from eating what should not be eaten.
One is liberated from all sins by the wearing of the five-faced [mantra]. || 13 ||
By wearing the six-faced Kārttikeya on the right arm, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. (24)
O Mahāsena, the king of serpents named Vāmana has seven mouths;
by him one is liberated from sins such as violating the teacher’s bed—of this there is no doubt. (25)
O Mahāsena, the eight-faced Vināyaka is the Lord himself;
he would even touch the wife of his guru with the back of his belly and hand. (26)
In this way, all such evils and even the most heinous sins are entirely destroyed;
his obstacles perish, and being liberated, he goes to the supreme goal.
Indeed, all these qualities belong to Aṣṭavaktra through its wearing;
one becomes Navavaktra Bhairava and should wear it on the left arm.
The Kāpila [mantra] is declared to bestow liberation; one shall become equal in power to me.
Even he who commits thousands of millions of crores of murders of Brahmins—by the wearing of the nine-faced [mantra], all that is quickly consumed. (29)
O Mahāsena, Janārdana himself is the ten-faced one;
by the wearing of the ten-faced [form], the planets, piśācas and others, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, and serpents are destroyed. (30)
Eleven Rudrākṣas on the face are known as the eleven Rudras;
one should always wear them on the crest-lock—listen now to the meritorious fruit thereof:
it is equal to the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of one hundred thousand golden-peaked [mountains],
that same fruit one attains by wearing the Vaktra-elephant with its eleven tusks.
One should wear a rudrākṣa with twelve faces on the region of the neck;
the Sun is constantly pleased, for he is established in twelve rays.
Kāma, who has thirteen faces, bestows the fruits of all desires; he who has fourteen mouths is the supreme one who effects the upliftment of the lineage.
One should wear ten Rudrākṣas around the neck, twenty-two on the head,
six on each ear, twelve on each of the two hands,
sixteen on each of the two arms according to the digits of the moon, and one on the crest-lock.
He who bears upon his chest eighteen marks of impurity is himself Nīlakaṇṭha.
Therein, the dhāraṇī-mantras in sequence are: Oṃ Aiṃ | 1 | Oṃ Śrīṃ | 2 |
Oṃ dhruṃ dhruṃ | 3 | Oṃ hrīṃ hraḥ | 4 | Oṃ hrīṃ | 5 |
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ | 6 | Oṃ hrāṃ | 7 | Oṃ kraṃ raṃ | 8 |
Oṃ hrāṃ | 9 | Oṃ hrīṃ | 10 | Oṃ śrīṃ | 11 ||
oṃ hāṃ hrāṃ | 12 | oṃ kṣauṃ stauṃ | 13 | oṃ ḍaṃ māṃ | 14 | || 35 ||
Now, regarding the expiation for the failure of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and so forth, it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"Whatever deficiency occurs in any rite, whether obligatory or occasional..."
One should recite the mantra a thousand times and the root-mantra ten thousand times.
For daily rites one should recite it a thousand times, and likewise ten thousand for occasional rites;
this refers to the domain of Viṣṇu.
But in another place, the *Tantrarāja* states:
"To pacify the faults arising from the transgression of daily rites, one should recite the Vidyā a hundred times;
upon the transgression of occasional rites, one should recite the mantra a thousand times."
But regarding the commingling of sins:
"When a commingling of all sins has occurred, the expiation consists of ten thousand recitations of the mantra as prescribed in the Tantra. (36)
Now, the technical rules (paribhāṣās):
In the work of Gautama,
I shall now declare the technical rules regarding the procedure for the ritual service of Hari.
The number of substances corresponds to the number of vessels, which are a collection of materials such as gold,
silver, copper, brass, clay, and so forth;
the wise declare that these are the materials for the performance of the ritual service.
Five flowers are for the seat; six or four *pala* weights are for the welcome offering (*svāgata*).
It is prepared with *śyāmāka*, *dūrvā*, lotus, and *viṣṇukrāntā*.
For the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*), there should likewise be water, fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and barley.
Dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, four tips of kuśa grass, white mustard seeds,

and the decoction of jātī, lavaṅga, and kakkola— these six palas are declared to be for the ritual rinsing (ācamana) in a bronze vessel; likewise, ghee and honey are included in the madhuparka offering.
One pala of curd together with pure water—likewise for me. (38)
The quantity of water for the purpose of bathing is fifty palas; furthermore, there must be complete sufficiency of pure water everywhere. (39)
In the ritual of worship for Hari, one should discard everything that is soiled or censurable;
likewise, the pair of garments should be new and no more than a span (vitasti) in length.
Ornaments made of gold and other metals, adorned with pearls and gems;
and the fragrance of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor paste, up to a weight of one pala. (41)
There were more than fifty kinds of various flowers,
placed in a vessel made of bell-metal or similar material, along with incense consisting of a karṣa of guggulu resin.
One should offer to Janārdana as much food as a man might eat,
consisting of various offerings of the four kinds of edibles, such as those to be chewed and so forth.

The wick, made of cotton and mixed with camphor and other ingredients, should be four finger-breadths long; the lamp, well-prepared, should be offered seven times. A person should likewise grind sandalwood paste and apply it seven times for the purpose of worship.
This should be performed in a vessel made of copper or similar metal for the pleasure of the Wearer of the Forest Garland (Kṛṣṇa).
The measure of the dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains should be known as exceeding one hundred;
this is declared to be the superior method, always to be followed when one possesses the means.
In the absence of all these, one should worship according to one's ability;
however, when wealth is available, one should avoid using substitutes for the ritual materials.
Whoever worships according to this rite with ritual offerings,
having become endowed with all enjoyments, shall at the end go to the city of Hari.
Now, the mantras for the propitiation of Viṣṇu;
therein, in the *Gautamīya*:
"O God, who dwells within all, [I offer] that which consists of the seed of all."
"I meditate upon the supreme, pure-minded one who abides within the self.
Thus is the seat. (1)
O Lord of the gods of gods, may you, whom Brahmā, Hara, and the other deities long to behold, manifest your presence before me out of compassion. O Supreme Lord, O Master, welcome, welcome to you!
Thus, welcome. || 2 ||

I have achieved my purpose and am graced; my life has become fruitful, O Lord of Gods, imperishable one consisting of consciousness and bliss, since you have come [to me]. Whether through ignorance, negligence, or deficiency in my spiritual practice, [may my transgressions be forgiven].
"Even if the rite should be incomplete, remain facing [me].
This is the invocation (āvāhana). || 3 ||
O Supreme Lord, I offer this water for the feet to You, the Pure One, through contact with even a fraction of whose devotion the arising of supreme bliss occurs.
Thus, the water for the feet (pādya). 4.
"To the God of even the gods, the divine self of the gods, O Lord, I offer water for sipping (ācamana) as nectar for the sake of hearing [the scriptures]. Thus ends the water for sipping. || 5 ||
"O Divine One, who removes the threefold suffering and is characterized by supreme bliss, I offer this *arghya* to you for liberation from the threefold suffering.
Thus is the *arghya*. (6)
"O Lord, I offer this madhuparka, which is free from all impurities and consists of perfect nectar; be gracious unto me.
Thus ends the madhuparka. (7)
"Even one who is defiled by remnants of food or is impure attains purity merely by the remembrance of You; to You, this water for sipping is offered again.
Thus, the water for sipping once more. 8.
"O Lord, I offer this bath, complete with its primary and secondary limbs, to You whose own form is immersed in the ocean of the awakening of supreme bliss.
Thus ends the offering for the bath. (9)
"To you whose secret brilliance is concealed by the variegated canvas of illusion, and who possess unobstructed consciousness, I offer this garment.
Thus, the garment. (10)
"Upon whom the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), which eternally deludes the world, depends—to that Supreme Lord I offer this upper garment. Thus [is the offering of] the upper garment. 11.
"By whose three powers this entire world is pervaded—to You, as the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), I offer this sacrificial thread. Thus ends the section on the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). 12.
"O you who are worshipped by the gods, whose limbs are beautiful by their very nature, and who are the locus of various powers, I fashion diverse ornaments for you.
Thus [ends the section on] ornaments. 13.
"O Lord of all the lords of gods, accept this supreme water, which brings satisfaction to all, and is filled with unbroken bliss. Thus [is the offering of] water. 14.
"O Supreme Lord, out of compassion, please accept this supreme fragrance, which fills the quarters of space with the sweet scent of supreme bliss. Thus is the offering of fragrance (gandha). 15.
"Please accept this supreme flower, endowed with the four qualities, enchanting with its manifold virtues, and possessing the fragrance of bliss. Thus ends the section on the flower (16).
"O divine essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, worthy of being smelled by all the gods, please accept this.
Thus is the incense offering (dhūpa). || 17 ||
"O great lamp, brilliantly illuminating, dispelling all darkness, this lamp, a light both internal and external—please accept it. Thus is the lamp offering. (18)
"O Lord of Gods, I offer this well-prepared, excellent oblation consisting of various and manifold foods to You and Your attendants; please accept it.
Thus is the food offering (naivedya). 19.
Then, with the words "O Lord of all the lords of gods," and so forth, [he offers] water. || 20 ||
Likewise, in the Gautamiya [Tantra]:
"Worship is said to be fivefold; hear from me its divisions:
approach (abhigamana), procurement (upādāna), application (yoga), and self-study (svādhyāya)."
I shall describe to you in sequence the fivefold worship known as *ijyā*.
Among these, *abhigamana* consists of cleaning the deity’s abode, as well as smearing it with unguents and removing the faded floral offerings (*nirmālya*). || 21 ||
"Upādāna" (gathering) refers to the collection of perfumes, flowers, and so forth; likewise, "yoga" refers to the meditation upon one's own deity as being identical with one's own self. (22)

Svādhyāya is defined as the recitation of mantras preceded by a contemplation of their meaning; it is likewise the chanting of hymns and praises, the congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana) of Hari, and the study of the scriptures concerning the ultimate reality and other such subjects. (23)
The worship of one's own deity according to its true nature is indeed called *ijyā*.
Thus, O lady of virtuous vows, the five types of worship have been described to you;
they grant, respectively, the states of *sārṣṭi*, *sāmīpya*, *sālokya*, *sāyujya*, and *sārūpya*. (24)
Now, the twelfth purification:
Now, the twelfth purification for the devotees of Viṣṇu is declared here;
it consists of approaching the temple and likewise following after Hari.
With devotion, one should perform circumambulation and again cleanse the feet. || 1 ||
Lifting up leaves and flowers for the sake of worshiping Hari with devotion alone—this purification of the hands is distinguished above all other purifications. (2)
The chanting of His name and the celebration of His qualities, performed with devotion toward Lord Kṛṣṇa, is held to be the purification of speech. (3)
Listening to his stories and beholding his festival are said here to be the complete purification of the ears and the eyes.
Furthermore, it is said that for one who has prostrated before Hari, the purification of the head consists of wearing the water from His feet as well as His flower garlands.
O ascetic, the smelling of offerings such as perfumes and flowers that have already been used is prescribed as a means for the purification of the inner self as well as the sense of smell.
Whatever leaves, flowers, and so forth are offered at the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, that alone is purifying in the world; for it indeed purifies everything.
A mace should be depicted on the forehead, and likewise a bow and arrows on the head;
the sword Nandaka in the middle of the chest, and the conch and discus on the two arms.
O Gautama, if a Brahmin who bears the conch and the discus dies in a cremation ground,
he attains that same destination which has been described for one who dies at Prayāga.
Now, the thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu,
as stated in another tantra: "Traveling by means of vehicles or sandals to the house of the Blessed One."
Not serving during the festivals of the gods, and not bowing down before them; || 10 ||

One should not perform the salutation of the Lord and so forth while impure from food remnants or during a state of ritual impurity; likewise, one should not offer a prostration with only one hand or circumambulate in his presence [in such a manner].
Stretching out the feet in front, likewise assuming the cross-legged posture, lying down, eating, and speaking falsely; || 12 ||
Speaking loudly, mutual chatter, weeping, and quarreling;
likewise, inflicting punishment and favor, and harsh speech toward women. (13)
Covering oneself with a blanket, censuring others, praising others, speaking indecently, and the emission of downward wind (flatus). || 14 ||

The secondary transgression regarding what is available, the eating of food that has not been offered, and the failure to offer the portions (kalā) and other elements arising at their respective times. || 15 ||
The giving away of what remains after [the guests] have been served, as well as the serving of condiments;
making one's seat clearly visible, reviling others, and praising others. (16)
Silence toward the guru, praising oneself, and likewise reviling the deity—these, along with [the aforementioned], are proclaimed as the thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu. (17)
This is an elliptical illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
In the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"Does he who does not perform dance and song before Keśava on the day of Hari not get burned by fire?"
Has he not gone to the netherworld? || 18 ||
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
"In the Kali age, remembrance and chanting of Viṣṇu, as well as the recitation of mantras and the like, and giving gifts—these alone lead to his pleasure; no other path is desired. (19)
In the Gautamīya:
"He who, without drinking the water from a Śālagrāma stone, merely pours it upon his head, is declared to be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa. (20)
The water from Viṣṇu’s feet, when drunk, destroys the sins of ten million births;
yet that very same water becomes eightfold sinful by the falling of even a single drop upon the ground.
The dhāraṇa-mantra is as follows:
"Having drunk the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, which removes untimely death and destroys all diseases, I wear it upon my head. (22)
O Agastya:

even the *tulasī* growing at his feet destroys the sin of killing; the water at his feet destroys theft; and the food offering (*naivedya*) destroys the sins born of excessive drinking of liquor and adultery with the wife of a guru.

O Sanatkumāra, obeisance is dependent on Śrī Śārṅgin, one’s abiding state is with the devotees of Hari, and the sin born of association with them is removed; such is this certain, world-transcending majesty of the Nṛsiṃha residing in the Śālagrāma stone.
The man who performs dance and song before Keśava in the Kali age obtains,
at every step, the fruit of a horse sacrifice perpetually.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Tantra], the time for sleeping and the time for awakening of the mantras are declared:
"The classes of mantras are of two kinds, according to the division of mantra and vidyā. (25)
Mantras are declared to have male deities, while Vidyās are remembered as having female deities;
all mantras are said to possess the nature of female, male, and neuter.
Mantras for males should end in *huṃ phaṭ*; those for females are considered to end in *svāhā* (dviṭha); and those for neuters should end in *namaḥ*. Thus, mantras are said to be of three kinds.
A mantra that lacks these [suffixes] is a *vidyā*, and it is celebrated as the "Great Sound" (*mahāśabda*).
Likewise, in the Tantra it is said:

"Mantras for cruel and gentle rites should be understood as having the nature of Agni and Soma; they are declared to consist primarily of the letters of fire (ra), the moon (sa), the end of the alphabet (kṣa), and the ether (ha). (28)
The *mantras* belonging to Agni are characterized by the letter *sa*, while those belonging to Soma consist predominantly of the syllables *im* and *amṛta*.
Those belonging to Agni awaken when the vital breath moves through the right nostril. (29)
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is situated in another portion, the gentle [deities] indeed attain awakening.
When the vital breath has entered both channels, they all attain awakening;
once awakened, they always bestow their fruit upon the practitioners (mantrins).
Alternatively:
From the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, and from the meeting of Śiva and Śakti, the time of awakening is to be known; the time of sleep follows thereafter. (31)
Likewise:
when the wind blows from the left, then the short [vowels] are joined with one *yojana*;
when the wind blows from the right, then the long [vowels] are joined.
When the wind resides in both, then it would possess the nature of both.
Having encapsulated [the mantra] with the mantra consisting of the letters from 'a' to 'la' along with the bindu, and again ending with the visarga, one should recite the letter *kṣa* alone.
If thus chanted as desired, it bestows swift accomplishment upon the awakened one. (33)
Thus ends the section on the time for awakening from sleep.
Now, the postures (āsanas) which are limbs of yoga: Padmāsana, the one called Svastika, Bhadra, and likewise Vajrāsana.
The heroic posture (vīrāsana) is thus declared; these are the five postures in their proper sequence. || 1 ||
Having placed both soles of the feet properly upon the thighs,
one should then bind the two big toes with the hands in a crossed manner;
this is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is dear to the hearts of yogins.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs, the yogi should sit with an upright body; that they call the Svastika posture. (3)
Having placed the pair of ankles very firmly on both sides of the perineum, one should bind the two feet below the scrotum with the hands;
this is declared as Bhadrāsana, devised by yogins. (4)
Placing the feet successively upon the thighs and the hands with fingers pointing forward upon the knees, one should rest them facing east; this is declared to be the unsurpassed Vajrāsana posture.
Placing one foot below and likewise resting the other upon the thigh,
with the body held straight, the practitioner of mantra enters the posture known as vīrāsana.
Now, the section on mudrās:
Regarding the etymological derivation of the word *mudrā*, the Tantra states:
"Because it gladdens (*modana*) all the gods and because it dissolves (*drāvaṇa*) the succession of sins..."
Therefore, she is celebrated as "Mudrā" by the sages who are knowers of the Tantras.
Now I shall explain the mudrās prescribed in all tantras,
by the performance of which the deities of the mantras rejoice.
And during the time of secret recitation, in meditation, in rites for specific desires, in bathing, in invocation, in the consecration of a conch, in protection, in the offering of food,
and likewise in other matters revealed in their respective ritual manuals.
The mudrās should be observed in their proper places, characterized by their respective individual marks. || 3 ||
The mudrās such as āvāhanī and others are not considered common;
likewise, one should employ the six-limbed mudrās in all mantras. (4)
Nineteen mudrās of Viṣṇu have been described by the wise:
the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the flute, the śrīvatsa, the kaustubha,
the garland of forest flowers, as well as the jñāna-mudrā and that called the bilva.
The supreme mudrā called Garuḍa increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu;
likewise, there are the Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, and Hayaśīrṣī mudrās, as well as the bow, the arrow, and the supreme axe-mudrā which deludes the world. || 5 ||
The Kāmamudrā is known as the supreme; these are the ten mudrās of Śiva:
the Liṅga, Yoni, Triśūla, Akṣamālā, Iṣṭa, Bhīma, Mṛga, Khaṭvāṅga, Kapāla, and the Ḍamaru, which grant satisfaction to Śiva.
For the Sun, there is only one mudrā called Padma; for the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa), there are seven:
known as Danta, Pāśa, Aṅkuśa, Vighna, Paraśu, Laḍḍuka, and the mudrā named Bījapūra—these should be understood for the worship of Vighna.
The noose, goad, boon-granting gesture, fear-dispelling gesture, sword, shield, bow, and arrow;
the mace and the ring—these are the mudrās of Durgā that bring about what is dear to Śakti.

In the worship of Lakṣmī, the Lakṣmīmudrā is used; likewise, in the worship of Vāg-vādinī, the Akṣamālā, Vīṇā, Vyākhyā, and Pustaka mudrās are employed. Furthermore, the mudrā known as Saptajihvā is to be understood for the worship of Agni.
The Matsya-mudrā, the one called Kūrma, the Lelihā, the one known as Muṇḍa, and the one renowned as Mahāyoni—these bestow the abundance of all siddhis. (10)
In the worship of Śakti, the Mahāyoni mudrā is used; for Śyāmā and others, the Muṇḍa and Mudrikā mudrās; while the mudrās known as Matsya, Kūrma, and Lelihā are considered common to all. || 11 ||
The specific details for the worship of Tārā are now being told: the five mudrās are the Yoni, the Bhūtinī, the one called Bījā, the Daityadhūminī, and the Lelihānā;
these are proclaimed as the five mudrās that have been observed. (12)
The tenth mudrā is to be known for the worship of Tripurā;
they are Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādinī, and Mahāṅkuśā. (13)
The *khecarī*, the *bīja*, and the *yoni* are proclaimed as the three sections (*trikhaṇḍā*).
The *kumbhamudrā* is used during consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and likewise the *padmamudrā* on the seat. The *kālakarṇī* should be employed for the rite of pacifying obstacles.
And the Gālinī mudrā should be employed in the rite of purifying the water. || 14 ||
In the worship of Śrī Gopāla, one should use the flute; for Nṛhari, the Nārasiṃhikā;
and in the worship of Varāha, one should employ that known as the Vārāhī.
In the worship of Hayagrīva, one should display the Hayagrīvī mudrā;
in the worship of Rāma, the bow and arrow mudrās; and likewise, in the worship of Paraśurāma, the paraśu (axe) mudrā is to be known as the Jaganmohanā.
The mudrā called Kumbha is for meditation on Vāsudeva, while [the same] is used for protection; and in all cases of supplication, one should employ the mudrā known as Prārthanā.
Now, their characteristics are described according to the order of their enumeration.
Having formed the añjali with both hands, one should place the two thumbs on the root joint of the ring fingers; this is known as the āvāhanī mudrā.
If this same [mudrā] were to be turned face downwards, it is known as the Sthāpanī (Installation) mudrā;
and from the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised, it becomes the Sannidhāpanī (Invocation) mudrā.
That same [mudrā], with the thumbs inserted within, is considered Saṃrodhinī;
with both fists turned upward and facing each other, it is considered Sammukhīkaraṇī.
The placement of the six limbs upon the body of the deity constitutes the rite of sakalīkṛti (the act of making complete).
The fist formed with the right hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downwards—
this is considered the avaguṇṭhana-mudrā when it is rotated all around.
Furthermore, when the little fingers and ring fingers are joined facing one another,
and likewise the index and middle fingers, this is proclaimed as the Dhenu-mudrā.
By means of it, the best of practitioners should perform the rite of consecration with nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa).

With the thumbs interlaced and the other fingers extended, this is declared by the wise to be the Mahāmudrā for the purpose of supreme transformation. One should employ these mudrās in the rite of invoking the deity.
The characteristics of the *aṅganyāsa* and the *mudrās* have been previously described; now, the characteristics of the Vaiṣṇava *mudrās* are being told.
Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist,
one should then turn the fist upward and extend the thumb;
likewise, the fingers of the left hand should be joined together and extended.
This [mudrā], known as the Śaṅkha-mudrā, is to be understood as that in which the right thumb is touched [to the fingers]. || 1 ||
Having brought the two hands together in front, well-bent and well-stretched out,
with the little fingers and thumbs joined— this is the mudrā known as Cakra.
Having placed the hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced,
and having again firmly joined and well-stretched the two thumbs upon the middle fingers— this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā* (mace gesture) of Viṣṇu, which increases his satisfaction.
Having brought the two hands together facing each other with the fingers slightly bent and raised,
and having joined the thumbs at the tips of the palms, this is the Padma-mudrā.
The two thumbs are placed upon the lips;
the left little finger is joined with the right thumb, while that same little finger is extended. The index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved.
This is the Veṇu-mudrā; it is well-guarded and is dear to Hari.
One should join the middle and ring fingers of the two hands back-to-back,
securing them at the base of the little fingers with the thumbs; one should then extend the two index fingers— this is the mudrā known as Śrīvatsa.
The right little finger is joined to the back of the ring finger;
it is bound by the other little finger and likewise by the right index finger;
and one should bind the left ring finger at the base of the right thumb.
Having joined the left thumb and middle finger together,
the other four fingers straightened and touching at their tips constitute the mudrā known as Kaustubha.
One should touch the area from the throat down to the feet with the thumb and index finger of both hands, like a rosary; this is the *vanamālikā* mudrā.
The wise one should place the index finger and thumb joined together at the front;
he should then place the lotus-hand of the left hand upon the crown of the left knee.
This shall be the Jñānamudrā, the beloved of Rāmacandra.
Having raised the left thumb and bound its tip with the thumb of the other hand,
and having pressed it firmly with the fingers as well as the fingers of the left hand,
one of pure intellect should place [the hand] firmly upon the heart while reciting the seed-syllable of Māra.
This ring, known as Bilva, has been clearly described here; it must be kept secret by those who know the ritual procedure. || 10 ||
Having turned the two hands away from each other and joined the two little fingers together,
with the two index fingers likewise joined and the two thumbs likewise joined,
one should move the two middle and ring fingers like two wings.
This shall be the Garuḍa-mudrā, which increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu. || 11 ||
Placing both hands between the knees with the chin and forehead level,
the hands resting on the ground, he should tremble again and again,
open his mouth wide, and lick his tongue.
This is the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which increases his delight. Another method:
having likewise pressed the two little fingers with the two thumbs of both hands...
This mudrā of Nṛhari is considered to consist of all [the fingers] with their palms facing downwards. || 12 ||
The wise practitioner, having placed the left hand above the right with the palm facing upward, should bend it downward;
this is declared to be the mudrā known as Vārāhī. An alternative method:
The right hand facing upwards and the left hand facing downwards,
with the tips of the fingers joined together, is the mudrā known as Vārāhī.
Having placed the fingers of the right hand with their palms downward upon the palm of the left hand,
one should raise the middle finger of those [fingers] and bend it downward;
this is the mudrā beloved by Hayagrīva, which imitates his form.
One should join the middle and index fingers of the left hand at their tips;
one should press the ring and little fingers with its thumb. This, displayed upon the left shoulder, is declared to be the Dhanur-mudrā (the Bow Gesture).
The arrow-seal is formed by the long index finger of the right fist. || 15 ||
Or as it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
"O beloved, make your hand like a bow held in the hand;
this is declared to be the mudrā of the bow, positioned in the left hand."
Just as arrows are held in the hand, so should you hold [the hand], O beloved;
this is declared to be the "arrow-gesture" (bāṇamudrā), which cuts down the host of enemies.
Having joined the fingers of the two hands crosswise, one should make them compact and extended; this is the mudrā known as the axe (paraśu). || 17 ||
The two mudrās, the fist with the thumb raised, are the Trailokyamohinī. || 18 ||
Having joined the two hands together with the fingers extended,
the two index fingers [should rest] on the backs of the middle fingers, and the two thumbs should lean against the middle fingers;
this is declared to be the Kāma-mudrā, which brings delight to all the gods.
Now, the characteristics of those dear to Mahādeva are described:
one should raise the right thumb and bind it with the left thumb;
one should also bind the fingers of the left hand with the fingers of the right hand.
This is declared to be the Liṅgamudrā, which brings about the presence of Śiva.
