Having bound the two little fingers together, [place] the two index fingers upon the ring fingers; with the ring fingers joined upward, place the tips of the two thumbs beneath the long middle fingers— this is declared to be the Yoni-mudrā.
Having bound the little finger with the thumb and keeping the three middle fingers joined together, one should extend them; this is proclaimed as the mudrā named Triśūla (the Trident).
Having interlaced three fingers at the tips of the thumb and the forefinger, one should extend [the remaining fingers]; this is proclaimed as the *akṣamālā* (rosary) mudrā.
The right hand, positioned below, is extended in the mudrā of granting boons. || 5 ||
The left hand is raised upward and extended in the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā). || 6 ||
One should join the ring fingers and the thumbs, and place them at the tips of the middle fingers;
with the other fingers joined and raised, this is declared to be the mṛgamudrā (deer mudrā).
The five fingers of the right hand joined together and raised upwards constitute the well-known Khaṭvāṅga mudrā, which is considered exceedingly dear to the Lord.
Having placed the left hand like a bowl upon the left shoulder and holding it aloft, this is considered the Kāpālikī mudrā.
Having formed a loose fist with the middle finger slightly raised, one should lift the right hand upward and wave it at the region of the ear;
this is the Ḍamaruka mudrā, which destroys all obstacles. 10.
Likewise, the characteristics of the Gaṇeśa mudrās are now described:
with the middle finger extended upward and palm facing up, held straight and with the fist clenched, this is declared by those learned in all the Āgamas to be the Danta-mudrā (Tusk Mudrā). || 1 ||
Having joined the index finger of the left fist with the index finger of the right fist, one should cast the tips of both thumbs onto the tips of their respective index fingers;
this is the mudrā called Pāśa, as proclaimed by the learned.
Having made the middle finger straight and joining the index finger at its middle joint, one should bend it slightly; this mudrā is known as the Aṅkuśa (the Hook).
The *vighnamudrā* consists of the ring, middle, and index fingers, with the little finger and thumb forming a fist;
it is downward-facing and elongated in form, with the middle finger extended.
The Parśu-mudrā has been described; the Laḍḍu-mudrikā is well known.
The mudrā called Bījapūra has been omitted because it is already well known.
Now, the characteristics of the Śākteyī mudrās are being described:
the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the boon-granting gesture (vara), the gesture of fearlessness (abhīti), the bow (dhanus), and the arrow (bāṇa) are proclaimed.
Having bound the little finger and the ring finger with one's own thumb on the right side,
while the remaining fingers are extended and joined together, this is the sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrikā).
Likewise, having placed the left hand across [the chest] and extended it, one should make the fingers contracted; this is declared to be the carma-mudrā.
Having formed fists with both hands, placing the right over the left,
one should perform this mace-mudrā (*muṣalamudrā*), which destroys all obstacles.
Having formed a fist with both hands, placing the right hand over the left, and joining them at the head— this is declared to be the mudrā of Durgā.
Having likewise formed the *cakramudrā* and extended the two middle fingers, one should bring the two little fingers together and place the two thumbs at their tips;
this is indeed the supreme *lakṣmīmudrā*, which bestows all prosperity. || 11 ||
Having bound the hands in the manner of playing the lute, one should move the head;
this is declared to be the Vīṇāmudrā, which brings pleasure to Sarasvatī. (1)
Having formed the left fist facing oneself, this is the book mudrā;
the thumb and index finger of the right hand are joined at their tips, while the other fingers [are extended].
With the fingers extended, joined, and turned upward—this is the Gesture of Exposition (vyākhyānamudrā), considered most beloved by Sarasvatī, the consort of Śrī Rāma. (3)
Placing the two hands with fingers extended at the wrist,
one should join the little fingers and thumbs together and extend them inward;
this is the mudrā called Saptajihvā, which is dear to Vaiśvānara.
The little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are held together and straight, without being bent.
This is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, which is moved over the conch.
Having placed the right thumb upon the left thumb with both hands, one should form a single fist with space between the fingers; that is the *kumbha-mudrā*.
With the thumbs raised in both fists, one should place them at the tips of the index fingers;
this is proclaimed as the Kumbha-mudrā, which indeed provides protection from all [evils]. || 3 ||
With the fingers extended and the two hands joined together facing each other, one should place them at one's own heart; this is the mudrā known as Prārthanā (the Request).
The añjali-mudrā, formed by joining the palms together, is also called vāsudeva.
Having raised the two thumbs while keeping the two fists joined together, one should turn those very thumbs toward each other; this is the mudrā known as Kālakarṇikā.
The *dakṣiṇā* [mudrā] consists of a tightly clenched fist with the index finger placed against the nose. || 7 ||
The mudrā known as Vismaya produces a state of wonder and inspires a sense of amazement. || 8 ||
The right fist with the thumb raised is the Nāda-mudrā;
the joining of the tips of the index finger and thumb is the Bindu-mudrā.
Having placed the right hand with its palm facing upward into the left hand which is turned downward,
and having interlaced the fingers of one hand with those of the other, one should turn them over;
this is the *saṃhāramudrā*, prescribed for the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*).
One should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand;
moving the two thumbs properly, this is the mudrā known as Matsyarūpiṇī.
One should join the right little finger with the left index finger,
and likewise place the left thumb upon the right index finger;
the right thumb should be raised, while the middle and other fingers of the left hand [are held straight].
One should join the fingers on the back of the right hand;
likewise, with the middle and ring fingers of the left hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*,
one should place them facing downward upon the right hand.
One should make the right hand equal to the back of a tortoise on all sides;
this is declared to be the *kūrmamudrā* for the practice of meditating upon the deity [on the back or chest]. (10)
Having formed a fist with the left hand, with the thumb inside,
one should then carefully grasp the tip of the right middle finger;
then, one should join the middle finger and the index finger with the tip of the thumb.
The practitioner should join the right hand into the left fist and display it on the right side; this is called the Muṇḍa-mudrā.
The mudrās of Tārā’s womb and so forth are as follows: the yoni-mudrā is to be described, and one should display it facing downwards;
Bhūtinī is to be described, and she is also called Bījā.
Having turned the hands over so that they are clear, with the middle fingers drawn back by the little fingers,
the pair of ring fingers below and the pair of index fingers separate,
having bound them tightly together with one another, then place the ring fingers upon the tips of the thumbs.
O beloved, this mudrā is called Dānavadhūmaketu;
by binding it, the practitioner of mantra is certainly released from bondage.
Having opened wide the mouth and moved the tongue downward,
with a pair of fists placed at the sides while licking [the lips], this is celebrated as *lelihānā*.
This is for the propitiation of Tārā; another, Lelihānā, must be described.
The wise know the sequence as: the Yoni, Māyādhara, the one with the dot (Bindu), and Dhuḥ, followed by Kūrca;
while pronouncing these seed-syllables, the mantra-reciter should perform the binding of the mudrās.
One should make the index, middle, and ring fingers equal and face them downward;
having made the little finger straight, one should place the thumb upon the ring finger.
This is the Lelihānā mudrā, proclaimed for the rite of bestowing life (jīvanyāsa).
Having joined the two hands starting from the base of the little fingers in the sequence of the index, ring, middle,
and little fingers,
and having placed the tips of the thumbs upon them, it is proclaimed as the Mahāyoni.
The mudrās taught in the Vāmakeśvaratantra are here being elucidated.
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall describe the mudrās that grant the accomplishment of all aims; by performing these, the presence of the Triple City (Tripurā) is attained. 1.
Having turned the two hands over, one should bring the two thumbs into contact and make them equal;
having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape within the ring fingers, O Maheśvarī, one should position the two little fingers in their own respective places.
This is declared to be the three-sectioned [mantra] for the practice of meditating upon Tripura.
Having placed the two middle fingers in the center, with the two little fingers pressed by the thumbs,
and having made the two index fingers like a staff above the middle fingers [with the ring fingers],
this is the supreme mudrā that causes universal agitation. (3)
O Supreme Goddess, when the two middle fingers of this very same mudrā are made straight,
it then becomes the Sarvavidrāviṇī.
O Supreme Goddess, with the middle and index fingers, and the little and ring fingers made equal,
the two middle fingers should be formed into the shape of a hook;
one should then place the thumbs upon the little and ring fingers.
This is the Ākarṣiṇī mudrā, the supreme attractor of the three worlds.
Having formed the hands in the shape of a casket (*puṭākāra*), with the two index fingers shaped like hooks,
and with the middle fingers positioned below them in a revolving sequence,
O Goddess, one should likewise proceed in that same order for the ring fingers and the little fingers.
Having joined all the fingers tightly together starting from the tips of the thumbs, O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is considered to be the bringer of total subjugation.
Having placed the two hands face-to-face, with the little fingers positioned between the middle fingers, the two ring fingers straight, and the two index fingers outside them;
then the two thumbs, shaped like staffs, should rest upon the nail-areas of the middle fingers.
This mudrā, known by the name Unmādinī, is the attractor of all women.
Having placed the pair of ring fingers below in the shape of a hook,
one should likewise apply the two index fingers in that same order;
this is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes all desired aims.
O Great Goddess, having placed the left arm on the right side and the right arm on the left side, and having rotated both hands,
one should join the little fingers and ring fingers, O Goddess, according to that sequence.
When the two index fingers press down upon both middle fingers from above,
O Maheśānī, one should also keep the two thumbs straight;
this is known as Khecarī when applied to the earthly posture.
O beloved, having turned the two hands over and touched them so they form the shape of a half-moon, one should then simultaneously join the pair of index fingers with the thumbs; then,
one should place the middle fingers upon the lowermost parts of the little fingers.
In the same way, the two ring fingers should be joined at the very base;
this is the Bījamudrā, which quickly increases all accomplishments.
Having made the two middle fingers curved and positioned above the index fingers, with the ring fingers likewise placed between them and the little fingers similarly situated,
one should join all [the fingers] together and press them with the thumbs.
This, however, is the supreme mudrā; it is celebrated as the yonimudrā. || 11 ||
O Great Goddess, these mudrās of Tripurā have been described by me;
they should be employed at the time of worship according to their sequential order.
Having formed a fist with the left hand at the region of the ear and extending the index finger straight, the best of mantra-knowers should rotate it;
this is the Saubhagyadaṇḍinī mudrā, which is also indicated at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having closed this forefinger with the fist formed by the inner thumb, this mudrā, which seizes the tongues of enemies, is also indicated at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa). 14.
Having indeed bound the yoni-mudrā, make the two middle fingers curved;
place the two thumbs at their tips—this mudrā is considered Bhūtinī.
Then, having formed the left fist of the Vidyā and extending the index and middle fingers from it, this is designated as the Tarjanī-mudrā by Vajrapāṇi. (16)
Thus ends the section on mudrās.
Now, regarding the dhāraṇā-yantras and so forth:
first among them is the Bhuvanēśvarī yantra.
In the *Śāradā*:

"Having drawn the eight 'bolts' (argalas) in the directions, one should write the three-syllable mantra beginning with the noose (*pāśa*) within the belly; then, in the other compartments, one should inscribe the six-limbed mantras and the two eight-syllable mantras."
Having written the six excellent pairs of letters from *a* to *ca*, starting from the front and the back,
upon the seats of space (*vyoma*) in the gates, one should then write two rows according to the qualities of the vessels of Indra, water, and so forth. || 1 ||

In the eight inner compartments, one should write the syllables of the mantra consisting of sixteen letters, together with the *ātman* (the seed-syllable), enclosed within pairs of vowels; one should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) in the pericarp and the root-mantra on the petals according to the sequence of three rows.
It should be encircled three times by the noose and the goad, and surrounded by the letters in both forward and reverse order.

With a jar resting upon a lotus, its opening covered by a lotus—this "Jar-Bolt" (*ghaṭārgala*) yantra is considered the bestower of the state of Śrī for practitioners of mantra. [The seed-syllables are:
Pāśa, Śrī, Śakti, Kandarpa, Kāma-śakti, Ramā, and Aṅkuśa.

The first mantra consists of eight syllables; then follows "kāminirañjini," ending with "svāhā. This second eight-syllable mantra is proclaimed by the wise as being preceded by "sadbhiḥ. [Then follows: *hrīṃ gauri rudradayite yogeśvari savarma phaṭ*.
This mantra, consisting of sixteen syllables with two 'tha's at its end, has been proclaimed by the virtuous. || 1-ka ||
Thus ends the Ghaṭārgala yantra.
Now, the Tvaritā yantra:
one should write "Tāre hūṃ" within the hollow of a lotus, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and [surrounded by] the syllables of the mantra.
Having drawn eight [syllables] corresponding to the Vasus upon the petals of the lotus,

and having encircled it three times with the Śakti [syllable] on its exterior, this yantra— situated within a jar, resting upon a lotus, and bearing the face of the Lotus-born (Brahmā)— is a subjugator, a remover of fear from planets and other such influences, a bestower of fortune, and a giver of splendor.
Thus ends the Tvaritāyantra.
Now, the Navadurgāyantra:
one should draw a lotus provided with twelve petals, and again, the *tāra* (the syllable Om) in its pericarp.

One should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) containing the power (*śakti*), together with the goal (*sādhya*), sequentially upon its filaments; then, having arranged the letters arising from the *Mardinī* mantra in pairs upon the petals, one should write the letters of the mantra three by three, placing the final letter on the final petal.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ, arise, O Puruṣa! Why do you sleep? A danger has come upon me.
Whether it be possible or impossible, pacify that for me, O Blessed One, svāhā!
The Yantra of Vindhyavāsinī, which bestows all prosperity, is said to be surrounded by the letters of the Mātṛkā and situated between two enclosures of the earth (Bhūpura);
it specifically provides protection and destroys minor spirits and other such beings.

It bestows sovereignty upon those who have lost their kingdom, subjugation for those desiring to bring others under their control, sons for those seeking offspring, and the pacification of disease for the sick. What is the use of saying more here? This Yantra is a wish-fulfilling jewel.
Thus ends the Yantra of Navadurgā (the diagram for the wearing of Navadurgā, Figure 52). Now, the Yantra of Lakṣmī:
[The name of] the Sadhya situated at the beginning of the Vedas, joined with the Śrī-Śakti-Māra mantras, [is placed] in the filaments.
Outside of that, one should draw a lotus whose petals shine with the mantra-syllables of the Sun (Dineśa), with consonants as its filaments and eight pairs of petals radiant with vowels;
this should be encircled by the two earth-mandalas, with the *vaṣaṭ* and the *Tvaritā* mantra written within the intervals.
The letters *ha* and *kṣa* should be written repeatedly in the corners of the two square enclosures.
This is the Mahālakṣmī yantra, which bestows the fruit of all sovereignty,
pacifies all suffering, and wards off all calamities.
What is the use of saying more here? There is nothing superior to us.
Thus ends the Lakṣmīyantra.
Now, the Tripurabhairavīyantra:
one should inscribe the seed-syllables and the letters of the Gāyatrī three times each within the nine triangles beginning from the center.
Furthermore, having written [the mantra] surrounded by syllables within the openings of eight petals,
and encircled at the corners by two earth-spheres joined with the god of love (manmatha), this is declared to be the Tripura Yantra, the glorious seat that agitates the three worlds.
(Tripurabhairavīyantra, Figure 53) As for the Gāyatrī: one should extract the word "manmatham," followed by the phrase "O Goddess Tripurā, we know [thee]."
Having uttered the word "Kāmeśvari," one should then say "dhīmahi";
and at the end, one should further say "tannaḥ kila pracodayāt. This is declared to be the Gāyatrī of Tripura, which bestows all perfections. || 5 ||

Now, the Tripurā Yantra: one should write the Māyā-bīja and the Vāgbhava-bīja within the abode situated between two houses of Fire; then, one should draw the syllable *blūṃ* in the six corners and at the junctions, and encircle it.

Impelled by the female seed-syllable (strībīja), this Yantra of the Triple City (traipura), which consists of the five forms of the Mind-born God (Kāmadeva), causes the agitation of the three worlds and bestows the wealth of beauty.
Thus ends the Tripurā-yantra.
Now, regarding the Śrīvidyā-yantra:
I shall describe to you, in this context, the specific yantra for wearing.

Between the letters *repha* (ṛ) and *hakāra* (ha), one should write the name of the Goddess facing [the practitioner], followed by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) ending in the accusative case; above that, one should write the mantra.
Right there, on the exterior of the wheel, one should write the entire *mātṛkā* (alphabet).
One should envelop [the object] with the root mantra using the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having established the vital breath (prāṇa) therein, one should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times.
Touching that, one should mutter the mantra while being intent upon the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyāna).
Having placed it in the middle of gold or alternatively in silver, if held in the hand, the world is brought under control; on the heart, one becomes beloved by women;
on the neck, one obtains wealth; and on the forehead, there shall be immobilization (stambhana).
One attains liberation through the crest-lock; therefore, one should wear it with great effort.
Thus ends the Śrīvidyā yantra.
Now, the Gaṇeśa yantra:
the seed-syllable, situated within the six corners in the center of a radiant fire-city, accompanied by the *tāra* (OM) in the cardinal directions...
Thereafter, one should draw the syllable *lakṣmī* (la), the seed-syllable of *māyā* (hrīṃ), and the seed-syllable of *kāmadeva* (klīṃ) within six compartments of nectar;

in the junctions thereof, the wise man should write the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in an eight-petaled lotus, and the remaining letters of the root-mantra, placing them by groups of three on the petals, with the final letter on the last petal.
This is the Yantra of the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa), written with the letters in direct and reverse order, enclosed by the noose and the goad, and surrounded by two circles of the earth;
it should be inscribed on the inner surface of birch bark or on gold using lac, saffron, yellow pigment, and musk.
By drawing [the diagram] and performing the ritual invocation, one obtains prosperity that is sought after by all.
Thus has been declared the rite of Mahāgaṇapati, which is honored by the gods, which grants all accomplishments to men, and bestows all human goals. 8.
Thus ends the Gaṇeśa yantra.
Now, the Śrīrāma yantra: one should write the *tāra* (OM) in the center, the mantra in the six corners, and the *aṅga-mantras* at the junctions.
Afterwards, one should write the syllable *māyā* (Hrīṃ) and the syllable *smara* (Klīṃ) on the corners and the flanks;
then, the group of *smara* syllables (*klīṃ*) on the tips of the petals, and in the middle of the petals, the letters of the *mālā-mantra* numbering nine, with five letters in the eighth [petal].
Having encircled it with the ten-syllable mantra and the letters beginning with *ka* in the outer square (*bhūpura*),

one should write the seed-mantras of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions. One should then utter "Salutation to the Blessed One" followed by the name of the Joy of the Raghus in the dative case.
At the end of "rakṣoghnaviśadāya," one should utter "madhurādi"; then "prasannavadanāya," followed by "amitatejase.
After that, "balāya," then "rāmāya," and immediately after that, "viṣṇave."
This garland-mantra (mālāmantra) is proclaimed to begin with the syllable Om (praṇava) and end with "namas. || 9-ka ||
Thus ends the Śrīrāma Yantra (the Dhāraṇa Yantra of Śrī Rāma, Figure 54). Now, the Nṛsiṃha Yantra:
One should first draw the seed-syllable (*bīja*) joined with the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center, and then [in] the eight petals.
One should write out the syllables of the mantra, dividing them according to the number of Vedic verses (four), and enclose them with the *lipi* (alphabet).

On the outside, it should be surrounded by two earth-palaces (*vasudhāgeha*) obstructed by the seed-syllable located in the corners; this is the Yantra that destroys minor poisons, planetary afflictions, diseases, and enemies, and bestows glory.
Thus ends the Nṛsiṃha Yantra (the Nṛsiṃha Dhāraṇa Yantra, Figure 55). Now, the Gopāla Yantra:
[The syllable] *piṇḍa* surrounded by the root mantra, with the six syllables shining in the corners within a pair of fire-purified triangles.
One should fashion a lotus with ten petals shimmering with the ten syllables, encircled by the seed-syllable of Kāma.

Upon the filaments of that lotus is another lotus with sixteen petals, radiant with the sixteen syllables of the *smaravikṛti* (the transformation of Smara), enriched with the consonants on the filaments, and the syllables of the *anuṣṭubh* verse placed upon the pairs of transformed petals.
Encircled by a noose and a goad, with the sixteenth vowel (au) at the corners of the pair of lotuses,
this diagram, radiant with the eight-syllabled mantra, has Gopāla as its presiding deity;
it bestows the fruits of virtue, wealth, and desire, and is the supreme provider of all protection.
The end of the five [letters] situated on the earth (Dha), adorned by the moon (U)—
this is declared to be the seed-syllable of the *piṇḍa*, the supreme bestower of all accomplishments.
Smara (Ka), for Kṛṣṇa (A), followed by the pair of *ṭha* (Ṭha-Ṭha)— this six-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed.
One should address the beloved [Kṛṣṇa] in the presence of the cowherd women with this ten-syllable mantra,
which bestows both seen and unseen fruits:
having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the heart-mantra (Hrīṃ), then "Kṛṣṇa," and thereafter the word ending in the dative case (Āya).

Such is the sixteen-syllable mantra of Govinda, consisting of "Devakīputra" joined with "huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Then follows the *piṇḍa* (the core) and the seed-syllable of the Lord of Rati, and thereafter "namo bhagavate."
"To the son of Nanda, who possesses a body like that of a child, who is dark-complexioned,
and who is the beloved at the end of the region of the cowherd women, ending with the *dviṭha* (svāhā)—
this is declared to be the *anuṣṭubh* mantra of Gopāla, the Lord of the Universe."
Anaṅga, Kṛṣṇa, and Govinda, ending in the dative case (ṅe), constitute the eight-syllable mantra. || 11 ||
Thus ends the Gopāla Yantra. Now, the Śrīkṛṣṇa Yantra:
one should duly draw four clear lines, oriented east-west and north-south, forming a square.

Having written the syllables of the verse— beginning with the center and ending with the east, joined with a trident rising from a corner and provided with a pair of bracelets— in the eight spaces between the eight squares in front,
and having subsequently surrounded that with twelve syllables on the outside, one has the Yantra of the Son of Devakī.
That which is the auspicious god of gods, praised in the Vedas, the beloved, the one established in passion, the renowned, the son of Devakī— this yantra,
written according to the prescribed rite upon birch bark or other materials, [is that very one].
Constantly held in the arm, it bestows the fruits of all desires.
Written upon a board made from the wood of the Palāśa tree and properly consecrated, one should bury it in a cow-pen; then an increase in cattle will occur. 12.
Thus ends the Śrīkṛṣṇa Yantra (Śrīkṛṣṇayantra, Figure 56). Now, the Śiva Yantra:
first, having drawn a hexagonal mandala, [one should place] within it the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).
Having written the seed-syllable of the palace (prāsādabīja), having written the letters of the five-syllabled mantra together with the *praṇava* within the six corners,
having written the mantras of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in the intervals between the corners, and having fashioned five petals outside of that, [one should place] *oṃ* on those petals.
"Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna; Oṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa; Oṃ, salutation to Aghora; Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta; Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva.
Thus, one should write these five mantras in order, starting from the east.
Having fashioned eight petals outside of that, one should write the eight letters of the Mātṛkā upon the petals. || 13 ||
One should encircle that with a circle by means of Tryambaka.
Having worshipped this yantra through recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and so forth, one should wear it;
thereupon, the attainment of the four aims of life—longevity, health, sovereignty, and the rest—shall come to pass. || 13-ka ||
Thus ends the Śiva-yantra (the dhāraṇā-yantrof Śiva, Figure 57). Now, the Mṛtyuñjaya-yantro:
one should write the central [syllable] *dhruva* (OM), enriched with the syllables of the person to be protected (*sādhya*), in the center.

In the cardinal directions and corners, one should place the final syllable of the mantra; then, in the cardinal directions, the abode of Manu (the letter *ma*), and in the intermediate directions, the lunar [syllable] (*ca*).
This machine, ending with the letter *ṭa*, is said to remove all fears.
It bestows the glorious state that grants renown and is gladdened by the pacification of the pain of poison, spirits, untimely death, disease, and delusion. || 14 ||
Thus ends the Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra (the Mṛtyuñjaya Dhāraṇa Yantra, Figure 58). Now, the Kālī Yantra; regarding this, it is said in the Yāmala:

The first seed-syllable, together with the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*), is in the first [square] of the eight; outside of that, in the eight triangles, are the eight seed-syllables starting from the east. Subsequently, in each pair of the eight squares, are six seed-syllables. The filaments are enriched with the vowels, and in the gaps between the eight petals are the six seed-syllables accompanied by *svāhā*.

Between the pair of earth-dwellings (the two squares) and the *vīta* (the surrounding frame), one should write the King of Yantras using two *kūrca* syllables; one should write the three seed-syllables of the Goddess in each cardinal direction, and the other two seed-syllables of Śakti in each corner—he who does this is a Guru even of Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu in the three worlds. (15)
Thus ends the *kālīyantra* (the *dhāraṇa*-yantra of Kālī,
Figure 59). Now, regarding the *tārādhāraṇa*-yantra for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
The mantra-practitioner should write the mantra with a golden stylus within the pair of triangles;
then, he should inscribe the long vowels, excluding the neuter ones, within the hexagon.
Next, he should place eight syllables upon the eight petals, and outside of that, two surrounding squares (bhūpura).
O lady of excellent vows, having drawn an eight-spoked vajra and a perimeter of earth (bhūpura), the supreme practitioner should inscribe [the mantra] upon a golden plate, birch bark, or silver,
using a clean pen and accompanied by the eight fragrances.
Or again, having drawn [the diagram] with a blade of *dūrvā* grass or with the root of *kuśa* grass. (The *dhāraṇayantra* of Tārā, Figure 60). From the *Ekavīrākalpa*.
One should wrap it with yellow cloth and enclose it in lac;

one should bind it with a silk thread as an ornament for the neck of children, or on the left arm of women, and likewise on the right arm of others— even a barren woman obtains a son by binding it thus.
One who is destitute shall become wealthy.
This supreme protection, once obtained, was [practiced] by Gautama and others for the sake of knowledge,
by other kings for the sake of pleasure, and by those desiring victory in battle.
The meaning of this is:
in the "pair of wombs," that is, the hexagon;
in its center, [one should write] on birch bark or similar material with a golden stylus or other tool.

Having prepared equal parts of saffron, gorocanā, red sandalwood, and jaṭāmāṃsī, and having written the root mantra in sequential order, one should write within the *repha* (the letter *r*) of the *hṛllekhā* [mantra]:
"Protect so-and-so! Protect! Cause a virtuous son to be born to so-and-so!"

Or, having written his name together with the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), such as "grant knowledge, grant knowledge" (*jñānaṃ kuru kuru*) and so forth, one should write each of the long vowels— *ā ī ū ai au aḥ*— one by one within the six corners, excluding the neuter vowels. As it has been said:
That which is situated in the middle of the vowels is the neuter tetrad.
One should write the eight syllables—*aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*—upon the eight petals.
As it has been said:

Vāgbhava, Kuladevī, Tāraka, Vāgbhava, and Hṛllekhā, followed by the Astra mantra at the end and concluding with the wife of Fire (Svāhā)— this is declared to be the eight-syllabled mantra, said to be the essence of all mantras. || 16 ||
Now, regarding the materials for drawing the yantras:
the preceptor should draw those yantras with saffron, yellow pigment (rocanā), lac, musk, elephant-ichor, and sandalwood, using a golden stylus.

A practitioner of mantra should never wear a yantra that has touched the ground, been touched by a corpse, been burnt, come into contact with discarded flower offerings (nirmālya), become cracked, or been stepped over; rather,
one should properly inscribe it upon a vessel of gold, silver, or on birch bark.
Alternatively, one should wear it fashioned into a pill with a copper plate;
for as long as one lives on gold, for twenty years on silver,
for twelve years on birch bark, and for half that duration on a copper plate.
Thus ends the materials for drawing the yantra. Now follows the ritual bath with water for pacification (śāntyudaka) after the application:
it is as follows:
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you;
may Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the omnipresent Saṅkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, grant you victory.
May Ākhaṇḍala, Agni, the Lord Yama,
Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth, and Śiva—
these guardians of the quarters together with Brahmā— protect you always.
Fame, Fortune, Fortitude, Intelligence, Nourishment, Faith, Forbearance, Thought, Wisdom, Modesty, Form, Peace, Illusion, Sleep, and Creative Imagination—
may these wives of the gods, having assembled here, consecrate you.

May Āditya, Candra, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, and Arkaja— may these, along with Rāhu and Ketu, being fully gratified, consecrate you. May the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas [consecrate you].
The sages, the ascetics, the cows, and the mothers of the gods;
the wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, and the celestial nymphs as women;
all weapons, all missiles, kings, and vehicles.
May medicinal herbs, jewels, and the divisions of time;
rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams—may these all consecrate you for the attainment of dharma, desire, and wealth. (18)
Thus end the consecration mantras as stated in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā.
Now, here is the procedure for the daily worship (nityapūjā) in brief;
it is said in the Yāmala:
First is the placement of the Ṛṣi and so forth; after that, the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi);

then the pervasive placement on the fingers (aṅgulivyāpaka-nyāsa) and the placement on the heart and other parts (hṛdādinyāsa); then the triple clapping of the palms (tālatraya) and the binding of the directions (digbandha); and after that, breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Meditation, worship, and recitation—this is the sequence in all tantras. || 1 ||
And the worship is for the root deity alone.
Furthermore, the nyāsa of the mātṛkās is also essential; likewise:
"Without the placement of the letters [of the alphabet], there is no efficacy for the recitation of any mantras."
One should know that such an act is fruitless; therefore, one should first inscribe the script.
The Concise Ritual Procedure for the Worship of Śrīvidyā:
As it is stated in the Svatantra Tantra:
"O Goddess, listen to the specific modes of worship proclaimed in the sequence of the daily practice."
O Goddess, for those who are incapable of extensive rites, as well as in times of adversity, this [practice] is recommended;
otherwise, worship performed with such contraction would lead to misfortune.
The first [wheel] would be from the spokes to the middle; the second is among the nine wombs (*yonis*);
the other, up to the fourteen spokes, is the third; and the fourth is according to the form already described.
The fifth destroys all suffering and pain and bestows what is desired.
The meaning of this is as follows:
for those who are incapable [of performing the full rite], there should be worship of the first and middle [deities] with weapons;
that is, the worship of the four deities accompanied by the four weapons.
The weapons are the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrows;
the deities are Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Śrī Mahātripurasundarī.
The meaning is that this initial worship consists of the adoration of the four deities.
He states the second [type of worship] as "in the nine wombs," [referring to] from Vaśinī up to Madhyamā.
He describes the third worship: the third worship consists of the service beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and ending with Madhyamā, situated upon the fourteen-spoked wheel.
"By the stated form" refers to the fourth [mandala]. In this context, it means "by the stated form," which extends from the sixteen-petaled lotus up to the central channel (madhyamā).

The fifth [type] extends from the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha) up to the middle and the end; thus, the fivefold worship has been described as bestowing the accomplishment of all aims. Therein, first, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), [is performed].
Having performed the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*), the four seats (*āsana-catuṣṭaya*), and the fourfold installation of the *Vaśinyā* and other goddesses (*vaśinyādinyāsa*),

one should purify the two offerings (*arghya*) with the *Bālā* mantra; then, having performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*) with the *Ṣaḍāsanavidyā*, one should invoke the Supreme Consciousness (*paraciti*) within the *bindu* by means of the *Hṛllekhā* mantra, as follows:
Having worshipped with offerings of power (śakti) as before, and having given the bali-offering to all beings, one should satisfy [the deity] with recitations and hymns. || 4 ||

Thus it is said in the *Navaratneśvara*: "O Śivā, having performed the three types of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and indeed having worshipped the wheel according to the prescribed seat, one should then offer the water for the feet and the respectful offering (*arghya*) with the *hṛllekhā* mantra."
Having invoked [the deity] into the center of the wheel, one should perform the abbreviated worship. || 5 ||
Alternatively, it is stated in the *Viśuddheśvaratantra*:
"O Sovereign of the Gods, I shall now describe the contraction of worship,
by the mere understanding of which one becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)."
First is Tripurā at the beginning; second is Tripureśvarī;
third is she who is endowed with Tripurādi in the Cakrarāja.
According to the sequence of the Goddess’s worship, there are also Sundarī and Vāsinī.
In the fifth [petal] is Tripurāśrī, and in the sixth is Tripuramālinī;
in the seventh is Tripurāsiddhā, and in the eighth is Tripurātmikā.
O Maheśānī, in the center of the Śakti is Mahātripurasundarī.
As it is stated in the Vārāhītantra:
"Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and having invoked the Goddess into the Bindu-cakra, one should invoke Aṇimā in the second [wheel],
Kāmakalā in the third, Brāhmī in the fourth, Sundarī in the fifth, and Ākarṣiṇī in the sixth."

Having worshipped Kāmeśvarī on the sixth [petal], Bheruṇḍā on the eight-petaled lotus, and Kuleśvarī on the sixteen-petaled [lotus], and having offered a handful of flowers to the Goddess, one should recite the mantra. Thus ends the sixth [section].
Thus concludes the brief ritual worship of Śrīvidyā.
Now follows the occasional (naimittika) procedure; regarding this, it is stated in the Gautamīya-tantra:
Nārada said:
Now I shall describe another ritual procedure; listen attentively, O Sage, by performing which even one of dull fortune may indeed obtain the fruits of the mantra.
One should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times situated between two *praṇavas*.
By merely reciting it three times, one becomes equal to Bṛhaspati;
one becomes an expounder of all the scriptures and even of the Vedas.
On a Sunday, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations at the root of an Aśvattha tree;
through this, peace shall arise again and again, and one shall live for more than a hundred years.
Peace will surely come to him for whose sake the rite is performed.
One should worship Kṛṣṇa for a month with pure garments;
by means of even soiled ones, one is released from difficult and most terrible sins.
One should worship with devotion using silken cloths and shall obtain incomparable prosperity;
by worshipping Kṛṣṇa with corals, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
One should worship with devotion using rubies; one shall become equal to a sovereign emperor.
By worshipping Kṛṣṇa with rubies (padmarāgas), one certainly becomes a king. (10)
A Kṣatriya shall become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth and conquer the entire world;
by worshipping with gems set in the form of Garuḍa, he becomes possessed of wisdom.

Indeed, what cannot be obtained by worshipping with diamonds and jewels? By honoring [the deity] for a month with flowers of gold, being devoted to such worship, one attains wealth equal to that of Kubera and rejoices before long.
At the end of the body, having attained the state of Hari, one reaches the station of Nirvāṇa.
On Sunday, with white lotuses; on Monday, with kahlāra lilies;
on Tuesday, with red lotuses; and on Wednesday, with those produced from the tagara plant.
On Thursday, the ascetic should worship with *campaka* flowers; on Friday, with *kumuda* blossoms; and on Saturday, he should worship with devotion using *śamī* flowers. (14)
On Sunday, one should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee;
on Monday, one should provide flour-cakes and similar foods combined with sugar;
on Tuesday, food enriched with many qualities and mixed with jaggery.
On Wednesday, [one should worship] with barley-gruel, and on Thursday, with those originating from soup.
On Friday, one should offer pure food, and on Saturday, milk-rice with ghee; in the month of Vaiśākha, one should duly perform the libation with water as cool as snow.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should diligently worship Hari with fruits;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Hari according to the rules with sacred threads (pavitrakas).
One should have each [thread] made with golden threads joined by knots;
alternatively, one may use silk threads or lotus fibers.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should offer them to the King of the Gods and to his queens.
Having given those to the couples, he should then hold a great festival;
he should satisfy the Brahmins of firm vows with various kinds of food and edibles.
By performing this for a year, the practitioner of mantra shall attain his desired goal. || 19 ||
If worship performed during the rainy season does not suffice for the sustenance of the Vāstu deity,
one should worship him with ketaka flowers in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
One should offer many cardamom, cloves, and kakkola fruits, which have been well-scented with moon-fragrance, sandalwood, musk, saffron, and other perfumes.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Viṣṇu with foods endowed with many excellent qualities;
in the month of Āśvina, one should worship Him with devotion using abundant varieties of foods and edibles.
When the sun is situated in Libra, one should worship Kṛṣṇa for the duration of one month with garments made of cotton and adorned with various ornaments.
At night, for the duration of a month, one should offer lamps and oblations combined with milk, flour, and other substances,
providing a most brilliant light that never flickers.
One should fast on the eleventh day and break the fast on the twelfth day.
On this lunar day, the wise man, having worshipped Viṣṇu with garments, ornaments, and other offerings during the bright fortnight, should perform the annual festival.
One should present various kinds of food and many delicacies to the Brāhmaṇas;
when this is done, the deity, being satisfied, bestows what is desired. (26)
One attains a peaceful world from which there is no return.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the God with fresh rice and auspicious side dishes.
[One should offer] coconut pulp mixed with jaggery and cumin.
One should offer that well-cooked food to the King of the Gods with devotion. || 27 ||
In the month of Pauṣa, one should indeed worship for an entire month with held flowers;
having quickly overcome the affliction of the planets, he shall become like a king. (28)
In the month of Māgha, one should worship Kṛṣṇa with unbroken white grains mixed with jaggery;
one should offer milk-rice with sugar and sweetened food.
On an auspicious day in this month, one should clothe the Lord with a garment.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship the Son of Devakī with golden lotuses,
fragrant flowers, incense, and lamps in great abundance.
In the month of Caitra, one should worship Vāsudeva with all kinds of flowers;
on the full moon day, one should offer worship with devotion using *damanaka* plants along with their clusters.
On this day, one intent on devotion should worship Rati and Kāma.
If the annual worship is not performed, it becomes fruitless for him. || 31 ||
Seeing Smara reduced to ashes, the virtuous Rati wept;
seeing her, Śiva himself was overcome with compassion and prepared to grant a boon.
He replied to Rati:
"O beautiful lady of Vraja, this handsome man shall attain great fortune for the sake of sporting throughout all the worlds."
From that water of weeping, the auspicious *damanaka* flower arose;
by the mere act of worshipping with it, one obtains the fruit of a year [of merit]. (34)
The knower of mantras who offers one hundred thousand oblations of flour cakes fried in ghee,
and having recited the mantra that same number of times, beholds Kṛṣṇa.
Thus has the complete worship arising from the rainy season been told to you;
having performed it according to this procedure, what on this earth will not be accomplished? (36)
Now, the worship of Śrīvidyā:
In the Jñānārṇava it is said: "O Maheśānī, I shall now describe the great worship of Śrīvidyā."
This is the unsurpassed atonement for faults such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, one should worship the supreme sequence with *brahma*-leaves, accompanied by all its rays and preceded by the eternal tradition (*nityāmnāya*). || 2 ||

O Goddess, adorned with camphor powder according to the traditional lineage practice, one shall destroy all the millions of great sins committed over many lifetimes within a single month; of this there is no doubt, O Mistress of the Gods. (3)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, Fortune shall remain firmly established and under his control in his house;
O Maheśānī, one should worship Śivā with hibiscus flowers as previously described.
By means of that very [practice], one should worship the Supreme Goddess for exactly one month in due order;
she destroys sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed in previous births—
of this there is no doubt— and the wise person becomes wealthy.
O beloved, one should worship as before with fresh ketakī flowers;
within just one month, he shall destroy all multitudes of minor sins (upapātaka),
and incomparable good fortune will arise for him— of this there is no doubt.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship for a period of one month with delightful hundred-petaled lotuses as before; this shall destroy all sin.
One should worship Śivā with Campaka flowers, as delightful as jasmine, as before;
within a single month, he surely destroys the [karmic effects] born of a hundred lifetimes.
By the grace of Tripurā, the practitioner of the mantra shall become possessed of good fortune.
O Great Goddess, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with large white lotuses;
O Beloved, she destroys the sins committed in twenty previous births within a single month,
and liberation stands within the grasp of such a person.
O Goddess, by worshipping for just one month with Bandhūka flowers,
a man brings the three worlds under his control and burns away his prior sins.
O Supreme Goddess, one who, with a tranquil mind, always worships for a full month as before with bilva leaves and parched grain,
shall become prosperous and will always be a destroyer of all sins. || 11 ||
One should worship for the duration of one month with mallikā, mālatī, and kunda flowers, as well as with śatapatra and white lotuses.

By the very sequence of family tradition, one destroys the sins born of a hundred lifetimes, including those produced by the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. O Goddess, liberation is in his hand, and by his word he becomes equal to Brahmā.

O beloved, having worshipped for one month with agasti, bāṇa, bandhūka, and red utpala flowers according to the previous sequence, the practitioner of mantra, with a tranquil mind, shall destroy his sins and become manifest as equal to Kāma himself. || 14 ||
O Goddess, one should worship with campaka, pāṭala, bakula, nāgakeśara, kahlāra, and sindhuvāra flowers, following the sequence as before.
In just one month, incomparable good fortune arises for him;
O Goddess, he shall destroy even the sin born of a thousand lifetimes.
On Sunday, with red lotuses; on Monday, with night-lilies;
on Tuesday, with red water-lilies;
on Wednesday, with tagara-flowers; on Thursday, with white lilies; and on Friday, with white lotuses.
One should worship with blue lotuses every Saturday for a year with devotion;
one should offer milk-rice, milk, plantain, fresh butter, sugar, and ghee on the seven days beginning with Sunday, as prescribed by the sequence.
Having thus propitiated the Goddess for a year in due order with perfumes and other offerings,
he quickly overcomes the affliction of the planets and enjoys all forms of happiness.
In the Matsyasūkta of Tārākālī:
"On the eighth and fourteenth [lunar days], one should worship with great care;
whatever the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) prays for, that he obtains constantly."
One obtains charming speech; one should always worship on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
In this context, following the daily worship (*nityārcanā*), the occasional rite (*naimittika*) should be performed.
Where no specific rule regarding time is observed, the occasional performance of the mandala ritual should be carried out every half-month, every month, or twice that period.
Thus it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"For half a month, or a month, or likewise for twice or thrice that duration, the yogi should practice in this manner until the attainment of the fruit. (19)
Elsewhere it is also said:
"In the case of rites performed for a specific purpose (naimittika) as well as those for desired results (kāmya), the attainment of the fruit extends up to the [completion of the] maṇḍala;
if not, [it does not follow]."
The wise person should perform twice that amount so as to become a partaker of the fruit.
Worship of the Goddess on the eighth day bestows the fruits of all desires.
[One should offer] plantains, jasmine, and citron, well-mixed with fragrant substances.
One should offer the oblation after mixing [the ingredients], especially on the eighth lunar day.
One should present a golden garland to Mahādevī with fragrant scents;
likewise, one should offer fruit and milk, with sugar added in abundance.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śivā for the sake of attaining perfection;
and for the sake of achieving imperishable results, one should diligently offer fruit to the Goddess.
Likewise, in the Nīlatantra:
"On the eighth and the fourteenth [lunar days], one should worship according to the rule;
thus one attains the accomplishment of the Command (ājñāsiddhi), as well as the javā flower and the varvarā."
One should offer sandalwood, *arka* flowers, and white *aparājitā*;
whoever especially worships Durgā on the Mahāṣṭamī will,
at that very moment, destroy the sin accumulated over three lifetimes.
"She is Durgā, the Savior," because this is supported by the context. || 21 ||
Now, the procedure for the ritual application (*prayoga*):
in every application, there is ten thousand recitations (*ayuta-japa*).
And so it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
The number of oblations (homa) should be ten thousand; the recitation (japa) is proclaimed to be of that same amount. || 22 ||
First, therein is the ritual application for Bhuvaneśvarī.
It is as follows:
the practitioner of mantra, having offered the best *aśvattha* fuel-sticks combined with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), [achieves his purpose].
One should quickly bring the Brahmins and the kings under one's control through the lotus-homa sacrifice.
Day after day, his wives and ministers should bathe with water over which the mantra has been recited twenty-five times, using *palāśa* flowers and also white lotuses (*kumuda*).

He who consecrates himself with this [mantra] shall possess all auspicious fortune. A man who drinks water over which the mantra has been recited twenty-five times in the morning, having attained great prosperity, shall become the foremost among poets. (25)
Likewise:
having offered oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one certainly obtains eloquence and prosperity.
Furthermore, he who drinks *brāhmī* ghee consecrated with the root mantra [attains the same].

The practitioner of mantra attains poetic skill within a year; of this there is no doubt. By offering white mustard seeds mixed with salt into the fire, the practitioner brings under his control a man, a woman, or a king—no deliberation is required here. (27)
Then, having quickly prepared a yoni-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to one's desire;
by offering oblations with jasmine flowers, one shall bring the entire world under control.
An oblation offered with Palāśa flowers pacifies sorcery, malice, and the like;
by offering auspicious stalks of sugarcane as an oblation, one attains great prosperity.
By performing a fire-oblation with dūrvā grass, the practitioner attains a long life;
by offering oblations with washed grains, he shall obtain his desired prosperity.
By offering *aśoka* flowers one obtains a son; by *madhuka* flowers one shall obtain what is desired;
and by sacrificing with fruits from the *jambū* tree, one attains the wealth one seeks.
With flowers produced from the bakula tree, one's fame shall be imperishable;
with mangoes, there shall be long life; and with campaka flowers, one shall obtain gold.
The wise man should perform a fire-oblation with mustard seeds, which brings about the destruction of enemies; by offering oblations with *vakula* leaves, he shall swiftly exterminate his foes. (33)
By the oblation of *śālmalī* leaves, one shall certainly destroy one's rivals;
by the oblation of black gram (*māṣa*), the enemy shall become mute, and by dice, he shall become insane.
Now, as for Durgā:
by means of an oblation of sesame seeds, one may subjugate men and even kings;
if the practitioner of mantra offers oblations with white mustard seeds, he shall be liberated from diseases at that very moment.
Having offered lotuses, one shall conquer enemies; with dūrvā grass, one shall obtain peace;
with palāśa flowers, nourishment; and with grains, one shall obtain an abundance of grain.
A homa performed with the feathers of a crow will spread hatred among men;
by a homa of black pepper (marīca), the enemy always meets his death.
Then Sarasvatī:
Having drunk that consecrated water, one should recite the mantra a thousand times every day;
within a year, the practitioner shall become a great poet—of this there is no doubt. (38)
Standing in water reaching only to the chest, one should meditate upon the Goddess seated within the orb of the sun;
reciting the mantra three thousand times every day, one obtains perfection from that orb as well as incomparable power of speech. (39)
One should offer oblations with *palāśa* and *bilva* flowers smeared with honey, or with fuel-sticks produced from those same trees; thus one attains fame and an expansion of speech. (40)
By offering oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one attains supreme mastery of speech;
likewise with *kadamba* flowers or fruits produced from the *bilva* tree, one quickly attains prosperity; and with those originating from the *kunda* flower, one gains eloquence of speech.
Or, by offering oblations with *nandyāvarta* flowers, one shall become beloved of speech.
Now, as for Lakṣmī:
having stood in water reaching up to her chest, she should recite this mantra.
Having meditated upon the Goddess in the solar orb, the practitioner of mantra should recite it three hundred thousand times;
he shall, in a short time, become a stable abode for Ramā.
Having propitiated the Goddess under the Uttara constellation with garlands, sandalwood, and other offerings,
he should then perform a thousand oblations with flowers from the *nandyāvarta* plant.
On the full moon day, he should offer oblations of bilva fruits soaked in honey.
On the fifth lunar day, falling on a Friday, with fragrant white lotuses or other pure flowers, one of vast intellect should worship every month;
within just one year, he shall become a perpetual treasury of all prosperity.
For one who constantly offers oblations of śāli rice one thousand and eight times, great prosperity will certainly arise before long. (44)
One should offer one thousand and eight oblations of Java flowers;
then, taking the ashes mixed with the juice of betel leaf, one should recite the mantra over them.
By applying a tilaka made from that, one will bring all beings under one's control.
The leaf of the betel vine. || 45 ||
Then Gaṇeśa:
One should daily satisfy the Lord of the Gaṇas with pure waters,
diligently offering four hundred and forty-four [libations].
A person shall obtain his desired goal, even more than that, before reaching the end of the maṇḍala.
A Homa performed with coconuts on the fourth lunar day brings about the attainment of prosperity.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, a wise person should perform the rite daily until the fourth day, using coconuts, powdered rice, parched grain, and sesame seeds in that order.
One should offer four hundred oblations; then all living beings will become submissive. || 47 ||
On the fourth lunar day, one becomes possessed of fortune by performing a fire-oblation with sesame seeds and rice;
by an oblation of lotuses, one gains kings; by auspicious blue lotuses, their queens;
by white water-lilies, ministers; and by flowers produced from the *pippala* tree, Brahmins.

With excellent fuel-sticks produced from the udumbara tree, a counselor should bring kings under his control; with those from the plakṣa tree, vaiśyas; and with those produced from the vaṭa tree, śūdras. (48)
Through honey, there shall be the acquisition of gold; through cow’s milk, one obtains cows.
By offering oblations of clarified butter (ājya), a human being attains great prosperity.
Through compassion, there shall be all-round success; through food offerings, one becomes a lord of food.
Then Sūrya said:
"In this manner, having duly worshipped Bhāskara, who is affectionate toward his devotees,"
One should offer the *arghya* daily, or when its [the deity’s] day has dawned;
having prepared a mandala at dawn, one should worship the pedestal as before. The vessel should be made of copper, holding one *prastha* of water, and be beautiful.
Having placed [these items] there, one should fill it with auspicious water; [namely:
saffron, gorocana, turmeric, red sandalwood, white water-lilies, oleander, hibiscus, rice, kusha grass, millet, and grains of rice.

Having conceived of oneness with the Sun, one who knows the ritual procedure should cast [the image] into that water and worship Bhāskara, possessing all his limbs and as described by the characteristics,
therein with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and so forth, according to the rules.
Having covered it, one should recite the mantra correctly one hundred and eight times.
Having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings, and having knelt upon the ground,
he should raise [the vessel] up to his head and fix his gaze upon the sun together with its enclosures in the sky, while muttering the root mantra with a sense of oneness.
With a serene inner soul, one should offer the arghya to the Lord of Day with compassion;
having offered a handful of flowers once more, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times,
until the Sun accepts the nectar of the arghya with his own rays.
The sun, satisfied by that, shall grant him his heart's desires.

This offering of the *arghya* increases the longevity and health of men; it bestows wealth, grain, cattle, fields, sons, friends, and wives; and it grants splendor, valor, fame, beauty, knowledge, prosperity, and good fortune. (51)
Then Śrī Rāma said:
"A man should offer oblations with *jātī* flowers for the attainment of fortune (*indirā*);
he should offer oblations with *jātī* flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water."
With lotuses, one gains control over kings; for the abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth, by means of an oblation of blue lotuses, one shall bring the entire world under one's power.
A person should offer oblations with bilva flowers to attain wealth;
by offering dūrvā grass, the practitioner of mantras shall become long-lived and free from disease. (53)
By offering red lotuses, the mantra-practitioner obtains his desired wealth;
one who desires intelligence should offer fresh palāśa flowers.
One who drinks water consecrated with that [mantra] becomes a poet after a year;
one who eats food consecrated with that [mantra] shall attain great health. (55)
Now, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
I shall describe the ritual applications common to both mantras,
by performing which the excellent practitioner becomes honored throughout the three worlds. (56)
I bow to that son of Devakī, who possesses the luster of a newly risen cloud,
who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and wears a garland of forest flowers;
having thus meditated upon this supreme mantra during the Brahma-muhūrta, one should recite it one hundred thousand times.
Having recited it, one attains supreme intelligence and becomes the foremost among poets.
Alternatively, having visualized her as having the luster of crystal and holding a manuscript and a writing tablet,
one should recite the root mantra one hundred thousand times during the Brahma-muhūrta;
having thus recited it, the practitioner of mantra becomes a knower of the three periods of time and equal to Bṛhaspati.
Meditating upon the Child (Bāla) during the Brāhma-muhūrta, while reciting the excellent mantra, the wise man becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures;
he certainly becomes proficient in the meaning of all Vedas and endowed with knowledge. || 59 ||

Meditating thus upon the best of men— who wanders through Nanda’s courtyard, grey with a mass of dust, radiant with a multitude of blazing jewels, and eager for Yaśodā’s gaze— one should recite the mantra while remaining firm in one's observances.
What on this earth cannot be accomplished by reciting this [mantra] one hundred thousand times? || 60 ||
Drinking water every morning while reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times,
even one who is extremely mute, evil-minded, or as dull-witted as a stone becomes directly like the Lord of Speech himself through this drinking of water.
This occurs; there is no doubt here—this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.

Having placed the cart upon his feet and meditating that it is weeping like an ordinary person, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; thus, he will certainly be liberated from calamities.
He has no fear from enemies, nor from kings, nor even from robbers;
he shall never experience any terror whatsoever, O observer of noble vows. (63)
One should constantly worship Kṛṣṇa, who delights in ritual action, with wild flowers;
then all [others], including Brāhmaṇas, become submissive—of this there is no doubt. (64)
One should mentally worship the one in the guise of a cowherd with jasmine flowers;
kings will become submissive—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (65)
Indeed, by means of flowers produced from the *tamāla* tree, Vaiśyas become submissive.
And Śūdras should worship [the deity] for a month with blue lotuses during the dark fortnight;
they should offer oblations of red flowers mixed with sesame seeds and rice,
and having recited the mantra eight thousand times, they should wear that sacred ash.
Indeed, when it is worn upon the forehead, all beings become subject to his control.
By means of this body, kings shall come under one's control; likewise, women, sons, and ministers will become submissive in every way. 68.
One who desires marriage should recite the mantra eight thousand times for one month,
while meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, who stands in Vraja situated in the center of the Rāsa-maṇḍala;
he shall thus marry a maiden of excellent form, radiant with all virtues.
One should meditate upon that Hari who, when entreated by a twice-born man saying, "Protect my son, protect him!",
restored the stolen son to him.
One desiring a son shall obtain a beautiful son within one month,
endowed with long life and unimpeded strength and vigor.
Having propitiated Kṛṣṇa with *kundapuṣpa* flowers, the maiden should meditate upon Him;
likewise, for two months she should mutter the mantra eight thousand times.
Having obtained her heart's desire as her husband, she sports with him for a long time.

Having touched collyrium, flowers, clothing, betel, sandalwood, and other such objects of enjoyment, one should recite the mantra one hundred times. To whomever these are given, that person will soon become submissive like a servant. (72)
O best of sages, women become submissive by this very [means];
likewise, a woman may bring a man under her control through this very procedure. (73)
One who desires food and drink should offer one thousand and eight oblations with *śrīpuṣpa* flowers mixed with white rice; he shall become possessed of abundant food. (74)

Having meditated upon the one who bears the universal form, the practitioner of mantra, with a concentrated mind, should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; one seeking glory shall obtain renown. One afflicted by spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and the like, or by the seizing grahas such as Skanda and others, [shall be liberated].
Having meditated upon the one who drank from the breast of Pūtanā, one should recite the mantra one hundred times. || 76 ||
Evil planetary influences perish and flee hither and thither;
even when bitten by a serpent or a swarm of snakes, or stung by mice and other such creatures,
a person should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of Kāliya, and recite [the mantra].
One should destroy the terrible poison that is threatening by means of the syllable HŪṂ. || 77 ||
In this regard, I shall declare the *apānya-mantra* beginning with the seed-syllable; listen to it according to its true nature.
I bow to that son of Devakī, the Lord Acyuta, the King of Dance, who performs divine dance in the midst of the hoods of Kāliya. (78)
One afflicted by fever should worship the mantra and likewise recite it one hundred and eight times;
thus [one is freed] from fever.
Having meditated upon the praised Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Bala and Pradyumna,
standing atop Garuḍa and burning the city of Bāṇa,
and being crushed by the Najajvara [fever], one destroys [the affliction] in an instant.

A mantra-expert, by the mere sight [of this], destroys chills, jaundice, and the like, as well as quartan fevers, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, worms, wind-disorders, epilepsy, and fear; of this there is no doubt. (79)

Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, whose feet are cherished by the cowherds and who stands holding his flute, one should recite the mantra; after a month, he shall possess cattle. This applies to one whose mind is set on becoming the royal priest of a king.
Having offered white flowers sprinkled with honey into that maṇḍala, one shall obtain great sovereignty;
furthermore, having attained it, one will certainly become world-renowned. (80)
Having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the upholder of Govardhana, a person should mutter the mantra when a terrible danger from wind, rain, and so forth has fully arisen;
his fear shall quickly perish—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (81)
Desiring rain, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa who has gone to Vṛndāvana and recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; one will undoubtedly obtain rain.
Thus, having meditated with the mind, one may bring down rain even during the dry season.
Having meditated thus upon the reservoir of water, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times;
even out of season, a great rain will fall—of this there is no doubt. || 83 ||
Desiring to sing, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa playing the flute;
having offered eight hundred oblations of clarified butter, one is sung of together with the Kinnaras.
He who desires victory should recite [the mantra] while meditating upon Acyuta, the wish-fulfilling tree being carried away,
who is praised by the deities and mounted upon Garuḍa;
that self-controlled practitioner should then offer oblations with fuel-sticks of red karavīra.
If one performs one thousand and eight oblations, the enemy is directly defeated;
when danger from kings and others has arisen, or in times of uncertainty, difficulty, or assembly,
by performing ten thousand oblations, one will certainly destroy that [danger] at that very moment.
Having offered one thousand and eight oblations of blue lotuses and other flowers,
and having meditated upon Hari— who is situated in the center of Dvārakā and accompanied by the treasures such as the conch—
one should perform a rite for pacification by offering oblations of rice and *dūrvā* grass.
Having meditated upon Janārdana, the cowherd adorned with a forest garland, singing at the foot of a kadamba tree and graced by kadamba flowers,
one should offer oblations with apāmārga leaves one thousand and eight times.
Having brought all the worlds under his control, he will quickly become wise. || 87 ||

At the king’s gate, in the assembly hall, and in legal proceedings, one who knows the mantra should first recite it one hundred and eight times and then utter his initial statement. By this very procedure, he shall be victorious everywhere. (88)
A man desiring liberation should diligently mutter the mantra of the lotus-eyed,
immutable Lord Kṛṣṇa, who is praised by Sanaka and others, who wears white garments,
and who holds the conch and the discus; having meditated upon Him, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

Having encased [the mantra] with the *tāra* (om) and occupied the proper place according to the rules, one should worship Kṛṣṇa within the maṇḍala of the lotus of the wheel while maintaining devotion;
he is immediately liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra—of this there is no doubt. || 89 ||
Then Dadhivāmana says:
One should offer a thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) and obtain prosperity;
by an oblation of grain, one obtains grain, as does one with oblations produced from a hundred flowers.
An oblation performed with seeds numbering one thousand destroys all fears.
Having offered oblations of pure curd-rice, one shall be liberated from an evil rebirth.
Recalling the form of the Three-Striding One (Viṣṇu), one should mutter the mantra with undistracted mind;
one shall be instantly freed from bondage—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Now, Hayagrīva:
A fire-offering performed with bilva fruits is proclaimed to bestow the state of prosperity.
One desiring imperishable glory of speech should offer kunda flowers as oblations.
Ghee consecrated by this mantra and boiled with the juices of *brāhmī* brings forth unimpeded poetic inspiration in men. One should daily consume *vacā* root consecrated by this mantra at dawn.
One soon becomes an expounder of all the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures. || 92 ||
Then, O Nṛsiṃha,
the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with flowers into a fire kindled with bilva wood;
he obtains prosperity by offering a thousand [oblations], or else with leaves produced from the bilva tree.
Śrīpuṣpa is the clove flower. || 93 ||
Likewise, through flowers or fruits, or by the offering of *dūrvā* grass, one attains freedom from disease.
When a bad dream occurs at night, one should bathe and recite the mantra one hundred times;
thereafter, the knower of the mantra, being free from sleepiness, experiences auspicious dreams.

In a great forest agitated by fear of tigers, thieves, wild beasts, and the like, this *mantra*— when recited— protects the practitioner from other dangers; likewise, ashes consecrated with this *mantra* [ward off] poisons, seizing spirits, and great serpents.
One shall destroy [it] very quickly indeed through the power of this mantra. || 95 ||
In cases of terrible sorcery, insanity, great portents, or great fear, one should recite the mantra and remember this; thus the person shall be liberated from suffering. (96)
Having visualized oneself as the all-pervading Lord in the form of a lion— extremely terrifying with claws and fangs that inspire great dread— one should then meditate upon the enemy as a young deer.
Having seized him by the throat, one should then swiftly cast him in all directions.
The eradication of enemies, including their sons, friends, wives, and others, occurs. (97)
Having first placed the name of the one to be subdued upon the seat of death, Hari himself,
visualizing the enemy being devoured by his own sharp claws, fangs, and so forth,
should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times without weariness.
Within the mandala, there arises the warding off of enemy armies. || 98 ||
When the fire is kindled with *vibhītaka* wood, one should meditate upon the god Nṛhari, the crusher of enemies,
worship him with flowers and other offerings,
and offer one thousand arrows, each cut together with their roots, individually into the fire.
As if devouring the enemy, one should mutter the mantra; as if piercing him, one should cast it down.
Having performed this for seven days, the practitioner of mantra, desiring victory over the foreign kingdom, should dispatch the king’s beloved army at an auspicious moment.
In front of her, one should perform the ritual visualization while recollecting Nṛhari slaying the circle of his enemies, until she returns again,
having conquered all foes and dwelling happily with the glory of heroism.

A victorious king, with a well-pleased mind, should properly gratify his minister with villages, fields, wealth, and other riches. If the minister is not satisfied, it will lead to disaster for the lord of the earth.
Now, regarding Varāha:
when the sun is in Leo, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
one should place a white stone in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), touch it, and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Facing north, one should bury that stone in the ground;
thus, one shall destroy the afflictions caused by enemies, thieves, and great spirits.
At sunrise on a Tuesday, one should collect earth from the site of the object to be accomplished while reciting the mantra; then, one should divide that earth into three parts:
having written [the mantra] on one part upon the hearth, and likewise on another part upon the cooking vessel.
Having thoroughly stirred [the milk] in divine cow’s milk, one should cast purified rice grains into it;
once the fire has been consecrated, the practitioner, reciting the mantra, should properly cook the *caru* offering.
Thereafter, having removed the *caru* from the fire, he should worship the deity according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped with incense, lamps, and other offerings,
one should again offer oblations of *caru* soaked in clarified butter into the kindled fire, up to one hundred and eight times.
In this manner, one should perform the oblation on seven consecutive Sundays for the sake of attaining mastery over the sacred field (*kṣetrasiddhi*).
In the morning, on a Saturday, the wise man should take earth from the ground where the object of the rite is to be accomplished,
prepare it as before, and offer oblations; thus,
opposition in the field, along with afflictions such as thieves and the like, shall perish.

With fuel-sticks produced from the rājavṛkṣa tree, this sage Manu should offer oblations three thousand times; for him, there shall be all prosperity. The practitioner of mantras should constantly offer oblations of śāli rice one hundred and eight times.
His mansion shines with an abundance of heaps of grain;
as long as one offers oblations of clarified butter from the maṇḍala, one shall obtain gold.

Now, regarding Mṛtyuñjaya: Having subdued his senses, the practitioner of mantra, having worshipped the fire according to the rules for one month, should offer a thousand oblations of pieces of Sudhā (Euphorbia) sprinkled with milk.
Sudhākhaṇḍa is guḍūcī.
With that, may the crane be satisfied, its body drenched in nectar;
[this shall] increase longevity, health, prosperity, fame, and sons. || 4 ||
One should diligently offer oblations for seven days with these seven substances mentioned— lime, banyan seeds, sesame, dūrvā grass, milk, clarified butter, and milk-offering (payo-havis)—
ten hundred times daily, each time increased by eight.

The practitioner of mantras should daily feed seven or more twice-born brahmins with sweet foods. He should increase the number of offering days in accordance with his specific transformation (vikāra).
He should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee consisting of reddish-brown, milch cows.
Having first worshipped the Guru with wealth and other offerings, regarding him as a deity,

one should then perform the rite for the accomplishment [of the goal] according to this procedure; thus, being liberated from sorcery, malice, and the like, one shall easily live for a full hundred autumns.
In cases of malevolent sorcery, acute fever, terrible insanity,
diseases of the head, incurable ailments, poison-induced affliction, delusion, burning sensations, and great fear—
this fire-oblation is declared to bestow peace and grant all prosperity.
One should offer oblations with these substances according to the prescribed rule throughout three lifetimes;
one should feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas with sweet foods. Thus, one attains long life and obtains desired prosperity.
A wise person should daily offer eleven oblations with dūrvā grass;
this shall surely conquer untimely death and increase longevity and health.
A fire sacrifice performed with the finest sacrificial fuel (samidh) produced from the nectar-creeper, saffron, and vakula flowers during three lifetimes removes all death and disease.
An oblation performed with *siddhārtha* seeds destroys even great fevers;
an oblation with fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* eradicates all diseases.
Now, as for Dakṣiṇāmūrti:
subsisting on alms and with his senses subdued, one should recite this mantra for a month, eight hundred times daily; he attains supreme excellence in speech.
The best of practitioners should drink water consecrated by reciting this mantra three times; he should daily meditate upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
and within a year he will attain the capacity to explain the scriptures.

Ghee cooked with the pastes of *brāhmī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, long pepper (*kaṇa*), and blue lotus (*utpala*), combined with fragrant substances, along with the juice of *brāhmī*—
this well-prepared ghee should be consecrated ten thousand times with this mantra.
When drunk, it bestows the splendor of poetry, strength, longevity, prosperity, and fortitude. || 11 ||
Then Bhairavī:
one should offer oblations with unblemished red lotuses soaked in honey, numbering one hundred thousand or more; thereafter, one should feed Brahmins every day.
One should please beautiful young women with the thought that they are deities;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should satisfy one's own preceptor with wealth, grain, and other offerings.
When this is done, the world becomes submissive and one shall attain the abode of Lakṣmī.

By performing a fire sacrifice with red lotuses or red flowers of the *hayāri* (flax) smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), along with milk, rice, and ghee, one brings the entire world under one's control.
The mantra-practitioner attains mastery over speech by performing oblations with *palāśa* flowers;
