the wise one should offer *guggulu* resin combined with camphor and agallochum.
By that very act, he attains divine knowledge and becomes a poet.
An oblation with pieces of *amṛtā* soaked in milk conquers all untimely death.
An oblation with *dūrvā* grass soaked in milk for three days bestows long life.
One will certainly bring Brahmins under one's influence by means of flowers from the *girikarṇī* plant.
By offering *kahlāra* flowers to kings, their wives with *karṇikāra* flowers, and their sons with *mālatī* blossoms, one shall bring them under one's control. (15)

The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations of *koraṇṭaka* flowers for Vaiśyas and *pāṭala* flowers for Śūdras, mixed with honey; having uttered the mantra accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) situated at the end of both the direct and reverse orders.
With mustard seeds mixed with pungent substances, one may bring kings under control in an instant. || 16 ||

By this very procedure, one shall certainly bring under control his wife and even his sons, as well as men, women, and kings, through oblations of *jātī* flowers, *bilva* fruits, and blossoms combined with the three sweets (*madhuratra*). (17)
By offering flowers produced from the *mālatī* and *vakula* trees mixed with sandalwood paste,
the practitioner of mantra obtains poetic skill within a year;
likewise, by offering fruits produced from the *bilva* tree combined with the three sweets (*madhuratrika*).
One should perform oblations; thus one shall subjugate the worlds and attain the desired prosperity.
He who offers oblations with *pāṭala* flowers, *kunda*, blue lotuses, *nāga-campaka*, blooming *nandyāvarta*, and *kṛtamāla* flowers [achieves these results].
Within a year, he is born as one who has surpassed earthly kings in prosperity. || 19 ||
One should offer oblations of food with clarified butter; one will then possess an abundance of food.
One who desires to subjugate others should offer camphor combined with musk and saffron;
such a person immediately attains a beauty even greater than that of Kandarpa.
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of parched grain soaked in curd, milk, and ghee;
having conquered all diseases, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Having ground together two parts of sandalwood (*malayaja*), one part of saffron filaments (*kuṅkumakeśara*),
and one part of yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*) with snow-water,
one should apply a tilaka-mark on the forehead; by this, those who see it and those by whom it is seen [are brought under one's influence].
Those whom he touches, or by whom he is touched, shall quickly come under his control.
One should prepare equal parts of camphor, *kapicora*, and *kaṅkola*; *jaṭāmāṃsī* is considered to be four parts, and *rocanā* is held to be the same amount;
saffron (*kuṅkuma*) should be seven parts, and sandalwood (*candana*) is considered to be one part.
Aguru should consist of nine parts according to this sequence of proportions.
All of this, well-prepared with snow-water and ground with *kanyā* [juice], should be taken; by applying it as a tilaka on the forehead, one shall bring kings and men under one's control.

By the mere sight of her, she shall bring under control women full of the pride of intoxication, elephants maddened by rut, lions and tigers of great courage, as well as bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (23)
Then Sundarī says in the Jñānārṇava:
"With jasmine, mālatī, and jātī flowers mixed with honey..."
O Goddess, by offering oblations with vessels filled with clarified butter, mastery of speech is produced;
for even one who is mute, dull-witted, or like a stone, it happens thus and not otherwise.
By performing oblations with javā flowers sprinkled with clarified butter, and likewise with karavīra flowers of the same kind,
the practitioner of mantras shall delude the inhabitants of the three worlds.
O Goddess, when camphor and saffron are mixed with musk and offered in the fire-oblation, O Goddess of good vows, the practitioner shall conquer Madana by means of his good fortune, charm, and power.
By offering *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers, the practitioner of mantra attains great, radiant prosperity that illuminates the heavens; he may even paralyze this entire world.
Then, one should offer oblations of śrīkhaṇḍa, guggulu, candana, and aguru;
by this, one shall bring under control the wives of the lords of the nāgas, asuras, and gods.
All the worlds become subject to him; of this there is no doubt.

By means of a hundred thousand oblations, one obtains a kingdom; and for one afflicted by the fear of poverty, O Goddess, there is the pacification of calamities through the offering of three *pala* measures of honey.
By performing a fire-oblation at night with the flesh of a goat smeared with blood and anointed with the three sweets, according to the procedure taught by the Guru,
one shall bring even a great fortress and an entire foreign kingdom under one's own control.
O fair-faced one, by offering cow’s milk, honey, curd, and clarified butter separately into the fire,
longevity, strength, health, and prosperity arise for men.
O Daughter of the Mountain, by means of milk and honey offered in sequence, death is destroyed;
by an oblation of curd and honey, one shall obtain good fortune and wealth.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, when the oblation is performed with only white sugar, along with curd, honey, milk, and parched grain, it causes the paralysis of enemies;
there is no doubt that it is the destroyer of time, the destroyer of disease, and the destroyer of death.
An oblation with red lotuses bestows complete prosperity;
with red water-lilies, the world is brought under control, and kings fall into subjection in an instant. (33)
O beloved, through oblations of blue lotuses, even the most wicked are brought under control; there is no other way. Through oblations of white lotuses, one obtains prosperity and eloquence.
Likewise:
having worshipped the rosary and then well-anointed it with sandalwood paste,
one should remain pure at all times and recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times while holding it.
Women certainly cause his mind to waver;
at that time, the best of practitioners should recite the second *lakṣa*.
Then, the daughters of the great serpent-kings from the depths of Pātāla will agitate him.

By a mere sidelong glance of them, she deludes the practitioner. Then, with a steady mind, the practitioner should perform three hundred thousand recitations. When the third hundred thousand has been completed, the celestial maidens cause him to wander.
By means of pride, which causes intoxication with beauty and good fortune, she indeed deludes the practitioner; yet therein, his mind remains steadfast.
Then, three hundred thousand [recitations] are effective for cutting away all sins.
When the practitioner, with a steady mind, has thus recited three hundred thousand times,
he deludes the inhabitants of the heavenly world (svarloka), the earthly world (bhūrloka), and the netherworld (talaloka).
O beloved, men and women, as well as all things moving and stationary, come under one's control.
One should draw the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) with substances such as gorocana and the like;
in its center, one should place an excellent image that is exceedingly beautiful and charming,
blazing, accompanied by the name, and interlaced with the great seed-syllable (mahābīja).
Then one should meditate upon the Goddess, even if she is a thousand *yojanas* away;
O Queen of the Gods, she who has never been seen before is difficult to attain even by mere hearing. Or [one may meditate on] a princess or a wife who is devoid of fear and shame.
O beloved, being deluded by the mantra, she comes to the practitioner in the proper manner.
Having placed himself in the center of the wheel, the practitioner should always contemplate himself as being red and possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns;
O Supreme Goddess, he should likewise contemplate the target as having become red.
By this sequential yoga, one becomes personally the embodiment of Kandarpa,
endowed with all auspiciousness and beauty, the subduer of all worlds,
and possesses a form accompanied by mudrās and all red offerings.
O Goddess, whoever should worship the Cakra while interweaving the name of another person,
that person shall become like a servant, whether he be wealthy or even a king.
Likewise, whoever should place the name of a woman within the center of the Cakra [shall likewise be subdued].
O Great Goddess, the wise practitioner who maintains the Yoni-mudrā swiftly compels by force even an unseen Yakṣiṇī, a princess,
a Nāga maiden, an Apsaras, a Khecarī, or a celestial nymph.
[He saw] a Vidyādharī of divine form, a daughter of the sages, the wife of his enemy,
whose broad hips were the site of the torment arising from passion,
her inner heart pierced by the arrows of Love, and her eyes darting restlessly. (40)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, through the yoga of meditating upon the Great Kāmakalā,
one may cause the women of the heavens, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld to tremble with passion.
Take one part of *rocanā* (yellow pigment) and one part of saffron;
then, O Goddess, grind two parts of sandalwood together with them. One should apply a *tilaka* made from this mixture, which brings the three worlds under one's control.
Having consecrated the mantra one hundred and eight times, one shall bring under control the king,
the city, and the village, however they may appear;
O Supreme Goddess, by means of this, all that shall come under his sway through the minister.
Betel leaf, incense, water, a leaf, a flower, fruit, curd, milk, merely the powder, cloth, camphor, musk,
saffron, cloves, and nutmeg.

O Supreme Goddess, whatever object there may be, whether it be water or anything else, if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and gives it to whomever, that person becomes submissive, O Goddess; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (43)
All women indeed become submissive and like female slaves;
this is called "forcible attraction," and it shall not be otherwise.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe that which destroys great sins.
O Devī, O beloved, one should worship Śivā with fragrant flowers;
one whose self is burdened by great sins becomes a destroyer of sin at that very moment. (45)
By means of śamī, dūrvā sprouts, aśvattha leaves, or those born from arka, a person destroys the impurity created over seven lifetimes within one month. (46)
One who performs the yoga bound by the mudrās through the previously described meditative yoga and recites [the mantra] exactly one hundred thousand times is liberated from great sins. (47)

By means of two hundred thousand [recitations], one shall destroy even the sins committed over seven lifetimes, including the foremost of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka); there is no doubt in this matter. || 48 ||
Then, O Mistress of the Kula, by reciting [the mantra] two hundred thousand times, one shall destroy ten million great sins; of this there is no doubt. (49)
O Goddess, by reciting it four hundred thousand times, one becomes a great lord of speech;
O Queen of the Gods, by five hundred thousand times, one becomes like Kubera—of this there is no doubt. (50)
By merely reciting it six hundred thousand times, one becomes a great Vidyādhara;
by seven hundred thousand recitations, the mantra-practitioner attains union with the Khecarīs. (51)
By reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times, the practitioner becomes worthy of worship by the gods;
O Dear One, he becomes the master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*. Kings and women, in particular, come under his control.
One should recite the mantra of Tripurasundarī one million times;
that practitioner becomes Rudra himself, the creator, manifest before one's eyes—of this there is no doubt.
He shall be ever worshipped by all, eternally well-established, and possessed of all auspicious fortune.
Now, regarding Chinnamastā:
a fire sacrifice (homa) using bilva fruits, palāśa leaves, and likewise those of the udumbara tree, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments, should be performed with great effort. (54)

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should thereafter perform the recitation (japa). The homa should be performed with jasmine flowers mixed with honey, or even with ghee; this bestows the status of the Lord of Speech.
An offering should always be given with food mixed with clarified butter and meat;
for six months, it should be combined with curd, and his prosperity shall become stable.
He who offers ten thousand oblations of goat meat mixed with blood, saturated with ghee, to the Goddess, shall bring her under his control. || 57 ||
He who performs the fire-oblation correctly one hundred thousand times with white oleander flowers according to the prescribed rite shall live for a hundred autumns.
The practitioner should offer oblations with sesame flowers and honey;
for him who offers them as many times as there are syllables in the mantra, success will come—of this there is no doubt. (59)
O beautiful goddess, he who offers thousands of *karṇikāra* flowers together with clarified butter attains supreme, desired perfection.
O beautiful one, one should perform the fire-oblation with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) along with clarified butter.
By practicing this for three periods of twilight for just one month, one shall attain mastery over speech.
Now, from the Śyāmākālītantra:
Next, I shall describe the ritual procedure for the attainment of desired objects, by which one becomes a master in all things.
The practitioner shall achieve success that is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The practitioner who, with a steady mind and in a state of complete secrecy, recites [the mantra] ten thousand times upon seeing the *Kulāgāra* of the *Puṣpitā*, shall become a treasury of knowledge.
Sanskrit words, Prakrit words, as well as worldly and Vedic ones—
all these come under the control of the practitioner, and not otherwise.
Alternatively, having consumed the sacrificial oblation with disheveled hair, a wise man who is well-restrained should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times; he shall obtain this very same fruit.
Seeing another woman naked, the practitioner should recite the mantra ten thousand times; he will quickly become a beloved of the Vidyā herself.
Merely by the sight of him, the disputants were rendered tongue-tied;
his speech, consisting of both prose and verse, arose within the assembly. (66)
All the wise, filled with joy, bow down to him by his name;
through familiarity with his speech, even the dull-witted become eloquent. (67)
In the *Kulacuḍāmaṇi*: Having approached a woman who is in her menses, and having worshipped the chosen deity upon her body during the dead of night, one should recite the mantra for three days.
O Goddess, one obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand sacred seats; there is no doubt about this.
O Bhairava, the most excellent practitioner should accomplish the siddhi of the vetāla, the sandals, and the sword, as well as the secret ointment and forehead mark;
he should recite [the mantra] every day one thousand and eight times—this is the meaning. || 69 ||
Where neither a number for recitation nor for fire-offerings is stated by those who satisfy the mind,
there the count is declared to be one thousand times eight thousand.
One who desires knowledge should offer oblations with lotuses mixed with honey;
one who desires wealth should offer oblations combined with sesame, clarified butter, and honey.
By means of an oblation of *vandhūka* flowers, one makes even a king a servant;
by an oblation of ghee and salt, one always attracts a beloved woman.
By performing oblations with *vakula* flowers alone, a man obtains good fortune;
by using *mallikā*, *jāti*, *punnāga*, and *kadamba* flowers, he shall attain nourishment.
Through oblations of milk, clarified butter, and tagara, one shall obtain great poetic skill.
Furthermore, by performing a fire sacrifice (homa) with sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, and camphor, the mantra-practitioner shall obtain all desired objects from Nīlasarasvatī.
The term "Nīlasarasvatī" is used here as an illustration [for other deities]. 75.
By performing a fire sacrifice with camphor, the practitioner of mantra shall obtain all desired objects.
Having worshipped with the root mantra, and having offered one thousand bilva leaves smeared with ghee every day, he attains the supreme goal.
"Daily" means up until the completion of the mandala. || 76 ||
Through the oblation (*homa*) of *mālatī* flowers smeared with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one becomes a swift poet.
In this context, wherever a specific number for the oblation is not mentioned, there it should be offered ten thousand times (*ayuta*).
This has been stated in that very same work:
However, for every single oblation, this rule applies to a number of ten thousand.
Now, regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*):
in the *Matsyasūkta*, it is said:
"One should perform the libation with honey; it fulfills all desires."
It directly brings about the accomplishment of mantras and destroys even the greatest of sins. || 78 ||
In the *Nīlatantra*:
"If one performs the libation for a full month with waters mixed with camphor, having brought all kings under one's control, one shall be an enjoyer of pleasures for as long as one lives. (79)
For the attainment of full longevity, one should offer ghee; for the attainment of health, milk;
by offering water mixed with agallochum (aguru), one shall be happy at all times. (80)
For the accomplishment of all goals, one should use water mixed with coconut water;
likewise, one may destroy enemies with water mixed with black pepper.
By means of these [mantras] alone belonging to the Uṣṇatīya [group], one may cause an enemy to vanish in an instant.
He shall become possessed by fever; by sprinkling him with milk, one should bring him back to normalcy.
In the *Siddhasārasvata*:
"By merely reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, a wise practitioner who applies a tilaka of yellow pigment (rocanā) will cause whomever he looks upon to become like a servant. (83)
With *pherakārī*, one may bring the king’s wife under control through specific ritual services;
the king by mere recitation (*japa*); and the entire world by means of an offering (*bali*).
"By means of a specific mode of worship" (upacāraviśeṣeṇa) should be understood as referring to the distinction between different types of practitioners (adhikāribheda).
"By mere recitation" (japamātreṇa) means outside of formal ritual worship (pūjāvahirbhāva). || 84 ||
Regarding the materials for the bali offering, the Matsyasūkta states:
"Having mixed together plantains, jasmine, citron, and fragrant substances, one should offer the bali, especially on the eighth lunar day. (85)
As for the mantra for the bali offering:
having first uttered the Praṇava, then [the name] Ugratārā,
one should subsequently recite the two words "vikaṭadaṣṭre mohaya."

"Kill! Eat the enemies! Cook the pair! Then say: 'Those who are intent on harming me—destroy them with the circles of Yoginīs! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! [Then] attract the rival's spell! Break the pair! Seize, seize the offering in the skull-cup! Svāhā!"
In the case of Ārāviṣaya, however, the materials for the bali offering should be understood as those described in the relevant chapter of the *Kālikā* and other [tantras].
Now, the method for subjugation and so forth,
as stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"Having taken charcoal from a cremation ground on a Tuesday at night..."
Having wrapped [the object] in black cloth, one should bind it with a red thread;
having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should cast it into the house of the enemy.
Within seven days, this shall effect his great expulsion.
Thus it is said in the Phetkārīya: "One should write the mantra on human bone with turmeric mixed with alkali; having recited it one thousand times at night on a Saturday."
In whosever house it is deposited, death shall come to him within two months. || 88 ||

In the field there will be loss of crops; in the case of a horse, there will be loss of the mount; in the treasury, there will be loss of wealth; and in the center of the village, there will be its destruction. "Kṣāra" refers to the excrement of a hawk, while "viṭalavaṇa" is fecal salt. || 89 ||
In the center of the letter *ra* situated below the *hṛllekhā*, one should write: "Create great hatred between so-and-so and so-and-so.
As it has been said:
"For the purpose of creating hatred, the wise man should write the mantra on a cloth from a corpse."
The names of the one who hates and the one who is hated [should be written]; his hatred shall become great.

One should write the mantra—having written the mantra, the meaning is that it should include the target (sādhya) such as "Kill so-and-so, kill," in the middle of the *hṛllekhā* and the letter *ra*. || 90 ||
Alternatively, having written the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), one should write at its end:
"Having recited [the mantra] a thousand times, kill, kill so-and-so. Thus, the recitation of the mantra is performed at the end.
For the purpose of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), however, one should recite it a thousand times at the end of the formula: "Create enmity between so-and-so and so-and-so."
Now, the accomplishment of the Vetāla and so forth:
as it is said in the *Kulacuḍāmaṇi*,
Bhairava said:
O Caṇḍikā, how does the great siddhi of the Vetālas and other powers come to be?
Tell me that, O Queen of the Gods, if you have affection for me. (92)
The Goddess said:
On a Tuesday at midnight, the best of practitioners, accompanied by his kula and his wife, should go to a cremation ground and take wood produced from a nimba tree.
Having dug [the ground], one should indeed recite the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī eight hundred thousand times;

likewise, one should offer a thousand oblations right there in that cemetery (pitṛkānana). Then, having extracted a wooden staff marked with the sign of a sandal (pāduka), one should place it therein.
Having performed [the rites] on the night of Durgāṣṭamī, he should then cast [the substance] into a cremation ground;
having placed a corpse upon it and worshipped according to the prescribed rule,
the hero, seated upon the corpse, should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Then, having offered the *mātṛbali*, one should address the wooden staff (*kāṣṭha*):
"Sphreṃ Sphreṃ! O Staff, O highly fortunate one, beloved of the heart of the Yoginīs!
O Lord, held in my hand, fulfill my command."
Having thus addressed it, wherever the vetāla is employed, the Kaulika, having reduced that very thing to powder, returns once again. (93-ka)
"Go, go, go quickly, O sandals of excellent hue!
By the mere touch of my feet, travel you a hundred yojanas,
having assumed a form of fifty finger-breadths made of the eight metals."
Having fashioned a sword and written the mantra upon it, one should recite that mantra a thousand times; then, having offered oblations over a great corpse,
one should bury the sword at the root of a living tree and, once bound there, contemplate it as dry.
At midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
having affectionately invoked [the deity] joined within the midst of the funeral pyre, one should then perform the oblation in the cemetery with bilva leaves combined with the three sweets.

From the feet up to the head, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should present the bali offering. At the end of the bali, the supreme Māyā, the goddess Mahiṣamardinī, arrives with her face full of the bali, her hand holding a boon-granting gesture, and her countenance smiling.
Saying "Take it, child," one should raise and hold up the sword [with the mantra]:
"O Ghoradaṃṣṭrā Mahākālī, you whose very form is the sword!
Āṃ Ghrāṃ Ghrīṃ Ghrūṃ Īṃ Ūṃ, perform auspiciousness!"
Having thus addressed the rhinoceros-horn [spear] for the sake of extensively cutting off opposing factors, the person who hurls it at its target—
having cut, cut, and cut again, it goes forth and is drawn back again. (94)
Alternatively, one should kill a black cat with a single blow and then bury it at a crossroads at night after consecrating it with mantras. Having planted a plantain tree there,
one shall enjoy [the fruit] as soon as its leaves begin to grow.
Every night, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times while consuming sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), remaining alone and avoiding the light of a lamp.
Upon seeing that a leaf has sprouted, one should cut it and bring it back without any holes.
Having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) on the bank of a river that day,
one should bring him there along with a circle of friends and wash [the bones] while reciting the mantra.
Then, O child, the bone proceeds toward the mouth of the stream.
Then, having brought [the substance] there, one should worship Kālikā, who possesses a terrible roar;
having diligently recited the Kālī-mantra a thousand times,
the practitioner of mantra will become possessed of *siddhāñjana*— of this there is no doubt.
Having ground the bone mixed with sandalwood, agallochum, and musk,
and having applied it as a *tilaka*, the practitioner conquers all,
O Lord of the Kula— O Kulamīna, Kulānna, and Kulamadya!
Having carefully brought [the substance] to the place of the family and offered it to the Goddess,
one should remain standing on the ground and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
by merely blowing upon the ground, a fissure will arise there.
Whether at a distance of a hundred yojanas or wherever the one to be accomplished may reside, he travels right there, gliding along the surface of the earth;
likewise, even through the midst of a chasm or within the cavity of a window-lattice.
Having encountered the contraction of desire, the man proceeds unhindered. || 96 ||
O child, O Lord of the Kula, without the Durgā-mantra and likewise the Kālī-mantra, the supernatural powers (siddhis) never arise by any means whatsoever.

Now, the consecration of the child (*bālakasaṃskāra*): prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord, one should [touch] the tongue or the lip of the child with honey and parched grain (*lāja*), using either a golden probe,
a tip of sacrificial wood (*yajñadāru*), or white *dūrvā* grass.
Having wiped it three times with the right hand, the father should write the root mantra there in the form of a row and worship the Goddess.
As it is said in the *Matsyasūkta*:

Alternatively, before the cutting of the umbilical cord, one should write [the mantra] on the tongue of the child with honey and parched grain using a golden stylus; the practitioner should write the root mantra on the child's lip with white dūrvā grass for the purpose of enabling the utterance of speech.
A fool may become eloquent and swift in speech. || 98 ||
In the *Mahogratārākalpa*, however, it is stated that the drawing of the mantra must be performed immediately after the occasional consecrations (*naimittika-saṃskāra*).
As it is said in the *Mahogra*: "The rite known as the 'Consecration of Birth' (*janma-saṃskāraka*) is highly praised when a son is born."
One should write the mantra upon the tongue using a twig of sacrificial wood or *kuśa* grass;
having wiped it three times with the right hand alone,
one should form each row beautifully while reciting the root mantra for each.
First, the consecration (saṃskāra) must be performed; at its conclusion, one should write down the mantra.
One should worship the auspicious Tāriṇī with perfumes, sandalwood, and flowers. 99.
Facing north, one should place the supreme pedestal;
one should worship the goddess Tāriṇī with various most beautiful offerings of food.
The son shall become a poet, eloquent, truthful in speech, and one who has conquered his senses.
In this context, the term *tāriṇī* is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Goddess alone;
this is because the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the child is observed in the *Bṛhatśrīkrama* and other tantras. 99-ka.
It is said in that very same place:
"Within three days, one should write [the mantra] upon the tongue of the child;
one should write it with honey and white dūrvā grass using a golden stylus."
One should indeed write this Vāgbhava-kūṭa on another piece of paper;
by this, it is indicated that [the rite] is effective within three nights when the power of the day has perished.
"This" (amuṃ) means the Vāgbhava-kūṭa of Bhairavī.
Now, some say that on the eleventh day, having fully worshipped the deity, one should write the mantra.
Furthermore, if the father is staying far away, then the paternal uncle or the maternal uncle should write the mantra.
Thus it is said in the Mahogra: "The father's brother or else the mother's brother should write the mantra;
one should have the mantra written by the father alone, and never by anyone else. (100)
Having carefully placed the child upon his mother’s lap and having spread darbha grass [there],
the practitioner should perform a rite for the child’s peace together with brahmins.
Now, the Peace Mantra:
"I know this son, born of desire, who desires [us] right here; he nourishes all this progeny for the sake of the gods. May there be auspicious peace through Tārā."
With this [mantra], "To the Keśavas, to Tārā, to the Rudras, to Umā, to Śiva, to the glory of Śiva," one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) using water with kuśa grass.
Now, regarding the offering of goats and other animals, the *Muṇḍamālā* states:
"When a goat is offered, one becomes eloquent; when a ram is offered, one becomes a poet."
In Mahiṣa there shall be abundance of wealth; in Mṛga there will be the fruit of liberation.
By the gift of a bird there shall be prosperity; by a lizard, great fruit;
by giving a man, there shall be great wealth and the unsurpassed eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi).
"Thus, O Supreme Goddess, only a king may offer a human sacrifice, and no other;
for by offering lions, tigers, or humans to a Brāhmaṇa, one would go to hell.
According to this statement, Brāhmaṇas have no authority to offer a human sacrifice.
Furthermore: "By means of the offering of a *caṇḍāla* as a sacrificial victim (*bali*), great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) arises.
Having stationed a sacrificial animal possessing the [proper] characteristics before the Goddess, according to the procedure to be described..."
One should release it.
As it is stated in the Yāmala:
"Having placed before the Goddess an animal endowed with the proper characteristics..."

Then, one should dispel the malevolent spirits by scattering white mustard seeds; thereafter, having sprinkled [the area] with water for the *arghya* offering, one performs protection with the *astra-mantra*,
covers it with the *kavaca-mantra*, and renders it nectar-like by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having worshipped the sacrificial animal (paśu) with perfumes, sandalwood paste, flowers, and other offerings,
he should then seize it with his left hand and sprinkle it seven times with the root mantra while employing the *tattvamudrā*. Thereafter, he should perform the worship.
Then, having performed the expulsion of obstructive spirits with white mustard seeds, having sprinkled [the site] with water for the *arghya* offering,
having protected it with the *astra-mantra*, having veiled it with the *kavaca-mantra*,
having rendered it nectar-like with the *dhenu-mudrā*, and having worshipped the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains;
Having performed the sprinkling with the root mantra and the *tattvamudrā*, one should recite this mantra into the ear:
"We know the one who binds the bound souls; we meditate upon Viśvakarman; may that Jīva inspire us.
Then: *Hrīṃ kāli kāli vajreśvari lauhadaṇḍāya namaḥ*.
With this mantra, one should worship the sword.
Then, one should worship the sword in the sequence of its tip, middle, and base as follows:
"Hūṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvarī and Brahmā."
Hūṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. Hūṃ, salutation to Umā and Maheśvara.
Then, salutation to the sword endowed with the powers of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Thus one should worship everywhere.
Then one should prostrate to the sword:
"O sword, you who are like a whetstone, intent upon the accomplishment of the task!"
"O Lord of the Sword, obeisance to you; by this [offering], may the animal be swiftly slaughtered.
Then the great formula:
"Desiring the pleasure of such-and-such deity, I offer this animal unto you."
Then one should offer it, saying: "By the prescribed rite, let this be offered unto you. Thereafter, one should cut the *bali* offering.
Then one should offer blood and meat as an oblation to the Goddess.
The determination of the locations for the offering of blood is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"One should place the goat on the left, while the buffalo should be in front."
Or one should give it on the right, or the blood from one's own body in front;
likewise, in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal.
Having placed it [there], one should offer that blood to the Goddess, preceded by the mantra.
Then one should offer the remainder to Vaṭuka and the others,
as follows: *Hūṃ vāṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka*.
Having thus worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer a bali-oblation in the northwest with the mantra as before.
Having worshipped with "HŪṂ YĀṂ NAMO YOGINĪBHYAḤ," one should offer a bali-oblation in the northeast with the previous mantra.
Having worshipped with "Hūṃ Kṣāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla," one should offer the bali-oblation in the southwest (nairṛtyā) using the previous mantra:
"Hūṃ Gāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati."
Having thus worshipped, one should offer an oblation (bali) to Gaṇeśa in the southeast.
Regarding the offering of blood from one's own body:
"O Dear One, the practitioner should never give blood from the area below the navel or from the back part of his body;
he should offer blood from his limbs."
One should offer blood to Durgā from the lips and the chin, likewise from the sense organs;
from below the throat and above the navel, from the region of the heart,
and also from both sides.
Nor indeed, O Bhairava, is there any other element that causes the limbs to be defiled by disease.
Furthermore, the result is stated in the Kumārītantra:
"Having taken the blood arising from one's own heart into a vessel, one should worship the goddess Tripurā for the sake of attaining all prosperity. (10)
Likewise:
by giving the blood from one's own limbs and bowing down, one shall attain sovereignty. || 11 ||
And furthermore:
"The man who, filled with devotion, gives flesh produced from his own heart, measuring a māṣa or even the size of a sesame or mung bean,"
Within six months, he shall obtain whatever desire he wishes for. || 12 ||
Furthermore:
Having given liquor to Mahādevī, a Brāhmaṇa shall go to hell;
having given the blood from his own body, he incurs the sin of suicide. || 13 ||
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the bali offering.
Now, the Kula tradition is described in the Kālītantra:
Now I shall proclaim the conduct by practicing which one partakes of the immortal;
one who is intent on the welfare of all beings, a protector of the rules of conduct and practice,
who has renounced transient actions, and is devoted to the performance of eternal duties.
By the mere propitiation of the mantra, being intent upon it with a spirit of devotion,
one offers all actions to the Supreme Deity;
yet there is faith in the worship of another mantra and the thorough adoration of another mantra.
A wise man should always avoid censuring noble women or heroes, seizing their property, showing anger toward women, and striking them. (14)

One should contemplate the entire world as consisting of women, and likewise contemplate oneself as such; the wise one should always contemplate everything— whether it be that which is drunk, chewed, sucked, eaten, or licked, as well as the home and pleasure— as being the form of a young woman.
Upon seeing a young woman of noble birth, one should offer salutation with a concentrated mind. O Goddess, if by the power of fortune the vision of the Kula arises,
then at that very moment one should perform mental worship of them there.
Of those goddesses, Bhagā and the others. || 16 ||
And likewise:
Bhaginī, Bhagacihnā, Bhagāsyā, Bhagamālinī,
Bhagadantā, Bhagākṣī, Bhagakarnī, and Bhagatvacā.
Having worshipped her who has a vulva-like nose, vulva-like breasts, and who moves like a vulva, with mental offerings of perfumes and the like,
and having paid homage to the Guru as well according to his meditation, the wise man himself remains unshaken.
Whether she be a young girl, one intoxicated by youth, an old woman, or a beautiful lady;
whether she be despicable or exceedingly wicked—one should meditate upon her after having paid obeisance.
One should likewise avoid striking them, censuring them, being deceitful toward them, or speaking what is unpleasant.
In every way, one must not act otherwise, for it would cause an obstruction to success.

Women are the gods, women are the vital breaths, and women are indeed the ornament. One must always remain attached to women; otherwise, even toward one's own wife, she will become averse in her affection and turn against one's heart.
One should offer to the deities flowers gathered by that hand, water gathered by that hand, and substances gathered by that hand. (18)
One must never harbor hatred toward women; rather, one should offer them great and special honor.
Having placed a large conch shell above the place of recitation, one should perform the *japa* while holding it aloft.
While approaching, touching, or especially looking at a woman—particularly one of noble birth and auspicious appearance;
while chewing betel, eating fish, or consuming other foods according to one's taste;
and having eaten all kinds of food such as rice and the like—one should perform the recitation (japa) with whatever remains. || 20 ||
In the *Vīra-tantra*:
"There is no restriction of direction or time, nor any restriction regarding the duration [of practice] and so forth.
There is no restriction of time for the recitation (*japa*), nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings (*bali*)."
In this practice for the accomplishment of the Great Mantra, self-willed discipline is prescribed.

One should not perform purification regarding clothing, seats, places, the body, touch, water, and so forth; therein, one should let the mind abide in the state free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
In the Kulārṇava:
Having gone to the house of the Kula-practice, one should with devotion request the Kaula nectar for the purification of sins; in its absence, one should drink water. (23)
Whatever is given according to family custom, one should receive it with devotion even from an unworthy recipient;
having offered salutations, one should accept it, otherwise one shall go to hell.
Elsewhere it is also said:
"A wise person should not waste time on such things as gambling and games;
rather, he should spend his time in the worship of deities, japa, sacrifice, hymns of praise, and so forth. (25)
For heroes, however, the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is praised at all times;
it should be performed in every land and at every sacred seat—of this there is no doubt. (26)
In the Śivāgama:
Śakti is Śiva, and Śiva is Śakti; Śakti is Brahmā and Janārdana;
Śakti is Indra, the Sun, the Moon, and the planets—this is certain.
He who does not know that the entire world is of the nature of Śakti goes to hell.
In the *Vīratantra*:
"Bathing and so forth are mental purity; mental is the source of recitation (*japa*);
worship is divine and mental; and the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites are likewise mental."
Every moment is indeed auspicious; nowhere is there found an inauspicious time.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between the twilights and the dead of night. One should always worship the Goddess, whether unwashed or having already eaten. (28)
At midnight, one should cause an offering to be presented with the mantra in a pure place. || 29 ||
As for that which was said:
"O you who are honored by heroes, the great worship must be performed only at night;
it should never be performed during the day, according to my teaching, O lady of excellent vows."
That, moreover, pertains to the domain of family worship. || 30 ||
Regarding the "Great Night" (mahāniśā), it is stated in that very same [text]:
"That which follows midnight for two muhūrtas is designated as the Great Night; what is given then becomes inexhaustible. (31)
In the Gāndharva [tradition]: "If, upon seeing a woman who has reached her menses, one should constantly [utter] 'A thousand!',
then that debater, defeated by his own tenet, shall go to the surface of the earth."
"Constantly" means for sixteen days. || 32 ||
Placing his hand upon the mountain, free from fear and with a restrained mind,
he too attains poetic inspiration and reaches the essence of immortality;
here, too, the connection is with the word "a thousand."
The earth, the lineage, the mountain, and the breast. || 33 ||
In the *Nīlatantra*, it is said:
"Having seen a verse, likewise a pierced Khañjana bird, a pinnacle, a chowrie,
the solar disc, a sesame flower, and a lotus."
Having beheld the trident and recited [the mantra] hundreds of times with a pure disposition,
one attains a gracious face, a beautiful countenance, lovely eyes, and a pleasant smile;
as well as a fine appearance, a noble gait, a fragrant scent, and indeed happiness itself.
And listen with respect, O Pārvatī, to what is obtained respectively:
the face is a lotus, the lower lip is a bimba fruit, the eyes are wagtails, the head is a mountain peak, and the hair is a chowrie.
The solar disc, vermilion, a sesame flower, the nose, a lotus, the navel, a trident, and the three folds of skin—these are to be understood [as the marks]. || 34 ||
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"One should always wander without hesitation in a solitary place, a desolate region, a cremation ground, a lonely forest, an empty house, or on a riverbank."
Having meditated upon the Goddess there at the great Chinese tree (mahācīnadruma), one should worship her;
one should worship with devotion using flowers produced from that tree. He shall become the family deity, pure and established within the family tree. || 35 ||
Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the prescribed rite at the great lotus of the Brahma-tree,
one should satisfy her in the forest of the Mātṛkās with a stream of that nectar-essence.
Enveloped by great Chinese trees and creepers, if the supreme practitioner recites the mantra at night, she herself becomes a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā). || 37 ||
If it is encircled by creepers numbering according to the sequence of the lunar days (tithis),
then success shall be attained within a month through a thousand recitations.
If it is seen to be double [in size] on the eighth and fourteenth days, there itself is a great accomplishment that is very difficult even for the deities to attain. (39)
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Listen, my son, to my secret, the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*) which arises from the Mother;
devoid of which, people do not attain success even in thousands of millions of births. (40)
A man who follows the family scriptures and the conduct of his lineage,
who possesses a noble mind, and is everywhere intent upon the practice of the Vaiṣṇavas,
should be patient with the censure of others and always devoted to doing good for others.
Whether on a mountain, in a forest, in a deserted place, in an empty pavilion, at a crossroads, or in the midst of a marketplace— if by chance one should find oneself there,
one should remain for a moment, recite the mantra, bow down, and then proceed as one pleases.

Upon seeing a vulture, one should unobserved pay homage to Mahākālī; likewise, upon seeing a jackal, one should pay homage to Kṣemaṅkarī, who is the messenger of Yama. One should also pay homage to Kurarī, to the hawk and the crow, and to the black cat.
O slender-waisted one, O greatly fierce one, O you with loosened hair, O lover of offerings!
O you whose face is pleased by the Kula practice, salutations to you, the beloved of Śaṅkara! 42.
Having seen a corpse in a cremation ground, the practitioner, circumambulating it to the right and bowing down with this mantra, shall attain happiness:
"O you of terrible fangs, of gaping mouth, resounding with the sound of 'kiṭi'!"
Salutations to you, O dweller in the cremation ground, who resounds with most terrible and fearsome cries! 43.
Upon seeing the red garment and the flower of Tripurāmbikā,
a person should prostrate like a staff upon the ground and recite this mantra:
"O Tripura, who resembles the Bandhūka flower, O destroyer of fear!"
Salutations to you, O lady of excellent complexion, who have arisen from the dawning of good fortune.
Upon seeing black clothing, flowers, a king,
a royal official, elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, shield-bearing heroic men,
a buffalo, a family deity, or the slayer of Mahiṣa (Mahiṣamardinī).
Having prostrated before Jayadurgā, he is not tainted by obstacles.
Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World, Primordial One of the three cities, embodiment of the three deities;
O Goddess who grants boons to your devotees, O Slayer of Mahiṣa, homage be unto you! (45)
Upon seeing a vessel of liquor, fish, meat, or a beautiful woman,
and having beheld the goddess Bhairavī and bowed down while reciting the mantra,
one should act for the destruction of terrible obstacles and the fulfillment of the Kula tradition.
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
I bow to you whose face is drenched with streams of blood.
O Goddess who removes all obstacles, salutations to you, the beloved of Hara!
If, upon seeing these [obstacles], they do not act in this manner by placing the Śakti-mantra at the forefront, no success (siddhi) arises for them.
Likewise, in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi:
"On the day of the Kula-planets, on the eighth lunar day of the Kula, and especially on the fourteenth, the worship of the Yoginīs and the primary worship of the Kula should be performed there. (48)
Just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day (tithi), grants all desires, so too Durgā, when worshipped on her own lunar day, bestows boons.
Regarding the rules for the days of the week (*kulavāra*) and so forth, it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"The Sun, the Moon, Jupiter, and Saturn—these four are called *akula*.
Mars and Venus are indeed termed *kula*, while Wednesday is both *kula* and *akula*. (50)
The second, tenth, and sixth lunar days are declared to be both *kula* and *akula*; all odd-numbered days are *akula*, and the remaining lunar days are *kula*.
Varuṇa, Ārdrā, Abhijit, and Mūla are declared to be both *kula* and *akula*.
Those constellations that possess a *dhiṣṇya* are *kula*, while the remaining ones are *akula*.
On the lunar day (tithi), the day of the week (vāra), and the asterism (nakṣatra), those who abide in the Akula state are invincible;
in the Kulākhyā state they are eternally victorious, and likewise in the Samyañcī Kulākula state.
Having thus understood the Kula-day and other such factors, the practitioner should perform his ritual action.
Now, regarding the *śivābali*:
it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"The practitioner [should perform it] at the root of a *bilva* tree, in a wilderness, or even in a cremation ground."
At the time of twilight, one should offer an oblation consisting primarily of meat.
When it was time to say "Kālī, Kālī," there Umā, in the form of Śiva,
arrived with her retinue of attendants, assuming the form of a beast.
Having eaten, she raised her beautiful face toward the northeast and cried out.
At that very moment his welfare is secured, and not otherwise, O ornament of the family. (55)
One must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with the gift of food;
likewise, the daily *śrāddha*, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā-vandana*), and the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*) are obligatory.
Similarly, there is a constant obligation to perform the family worship for those deities traditionally served by one's lineage.
Whoever does not worship the goddess Śivā in the form of a female animal in a secluded place, everything of his will certainly perish instantly through the howling of the jackal. 56.
Taking with her whatever merits were gained from the performance of recitations and worship,
Śivā took a curse and wept in a secluded place.
O God Bhairava, where Śivā alone is enjoyed, there alone is the supreme and most difficult-to-attain delight of all the Śaktis. (58)
Since the worship of the animal power (paśu-śakti), the bird power (pakṣi-śakti), and the human power (nara-śakti) in due order accomplishes auspicious rites with threefold efficacy,
therefore this great worship should be performed with every possible effort.
When one has encountered fear from kings and the like, or fear arising from traveling to another land and so forth,
one should offer the bali-oblation after reflecting upon one's auspicious and inauspicious karmas.
The mantra is as follows:
"O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O Śivā, whose form is the fire of time!
Make manifest the fruit of the auspicious and inauspicious; accept this bali offering of yours."
Having recited this, O dear one, the bali offering should be given, which is pleasing to the family deities;
if it is not consumed, then no auspiciousness whatsoever will occur.
If there is merit therein, it is enjoyed in its entirety;
knowing this, O Mahādeva, one should perform rites for peace and well-being.
Thus ends the *śivābali*.
Regarding the secrecy of the *kulavartman*:
the path of the *kula* must be concealed everywhere.
And so it is stated in the Nīlatantra:
"It should be performed in a secluded place and never in the presence of people;
furthermore, one should not perform it at all when birds, insects, or the like are visible. (63)
It should be performed either in a pavilion of Pātāla, or in a well-restrained cave, or even in a leak-proof pavilion; however, it must not be done in the immediate vicinity [of a fire].
One should never, under any circumstances, reveal the family flower, the family substance, the family worship, the recitation (*japa*), the family lineage,
the master of the family, the family garland, the family and non-family,
the family wheel, or the family meditation.
From disclosure comes the loss of accomplishment; from disclosure comes death and the like;
from disclosure comes the destruction of the mantra; from disclosure comes the ruin of one's lineage;
from disclosure comes the attainment of death. Therefore, it must never be disclosed.
O Goddess of gods, if anyone should enter here at the time of worship,
one should show them the Vaiṣṇavī mudrā, as well as the Viṣṇu-nyāsa and the hymn. If there is concealment because of public exposure, there is no fault arising from that exposure.
If manifestation were to occur through concealment, then that concealment would not be established as such. || 67 ||
Sometimes there may be loss of the body, but never a lack of manifestation; it is better not to perform worship at all than to have no manifestation whatsoever. (68)
Now, the morning ritual:
having risen in the morning and bowed to the family tree (kulavṛkṣa), the practitioner [proceeds].
As for the family tree:
The Aśoka tree [blooms] from the strike of a foot; the Keśara and Karṇikāra from the wine of the face; the Cūta and Nimba from laughter;
the Tilaka tree, Nameru, and Piyāla from singing;
the Karṇikāra from conversation; and the Kuruvaka tree from an embrace.
The *sindhuvāra* and the *kādamba*, as well as the *campaka* tree, certainly blossom for women upon being touched. (69)
And so says the Śruti:
"There is no calamity for ten generations of trees.
As for the tree of ten generations: [it is as follows].
Śleṣmātaka, Karañja, Bilva, Aśvattha, Kadambaka, Nimba, Vaṭa, Udumbara, Dhātrī, and Ciñcā are remembered as the ten [trees].
Having meditated upon the Kula from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should remember the Guru. (70)
The one named Prahlādānandanātha, as well as Sanakānanda;
the one named Kumārānandanātha, Vasiṣṭhānandanātha,
Krodhānanda, Sukhānanda, and beyond that, Jñānānanda.
Then, having worshipped the bliss of awakening, one should meditate upon the Kula-mukha;
[the goddesses there] have hearts overflowing with the great nectar of passion, their eyes rolling,
and all their darkness completely pulverized by the embrace of the Kula.

With their inner hearts filled with compassion for their noble disciples and striving [to help them], with hands raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and being knowers of the meaning of the Kula Tantras—
having thus bowed to the Kula Guru and dismissed the Kula-nāyikā, [one should proceed].
Having taken refuge in his family's traditional place, he should resort to a sacred bathing site for the purpose of ritual ablution.
Having sipped water with the mantras *ātmavidyāśiva*, one should perform the other rites.
In the Kulārṇava:
"One should cause the arghya offering to be presented three times to the divine Kulasūrya;
one should likewise satisfy the gods, the sages, and the ancestors with the water of the Kula. (73)
Having sipped water with a *kuladarbha* blade, and having taken up a *kulapuṇḍraka* mark along with a *darbha*,
as well as a *kulapātra* containing *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and water;
And for the pleasure of the family deity (kuladevī), one should perform a ritual bath.
Having thus made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should place the family-circle (kulacakra) in the water,
having brought it from the family-place by means of the family-goad-seal (kulamudrāṅkuśa).
Likewise, having invoked the family-tirthas as being of the nature of Śiva,
one should drink that water three times and perform the sprinkling of the body three times.
Also in the *Svatantra*:

"O Goddess, while reciting the root mantra, the foremost of practitioners should pour water upon his head with the mudrā known as the 'water-pot' (*kumbha*), and having offered it three times, he should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*). (76)
Thus is the family tradition (*kulācāra*).
Now, the sacrifice to the messenger (*dūtīyāga*) is described;
therein, first, is the acceptance of *vijayā*.
And so it is stated in the *Vijayākalpa*:
"Between consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the liquor (*āsava*), consciousness alone is more important;
therefore, the best of practitioners should employ consciousness here in worship and other rites."
And a great worship must be performed by those who are well-resolved;
this ritual application at the beginning of worship must be performed everywhere by those of noble family. || 77 ||
Elsewhere as well:
"Without bliss there is no falling away, and the deities are not satisfied. (78)
And she is fourfold:
Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, and Śūdrā,
distinguished by white, red, yellow, and black flowers respectively.
The purification of these [threads] is stated in the Vijayākalpa:
"O Consciousness, born of Brahman, daughter of Brahman, ever sinless!
For the sake of the satisfaction of the Bhairavas, be forever pure."

Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmaṇī, svāhā—thus one should purify. Then: O Goddess who possesses perfected roots, O awakener of the awakening of the root, O Princess, O subduer, O trident-wielder against the throats of enemies!
Aiṃ, obeisance to the Kṣatriyā, Svāhā; thereafter, one should purify the Aparā. || 79 ||
O you whose form is the blazing fire of the flame of knowledge, kindled by the fuel of ignorance—considering this an oblation of the clarified butter of bliss, grant me the food of perfect knowledge.
Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vaiśyā, Svāhā! Thereafter, one should purify Vaiśyā.
I pay homage to Mahāmāyā, who reveals the path of Yoga; O Mother, victorious over the three worlds, grant me the fruit of samādhi. With "Śrīṃ, obeisance to Śūdrā, svāhā," one should purify the Śūdrā.
Then follows the purification of all [the offerings]:
*oṃ amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi*, then the word *padaṃ*,
then the pair *amṛtam ākarṣaya*, and after that, *siddhiṃ dehi*.
Then one should say, "Bring such-and-such under my control";
this mantra, ending with *dviṭha*, is declared here for the purification of all [the goddesses].
If [the practitioner] possesses knowledge, he should purify each one individually with their respective mantra; however, if he lacks knowledge, he should do so with this [mantra].
One should purify. || 79-ka ||
In the Uttaratantra:
One should apply the root mantra seven times over that [image];
then, one should perform the mudrās for invocation and so forth, followed by the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās.
Having performed the binding of the directions with finger-snaps preceded by three claps,
and having dispelled all obstacles with divine vision and strikes of the heels,
one should satisfy [the deities] seven times at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) while reciting the root mantra.
The practitioner, for the sake of attaining accomplishment, should with devotion offer libations three times to the Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus using the *saṅketamudrā*.
Having recited the root mantra of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should say: "I offer libations to such-and-such deity. Thus.
And one should satisfy the Guru.
Then, one should accept that [offering] with the Saṅketa-mudrā and the Tattva-mudrā,
as follows:
Aiṃ vada vada vāgvādini, be firm upon the tip of my tongue, O subduer of all beings, svāhā!
And likewise:
One should utter "Aiṃ vada vada padaṃ," followed by the word "vāgvādini.
Then, one should say "mama jihvāgre sthirībhava" and thereafter the word "sarva. With the mantra ending in "sattvavaśaṅkari svāhā," one should offer oblations into the mouth.
In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having encountered [the consort] without a [proper] cause, Maheśvara becomes agitated;
he should perform neither worship nor fire-offerings, nor meditation, nor contemplation."
Therefore, having eaten and having drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess; "having drunk" refers specifically to *vijayā*, because of the context. (81)
Now, the method of worship:
there, when one watch of the night has passed, having his mouth filled with betel, he should worship the Mistress of the Family (Kulanāyikā). || 82 ||
In the *Uttaratantra*:
"When only one watch of the night has passed, the man should then go to the house of the Kula woman,
his mouth filled with betel and fragrant with the scent of incense."
His limbs smeared with red sandalwood, adorned with red garlands,
clad in red garments, having entered a house of lac-dye,
he was enveloped in a red wreath and decorated with red flowers.
One should worship the Mistress of the Kula with the conventions of the fivefold process (pañcīkaraṇa). || 83 ||
Regarding the leaders of the families (*kulanāyikā*), it is said in that very same [text]:
"The actress, the *kāpālikā*, the courtesan, the *pukvasī*, the barber’s wife, the washerwoman, the dyer, the servant-woman, and the newlywed wife."
Ghaṭikā, Ghaṭikā, and likewise Gopālakanyakā—
all these noble women were endowed with exceptional cleverness;
they were devoted to their elders and the gods, yet devoid of compassion and shame.
Young women who are generally devoted to secrecy grant all accomplishments.
[One should choose] one who is endowed with unimpaired conduct, possessed of virtue and good fortune,
dedicated to right practice, of a sattvic nature, and filled with devotion.
One should make her free from impurity, devoted to the observances, and affectionate toward her devotees;
endowed with qualities such as cleverness, magnanimity, courtesy, and compassion;
perfected in beauty and youth, and distinguished by virtuous conduct and good fortune.
Whether she has been constantly cherished, or has arrived by appointment,
or has come at that very moment, tormented by the fire of passion—
smeared with red perfume and adorned with red garments.
One should employ a slender woman who possesses fragrant red flowers, is adorned with all ornaments, and is perfumed with excellent incense for the rites of a female messenger.
In the *Kumārītantra*:
"The dancer, the Kāpālikā, the prostitute, the washerwoman, the barber’s wife,
the Brāhmaṇī, the Śūdra maiden, and likewise the cowherd’s daughter."
The daughter of the gardener and the nine maidens are proclaimed;
however, the term "Brāhmaṇī" refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa caste. || 85 ||
One should worship her who is of such a nature upon a cushion of flowers—
she whose limbs are defective or deformed, whose mind is full of conceptual constructions,
who is aged, devoted to sin, and greedy for the objects of sense through the syllable *hūṃ*.
The best of practitioners should avoid one who is dejected and whose mind is devoid of devotion. || 86 ||
Whether for the sake of wealth, or out of desire, or even for the sake of pleasure, that practitioner who is devoted to the male and female organs shall go to the Raurava hell. (87)
O Goddess, when a daughter or maiden has been instructed [in sacred knowledge], and when she is worthy of worship, then she is no different from a mother; of this there is no doubt. (88)
Having brought such a woman of noble family and performed the ritual of anointing with unguents and so forth, one should place her upon a couch.
Likewise, in the *Uttaratantra*: "Then, having properly brought [the disciple] to the family (*kula*), immediately after the ritual anointing (*udvartana*),
he has bathed, is adorned with pure silk garments and the like, and beautified by the application of fragrant unguents."
Having seated him— who was adorned, free from fatigue, and welcomed—
upon a seat consisting of a mattress in the midst of various fragrant flowers,
[anointed] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, and other such substances;
Then, having seated the Mistress of the Family in the midst of the assembly, one should worship her.
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the limbs of the respective deity family.
It is as follows:
first, the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), and after that, breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should also perform it upon the limbs of the *kula*. Then, having brought the five *makāras*, one should purify them. The five *makāras* are as follows:
Alcohol, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union—this group of five beginning with the letter *ma* is the destroyer of great sins.
Regarding that, the purification of the liquor is as follows: holding the jar, one should recite:

The Supreme Brahman alone is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle. O you who are born from the solar disc, O you who are born from the abode of Varuṇa, by what means shall I destroy this sin of Brahmin-slaughter arising from a mere flash of light?
O Goddess, who consists of the seed-syllable *amā*, may [this person] be released from the curse of Śukra.
If the *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman,
by that truth, O Goddess, may it remove the sin of killing a Brahmin from you.
Then, one should recite ten times over that [the mantra]: *oṃ vāṃ vīṃ vūṃ vaiṃ vauṃ vaḥ, obeisance to the goddess Sudhā, who is liberated from the curse of Brahmā*.
Then, one should recite ten times over that [the nectar]: *Oṃ śāṃ śīṃ śūṃ śaiṃ śauṃ śaḥ, obeisance to the Goddess Sudhā, who is liberated from the curse of Śukra*.
Thus, one should recite ten times: *evaṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ krāṃ krīṃ krūṃ kraiṃ krauṃ kraḥ kṛṣṇaśāpaṃ vimocayāmṛtaṃ srāvaya svāhā*.
Then, having recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) over that eight times, one should visualize it as being composed of the deity.
Thus ends the purification of substances. || 91 ||
This gift of substances, however, pertains only to the Śūdra.
Thus it is stated in the Śrīkrama:
"A Brāhmaṇa should never, under any circumstances, give liquor to Mahādevī."
For a Brahmin who desires the [highest] state, one should not consume liquor or meat. || 92 ||
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "Where liquor must necessarily be drunk, especially by a Brāhmaṇa,
one should then offer jaggery and ginger, or pour honey into a copper vessel."
One should offer this substance on the right side of the Goddess, at the side of the discus;
however, this is for a Śūdra alone and never for others.
For a Vaiśya it is pure honey, while for a Kṣatriya it is accompanied by ghee.
A Brāhmaṇa may pour cow’s milk or honey into copper;
coconut water into bell-metal; for all [castes], this is the purification of substances.
However, for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, liquor made from molasses (gauḍī) and that made from honey (mādhvī) should be given there, because they have the entitlement to those.
In the absence of that, there is the prescription of a secondary alternative (anukalpa).
And so it is said:
"A Brāhmaṇa should give cow's milk, and a Bāhuja (Kṣatriya) should give cow's ghee."
Honey is the substance for a Śūdra, and furthermore, [substances] such as those for nourishment;
therefore, this is the secondary rule (anukalpa) for a Śūdra. || 93 ||
In the Kulārṇava: "O auspicious lady, [the substances are] water, milk, ghee, honey, maireya wine, sugarcane juice,
that which comes from flowers, that which comes from trees, that which arises from grains, and that produced by the churning wheel."

O Goddess, O fair-eyed one, the intoxicant derived from the *sahakāra* tree is of three kinds and has many varieties; because it causes the confusion of dharma, it was to be avoided. However, when that same substance is consecrated by knowledge (*jñāna*), it becomes the destroyer of great sins.

In giving that [fruit], there is an absence of sin, or rather, it pertains to a divine state. O Goddess of the Gods, the delightful substance produced from the fruit of the mango tree should be consumed by the twice-born; however, because it does not cause intoxication, sugarcane juice is consumed by the wise.
By this it is shown that Kṣatriyas and others should consume non-intoxicating substances;
for it has been stated that intoxication is a cause of sin. || 94 ||
In the Bhairavatantra:
"O child, without wine and meat, whatever Kula practice there may be,
one should give it to the Śakti, and then offer the remainder to the Guru."
Placing their permission upon one's head, one should apply it to oneself;
by that, the Kṣatriyas and others have the authority for the primary act of giving, but not for drinking.
As for that which says:
"Having drunk again and again, having drunk once more and fallen upon the earth, and having risen and drunk yet again—there is no further rebirth. (96)
In the Bhairavatantra:
"He who experiences delusion regarding drinking, who feels loathing for blood and semen,
who perceives impurity in what is pure, and who harbors sinful apprehension toward sexual union [is unfit]."
One who has fallen from his status should worship the Goddess; how should he recite the Caṇḍī mantra? || 97 ||

Likewise: "One should not practice the conduct of one's caste in relation to liquor or sexual intercourse. This, however, refers specifically to those in the fourth stage of life (the *caturthāśramin*).
One should not concern oneself with the generic class (*jāti*) when taking those respective substances,
because their purification is mandatory.
And so it is said:
Without having performed purification, the practitioner [should engage] with women and wines; by performing it,
there would be a loss of accomplishment, and Sundarī becomes angry—
this applies to both primary and secondary types of wine.
Likewise:
his necessity for the worship of the Kula is established. || 99 ||
And so it is said:
"O Goddess, one should commence the Kula worship without honey or meat;
otherwise, the merit accumulated over a thousand lifetimes perishes for him. (100)
Now, the purification of meat and so forth:
Meat is to be known as threefold—of aquatic, aerial, and terrestrial creatures.
This threefold meat is declared to be that which causes the gratification of the deities. (1)
O Goddess, fish are of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling. O Goddess, the superior kind is of three types: the śāla, the pāṭhīna, and the rohita.
It is devoid of scales and bones, smeared with oil, and accompanied by its own juices.
That which brings pleasure to the Goddess is the middle type, and it is of four kinds;
all those minor ones, the wise know, are the inferior types.
The flesh of the earth-bearer (the elephant) and that produced from the cow, man, ram, horse, buffalo, boar, goat, and deer—
this is declared to be the eightfold "great meat" (*mahāmāṃsa*), which causes delight to the deities. (3)
In the absence of meat,
there is a substitute according to the traditional practice:
salt, fresh ginger, oil-cake, sesame, wheat, and black gram.
And garlic, O Great Goddess, is traditionally considered a substitute for meat. || 4 ||
Mudrā, however, is of two kinds.
As stated in the Kulārṇava:
"The *kṛṣara* is circular in shape, auspicious, and resembling the orb of the moon."
Beautifully cooked, heart-stealing, and filled with sugar and other ingredients—
this is proclaimed as the mudrā for the deity at the time of worship.
In the *Yāmala*:
"From ground grains and so forth, up to whatever may be prepared as food for chewing—for these, the designation 'mudrā' has been established, which bestows great delight. (6)
The purification of these is as follows in the *Svatantra-tantra*: with the mantra beginning "Oṃ pratadviṣṇu... for meat;
and with the mantra beginning "Oṃ tryambakam... for fish.
One should purify the mudrā with the mantra beginning with "oṃ tad viṣṇoḥ," and so forth. || 7 ||
Now, regarding the purification of the *śakti*:
in that regard, the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* states:
"From association with those of the *kula* who have not received initiation, the loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises."
If one were to hear her stories, or if one were to go to her bedchamber— how, O Goddess, could such a person of noble birth worship the Supreme Sovereign?
In the Śrīkrama: one should not perform the worship of the Kula without first having carried out the purification. || 8 ||
In the Kaulika Tantra:
"Purification occurs through initiation by means of the utterance of mantras and drops;
one should perform the initiation either forcefully or with effort. (9)
The initiation mantra (abhiṣeka-mantra) is as follows:
First, having uttered *Bālā*, one should extract [the name] for *Tripurā*.
Having uttered the word *namaḥ*, one should then say "this power" (*imāṃ śaktim*).

O Dear One, at the end of the word *pavitrīkuru*, say "grant me success" (*mama siddhiṃ kuru*). O Sovereign of the Gods, having uttered the *vahnijāyā* (the fire-wife, *svāhā*), this is the purification mantra (*śuddhimantra*).
With the thought of non-difference, one should utter the *māyābīja* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) into her ear.
Thus ends the purification of the power (śakti). || 10 ||
Then one should place the purified substance into the *arghya*.
Regarding the procedure for the *arghya* in the *Śrīkrama*:
"One should indeed pour the previously purified substance into it in a secret manner. (11)
In the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"The wise and disciplined practitioner, having placed the primary substance in the arghya vessel,
[should offer] the substance produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, as well as the *svayambhū* flower."
O Maheśānī, by offering the *arghya*, one becomes a master of all *siddhis*.
By offering *arghya* with nectar (*sudhā*), one becomes dear to the *yoginīs*.
O Goddess, by means of the water used for washing the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), one becomes a great *yogī*. (12)
In the Bhairava Tantra: "There is nothing superior to the fifth [element] for the Śāktas regarding bliss and liberation;
even by means of the five alone, the practitioner becomes accomplished."
With those five kinds of substances, worship should be performed. || 13 ||
Then, immediately after the placement of the *arghya*, one should worship the pedestal (*pīṭha*) in the center of the *paryaṅka* in the sequence beginning with "Salutation to Maṇḍūkī.
As it has been said:
Then, one should worship Maṇḍūka in the center of the lotus seat,
followed by Kālāgnirudra, Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, Ananta,
Varāha, Pṛthivī, the bulb (kanda), the stalk (nāla), and the filaments (keśara).
One should worship the lotus, the pericarp, and the mandala;
one should also worship Dharma, dispassion, sovereignty, knowledge, ignorance,
lack of sovereignty, lack of dispassion, and even non-dharma.
One should worship the Self, which consists of gnosis and wisdom;
having offered perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth, one should worship right there. Then, having placed the *kula* upon the brush (*tulikā*), one should worship it.
And likewise: Having placed the *kula* upon it and performed the ritual worship,
one should then, with a concentrated mind, worship the five objects of desire within that [liṅga].
Hrīṃ Kāmarāja, Klīṃ Kandarpa, Aiṃ Manmatha,
Blūṃ Makaradhvaja, and Strīṃ Manobhava—
preceded by Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ— one should worship these with flowers combined with fragrant scents.
Having performed worship, one should honor the Mistress of the Kula in the four directions—
namely Vaṭuka, Bhairavī, Durgā, and Kṣetrapālaka.
The words for worship are: *oṃ hrīṃ kāmarājāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
Then: *aiṃ klīṃ strīṃ klīṃ blūṃ ādhāraśaktiśrīpādukāṃ*.
With the words "I worship," one should draw a triangle on her forehead.
And so it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*: "The Vāgbhava, the Kāmabīja, and the Strībīja, which is the Kāmarāja."
Then, having offered that which consists of the syllable *blūṃ*, one should extract the *ādhāra-śakti*.
Then, having offered the *śrīpādukā*, one should say, "I worship.
O Goddess, with this mantra, [one should place] something very beautiful on the forehead.
O fair-faced one, having drawn a triangle there with vermilion and other substances;
as stated in the *Uttaratantro*:
"The practitioner, having drawn a triangular yantra upon its head..."

Then one should worship Bālā upon the great corpse-seat (mahāpreta-āsana) in the center; thereafter, one should worship with the mantra "Hsrauḥ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of Sadāśiva-mahāpreta," and then worship Bālā and Kāmeśvarī. || 15 ||
In the Kulārṇava: "O Dear One, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Lord of the Kula, Durgā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī, as well as Vasanta and Madana, within the triangles."
Thereafter, one should worship the Moon (Sudhākara) upon her face.
According to the *Uttaratantro*:
"One should worship Gaṇeśa on the crown of the head, Kulādhyakṣa at the tips of the hair, and [the deity] on the forehead."
"Durgā in the eyebrows, Lakṣmī likewise in the tongue, and Sarasvatī"—this inversion of their locations is according to one's own preference. (16)
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O beautiful one, one should worship all the digits (*kalā*) of both Kāma and Soma, beginning from the right foot up to the head, and from the left head down to the foot."
Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Bhūti, Kānti, Manobhavā,
Manoharā, Manoramā, Madanotpādinī, as well as Mohinī, Dīpanā, Śodhanī, and Vaśaṅkarī.
O Goddess of gods, one should worship these Kāmakalās: Rañjanī, Ṣoḍaśī, and Priyadarśanā, conjoined with the sixteen vowels. And the statement is:
Aṃ, salutation to Śraddhā; Āṃ, salutation to Prīti, and so forth.
Thereafter, the digits of the moon (candrakalās) are to be worshipped from the head down to the feet:
Pūṣā, Vaśā, Sumanas, Rati, Prīti, and Dhṛti.
Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, Aṃśumālinī on Śailajā; Aṅgirā, Vaśinī, Chāyā, and Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā;
likewise Tuṣṭi and Amṛtā—these are the sixteen digits (kalās) of the Moon.
In place of "Aṅgirā," there is also a reading of "Madirā. || 17 ||
In the *Uttaratantro*:
"Indeed, she should be worshipped by means of the vowels alone for the sake of accomplishing all purposes.
In the *Lalitātantra*:
Within your womb, three channels of flow are to be known:
one is the lunar channel (cāndrī), another is the solar channel (saurī), and the other is to be known as the fiery channel (āgneyī). The practitioner should worship them.
The lunar [energy] flows as water, the solar [energy] flows as flower, and the fiery [energy] flows as seed; one should worship those [energies] at the navel.
(From the Lalitātantra)
With a serene mind, one should worship them with the [seed-syllables] beginning with Vāgbhava (Aiṃ), joined with "namaḥ.
Thus: Aiṃ Cāndryai namaḥ;
Aiṃ Sauryai namaḥ.
Aiṃ, salutation to Āgneyī. || 18 ||
In the *Uttaratantra*:
"One should worship in the temple of Madana, which is smeared with red sandalwood;
having first uttered the *Bhagamālā* mantra, followed by the *Tritārā*."
Likewise:
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ Jaṃ Blūṃ Klinne; after that, "sarvāṇi" (all), then "bhagāni" (the vulvae), and after that, "vaśamānaya" (bring under control).

One should worship her with perfumes and other offerings using the mantra: *strīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ bhagamālinyai namaḥ* and *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. Thereafter, one should worship the root-mantra (*mūla*) at that very spot.
In another tantra it is said:
"O Maheśvarī, here too there is no invocation (āvāhana), nor the placement of the vital breaths (jīvanyāsa).
In that very manner, according to this procedure, one should worship her with the sixteen types of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra)."
Having worshipped one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevī), one shall then become a master of all accomplishments (sarvasiddhīśvara).
Thereafter, one should worship one's own liṅga;
immediately following that, one should honor one's own Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The root mantra is "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," followed by which one should worship with those known as Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, and Sadyojāta;
however, in the case of Śrīvidyā:
*Tāram* (Om), *Bhuvaneśānīm*, and likewise *Tripurasundarīm*;
"Obeisance to Śiva"—this is proclaimed as the ten-syllable *vidyā*.
This is the distinction.
Sundarī and Sundarītrikūṭa;
the mantras for Tatpuruṣa and the others have been stated previously.
Immediately after that, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and Vidyā.
Immediately after that, one should worship Śakti and Śāntyatītā upon her limbs;
then, having uttered the entire Vidyā, one should worship the triangle itself,
as well as Avadhūteśvarī, Kubjā, Kāmākhyā, and Samayā.
There, the practitioner should worship Cakreśvarī, Kālikā, as well as Dikvaravāsinī, Mahācaṇḍeśvarī, and Tārā; then,
having obtained their permission and offered betel-leaf, he should proceed.
Having placed Śiva there with the mudrā called Gajatuṇḍa,

I perpetually offer the functions of the senses as oblations into the fire of the Self— which is kindled by the fuel of dharma and adharma— using the mind as a sacrificial ladle along the path of the Suṣumṇā.
This great mantra, ending with "svāhā," has been proclaimed for recitation at the commencement [of the rite].
Then, while approaching his wife, he should mutter the Vidyā of the Sovereign of the Three Worlds.
Regarding the instruction "he should mutter": he should mutter it one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times, remaining undisturbed.
And likewise, in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, which removes agitation;
or, with a pure mind, one should recite it one hundred and eight times."
