Holding Unmanī with the hands of Light and Space, I offer her—who is filled with the oil of the digits of merit and demerit—into the fire as an oblation with the *sruc* ladle.
This great mantra, ending with *svāhā*, is proclaimed for the emission of the seed (*śukra*). (18-ka)
The specific detail is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The union of Śiva and Śakti is indeed yoga, without a doubt;
the sound 'sīt' is the recitation of mantra, and speech becomes hymn."

Know that embracing is musk, kissing is camphor, the nail-marks and tooth-wounds are various flowers, churning is libation (tarpaṇa), and the emission of the seed is the ritual dismissal (visarjana). (18-kha)
In the Kulārṇava: embracing, kissing, the pressing of the breasts,
as well as the sight of, the touching of, the opening of the vulva, and the rubbing of the linga.
The entry and the installation of the power, and the nine flowers in the worship. (19)
In the *Yāmala*: "From union arises bliss characterized by supreme bliss;
a man should diligently grasp the *kulāmṛta*, which is difficult to obtain."
Indeed, by that divine nectar, all become satisfied;
whatever desire the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) undertakes, that very thing is accomplished at that very moment.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Dear One, having purified the substance of the Kula, which consists of Śiva and Śakti,
O Beautiful One, one should pour in the supreme nectar of life, whose nature is Brahman."

Having worshipped with the nectars from the *arghya* vessel, the man who is always free of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), having fully honored the sequence of Śrīvidyā, becomes one with the Supreme Brahman.
"Śrīvidyā" is used here as an illustration [for other such sequences]. (21)
Thus, O fair-faced one, I have told you all this delightful knowledge.
However, a man who is constantly possessed of conceptual thought becomes a partaker of sin;
a practitioner of mantra who is intent on doubt becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed.
Therefore, O lady of excellent hips, one should always remain free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). || 22 ||
In the conduct of the *samaya*: having taken the *kulāmṛta*, one should then place it into the *arghya* water;
having propitiated [the deity] with that *arghya*, one should perform the remainder of the worship.
The nectar of the family has been purified. || 23 ||
The purification mantra in the Śrīkrama is as follows: *amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi priye*,
followed by the two words *devīpadaṃ śukraśāpaṃ pramocaya*.
Causing the pair [of syllables] to flow as nectar, one forms the "pair of nectars"; then, O Goddess, the word *svāhā* follows, whereby the purification of the semen occurs, O Beloved. (24)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship the Goddess in the yoni with white unbroken rice grains, fragrant flowers, and substances for the arghya offering. || 25 ||
In the Uttaratantra:
"The Kula practitioner, having offered incense, lamps, and various food offerings, and having performed her worship, should himself partake of her remains. (26)
And in the Śivāgama:
"If a person does not drink the *śaktyucchiṣṭa* without deliberation,
he goes to a terrible hell and will certainly fall from the path of the Kula."
Therefore, having investigated with effort, the wise one should partake of the remnant of his power;
he should cause bliss to arise and drink the reality without delusion. (27)
In the *Kulāmṛta*:
"Except at the time of worship, one should never look upon the naked Śakti;
except at the time of worship, she should never be drunk by practitioners."
By touching [it] or drinking [it], one's lifespan is diminished and one goes to hell.
Thus ends the worship of the lineage (kulapūjā). 28.
In the *Yāmala*: "The gods always desire an offering of food for the Goddess Tripurā;
therefore, O best of men, perform it likewise for Brahmā and Viṣṇu as well."
O Great Goddess, one should cause [the offering] to be given to Mahāśuddha, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Dhanada, and Īśāna, as well as to the practitioner (sādhaka).
The term "Tripura" is an illustration (upalakṣaṇa). || 29 ||
Now, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for heroes:
therein, first of all, one should worship a woman belonging to another who has been initiated.
And so it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
Indeed, during the period of *puraścaraṇa*, one should worship the wives of others who have been initiated,
honoring them with garments, ornaments, and foods made of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
However, at the time of commencement, one must strictly observe eating only food cooked by oneself.
Various kinds of flour-based sweets endowed with diverse flavors;
milk, curd, ghee, buttermilk, fresh butter with sugar;
pieces of stone-sugar, mangoes, and various kinds of elixirs.
Coconut, wood-apple, orange, *sudarśana*,
*limpāka*, citron, and the excellent pomegranate fruit;
likewise, various delightful fruits and various fragrant ointments.
Sandalwood, musk, śrīkhaṇḍa, fresh sprouts,
ṭaṅkaṇa, and lodhra— both aquatic and forest-born—
as well as various minerals produced from different mountains, all adorned with diverse ornaments.
Having brought her into an empty house and purified her with arghya water,
one should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) and lead the Śakti before oneself.

A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrā who adorned her family; a Vaiśyā, the daughter of a barber, a washerwoman, and likewise a dancer—all of these were noble women endowed with exceptional skill. (31)

Then, having consecrated himself, the initiate should sequentially establish the eight Śaktis, place the vessel for the *arghya* offering, sprinkle them with the *arghya* water, transform [the water] into nectar using the syllable "Vam" and the *dhenu-mudrā*, and effect the differentiation into the forms of the eight Śaktis.
Having performed the naming ceremony for the eight powers, beginning with Brāhmaṇī, by means of their respective names, one should offer the seat and so forth in due order.
This is stated in that very same [text]:
Beholding the eightfold manifestation of the forms of the maidens, which was enveloped in indignation,
he first offered a seat and repeatedly welcomed them by addressing them with the names of the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmaṇī.

Then one should offer the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), drinking water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water for bathing; likewise, one should perform the refinement of the hair with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having then fumigated the hair, one should present a silken garment (kauṣeya).
Then, having spread a seat in another place and placed a pair of sandals there,
she should sit upon it; having adorned her with various ornaments and decorations,
she should offer her unguents, perfumes, and garlands.

Then, having invoked each respective Śakti in due order in the form of Brahmāṇī and the others, and having performed the *jīvanyāsa* and other rites, one should offer them perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food, side-dishes, and so forth.
One should recite the hymn in sequence at the left ear.
As it is stated in that very same source: "Having invoked each respective Śakti, one should bring them together upon the head."
One should present the food— namely that which is to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, eaten, and consumed— within the center of the maṇḍala in a beautiful golden vessel.
However, if there is one who is uninitiated, then one should offer her an illusion (māyā).
Then, one should perform the hymn of praise upon their left ears.
Oṃ! O Mother Goddess, salutations to you, O sinless one who bears the form of Brahman;
out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra.
Oṃ, O Māheśī, O Goddess who grants boons, whose form is supreme bliss; through your grace... and so forth.
Oṃ, O Kaumāri, sovereign of all vidyās, you who sport like a maiden, O excellent one;
[grant your] grace, etc.
Oṃ! O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, who carries the son of Vinatā; through your grace... [and so forth].
Oṃ Vārāhī, O boon-granting goddess, O you who lifted up the earth with your tusks!
Out of compassion... [and so forth].
Oṃ! O Goddess who assumes the form of an enemy, worshipped by Śakra and the other gods;
[grant] grace, etc.
Oṃ Cāmuṇḍe, O you who are adorned with garlands of severed heads and blood, O destroyer of obstacles! [Grant your grace... and so forth.
Oṃ, O Mahālakṣmī, O you of great energy, who removes agitation and torment;
[grant your] grace, etc.
O Goddess, who consist of measure and the measurer, yet are beyond measure and the measurer; O Goddess, who are both one and manifold, whose form is the universe—salutations be unto you!
He who, being self-controlled, recites this hymn at the commencement of his undertakings, [attains success].
Or, upon seeing a learned woman, no obstacle arises for him.
O son, these are said by you to be the door-deities of one of noble birth;
if one does not worship them at the time of initiation or during the occasion of daily worship, [an obstacle occurs].
O child, the fruit of his worship is carried away by yakṣas and rākṣasas.
If she is overcome by modesty regarding the meal, he should remain outside her house and recite the hymn of praise until satisfaction arises.
Having sipped water (ācamana), he should offer mouth-fresheners and the like, as well as betel leaf.
Then one should offer a garland again, along with sandalwood paste mixed with fragrant scents;
having released [the deity], performed circumambulation, and requested a boon, one shall become happy. || 34 ||
If no other woman is available, one's own daughter, one's own younger sister,
an elder sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, or one's mother or her co-wife should be worshipped;
in the absence of each preceding one, the next is to be honored, for these women are considered to be portions of myself.
O Bhairava, if there is only one person— whether it be an elder sister, a maternal aunt, a mother, or her co-wife— who is worthy of worship according to the family tradition and the scriptures,
then all the gods, including Brahmā, Śiva, and the rest, are truly worshipped. 35.
And there, O Kulabhairava, the goddess Ekācī was worshipped and beheld;
indeed, all the supreme goddesses were worshipped—
at the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, especially upon the completion of the hundred thousand recitations.
If one does not honor one's beloved, then one is besmeared by obstacles. || 36 ||
There is no fruit from what was earned in the past; what need is there to speak of another birth?
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship Kulasundarī.
Then, in this manner, during the course of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*) and so forth, one should worship Śakti at the beginning, the middle, and the end.
"One hundred thousand" is an illustrative term (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Thereafter, at night, having fully worshipped the Goddess with the fifth [mantra] and the secret rosary (*rahasyamālā*), together with the *kula*...
Having meditated on the Guru at the head and the Goddess in the heart, and contemplating "I am Śiva," one should perform the recitation (japa). || 38 ||
In the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"When the first watch has passed, up until the third watch of the night, one should perform the recitation; however, one should not recite during the remainder of the night. (39)
In the *Svatantratantra*:
"Having worshipped the Goddess at night according to the ritual with meat and liquor,
then, naked and even if moist with sexual fluids, one should enjoy a naked woman."
Then, having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, the practitioner should perform a fire sacrifice for the Goddess using water-wood as fuel in a yoni-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
He should offer copious quantities of ghee, meat, and fish,
and satisfy the deity with substances mixed with meat in a portion equal to one-tenth of the recitation.
Having performed the consecration of the one who embodies the universe with a tenth part of the libation (tarpaṇa),
one should properly feed a tenth part [of that number] of practitioners who are dear to the deity;
one should cause divine meat, fish, and solid food (carvaṇa) to be offered.
At the conclusion of that, O beloved, one should gratify the Guru with devotion by means of gold and other offerings;
by this ritual method, O Great Goddess, the mantra is certainly perfected.
Thus ends the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the Kula.
Now, regarding the mantra-bath for practitioners,
it is said in another Tantra:
One should bathe in the stainless holy site (tīrtha) of Puṣkara, which resides within the heart;
or, having bathed in Bindu-tīrtha, there is no rebirth again.
"In this body, which is a sacred ford of Śiva filled with the water of knowledge, the *iḍā* and *suṣumnā* channels flow;
he who always bathes in those two with the waters of Brahman—what need has he for the waters of the Gaṅgā or even the Puṣkara lakes?
Thus is the description of bathing.
Now, regarding the twilight (sandhyā):
at whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs, that is the twilight; for those established in Kula, it arises as their meditative absorption (samādhi). || 43 ||
As for the libation (tarpaṇa): having raised the Kuṇḍalinī, blazing from the Mūlādhāra and consisting of the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire,
and having caused the Supreme Bindu to descend [into it].
One should satisfy the deity of the body with the very nectar produced from that.
Thus it is said in the Navaratneśvara:
"The supreme nectar that has flowed forth from the union of the moon, the sun, and fire—one should satisfy one's chosen deity with that divine nectar. (45)
In the lower portion of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is the supreme lunar vessel;
having filled it with the essence of the digits (kalās), one should satisfy the Khecarī with that.
As for meditation:

having brought about dissolution in the great void—that which resides in the rays, that which resides in fire, and that which is situated between the moon and the sun—the king of yogis remains full. (47)
Alternatively:
"That radiance which arises in the supportless, void state—one should constantly practice that as the 'womb' (garbha);
for this is indeed the meditation of yogins."
One should practice that which is "within its womb," meaning that which resides within the internal organ (antahkarana). || 48 ||
Now, the intermediate worship (*antarapūjā*):

having raised the *kulakuṇḍalinī* from the *mūlādhāra*, and having led her to the solar orb in the heart, [one should recite] the root mantra with the stream of lunar nectar situated within the thousand-petaled lotus.
One should sprinkle while recollecting [the deity]. || 49 ||
By worshipping with the flowers of the sense-objects, one becomes identical with that in an instant. Nyāsa is the realization of identity with that; one should worship with the feeling "I am He.
"Identical with that" refers to the knowledge of oneness with that, while "I am He" refers to the state of being that very self.
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as being strung upon the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
That very [power], in the supreme void (paramavyoman) which is expanded by supreme bliss, reveals the true nature of the Self without [the need for] worship, fire-offerings, and so forth. (49-ka)

The flowers of the sense objects are as follows: freedom from deceit, freedom from egoism, freedom from passion, freedom from pride, and likewise freedom from delusion, freedom from hypocrisy, and likewise freedom from censure and agitation.
The wise know that the ten flowers are non-miserliness and non-greed;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower; compassion is a flower, forgiveness is a flower, and knowledge is the fifth flower. (50)
Now, the fire-oblation (*homa*):
having visualized oneself as undivided,
consisting of the forms of the self (*ātman*), the inner self (*antarātman*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), and the knowledge-self (*jñānātman*), which is square;

Having meditated upon the fire-pit of consciousness (citkuṇḍa) at the navel— endowed with the girdle of bliss (ānandamekhalā) and adorned by the womb (yoni) in the form of the half-measure (ardhamātrā)— one should offer oblations into the fire of gnosis (jñānāgni) situated in its center.
As it says at the end of the *Mūla*: "With the mind as the sacrificial ladle and consciousness at the navel as the fire,
I perpetually offer the activity of the senses as an oblation into that fire kindled by knowledge— *svāhā*!"
Thus is the first oblation. At the end of the root mantra:
"In the fire of the self, kindled by the fuel of dharma and adharma, with the mind as the ladle..."
"By means of the path of the *suṣumnā*, I constantly offer the functions of the senses; *svāhā*—thus is the second oblation—at the end of the root [mantra]:
'Into the fire of the Self, kindled by the fuel of merit and demerit, I offer with the mind as the sacrificial ladle.'"
"By means of the path of Suṣumnā, I perpetually offer the sensory functions; Svāhā!"—with this, he makes the second oblation at the end of the root-mantra:
"Having grasped Unmanī with the ladle of the hand of luminous space."
"I offer into the fire that which is filled with the oil of the portions of merit and demerit; svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer the third oblation.
Then, at the end of the root mantra:
Into the fire of consciousness— which blazes within without external fuel, which dispels the darkness of illusion,
and which is the ground for the manifestation of the rays of all that exists— I offer the entire universe as a libation.
"Beginning with the earth and ending with Śivā"—
with these words, one should offer the fourth oblation.
Having performed this internal sacrifice (antaryajana), one becomes directly composed of Brahman;
for such a person there are neither sins nor merits, and he certainly becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
This internal sacrifice belongs only to those who possess knowledge.
Now follows the method of the internal sacrifice of the five *k*’s (*antaḥ-pañcamakāra-yajana*).
As it is stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "In the internal sacrifice, wine is the Śakti, meat is Śiva, and the one who consumes them is Bhairava himself."
The bliss arising from the unity of these two is called liberation. || 52 ||
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and it is established within the body;
that substance which manifests it is drunk by the yogis.
He who knows the distinctions of the three marks and pierces the lotuses of the six cakras [attains this].
Having arrived at the locations of the *pīṭhas*, one should proceed to the Great Lotus Grove (*mahāpadmavana*).
Moving again and again from the *mūlādhāra* up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*),
there arises the great exaltation of the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between Consciousness (*cit*), the Moon, and the Kuṇḍalinī energy.
O Goddess, the man who delights in drinking the nectar flowing from the sky-lotus drinks this true wine; all else is merely the drinking of intoxicants. (53)
Having slain the sacrificial animal of merit and demerit with the sword of knowledge, the knower of yoga leads the mind to dissolution in the Supreme; he is called a "Palāśin. || 54 ||
Having restrained the group of senses beginning with the mind, one should unite them within the Self;
he, O Goddess, becomes a "meat-eater" (māṃsāśin), while others are merely slayers of living beings.

Those who are filled with the bliss of the union of the couple consisting of Paraśakti and the Self are liberated; that indeed is true sexual union, while others are merely those who indulge in women.
Now, regarding the worship of the maiden (*kumārī-pūjā*),
the *Jñānārṇava* states:
"Indeed, all rites such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth [are incomplete] without the worship of the maiden."
The fruit would not be complete through [ordinary] worship;
that fruit would certainly be attained by worshipping a maiden, O Goddess—the fruit becomes ten millionfold. (57)
The fruit of a flower given to a young maiden is equal to Mount Meru;
by him who has fed a young maiden, the three worlds have been fed.
Regarding that, the determination of the maiden is stated in the *Yāmala*: "A one-year-old girl is Sandhyā; she who is two years old is Sarasvatī;
she who is three years old is Tridhāmūrti; and she who is four years old is Kālikā."
At five years she is Subhagā, while at six she becomes Umā; at seven she is Mālinī in person, and at eight she is Kubjikā. At nine she is Kālasandarbha, and at ten she is Aparājitā.
In the eleventh year she is Rudrāṇī, and in the twelfth year she is Bhairavī;
in the thirteenth year she is Mahālakṣmī, and at twenty-two she is the Mistress of the Pīṭha;
with fifteen [years] she is Kṣetrajñā, and in the sixteenth year she is remembered as Ambikā.
In this manner, one should worship in sequence until no flowers remain.
One should worship [the goddess] from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the full moon according to the various stages of her growth;
especially during all the great festivals (mahāparvan), and particularly during the Pavitraka rite.
O Goddess of gods, on the Mahānavamī day, one should also worship the Kumārī.
Now, the sequence of worship:
having brought a young girl there, one should offer water with the syllable *aiṃ* while perceiving her as the Goddess, using her respective name.

One should offer water for the feet with the syllable *hrīṃ*, the water of honor (*arghya*) with the syllable *śrīṃ*, sandalwood paste with the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, flowers with the syllable *hrīṃ*, and incense and lamps with the mantra *hsauḥ*. Thereafter, one should worship with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Namely:
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Hsauḥ, obeisance to the heart of Kulakumārīke;
Haiṃ Vaiṃ Hraiṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Aiṃ Svāhā, Svāhā to the head.
Oṃ śrīṃ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair (śikhā).
Aiṃ, huṃ to the armor (kavaca) of Kulavāgīśvarī.
Aiṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya) of Kuleśvarī.
Hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ.
Then: Aiṃ siddhajayāya pūrvavaktrāya namaḥ. Aiṃ jayāya uttaravaktrāya namaḥ.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrī Kubjike, salutation to the western face. Aiṃ Kālike, salutation to the southern face.
Through the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] there is the agitation of the city; in the Māyā-bīja, the eight qualities.

From the seed-syllable Śrī comes the attainment of fortune; by the seed-syllable Hūṃ, there is the destruction of enemies. And by the Bhairava seed-syllable, one attains the state of moving through the air like the immortals and others.
O Lord, I am indeed the Virgin (Kumārikā), for you are always the Virgin.
One should worship either one hundred and eight or even just one;
when worshipped, they return the worship, but if treated with contempt, they consume [the offender].
The maiden is a yoginī, the maiden herself is the supreme deity.

The Asuras and wicked Nāgas, whatever malevolent planets there may be, Bhūtas, Vetālas, Gandharvas, Ḍākinīs, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas, and all other deities belonging to the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar who are terrifying— [may they all be pacified].
The entire earth and other elements, the cosmic egg with all its moving and non-moving beings,
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
all these are pleased and all are satisfied by one who worships a maiden. (61-ka)
One should feed the Bhairavī [image] according to the prescribed rites along with young maidens;
having worshipped with devotion, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), the respectful oblation (arghya), incense, and auspicious saffron and sandalwood paste to the maidens.
One should perform three circumambulations—at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end.
Afterwards, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of silver, gold, and pearls should be given;
and one should likewise give sacrificial fees to young maidens in due order.
Likewise, in that very same [text]:
"If he himself marries off a maiden, he removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
the sin of killing cows, the sin of killing a woman, and all evil are destroyed."
Whoever bestows the gift of a daughter during an auspicious time shall obtain the fruit of worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as good fortune and all prosperity.
The three-eyed Lord Hara dwells eternally in the world of Rudra;
that mortal who marries off a daughter obtains the fruit of thousands of crores of holy fords and hundreds of horse-sacrifices.
It should be known that for as many thousands of years as there are grains of sand in the ocean,
each individual family is uplifted and honored in the world of Rudra.

The experts of tradition maintain that the giving of a maiden is for the sake of pleasing the respective deity. In reality, however, the secret meaning is that one should give the maiden of the corresponding age after contemplating her as being of the nature of Śiva, through the mental identification of her with that particular deity. || 67 ||
Now, the method of yoga: in the *Gautamīya*,
Gautama said:
O divine sage, whose self is united in yoga, who reveals the experience of yoga,
who possesses specialized knowledge of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and who practices the yoga of action—
O Lord, without yoga, that movement of Kuṇḍalinī cannot be perfected.

O Lord, as long as Kuṇḍalinī remains asleep within the root-lotus, nothing at all— whether yantras, mantras, worship, or other rites— will succeed. If that Goddess awakens through the accumulation of many merits, [then success is attained].
Then the mechanical devices, mantras, ritual worship, and so forth, attain their efficacy. || 68 ||
Endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), one shall roam through the worlds like Śiva.

Through the application of yoga, liberation arises, as does unimpeded perfection in mantra. When the mantra is perfected, there is the attainment of the Supreme (*parā*); such is the determination of the meaning of the teaching.
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, please explain the supreme yoga which must be practiced,
by means of which the liberated soul may roam in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld,
and which allows one who is liberated while living to attain the state of Nirvāṇa at the end of the body. (69)
Nārada said:
Out of affection for you, I shall speak, O Gautama, for you are worthy of yoga.
The method for crossing over the cycle of worldly existence is designated by the word "yoga."
Those proficient in yoga declare that the union of the individual soul and the Self is oneness.

Out of affection for you, I have described these obstacles to yoga, known as desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. By conquering them through these limbs of yoga, practitioners attain yoga. (71)
Yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma,
followed by pratyāhāra, that which is called dhāraṇā, dhyāna, together with samādhi—
these they declare to be the eight limbs for the yogi in the practice of yoga.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten restraints (yamas). || 73 ||
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the deity, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings—
these ten are declared as the observances (niyamas) by those expert in the Yoga scriptures. (74)
The postures are those previously described.
One should draw in the external air through the *iḍā* with sixteen measures;
the yogi should retain the filled breath for sixty-four measures.
The best among those who know yoga should slowly exhale this [breath] through the piṅgalā channel, which is correctly situated in the middle of the suṣumnā for thirty-two mātrās;
those learned in the yoga scriptures call this prāṇāyāma.
One should perform this repeatedly and gradually, alternating its sequence; according to the progressive increase of the measures (mātrā), twelve or sixteen [repetitions] performed properly,
joined with recitation (japa), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth— the wise know that as "with seed" (sagarbha).
They know that breath control (prāṇāyāma) which is free from that [leakage] and devoid of internal emission (nirgarbha) to be supreme. || 76 ||
Through gradual practice, the emergence of sweat in a person's body is considered the lowest [stage];
the middle is accompanied by trembling; and the highest is regarded as the abandonment of the ground.
The attainment of the qualities of the supreme [stage] continues as long as the practice is maintained. (77)
The withdrawal of the senses as they roam unimpeded among their objects, forcibly drawing them back from those [objects], is prescribed as *pratyāhāra*. (78)
In the thumb, the ankle, the knee, the thigh, the suture, the navel, the genitals, the anus, the heart, the neck, the throat region, the uvula, as well as the nose,
between the eyebrows, on the forehead, at the crown of the head, and at the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta), according to the prescribed rule.
The retention of the vital breath is designated as "dhāraṇā" (retention). || 79 ||
Meditation here is said to be the contemplation of one's chosen deities within the self, by means of a concentrated mind abiding in inner consciousness.
The sages declare that the constant cultivation of the equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman),
characterized by the eight limbs as previously described, is called samādhi.
O Brahmin, thus has been described the destruction of the sixfold group beginning with desire;
now I shall tell you the unsurpassed yoga of mantra. (82)

O Sage, the body is said to be the universe, composed of the five elements; through the splendors of the moon, sun, and fire, it is the embodiment of the unity of the individual soul and Brahman. It is held that there are thirty-five million channels within the body.
Among them, ten are declared to be the principal ones; among those, three are established [as the most important]. || 83 ||

Here, within the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), the principal channel has the form of the moon, sun, and fire. The white channel Iḍā is situated on the left; it has the form of the moon, is of the nature of Śakti, and is the very embodiment of nectar.
To the south, however, is the one named Piṅgalā, who has a male form and the appearance of the sun;
she resembles the filaments of a pomegranate flower and is remembered by the sages as Viṣā. || 84 ||
Situated in the center of Meru, extending from the base up to the form of Brahmā,
that Suṣumnā is composed of all splendor and possesses many forms.
In its center is the auspicious one called Vicitrā, which flows with nectar;
she consists of all the gods and reaches the hearts of yogins.
In reality, she abides from the point of emission (visarga) up to the bindu.
In the Mūlādhāra, known as the triangle and consisting of will, knowledge, and action,
is the self-manifested Liṅga (Svayambhūliṅga) in its center, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), ending with the jar (kalaśa), the moon (indu), and the nasal sound (nāda).
Above that is Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is like a flame, the very embodiment of Brahman.
Outside of that, one should visualize a four-petalled lotus with the color of gold, possessing the hue of the Vasus, and shining like molten gold. (89)
Above that is the [cakra] known as Adhiṣṭhāna, resembling fire in brilliance, possessing six petals with the luster of a diamond,
and joined with the six syllables beginning with ba and ending with la.
Among the six root-supports (mūlādhāras), they know the first to be the *mūlādhāra*;
by the word "self" (*sva*), they know the supreme *liṅga* to be the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. || 91 ||
Above that, in the region of the navel, is the Maṇipūra, of great luster,
resembling a cloud and shining like lightning, composed entirely of manifold splendor.
Because that lotus is pierced like a gem, it is likewise called Maṇipūra.
The lotus, endowed with ten petals and possessed of the letters beginning with 'ḍa' and ending with 'pha', is presided over by Śiva and is the sole cause of the entire world. (93)
Above that is the Anāhata lotus, resembling the rising sun,
presided over by twelve petals consisting of the letters from 'ka' to 'ṭha'.
In its center is the Bāṇaliṅga, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns;
there the unstruck sound (anāhata) is perceived, consisting of the Śabdabrahman.
That is proclaimed by the sages as the lotus known as Anāhata. || 95 ||
That is indeed the abode of bliss, presided over by the Supreme Puruṣa.
Above that is the petal known as Viśuddha, a sixteen-petaled lotus,
endowed with the sixteen vowels, smoke-colored and of great luster.
Because it extends purity through the vision of the *haṃsa* by the individual soul (*jīva*), the lotus called "Space" is declared to be pure and most wonderful. (96)
Above that is the wheel of command (ājñācakra), the supreme, presided over by the Self;
the transmission of command therein is celebrated as the "Command of the Guru. (97)
Above that is the one called Kailāsa, and above that is Bodhanī;
thus, O you of noble vows, the Śiva-cakras have been described to you.
The thousand-petaled lotus, the abode of the Bindu, is said to be situated above that. || 99 ||
First, by means of the practice of inhalation (pūraka), one should fix the mind upon the foundational center (svādhiṣṭhāna).
Having contracted that power (śakti) located between the anus and the genitals, one should awaken it. 100.
Following the sequence of the division of the *liṅgas*, one should lead [the energy] to the *binducakra*;
one should contemplate that supreme power (*parā śakti*) as being in a state of oneness with Śambhu. || 1 ||
There, having caused that spear named Kṛṣṇā— which bestows the perfection of practice— to drink the nectar-essence arisen therein, which resembles molten lac,
one should satiate the deities of the six wheels there with a stream of nectar.
Then the wise one should lead it by that same path back to the mūlādhāra.
For one who practices in this manner day after day, the vital breath (māruta) is released from the bondage of existence through [the cessation of] the sufferings of old age, death, and the like. (3)
All mantras corrupted as previously described will not succeed otherwise.
Whatever qualities belong to the God who performs the fivefold cosmic act,
those very qualities indeed come to exist in the excellent practitioner, and not otherwise.
Thus has this entire unsurpassed path of yoga been described. || 4 ||
Now listen attentively to me as I describe that which is called *dhāraṇā*:
by fixing the mind upon Kṛṣṇa, who is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, one quickly becomes absorbed in Him through the union of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. (5)
Alternatively, when the mind is defiled and does not quickly attain success,
then the yogi should practice the yogas through the application of its constituent parts.
One should fix the mind upon the lotus-feet, variegated with the filaments of the toenails;
likewise upon the pair of shanks, beautiful as the stalks of the *rāmaka* plantain;
and upon the two thighs, possessing a luster equal to the trunk of an elephant in rut.
Then, in the navel deep as a whirlpool of the Gaṅgā, in the cave of the perfected ones (siddhas),
likewise in the belly, the chest, the neck-ornament, the Śrīvatsa, and the Kaustubha gem; and on the forehead, which resembles ten thousand full moons, and upon the beautiful locks of hair.

The pure practitioner, with a purified mind, should place [the deities] in their proper positions upon the crown and the pair of earrings— which are adorned by the staff-like arms holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and which resemble a thousand suns.

Having fixed the mind upon Kṛṣṇa, one certainly becomes absorbed in Him. As long as the mind has not reached dissolution in Kṛṣṇa— the Self, who is composed of consciousness— the practitioner of mantra should diligently perform recitation and fire-offerings according to his desire.
"Kṛṣṇa" is an illustrative designation. || 8 ||
Beyond this, there is nothing further to be done for Hari;
once the supreme reality is known, all restrictive observances are superfluous.
What need is there for a palm-leaf fan when the Malaya breeze has been obtained?
Through the practice of mantra and yoga, knowledge leads to [higher] knowledge.
There is no mantra without yoga, nor indeed is there yoga without mantra;
for the combined practice of both is the cause of the perfect realization of Brahman. (10)
Just as a jar in a house enveloped by darkness becomes visible through a lamp, so too the Self, though veiled by māyā, is brought within the range of perception by means of the mantra. 11.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have explained to you this unsurpassed yoga of mantras,
which is difficult to attain for those attached to sense-objects, yet easily accessible even for those such as yourself.
Now, another method from the *Śāradā*:
"The body, which consists of both [aspects], is ninety-six finger-breadths in length."
Within the region of the guḍadhvaja, they know the bulb (kanda) to be two finger-breadths in height;
its width is twice that, adorned in a circular form.
From it, channels arise, of which three are proclaimed as the principal ones. (13)
The channel *iḍā* is situated on the left, while *piṅgalā* is considered to be on the right;
between these two is the channel *suṣumnā*, which rests upon the spinal column.
Having reached the two big toes, then the two crests, and finally the head,
she attained the station of Brahman, manifesting in the form of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
Situated in its center is the channel named Citrā, beloved by yogins;
they know the supreme Brahmarandhra within it, resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk.
They also recognize various bases therein in many ways according to different traditions.
They call this the path of the gods, the cause of the bliss of immortality.
The Moon moves in the iḍā and the Sun in the piṅgalā;
those who know the principles of yoga recognize both of them as being within the suṣumnā.
Those who know the scriptures say that there is a most beautiful triangle situated in the middle of the foundation-root (ādhārakanda), a divine abode of all luminaries. 18.
There, the Supreme Deity Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is like a streak of lightning, vibrates as the soul of all, appearing like a sleeping serpent. (19)
The Kuṇḍalinī energy, resting upon the Haṃsa, sustains the Self;
the Haṃsa is eternally supported by the vital breath (prāṇa), and the vital breaths are supported by the pathways of the channels (nāḍīs).
The wind, having arisen from the *ādhāra* (the foundational center) of all embodied beings, enters the body through its own channels and proceeds outward. (21)
Because it measures twelve finger-breadths, it is therefore called *prāṇa*.
Having thus secured his posture upon a pleasant, pure, and soft seat covered with a silk cloth, an antelope skin, and *kuśa* grass, the yogi should become intent on the path of yoga. (22)
Having correctly understood the emergence of the elements within the body by means of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu),
the wise person should worship each respective element within the body for the sake of attaining firmness;
this refers to the previously mentioned emergence of the elements during the performance of the āsana.
With the senses composed, one should firmly bind them with the fingers:
both ears with the two thumbs, the eyes with the two index fingers, the nostrils with the two middle fingers, and the mouth firmly with the remaining fingers.
Constantly recollecting the oneness of the exhaled breath, the inhaled breath, and the mind, one should properly restrain the vital air; this is yoga, beloved by practitioners of yoga. (24)
As he practices gradually and slowly, a resonance arises for him;
the first sound is like the song of a swarm of intoxicated bees. (25)
Another [sound] resembles the resonance of a bamboo flute filled with wind from a bell-metal vessel;
after that, one equal to the ringing of a bell, and another like the roar of thick clouds.
For a man practicing in this manner, there occurs the destruction of the darkness of saṃsāra.
First, the imperishable knowledge characterized by the swan arises. || 26 ||
The wise have declared that the *bindu* and the *sarga* consist of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti respectively.
From these two, in due order, arise [the other letters] ending with the *bindu* and the *sarga*.
Those two, known as Puruṣa and Prakṛti, are the two *haṃsas*; "haṃ" is the Puruṣa, and "sa" is Prakṛti.
The Ajapā [mantra] has been described by those two; it is that which the individual soul (jīva) attends upon.
When, regarding the Puruṣa as the eternal support of the self and considering Prakṛti as its own, it attains that state, then she becomes "I am this [Puruṣa]. (28)
Having elided the letter *sa* and the letter *ha*, one should then perform the sandhi as the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*); thus it becomes the *praṇava*. || 29 ||
The yogi should always contemplate the Praṇava, which consists of supreme bliss, is eternal, has consciousness as its sole quality, and abides in non-difference from the Self. (30)

The virtuous, established in the Self and intent on liberation, behold within themselves that primordial Tāraka— the goal of knowledge which lies far beyond the reach of the words of the scriptures— by means of the quality of perfect realization, as the singular ocean of the essence of bliss.
Truth, devoid of cause, the primordial source of the words of scripture, the cause of the universe, pervading all that is moving and unmoving, incomparable, and containing within it consciousness;
the Self, whose form is the sun, moon, and fire, and who is the essence of the stars— [I bow to] that eternal one.
Those of merit, with their senses restrained, behold the virtuous one, the abode of the qualities of eternal bliss. || 32 ||
Worship that supreme splendor of Tārā, which is being perceived through its five manifestations, which is constantly accessible only through humility,
which is sought after by the crest-jewels of the Vedas,
which is the totality of consciousness, stainless, and descended from the sky.
A dense mass of nectar-water.
They worship the golden, radiant Being, who possesses manifold colors, whose root is the triple form (Trimūrti), and who is the seed of the Vedas and other scriptures;
he is the Person (Puruṣa) the size of a thumb, pure consciousness alone, situated within the solar orb. 34.

They meditate upon the Primordial One, who reclines upon the coils of the serpent born from the Milk Ocean, accompanied by Kamalā; whose eyes are like blossoming lotuses, who resembles the color of collyrium, and whose navel-lotus is occupied by his four faces.

The wise behold that Supreme Person, who is established in the sacred tradition, whose three-quarters are the manifest world, who is dark as a rain cloud, and who displays the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, the lotus, the conch, and the discus; he whose abode is the white lotus of the heart and who is the sole root of the universe.
The Purāṇa. || 36 ||

May that body of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva)—which is the source of the sound of the *vindu*, which, when the sound has arisen, is the cause of the universe; which is the high-pitched reality (*tāra-tattva*) with the lotus-face surrounded by a multitude of arms consisting of the phonemes (*varṇa*);
and which has the Vedas as its four feet—protect us! It is a form whose root is bliss.
It was submerged in a flood of divine nectar shimmering from the crescent moon upon his crown.
The *piṇḍa* is Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is Śiva; the *pada* is Haṃsa, the inner self of all.
Bindu is remembered as the form, possessing intense splendor and a most excellent appearance—the state of equilibrium with Śiva (*śivasāmarasya*).
The wise declare that the yoga of the *piṇḍa* and so forth is the yoga of the seed-syllables (*bījayoga*), which is essentially the equilibrium with Śiva.
One attains absorption in Śiva, who is eternally endowed with auspicious qualities, through seedless yoga that is indifferent to fruits. || 39 ||
Resembling the king of serpents with its root fully awakened, she moves through the interior of the *suṣumnā*,
swiftly piercing the collection of foundational centers like a shimmering flash of lightning;
she is drenched by the floods of divine nectar flowing from the lunar orb situated within the lotus of the sky.
Having honored her, once she has returned to her own abode, one should again contemplate this Kuṇḍalinī.
Having taken hold of that Swan— who is eternal, infinite, and possessed of imperishable qualities— by its own support, the Kuṇḍalinī Śakti, the mother of all,
departed for the abode of Śambhu; and while going, she herself experienced that supreme bliss.
Resplendent with the brilliance of ten million suns within her own abode, she who deludes the world should be meditated upon. || 41 ||

Having led the Unmanifest, whose splendor is accumulated from the supreme bindu, to the abode of Śiva, the Kuṇḍalinī energy— whose body consists of the three qualities and who resembles a flash of lightning—
[reaches] the Destroyer of Cities, who dwells in the midst of the nectar of bliss and possesses the radiance of ten million moons and suns.
Having gazed [upon him], the Blessed One, who is faultless in her virtues, went to her own city; she is to be meditated upon. 42.

In the midst of the path, having transcended the mass of sounds born from the agitation of the mutual friction of the two winds, we worship Her as She rises in the light resplendent with the brilliance of ten million lightning flashes—
reddened by the twilight of fresh saffron.

The supreme goddess Kuṇḍalī, who consists of the nectar of intense bliss and has reached Paraśiva, bestows the fruits of yoga through her coming and going. This Kulakāmadhenu, once arisen, is a wish-fulfilling creeper for those who worship her, granting whatever they desire. || 43–44 ||
Now, he states the praise [of the Āgama] in the *Yāmala*:
"All sciences (*vidyā*) are in the Āgama, and all treatises (*śāstra*) are in the Āgama."
Indeed, in the scripture of the God and Goddess, the supreme goal is attained through the scripture. || 45 ||
For those who practice this scripture, read it, or cause it to be read,
the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), as well as wealth, grain, and sons, are in the palm of their hands.
Respected in all the worlds, enjoyers [of worldly pleasures], and agitating others, those who are experts in all the scriptures attain the Supreme Brahman. || 47 ||
O Mother, having observed the frequent occurrence of the loss of sacrifice due to the study of treatises contrary to the meaning of the Vedas,
please forgive the faults arising from my attempt to clarify those hidden deceptions.
I entreat you at your pair of feet. || 48 ||

O Lord, if I, with a deluded mind, have made clear that which is most secret in the tantra, this must be forgiven by you, O treasury of compassion; for anger is truly not appropriate toward the foolish. (49)
Thus ends the *Tantrasāra*, composed by the Great Professor (Mahāmahopādhyāya) Śrī Kṛṣṇānanda Vāgīśa Bhaṭṭācārya.
The Supplement: A Section on the Mantras, Hymns, and Other Liturgies for Specific Deities;
Now, the Gaṅgā-mantra:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim Gaṅgā, the purifier of the world,
who is to be meditated upon with the prescribed contemplation, and who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the *Brahmasaṃhitā*:

Having extracted the seed-syllable of poison (*viṣabīja*) and then *māyā*, which is dear to Viṣṇu, followed by the word *gaṅgā* ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, [the mantra] concludes with the consort of Fire (*vahnijāyā*). This is the mantra.
This eight-syllabled great vidyā is difficult to obtain on earth even from the Gaṅgā.
The seed-syllable of poison is *praṇava* (oṃ); *māyā* is *hrīṃ*; and *viṣṇupriyā* is *śrīṃ*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows, according to the *Kriyāyogasāra*:
"He beheld Gaṅgā before him, two-armed and seated upon a crocodile."
White as a jasmine flower, a conch shell, or snow, and adorned with all ornaments. || 3 ||
(Other forms of meditation may be found in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* and other texts).
Having meditated upon the auspicious river that flows through the three paths by means of this very meditation,
O Brahmin, one should offer her the sixteen types of ritual services (*upacāra*) after having made the gift.
A seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), bathing materials, unguents, incense and lamps, food offerings, betel leaf, and cool water. || 5 ||
Garment, ornament, garland, perfume, water for rinsing the mouth,
and a beautiful, excellent bed— these sixteen items are to be given.
Having offered [the gift] with devotion, one should prostrate and offer praise with palms joined in the *sampuṭa* gesture;
by thus worshipping with the syllable *pakāra*, one obtains the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
All else is as described in the general ritual manual (*sāmānyapaddhati*).
Now, the mantra of Kārttikeya from the Bhūtaḍāmara:
"Viṣaṃ raudraṃ krodhapadaṃ dhāriṇe," and after that [the name].
This mantra of the one in the form of Kumāra is said to end with the wife of Vahni (the letter *i*);
*viṣa* is the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), and *raudra* is the *māyābīja* (*hrīṃ*). || 1 ||
One should meditate as follows:
on the highly fortunate Kārttikeya, seated upon a peacock,
possessing the luster of molten gold, holding a spear in his hand, and bestowing boons.
Two-armed, the slayer of enemies, adorned with various ornaments, six-faced, with prominent eyes, and placed at the head of all the armies. || 2 ||
Having meditated thus and performed everything as before, one should prostrate: "Oṃ, I pay homage to Kārttikeya, the son of Gaurī, the bestower of auspiciousness,
the six-faced one, the highly fortunate, the destroyer of the pride of the Daityas."
The sixth is Maṅgalacaṇḍī; these are the portions of Prakṛti manifested through the mind.
This account of the Goddess, however, bestows all perfections upon men. (3)
Now, the sixth mantra is as follows:
having extracted the seed-syllable at the beginning of the Vedas (Om), the Māyā-bīja (Hrīm) follows thereafter.
The word "Ṣaṣṭhīdevī" ending in the dative case (ṅe), conjoined with the "fire-born wife" (svāhā), is the eight-syllabled great mantra proclaimed for the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. || 1 ||
The meditation is as follows:
[one should meditate on] Prakṛti, who possesses a sixth part, who is pure, well-established, and radiant;
who bestows excellent sons, who grants auspiciousness, whose form is compassion, and who is the mother of the world.
I worship Devasenā, who possesses the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, who is adorned with jewel ornaments, and who is of supremely pure form. || 2 ||
Everything else is as before.
The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
[This is stated] in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
"O Sage, he who recites the eight-syllabled great mantra one hundred thousand times certainly obtains a son; so said the Lotus-born One.
This should be understood from the Maṅgalacaṇḍī section of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa. (3)
Now, the mantra of Viṣaharī-Jagadgaurī-Manasā:
Having extracted "Halāhalam," followed by the seed-syllable of Lañjā (Lauṃ),
then the word "Namaḥ," and thereafter one should utter "Manasāyai."
The supreme knowledge ending in *svāhā* destroys the poison of all embodied beings. This ten-syllabled mantra is declared to be the presiding deity of all;
*halāhala* is the *praṇava*.
The meditation on her is as follows:
she has the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, is adorned with jewel ornaments,
wears garments of fire-purified silk, and has a serpent as her sacred thread.
I worship the one endowed with great wisdom, the most excellent among the wise, who is truly real; the goddess who presides over the Siddhas, herself a Siddha, the bestower of success.
Worship and other rites are as before.
In this manner, one should worship Jaratkāru, the sage Āstīka, the serpent, and the other surrounding deities. || 2 ||
Now, the Svāhā mantra from the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the goddess Vahnijāyā; after that [the following].
The twelve-syllable Mahāvidyā of the goddess Svāhā has been proclaimed. The meditation on her is as follows:
[one should meditate upon] Svāhā, who has become a limb of the mantra and whose very nature is the accomplishment of the mantra.
I worship her who is perfected, who bestows perfection upon men, and who grants the fruits of action;
all [rites] such as worship and so forth are to be performed as before. || 3 ||
Now, the mantra for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the rites is as follows,
in that same [text]:
"Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ dakṣiṇāyai svāhā," which consists of ten syllables.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[She who] was born from a portion of Lakṣmī and Dakṣa, the Dakṣiṇā who is a digit of Kamalā,
skillful in all rites, and the bestower of the fruits of all actions.
I worship Suśīlā, who is the very embodiment of Viṣṇu’s power and the bestower of auspiciousness;
the worship and other rites are as before. || 4 ||
Now, the mantra of Krodharāja as it appears in the Bhūtaḍāmara:
"Viṣañca vajrajvālena hanayugmamataḥ param. (And poison with the vajra-flame; thereafter, the pair *hana*.)
The mantra beginning with *sarvabhūtāntataḥ* and ending with the *kūrca* mantra has been proclaimed.
Meditation, worship, and so forth should be understood as pertaining to that very [mantra].
A hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajapa*) of this mantra are for the sake of accomplishing all aims; at the outset, they are for the purpose of self-protection.
It should be performed everywhere.
Now, the Gaṅgā-kavaca: Oṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā.
For the Gaṅgākavaca, Viṣṇu is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ), and its application (viniyoga) is in the recitation for the purpose of uplifting fourteen persons.
Oṃ, you who are of the nature of substance, highly fortunate one, present both in the ritual bath and in the libation (tarpaṇa).
May she who is white in form protect me during consecration and worship. || 1 ||
You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu, bearing the name Vaiṣṇavī;
may Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, protect me and guard me from all sides.
May Mandākinī, who is beloved of heaven, protect [me] always at the end of the body; and may Alakanandā, who dwells upon the earth on its left side, protect me. || 3 ||
In Pātāla there is Bhogavatī, and likewise Mandākinī in Svarga;
whoever recites or even hears this five-syllabled mantra [attains these].
The sick shall be liberated from disease; the bound shall be released from bondage;
the pregnant woman shall give birth to a son, and the barren woman shall become possessed of sons.
Merely by remembering the Gaṅgā, a man becomes free from sin;
he who recites this within his home shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.

Whoever recites this at the time of bathing shall obtain the fruit of a hundred crores; whoever recites it with devotion while self-restrained shall be liberated along with ten million members of his lineage.
Thus ends the Gaṅgākavaca, from the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī in the Viṣṇuyāmala.
Now, the Inexhaustible Armor of Kārttikeya:
the Goddess said:
"Whichever sons were born to me, each one was struck down by Kaṃsa."
"O bull among sages, tell me how my mental continuum may remain stable."
Nārada said:
By whatever means the progeny of people may live for a long time, all of that I shall declare to you; listen with focused attention.
Of this armor that exhausts the aggregates (skandhas), Nārada is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, Senānī is the deity, and its application is for the protection of the calf.
Om! May the son of Bāhulā protect the head; may the delighter of Śaṅkara protect the shoulders. (3)
The son of Pārvatī has my head; the one whose vehicle is the peacock has my heart; the wielder of the spear protects my waist; and the destroyer of Tāraka guards my shanks.
May Guha protect my feet; may Senānī, the supreme child, protect them. May Skanda protect my limbs, and may he who is the fire of the ten directions protect me.
May Kumāra, who is six-faced, protect us from terrible fear in the cremation ground.
"O auspicious lady, I have thus told you this most excellent armor (kavaca).
By wearing it, one obtains a virtuous son who is long-lived. (7)
Having heard the words of Nārada, she put on the armor;
by the grace of that armor, the virtuous woman shall have living children.
By the grace of that armor, Janārdana became her son;
likewise, Dhārikā’s son was invincible even by the gods.
Thus ends the *Kārtikeyākṣayakavaca* from the *Umāyamala*. Now begins the *Vaṃśalābhākya-kavaca*:
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, beloved as life itself to Pārvatī,
please reveal to me the armor known as Vaṃśalābha.
Īśvara said:
This armor known as Vaṃśalābha is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
by its grace, Kamalā obtained an excellent son.
Kāmadeva and Aparṇā, Vināyaka and Ṣaḍānana, Jayanta and Indravanitā, as well as the wives of the gods and their sons. (3)

For this armor known as *Vaṃśalābha*, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śrī Pārvatī is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of obtaining a living son.
Oṃ! May Pārvatī protect my head; may Maheśvarī protect my face.
May Bhavānī protect my eyes; may the beautiful consort of Śaṅkara protect my eyebrows.
O Maheśānī, praised by the gods, protect my waist;
may Gaurī always protect my thighs, and Kauṣikī protect the pair of my knees. || 5 ||
May Sumukhī protect my two arms; may Subhāvinī protect the pair of my hands;
may Brahmamayī protect my feet; and may Bhuvaneśvarī protect my ears.
May Lalitā protect the nostrils; may Tripurasundarī protect the throat; may Rudrāṇī protect the heart; and may Maheśvarī protect the pair of breasts.
May Sarvamaṅgalā protect [me] from head to foot and all my limbs.
O Brahmin, thus has this armor (kavaca), worshipped by the gods, been recounted to you. Oṃ!
By reciting and retaining [this], one shall obtain imperishable progeny;
I shall now declare its meditation, so that a person may recite it while meditating upon it.

Oṃ! [I meditate upon her] who resembles a thousand suns, adorned with all ornaments, three-eyed, and holding in her hands the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness. 10.
Thus ends the armor known as Vaṃśalābha, from the Śrī Bhairava Tantra, in the dialogue between Śiva and Nārada.
Now begins the sixth hymn:
Listen, O best of sages, to this hymn which brings about all desires and auspiciousness, which grants the wishes of all, and which is hidden within the Vedas, O Nārada. (1)
Priyavrata said:
Oṃ, salutations to the Goddess, the Great Goddess; salutations again and again to Siddhi and Śānti.
Salutations again and again to the auspicious Devasenā and to the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. || 2 ||
Salutations again and again to the giver of boons, the giver of sons, and the giver of wealth;
salutations again and again to the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the giver of happiness and the giver of liberation. || 3 ||
Salutations again and again to her whose nature is Śakti and Ṣaṣṭhī, and who is the perfected one (Siddhā); salutations again and again to Māyā, the Siddha-yoginī, and the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. || 4 ||
Salutations again and again to Sārā, to Sāradā, to Parā, and to the goddess who presides over all actions;
salutations again and again to the goddess Bālādhiṣṭhātṛ and to the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
Salutations again and again to the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the bestower of auspiciousness, the auspicious one;
salutations again and again to the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, who grants the fruits of actions, who is the embodiment of fruitfulness, and who is directly manifest to her devotees. || 6 ||
Salutations again and again to the venerable Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the beloved of Skanda, who performs divine protection in all matters and in all rites. || 7 ||
Salutations again and again to her who is the very nature of pure being and who has been saluted;
O Sovereign of the Gods, grant me wealth, grant me prosperity, and grant me a son.
Grant me Dharma, grant me glory; salutations again and again to Goddess Shashthi!
Grant me land, grant me progeny, grant me sovereignty, O highly honored one!
Grant me auspiciousness and victory; salutations again and again to Goddess Shashthi. (9)
Having thus praised the Goddess with "Oṃ," Priyavrata obtained a son, a renowned lord of kings, by the grace of Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. || 10 ||
Whoever hears this hymn to the Sixth [Brahmāṇī] day by day, O Brahmin, a sonless man obtains a son who is excellent and long-lived. (11)
And he who recites this hymn with devotion for one year shall be liberated from all sins; even a woman long barren shall give birth.
And by the grace of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, [he shall have] a son who is heroic, virtuous, learned, illustrious, and indeed possessed of a very long life.
Thus ends the Hymn to the Sixth [Day] in the *Prakṛtikhaṇḍa* of the *Brahmavaivarta Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada.
Now begins the *Viṣaharīmanasā-stotra*:
Oṃ! Jaratkāru, Jagadgaurī, Siddhayoginī in thought, Viṣṇavī, sister of the Nāgas, Śaivā, and likewise Nāgeśvarī. || 1 ||
She is beloved by the Creator of the World, the mother of Astika, and the remover of poison;
endowed with great wisdom, that Goddess is worshipped by the universe.
Oṃ!
Whoever recites these twelve names at the time of worship,
for him and for those born in his lineage, there is no fear of nāgas.
In a bed terrified by a nāga, in a dwelling seized by a nāga, in a great fortress destroyed by a nāga, or in a body encircled by a nāga; || 4 ||
Having recited this hymn, one is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
If one recites this constantly after seeing a site, the host of nāgas flees.
By merely reciting this hymn one million times, men shall achieve perfection in the hymn;
he who has achieved perfection in the hymn is capable of consuming poison.
Having made the multitude of serpents his ornament, he shall have the serpent as his vehicle;
when one has accomplished the hymn, even poison becomes equal to nectar.
Thus ends the *Manasā-stotra* in the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*. Now begins the *Svāhā-stotra*:
Vahni said:
Oṃ svāhā and the others are portions of Prakṛti, embodied within other mantras;
she is the bestower of the fruits of mantras and the sustainer of the worlds, the virtuous Satī. (1)
She is the very nature of accomplishment, the perfected one, and the bestower of success upon men at all times;
she is the power of burning fire, whose form exceeds even their vital breath.
She is the very essence of saṃsāra, yet she is the one who carries one across the terrible ocean of saṃsāra;
she is the life-force of the gods, yet she is the stone that brings the gods [to rest]. || 3 ||
Oṃ!
Whoever recites these sixteen names endowed with devotion shall attain all accomplishments, and all his actions will be auspicious.
One without a son obtains a son; one without a wife obtains a beloved.
Thus ends the Svāhā-stotra in the Prakṛti-khaṇḍa of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. Now begins the Dakṣiṇā-stotra:
The Yakṣa said:
Oṃ! You are the goddess of Goloka, the supreme and foremost among the gopīs;
you are equal to Rādhā, her dear friend, and the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O dear one.
During the great festival of Rādhā on the full moon day of Kīrtika, she manifested from the right shoulder of Kṛṣṇa; therefore, she is called Dakṣiṇā.
Formerly, you were named Suśīlā on account of your beautiful character; however, due to Kṛṣṇa’s wearing your garment over his shoulder and due to Rādhā’s curse, you became Dakṣiṇā.
"O highly fortunate one, you have descended from Goloka and appeared before me through my good fortune;
show mercy, O noble lady, and make me alone your husband."
O Goddess, you alone are the bestower of fruits for the actions of those who perform them;
without you, all the actions of everyone are fruitless.
Just as a tree on the surface of the earth is not beautiful when deprived of its fruit and branches,
so too is action not beautiful for those who perform it without you.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and even the guardians of the quarters and others are not capable of bestowing the fruit of action without you.
Brahmā himself is the embodiment of action, Maheśvara is the embodiment of the fruit,
Viṣṇu is the embodiment of sacrifice, and I am you— the embodiment of their essence.
The giver of the fruit is the Supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities and beyond primordial nature;
he is the Lord Kṛṣṇa himself, who is capable [of granting it] along with you.
O beloved, you alone are my power in birth after birth;
O fair-faced one, I am capable in every action only when together with you.
Having spoken thus, the presiding deity of the sacrifice remained intent upon that;
the Goddess became pleased, so one should worship that portion of Kamalā.
Oṃ!
Whoever recites this hymn of praise for the sacrificial fee at the time of a sacrifice shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. || 12 ||
In the Rājasūya, Bājapeya, Gomedha, and Naramedha sacrifices;
in the Aśvamedha, the Maṅgala, and the illustrious Viṣṇuyajña. || 13 ||

In the case of one who bestows wealth, one who bestows land, one who is fruitful, one whose desires are fulfilled, one who performs the elephant-sacrifice or the horse-sacrifice, one who performs an iron-sacrifice or a gold-sacrifice, and one who causes the cutting [of trees] or the destruction of the Veda; || 14 ||
In the Śivayajña, the Rudrayajña, and the Śatruyajña; at Bandhuka, at the Varuṇayāga, at Kaṇṭaka, and at Vairimardana. (15)
In the Śuci sacrifice, the Dharma sacrifice, the Rocana, the Pāpamocana, the Bandhana, the Karma sacrifice, and the auspicious Maṇi sacrifice; 16.
And whoever recites this hymn at the commencement of these [rites], that ritual action will certainly be accomplished without obstacles and with all its constituent parts complete. || 17 ||
Thus ends the hymn to Dakṣiṇā in the Prakṛtikhaṇḍa of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Nārada. Now follows the hymn to Balarāma:
Oṃ, salutations to you, Rāma, the wielder of the plow; salutations to you, whose weapon is the mace.
Salutations to you, beloved of Revatī; salutations to you, who are affectionate toward your devotees. || 1 ||
Salutations to you, O best among the strong; salutations to you, O upholder of the earth! Salutations be to you, O enemy of Pralamba; protect me, O elder brother of Kṛṣṇa!
Oṃ!
This supreme hymn is meritorious and brings about all accomplishments for human beings;
he who recites it with devotion and self-restraint becomes a vessel for all success.
Thus ends the Balarāma-stotra in the Utkala-khaṇḍa.
Now follows the Mahākālī-stotra:
Mahākālarudra said:
Oṃ! You are the embodiment of inconceivable, immeasurable, and infinite power; you are the singular form whose essence is the presiding principle within every individual being.
Transcending the qualities (*guṇas*) and free from dualities, you are accessible through pure consciousness alone; you are the one, existing in the form of the Supreme Brahman.
It is established. || 1 ||

Because it is not of the nature of a lineage (*agotra*), because it is non-erroneous (*anaikāntika*), because it is beyond the reach of defining characteristics (*alakṣyāgama*), and because it is the source of all without remainder;
because it is free from the exhaustion of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), because it is without beginning, because it is established as the singular form of the Supreme Brahman,
because it is unique, because it is without connection, because it has no separate substratum, and because it is without causal agency.
Because you consist of ignorance and because you are beginningless, you alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
When there is neither the Creator, nor Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor Time, nor the five elements, nor even destruction;
Then you alone, whose single form is the being that has become the cause, were established as the Supreme Brahman;
neither the followers of the Mīmāṃsā, nor those of Time and other systems of logic, nor the Sāṃkhyas, nor the Yogas, nor the Vedāntins existed.
The gods do not know your formless state; you alone are perfected as the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
You have no name or lineage; you have no birth or death; you have no station or activity; you have no pain or pleasure;
you have no friends or enemies; you have no bondage or liberation. You alone are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.
You are neither a child, nor are you one in the prime of youth, nor are you old; you are neither woman, nor eunuch, nor indeed are you a man.
You are neither a god, nor an asura, nor a human; you alone are perfected in the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Coolness in water, burning power in fire, purity in the moon, and the power to stop movement in the sun—
O Mother, whatever power belongs to anyone, it is yours alone; you are established as the one Supreme Brahman.
That fierce poison which Maheśa drank in ancient times, and by which he again withdraws the universe at the time of dissolution—
that occurred solely through your grace and not by his own power; for you alone exist in the form of the Supreme Brahman.
It is established. || 9 ||

Assuming faces of terrifying form and possessing a multitude of hands, weapons, and other attributes for the protection of the world and the slaying of the asuras, you alone are established as the Supreme Brahman in the form of Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī,
Guhyakālī, Karālī, Mahāḍāmarī, and the one with boisterous laughter.
You alone, O Caṇḍikā who illumines the world and protects it, are established as the form of the Supreme Brahman.

Crying out with auspicious sounds, carrying a skull-cup, conquering the enemies of the gods, speaking with a gracious mind, dancing, moving with grace, and laughing—you alone are perfected as the form of the Supreme Brahman. Though footless, you run faster than the wind; though devoid of ears, you hear sound.
You hear;
though without a nose you smell, and though without eyes you see, and though without a tongue you perceive the discernment of various tastes.
Just as a single orb of the sun situated in the sky appears through its reflection in as many bodies of water as there are.
She who shines forth in manifold forms is established as the one supreme Brahman in its true nature. || 14 ||
Just as a potter, having whirled the clay, fashions a shallow bowl and a jar within the center of the wheel,
so do you [fashion] all beings and humans within the great mechanical engines of delusion.
You create at the beginning of creation. || 15 ||
Just as for men, through a sudden optical illusion regarding colored cloth, lotuses, and the sun, there may arise the delusion that they are silver, a serpent, or water;
so too in this world which consists of those very things, you alone are everything when each of those [delusions] is sublated. 16.

O you of fierce form, because you cause your own gods to mount the lion-throne that has the appearance of great light, and remain standing by firmly pressing upon Śiva and Bhairava with your two feet, you are indeed the preeminent one in the center.

O Mother of the World, how can your unprecedented play— manifesting as the Yogamudrā in a base yogic posture and as the lion-faced [deity] upon the carcass of a jackal— be comprehended by those like us? O Goddess, you are pure, supreme consciousness, consisting of self-luminous nectar-bliss, and all-pervading throughout the universe.
And as for this form of yours, which is your own essential nature— should we meditate upon it within our hearts?
It is a great, loud laughter, dwelling within a mass of flames like the most terrible fire of time.
O Mother, you whose mass of matted hair is dark, who wear a great garland of skulls, and who are vast— such as you I meditate upon.
Performing penance, I do not weary my body; even when visiting sacred fords, I limp at every step;
and though reciting the Vedas, I merely pass my life—yet your two feet are the source of all auspiciousness.
I shall accomplish it. || 21 ||
For this person who has set aside the worship and rites of other gods, who has abandoned the sacrifice of dharma,
and whose mind is fixed solely on your service— what can these messengers of Dharmarāja do to him?
The messengers. || 22 ||
I do not consider Hari, nor the Creator, nor Īśa, nor Vahni, nor Arka, nor the Moon and other gods;
O Mother, let the injunction for your worship enter [my heart] through the many series of words uttered by Śiva.
In the case of "mati" [the rule applies]. || 23 ||
Let men indeed revile me; let kinsmen and relatives abandon me;
let the messengers of Yama cast me into hell—You alone are my refuge, You alone are my refuge.

Oṃ! That devotee who always recites this hymn proclaimed by Mahākālarudra with a spirit of devotion shall be free from sorrow, disease, and death; and in the end, there shall be spiritual perfection and the attainment of liberation.
This hymn to Śivā, called the "Stream of Nectar," has been told;
by its constant practice, spiritual perfection rests in the palm of one's hand. (26)
This hymn, this armor-verse, and these three verses— all of them—
should be recited with effort during occasional worship.

With the mass of her hair swaying upon her hips, she is that Kālī who possesses the splendor of a hand dark as a sword-blade; she is Caṇḍikā, whose festive and auspicious sounds of intoxication arise from the dance of her body’s intense radiance, which is like a cluster of gentle blue lotuses and dark rain clouds.
May Jayakālikā protect you— she who is dark, who causes fury, who is the abode of the madness of fear inspired by the terrible Time (Kāla),
whose eyes put to flight the hosts of Daityas led by Kṛtānta, whose body is most formidable and fearless,
who is the foremost of goddesses, and whose face is terrible with the sound "Hūṃ."
The bestower of fearlessness to her devotees, the giver of victory, she who occupies the Siddhāsana of the Lord of the Universe. || 29 ||
May Kālikā— terrible with her upturned face, both fearsome and beautiful, clad in a tiger skin around her waist, the ender of the Dānavas,
and sounding "Hūṃ Hūṃ Kaṃ Maḍī"— be ever gracious toward us who have sought refuge in her.
May it purify! || 30 ||
Thus ends the hymn to Kālī titled *Sudhādhārā*, composed by Mahākāla Rudra, within the *Śrī Mahākālasaṃhitā*.
Now follows the *Nāyikā-kavaca*:
Unmattabhairava said:
Listen, O auspicious one, to my words concerning this armor (kavaca), difficult even for the gods to obtain,
which bestows success in brief upon the leaders of the Yakṣiṇīs.
O Goddess of gods, one certainly attains perfection through mere knowledge;
Yakṣiṇī herself comes forth merely from the knowledge of this armor-mantra.
O Goddess, this which has been revealed in the Ḍāmaras is difficult to find anywhere;
by reciting and retaining it, a mortal may bring a Yakṣiṇī under his control.
Garga is declared to be the seer of the armor-mantra; the Gāyatrī is said to be its meter;
and the deity is the goddess Yakṣiṇī, the bestower of all accomplishments. || 4 ||
The application for the sake of attaining direct success and prosperity is proclaimed as follows:
"Oṃ! May Yakṣiṇī protect my head; may Yakṣakanyakā protect my forehead. (5)
May Śrīdhanadā protect my face; may Kulanāyikā protect my ears; may Varadā protect my eyes; and may Bhaktavatsalā protect my nose.
May Piṅgalā protect the tips of my hair; may Śrī Maheśvarī, the giver of wealth, protect [my head];
may Kulālapā protect my shoulders; and may Kamalānanā protect my throat.
May Kirātinī always protect my pair of arms; may Jaṭeśvarī always protect me;
and may Vikṛtāsyā, the beloved of Mahāvakra, always protect me. (8)
May Bheruṇḍā, the goddess with weapons in her hands, who is honored by the gods, protect the back and the region of the belly, as well as the heart. 9.
May Compassion, adorned with ornaments, protect my hips;
may the celestial maiden protect the private region of my virtuous self with her pair of sandals.
May she who is the very form of the Mother of Mantras always protect me in empty dwellings;
may she who is stainless and dwells in the waters always protect my entire body. 11.
May she who bestows wealth in the wilderness protect me, revealing her own seed-syllable;
may she whose essence is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī protect me, revealing her own seed-syllable. (12)
May she whose essence is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, who holds a sword in her hand, protect [me] in the cremation ground;
may the daughter of the great Yakṣa-lord protect me in an empty house or on a riverbank. 13.
May she known as Varadā protect me; may Mohinī protect all my limbs, especially in the midst of great peril, in battle, and amidst a multitude of enemies. 14.
May she who has the form of wrath, the constant attendant of Mahādeva, protect me;
may Bhavānī, the bestower of the lineage, protect me everywhere and at all times. 15.
Oṃ! O Goddess, this armor (kavaca) is the embodiment of a multitude of great mantras;
by its mere recollection, one attains kingship before long. 16.
He remains firm upon the earth for five thousand years;
he certainly becomes a knower of the Vedas and a master of all the scriptures. || 17 ||
In the forest, one attains perfection through the recitation of the Great Armor;
and the Yakṣiṇī, the family lore, arrives, bestowing excellent accomplishment.
One shall obtain the fruits of the supernatural powers of *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and *prāpti*, as well as the attainment of happiness,

by reciting and retaining [this mantra] in a solitary place, on a mountain peak in the forest; staying there, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times at night and obtain the desired success.
By the recitation of the Great Armor (Mahākavaca), that goddess becomes one's wife;

O Goddess, what else is difficult for yogins to obtain, such as spiritual accomplishments (sādhana) and the like? Success shall arise from its mere grasping; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 20 ||
Thus ends the Armor of the Yoginī Leader in the *Bṛhadbhūtasandhāna-Ḍāmara*, the Great Tantra.
Now follows the Hymn to the Leader:
I shall proclaim her hymn of praise; listen with careful attention.
By reciting this hymn to the Yoginī, one attains direct spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). || 1 ||
Unmattabhairava said:

Oṃ! I bow to you, O Yoginī, who bestows the wealth of the perfection of yoga; you who blaze like a bandhūka flower, whose body is adorned with various ornaments, the divine jewel, the daughter of the gods, the Beloved.
O Mother, destroy my poverty; grant me happiness and the attainment of my desired goals, such as sovereignty, friends, wife, sons, and wealth—please bring these to fulfillment for me.
O youthful goddess, I worship your two lotus feet on this earth, which dispel the terrible affliction of great fear;
have mercy upon my home and always be my sister along with your retinue of deities.
Joyfully endure the distress caused by the family. || 3 ||
You alone are the Yoginī, the maiden Piṅgalā, the youthful Rati, Gaurī, the Vidyādharī, and Śyāmā; be ever gracious. || 4 ||
You are Sandhyā, Khecarī, Vidyā, Yakṣiṇī, Bhūtinī, and Priyā;
