may you alone, the Protectress (Dhātrī), with a golden vessel in your lotus-hand, protect me.
Hiraṇyākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Capalā, Nāginī, Jayā, Prasannā, she who is called Śabdā, Kāminī, and the bestower of desires—be gracious! (6)
O Ḍākinī, become Khecarī, the bestower of success upon the Kula-mantras;
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess, served by the hosts of Yoginīs. (7)
O Beloved One, you whose beautiful garland possesses the luster of the moon; O Goddess, you who dwell upon two stainless lotuses and shatter the evil of poverty.
I worship you with my mind and my speech; be gracious, O beautiful one!
O Goddess, leader of hundreds of sky-faring beings, [protect us] from the effects of the Kali age. (9)
Grant me the attainment of wealth quickly; come to my home, you who bestow success upon the distressed and destroy untimely death. (10)
"O Goddess who bestows the fulfillment of speech, garlanded with excellent rubies, remain firm in my lineage for ten thousand years. (11)
With all your limbs adorned with ornaments, remain forever serene;
O Goddess whose essence is the seed-syllable of Māyā, you who are filled with the seed-syllable of Vadhū.
Always grant me the substance of accomplishment; be my beloved in my abode, your limbs adorned with various garments and arrayed in diverse ornaments. (13)
O Kāmeśī, whose face is a lotus blooming with smiles, resplendent with the luster of the moon and shining like the sun reflected in a ruby— command me, even that which is difficult to attain.
O Mistress of Desire, bestower of the enjoyment of the King of Supreme Bliss, grant me success and the boon; O Mother, be my beloved sister. 15.
O Goddess, I, your servant at your command, worship you with devotion;
remaining firmly established before me, grant me success at all times. 16.
O Kaulinī, you who dwell in the sky, become my companion;
protect me alone as your servant for a hundred thousand years. (17)
One should meditate upon Tripurā, who possesses lotus-like eyes, is endowed with fresh youth, is adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells, within the lotus of the heart. 18.
O Goddess, I bow to you alone—the blessed Yoginī who moves at will, who bestows boons and fearlessness, and who is the perfected knowledge of the worlds. (19)
"O lotus-eyed one, once you have attained perfection, become my beloved, always remaining by my side upon my body for ten thousand years. (20)
"O beloved, always be my wife; always grant me a body.
A wise man, endowed with the practice of meditation, should recite this hymn. (21)
One should offer cooked rice or coconut mixed with sugar;
by the power of this hymn and worship, the Bhūtinīs grant success.
Thus ends the hymn to the Nāyikās in the *Vadbhūtasandhānaḍāmara*, the great tantra, within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava.
Now follows the *Gurukavaca*:
Nārada said:
O Brahman, I have duly mastered the hymn of praise to Guru as taught by Manu;
now, please tell me about the armor (kavaca), for I have faith in hearing it.
Brahmā said:
Listen to me as I describe the secret armor (kavaca) of the venerable Guru;
it must never be given to one who is not a devotee, but should always be bestowed upon one who possesses devotion.
For this armor (kavaca) of the illustrious Guru, the Brahman-sage is proclaimed; the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is the Guru himself, whose essence is the three gods.
Oṃ! May the Guru, beautiful in all his limbs, always protect my head;
may his compassionate gaze protect my forehead and my two eyes.

May his gentle smile protect my face, and his sweet speech protect my ears; may his utterance of mantras protect my heart, and his hands, bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, protect my two arms.
May the lotus-throne of the Guru protect [me] from the navel down to the feet;
may the moonlight of the nails of the Guru’s feet protect every limb at all times.
May the seed-syllable of Speech protect me always, and may Khecarī protect the beginning and end of my desires;
may Ānandabhairava always protect the temple of bliss.
May Ānandabhairavī always protect my bliss;
may the mantra supreme to the Śrīprāsāda always protect me from violent beings. (8)
May the mantra of Parā-prāsāda protect [me] constantly from states of calamity;
may Haṃsa protect the seat above, and may it always protect [me] in all directions.
May the Gurus protect the family; may the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) protect below.
May the Divine Current (Divyaugha) protect knowledge, and those known as the Siddha Current (Siddhaugha) protect the will.
May the Human Current (Mānavaugha) protect ritual action, and may the Illustrious Guru protect [me] at all times.
Oṃ!
That man who daily recites this armor-mantra (kavaca) with devotion at the conclusion of his morning rites shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
For him, there shall be success in mantra, and the deity becomes propitious;
this is the truth, the truth, and again the truth—no doubt should be entertained here. (11)
If the recitation is performed without knowing the armor-mantra (kavaca) containing the names of the Guru, his exertion will be in vain;
there will be no success in the mantra worship.
Placing the feet of the Guru before one, the auspicious armor-mantra (kavaca) is recited;
then, the accomplishment of the mantra and the yantra occurs, and not otherwise. (13)
And that which is to be kept secret from the Guru must never be spoken. || 14 ||
It must never be given to just anyone, nor should it ever be disclosed;
it should be given specifically to one endowed with devotion and, above all, to one of noble birth.

This armor of the Guru, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, yields the merit of all sacred pilgrimage sites for whoever recites it;
thus it has been told to you, my son—listen with careful attention. (16)
Thus ends the Śrīmad-gurukavaca in the Brahmayāmala. Now, the visualization of the female Guru (yoṣid-guru-dhyāna),
as follows:
Oṃ. One should meditate upon the Guru as Śivā—her eyes like the petals of a full-blown lotus, her breasts firm and plump, her face serene, and her waist slender. 1.
She has a luster like a ruby, is beautifully adorned with red garments, has hands with red bracelets, and is graced by jeweled anklets. || 2 ||
Her form was brilliantly adorned by lotus-feet resembling land-lotuses,
and her body was illuminated by a face resembling a white water-lily.
Having thus meditated upon her who stands on the left side of her own Lord, with her lotus-hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, one should worship her. || 4 ||

Now, the Armor of the Female Guru (*strīguru-kavaca*): For this Armor of the Female Guru, the deity is the Female Guru; the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of the four aims of human life.
On the head: salutation to Sadāśiva, the seer (*ṛṣi*).
In the heart: *Namaḥ* to the woman, the guru, and the deity.
The Lord said: Sadāśiva is traditionally remembered as the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this armor (*kavaca*) of the woman-guru.
The deity named after that [mantra] is said to bestow the fruits of the four aims of human life. || 1 ||
Oṃ Klīṃ: may the seed-syllable protect my head, and its name protect my forehead.
May the seed-syllable Klīṃ protect my two eyes, and may Sadāśiva protect all my limbs. || 2 ||
May the seed-syllable Aiṃ protect my mouth; may Hrīṃ thoroughly guard my tongue;
may the seed-syllable Śrīṃ protect the region of my shoulders; and may Hasakhaphreṃ protect my two arms. (3)
May the letter *ha* protect the region of my throat, may the letter *sa* protect the sixteenth petal, may the syllable *kṣa* protect what is below that, and may the letter *la* protect my heart. (4)
The letter *va* is the region of the back, the letter *ra* is the right side, the syllable *hūṃ* is the left side, and the letter *sa* is Mount Meru itself. (5)
May the syllable *ha* protect my right arm, and the syllable *kṣa* my left hand;
may the syllable *ma* protect my fingers, and the syllable *la* protect my nails.
May the syllable *va* protect my hips, the syllable *ra* my belly, the syllable *yīṃ* my pair of feet, and may *hsauḥ* protect all my limbs. (7)
May *hsauḥ* protect my genitals, body hair, and hair;
may the seed-syllable *aiṃ* protect me in the east, and may the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* protect me in the south.
May the seed-syllable Śrīṃ protect [me] in the west; may that which originates from the Bhūtas protect me in the north.
May Aiṃ protect me in the southeast, and may Vedādya protect me in the southwest.
May the Mother Goddess protect [me] in the northwest, and likewise may Śambhu’s auspicious sandals protect me;
I worship them above, and may they always protect me from below with their salutation.
Oṃ!
Thus, O beloved, this most wonderful armor has been recounted to you.
If one recites the armor after having chanted the guru-mantra, [the result is attained].
He is a perfected one (siddha), he is a member of the retinue (gaṇa), and he is Śiva himself in person; of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
O Goddess of the Suras, he who recites this armor (kavaca), which is the embodiment of mantra, at the time of worship shall obtain the fruit of that worship; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
O Goddess, he who recites it at the three junctions of the day becomes a perfected one (siddha); of this there is no doubt.
If one writes [this mantra] on birch bark, places it inside a pill, and wears it within gold, debaters will lose their luster at the mere sight of him. (13)
In dispute he attains victory, and in battle like that of Nairṛta;
in the assembly he attains victory—he is my equal, without a doubt. (14)
If one who meditates upon the thousand-spoked [wheel] recites this at the three junctions of the day, he alone becomes a Lord of the World of Siddhas and attains the state of Nirvāṇa. || 15 ||
This most wonderful armor named Samastamaṅgala must never be given to just anyone, nor should it ever be disclosed.
It should be given to a disciple who is peaceful; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should not show it even to one's own sons if they are not devoted.
He who recites this mantra without knowing this armor (kavaca) and the vidyā itself does not obtain its fruit; moreover, he shall go to hell. || 18 ||
Thus ends the Śrīmat-Strī-guru-kavaca, from the *Brahmayāmala*, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Īśvara.
Now follows the Guru-stotra:

O beautiful mother, though one knows the Supreme Self whose nature is knowledge—[who is] charity, meditation, yoga, and wisdom—there is nothing greater than that Guru; indeed, there is nothing greater than the Guru. || 1 ||

I consider life, body, home, kingdom, enjoyment, liberation, power, son, friend, wealth, and wife to be nothing more than the Guru; nothing is greater than the Guru, nothing is greater than the Guru. (2)
The dharma of the forest-dweller, the various duties of the ascetic, the state of the paramahaṃsa, and the conduct of the mendicant;
service to the virtuous, devotion to many gods—there is nothing superior to the guru, nothing superior to the guru. (3)

Devotion to Viṣṇu, the practice of worship, service to Vaiṣṇavas, and devotion toward one’s mother; the manner of serving one’s father is like that toward Viṣṇu—there is nothing superior to the guru, there is nothing superior to the guru. (4)
Withdrawal of the senses and mastery over the faculties, breath control and the ritual of placement;
worship through sacrifice, recitation, austerity, and devotion—there is nothing superior to the Guru, nothing superior to the Guru. (5)

Kālī, Durgā, Kamalā, Bhuvanā, Tripurā, Bhīmā, Bagalā, Pūrṇā, Śrīmātaṅgī, Dhūmā, and Tārā— these are the Vidyās that are the essence of the three worlds; there is nothing superior to the Guru, nothing superior to the Guru.

The Fish incarnation, the Tortoise, the glorious Boar, the form of Narasimha, the deeds of Vamana, and all other incarnations and so forth—none of these are superior to the Guru, none are superior to the Guru. (7)

I consider the ten incarnations—Śrī Raghunātha, Śrī Yadunātha, Śrī Bhṛgudeva, Buddha, and Kalki—to be none other than my Guru; indeed, there is nothing superior to the Guru, truly, there is nothing superior to the Guru. (8)
The Gaṅgā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Dvārā, Māyā, Ayodhyā, Avantī, Mathurā, Yamunā, and Revā—there is no holy place superior to these, none greater than the Guru, none greater than the Guru. (9)

The journey to Gokula, the sporting with the cowherd girls, and the wandering through the honey-filled city of Śrī Vṛndāvana—all this, O beautiful Mother, is nothing more than the Guru; it is nothing more than the Guru. 10.

Service to Tulasī, devotion to Hari and Hara, and liberation at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—what else is greater than this? O Mother Kṛṣṇa, O beautiful one, all of this is nothing more than devotion;
there is nothing greater than the Guru, nothing greater than the Guru. (11)
He who recites this hymn daily is a knower of liberation and is exceedingly blessed;
for whatever is to be known within the entire universe is not greater than the Guru. (12)
Thus ends the Śrīgurustotra within the Bṛhatpāramahaṃsya Saṃhitā, in the dialogue between Śrī Śiva and Pārvatī.
Now begins the Śrīhanūmatstotra:
The Lord said: He is one whose preeminent and incomparable fortitude is most intensely manifested, and who is celebrated as the sole hero in accomplishing the work of Śrī Rāma.
Having leaped across the shore of the ocean by his speed, may that glorious Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, be victorious! || 1 ||

Victorious is that illustrious son of the Wind-god, who at the very moment of birth, beholding the orb of the sun, grasped it suddenly with both hands without hesitation as to its consequences, and then released it.
Hanumān || 2 ||
Ever manifesting upon his body the power of his companions within the multitude of Vraja, that mighty and glorious one—
who set Lanka ablaze in the very presence of the assembly of the Ten-faced one— triumphs.
Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god. || 3 ||
Victorious is that illustrious son of the Wind-god, who, when the great younger brother of Rāma was struck by the ten-headed Rāvaṇa at the front of the battle with his power,
quickly brought medicinal herbs and restored him to life.
Hanumān || 4 ||
Having presented the crest-jewel that had come from the daughter of King Janaka and was marked with the name of the Joy of the Raghus,
the heroic and illustrious son of Vāyu brought Rāma forward and introduced him, saying, "Victory to him!"
Hanumān || 5 ||
Slaying the guardians of the Ashoka grove, breaking hundreds of thousands of great-armed beasts,
and indeed eating various fruits— seeing him thus, this glorious one triumphs as he gazes upon Sita.
Hanumān, the son of Vāyu. || 6 ||
Victorious is that illustrious son of the Wind, who, merely by being thought of in the heart while one is imprisoned in a jail, grants immediate liberation from it;
he is the remover of fear from flesh-eaters, yakṣas, wind-gods, and other such beings.
Hanumān. || 7 ||
Salutations to you, the bestower of all auspiciousness; salutations be to you, who are born from wind and fire;
salutations to you, the supreme benefactor of the worlds, who removes the suffering and pain of all beings.
Homage, homage to you! || 8 ||
This hymn of praise to Hanumān destroys great sins, grants victory in battle, is meritorious, and is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (9)
Whoever recites this upon rising in the morning, whether while bathing or lying down,
poison shall not afflict him, nor shall any harmful beings injure him.
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking a son obtains a son; and a woman becomes dear to her husband. 11.
The sick shall be liberated from disease; the bound shall be released from bondage;
the weak shall attain strength, and one shall become like the son of Āyu. 12.
Upon seeing him, all obstacles flee; of this there is no doubt.
In battle and in legal disputes, victory comes to him.
He attains liberation from bondage, and in his travels, he surely achieves success. (13)
Thus ends the Hanumat-stotra in the Hanumat-kalpa of the Śrī-Garuḍa-tantra. Now begins the Mātaṅgī-stava.
Īśvara said:
Oṃ! By worshipping your lotus feet, O Mother, Brahmā and the other gods attained world-renowned fame;
other lords of sages attained supreme power, and others, through the weight of their devotion, attained supreme glory. (1)
I bow to the Goddess Mātaṅginī, who wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament;
she who, with words that never fade, respectfully awakens her beloved by explaining the meaning [of his state].
Your lotus-feet shine, adorned by the jewels in the crowns of the prostrate gods and asuras.
O Goddess, those who serve the lords of the earth attain prosperity with diligence. || 3 ||
O Mother, as you walk with the Mātaṅginīs, I take refuge in these tinkling anklets of yours;
I worship your lotus feet, which are the pure speech of those who are unartificial.
I condemn that virtuous-hearted Mātaṅginī, who makes her path purposeful with her feet by means of her tinkling anklets, and who strikes her sweet lute.

I bow to the consort of Śambhu, whose rounded hips are bound with playful silks, who wears an ornament of palm-leaf upon her ear, whose lotus-eyes are perpetually rolling from the intoxication of honeyed wine, and who possesses full, firm breasts.

O Mother, Sovereign of the worlds, with devotion I remember your waist, which is embraced by the streaks of lightning, whose ornaments are imperceptible, which after a long time becomes visible through the line of fresh hair, and which is marked by the three folds.

I meditate in my heart upon the daughter of the mountain, who bears the splendor of blue lotuses with her beauty and the side-glances of the lotus-pools, and whose mass of hair is adorned with garlands of kadamba flowers.

O Great Goddess, I would meditate upon your face—with its bimba-fruit lips adorned with a beautiful tilaka, its long eyes, its gently smiling expression, its dark, curling locks, and its cheeks like rosy lotuses. (9)
Those people who, endowed with devotion, praise Mātaṅginī— the consort of Śaṅkara and the presiding deity of speech— with this hymn, always attain supreme prosperity.
Oṃ.
Thus ends the Śrīmātaṅgīstotra from the Rudrayāmala.
Now follows the Dhūmāvatīstotra:
Īśvara said:
Oṃ! In the morning she is a maiden, chanting her rosary with a flower bud;
at midday she is full-grown, with a blossoming face and beautiful eyes; and at night, she is as she is.

At twilight, may that Goddess Caṇḍikā—the mother of the three worlds and the God of gods—protect you; she appears in the form of an old woman with sagging breasts, wearing a garland of skulls. || 1 ||

Having bound the mass of Kapila’s finest matted locks to the tip of his skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), having made a garland for his chest from the heads of the foremost Daityas and a crest for his head from the feathers of Garuḍa,
and having taken in his hand the great horn of Yama’s buffalo, filled with the blood of the gods;
May Bhairava protect you both, being praised by Kālarātri, who rejoices at the dissolution of the universe. || 2 ||
Chewing upon a mass of knotted fragments with a fierce and continuous *kaṭakaṭa* sound,
the slender-limbed one laughs a terrible *kakaha-kakaha-kaha* among the spirits;
ever intoxicated by dancing, she causes her lotus-face to emit the resonant *ḍima-ḍima* of the hand-drum.
May this Caṇḍikā protect us, wandering about while uttering the sounds "jhajha-ma-jhama-jhama-jham. || 3 ||
With the sounds *ṭaṇṭaṭ-ṭaṇṭaṭ-ṭaṭaṇṭā* and the manifest *maṭamaṭā* of her ringing bell,

uttering the sounds *spheṃ spheṃ spheṃ*, laughing with a *ṭakaṭakiṭa* laugh, terrifying with the clashing of her teeth, wearing a swaying garland of severed heads, and devouring with a *lalaha-lahala-haha* sound and a restless, fierce roar— she moves.
May she, chewing upon Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa who have been repeatedly crushed and masticated, purify [us]. || 4 ||
In his left ear the moon eclipsed by the dissolution, in his right the solar disc;
around his neck a necklace of stars, and on his formidable mass of human matted hair a garland of skulls;
upon his shoulder he bears the burden of Brahma’s skeleton, accompanied by the hand holding the banner of the lord of serpents.
May Bhadrakālī, the bestower of auspiciousness, who sustains all during the dissolution, take away my fear. || 5 ||
With a single braid anointed with oil, her ears adorned with shining earrings made of tin, and having fashioned the beauty of her lotus-feet from a single piece of iron—
she who is naked and mounted upon a donkey devours this entire world.
With ears adorned by the *javā* flower, with arms raised and outstretched like a banner, O Goddess, you alone are she who wields the sword.
Having fashioned a garland for your head from the blood-stained heads of warriors severed by weapons in battle, you entered the cremation ground with your arms outstretched like a banner.
Having seen her at night, accompanied by numerous spirits, with broad hips and heavy breasts,
wearing a girdle of great lordly serpents, her hands grasping the tips of tridents, intoxicated by sweet blood,
and her eyes copper-red— || 7 ||
O Goddess, when this world enters your mouth, fierce with fangs, in half a moment at the end of saṃsāra— smoky-grey and overflowing with human blood and fat—
you are Kālī, the Kāpālikī, the Yoginī devoted to reclining upon corpses, sealed in yoga, red-hued, and possessed of supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
O Virgin, you are the remover of the fear of death; you are Śivā, the fierce-bell.
Oṃ! This meritorious *Dhūmāvatyaṣṭaka*, which wards off all calamities—
whatever practitioner recites it with devotion finds his desired accomplishment even in the face of great adversity.
In times of great terror, great disease, and great battle; in the expulsion of enemies, in killing and the like, as well as in the deluding of living beings. || 10 ||
O Goddess, by reciting this hymn one shall attain success everywhere;
[one will overcome] gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas. || 11 ||
By the mere recollection of this hymn, all beings such as lions and tigers flee to a distance even further than far; how much more so, then, humans and the like? (12)
O Goddess of gods, what on this earth cannot be accomplished by means of this hymn?
O Goddess, all peace shall prevail, and in the end, one shall attain nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the *Dhūmāvatyaṣṭaka*, the essence of hymns, from the *Dhūmāvatīkalpa* within the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*.
[Now follows] the installation of the jar (*ghaṭasthāpana*).
As stated in the *Āgama-tattva-vilāsa*,

following the word "pot" (*ghaṭam*) in the section on the Śākta initiation (*śāktābhiṣeka-prakaraṇa*) in the *Rājeśvarī-tantra*: "Neither too short nor too long, it should be made of clay, copper, or gold."
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāmabīja), one should strike it with the Vāgbhava syllable;
having placed the jar upon the Śakti, one should fill it with water using the Māyā syllable.
With this mantra, the preceptor should then invoke the sacred waters (tīrthas) therein.
All rivers such as the Gaṅgā, all oceans, and all lakes;
all seas, streams, lakes, clouds, and rivers;
and sacred pools and springs located in heaven, the netherworld, and on earth.
May all the meritorious holy fords (tīrthas) be present within the jar.
One should offer the sprouts while reciting the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrī-bīja).
The offering of fruit should be performed with the Kūrca-mantra, and stabilization with the seed-syllable of the Woman (Strī-bīja).
One should offer vermilion with the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ), and flowers with the Śavānu mantra;
one should offer Dūrvā grass with the Mūla-mantra, and then perform sprinkling with the Praṇavas.
Then, one should perform the striking with Darbha grass using the mantra "Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā."

Having meditated upon the seat of the Goddess (devīpīṭha), one should invoke her there and worship her with the seed-syllable *sauḥ* along with the power (*śakti*). In this context, "with *śavānu*" means "with *śarānu*."
This is the reading maintained by the *Āgama-tattva*;
its meaning is "with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) called Śarānu. || 1 ||
The consecration of the armor (*kavaca-saṃskāra*):
In another Tantra cited in the *Dīpikā*: "O Goddess, having written the armor-mantra, one should wrap it with a red thread."
Then, O Goddess, having wrapped it, one should place it in gold or another such vessel;
then, on an auspicious day, having bathed it with the five earths and the five products of the cow,
one should worship the pill, which has the form of the deity and grants all desires.
One should enjoin the vital breaths there with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra;
then, having meditated upon the inner womb (*antaryoni*), the wise one should establish [the deity] therein.
O Goddess, this pill, when worn around the neck, bestows happiness. (1)
Now, the examination of the mantras' ears and other faculties; as stated in the *Yakṣaḍāmara*:
"For the benefit of mortals, [this] is difficult to obtain in the three worlds."
The Blessed One further explained the investigation of the ear and the other [senses]. || 1 ||
Taking his seat in the heart, firm-minded and composed,
the practitioner should gaze at the tip of his own nose without looking toward the directions,
having subdued the mind along with the senses and other faculties through his entire being.
The ear perceives sound through dissolution [into its source]; otherwise, it could not hear speech.
In the Saura, Gāṇapatya, Daurga, Śaiva,
and likewise in the Bhautika [tantras], this heart and eye [mantra] shines forth within the mind. This investigation regarding the root-syllable is called the seed of all roots.
Mental reflection must be performed when the seed-syllable contains poison;
for Rudrahaṃsī, who has become the seed-syllable, is [composed of] Ḍiṇḍima and Vidruma.
Here, one should perform the visualization of the face and other features according to the sequence of the city with the moon.
One should perform the investigation of the seeds beginning with Yamasthāgin, Śuka, Daṇḍin, Maṇibhadra, Ghaṭotkaca, Bhṛṅgin, and so forth, as previously described.
Wherever Yakṣeśvara occurs in the mantra, there his mouth is primarily located.
In the absence of Caṇḍikā here, [the mantra consists of] vidyut, netra, hṛt, and āsava. || 4 ||
Jyotiḥkapardin, Khadyota, Grāsinī, and Surāntaka;
Vaivasvata, the one named Ketu, Śikhin, and Prāṇaprahāriṇī;
in whom [are] Ulkāmukhī, Jālandharī, Caṇḍa, and Yugāntaka?
Kiṅkarī, Piśitākṣī, Sukinnara, Manoharī,
Dhvāṅkṣyā, Vaitānikī, Phetkāriṇī, Śūla, and Payodharā—
these are the twenty-four seed-syllables that should be in the mantra of the Yakṣa-Ḍāmara.
By means of these, the heart, eyes, and mouth of all mantras are to be fully understood; they are the seed-syllables (anava) of this [deity], kept secret in all tantras. (5)
Likewise, the root-syllable is designated as the "mouth," and that which is called the vowels is the "heart.
The meaning is that the root-syllable is the *praṇava* (Om), which is the mouth of the mantra;
and the "heart" refers to the powers of the vowels, which are the sixteen syllabic powers (*śakti*) of the mantra.
The meaning is "the heart. And thus, that which is called the root-syllable and the mouth is the heart; its own powers—the powers of the vowels—are to be spoken.
Now, regarding the absence of the *praṇava*, he states the specific nature of its seed-syllables (*bīja*) in that very same [text]:
"At the beginning, middle, and end; in the absence of the former, likewise the latter;
it is called Kīrti, accomplished by Kālavaktra, that is, Mahākāla."

That seed-syllable of Viṣṇu’s beloved is beginningless, consisting of five rays, the imperishable cause of creation and maintenance, and the poison [of the serpent]. It is the secret one, joined with Śūlinī, being Caṇḍīśa marked by fire, the moon, and the bindu; it is honored by the world and dear to the world.

Regarding the phrase "at the beginning, middle, and end": if the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) is present at the beginning, the middle, or the end of the mantra, then that alone constitutes its "face" (*mukha*).
According to the rule "in the absence of the preceding, [use] the succeeding," if the *praṇava* is absent, the subsequent procedure is as follows.
The phrase "by Kīrti, known as the mouth of Time" refers to the letters *a* and *u*; "by Mahākāla" refers to the letter *m*.
That which is accomplished by these is the beginningless five-rayed [syllable], which is indeed the *praṇava*.
This is the seed-syllable dear to Viṣṇu, known as the *śrībīja*; such is the syntactical connection across two and a half verses.

And likewise, in whichever mantra the *śrībīja* and so forth are present, that very [seed-syllable] is the "mouth," because it is of the nature of the *praṇava*; therefore, he states the seed-syllables that constitute the "mouth" of the mantra in their proper order, and therein the *śrībīja* is mentioned.
That supreme [mantra] is as follows: "Blood" (kṣataja), "sky-face" (vyomavaktra), adorned with Caṇḍa, Ugra, Indu, and so forth;
"moist" (ārdra), "fierce" (raudra), and "elemental" (bhūta)—this is remembered as the primary seed-syllable.
*Kṣataja* (blood) is the letter *ra*; *vyomavaktra* (sky-face) is the letter *ha*; *caṇḍogrā* (fierce and terrible) is the letter *i*.
"Adorned with the moon and so forth" means adorned with the moon (*bindu*) and the *nāda*, which is the *māyābīja* (*hrīṃ*).

*Krodhīśa* (the Lord of Wrath) is the letter *ka*; "red-going" is the letter *ra*; it is further adorned by *dhūmra-bhairavī* (the smoke-colored Bhairavī), which is the letter *ī*, and the moon and so forth.
The seed-syllable of Pitṛbhūvāsinī consists of the letter *ka* (the first part of Kāleya), followed by *pa* (the food), and *la*.
Krodhīśa is the letter *ka*; Raktaga is the letter *ra*, and Dhūmrabhairavī is the letter *i*. Through the union of the *bindu* and *nāda*, this forms the seed-syllable of Kālī.

[One should worship] Ugrabhairavī, who is joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, together with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable pertaining to the elements, which increases supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and intelligence (*buddhi*).
"Ugrabhairavī" refers to the vowel *ai*; thus, the meaning is that [the mantra consists of] the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable.
*Phaṭ* is the well-known *astra* (weapon-mantra), while *kāli*, *agni*, *vyāpaka*, and *aṅkuśa* [are other components].
*Śiras* is *svāhā*; the two *ṭha*s are the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*), the beloved of the blazing one.
Brahmā seated upon the throne of Indra—that is the Trimūrti—and that is Manmatha.
The sky (ha) is its face, enriched by the mouth of time (ra), and joined with the dot and the bindu of armor (va);
by this [is formed] the Kāma-bīja and the Kūrca-bīja.
The Void (śa) is mounted upon blood (ra) and adorned by Caṇḍabhairavī (i).
The mantra of light, adorned with the *vindu* (bindu) at its head, has been proclaimed.
*Śūnya* is the letter *ha*; *kṣataja* is the letter *ra*; and *Caṇḍabhairavī* is the vowel *ai*.
This unsurpassed treasury of mantras was taught by the Primordial God.
That which is most secret among these has been proclaimed by me here:
the analysis of the treasury of mantras for the Yakṣa-Ḍāmara,
as it was spoken by the Lord of Wrath (Krodhādhipa) to the great-souled Bhairava.
Thus, for this very reason, wherever a particular mantra exists among the Praṇava, Śrībīja, Māyā, Kālī, Vāgbhava, Astra, Vahnijāyā, Kāma, Kūrca, and Jyotirmantras, therein that [mantra] resides.
The state of being the *āsya* (mouth) has been explained.
Wherever two or three of these seeds reside,
there, by means of the aforementioned mantra, the extraction of that preceding seed is performed.
Now follows the determination of the eyes (*netra*):
it is stated in that very same [text]:
"In the seed-syllable, all are red-faced; the root-syllables are the heart, and the vowels [are the eyes]."
If the right and left eyes are not deficient in Caṇḍī, and the middle one is absent;
if there is an absence of seed-syllables (bīja), the mind is like lightning, and its eye is Manoharī;
the root syllable is the heart, Daṇḍin is the vital breath, and the vowels are the powers (śakti).

"In the seed-syllable, those with red faces" means that all the root-syllables, beginning with the Śrī-bīja and others, become "red-faced" when the seed-syllable is present; that is, when the mantra itself is present.
"In Caṇḍīvikala, if not in the middle of the visarga and bindu" means that [the red faces] are not located in the middle of the mantra.
If that is so, it means his right and left eyes.

"In the absence of the seed-syllables" (bījābhāve) means in the absence of the seed-syllables consisting of the faces and eyes. "The eye of the lightning of Manu" (manor vidyunnetram) refers to the eye of the mantra.
"Lightning" refers to the vowel *a*;

"the mouth is charming" refers to the fire-born consort (the letter *i*); by the statement "it is the root-syllable," the heart is the "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), which is the *anusvāra*; and "the vital breath is also the power of the vowels" refers to both the staff-bearer and the powers of the vowels.
"The state of being the heart and the vital breath"—this is the secret teaching.
Here, there should be no deliberation regarding Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha.
And so it is said: "Those known as Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha are [located] in the ears, the mouth, and the eyes, excluding the [other] sense organs."
Wherever the seed-syllable mantra is found, there indeed it is in its entirety;
wherever a form is seen preceded by the primary [syllable] and ending with the supreme [syllable], yet appearing incomplete,
one should recognize that as the Eye (netra), its face smeared with blood.

In this context, "seed-syllable" refers to a mantra consisting solely of the venerable seed-syllable (*śrībīja*) and so forth. Wherever there is a primary [mantra] preceded and followed by [the seed-syllable], and where Caṇḍī is seen to be both preceding and following [it] herself, one should know that very place to be the "eye. Furthermore, the "mouth" is the letter *ra* (repha), which is smeared with blood.
This is the meaning.
Regarding the mantra *manu* when deprived of the letter *ra*, he states in that very same place: "In the *manu* devoid of the color red, the root-syllable is proclaimed to be the mouth."
The "lightning-eye" (vidyunnetra) is specified when [the goddess] Caṇḍīvikalā is excluded;
furthermore,
Garjinī and Dhūmrabhairavī are remembered as the two eyes in the state of Abhāva.
*Garjinī* is the third vowel (*i*), and *Dhūmabhairavī* is the fourth vowel (*ī*).
Even these two, in the absence of the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the visarga, signify "the two eyes.
Wherever Yakṣeśvara is in the mantra, there alone is his face, primarily.
In the absence of Caṇḍikā here, [the mantra is] vidyut-netra-hṛd-āsavaḥ.
Regarding that very point, Sugrīva says: "The two [syllables] are the ear, hṛṃ is the void, and the eyes are vikalā."
In the absence of Vikalā, there would be Gaurī and Pārvatī.

Yakṣeśvara is the letter *ha*; Caṇḍikā is the visarga; Vidyut is the letter *a*; Sugrīva is the letter *ra*; Śūnya is the letter *ha*; Vikalā is the two dots (*bindu*); Gaurī is the third vowel (*i*); and Pārvatī is [the letter *u*].
The fourth vowel:
the meaning is that in the absence of all [other vowels], the letter *a* alone is to be understood as having those respective forms.
And thus:
"Vidyut alone is said to be the heart, the eye, and the breath when [the body] is devoid of the heart, mouth, and breath.
By this, it is established that the heart, the eye, and the breath are Vidyut alone, according to the statement: "The breaths are also the powers of sound (svara-śaktayaḥ).
Thus ends the knowledge of the ear and the other senses. || 7 ||
He states the permanence of this knowledge in that very same place: "Without which knowledge, one is not capable of the application of recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*).
Likewise:
Through knowledge of the mantra’s hearing, mouth, heart, and eyes, liberation comes to Manu immediately;
all kinds of supernatural powers (siddhis) shall arise, for he is Śiva himself, as is the practitioner.
Even in the absence of knowledge through the ears and other senses, [liberation occurs] from the mere grasping of the mantra.
Poverty, misfortune, falling into hell, loss of fame, being wretched,
extremely miserable, defeated, oppressed by enemies, and grieving—
one who possesses such a mind should indeed practice that mantra which brings knowledge of the divine ear and other faculties.
Such [passages] are to be understood.
Now, regarding the powers of the vowels (*svara-śaktayaḥ*): in that same [work]:
In the letter *a* is Bhīṣaṇā, renowned as Vidyujjihvā; *a*.
In the letter *ā* is Tāmasī, the fierce Kālarātri, the Bhairavī of Time;
*ā*. In the letter *i* is Garjinī, to be known as Caṇḍā, who causes fear even to Rudra; *i*.
In the letter *ī* is known Śūlinī, Caṇḍogrā, and Dhūmrabhairavī; *ī*.
In the letter *u* is she called Kālavaktrā, Pracaṇḍā, and Caṇḍavallabhā; *u*. In the letter *ū* is to be known Vidārī, Tālajaṅghā, and Kapālinī; *ū*.
In the letter *ṛ* there is Mahāradrī and also the Yoginī Jvālinī; *ṛ*.
In the letter *ṝ* is the goddess Kālikā, Pitṛkālī, the Terrifying One; *ṝ*.
In the letter *ḷ* there is Saṃhāriṇī, Meghanādā, and Grahāsinī; *ḷ*.
Rudracaṇḍā and Kālajihvā reside in the syllable *ḷ*; Karālinī is in *ḹ*.
(*ḹ*) Urdhvakeśī and Cāmuṇḍā are known to abide in the sound (*nādinī*) of the syllable *e*.
(*e*) Koṭarākṣī, Māninī, and Uttamabhairavī reside in the syllable *ai*. (*ai*)
Jvālāsyā, who goes to the syllable *o*, should be known as Bhīmākṣī, wearing a garland of severed heads; *o*.
In the syllable *au* is Ḍākinī, Siṃhanādinī, and Caṇḍabhairavī;
*au*. In the syllable *aṃ* is Rudraḍākinī, called Akrūra and Vikārī; *aṃ*.
The remainder consists of Kapālinī in the south and Caṇḍikā as the two earrings;
the visarga, the *ā* (long vowel), the anusvāra, the kalās, and the powers of the vowels—namely *aḥ*.
Whichever of these are joined to whichever part of this mantra, those very ones constitute its heart.
"They are to be cultivated" is the secret meaning.
Thus, having understood the mantra's ear and other [senses] in this sequence, one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraskriyā*).
And so it is said:
Having received the mantra from the presence of the Guru, one who is devoted to the Guru should diligently discern the heart,
eyes, and life-force of the mantra-hearer; and having understood the mantra and its *kīlaka*, one should perform the preliminary rites for the mantra.
Having completed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), one should practice for heroic accomplishment (vīrasiddhi).
Thus is the thorough knowledge of the ears and other [senses] regarding the mantra.
Now, the convention concerning the limbs of the mantra,
as stated in the Jñānatantre:
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, frequented by hosts of Gandharvas,
the daughter of the mountain, seated upon the chest of Sthāṇu, questioned the God.
Pārvatī said:
O Gaṇeśa, Nandi, Candreśa, Bhūtanātha, and Madīśvara! [I shall explain] the illumination of the many Tantras and Mantras, as well as their internal sections,
their divisions, their *kīlakas*, and the removal of curses.
"O Lord, by your grace I have understood this without doubt;
O Lord of Gods, it is recorded in various tantras that the Vidyā consists of letters.
Now I desire to hear the determination of the names of the limbs of the mantra."
The symbolic convention of mantras has been indicated by me in many ways; however,
O Mahādeva, if you have affection for me, then speak of it in this secluded place— there is no need for hesitation here.
"If I do not speak the truth today, placing it before you, I shall give up my life; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
The Lord said:
"Excellent, O blessed lady, you have asked that which was in my mind. O Goddess, because of a woman's fickleness, I did not previously speak of it to you, my dear;
but now, knowing your steadfastness, I shall tell it to you, O sinless one."
O Great Goddess Pārvatī, this must never be revealed;
O Great Goddess, if the Great Reality (mahātattva) is disclosed, your supernatural powers (siddhis) will perish.
It has been stated again, O Great Goddess: it is certain that this must not be spoken.

O compassionate one, by means of mere realization— without recitation, fire-offerings, or worship— the perfection of the mantra is produced. He who recites the king of mantras without knowing the secret convention (*saṃketa*) of the mantra [attains nothing].
The accomplishment of the mantra does not arise merely by reciting it one million times;
therefore, with every effort, the visualization of the limbs [of the deity] must be understood.
O virtuous lady, out of great respect for you and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, [I shall explain it].

I shall speak, O Goddess of gods; listen to this great essence of essences. One should contemplate the complete form of the body within the single-syllable Great Mantra, O Maheśānī, and think of nothing else.
One should contemplate [the body] in sequence: first ending at the base of the arms, second ending at the waist, and third ending at the base of the feet.
Among the four-syllable mantras, the first [syllable] corresponds to the end of the cheek.
The second [should extend] to the end of the arms, and the third should reach to the navel; O Goddess, one should then contemplate the fourth as reaching to the ends of the feet. || 1 ||
In the case of the five-syllable mantra, one should visualize it in five parts:
O Goddess, the first extends to the neck, the second should extend to the ends of the arms,
the third extends to the region of the belly, and the fourth extends to the thighs.

O Goddess, the fifth [syllable] reaches the end of the feet; of this there is no doubt. In the six-syllable mantra, the first [syllable] reaches the end of the mouth, the second reaches the end of the throat, and the third reaches the end of the arms.
One should contemplate the fourth [syllable] ending at the heart, the fifth ending at the thighs,
and the sixth syllable as the feet, in due order;
in the seven-syllable mantra, the first [syllable] ends at the mouth.
The second reaches the throat; the third, the ends of the arms;
the fourth, the back; the fifth, the belly;
the sixth, the thighs; and the seventh reaches the feet.
In the great eight-syllable mantra, the first [syllable] extends to the mouth; the second extends to the chin; the third extends to the throat;
the fourth extends to the end of the arms; and the fifth extends to the back.
The sixth [syllable] is within the belly, and that which is being born becomes the seventh;
the eighth is at the end of the feet—of this there is no doubt even regarding the limbs of the manifestation. In a nine-syllabled mantra, however, the first is at the end of the nose.
The second [portion] should end at the mouth, and the third should extend to the neck.
The fourth extends to the arms, and the fifth should end at the belly.
The sixth is known as the head, and the seventh should extend to the breasts.
The eighth [syllable] is the "widest" (urvantam), and the ninth should be at the end of the foot.
In a ten-syllable mantra, the first [syllable] is at the end of the head (śiro'ntam);
the second should be at the end of the chin (cibukāntam), and the third is the pair of ears (karṇayugmakam).
The fourth should be the neck, the fifth the pair of arms;
one should know the sixth as the back, the seventh as the region of the breasts,
the eighth as ending at the abdomen, and the ninth as ending at the thighs.
The ninth [syllable] should be known as the end of the feet; such is the meditation on the limbs of the mantra.

Having thus performed the visualization of the external limbs for mantras consisting of eleven syllables and so forth in this sequence, one should perform the recitation of the mantra and other rites. || 2 ||
For fear of excessive length, other [details] have not been stated; thus ends the convention regarding the external limbs of the deity.
The supplement is complete.
